14442-memoirs-of-major-alexander-ramkins:
This 1719 memoir presents Alexander Ramkins, a Highland officer then held prisoner at Avignon, telling his own life across nearly three decades of soldiering. The publisher claims the papers reached him through a kinsman of the author.

Ramkins serves in Scotland, Germany, Italy, Flanders, and Ireland, and he recounts battles, escapes, love affairs, debts, and spells in prison with frank humor. His reflections on loyalty, fortune, and the court of the exiled Stuarts run through the tale. The book reads as a rogue's life, part adventure and part moral lesson. Modern readers may doubt some of his taller tales.
14753-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for September 1843 opens with a two-part tale of the assizes, headed with the line about low people. Its narrator returns on business to a populous city tied to his childhood and to his mother's death there, and the place still carries that grief.

As a monthly magazine issue, the number mixes fiction with the periodical's usual range of essays, reviews and commentary on public life. The opening story leans on memory, guilt and local feeling rather than on courtroom procedure alone. Readers get a vivid sample of Victorian magazine storytelling, with its slow build, moral shading and eye for provincial character.
15307-the-narrative-of-gordon-sellar-who:
Gordon Sellar's narrative, printed at Huntingdon, Quebec, in 1915, tells of a boy who emigrated to Canada in 1825. His mother, a Glasgow servant, married a soldier in a red coat who tossed him to the ceiling. When the regiment sailed for Belgium, Waterloo news filled the streets with lights and cheers.

Sellar recalls his mother's shiver past drunken men at the Cross, a fear he understood only later. The narrative then follows a young immigrant's life in Canada, with hardship, work, and settlement. Family historians will find the book a vivid, personal record of Scottish emigration.
15386-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Dated March 11, 1897, this eighteenth number of The Great Round World, a weekly paper for boys and girls, costs five cents. Publisher Harison, at West 18th Street, prints a notice for a handy nature study book by I. G. Oakley, praised for giving children genuine lessons from what they can see and touch.

Nature lessons, the notice says, must deal with real things, not mere book talk. News, stories, and school notes fill the rest. The issue shows a children's paper linking reading to outdoor observation. Young naturalists and print historians will enjoy its earnest, bright tone.
15464-foods-that-will-win-the-war-and-ho:
C. Houston Goudiss and Alberta M. Goudiss published this wartime cookbook in 1918, through the Forecast Publishing Company. Its front pages carry Food Administration slogans: save wheat and use more corn, save meat and use more fish and beans, use just enough fat, and use syrups for sugar. The aim was plain: send more food to Europe, or they will starve.

Chapters give reasons for each saving, then practical recipes: corn, oats, rye, barley, and potato breads, pancakes and waffles, meat economy dishes, and fish as a meat substitute. Rules for buying with thought, cooking with care, and serving just enough run through the book. As a home-front manual, it shows how American kitchens were asked to serve the cause of freedom, one meal at a time.
16401-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Dated February 18, 1920, this weekly issue of Punch opens with Charivaria, a run of short jokes on the news of the day. Lloyd George, Churchill, and the ex-Crown Prince all get a jab, as do the America Cup, jobless pay, and a will that left a large sum in very few words. The humor is dry, brief, and aimed at readers who kept up with politics and London life.

Later pages keep the same tone, with cartoons, verse, and short comic pieces that poke fun at spring suits, boxing promoters, and the League-era talk of the time. Read as a whole, the issue shows a London paper laughing at its own public men and daily headlines. Each joke is small, and the issue comes just after the First World War.
16762-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-2-of-6-:
This slice of Holinshed's Chronicles covers Richard I, second son of Henry II, from his reign's start on July 6, 1189. The text, in old spelling, sets his crowning against the reigns of Emperor Frederick, Philip of France, and William the Lion of Scotland. After his father's funeral, Richard hastened to Rouen, where he was joyfully received and proclaimed duke of Normandy.

Richard then set affairs in order across the sea, hunting for his father's treasure and seizing Stephen de Turnham, steward of Anjou, to answer for it. The slice shows a king who prized order, money, and war in equal share. Readers who push through the old spelling get a reign opening in full chronicle style, with dates and deeds in one long march.
20906-the-journal-of-negro-history-volum:
No truth rings stronger, says volume three of The Journal of Negro History, than Bremer's line on America. The fate of the Negro, she said, is the romance of your history. The 1918 volume opens its work under that bold banner.

Hero sketches show lives once used and scorned by Christian men, the editors note. Studies here trace how a distinct American culture grew from that pain. Woodson's journal kept building Black history on records, not myth. Volume three shows the field in its third year, already rich, rigorous, and set on reshaping how America told its own past.
2118-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Carlyle carries the Seven Years' War to its height in this volume, covering 1757 to 1759, when nearly all Europe combined against Frederick. Powers that once hesitated, including Sweden, joined the plan to partition Prussia. The coalition against Frederick included Austria, France, Russia, and Sweden, a daunting array.

The campaign opens amid fulminations in the Reichstag and across the continent, with England alone excepted. Carlyle follows battles and alliances in his dense, driving style, showing a king beset on every side yet still fighting. Carlyle's partisanship shows here, since he treats Frederick's foes as a league of envy.
21833-experiences-of-a-dug-out-1914-1918:
A senior staff officer tells what the Great War looked like from headquarters in Experiences of a Dug-Out, by Major-General Sir C. E. Callwell, published in 1920. Callwell had written lives of generals and studies of the Dardanelles before this memoir. Here he looks back on 1914 to 1918 from inside the machine that ran the British war effort. Some pieces first ran in Blackwood's Magazine.

He defends the soldiers' view against critics who, he says, had it all their own way during the fight. Grievances could be aired freely while serving men stayed silent, he notes. The frontispiece shows him at the Crow's Nest with Russian allies. It is a frank, professional memoir of the war behind the lines.
21880-the-medallic-history-of-the-united:
America's first century is told in medals in J. F. Loubat's Medallic History of the United States, covering 1776 to 1876. One hundred seventy etchings by Jules Jacquemart picture the coins and medals of honor struck for the nation's deeds. Loubat, a member of the New York Historical Society and a knight of several orders, dedicated the work to Elihu B. Washburne, late minister to France.

A hundred years of history, he argues, already holds deeds and names enough to make the medals a valuable record. Battles, treaties, and great citizens appear in bronze and gold. The book is at once a catalog for collectors and a patriotic history. Each medal fixes a moment the young republic chose to remember in metal.
23926-st-nicholas-magazine-for-boys-and-:
St. Nicholas Magazine for April 1878 opens with Sara Keables Hunt's story How Kitty Was Lost in a Turkish Bazaar. Kitty is a pretty child with laughing gray eyes and dimples, dangerously fond of running away from home from the time she first toddled alone.

Let a door stand ajar and out pattered tiny feet into city streets and dangers. Papa and mamma consult long over correction, while Aunt Martha, over her spectacles, timidly suggests a little birch tea. Mamma will not hear of it for so small a child. Kitty reaches her fifth year unharmed, but a time of great anxiety comes, and the bazaar of the title awaits her wandering feet.
24393-our-casualty-and-other-stories-191:
G. A. Birmingham wrote these stories in 1918, opening with Our Casualty. The Ballyhaine Veterans' Corps, he writes, is the most efficient military body in the whole British Isles. The men look like soldiers in grey uniforms with brassards, talk like soldiers, and have the true military spirit. Not a man in the company is under fifty, yet if the Germans try a landing at Ballyhaine beach, by submarine or any other way, they will regret it afterwards.

Ballyhaine is a suburb of better villas, each with a garden, where in peacetime men discuss sweet peas, winter spinach, and chrysanthemums on the 9.45 train, first class. When their boys went off early in the war, the older men felt it time to do something too. All joined, even poor old Cotter, near seventy, retired three years, who dropped his rheumatism talk and was made corporal. Readers get wartime volunteers, gently mocked.
24421-the-story-of-gunnlaug-the-worm-ton:
Eirikr Magnusson and William Morris translated this Icelandic saga from the original Old Norse in 1875, retelling a tale thought to date from the thirteenth century. It follows Gunnlaug, a gifted young poet nicknamed Worm-tongue for his sharp verse, and his rival Raven, both skalds, or court poets, competing for the hand of Helga the Fair.

The story moves between Iceland and the courts of Norway, England, and Sweden, where the two poets seek fame and favour from kings and earls. Pride, broken promises, and a duel drive the plot toward its tragic close. Readers meet a world ruled by honour, poetry, and kinship, in prose that keeps much of the saga's stark, old-fashioned flavour.
25528-q-6-a-and-other-places-recollectio:
Francis Buckley recalls his war years of 1916, 1917, and 1918 in this 1920 memoir, named for Q. 6. A and other posts where he served. Opening chapters cover the start of his service, the men of the north country who served beside him, and Alnwick, grounding the book in place and comradeship.

Buckley writes from memory rather than from official history, so daily routine, humour, fear, and slang shape the account. A note explains period slang, such as the morning hate for the dawn stand-to-arms, helping civilian readers follow soldiers' talk. Later chapters move on to other posts, keeping men and places at the centre.
26838-a-history-of-the-french-novel-vol-:
George Saintsbury, late professor of rhetoric and English literature at Edinburgh, wrote this first volume of his history of the French novel, published by Macmillan in 1917. It runs from the beginnings of French fiction to 1800. It opens with the Matters of France, Rome, and Britain, then turns to the romans d'aventures that carried those tales forward. Saintsbury corrects and adds to his own text in a prefatory list of addenda.

Later chapters reach the seventeenth century, where backward-looking, semi-chivalrous novels still dress heroes as knights, and where Jean de Lannoi's Roman Satirique of 1624 runs to some 1100 pages. Saintsbury treats the long French tradition as one story, not a shelf of separate books, and judges each stage by what it added to the novel's art.
30026-a-story-of-one-short-life-1783-to-:
Elisabeth G. Stryker wrote A Story of One Short Life, 1783 to 1818, for the Missionary Annals series, printed in Chicago in 1888 by the Woman's Presbyterian Board of Foreign Missions of the Northwest. Ten chapters carry the life: ancestry, birth, boyhood, and conversion; college, the haystack, and efforts to spread interest in foreign missions; and Obookiah in Hawaii and in America. The Sandwich Islands with and without the gospel follow, with Mills at Andover and the American Board.

An apostolic journey in the United States, Mills's second tour, and the American Bible Society with the United Foreign Missionary Society follow. The American Colonization Society, with Mills as its agent visiting Africa, leads to the last journey. These are her real friends, she says, and beyond them rows of boys and girls whose sympathies she would gladly claim.
30221-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
Birds Illustrated by Color Photography opens its first volume in January 1897. The monthly serial promotes knowledge of bird life, priced at fifteen cents or a dollar fifty a year. Nature Study Publishing of Chicago issued the handsome little magazine from the Fisher Building, and its first number carries a color picture of the nonpareil. A verse on the cover sends birds hopping from perch to spray, sporting along the meads in social flocks.

A letter from the president of the National Teachers' Association, written from Albany in December 1896, thanks the publishers for a first copy. He asks to be entered as a regular subscriber. He praises the magazine as beautiful and interesting beyond any publication yet attempted in its line, sure to win popular favor. The number suits readers who want birds in color, with nature study made attractive.
30552-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
Birds Illustrated by Color Photography, volume two, number four, for October, opens with an article on birds in captivity. The editors had planned pathetic instances of suffering among species kept confined in cages by many people.

They argue that such cages are totally inadequate for any purpose other than cruelty, and question whether humans may rightly cage an innocent creature. The issue pairs color photographs with popular text, teaching bird life while urging kindness. It suits families and young naturalists who learn from pictures and plain words. Caged birds in the issue stand for a wider plea for humane care.
31430-the-church-of-england-magazine-vol:
Volume ten, number 263, of The Church of England Magazine, dated January 9, 1841, was issued under the superintendence of clergymen of the United Church of England and Ireland. Its motto, printed on the page, reads "Her foundations are upon the holy hills." The issue sold for one penny halfpenny and opened with a piece on the Christian's obligation to seek the spiritual benefit of others.

Inside, readers find sacred philosophy and contributions to natural theology, alongside the usual mix of sermons, notices, and church news. The magazine served Anglican clergy and lay readers who wanted doctrine, devotion, and argument in a short weekly form. As a single issue, it captures the concerns of the established church in early Victorian England.
31511-a-history-of-witchcraft-in-england:
Wallace Notestein's history of witchcraft in England, from 1558 to 1718, won the Herbert Baxter Adams Prize in European history for 1909. It was published by the American Historical Association at Washington in 1911. Notestein was then assistant professor of history at the University of Minnesota, and his essay runs in fourteen chapters.

The book traces English witch belief and witch prosecution across a century and a half, from the reign of Elizabeth into the early eighteenth century. It treats the subject as history rather than as marvel, weighing how courts, clergy, and common people understood charges of witchcraft and what changed as the prosecutions faded.
31557-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Volume eighteen of the Swanston Edition of the Works of Robert Louis Stevenson, published in London in 1912, the year given as MDCCCCXII, contains In the South Seas. The edition was printed in twenty-five volumes, with 2,060 copies in all, of which 2,000 were for sale. A map illustrating Stevenson's life in the South Seas fronts the volume. Its parts carry the reader through the Marquesas, the Paumotus, the Eight Islands, and the Gilberts, including Apemama.

Stevenson's South Seas book records his voyages among Pacific islands, their peoples, and their customs, with the novelist's eye for character and place. It is travel writing of a high order, and a document of a Pacific already changing under European contact. Readers will find adventure, ethnography, and reflection joined in Stevenson's most personal travel book.
32738-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
This September 1845 number of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume fifty-eight, gathers ten pieces. It opens with English landscape and Constable. It judges Leslie's life of the painter, built largely from Constable's own notes, journals, and letters.

Other items include a poem on Mahmood the Ghaznavide and part nineteen of Marston's memoirs of a statesman. Waterton's essays and Warren's law studies follow, with pieces on Margaret of Valois, Baron von Stein, and the historical romance. A closing supplement to Mac-Flecnoe and the Dunciad rounds out a month of criticism, history, and verse. The number suits readers who enjoy art, history, and sharp monthly comment.
33199-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for September 1847, number 383 of volume sixty-two, opens with How I Stood for the Dreepdaily Burghs, a comic tale of finance and politics. Its narrator learns from his friend Robert M'Corkindale that things in Liverpool look as black as thunder. Bullion is leaving the country and banks are refusing to discount, news he already knows painfully well. Six weeks earlier, confident the panic was subsiding, he had recklessly invested his whole capital in railway shares now sinking to Erebus.

The story that follows mixes money panic, sporting folly at Paisley, and a run for a burgh seat, in Blackwood's characteristic blend of humor and political comment. The number gives readers a vivid picture of the railway mania's aftermath, when tradesmen quaked and investors hid from their creditors. For students of Victorian fiction and finance, it is a lively, instructive issue.
34165-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
The Nature Study Publishing Company of Chicago issued this January number of Birds. It is a monthly serial illustrated by color photography, designed to promote knowledge of bird life, with volume three copyrighted in 1897. An introduction notes testimonials from competent judges, many of them scientists, praising the pictures as true to life.

One writer, who owned a fresh copy of Audubon's Birds, compared the magazine's wood-duck and wood-cock pictures with mounted birds and found every marking matched. The serial serves children and adults alike. It remains a charming early use of color photography for nature study.
3598-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volum:
This eighteenth volume of Montaigne's Essays gathers chapters ten through twelve of Book Three. They treat managing the will, cripples, and physiognomy, the art of reading character from faces. Montaigne opens the first essay by noting that few things move or possess him compared with other men. He has worked by study and argument to enlarge his natural privilege of calm.

The essays ask how much of life we can govern, what bodily difference teaches about fortune, and whether faces reveal souls. Montaigne doubts physiognomy even as he practices it, testing proverbs against his own friends. The volume suits readers who want his late reflections on self command and on judging others.
5292-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
Jean de La Fontaine's Tales and Novels continue in this eighteenth volume, in English verse translation. Its contents are The Case of Conscience, The Devil of Pope-fig Island. Feronde opens the set, with a reflection on how writers of fables bestow names and titles freely, making nymphs, shepherdesses, and even goddesses of their characters.

La Fontaine's tales turn conscience, devils, and island trickery into comedy, with Horace invoked as a model of superior art. Readers get three tales in which moral questions are settled by wit rather than sermon, in the author's most playful manner.
57176-the-wisconsin-magazine-of-history-:
The first year of the Wisconsin Magazine of History, 1917 to 1918, fills this book. Milo M. Quaife, the head of the State Historical Society of Wisconsin, set it in order. The list of main pieces shows the scope of the new sheet. A life of Increase Allen Lapham, the first man of study of the state, stands at its head, by Quaife. A fire in the woods of the north of the state comes next.

More pieces treat of the aid of banks in the war years of 1861 and 1862, and of the wild edge of the land as a world theme, by Carl Russell Fish. First thoughts of Lake Geneva, a trip to North America told by two men from the north of Europe, and a tale of Dutch towns in Sheboygan County fill the mid pages.
5920-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
Two closing chapters fill this Don Quixote portion, fifty-one and fifty-two, at volume one's end. Chapter fifty-one deals with what the goatherd told those carrying off Don Quixote, opening three leagues from a valley where a small but rich village holds a worthy, respected farmer. Chapter fifty-two treats the quarrel Quixote had with the goatherd, together with other rare incidents, as the caged knight nears home.

Readers reach volume one's conclusion through talk rather than triumph, as a goatherd's village tale and a quarrel close the journey. The chapters favor anecdote and character over battle, letting ordinary people have the last word before Quixote's return. This part suits readers finishing volume one, since it delivers the knight home, chastened but unconverted, ready for part two.
6826-neville-trueman-the-pioneer-preache:
W. H. Withrow tells of Neville Trueman, pioneer preacher, in a tale of the War of 1812, dedicated to Egerton Ryerson, whose long life served his country and whose pen recorded that war. The preface says the short story aims to show phases of Canadian life. It covers the heroic struggle against foreign invasion. That struggle first stirred a common national life in Canada, later grown sturdy in confederation.

Trueman preaches, rides, and endures through invasion and hardship, with faith as his weapon. Withrow writes with patriotic warmth. Neville Trueman is a stirring, earnest Canadian tale of war, faith, and a nation's first pulse.
6962-military-reminiscences-of-the-civil:
Jacob Dolson Cox, formerly major general commanding the Twenty Third Army Corps, carries his Civil War memories forward in this second volume, from November 1863 to June 1865. Chapter twenty seven opens with Grant in command and Rosecrans relieved, weighing unity of command, the troubles of a double organization, and Burnside's separate problem. Grant's voyage to Cairo, his meeting with Stanton at Louisville, and the creation of the Division of the Mississippi follow.

Cox sketches Grant's mind at work, his taciturn patience, clear judgments, and good anecdote, with Garfield sent to Washington amid talk of congressman or general. Only this volume's span is told here, from Grant's rise to the war's closing months, in the voice of a corps commander who lived the campaign.
7604-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Part eighteen closes the Caxtons' emigrant story with a farewell to a beautiful new land. Lytton presents the country as a cradle for a people, with a wide heritage still ahead of them in time. It may renew, he suggests, a civilization that feels worn by its own sins and sorrows. The farewell carries that hope forward through cycles of change.

The settlers' life, as the part recalls it, mixes risk with vigor: danger, strong health, bursts of adventure, and intervals of careless rest. A fierce gallop across wide, rolling plains stands for that energy. The part ends the family's story on an expansive note, looking to a place where a family might begin again. It is Lytton's broadest farewell in the novel.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: James Garfield and the first Cleveland term fill this eighth volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. The period runs from 1881 to 1889, and Garfield's death by an assassin brought the vice president to office for the fourth time. The volume records a national shock met without strain on institutions. Richardson presents the messages of both administrations in full.
a-suggestive-inquiry-into-the-hermetic-m:
A Suggestive Inquiry into the Hermetic Mystery is Mary Anne Atwood's study of alchemy, presented here in the later edition published at London by W Tait in 1918. The work first appeared anonymously in 1850; in this edition the author's name stands with the book at last. Its dissertation on the more celebrated of the alchemical philosophers accompanies the inquiry itself.

Atwood's attempt toward the recovery of the ancient experiment of nature reads the adepts as witnesses to a spiritual science. By 1918 the book had become a classic of occult literature, and the Tait edition served a new generation of hermetic readers. The text is the same inquiry that the 1850 volume in this library preserves in its first, anonymous form.
arxiv-2412-02118:
Hussein Behzadipour, Henk Koppelaar, and Peyman Nasehpour wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-four introducing a new algebraic structure. The structure is called an Indigenous semiring. A semiring is like a number system where subtraction and division may not work, and such systems show up in computer science and information theory.

The authors show that these semirings can serve as information algebras. They attach a graph to each one and study its width, shortest cycles, and largest fully linked sets. They also work out the ideals of the structure and describe its units and stable elements in power series built over it.
arxiv-2412-03818:
Joseph Dill and colleagues show that a puzzling drop in carriers in a gallium nitride hole gas was an artifact of counting with the wrong model. The material hosts a dense two-dimensional sheet of holes created by polarization at an interface, a candidate for nitride electronics. Earlier Hall effect studies saw the carrier count halve between room temperature and cryogenic cold. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team fits the magnetotransport with a two-carrier model, acknowledging light and heavy holes, and checks the numbers against self-consistent band simulations.

With two carriers, the densities stay consistent across temperatures, and the mobilities separate cleanly at low temperature, the light holes moving several times faster. The authors identify their measurement as the first experimental sign of light-hole band conduction in gallium nitride. The caution for the field: single-carrier Hall analysis can invent physics that is not there.
arxiv-2412-04318:
Fredrik Carlsson and four colleagues wrote a 2024 paper on a surprising training trick for large language models, which they call hyperfitting. When language models write open-ended text, they often fall into repetitive, dull loops, especially when they always pick the most likely next word. This happens even in the largest modern models.

The team found that fine-tuning a model on a very small data set until its training loss is nearly zero changes this behavior. Rather than ruining the model, as classic overfitting would, the sharpened model writes more varied and stable text. The result is counter-intuitive and challenges standard advice about overfitting. It suggests new, cheap ways to improve the feel of generated text.
arxiv-2412-04418:
Spencer Clark, Oliver Watt-Meyer, and seven co-authors teach a machine learning climate model to feel carbon dioxide changes. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, couples the ACE2 emulator to a simple slab ocean. Past emulators mimicked today's climate but not its response to new gas levels. Training data come from physics simulations run at several carbon dioxide levels.

The coupled model is tested in steady and shifting climates. It handles gas levels inside and beyond its training set. Warming and rain patterns match the physics model under doubled, tripled, and quadrupled gas. Even extreme rain rates track well. The work opens cheap, fast climate sensitivity tests.
arxiv-2412-05218:
Jakub Peleška and Gustav Šír bring transformer models to relational databases. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Transformers have spread to many fields by turning data into sequences. Tables can be cast that way, but linked databases, with many tables tied by keys, do not fit a flat sequence well.

They give a neural message-passing scheme that sticks close to the formal model of a database. It lets a tabular transformer learn end to end, straight from the stored data. They face the hard parts of how to shape and load the data for learning. On a wide range of sets, the new build beats models from kin fields.
arxiv-2412-06918:
Elena Titova and a team of ten co-authors test graphene detectors for faint sub-terahertz waves. Their twenty twenty-four paper uses bilayer graphene, two sheets of carbon one atom thick. A voltage can open a band gap in the bilayer, and junctions in it have shown strong response to such waves when cold.

The team pushed the gap to near the largest values seen in transport tests, with a high-grade gate layer below. As the gap grew, the noise floor fell by about tenfold, and the response did not level off. Wiggles in the response from plasma waves also showed up at the largest gaps, which matter for tuning the device.
arxiv-2412-08418:
Ohland leads a team of seven on this paper from two thousand twenty-four, with given names in fuller form in its text. It brings adaptive optics, the trick that steadies starlight, to the Apollon laser in real time.

Big lasers warp their own beams, and shot-to-shot wobble spoils fine work. Slow fixes force long cool-downs, which hurts as fast firing grows key for fusion work. The Apollon rig shines a steady pilot beam through the path, split off by color from the main shots. A graphics-chip controller runs the loop, bending a mirror against a fast wavefront sensor's reads. Bench tests held steady and cleaned the wave well. Mounted on the laser, though, new hazards showed that must be solved before full-power shots are safe.
arxiv-2412-08518:
Grigor Adamyan takes up edge modes on rough bounds in a piece from twenty twenty-four. Edge modes bear signs down a bound, but true bounds are rough. The rough bits throw the mode off into the bulk, and the mode fades as it goes. To call that loss in advance is the task here.

Adamyan builds a conformal map tool for the task. In systems where the stored work has conformal invariance, a change of form can pull the bound straight. Once straight, the terms at the bound turn much more plain. He tries the thought on edge modes in a plain field theory model. The throw off into the bulk is worked through, and the terms that keep a mode safe from fade are found. The tool may serve for more edge mode tasks set in two space axes and one time axis.
arxiv-2412-08918:
Jianwei Cui and five co-authors present a singing voice system in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Singing voice synthesis aims to make sung audio that sounds rich and expressive. Older systems used two stages: a model turned a score into sound features, then a vocoder built the voice. End-to-end systems that skip that split have worked well in singing and in speech.

Their system, CSSinger, is fully end-to-end and works in chunks as it streams. Streaming cuts the wait for listeners in real use. The authors say this is the first full end-to-end streaming attempt using latent forms from a variational autoencoder. They made targeted changes to lift quality in that setting. Tests showed expressive output with high fidelity.
arxiv-2412-09318:
Jing Liu and Abdellah Fourtassi benchmarked language models in twenty twenty-four on how well they mimic child-caregiver conversation. Such dialogue has distinctive traits — short turns, repetition, scaffolding — that matter for child-oriented AI. Using static tests and live interaction setups, they probed whether leading models reproduce those traits.

Top models like Llama 3 and GPT-4o approximated the talk at word and utterance level. But they missed the discursive patterns of real children and caregivers, exaggerated how much the partners align, and produced less diverse language than humans. The authors frame the study as the seed of a fuller benchmark for language models in early childhood applications, where fidelity to developmental patterns is the whole point.
arxiv-2412-09918:
Assouline and a large team of co-authors demonstrated control of a single-electron flying qubit in graphene in twenty twenty-four. Flying qubits carry quantum information in moving states rather than fixed ones. Light-based versions interact too weakly for easy gates, while electrons interact strongly but usually lose coherence fast in standard materials.

Their qubit is a leviton, a clean single-electron pulse, traveling along the edge channels of a high-mobility graphene sheet in the quantum Hall regime. The team injected levitons on demand and steered the qubit state around the Bloch sphere, the standard map of a qubit's settings. Single-shot readout and two-qubit gates remain to be shown. Still, coherent control of one moving electron marks a strong step toward electron-based quantum circuits.
arxiv-2412-13718:
Jonas Allerbeck, Laric Bobzien, and six co-authors flip the charge state of single atomic defects at ultrafast speed, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Steering electrons at light-wave pace is a core challenge for future nanoelectronics. The team used terahertz pulses fired into a scanning tunneling microscope's tiny gap.

Their targets were missing selenium atoms in atom-thin tungsten diselenide sheets. Pulse pairs snapped snapshots of the fleeting blockade that signals charge moving through the defect's fixed states. Charges leaking back to the tip posed a problem, but a vibration-based blockade curbed it and pushed flow one way. A rate model matched the timing throughout. The work opens paths to probing charge motion in thin materials.
arxiv-2412-15118:
Zhuohao Yu and seven co-authors address a weakness of large language models: they write code well but stumble on tasks needing careful multi-step reasoning. Process supervision usually needs costly trained reward models, while judging only the final output misses the steps in between. Their method tries to get both benefits at once.

Called Outcome Refining Process Supervision, the approach searches through a tree of candidate solutions and actually runs the code. Execution metrics and self-critique then score each branch using real runtime feedback. Across five models and three benchmarks, correctness rose by about twenty-seven percent. Code efficiency improved even more, and the authors released their code openly.
arxiv-2412-15318:
Marco Ambrosini, Eliezer Rabinovici, and three colleagues link two ways of measuring how complex a quantum operator grows over time, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Their arena is the double-scaled SYK model, a solvable stand-in for chaotic quantum systems with holographic duals.

Inserting a single-particle operator splits the model into left and right sectors, pictured as a chord crossing the diagram. The team computes two Krylov complexities for that insertion: one for the operator itself, and one for a state made by acting on a doubled thermal state. They prove, and back with detailed numerics, that both grow from the same recursive ladder of states. The ladder is labeled by a fixed total chord count. As a result, Krylov complexity in this model turns out to equal a length in the dual space. The finding ties a quantum information measure to geometry.
arxiv-2412-16518:
Sahoo, Srivastava, Shimizu, and Utsuno ran large shell-model sums in twenty twenty-four on mercury cores with mass from one ninety-three to two hundred. The shell model treats each core part as moving in set shells. They used a wide shell range and a cut rule to keep the sums in reach.

They report low-state energy sets, trends in those sets, and shared traits like jump odds and pull traits. They trace how the wave mix shifts with spin in the even-mass cores. Results match known lab data in fair ways, and they give forecasts where no data yet exist. Core shapes are shown through energy maps too.
arxiv-2412-17518:
Mike Nguyen and Nicole Mücke analyze how fast two-layer neural operators learn, using the neural tangent kernel framework. Neural operators are used as fast stand-ins for the solution maps of partial differential equations. Good theory for their generalization has lagged behind practice.

Working in the kernel regime, the authors derive convergence rates for early-stopped gradient descent that match known optimal rates in kernel regression. They also bound how many hidden neurons and second-stage samples are needed. A supporting result shows any operator a neural operator can approximate also lies within reach of the kernel space. Simulations on the Poisson equation illustrate the theory.
arxiv-2412-18018:
Veronika Hubeny and Massimiliano Rota wrote this physics paper, published in 2024. It offers a new way to picture patterns of independence among the parts of a quantum system, using a structure called a correlation hypergraph.

The wider question asks which patterns of independence quantum states can actually realize, given the rules that govern entropy. Older pictures of these patterns are clumsy. The new hypergraph picture is leaner and ties more neatly to the strong subadditivity rule. It also mirrors a known link in holography, where shared information between regions matches how their space-like wedges connect. From the picture, the authors extract new facts about groups of parts that can be independent all at once. They also derive a test, based on graph shape, that certain simple models of holographic entropy must pass.
arxiv-2501-00618:
Bradley Fox and Benjamin Bruyns wrote this paper, listed in two thousand twenty-four in its head. It weighs variants of the Borda count, a points-based voting rule, against real ranked choice election data from the United States.

Plurality and instant runoff rules can fail in set ways: the broad favorite can lose, and odd paradoxes crop up. Borda variants dodge the monotonicity paradox, but differ in how partial ballots count and how rank points spread. The authors show which failures each variant allows in theory. They then run hundreds of real ranked elections through five variants. Majority failures prove rare or absent, while other failure kinds grow as the price of the gain.
arxiv-2501-01718:
Yau and Yin prove that the eigenvectors of large one-dimensional random band matrices spread out rather than localize. These matrices have random entries only within a band around the diagonal. The band must be wider than the square root of the matrix size, by some small power. Four results are shown for the middle of the spectrum. First, the eigenvalue density follows the semicircle law down to tiny scales.

Second, every normalized eigenvector is delocalized with high probability. Third, their local mass evens out, a property called quantum unique ergodicity. Fourth, local eigenvalue patterns match those of a standard Gaussian ensemble. The package settles key questions for this matrix class.
arxiv-2501-02118:
Kevin Lopez and Amin Rezaei wrote a paper in 2025 on K-Gate Lock, a multi-key logic locking method for protecting chip designs against oracle-guided attacks. Chip designs are drawn by a design house and manufactured at a foundry that may not be trusted. Logic locking scrambles a design so that it works correctly only with the right key, preventing piracy and overproduction.

Earlier methods used a single global key for the circuit. Oracle-guided attacks, helped by a working chip purchased on the market, have extracted the key from sophisticated single-key schemes. The method encodes input patterns using multiple keys applied to one set of key inputs at different operating times. Experiments confirm that the multi-key approach withstands oracle-guided attacks, forcing an exponentially time-consuming brute force search. Overhead in power and performance remained reasonable, making the scheme practical for hardware protection.
arxiv-2501-02518:
Ao Sun presents CHAIR, a tool to catch made-up claims in text from language models, in a solo twenty twenty-five paper. Such false claims are called hallucinations. Rather than read the final text alone, CHAIR looks inside the model, at the scores it gives each word as it writes.

From those inner scores, for each token and each layer, CHAIR pulls a small set of stats: the max, min, mean, spread, and slope. A trained classifier then flags likely false text. On the TruthfulQA and MMLU test sets, CHAIR lifts detection a lot, above all when no examples are given. Sun also sketches how such inner signals could steer writing itself.
arxiv-2501-06618:
Maria De Iorio, Andreas Heinecke, Beatrice Franzolini, and Rafael Cabral examine shrinkage priors in a 2025 arXiv paper. These priors push small effects toward zero while keeping large ones intact. Horseshoe-type priors are popular, yet users lack clear guidance on which prior fits a given task.

The team builds a framework that covers a large class of such priors, with and without a spike at zero. They recast the priors through ideas from reliability theory and wealth distributions. A folded form, which they call the Gambel distribution, can be written as a ratio of two known distributions. That form reveals behavior near zero and in the tails, supports new consistency results, and leads to sampling schemes. The paper ends with guidance on setting the prior's parameters.
arxiv-2501-08118:
Seamie Hayes, Ganesh Sistu, and Ciarán Eising test whether frozen foundation models can strengthen bird's-eye view perception for cars, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Bird's-eye view models fuse camera images into a top-down scene map. They usually need large amounts of driving data to generalize.

The authors modified two architectures, Lift-Splat-Shoot and Simple-BEV. Into the first they plugged frozen DINOv2 features and Metric3Dv2 depth estimates. That version beat its baseline by a wide margin while using half the training data. For the second, they turned Metric3Dv2 depth into a pseudo-LiDAR point cloud replacing real LiDAR. The camera-only model gained several points of overlap accuracy. Careful reuse of big pretrained models pays off.
arxiv-2501-08618:
Aruna Sankaranarayanan, Dylan Hadfield-Menell, and Aaron Mueller test whether language models keep layered grammar apart from flat grammar inside, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Human brains react only to layered rules when word sets match. Test text came in three languages plus made-up words, under both rule types.

Models behaved distinctly on layered versus flat inputs. The parts driving layered handling differed from flat parts, and cutting tests proved the split causal. Layered parts also fired on nonsense grammars, so the trait is not tied to sense or training likeness. Exposure to big text alone bred the split. Readers get a brain-like hint inside model wiring.
arxiv-2501-09018:
Grossmann and a large team of colleagues pin down the age of the red giant binary KIC 9163796 by combining binary and seismic constraints. Ages of single giants from standard fitting carry thirty to fifty percent uncertainties. This double-lined binary helps: its two stars have nearly equal mass yet sit at clearly different places in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.

A multidimensional grid of stellar models was fit against binary, spectroscopic, and asteroseismic information together. The combined approach gives an age of about 2.44 billion years with only nine percent relative error. Both stars share an initial helium abundance well above the primordial value, and their masses agree with seismic scaling relations. Precision below ten percent for a giant is the headline.
arxiv-2501-10318:
Zhang and colleagues cut in twenty twenty-five the computing cost of large vision-language models by rethinking how image data flows through them. In current models, long strings of image tokens pass through every layer of the text decoder, which dominates the cost. Their design lets only the text stream run the full path, while image data joins at set stages inside each layer through a mixed attention step.

Across several model families, the decoder's computing cost fell about tenfold. Output quality stayed close to the original models on standard tests. The authors argue the image stream carries much redundancy that full processing wastes effort on. They hope the trick opens new angles on efficient vision-language design.
arxiv-2501-10918:
In a directed network, a dicut is a set of arcs all crossing one way between two camps, and a dijoin is a set of arcs meeting every dicut. Gérard Cornuéjols, Siyue Liu, and Ravi study an old guess linking the two: that the lightest dicut weighs the same as the largest packing of dijoins. The guess was disproved in general, and its unweighted form is still open after decades.

For one family of networks, those whose underlying undirected graph is chordal, the three prove the guess true. Chordal graphs are built from overlapping cliques in a tree-like way. They also give a fast method, running in strongly polynomial time, that builds the matching packing. The result settles the question for a broad and useful graph family.
arxiv-2501-11418:
Jan Nowosielski and three co-authors build a radio receiver from atoms in twenty twenty-five. Rydberg atom sensors can detect radio signals with extreme sensitivity. The best mode, superheterodyne reception, needs a local oscillator inside the vapor cell. That oscillator undercuts stealthy, all-optical operation.

Their scheme avoids a same-frequency local oscillator by mixing multiple tones. An atomic transition loop does the mixing inside the atoms themselves. The receiver works at S-band frequencies, the range used by Wi-Fi networks. It operates without interfering with the signal it senses. Efficient theory predicts the sensor's performance. Readers in quantum sensing get a practical detector that keeps the advantages of atomic receivers while dropping a key drawback.
arxiv-2501-11918:
Md Kamrujjaman Mobin and Md Saiful Islam wrote this paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, as their entry to a shared task on spotting machine-written text. The hard part is doing it across many kinds of writing, where style and topic shift.

Their system, LuxVeri, blends several fine-tuned transformer models into one ensemble. Each model's vote is weighted by the inverse of its perplexity, a measure of how surprised it is by the text, so more confident models count more. In the plain detection round the blend placed tenth of twenty-three entries. In the harder round, where texts were tweaked to fool detectors, their single best model placed eighth of twenty-two. The authors say the weighting scheme is what helps the detector carry across domains.
arxiv-2501-12318:
Tamas Karacsony, Joao Carmona, and Joao Paulo Silva Cunha blanket a human motion data set, digitally, so pose-estimation models can learn to see patients under covers. Clinicians want skeleton tracking of people in bed from ordinary cameras, but blankets hide the body and labeled examples are rare. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team generated over a million frames with photorealistic synthetic blankets draped over body-model meshes and laid over a standard exercise data set. A strong pose model was then fine-tuned with and without the augmented frames.

Adding the synthetic blankets lifted accuracy sharply on the synthetic test and by a smaller but real margin on a genuine in-bed patient data set, the authors report. The two-step gain, big on fake data and confirmed on real data, is the paper's evidence that manufactured occlusion can substitute for scarce clinical labels.
arxiv-2501-14218:
Wenqian Zhang, writing alone in 2025, studies the shape of graphs that push a spectral limit as high as possible without containing banned patterns. A graph is a web of points and links. Its spectral radius is a single number from its link matrix that captures how densely connected the web is.

Zhang works with families of banned graphs that need a set number of colors to draw. Building on classic results about the most-edged graphs that dodge such families, the paper pins down the exact structure of the graphs with the largest spectral radius. These extremal graphs turn out to hug a balanced split form with a small twist inside one part. Several uses of the result follow.
arxiv-2501-14718:
Yijie Zhu and Shan Raza segment glands with a foundation model in twenty twenty-five. Cancer grade guides how malignant a tumor is judged to be. Precise gland segmentation in pathology images supports that grading. The authors turn the dependency around: the grade itself can guide segmentation.

They use the Segment Anything Model, whose strength is following prompts. Feeding the benign-or-malignant class as a prompt gives the model prior knowledge of the target's likely look. Modifications to structure and training adapt the model to the task. The approach improves on a fine-tuned baseline and reaches state-of-the-art results, they report. Readers in medical imaging get a loop where classification and segmentation strengthen each other.
arxiv-2501-14818:
Zhiqi Li and a large team of co-authors build Eagle 2, a family of vision language models, by crafting the post training data plan from scratch. Open models have neared closed frontier models, but most share only final weights, which hides the data craft. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team treats data as the core driver and walks through how the plan was built step by step. That plan, with training recipes and model design, yields the Eagle2 family. Its mid size member hits top scores across many multimodal test sets. It matches some rival models that are many times larger, the authors report.
arxiv-2501-15218:
Jeongsoo Kang and Younghun Kwon design a new CNOT gate for a hybrid superconducting qubit system, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Transmons are the workhorse qubits of superconducting processors, with fast operations. Their coherence times and gate fidelities still need improvement for fault-tolerant computing. A newer parity-protected qubit offers better coherence but lacked an efficient hybrid design.

The authors pair a tunable transmon with the parity-protected qubit and apply a cross-resonance pulse. They provide the hardware specifications and pulse parameters needed for the two-qubit gate. The resulting CNOT reaches an average fidelity above zero point nine nine eight. That performance suggests the hybrid system could become a new platform for quantum computers. It combines the transmon's practicality with the protected qubit's coherence advantages.
arxiv-2501-15618:
Mohamad Qadri and four co-authors show that learned constraints are backward reachable tubes in two thousand twenty-five. Inverse constraint learning infers rules from safe example acts. Learned rules should guide safe plans for new tasks and new dynamics. The team asks what object the learning truly recovers.

In theory and in tests, it recovers where failure is doomed, not where it has hit. Safe control calls that set a backward reachable tube. That tube rests on the dynamics of the data source system. The twist shapes how well rules transfer and how fast plans can be found. Both gains and limits follow.
arxiv-2501-16318:
Milan Krstajić and five co-authors measure a condensation temperature shift in a 2025 paper. Ultracold atom clouds condense at a critical temperature, and magnetic dipole forces between atoms should move that point. Using erbium atoms, whose dipole forces are strong and whose contact forces are tunable, they trapped clouds in a stretched trap. The critical temperature clearly depended on which way the dipoles pointed relative to the trap.

Standard theory matched the shift across contact strengths. The authors say the result opens study of stronger dipolar regimes, where exotic states like supersolids and droplets appear.
arxiv-2501-17218:
Samuel Alipour-fard and Wouter Waalewijn stretch a set of particle physics measures in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Energy correlators are measures that link tests and theory in collider physics. They have given the most exact jet-based call of the strong coupling constant, and may pin down the top quark mass. But all past forms link particles by angle. So mass and like values must be read in a round way, through steps.

The measures are called Energy Weighted Observable Correlations. They track non-angular links, linking subjets, not particles, to stay collinear safe. Tuning the subjet radius steers which scales are probed and how keen the measure is to non-perturbative effects. In a test hunt for the W boson mass in jets, the mass form beat the angle-based correlator and matched the groomed jet mass. Sums on light-quark jets go with the plan.
arxiv-2501-17318:
Mohammad Ramadan, Evan Toler, and Mihai Anitescu wrote this control theory paper, published in 2025. It proposes a safety guard for controllers that learn straight from data, warning that such methods quietly assume the machine being steered behaves linearly.

Data-driven predictive control designs a controller from recorded behavior. If the new controller pushes the machine into states the data never covered, hidden nonlinear behavior can switch on and endanger the system. The authors add quadratic penalty terms, nicknamed floodgates, to the control design. These slow how fast the system's behavior drifts away from the recorded regime. Slower drift means slower exploration, a trade-off the paper compares to the explore-versus-exploit balance in machine learning. The method keeps data-based control honest about the limits of what it has seen.
arxiv-2501-18118:
Lei Shen, Bo-Song Huang, and Yu-Gang Ma wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about what happens when a proton strikes a carbon nucleus. Carbon-12 can take a triangular form built from three alpha clusters, or a round form. The team asked whether that inner shape leaves a visible mark on the reaction products.

They simulated the collision across a wide range of incoming energies using a molecular dynamics model plus a decay code. The triangular form showed an extra share of near-elastic reactions that the round form lacked. That oddity appeared as a small dent in curves of event information entropy, a measure of outcome spread. The authors propose entropy as a probe for alpha-cluster structure in nuclei.
arxiv-2501-18518:
Ferdinand Thein and Gerald Warnecke give balance laws for flows with singular interfaces in two thousand twenty-five. A control volume is split in two by a surface of jump. States on each side of that surface can differ sharply. Such setups model phase fronts and shocks in fluids.

Geometry facts are summed in one unified account first. Transport theorems for generic balance laws follow, with proofs. Those theorems show how integrals move with the volume. The step from integral balances to differential equations is spelled out. The paper is a concise, rigorous reference for the topic.
arxiv-2501-19018:
Ahmed Kadhim and co-authors present a scalable word embedding method in two thousand twenty-five built on a logic-based learning machine. The Tsetlin Machine learns rules as plain logical clauses, so its decisions stay readable. Earlier work used it to build word embeddings, but the approach slowed as inputs grew longer.

Their two-phase method first stores what each word in the vocabulary means, then builds sequence embeddings from that stored knowledge. The design scales better while keeping the transparency that sets the machine apart. Tests showed performance matching earlier approaches and comparing well against human-made benchmarks. Applied to movie review sentiment, the embedding plus readable classifiers gave an end-to-end solution that competes with black-box rivals.
arxiv-2502-00118:
Matteo Becchetti, Federico Coro, Christoph Nega, Lorenzo Tancredi, and Fabian Wagner work out two-photon production in full, on paper, two loops deep. Their 2025 paper covers two routes. A quark and an antiquark can meet and make two photons. Two gluons can do the same. Both routes run through loops of heavy quarks.

Elliptic integrals blocked this work in the past. So past work used semi-numerical methods for part of the job. New theory for the differential equations of such integrals clears the path here. The team builds a canonical basis for each integral in play. The answers come as iterated integrals over elliptic and polylog forms. Once they are written this way, the physical terms show neat cancellations. Series expansions then give fast, sound numbers across much of the phase space.
arxiv-2502-02118:
Hoang Nguyen and eight co-authors improve self-supervised audio learning in twenty twenty-five. Models like BEATs learn from unlabeled audio by predicting quantized tokens. Their bidirectional training borrows the BERT recipe from language. A single quantization codebook, though, may be too crude for rich signals, and many code vectors go unused.

Their framework, BRIDLE, interleaves bidirectional learning with residual quantization. Multiple codebooks capture different facets of a signal in stages. Better codebook use is a design goal. The approach generalizes the masked prediction recipe beyond audio in principle. Readers in representation learning get a fix for a quiet inefficiency: learned codebooks where much of the vocabulary is never spoken. The method targets richer discrete tokens for downstream tasks.
arxiv-2502-02918:
Jeewon Heo and five colleagues wrote a 2025 particle physics paper on measuring a small quantity called |Vts|. This value helps test how quarks change type, but it is hard to measure straight from data. One route uses top quark pairs made in proton collisions.

The hard part is spotting the rare strange jets that come from top quark decay. The team built deep learning tools, named DISAJA, to sort these jets from all the rest. One tool uses whole-event data, while a second uses the fine detail of each jet's parts. Both sharpen the sorting. Better sorting should make the direct measure of |Vts| more exact in future collider data.
arxiv-2502-03718:
Zhang, He, Hu, Ma, and Wang hunted crypto attacks before they strike in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Price manipulation lets attackers trade tokens at wildly rigged prices on decentralized exchanges. Most defenses spot the theft only after it happens. The authors note attackers must first deploy a rigged contract, which leaves an early footprint.

Their tool, SMARTCAT, scans contract bytecode for that footprint. It maps how tokens flow through the contract's calls into a graph. Suspicious paths get deeper checks across contracts. In tests it caught over ninety percent of attacks with near-perfect precision. Field scans found hundreds of attack contracts worth millions in losses. Live use raised alarms about ninety-nine seconds after deployment on average.
arxiv-2502-05318:
Kevin Han Huang and four co-authors tested how to bake symmetry into neural solvers for many electron problems. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with the Schrödinger equation for many electrons. Diagonal symmetry, where many objects move as one, is key in such systems. Yet it lacks a plain in built map for nets, save in rare cases. The team tried three ways to add it: more data, group means, and a canonical fix of inputs.

They trained the nets by variational Monte Carlo. Against the norm, symmetry forced in mid training made training less stable and scores worse. Their theory backs that twist. Readers in AI for science get a warning: a trick that helps in plain learning can hurt in quantum solvers.
arxiv-2502-07118:
Tabassum Mahmud and six co-authors dissect how file system settings depend on each other, and build a tool to extract those links. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies Ext4 and XFS, two major file systems. Rich setting lists grant flexibility but breed subtle faults. A pattern stands out: dependencies stack across levels, so one knob's valid range rides on others.

Their ConfD tool pulls such dependencies out on its own. Plugins then use the map to catch mishandled settings and test failures sparked by valid choices. Tests add ZFS, a modern copy-on-write system, to the pair. The tool found a large set of dependencies with few false hits. A trial on the WiredTiger storage engine checks wider reach. The authors offer the study as a guide for storage teams.
arxiv-2502-09918:
Jacob Knaup and five co-authors help self-driving cars merge into traffic with human drivers. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, tackles a hard part of driving. The car must guess what nearby drivers will do while it plans its own move. Guessing first and acting next is too slow and often wrong.

Their method learns from the back-and-forth as it drives. A new solver based on diffusion models plans moves in real time. Tests moved from computer runs to real hardware with human-driven cars. The car read driver behavior and adapted its plan. The authors report smoother, safer merges under doubt about what others will do.
arxiv-2502-10118:
Sania Waheed and Na Min An made small vision-language models write richer image captions in a 2025 paper, with no retraining. Top captioning models are heavy, which shuts out phones and assistive devices, while small models tend to give one bland, high-level description and miss detail. Their training-free framework instead samples the image's internal representation region by region.

Structured segmentation builds a hierarchy from whole scene down to local patches, and the model captions across those levels. On three standard datasets the small backbone matched larger models on alignment and faithfulness to human captions, while diversity scores stayed high. Varied, detailed captions from a compact model suit on-device accessibility tools.
arxiv-2502-10318:
Debasish Borah, Satyabrata Mahapatra, Dibyendu Nanda, Sujit Kumar Sahoo, and Narendra Sahu study dark matter that talks to the standard model through neutrinos in two thousand twenty-five. In their setup, neutrinos are Dirac type, so each has a right-handed partner. That partner also serves as the bridge to a lone dark matter particle.

All allowed links at a set order are written down under rules that keep the dark particle stable and lepton count fixed. The bridge particle heats up along with the dark matter, which adds to the early universe's radiation load. That extra load sits within reach of near-future sky surveys. The team maps how dark matter hunts and cosmic tests back each other, and offers a full model behind the shorthand.
arxiv-2502-10818:
Alvaro Arroyo and co-authors trace three graph network diseases, vanishing gradients, over smoothing, and over squashing, to one root in training dynamics, in work from twenty twenty-five. Graph networks pass messages between nodes, but deep stacks blur node identities and strangle far away signals. The trio of flaws was usually treated apart.

Reading graph networks as recurrent models, they apply control theory tools to the message flow. Proofs and tests show gradients die within a few layers by design. Over smoothing follows from the same mechanism. A plain state space rewrite of the network eased both flaws at no extra parameter cost. Over squashing yields best to rewiring plus gradient care together.
arxiv-2502-11518:
Di Wu and a large team take stock of how base models lift teams of agents with bodies. Such teams place more than one agent, real or in a sim, in one shared world. They aim at freight and robot tasks no lone agent does well. Base models pledge richer talk and more flex in how snags get solved. The stock-take sorts the field by frame type and by body type.

Four blocks get deep looks: sense, plan, talk, and notes back. For each, the team shows how make-new tech adds strength and flex. Real rigs show the shift base models bring. Teams that span real and sim worlds are a theme that comes back. Open snags and paths ahead close the stock-take. The field, they say, moves from scripted teamwork to work that is made up on the fly, in a true sense.
arxiv-2502-12218:
Yusheng He, Jia-Hui Huang, and Jinbo Yang study black holes whose horizons are not perfectly round. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. The objects are Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton black holes set in anti-de Sitter space. A method borrowed from axion-supported solutions warps the horizon's angular part. The radial part stays the same, while the angular curvature varies from place to place. That unevenness signals anisotropy in the spacetime.

The team works out what the warping does to the hole's thermodynamics. Heat, entropy, and related traits all shift with the deformed shape. They also check two tools used to define mass and energy flow. The Misner-Sharp mass and the unified first law are tested for validity here. The paper extends black hole physics beyond the symmetric cases.
arxiv-2502-16218:
Maarten Bosten and Bennett Kleinberg count how much of the field of language technology research is tied to firms, over a span of more than two decades. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The field leans more and more on huge data and compute, and many gains came from joint work with tech firms. That tie can bend what gets asked and told. The team tagged each author's base as school or firm for papers from two thousand to two thousand twenty-four. Just over a quarter had at least one firm-linked author. By the last year, the share was more than one in three. Top venues drove the trend most.
arxiv-2502-19718:
Tao Huang, Yanxiang Ma, Shan You, and Chang Xu gave a fresh account of why masked image models work. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with masked autoencoders. These models learn by hiding parts of an image and guessing them back. They score well, but why they work has stayed dim. Past reads lean on contrast or feature views that give hints, not plain truth.

The pair frame the trick through the information bottleneck idea. Their proofs show that the key is a balance: keep the facts that matter, drop the rest. From that they built MI-MAE, which tunes that balance through mutual information terms. Readers in vision get both a theory and a tweak for a core self taught model.
arxiv-2502-20718:
Xiao Tan and colleagues kept linear systems safe under heavy sensor attacks in a 2025 control paper. Attackers who corrupt sensor readings can steer a physical system into danger. The standard fix rebuilds the true state from scratch, a secure reconstruction that is thorough but too slow for real-time control, since the search explodes combinatorially.

Instead of full reconstruction, the authors compute control actions straight from past input-output data, guarding safety with a barrier condition. Conservative bounds from a spectral shortcut keep the guarantee, and a smaller subproblem can be solved when tighter action is worth some cost. Comparisons confirm the speed gain while safety holds. The approach suits fast systems where delays themselves are risky.
arxiv-2502-20918:
Luis Alberto Razo López and four co-authors watch protected edge currents move in time, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Some materials host states that live only on their boundary and shrug off defects. A two-dimensional effect with time symmetry is the classic home for such states, but their motion over time was little explored.

The team built a microwave stand-in for the effect. Signals carrying a handedness traveled one way along the edge and passed planted defects without scattering. Their speed, though, was hundreds of times slower than light in open space. The authors note that slowness could matter for real devices that hope to use these edge states in optics or quantum information.
arxiv-2503-03618:
Noel Portillo designs a solar-powered server cluster from small Raspberry Pi boards. His paper is from two thousand twenty-five, and the work is a theory-based plan rather than a field test. The aim is a low-power hub for web-of-things tasks and edge services, with less call on big data centres.

The build pairs a solar panel and a lithium battery with a light cluster tool and container software. Study rests on theory and on data from past work, not on a live build. It weighs power use, load share, and uptime in varied scenes. The plan looks workable and green, with a far lower carbon load than a classic centre.
arxiv-2503-05318:
Nico Daheim and co-authors improve how language models pick their final answer in 2025. Models still blurt out wrong or made-up text at times, and such slips have been tied to uncertainty the model does not report. A method called Minimum Bayes Risk already picks the answer with the lowest expected error among samples.

The team extends that method to fold in doubt about the model itself, not just about the wording. The richer score helps choose outputs and also tells the model when to stay silent rather than guess. Tests showed gains with no added running cost. How the doubt was learned mattered, and more varied samples helped most. The code is public.
arxiv-2503-05818:
Bassel El Mabsout, Abdelrahman Abdelgawad, and Renato Mancuso give reinforcement learning designers a logic for stating what they actually want, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The chronic problem is translation: a designer's intent usually involves several goals at once, but reward functions are typically built by gluing single-goal scores together with weights.

That gluing is laborious and brittle, especially when goals fight each other, as speed and energy saving do in robotics. The authors build on the notion of objective fulfillment and define Fulfillment Priority Logic around it. A designer writes a logical formula that states the intentions and which goal outranks which. Their Balanced Policy Gradient algorithm then trains policies directly from such formulas. The authors report far better fulfillment of the stated intent than weighted rewards achieve. The work targets robots and other systems where trade-offs are the whole design problem.
arxiv-2503-06018:
Shneyder and four co-authors modeled in twenty twenty-five how lattice vibrations shape the pseudogap state in strongly correlated electron systems. The pseudogap — a partial suppression of states near the Fermi level — haunts cuprate physics, and electrons dressed by phonons, polarons, are candidate players. The team applied a polaronic generalized tight-binding method to a realistic two-dimensional multiband model with both Holstein and Peierls type couplings.

As coupling and doping vary, polaronic effects first appear as modulations of spectral intensity. In one region of the phase diagram, coherent polaron excitations flatten part of the band near the Fermi level, reshaping the Fermi surface's topology and leaving fingerprints in the density of states. The study maps where lattice dressing merely decorates the pseudogap and where it rebuilds it.
arxiv-2503-07318:
Nicholas Braun Rodrigues and Gregorio Chinni prove that a family of differential operators on the torus forces its solutions to be analytic at all points. The operators are of second order with a non-negative characteristic form, set out globally on the torus. Global analytic hypoellipticity is a strong regularity property. It does not come for free for such equations.

The class they treat extends past sum-of-squares groups studied by Bove and Chinni and by Cordaro and Himonas. To extend those results widens the known ground where rough data still yield analytic solutions. The work sits in the regularity theory of partial differential equations, where characteristic geometry decides smoothness. What it adds is a larger proved class, not a new method.
arxiv-2503-08418:
Hao Wang studies how city locations rise and fall in visitor rankings through the day, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Human mobility shapes city life and sustainability, yet the ranking dynamics of inflows had drawn little study. Wang tracked hourly inflows across sixty Chinese cities.

The rank-size pattern of inflows stayed stable across cities over the day. Beneath that calm surface, busy places showed clear trends: their inflows rose or fell in a steady direction hour to hour. Rank changes, though, were most stable at the top, the bottom, and the middle of the table. Wang compares cities using a rank turnover metric. The results may inform urban planning and traffic work.
arxiv-2503-09018:
Takahashi, Sasaki, and Matsubara wrote in twenty twenty-five about teaching robots by demonstration without asking for impossible moves. Humans and robots move differently, so a human demo may exceed the robot's ability. Their framework, FABCO, judges each demo's feasibility using the robot's own dynamics models. Visual feedback shows demonstrators which parts the robot cannot copy. People can then refine their demonstrations on the spot. During learning, feasible demos count more than infeasible ones.

The team tested the approach on a pipette insertion task. Four participants gave demonstrations with and without the feedback. Workload was measured with a standard NASA index. Feasibility feedback and weighted learning improved the resulting policies. Data efficiency and robustness both gained from the weighting. The method aims to make intuitive teaching safer for automation.
arxiv-2503-12318:
Zerong Huang led a team probing a shell-shaped quantum gas in a 2025 paper. The gas is a Bose-Einstein condensate formed into a hollow shell using a two-species mixture that will not mix. Its hollowness can be tuned by adjusting how strongly the species repel each other. The team used collective vibrations to detect the change from filled to hollow.

They found two vibration modes, one where the two gases move together and one where they move in opposition. The second mode's tone rose and fell in a distinctive way as the repulsion grew, marking the topology change clearly. The critical point also shifted strongly with the ratio of the two species.
arxiv-2503-14918:
Matija Bucić, Vanshika Jain, and Varun Sivashankar settle a hypergraph question in twenty twenty-five. In nineteen seventy-four, Erdős and Lovász asked a question Erdős later called a favorite. It asked for the fewest edges in an intersecting hypergraph whose cover number matches its uniformity. Kahn solved it up to a constant factor in nineteen ninety-four.

A newer version adds a limit on how many vertices the hypergraph may use. That twist came from work on a problem about many colors posed by Bollobás. The authors settle this version asymptotically, for the whole range of parameters. Their answer is tight up to a logarithmic factor in the exponent. Readers in combinatorics get closure on a fifty-year line of questions.
arxiv-2503-15218:
Li, Xu, and Calhoun match sight brain acts tween man and small ape kin in this twenty twenty-five paper. Both kinds watch films while brain scans track their sight zones. Shared sight acts would back the ape as a model for man's sight.

Inside, pair and group marks weigh shared facts and joint-only facts in the scans. Sight acts matched hard tween the kinds in zone after zone. One man's deep zone paired most with the ape's high sight zones. Shared-fact hubs held firm while joint acts shifted up the sight chain. The team reads the ape as a close sight kin of man.
arxiv-2503-16218:
Yu Cao, Zengqun Zhao, Ioannis Patras, and Shaogang Gong wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It explains why AI image generators leave artifacts, warped hands and smeared faces, by watching how an image forms over time inside the model.

The authors split the image-building process into three phases: profiling, mutation, and refinement. Artifacts, they find, are born in the middle phase, where some regions show odd jumps in the model's guiding scores. That is why fixes that only inspect the finished image miss the trouble spots. Their method, ASCED, watches score behavior during generation, flags the bad regions, and repairs them on the fly with fresh noise. In tests it cut artifacts across many kinds of images, matching or beating detector-based fixes without extra training.
arxiv-2503-17218:
Regaly, Frohlich, and Kiss simulate rings around small worlds in this two thousand twenty-five astronomy paper. Giant planets host rings, but so do the Centaur Chariklo, Chiron, the dwarf planet Haumea, and the object Quaoar. This is odd, since solar radiation pressure should break up such rings by exciting particle eccentricities. The authors evolve rings around Chariklo and Haumea analogs with a GPU-based N-body integrator. The runs add planet and solar gravity, radiation pressure, and the shadow, over thousands of years.

Two ring families emerged, sorted by tilt. Slightly tilted rings fail for particles below a critical size. Highly tilted rings are unstable only across a middle band of particle sizes, and the planetary shadow shrinks the critical size fivefold. The survivors stabilize because radiation forces their plane perpendicular to the sunlight, so the ring plane forever faces the Sun as the body orbits, a celestial sunflower.
arxiv-2503-17818:
Sipaz Sharma looks at a fine point in lattice sums in quantum chromodynamics in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The key value is the fourth-order charm fluctuation. It is a generalized susceptibility. It tells how charm quark number shifts when terms shift. Lattice sums rest on the bare charm quark mass put in at the start. Sharma tests how much that choice counts, in depth.

He works toward the continuum limit on four distinct lines of constant physics. He measures cut-off effects from the bare charm mass on coarse and fine lattices. The key find is of use in practice. Ratios of generalized charm susceptibilities from coarse lattices will do. Pair them with the continuum-extrapolated fourth-order fluctuation. Then all key values for open charm physics can be got in the continuum limit. That saves much computer time.
arxiv-2503-18718:
Lijiang Li and co-authors offered GS-Marker in 2025, a watermarking system for 3D scenes built with Gaussian splatting, a popular modern way to represent 3D content. Protecting 3D models matters as content-making tools spread, but watermarking them is harder than watermarking flat images. Because a renderer sits between the 3D data and any picture a checker can inspect, blocking straightforward training.

Earlier 3D methods optimized each scene separately, which is slow and does not broaden. GS-Marker instead works in a single pass: a 3D encoder embeds the message, warping layers during training harden it against damage. And a 2D decoder reads the watermark back from rendered views from any angle. A self-tuning control process adjusts the marking to the scene, aiming for watermarks that survive warping across many varied models.
arxiv-2503-20818:
Lucas Williams wrote a solo mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five that extends a classic theorem. The Pontryagin-Thom theorem links two worlds: shapes called framed manifolds, grouped by how they can deform into each other, and a deep object in algebra known as the sphere spectrum. The link is an exact match between the two groupings.
