Williams proves the same kind of match for whole families of shapes at once. The families vary over a compact base space, and the shapes carry symmetry, which is the equivariant part of the title. His result widens a bridge that mathematicians use to turn shape problems into algebra.
arxiv-2503-21418:
Sylwia Czach, Jakub Rydzewski, and Wiesław Nowak review computational methods for photoactive proteins in two thousand twenty-five. Such proteins soak up light and change shape to do their work. They drive key acts in living systems and draw biotech and medical eyes. Experiments alone miss fast, fine steps in those changes.

Computing gives atom level views of structure, electrons, and motion. The review maps the main families of these proteins first. It then walks through bioinformatics, molecular dynamics, and enhanced sampling tools. Hard steps like pigment flips and shape shifts get focus. The piece is pitched as a first guide for new researchers.
arxiv-2503-21718:
Iuri Macocco and colleagues explained a quirk of language models in a 2025 study: a few standout internal dimensions that fire strongly for almost every input. Such outlier dimensions look like defects, since they swamp the signal from other dimensions. The team traced them across many modern models and asked what job they do.

Turns out they push the model to favor common words, a handy default when context gives little guidance. When context demands a rare word instead, the model cancels the push with weight spread across the remaining dimensions. The authors also track which settings feed the outliers and when they appear in training. A seeming flaw is really a learned shortcut.
arxiv-2503-22918: Sourav Ghosh proved a uniqueness result for a geometric flow in a 2025 paper. Lagrangian mean bend flow moves a special class of faces so as to shrink area fast. At points where the flow breaks down, analysts rescale time and space to see a limiting tangent flow. Ghosh shows that when the mean bend stays uniformly bounded along a zero-Maslov flow in 4D complex space. That tangent flow at a singular point is unique: every rescaling sequence leads to the same limit.
arxiv-2504-02718:
Kaname Matsue gives a simple test for blow-up solutions in nonautonomous equations in two thousand twenty-five. Blow-up means a solution grows without bound in finite time. Past work set geometric rules for such acts via dynamics at infinity. The present paper links those rules to leading term equations.

Leading terms come from the assumed shape of the blow-up near its end. The focus is on cases where those terms have constant coefficients. Known simple rules for autonomous equations then carry over. The result is a plain criterion for when type one blow-ups exist. It trims a heavy theory down to a check that is easy to apply.
arxiv-2504-02918:
Antonios Tragoudaras and a team of co-authors test video generators on physics in twenty twenty-five. Video models are hoped to be world models that grasp how things move. Before trusting them in robotics or driving, their grip on physical law must be measured. Older evaluations used subjective judgment or trajectory matching, both weak tools for physics.

Their framework, Morpheus, is among the first physics-informed evaluators. It uses one hundred thirty real-world videos of physical phenomena on real systems. Generated videos can then be scored against Newtonian mechanics directly. Many physically plausible generations must be distinguished from correct ones. Readers get a rigorous way to ask whether a video model has learned Newton, or merely learned to look plausible.
arxiv-2504-03618:
Pourbabaee, Sheng, McCrory, Simon, and Mo weigh fit against pay in how LinkedIn ranks jobs for each seeker, in work from twenty twenty-five. The site must rank jobs so paid spots earn cash now, while good fit keeps seekers coming back for years. Cash funds the jobs marketplace today. The rules for selling top spots set how that pull plays out.

Two shifts lift fit at very small cost in pay. First, the ranks can fold in what each seeker wants, which lifts match quality with care. Next, position-aware auctions price each slot by the true worth of the eyes it draws. The team builds ways to gauge and to tune both levers. Their work shows a jobs site need not give up much pay to gain a lot of fit.
arxiv-2504-06518:
Misak Sargsian studied in twenty twenty-five what lives inside a deuteron at distances too short for protons and neutrons to remain themselves. Nuclear forces repel fiercely below about half a femtometer, keeping nuclei from collapsing, but the nature of that core is unresolved. At the extreme internal momenta reached in high-energy electron scattering, the deuteron behaves as a pseudo-vector composite rather than a proton-neutron pair.

Sargsian shows this description implies a new structure in the deuteron, one that can exist only if a non-nucleonic component was present beforehand — constituents beyond the familiar two nucleons. He develops the dynamics of the predicted structure and asks whether it explains an anomaly in a recent Jefferson Lab experiment probing momenta above eight hundred mega-electronvolts. The answer would reshape pictures of the nuclear core.
arxiv-2504-10618: Pálvölgyi and Zólomy show a set clan of plane forms can be hit by few points. The forms are joined, flat, and non-pierce in the clan set. Their lone count is bound in the clan frame. A fixed count of points hits all forms in that clan. That end solves a past ask from Axenovich and two peers. Their ask was the top face length in a chart. That chart is edge-full with loop span at least a set mark.
arxiv-2504-11318:
Vishnu Iyer wrote this quantum computing paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on learning what a fermionic machine is doing. The simplest fermionic circuits, called Gaussian, are already known to be learnable fast; real chemistry needs circuits a bit beyond them.

Iyer gives the first algorithm that learns unitaries built with a sprinkling of non-Gaussian gates. It queries the unknown process and returns a circuit close to it in the strictest distance measure, in time that grows mildly with system size. The key is a new measure, Gaussian dimension, which grades how much of a process stays Gaussian. The algorithm covers a class wider than the sprinkled-gate one, including processes that would take far more gates to build directly. A companion test tells whether a process sits in the class at all. The paper settles an open problem in the field.
arxiv-2504-13018:
Chengde Qian, Yanhong Liu, and Long Feng made a classic multivariate method safe for heavy-tailed data in 2025. Canonical link study finds the strongest linear relationships between two sets of factors, but in high sizes it needs thinness to stay clear. And its usual covariance figures collapse when the data have heavy tails, as financial and genomic data often do. The authors restrict focus to elliptically balanced spreads, a broad group that includes such heavy tails.

Their method swaps the sample covariance for a spatial-sign covariance, a robust substitute that downweights extreme points, and adds a thinness penalty to select the major factors. Theory shows the estimator is steady and converges at the optimal rate even with heavy tails. Models put it ahead of current sparse methods exactly where tails are heaviest, and a real-data application confirms the useful gain.
arxiv-2504-15018:
Luiz Czelusniak, Tim Bingert, Mathias Krause, and Stephan Simonis put a popular multiphase flow method, in a 2025 preprint, on firm mathematical footing. The pseudo-potential lattice Boltzmann method simulates fluids that split into liquid and vapor. Users long tuned its knobs by trial and error. The authors derive the exact equation the method solves under diffusive scaling. That derivation ties each knob to a physical trait: phase densities, interface thickness, and surface tension. Users can now set properties in real units from the start.

The approach ships inside the OpenLB software with a unit converter for multiphase work. Benchmarks use a refrigerant as the working fluid, with all properties in physical units. A flat interface, a still droplet, and flow between plates all behave as theory predicts. The method converges at second order to the derived equation. The authors call it ready for accurate, user-friendly multiphase simulation.
arxiv-2504-15118:
Inho Kim, Youngkil Song, Jicheol Park, Won Hwa Kim, and Suha Kwak work on sound source localization. Their twenty twenty-five paper asks a model to find, in an image, the thing that is making a sound. No labels mark the right spot, so models learn by matching image and audio traits.

Past methods squash each input into one vector, which lets noise and clutter leak in. The new method uses joint slot attention: two slots compete for the image and audio traits and split them into target and off-target parts. Only the target parts are matched in training. On three public benchmarks the method topped nearly all past work.
arxiv-2504-17518:
Martin Karuhanga and Catherine Ashabahebwa bound the trapped energy levels of a particle moving in a thin, strip-like guide. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Such guides, called quantum waveguides, can be straight or bent. The levels of interest sit below the floor of the free motion range.

The pair give upper bounds for both the count of these levels and their total sum. The bounds are stated in terms of the strength of the pull acting inside the guide. For bent guides, they assume the strip does not cross itself and its bend varies in a smooth, bounded way. The bounds for the bent case are new. Results of this kind help physicists predict when a bent wire or channel will trap waves.
arxiv-2504-19718:
Chen and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about separating skin from non-skin parts on three-dimensional head scans. Face registration warps a template mesh to fit a scan. Hair, beards, and accessories pull that fit off course and lower its quality. Image-only methods give masks that disagree across views. Scan-only methods lack the fine detail images provide. Their method lifts image features into three dimensions and fuses them with shape features.

A frozen image model supplies the two-dimensional features from many views. The fused features predict a mask directly on the scan mesh. Their masks improved registration accuracy over both single-source methods. The model trained only on synthetic data, yet worked well on real scans. Cleaner skin masks could help face modeling for graphics and medicine.
arxiv-2504-21518:
Patrick Sabanic and co-authors make in 2025 short-lived cloud functions safe for sensitive data. Serverless computing is cheap and simple, but data flows through fleeting executions on untrusted machines. Sealed virtual machines protect data, yet they fit serverless poorly.

Their system, WALLET, nests tiny protected compartments, called trustlets, inside a sealed machine, one per function. A light operating layer handles input and output efficiently. Against plain sealed-machine setups, the trusted code base shrank over fourfold. End-to-end delay fell, far more functions fit per machine, and chained calls ran many times faster. The authors offer WALLET as a practical base for private serverless work.
arxiv-2505-00118:
Kao, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, takes a new look at a famed lone-pole solution in a gauge model with two force groups. Such a pole is a point source of a magnetic-like field.

The model holds a scalar pair. Kao shows an eigenvalue rule for that pair births a set of pole forms, each set by a path in space. The pole turns out to rest on that rule and on a sole matched blend of the non-plain gauge field. He gives a new set of pole forms that stretches a known one. The field of that known form is shown to be the same as his matched field. He weighs what the match may mean.
arxiv-2505-00618:
Gurjot Singh, Alim Dhanani, and Diogo Barradas present RevealNet, a system for finding who is behind network attacks, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Attackers hide behind proxy chains, VPNs, and anonymity networks. Traffic correlation can unmask an attacker's true location. Past systems for this are centralized. They take in flows from many probes, and they scale poorly on fast networks.

RevealNet instead runs a fleet of P4-programmable switches. The switches correlate traffic inside the network itself. Its building blocks compute and compare flow sketches. A sketch is a compact summary of a flow's key traits. So correlation happens in a spread-out, in-network way. Tests suggest accuracy on a par with centralized systems for attribution. At the same time, the compute cost and bandwidth overhead drop sharply. The work points toward attack attribution that keeps pace with large, high-speed networks.
arxiv-2505-03418:
Da Zheng and eight co-authors survey, in a 2025 preprint, how outside knowledge can help language models solve hard problems. Language models pair raw computing power with a rough form of reasoning. They stumble, though, on tasks needing many steps, deep domain facts, or checked answers. The survey maps the fixes now in use. These include chain-of-thought prompting, ways to fetch or inject knowledge, and tools that verify each step or the final result.

The authors then walk through fields where the problems bite hardest. Software work, math proving, data modeling, and lab science each get a section. Recurring limits include shaky multi-step logic and knowledge that goes stale. Verification stays hard when no ground truth is cheap. The paper closes with future directions grouped by its three themes. It aims to give researchers a shared map of a fast-moving area.
arxiv-2505-03818:
Antonio Valerio Miceli-Barone, Vaishak Belle, and Ali Payani present a game-based way to teach language models about code in a 2025 arXiv paper. Models do well on everyday coding tasks but can fail when a task needs deep reasoning about what code does. Good training examples for such reasoning are hard to find.

Their game, called SInQ, pits two agents against each other. One agent makes variants of real programs that behave in distinct ways. The other must find inputs where the variants act differently. Training this way improved results on several benchmarks. Gains appeared even in spotting flaws in C and C++ code, though training used only Python.
arxiv-2505-05818:
Vladimir Dzhunushaliev, Vladimir Folomeev, and Sayabek Sakhiyev build odd star like things that join a Dirac star with the form of a worm hole. Their set pairs a spin field with weight and a curve that is not straight. It adds a ghost field with no mass that gives the odd form. They get groups of flat at the ends, off same on each side, fixes.

Three input traits fix each build's traits. They are the curve strength of the spin field, its wave rate, and the throat size. Based on the picks, fixes are smooth or sharp edged. They have one or two throats and may have bounds of more than one kind. The two mouths can show far off mass and size. For strong bad curve strength, mass comes near the Chandrasekhar scale. Widths are on the scale of a few miles of ground.
arxiv-2505-07018:
Nicholas Boardman, Vivienne Wild, Natalia Vale Asari, and Francesco D'Eugenio wrote a 2025 astronomy paper on what sets the metal content of galaxies. Metals here means elements heavier than hydrogen and helium, built up by past stars. A known three-way trend ties metal levels to galaxy mass and star birth rate.

The team asks how much of that trend comes from a galaxy's recent star birth versus its long past. They use MaNGA survey data, which maps light across each galaxy's face. Oxygen, nitrogen, and the metals inside stars each tell a part of the story. Splitting the effects helps test whether slow gas inflow over time explains the trend.
arxiv-2505-07918:
Ryan Brady and Michael Zingale set a benchmark for how supernova codes should handle burning inside shocks. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. In double-detonation models of type Ia explosions, letting fuel ignite inside a shock front can corrupt the whole simulation.

A layered white dwarf model carried a tunable switch that suppresses burning where compression and pressure gradients spike. Three settings ran at three resolutions, down to a third of a kilometer per cell. At the finest grid, full burning and the strictest suppression agreed, while the looser setting drifted. Working resolutions are far coarser, so the pair advise always disabling shock burning in practice. Low-resolution runs proved touchy about the switch value.
arxiv-2505-08418:
The Belle and Belle II teams search for a rare decay that would break a known rule of particle physics. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, looks at B mesons made in collider runs in Japan. The decay they seek swaps one kind of lepton for another. No such swap has ever been confirmed, so any find would be big news.

The teams tag the partner B meson from its own decay products. That lets them spot the rare event in a messy mix. They hunt for a tau lepton paired with an electron or a muon, plus a known particle. The search method itself is the core of the report, with data from two runs of the machine.
arxiv-2505-10418:
Sahrish Naqvi and four co-authors study how fast flow through tight, stony material stops behaving in the simple linear way. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. The setup is a flat bed packed with stubby grains, driven by gravity, with only small gaps between stones.

At high flow speeds, push effects take over even though standard friction checks still look linear. The flow carves favored channels through the bed. Energy piles up unevenly, and swirls form behind grains. A vorticity analysis exposes a growing lopsidedness in the field. Oddly, the more the path winds, the higher the apparent ease of flow in this fast regime. The findings matter for filters, soils, and oil-bearing rock.
arxiv-2505-10718:
Suresh and six colleagues enrich word feature lists with language model help in twenty twenty-five. Feature norms, the traits people list for a concept, ground the study of how minds store meaning. Hand made lists are deep but small, since the work is slow. Their set, NOVA, covers near eight hundred concepts.

Model drafted traits were checked against trusted human calls. The blend packs far denser traits per concept than human only lists. It also predicts human likeness ratings better than the old lists and word vectors. The team argues minds hold richer concept detail than past lists showed. Checked model help can speed cognitive science, they say.
arxiv-2505-11718:
Pawin Taechoyotin and Daniel Acuna build an AI system that writes peer reviews in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Automated reviewers today tend to be shallow and overly kind. Real reviews press on weak points and judge novelty. The authors train a reasoning language model to do better. Their reward function scores reviews on many aspects, from quality of criticism to fit with the paper.

They first fine-tune the model on a new data set of strong conference reviews with reasoning traces. Then they train two variants with reinforcement learning, one on the human-aligned reward and one on a flat reward. A surprise emerged: the human-aligned reward penalized traits often found in strong reviews. The study opens a window on how reward design shapes machine judgment.
arxiv-2505-12018:
Yuwei Yang and co-authors plant mind traps in a web hacking game to see if bias can blunt attackers, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Players hunted flags in a flawed web app built for the test. Two biases were targeted: settling after a first find, and fear of loss.

Many players showed the settling bias, and it cost them clear success. Biased players found a quarter fewer flags than clean players on average. Both number and story data back the read. The team frames bias as a tool for training and defense design. Readers in security teaching get proof that minds, not just code, guard the gate.
arxiv-2505-15618:
Bernard Derrida's lecture notes teach non-equilibrium physics in twenty twenty-five. The notes were written for a summer school held at Les Houches in twenty twenty-four. They draw on twenty-five years of work on systems held out of equilibrium. Such systems touch several heat baths at different temperatures, or particle reservoirs at different densities.

Classical tools come first: tilted matrices, the fluctuation theorem, and transport coefficients. Einstein relations and fluctuating hydrodynamics are also recalled. The notes then present macroscopic fluctuation theory. That theory yields large deviation functions for density and current in diffusive systems. Readers get a compact course on how rare fluctuations in driven systems can be computed, from a leading figure in the field.
arxiv-2505-16918:
Nikola Tankovic and Robert Sajina wrote this paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on picking the right retail offer for each shopper when offers change fast. The tool for this is the contextual bandit, an algorithm that learns from each choice's outcome while using context about the user.

The paper first reviews the field, then presents a working prototype. It describes shoppers at the product category level, so what is learned from one offer can carry to like offers in the same class. Added features track how long a member has gone without buying a class, plus taste patterns from matrix factorization. Plain logistic models keep every choice explainable, and a language model front end lets staff ask why a profile shifted. The authors place the design next to classic methods and argue it fits live retail use.
arxiv-2505-17318:
Giovanni Ferrami and a large team search for galaxy scale lenses in two thousand twenty five. Two JWST fields host the hunt: PEARLS and CEERS. Visual checks of NIRCam images yield sixteen candidates at first pass. Lens modeling and redshift data trim the list hard.

Four lenses stand as the paper's main report here. Five high confidence candidates survive the full screening process. JWST yields about one lens per three to four pointings. That rate far exceeds ground based searches per area. A pure parallel survey could find some eighty lenses.
arxiv-2505-19118:
Sota Shimamura, Nen Saito, and Shuji Ishihara study active particles with attractive forces in two thousand twenty-five. The particles are active Brownian ones that pull toward each other. Plain sense says pull should build one big cluster. Phase splits of self driven crowds do just that in past work.

Their simulations show the pull breaks the single cluster apart. Many clusters form in its place, with sizes spread by a power law. Inside each cluster, swim directions align on their own. No alignment rule was built into the model. That inner accord makes each cluster move faster as a unit.
arxiv-2505-19818:
Luc Dessart, writing solo, computes what dying massive stars should look like in infrared light months after exploding. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. His models cover red supergiants and helium stars. Progenitor masses run from ten to about forty Suns. Explosions end as Type II or Type Ibc supernovae. The nebular phase, a few hundred days in, is the focus.

Full radiative transfer without thermal equilibrium assumptions does the work. Molecules and dust are left out by design. Type II models stay bright in visible light throughout. Type Ibc models shift most of their glow into the infrared. Strong lines from neon and nickel ions mark the spectra. Observers gain templates for reading late supernova light.
arxiv-2505-19918:
Amirali Kaboli, Alex Mascolo, and Amir Shaikhha unify two families of database join algorithms in a 2025 computer science study. Joins combine tables, and hard queries can create intermediate results vastly larger than the final answer. Worst-case optimal algorithms avoid that blow-up in theory, while classic binary joins are fast and simple in practice, leaving engine builders torn.

A single architecture that runs both styles efficiently is the authors' goal. Switching strategy per query, inside one system, could give worst-case guarantees without giving up everyday speed. The design speaks to the core of every relational database engine.
arxiv-2505-22218:
Jiří Ajgl and Ondřej Straka wrote a 2025 paper on a compression trick for state estimates in high-dimensional tasks. A state estimate weighs how sure we are of the state of a thing, as a spread of probability over a grid. Fine grids blow up in size as dimensions grow. The compression stores the spread as a chain of small grids, multiplied out, which cuts the count sharply.

Three snags draw the attention of the team. Compression can let bad, negative weights creep in, and spoil the spread. Square spreads and bell-shaped spreads are then set side by side in the compression, with a look at how correlation strength sets the ranks of the chain. Last, the team studies what it costs to shift the spread from one grid to a fresh one. The study is a guide for tracking tools in hard, high-dimensional work.
arxiv-2505-22418:
Jeongwon Jo and three co-authors study AI in public benefits in twenty twenty-five. The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program supports forty-one million low-income applicants in the United States. Applying brings administrative burdens: forms, rules, and stress. The authors interviewed applicants with diverse experiences of the system.

Language model tools can ease old burdens, they find, but they also create new ones. New learning, compliance, and psychological costs transform what applicants face. Trust in AI, across competence, integrity, and benevolence, seemed to reduce burdens. Some of that relief may stem from excessive, unintended trust in the system. The authors discuss calibrating trust to a proper level. Readers get a grounded view of AI help in welfare offices.
arxiv-2505-22518:
Agnideep Aich sets out IGNIS, a neural network tool that finds the key value in a class of models for linked risk, called Archimedean copulas. Old methods can fail on these models when their math turns unstable or their links are too weak. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

IGNIS learns a direct map from simple signs of link strength in the data to the model value. Its design forces the output to stay in the valid range. Trained on four model types, two of them known to be hard, it gave steady and close results on real finance and health data. The author presents it as a stand alone tool for cases where old methods break.
arxiv-2505-23518:
Hangoo Kang, Jehyeok Yeon, and Gagandeep Singh set out TRAP, an attack that steers the choices of smart agents by planting sense in an image. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Agents run by sight-language models are near real use, but their cross-channel thought opens new attack paths. Past attacks mar pixels in plain sight, or need deep access to the model or its world. TRAP makes images that look natural, yet bend an agent's picks in a set way. It joins a prompt that drags quality down with a push that lifts a target sense. A twin net and a layout mask guide the plant. No reach into the model is needed.
arxiv-2505-23618:
Amir Said, Hilmi Egilmez, and Yung-Hsuan Chao find a cheaper way, in a 2025 preprint, to run the math transforms inside modern video codecs. Codecs shrink video by restating blocks of leftover signal with wave-like patterns. Using several pattern types, including uneven ones, improves compression. But the uneven transforms cost far more to compute than the standard one, above all on large blocks. That cost hits both software and hardware designs.

The authors design near-copies of those transforms that start from the cheap standard transform. Small orthogonal tweaks then bend its most important patterns toward the target shapes. The result keeps the speed of the standard path while acting almost like the costly one. Tests in the Versatile Video Coding reference software showed large savings in computation. Coding quality stayed practically the same as with the full transforms.
arxiv-2505-24518:
Jiatong Shi and co-authors built ARECHO in 2025, a system that grades logged speech on many quality scales at once. Builders track several measures of speech, covering overall quality, intelligibility. And listener opinion scores, but each metric has its own scale and starting claims. And they influence one another, so estimating them jointly is not straightforward. Separate clues ignore those dependencies.

ARECHO models the dependencies with an autoregressive design. A tokenization workflow first converts the speech signal into a rich set of information tokens. A dynamic classifier chain then predicts the metrics in sequence, each estimate informed by the ones before it. And a two-step reading method uses confidence to make the final inference more reliable. In tests the system greatly outperformed the baseline method across a diverse range of testing settings.
arxiv-2506-02318:
Yuchen Liang and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on diffusion models that work with discrete data, such as words. These models add noise step by step, then learn to undo it. One choice shapes the noise path: a uniform path or an absorbing path. The absorbing path often gives better output, but proofs for it were missing.

The team gives the first time bounds and error rates for the absorbing case. They use a stand-in start point to tame a math snag at the start state. Two sampling methods get proofs with better rates than in the uniform case. Under fair terms, the proofs hold with no need to stop early. New proof tools for score bounds form part of the work.
arxiv-2506-05418:
Agents that learn from images often latch onto the wrong details, such as shadows or clouds, and then fail when the scene changes. Kyungsoo Kim, Jeongsoo Ha, and Yusung Kim offer a method called Self-Predictive Dynamics that teaches an agent to keep only the features tied to the task. The method pairs mild and strong altered views of each image and learns by predicting how the agent's own actions move it between those views.

Tests covered simulated control tasks and a driving simulator. In both, the method beat earlier work on scenes with complex, distracting detail. Its lead grew on scenes the agent had never seen, which is the weak point the work targets.
arxiv-2506-06518:
Neil Fendley and co-authors wrote a 2025 systematic review of poisoning attacks against large language models. In such an attack, an attacker slips a flaw into the training process to make the model behave badly on command. Such models and their training sets are now widespread and freely available. The risk grows with the spread. The vocabulary for this risk comes from older work on classification, which fits poorly with free-text models.

The team reviewed the published literature on such attacks and built a clean threat framework to sort them. The framework names four specifications of an attack, covering its logistics and manipulation moves. It also names six metrics for the marks of an attack. Within the framework, the field is read in four groups: plain concept harm, hidden stealthy harm, long-lasting persistent harm, and task-specific harm. The aim is a shared language for a young field.
arxiv-2506-07118:
Yu-Xuan Wu, Ziyan Huang, Bin Hu, and Zhi-Hong Guan build a sound-based tool to help diagnose depression, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Most top diagnostic models lean on images, while the clues carried in a person's voice often get less attention.

Their model, called RBA-FE, pulls six kinds of acoustic features from raw audio, catching both the shape of sounds and how they unfold over time. Noise is the central enemy, since real recordings are messy. To fight it, the design uses a spiking neuron model tuned to mimic how the brain sharpens its focus on chosen signals. This adaptive neuron helps the features stay clean where older networks lose precision. The result is a brain-inspired extractor meant to keep depression screening from voice steady in noisy settings.
arxiv-2506-08118:
Ankit Srivastava, Victor Jimenez-Fernandez, Louis Cattafesta, and Scott Dawson measure cause and effect inside fluid flows in a 2025 study. Their framework works with linearized dynamics, the simplified equations that govern small disturbances around a steady flow. The matrix exponential of those equations tells how each mode influences others at any later time, which the authors turn into a causal score between modes.

An upper bound further quantifies how much causality a mode can exert. Specializing a general dynamic causal effect analysis to operators makes the method fast enough for engineering flows, where knowing what drives an oscillation guides control design.
arxiv-2506-08818:
Quentin Bizot and Noel Jakse simulated how crystals first form in aluminum-silicon alloys in 2025. How a molten alloy freezes sets the grain pattern, and with it the strength, of cast parts. The first tiny crystals appear at scales too small and fast for lab tools to watch directly, so the team turned to atom-level simulation.

A machine-learned force model, trained on quantum-accurate runs, let them simulate large samples of cooling liquid near the balanced alloy mix. On the aluminum-rich side, aluminum crystals started first and grew round. On the silicon-rich side, silicon started first and grew with flat, polygonal faces. The contrast guides how casters might steer freezing.
arxiv-2506-09018:
Havasi, Karrer, Gat, and Chen propose Edit Flows in twenty twenty-five, a new way to generate sequences. Models that write one token at a time handle varied lengths with ease. Models that write all at once often force a fixed, rigid shape. That shape fits sequence data poorly.

Edit Flows builds sequences through edits: it inserts, deletes, and swaps tokens. The process is framed as a chain that moves through sequence space over time. A training trick with extra variables makes learning fast and tractable. In tests, the method beat both step by step models and mask models on image captions. It also did much better than the mask method on text and code tasks.
arxiv-2506-09218:
Bruno Ferenc Šegedin, a solo author, studies how a generative network learns sound patterns in words, in two thousand twenty-five. The network was trained on raw audio of words. The open question is whether such networks pick up general sound rules that go beyond the words they learned from.

Šegedin shrank a key layer of the network to a narrow bottleneck before training. Under that narrow shape, a new probing trick works: skip the bottleneck and feed random feature maps into the sound-building layers. The outputs still obeyed a sound restriction from training, just as normal outputs did. That shows the sound-building layers themselves can generalize sound patterns.
arxiv-2506-09718:
Xulin Ma and nine co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on health checks with no touch, done in front of a mirror. A camera method reads pulse from small shifts in face color. Daily care routines are a good slot for such checks. But light shifts, hand blocks, and face moves make the reads hard, above all at high altitude.

The team built the first long term data set for this case. It holds paired color and infrared face videos from a group of adults in five care scenes. True pulse, breath, and blood oxygen reads come with the videos. Mixed color and infrared input cut heart rate error a lot. Learning all signs at once helped each one.
arxiv-2506-10918:
Morris Yau and five co-authors characterized a broad family of sequence models in twenty twenty-five that train in parallel yet infer step by step with little memory. Architectures like Mamba and gated linear attention achieve this balance, but the full class was undefined. The authors start from state space models, whose updates fit the classic parallel prefix scan with a custom combining rule.

Relaxing that rule to allow arbitrary functions, even softmax attention, defines Prefix-Scannable Models, a class unifying many known designs and adding new ones. Some new members use constant amortized compute per token with only logarithmic memory. On small language modeling and synthetic tasks like state tracking, these models matched transformer expressivity with state space efficiency, and sometimes generalized to longer sequences better than either.
arxiv-2506-11318:
Bruno Monteiro and Vinicius dos Santos wrote a computer science paper in two thousand twenty-five on searching for a pattern that keeps changing. Classic string matching counts how often a fixed pattern occurs in a fixed text. Here the text stays put, but letters can be added to or removed from the pattern at any time.

After each change, their method recounts the matches in the text. It rests on suffix arrays, a sorted index of all text endings. Setup takes time tied to the text length, and each update then runs very fast. They extend the method to deleting, moving, and copying blocks of the pattern, and to texts that keep growing.
arxiv-2506-12218:
Samuel Rey, Hamed Ajorlou, and Gonzalo Mateos set out the DAG Convolutional Network, a graph neural network built for directed acyclic graphs. Such graphs sit at the base of causal work, scheduling, and neural network search. Plain graph networks do not respect the partial order that defines these graphs.

The new design uses causal graph filters to learn node values that take that order into account. That order is a strong built-in bias. In contrast to past machine learning on such graphs, it rests on formal operations with spectral forms. The team also gives a parallel form. It feeds signals to a bank of causal graph-shift operators, worked on by a shared multilayer perceptron. Tests across tasks showed good scores on accuracy, robustness, and speed.
arxiv-2506-13618:
Lauren Rhodes led a large team tracking a torn-apart star in a 2025 paper. A star that strays too close to a giant black hole gets shredded, and some shredded matter can launch a fast jet. Their target was the fifth such jetted event known, and it glowed at radio wavelengths for a long time.

They fit three models to their long run of observations. A fast round outflow, holding both hot normal electrons and faster ones, fit best. The space around the event thins outward in a pattern like other such events, but this one carried twice the energy of the best-studied case. Heat-based electrons were inferred here for the first time.
arxiv-2506-16118:
Partha Mondal, Omar Alkhazragi, and Hakan Bagci wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It designs a tiny layered absorber that soaks up light from the ultraviolet through the near-infrared, to boost thin-film silicon solar cells.

The stack has a grid of titanium on top, a thin glass-like spacer, and an aluminum back that acts as a mirror. Tuned with care, it takes in nearly all light across a broad band, works for any light angle of tilt or twist, and was built with electron beam tools. Bench tests match the models well. Set into a thin-film cell, it lifts the light caught in the active layer by a large margin.
arxiv-2506-16618:
Meysam Alizadeh and Fabrizio Gilardi test whether a data market lifts people's will to sell their social media data, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Two pre-set online trials compared market offers with free donation and one-off buys. Research access to such data has tightened while user worry grows.

The market raised will to sell by twelve to twenty-five points over donation. It also beat one-off offers by near seven points. Most sellers set prices inside the low range the market showed, far below past one-off sums. Buyer type and privacy shields did not move choices in the market arm. Readers get a workable price path for user data.
arxiv-2506-17218:
Zeyuan Yang and colleagues let a vision-language model daydream in pictures it never has to draw. Text-only decoding forces models to verbalize visual reasoning, which hobbles tasks needing imagination. Rendering real images is expensive and can damage reasoning. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their framework inserts latent visual tokens into the output stream. When the model chooses to think visually, its own hidden states become the next tokens. The trajectory stays multimodal without a single pixel being produced. Training begins by distilling true image embeddings into those tokens, then switches to text-only supervision.

A reinforcement learning stage sharpens the skill further. Across diverse benchmarks, the mental imagery models reasoned better than their text-bound counterparts, the authors report. No explicit image generation was involved. The paper takes its cue from human cognition, where mental pictures guide thought invisibly.
arxiv-2506-17318:
Atharv Singh Patlan, Ashwin Hebbar, Pramod Viswanath, and Prateek Mittal show that web agents can be attacked through their stored context, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Autonomous web agents turn language instructions into browser actions for shopping, search, and discovery tasks. Because language models are stateless, agents depend on external memory. That memory often sits client-side or with third parties, exposed to tampering.

The authors formalize plan injection, an attack that corrupts an agent's internal task representation. Testing two popular web agents, they find plan injections bypass strong prompt injection defenses. Success rates ran up to three times higher than comparable prompt attacks. A chained variant builds logical bridges from user goals to attacker objectives. It raised the success rate for privacy exfiltration tasks by seventeen point seven percent. The authors conclude secure memory handling must be a first-class design concern.
arxiv-2506-17518:
A robot that sees the world as raw pixels must first boil each view down to a compact summary of where things stand. Ayoub Echchahed and Pablo Samuel Castro survey the methods that learn such summaries for deep reinforcement learning, the field where agents learn by trial and error. They limit the survey to agents that learn while acting, without a model of the world handed to them.

The methods fall into six broad classes, and the survey lays out how each works, where it helps, and where it breaks down. It also covers ways to judge whether a learned summary is any good. The authors close with open problems meant to guide new researchers entering the field.
arxiv-2506-19518:
Ming-Chun Lee and a team of co-authors survey wireless networks that sense, send, and compute at once, in two thousand twenty-five. Such systems could serve robot networks, smart transport, smart factories, and virtual reality. Most work so far chases speed and efficiency in their joint design.

The survey turns instead to strength under strain, with limited resources in view. The authors first define what it means for such a network to stay robust under doubt. They also define resilience, the power to keep a basic service through major disruption. Design approaches for both traits follow, and a case study and open problems close the piece.
arxiv-2506-19918:
Kun-Feng Lyu and Yue Zhao ask what a super-cooled phase shift in the young cosmos would do to the QCD axion. The work came out in 2025. The axion is a guessed speck put forth to fix a flaw in the strong force. It is also a top pick for dark stuff.

How many axions last turns on the heat path of the cosmos near the QCD scale, when quarks got bound in tight groups. The NANOGrav team has found a faint hum of waves in space. One source could be a phase shift that cooled too far before it closed. The team tracks how such a shift would stir the axion field. It could spark a brief stage where the field's move is out of line. In part of the range, axion walls would form with near force of fate. Those walls would leave marks on both counts.
arxiv-2506-21118:
Tatsuya Gima, Soh Kumabe, and Yuichi Yoshida published a computer science paper in 2025 on stable algorithms. A stable algorithm barely changes its answer when inputs shift slightly. That property, called Lipschitz continuity, supports reliable decisions. Until now, stable algorithms were designed separately for each problem.

The authors prove a broad meta-theorem for the field. It parallels a classic result about graphs with small tree-like structure. For weighted vertex problems stated in a standard logic, good stable approximations exist. The guarantee holds on graphs of bounded treewidth. Similar results cover a second graph measure, clique-width. Their method beats most earlier problem-specific designs on quality, stability, or both.
arxiv-2506-23618:
Zhongdao Wang and five colleagues present TurboVSR, a diffusion-based model for video super-resolution, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Diffusion models produce excellent detail in upscaled video. They are also painfully slow, sometimes taking tens of minutes for a two-second clip. TurboVSR aims to keep the quality while removing the wait.

Three design choices drive the speedup. A highly compressing autoencoder cuts the number of tokens the model must process. Factorized conditioning teaches the model to restore the first frame, then guides later frames using it. Finally, the pretrained diffusion model is converted into a shortcut model needing fewer sampling steps. The result matches leading methods on quality while running over a hundred times faster. It upscales a two-second high-definition clip in about seven seconds and even handles 4K images.
arxiv-2506-24118:
Haiwen Li and eight co-authors proposed in twenty twenty-five a new design for Community Notes, the crowd-sourced fact-checking system, in the age of language models. Their paradigm is an open ecosystem: humans and AI models alike may draft notes, but diverse human raters still decide which notes are helpful enough to display. That keeps trust anchored in the community principle the system was built on.

AI drafting could deliver context far faster, while human judgment guards quality. The feedback loop runs both ways: ratings of AI notes become training signal, a scheme they call reinforcement learning from community feedback. The paper describes how such a system would work, its benefits, and the fresh risks it brings, and closes with a research agenda for handling them.
arxiv-2507-01118:
Bhagyalekshmy S and Rutuja Kshirsagar give the first sharp decoding method for a broad family of error-correcting codes. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Quasi-twisted codes cover several well-known code families in one frame. They guard data against noise in storage and transit. Yet no fast way to decode them was known.

Their method works from the error pattern, called the syndrome, and fixes up to a set limit of errors. The limit rests on a new lower bound for how far apart code words must sit. The pair then build a code-based lock system in the style of a classic design. The system stands up to known classic attacks and to some quantum ones. Code-based locks are prized as backups if quantum machines break today's codes.
arxiv-2507-04818:
Ferraro and co-authors explore stronger security for edge devices in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Small linked devices now run drones, factories, and key public systems, so a break-in can cause real harm. Their tool is CHERI, a chip design that guards memory and splits software into sealed parts.

The team applied this split to the network stack, the part of a system most often attacked. They isolated apps, network libraries, and drivers on a test system and measured the trade-offs. The results suggest the approach can raise security while keeping speed in settings much like embedded ones. The authors present it as a path to safer devices at the edge.
arxiv-2507-04918: Tomasi and a very large team of co-authors present a simulation framework for the LiteBIRD instruments in two thousand twenty-five. The work describes the software frame used to model how the mission's instruments behave before flight. The long author list reflects the scale of the joint team behind the instruments. Papers of this kind let mission teams test analysis steps on fake data that mimics the real signal chain.
arxiv-2507-07218:
Alfredo Scigliani and Hadi Mohammadigoushki study the flow of wormlike micelle solutions in a two thousand twenty-five paper. These soapy fluids form long, flexible structures that can split into bands flowing at different speeds. The phenomenon, shear banding, matters in products from shampoo to enhanced oil recovery.

Two solutions with similar bulk behavior but different surfactant chemistry were tested. The setup was a Taylor-Couette cell, and the gap size varied to change elasticity and curvature. Both fluids showed a stress overshoot after startup, then growing flow irregularities. Past a threshold, one solution briefly flowed backward while the other never did. The authors blame stronger electrostatic repulsion between the second fluid's molecular head groups.
arxiv-2507-07718:
Alberto Rota, Ke Fan, and Elena De Momi build and test a virtual reality trainer for surgical robotics with haptic guidance built in. Their paper from twenty twenty-five argues that high-level assistance tools can give trainees a broader, sturdier skill set. Better training should carry into better clinical work. Their simulator holds eight surgical tasks driven by a physics engine.

Trainees feel guidance through haptic interfaces on their hands and wrists. The system steers motion toward targets and away from obstacles. Each task ends with a numeric performance score. A study with trainees shows the guidance lifts scores during training. More telling, skills carried over to unassisted runs that mimic clinic work. The authors pitch assisted curricula as a route to safer first steps in robotic surgery.
arxiv-2507-09118:
Linlan Huang, Xusheng Cao, Haori Lu, Yifan Meng, Fei Yang, and Xialei Liu present MG-CLIP in two thousand twenty five. Continual learning adds new tasks without erasing old skill. CLIP based versions often ignore the modality gap inside CLIP. That gap tracks how much pretrained knowledge survives fine tuning.

Their method preserves the gap to fight forgetting of old classes. It also compensates the gap to fit new data better. No replay data is needed for the gains shown. Tests across benchmarks beat prior continual learning methods. The modality gap becomes a design lens for the field.
arxiv-2507-13518:
Thomas Belvin and Peter Shawhan explore catching dark matter by listening to a taut wire. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A heavy particle passing near Earth would tug the wire by gravity alone. That tug starts waves along the wire. The team asks whether the waves could reveal the passerby. The wire in their study is a fine copper beryllium strand.

Both transverse and longitudinal waves form after the pass. Each carries a distinct time pattern of displacement. Together they allow a full three-dimensional track reconstruction. The particle's mass-to-speed ratio comes out as well. At very close range, Planck-scale particles are the target. Their displacements prove immeasurably small in this setup. The paper maps the idea's limits honestly.
arxiv-2507-13718:
Danilo Avola, Muhammad Bilal, Emad Emam, Cristina Lakasz, Daniele Pannone, and Amedeo Ranaldi catch lies from brainwaves with a bidirectional recurrent network. Their paper from twenty twenty-five trains on the Bag-of-Lies dataset, a multimodal corpus of casual, natural deception. The classifier reads EEG signals only. A Bi-GRU network scans each signal forward and backward, catching patterns that one-way passes miss.

Test accuracy lands at ninety-seven percent, with precision, recall, and F1-scores high for both truth and lies. The authors credit bidirectional time modeling for the strength. Real-time deception screening is floated as a use, alongside richer architectures later. Security, psychology, and forensics all watch this space, and the result is a strong mark on a public benchmark.
arxiv-2507-16018:
Lu and four colleagues turn odd tokens inside vision transformers into a speed trick in twenty twenty-five. A few tokens grow huge and act as attention sinks. Others arise as artifacts of the process. The two kinds suppress each other through attention, shaping the flow of information.

Their Fast Nyström Attention uses that structure to sketch self attention in linear time and space. No retraining is needed. A masking step cuts noise from the odd tokens for small gains at near no cost. Tests span retrieval, classing, segmentation, and visual questions. Scores stayed competitive while compute fell.
arxiv-2507-17818:
Hyerin Cho, Ben S. Prather, Ramesh Narayan, Kung-Yi Su, and Priyamvada Natarajan simulate black hole accretion and feedback from the event horizon to the host galaxy, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Spanning that range of scales in one simulation is extremely challenging. Their multizone method previously reached steady states for non-spinning black holes. Here they improve the method and apply it to rapidly spinning black holes that power relativistic jets.

The strongly magnetized accretion launches a jet with an intermediate feedback efficiency near thirty percent. Prograde and retrograde setups eventually converge to the same efficiency as magnetic fields remove gas rotation. Extending simulations to much larger Bondi radii, accretion falls below the Bondi rate in a clean scaling. Yet the time-averaged feedback efficiency stays near thirty percent regardless of radius. Spin, the authors conclude, mainly governs how efficiently black holes return energy to their galaxies.
arxiv-2507-19118:
Abu Sadat Mohammad Salehin Amit, Zhaojun Liu, and four co-authors propose a method for matching features between remote sensing images taken in different modes, such as optical and radar. Their paper came out in 2025. Large differences in geometry and brightness between such images make matching hard.

Their mechanism detects distinctive keypoints in each image separately, then builds maps that relate regions across the pair. The matching step is recast as a classification task handled by a fully convolutional network, a network that labels every point in an image. This keeps sensitivity to local detail while carrying broader context. Tested on object detection in two standard datasets, the method reached state-of-the-art accuracy while still running at usable speed. Better matching directly improved the downstream detection task.
arxiv-2507-22918:
Daniel Son and co-authors test whether two Gemma language models of unlike size carve the world into like inner features, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Sparse autoencoders pulled clean single-sense features from each model's stream. Matched features were then compared by two gauges.

Middle layers overlapped most, while first and last layers split apart. Word chunks with like sense also met the models alike in early side tests. The pattern backs a shared feature world across scale. That sharing could ground tools that move insight between models. Readers get size-proof hints of one inner map.
arxiv-2508-00318:
Shivakumar Athani, Benjy Marks, François Guillard, Alistair Gillespie, and Itai Einav look at a puzzle in grain flow in this two thousand twenty-five paper. In lab tests, when a silo fills, large grains move to the walls. Small ones gather near the center. Yet big silos often show the reverse. The team ran set tests with grains of two sizes in flat, near two-dimensional silos. The tests ran dry and under fluid.

They changed the shape of the box and how thick the fluid was. They read the fill marks from images. Two key dimensionless numbers stood out. One is how slim the silo is. The other is the Stokes number. It sets grain push and pull against drag from the fluid. The result is one scaling frame that fits both lab and field marks. It also shows how fluids shift how grains sort as they fill.
arxiv-2508-01218:
Yujian Liu and colleagues rebuilt digital head avatars with steadier geometry in a 2025 paper called MoGaFace. Standard pipelines first track a parametric face mesh from landmarks, then render with Gaussian splats, but the tracked mesh often sits slightly off the photos, blurring detail and breaking consistency across views. Their framework keeps refining shape and texture during rendering instead of freezing the mesh first.

A momentum-updated expression bank and a correction step keep geometry consistent over time and across angles. A latent texture module folds multi-view features into each Gaussian so texture sharpens in step with geometry. Experiments show high-fidelity avatars and better novel-view synthesis, even when the starting mesh is inaccurate.
arxiv-2508-02718:
Zahra Mohammadi and Siamak Mohammadi present a low-power method for classifying sleep apnea in a 2025 medical computing study. Apnea interrupts breathing during sleep, and its obstructive, central, and mixed forms need different care. Wearable devices must spot the forms quickly while using little energy and only a single heart signal lead.

The authors compare many classical and deep learning methods on one-second windows of electrocardiogram data. They weigh accuracy, complexity, and energy use together. Their compact network, SleepLiteCNN, comes out of that comparison. It aims for fine time resolution and low power, suiting overnight monitoring on small wearable hardware.
arxiv-2508-03618:
Nassim Ali Ousalah, Peyman Rostami, and four colleagues let an algorithm design pose-estimation networks that fit a strict computing budget, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Estimating an object's full six-degree-of-freedom pose, its rotation and translation, from one image is vital for robotics and augmented reality, but heavy networks exclude small devices.

Their framework, FPG-NAS, searches architectures differentiably, so the search itself is fast. A gating mechanism picks among candidate operations in a discrete way, widening the variety of designs explored. A penalty on floating-point operations keeps the accuracy-efficiency trade-off honest. The search space is astronomically large, around ten to the ninety-second power possibilities. Tests on the LINEMOD and SPEED+ benchmarks validate the found architectures. Automated design under a FLOPs budget brings pose estimation to hardware that could never run a hand-designed giant.
arxiv-2508-03818:
Toby Walsh wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It designs fair rules for placing a facility, such as a clinic, when a prediction of the best spot is at hand and agents may game their stated spots.

Walsh takes an egalitarian view, weighing both the worst distance any agent must travel and the worst share of benefit any agent gets. Rules are graded on how well they do when the forecast is right, and how badly they can fail when it is wrong. By studying the failure modes, he builds rules that trade the two off by a dial. He then gives honest rules for two facilities, fed by two forecasts, with both traits bounded.
arxiv-2508-03918:
Jack Anderson and co-authors trace a carbon molecule in young stars in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The molecule, a two-carbon radical, is a useful tracer of gas shaped by starlight in older disks around stars. Much less is known about it in younger, still-embedded protostars.

The team used survey data and new telescope observations for thirty-five young low-mass protostars in Perseus. The molecule's glow lined up with the walls of outflow cavities and avoided areas rich in another molecule. This shows it marks light-active, oxygen-poor gas even at this early stage. Its glow stayed spread out at all ages sampled, so the shift to compact patterns in older disks must happen quickly.
arxiv-2508-06918: Stefano Fioravanti, Michael Kompatscher, Bernardo Rossi, and Albert Vucaj sort all Mal'cev clones on a three-item set up to a loose form of sameness, in twenty twenty-five. A clone is a closed set of operations, and the Mal'cev kind has a key three-input rule. The sort is one step toward a full sort of three-item structures by a broad build test. They also give a fresh proof of Bulatov's known result, which caps the size of a base set of links for such clones.
arxiv-2508-08018: Allan Berele, a solo author, proves trace identities for matrix-like structures in a 2025 paper. Given a set of weights in a field, he defines a weighted trace that adds up scaled inputs. He shows this space satisfies two kinds of identity. In one, a high power of a variable equals a mix of lower powers. In the other, a product of traces equals a mix with fewer traces. The proofs run through specialized symmetric functions.
arxiv-2508-08218:
Ellie Pond, Yichen Zhao, and Matthew Hale design a distributed optimization method that needs no delay bounds in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. In distributed computing, workers update at uneven pace, and proofs often assume delays stay capped. Real caps are hard to know.

Their generalized momentum method covers classic schemes like heavy ball and Nesterov's method as special cases. It allows any finite delay. The authors first give settings that guarantee the method settles, then show its speed grows linearly with work done. In tests on a text sorting task with unbounded delays, it beat plain descent by over a third in rounds and also beat both classic rivals.
arxiv-2508-08418:
Emma Prevot, Dieter Haring, and colleagues model treatment effects over time in multiple sclerosis trials in a 2025 biostatistics study. Long trials can show how and when a therapy bends a patient's disease course, but follow-up is irregular, patients differ, and confounders change with time. Bayesian causal forests estimate differing effects across patients by splitting the job between prognosis and treatment effect trees.

Their hierarchical extension adapts that machinery to repeated measurements on the same patients. The multiple sclerosis case study grounds the method in real trial structure. Better causal estimates from long trials help clinicians match treatments to the patients most likely to benefit.
arxiv-2508-10418:
Song and Kawashima gave a sharper shrink tool in twenty twenty-five for flat nets of small math blocks used in physics sims. Such shrink steps let vast grids fit in small models. Their new step uses best-fit edge blocks for the whole net as the work frame.

From that frame they build shrink maps with less loss than past top ways. The cost stays the same as the base method's, they show. No weave-cut step is needed for the gain. The path can stretch the method to higher dims at sane cost.
arxiv-2508-12218:
Azam Nouri sorts all positive solutions of a critical nonlinear equation on a half-space in a 2025 math study. The equation pairs a Laplacian with a power term at the critical exponent, where compactness fails and solution shapes become rigid. A boundary rule links the outward slope to another critical power on the flat edge of the half-space.

Nouri proves every positive solution has one stated bubble form, set by a scale and a center placed below the boundary. Uniqueness of that form is the whole content: no exotic solutions hide. Such rigid results anchor blow-up analysis for geometric equations.
arxiv-2508-12418:
Rachael DeVries, Casper Christensen, Marie Lisandra Zepeda Mendoza, and Ole Winther wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It classifies patients from electronic health records with a transformer that reads along two axes at once.

Health records keep growing: more fields, longer spans, more data kinds. Transformers fit such bulk, but the way records are fed in can waste the gaps, which often carry signal. Their Bi-Axial Transformer attends to both the clinical fields and the time points. On sepsis warning it sets the best score known. On death risk it matches the top methods. It shrugs off missing data better than rival transformers. Its learned sensor codes can also move to new tasks.
arxiv-2508-14218:
Mustafa Mohammadi Gharasuie and Luis Rueda speed up image sorting with graph neural nets and Voronoi diagrams. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Graph methods treat an image as a web of linked points, which fits complex data well. Classic image nets do not use that web form.

Their frame turns pixels or zones into graph points, then trims the web with a Delaunay form tied to the Voronoi split. A new graph layer they name works faster than the standard one. On several test sets, their model cuts pre-work time and lifts accuracy past past best models. Gains are largest on complex scenes and fine classes.
arxiv-2508-14818:
Jihao Andreas Lin and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on faster tuning of neural networks. A known method, successive halving, gives more compute to the best early runners and cuts the rest. Its flaw is that slow starters may be cut too soon, though they could win in the end. The team tests if forecasts of full learning curves can fix that flaw.

Their curves come from a latent Gaussian process with a Kronecker form. In a large test on many network types and a click data set, the forecast route did about as well as the plain route. It did not beat just spending more on the plain route, since it needs full curves to train on. Old curve data could ease that cost.
arxiv-2508-15018:
Stefanie Heyden, Mohit Pundir, Eric Dufresne, and David Kammer show how the type of disorder in an elastic network stamps its rest shape and stiffness, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Networks were built with disorder in length, in links, or in stiffness, then let settle under full motion math. Each class was checked after settling.

Settled shapes differed clearly by disorder class. That split hints that easy lab measures on a settled net can reveal hidden build detail. Macroscopic stiffness also bore the class stamp. The work turns disorder from noise into a design code. Readers who craft soft nets get a map from build mess to final behavior.
arxiv-2508-15918:
Christy, Dent, Ghosh, Kumar, and Ward study thermal corrections at low temperature in phase transitions of the early cosmos, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. First-order transitions in the early universe send out gravitational waves. Heavy particles can shift the effective potential in subtle ways when it is cold. Their focus is the thin-wall regime, where the vacuum structure stays as it was.

In this limit, all such corrections are modeled by one new parameter. Shifts in the values that mark the transition follow from that single quantity. Gravitational wave signals and other things we can observe shift in step. The shortcut covers tangled forms of correction in one even way. Builders of models gain a quick tool for a first estimate.
arxiv-2508-17018:
Seamus Somerstep, Ya'acov Ritov, Mikhail Yurochkin, Subha Maity, and Yuekai Sun wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It probes the limits of label refinement and weak training, two paths meant to let strong AI models learn from weaker guides.

The worry is that human-made data caps a model at human level, a snag called the superalignment problem. Under the standard probability setup used to study refinement, the authors show both paths carry error that cannot be removed. An ideal oracle method, too costly to run, would do better, so a real gap stays open. The result pushes the field to seek new ways to grow from weak to strong that keep the ease but close the gap.
arxiv-2508-17318:
Yu Wu and colleagues proposed a design recipe in 2025 for crystals that barely conduct heat, by sabotaging both ways heat travels. In a crystal, heat moves as particle-like phonons and as wave-like vibrations that tunnel between modes. Most low-conductivity designs attack only one channel. Their recipe, called heavy-light and soft-stiff, mixes heavy atoms with light ones and soft bonds with stiff ones inside the same structure.

Calculations show the heavy, softly bonded atoms crowd the low-frequency range, scattering the particle-like flow. The light, stiffly bonded atoms spread thin high-frequency branches that break the wave-like coherence. High-throughput screening then searched for real compounds matching the motif. Ultralow thermal conductivity is the key property for thermoelectric generators and thermal barrier coatings. A recipe that suppresses both channels at once could widen the menu of candidate materials.
arxiv-2508-17518:
Thomas Gassmann, Stefanos Chaliasos, Thodoris Sotiropoulos, and Zhendong Su run the first broad study of how compiler optimizations affect zero knowledge virtual machines. These machines turn zero knowledge proofs into a plain back end for normal code. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team tests dozens of LLVM passes, six standard levels, and an unoptimized base across many benchmarks on two RISC-V based machines. Standard levels did lift speed by a wide margin, yet far less than on normal chips. The cause is that compiler choices lean on hardware traits, like caches, that proof systems lack. The authors draw guidance for proof aware tuning.
arxiv-2508-18418:
Pedro Meyer Tokoro studied in twenty twenty-five whether a class of math operators keeps its good behavior when slightly disturbed. The operators are pseudo-differential operators on flat space, used to state and solve equations from physics. An operator is called globally hypoelliptic when rough inputs still yield smooth outputs in a strong, whole-space sense.

Tokoro proves that if such an operator is perturbed by a much weaker one, the strong smoothness property survives. The result covers named families such as the Shubin and SG classes. He also explains why the same claim fails for the standard Hörmander classes. Results like this matter because real models are never exact; a small error should not break the theory built on them.
arxiv-2508-20318:
Bibandhan Poudyal and Gourab Ghoshal modeled what sets off outbreaks of vector borne disease. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with ills carried by mosquitoes. Such outbreaks grow from two linked flows: how people move and how mosquitoes live. The pair cut the map down to a hub and leaf form, which strips the system to its core. From it they derived an equation for outbreak risk.

The math shows risk rests on the ratio of people to vectors and on how time splits between hub and leaf. Even flows of people between spots kept risk at its least. A pile up of vectors can shift the top risk to one spot. Readers get plain rules inside a messy spread system.
arxiv-2508-20518:
Zhaopeng Shi and co-authors achieved a long-chased state of matter in 2025: a Bose-Einstein condensate made of molecules. Polar molecules, with their strong electric dipoles, are prized for quantum model, but molecule samples usually destroy themselves through near-universal two-body collision losses before they can condense. The team worked with ground-state sodium-rubidium molecules and tamed the losses with a dual microwave shielding method, dressing the molecules so collisions turn non-destructive. Then cooled them by evaporation with high efficiency.

Crucially, the dipole-dipole contact between the molecules could be tuned, and tuning proved needed to reaching condensation. With that knob the authors explored distinct regimes of the condensate: a normal gas phase and a quantum droplet phase, where the dipolar attraction balances into self-bound droplets. The result opens test access to quantum matter ruled by strong, long-range, directional forces.
arxiv-2508-21418:
Gernot Fiala and a large team of co-authors propose standard tissue maps as metadata for whole slide image archives. Their paper from twenty twenty-five addresses a bottleneck in digital pathology. Slide scans pile into the millions, yet no standard says what each slide holds. Picking cohorts for AI training still leans on hand checks. Their maps describe slide content in a shared syntax.

Three layers stack the facts: the source, the tissue type, and the disease changes. Each layer tags slide segments with set classes. AI extraction fills the maps from the scans themselves. A live archive demo shows search gains from the added metadata. Training sets can then be built faster, with better balance and aim. The standard claims reach across cancer work and many other slide-based fields.
arxiv-2509-00418:
Miklos Eper and Szilard Szabo study rank three representations of Painlevé systems in 2025, focusing on their Dolbeault structure and spectral correspondence. Painlevé systems are special differential equations whose solutions define new functions of wide use in physics. Their representation spaces carry rich geometry in several complex structures at once.

The authors prove a holomorphic symplectic isomorphism between the rank two and rank three representation spaces in the Dolbeault structure. Explicit descriptions of the corresponding elliptic fibrations are given. Combined with a de Rham description from a prior part, the moduli spaces are shown to be hyperKähler isometric to each other. Such dualities can transfer hard problems between ranks.
arxiv-2509-00718:
Ananda Prakash Verma, writing alone, builds theory for an Exam Readiness Index. The index is a single score from zero to one hundred. It sums up how ready a learner is for a high-stakes exam. The score stays interpretable and actionable by design. It is also blueprint-aware, so it respects the exam's topic plan.

Verma builds the index from six signals. The signals are mastery, coverage, retention, pace, volatility, and endurance. They come from practice tests and mock exams. He states axioms for each part and for the whole. He proves the composite is monotone and stable. Drift stays bounded when blueprint weights change. A unique best linear composite exists under convex design limits. Empirical study is left to future work.
arxiv-2509-00818:
Qi-Ming Wu leads five authors in total, with Ye-Wei Mao, Lin Lin, Hu Zou, and Shu-Ting Wang, in analyzing H II regions in the spiral galaxy NGC 2403. H II regions are ionized nebulae where stars form, serving as laboratories for star formation and photoionization and as tracers of their host galaxy's evolution.

Wu and his co-authors combine spectra from a 2.16 meter telescope at the National Astronomical Observatories of China with published data, and add photoionization modeling to diagnose the emission lines. They estimate parameters such as metallicity and ionization parameter, infer evolution stages for the regions, and show how distinct spectral features respond to specific parameters. The work offers guidance for using emission-line diagnostics on nearby and distant galaxies.
arxiv-2509-01018:
Matthew Varona leads a team of seven authors on visualization literacy. This field studies the skills needed to engage with charts and graphs. The report surveys the current literature in depth. It aims to give a comprehensive overview of the field. The term itself remains ambiguous across studies, the team notes.

Their taxonomy organizes the field into themes and research categories. Literacy is pinned down by context: domain, scenario, and audience. Skills fall under consumption, construction, critique, and connection. Work is grouped into five categories. They are ontology, assessment, mechanisms, populiteracy, and intervention. For each, key trends and open challenges are named. The report shows how advances in one area inform the others.
arxiv-2509-01518:
When an electron beam strikes a material, it can emit light. Most such light comes from direct hits by the beam's fast electrons. Sven Ebel, N. Asger Mortensen, and Sergii Morozov explore a gentler route. Here, electrons made in the substrate do the exciting instead. Color centers in diamond serve as hardy local probes of that indirect light.

The team maps how the indirect light spreads across several shapes and substrates. Photon tests show the emitters sync more strongly at reduced currents. The authors propose using that effect to extract the tiny currents the emitters feel. Currents as low as a tenth of a picoampere could be estimated. The approach promises probing of delicate emitters with little harm. It could serve work inside luminescence microscopes.
arxiv-2509-01918:
Nicolas Andruskiewitsch and Francois Dumas study the algebra of the super Jordan plane, a noncommutative structure with graded signs. Noncommutative means the order of multiplication matters, and super adds a sign rule for odd parts. The structure was introduced by Angiono, Heckenberger, and Andruskiewitsch himself. Their approach embeds the classic Jordan plane inside it as a subalgebra.

They prove the super plane is super-prime, a graded version of having no zero divisors in a strong sense. Its ring of fractions, where division is allowed, turns out super-simple and super-artinian, both strong finiteness traits. Groups of symmetries are computed for both plain algebra maps and braided Hopf maps. The embedding drives each step of the argument.
arxiv-2509-02018:
Stanley Mugisha, Rashid Kisitu, Francis Komakech, and Excellence Favor build a camera based monitor for preterm infants in low resource wards. Preterm birth drives newborn deaths, above all where advanced intensive care is scarce. Watching sleep, wake, and crying states now relies on manual checks or skin sensors that can harm fragile skin. Their system runs a compact neural model on a small single board computer.

The shrunk model, cut down by quantization to save memory, spots sleep and crying states with high accuracy. Tests on public newborn image sets beat larger rivals once cost is weighed. Bigger networks gain little accuracy but run too slowly for live edge use. Secure wireless alerts link the device to clinical staff. The design favors cheap, scalable monitoring for constrained wards.
arxiv-2509-02118:
Hannah Elfner summarizes theory progress in heavy ion physics as presented at the Quark Matter 2025 conference. Heavy ion collisions recreate extreme matter to probe quantum chromodynamics, the theory of strong interactions. Her write-up records the summary talk on theory activities for the community. A personally selected set of parallel session results anchors the report.

Progress is reported across three areas: bulk dynamics with initial state modeling, hard probes like jets and heavy flavor, and the phase diagram with its observables. Electromagnetic probes join the second area coverage. Major achievements in each area are conveyed with an eye to future directions. As a conference summary, the piece maps where the field stands and where it heads next.
arxiv-2509-02318:
Márton Guba and Tibor Höltzl present a 2025 computational chemistry paper on simulating catalysts for electrochemical reactions, where voltage at an electrode drives the chemistry. Older tools assume the charge storage at a surface stays fixed as voltage changes, which real catalysts often break.

Their method, called mu-GCP-K, drops that fixed assumption and lets charge storage vary freely with voltage. They test it on graphene, a single sheet of carbon atoms, and recover both surface charge and varying capacitance. The work also stresses accurate stability checks for reaction intermediates, the short-lived species formed mid-reaction, during carbon dioxide electroreduction. Better voltage handling should make catalyst screening more trustworthy.
arxiv-2509-02418:
