Yilang Zhang, Bingcong Li, and Georgios B. Giannakis present a 2025 meta-learning paper on adapting prior knowledge to a new task from very few examples. Fast adaptation often relies on preconditioning, which reshapes the loss surface so training converges in a few steps.

Simple linear preconditioners assume a quadratic loss shape and struggle with complex geometry. The authors instead learn a distance-generating function, realised by a neural network whose output is guaranteed to define a genuine distance. That function induces a nonlinear mirror map able to follow varied loss shapes. Theory proves convergence for their method and, more broadly, for preconditioning-based meta-learning, at a standard rate. Few-shot tests show stronger accuracy and faster per-task adaptation, cutting the steps each new task needs.
arxiv-2509-02618:
Jiayi Qin and twenty-one co-authors present a 2025 materials science paper on patterning epitaxial oxide films, single-crystal layers prized for electronic and magnetic functions. Standard patterning etches the film, risking damage, undercutting, and extra cost.

Their dual-lift-off method avoids etching entirely. A sacrificial layer of amorphous strontium aluminate acts like a photoresist that survives high growth temperatures. After the first lift-off clears the resist pattern, the oxide film is deposited, then the sacrificial layer is dissolved to lift away unwanted oxide. Patterns matched the resist shape closely. Demonstrations cover a ferromagnetic manganite film and a ferroelectric bismuth ferrite film. The authors describe the route as simple, precise, flexible, and cheaper than etching.
arxiv-2509-02818:
Grigory Koroteev wrote a 2025 solo materials informatics paper on improving machine learning predictions of the density of states, the count of electron energy levels available in a material. Graph neural networks predict that density, and its projected variants, but sharp features are often missed.

Koroteev extends the idea of van Hove singularities, points where the density of states spikes, into a quasi form usable as prior information for learning models. Instead of computing the density exactly, the method works with model estimates and adds a post-processing step guided by that extra information. Regularisation, described as close in spirit to Fisher information weighting, redistributes what the model knows about the system. The author reports significantly better prediction quality, with the gain likened to higher-order singularity effects.
arxiv-2509-02918:
Midhat Urooj and 4 co-authors proposed a 2025 method for grading diabetic retinopathy, an eye disease that can blind people with diabetes. Their system, KG-DG, aims to keep working when photos come from a new clinic or camera. Models often fail after such shifts in image style.

The design mixes vision transformers, software that reads images in patches, with expert rules drawn from clinical knowledge of lesions. It also uses maps of retinal blood vessels and blends both streams by confidence. Tests across four public photo sets showed gains over plain vision models. Rule-based parts alone did surprisingly well, which suggests the clinical features steady the system, not just explain it.
arxiv-2509-03218:
Yufan Luo wrote a 2025 number theory paper on a refined counting quantity for Galois cohomology. Galois groups encode the symmetries of number fields, the number systems built from rationals with algebraic numbers added. An Euler-Poincaré characteristic summarizes the sizes of a group's cohomology, its higher algebraic invariants, in one alternating total.

Luo studies a second partial version of that total for modules over a Galois group tied to primes outside a chosen set. Earlier formulas needed a side condition on the module's size, which he drops. By adjoining extra primes, chosen away from any thin prescribed set, he obtains an explicit formula. Applications concern how the Galois group can be presented with generators and relations. He also builds counterexamples to a dimension conjecture about deformation rings.
arxiv-2509-03818:
Sherwan Jalal Abdullah and four co-authors devote a 2025 research paper to a drone-based platform for measuring cellular network performance from the air. Drive testing coverage on the ground is slow, labour-heavy, and sometimes hazardous. Crowdsourced data, the usual alternative, fails in rural areas where few people live and terrain is difficult.

Their drone platform carries an onboard computer and a commercial cellular modem, recording radio signals and end-to-end service metrics in flight. Mapping tools and statistics turn the logs into coverage observations. Signal power improves at higher altitude, thanks to clearer line of sight. Signal quality degrades at the same time, because interference from neighbouring cells grows. Across most of the tested area, quality stayed acceptable, with adequate throughput both ways and satisfactory round-trip times. One caution stands out: a strong signal reading for a cell does not guarantee consistent coverage across space.
arxiv-2509-04018:
FPC-VLA, a robot control framework that adds a supervising model to a vision-language-action system, occupies a 2025 research paper by Yifan Yang and ten co-authors. A single end-to-end model, mapping images and instructions to actions, is flexible on open-ended tasks. What they lack is foresight: mechanisms to anticipate failure and recover when a grasp goes wrong.

The supervisor evaluates whether planned actions are viable, asking vision-language queries about the scene, and drafts corrections when risks appear. It is trained efficiently, without manual labelling of failures. A dual-stream fusion module refines actions by drawing on past predictions, so earlier judgements inform the current motion. Evaluation spans the SIMPLER and LIBERO simulators and three robot bodies: WidowX, Google Robot, and Franka arms. The framework beats leading models under zero-shot and fine-tuned regimes alike. Real robots succeed on diverse, long-horizon tasks.
arxiv-2509-04218:
Yejing Zhan and five co-authors show how a future space network could measure the universe's expansion without any light signal in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Gravitational waves from merging black holes carry distance information, while light from the host galaxy gives redshift, the stretching of light by expansion. Pairing both yields the Hubble constant, but spotting the right galaxy is usually hard. Three planned space detectors, LISA, Taiji, and TianQin, would locate sources with extreme precision when working as a network.

That sharp aim alone can single out one host galaxy, making the event a bright siren without a light counterpart. Five population models for massive black hole pairs were folded in. The best cases reach galaxies quite far away and pin expansion to under one percent.
arxiv-2509-04418:
Alessio Squarcini and two co-authors add a long-missed entropic term to the physics of wetting in a 2025 research paper. Wetting describes how a liquid film binds to a wall, and its binding potential summarizes the forces holding the interface in place. Standard theory used a mean-field contribution alone. The authors derive an additional Casimir-like term from the many microscopic arrangements hiding behind one average interface shape, starting from a microscopic Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson model, a standard energy description.

A boundary integral method organizes the new term into a ladder of fading contributions. Its decay differs sharply between first-order and critical wetting, switching form at the tricritical point. Including the term preserves the overall phase diagram but radically changes fluctuation predictions.
arxiv-2509-04518:
Dhruvi Paprunia and two co-authors teach small language models to use external tools accurately through reinforcement learning in a 2025 research paper. Tool use lets AI agents fetch data and call functions, but small models often fumble the structured output, wrong tool choice, or sloppy parameters. Their method applies Group Relative Policy Optimization, which scores groups of candidate answers against each other. A designed reward system pays for valid JSON formatting, the right tool choice, and careful parameter use.

Training stayed computationally cheap while tool-use capability rose significantly in their tests. The work matters most for resource-constrained deployments, where giant models are impractical. Function calling, the backbone of agent systems, becomes accessible to modest hardware.
arxiv-2509-04618:
Ground-state energies are well known to be hard to estimate, even for quantum computers. Gerard McCaul examines a newer method for that problem in a solo-authored 2025 paper on Hamiltonian complexity. The method, imaginary-time quantum dynamical emulation, estimates spectral densities, partition functions, and low-lying gaps with minimal coherent control.

McCaul derives scaling and stability rules that show when its estimates can be trusted. He also adds a controlled smoothing that balances bias and variance. The result identifies a practical middle regime, his free snack, where coarse spectral information needs only polynomial resources on near-term hardware.
arxiv-2509-04818:
Turbulence inside molecular clouds helps regulate how stars form, but observers must infer it from spectral data. Jayashree Narayan, lead author with two co-authors, test how carbon monoxide lines affect that inference in a 2025 paper. Earlier methods got three-dimensional velocity spread from observations while assuming the gas was optically thin.

The authors post-process a chemo-dynamical cloud run with a radiative transfer code. That builds spectral cubes for two carbon monoxide lines. Smoothing isolates turbulence in the resulting maps. They find the measured velocity spread needs a correction factor. They also measure how opacity and chemistry shift the result.
arxiv-2509-05118:
Thick sprays, where droplets occupy a non-negligible volume, are widely modelled by an Euler-Vlasov system in engineering. Zhe Chen derives that model formally from a more basic kinetic description in a solo-authored 2025 applied mathematics paper. A specific scaling takes the Boltzmann-Enskog system for the dispersed phase toward the engineering equations.

Beyond validating the kinetic-fluid model, Chen identifies higher-order corrections to the viscous force. Those corrections scale with the volume of the dispersed phase and are normally neglected through a volume fraction function. The work builds on an earlier formal passage for thin sprays in binary mixtures.
arxiv-2509-05418:
Solving equations whose answers are very sensitive to noise is regularised by Robert Plato in a solo 2025 mathematics paper. The setting is Banach spaces, general spaces where size is measured but angles need not exist. The focus is solutions described by a logarithmic source condition, typical of severely ill-posed problems like running heat flow backwards.

Plato sets out the operator logarithm framework and proves rates for a family of regularisation schemes. The family includes an iterated version of Lavrentiev's method and a method based on an abstract evolution equation. Both advance choice of the tuning parameter and data-driven choice are covered. An example built on the integration operator shows a function meeting that condition.
arxiv-2509-05518:
Ions gain energy across their magnetic field lines when fluctuations are sharp in space and time, Alfred Mallet and four co-authors explain in a 2025 plasma physics paper. Heating of this kind matters in turbulence and in reconnection, where magnetic fields snap into new shapes.

The authors study one ion meeting a localised electromagnetic fluctuation and derive a general formula for its energy change. An exponential cutoff depends on the fluctuation's timescale, and the outcome spreads energy in both perpendicular and parallel directions. Applied to Alfvénic turbulence and reconnection settings, the framework unifies earlier models of stochastic heating, cyclotron heating, and reconnection heating. One theory now covers mechanisms long treated separately.
arxiv-2509-05618:
Black holes born in the infant universe and evaporating before the first elements formed are constrained by Quan-feng Wu and Xun-Jie Xu in a 2025 cosmology paper. Their Hawking radiation would have disturbed big bang nucleosynthesis, the process that set the amounts of light elements, leaving measurable traces.

Working through the intermediate steps analytically, the authors find an effect needs a mass above a stated threshold, higher than some earlier studies reported. Sensitivity rises steeply just above that threshold, peaks, then falls, and current element measurements cap the initial share of such black holes across the studied mass range. Their code is public for use with updated nuclear and cosmological inputs.
arxiv-2509-05718:
Charts are sorted by vision-language models much as humans sort them, except for chart type itself, in a 2025 study by Péter Ferenc Gyarmati and three co-authors. Shared perception of visual material is a base requirement for useful human and AI collaboration on data displays.

Thirteen diverse models classified scientific visualisations from the picture alone by purpose, encoding, and dimensionality, against expert labels from a human-centred typology. Purpose and dimensionality were often right, while specific encodings like bar or node-link caused trouble. Larger models did not always win. Earlier work found these models lean on text cues over visual analysis, and the authors urge human supervision in visualisation tools.
arxiv-2509-05818:
Helping patients actually understand their medical notes is the aim of NoteAid-Chatbot, presented in a 2025 paper led by Won Seok Jang with nine co-authors. Many patients cannot join fully in their care because records are hard to read. The chatbot teaches through conversation rather than handing over a simplified printout.

It runs on a small LLaMA language model trained in two stages. The first stage uses synthetic dialogues built from teaching strategies. The second uses reinforcement learning scored on simulated discharge talks, with no human-labeled data. Judges found clear, relevant, well-structured teaching even though those traits were never directly trained. In a Turing-style test it outdid non-expert humans. The authors argue cheap reinforcement learning can shape small, focused chatbots for open-ended conversation.
arxiv-2509-06318:
A quantum computer can be attacked through its neighbors' crosstalk, demonstrates Devon Campbell in a 2025 paper on the Quantum Rowhammer. Superconducting processors leak residual coupling between qubits, and cloud services increasingly share machines among tenants. Campbell's attack uses only ordinary X and CNOT gates, no pulse-level access, on IBM's 127-qubit Eagle processors.

Targeted hammering injects localized phase errors confined to the attack cycle, with near fifty percent flip rates under Hadamard-basis probing. A full lattice sweep shows reproducible corruption within two coupling hops of the target and rapid recovery in later benign cycles. Those properties support a prime-and-probe covert channel between tenants. The author argues hardware isolation and scheduler-aware defenses must arrive before multi-tenant quantum computing becomes standard.
arxiv-2509-06518:
Uneven layer sizes inside a language model are tested by Andrei Baroian and one co-author in a 2025 machine learning paper. Standard transformers give every layer the same width, ignoring that shallow and deep layers may do different jobs. Earlier layer-wise scaling work suggested redistributing width, but options were few.

Three new layouts are introduced. Crown, Frame, and Reverse shift feed-forward widths and attention head counts across depth using simple interpolation between two or three anchor points, all before training begins. Every variant is trained under the same budget of parameters and data tokens, in the first systematic comparison of its kind. All reach losses similar to each other and beat an equal-cost uniform model, with little slowdown in training. The authors frame this as an early step and call for tests at much larger scales.
arxiv-2509-06818:
Custom images containing several specific people, each keeping the right face, are the goal of a 2025 image generation paper led by Yufeng Cheng, with five co-authors. Humans are acutely sensitive to faces, and models that customize images often mix identities up when several reference photos are given. Scaling to many identities has lagged.

Their framework, UMO, recasts multi-identity generation as a global assignment problem: references and generated faces are matched many-to-many, and a matching reward drives reinforcement learning on the diffusion model. A scalable dataset with multiple reference images, part synthetic and part real, supports training, and a new metric measures identity confusion directly. Experiments show stronger identity consistency and less confusion across several existing customization methods. The authors report a new state of the art among open-source systems for identity preservation.
arxiv-2509-06918:
Spotting inputs from classes a model never trained on, when the training labels themselves are noisy, is tackled by Tarhib Al Azad and one co-author in a 2025 machine learning paper. Out-of-distribution detection is vital in safety-critical systems. Label noise is known to degrade it, yet principled remedies were lacking.

Simply bolting existing noise-robust methods onto existing detectors does not solve the problem, the authors show. Their framework instead combines loss correction, borrowed from noisy-label learning, with low-rank and sparse decomposition from signal processing. The idea is to clean the training signal while separating the structured part of the data from the corrupted part. On synthetic and real-world datasets, the method significantly beat leading detectors, with the largest advantages under severe label noise. Robust detection under messy training data is the practical payoff.
arxiv-2509-07018:
Jun Gao and Jie Ding present sigma-counting in a 2025 paper on answering counting queries without exposing private data. Many applications ask a database how many items fall inside a range of values that a client picks. If a program answers many such queries, its answers can leak facts about single people in the data.

One common defence adds random noise to each answer, spending from a fixed privacy budget over time. That can cap how many queries are allowed and can blur accuracy. Answers can also break the ordering that nested queries should keep. Sigma-counting instead builds on sigma-algebra, the mathematics of set collections. The authors show their design can sharpen accuracy a great deal while still holding the promised privacy level, even under very many queries.
arxiv-2509-07118:
Rings around planets outside our solar system, called exorings, might be easier to spot than the planets themselves. Rachel Bowens-Rubin and 6 co-authors explore that claim in a 2025 paper. When a cold giant planet wears a ring, reflected light from the ring can outshine the planet in near-infrared light, the part of the spectrum just past red.

The team simulates the NIRCam camera on the James Webb Space Telescope watching two nearby stars, Proxima Centauri and Tau Ceti. Under the best conditions, the camera could spot a ring about 2.8 times the size of Saturn's A ring around a planet at a certain distance. Much larger ring systems could also be within reach. Finding how common such rings are would teach scientists how planetary systems form and change.
arxiv-2509-07318:
Jonathan Quang Tran and 2 co-authors use optimal transport to compare flow fields in a 2025 fluid mechanics paper. Optimal transport is a math framework that measures how much work it takes to reshape one distribution into another. Simple point-by-point distance scores can miss broad shifts in a flow pattern, such as a bubble of separated air growing or shrinking behind a wing.

An autoencoder, a neural network that compresses data, first maps each flow field into a compact latent code. The training aligns plain distances between codes with optimal transport distances between the full fields. Tests use controlled flow past a NACA 0012 airfoil at two angles of attack. A two-dimensional code captures the main regimes, including how far a control suppresses the separation bubble. Consistent readings across both angles suggest the method could grade flow control designs fairly.
arxiv-2509-07718:
Erina Nanyonga and 1 co-author ask in 2025 whether an option on a two-asset portfolio can be hedged by trading only one of the assets. Options are contracts tied to underlying asset values. The classic Black-Scholes argument prices them by delta hedging. That means holding an offsetting position in the underlying asset itself. When that asset is costly to trade, hedging with a cheaper, correlated asset may be smarter.

The portfolio mixes two correlated assets. The hedge uses just one of them. At the extremes, that covers hedging with the right asset and with the wrong one. The authors work on simulated data. They vary trading intervals, the correlation between the assets, and transaction costs. They then compute risk-adjusted values for each choice. The study maps when the cheaper cross-hedge keeps risk at an acceptable level. That is a practical question for traders in costly markets.
arxiv-2509-07818:
Counting the points a surface map leaves unmoved is the subject of a 2025 mathematics paper by Tarik Aougab and 2 co-authors. The maps are pseudo-Anosov homeomorphisms, which stretch and fold a surface in a structured, chaotic way. Knowing how many fixed points such a map must have connects geometry with dynamics.

The authors give a formula estimating that count. When the map is strongly irreducible, the logarithm of the fixed-point count roughly equals its Teichmüller translation length, a measure of how far the map moves shapes. Applications follow, including an inequality linking the volume of a related three-dimensional space to the rank of a homology theory. Results like these tie surface dynamics to the geometry of spaces built from them.
arxiv-2509-08118:
Stars in close pairs can pour matter onto each other, changing both stars' fates, but catching that transfer in action is rare. G. Garcia-Moreno and 6 co-authors hunt for such systems across the Milky Way in a 2025 research paper. They start with stars in the Hertzsprung gap, a short-lived phase between the main sequence and giant stage. The method was inspired by the slow brightening seen before stellar mergers.

Candidate systems had to show hydrogen emission, excess mid-infrared light, and photometric variability together. That filter produced a sample of several dozen candidates. Follow-up data revealed eclipsing binaries, likely binaries, and systems that may host compact companions. The team also published a refined catalogue of bona fide gap stars. Contamination from hot, reddened stars remains the main nuisance. The catalogue should contain a richer share of true mass-transferring pairs for future study.
arxiv-2509-08218:
Indian policy news becomes a readable timeline in PolicyStory, a 2025 tool paper by Aatif Nisar Dar and 2 co-authors. Ordinary news consumption, online or in print, rarely gives a structured, long-run view of a complex policy fight. Articles arrive scattered across outlets and days, and the thread of an issue is easy to lose.

PolicyStory gathers articles from diverse sources, clusters them by topic, and uses open-source language models to build summaries at three levels of depth from the long-run media discussion. A user study found the tool genuinely helped readers understand policy issues. Citizens following land, health, or education reforms could track how a debate evolved instead of meeting it fresh each morning.
arxiv-2509-09018:
Xueyi Wang and colleagues present a personalized sleep prediction model in a 2025 paper. Forecasting sleep can help people and clinicians act early on poor rest. Their AdaST-Sleep model uses sparse data from commercial wearable devices.

Convolutional layers capture interactions between health features, while recurrent layers handle longer time patterns. A domain classifier helps the model generalize across different subjects. Experiments vary input windows from three to eleven days and forecast windows up to nine days. The best setup uses seven days in and one day out. The model beats four baselines and tracks both level and daily swings of sleep scores.
arxiv-2509-09118:
Tianlu Zheng and 5 co-authors advance CLIP for text based person retrieval in a 2025 paper. Retrieving a person from a text description needs fine grained matching. Large annotated person image text data are scarce, and global contrastive learning can lose local detail.

A data pipeline uses multimodal models to filter and caption web images, yielding WebPerson, five million high quality person pairs. Their GA-DMS framework masks noisy text tokens using gradient attention scores. Masked token prediction forces the model to learn informative tokens. Together, data and model reach state of the art results across multiple benchmarks for person retrieval.
arxiv-2509-09618:
Marvin Schnubel and 1 co-author compute electron and photon structure functions to second order in 2025. The work is a step in exact quantum electrodynamics. These functions say how likely an electron is to be found with a share of the energy of a larger particle. They are also called lepton parton laws. Getting them in full at two loops was an open analytic task.

The pair cut the problem down to a set of master integrals. They solve those with differential equations. The result gives plain formulas for five such laws. The laws cover electrons and photons found inside electrons and photons. It also covers positrons found inside electrons. Checks against one-loop work all line up. So do checks against a recent theory study. Such laws feed the precision of collider forecasts.
arxiv-2509-09918:
Seyed Moein Abtahi and 1 co-author present WALL in 2025, a web tool that pairs a code scanner with language models to clean up software automatically. Growing projects collect thousands of small defects, and finding, fixing, and grading fixes by hand eats developer time. WALL chains three parts together: one pulls issues out of files with SonarQube, one rewrites the code, and one compares the rewrite against the original.

Trials covered 563 files carrying more than seven thousand flagged issues. Mixing a cheap model with an advanced one cut costs while raising the share of successful revisions, the authors report. Human effort fell without quality slipping. Planned upgrades add open models and remove the human checkpoint entirely, aiming at fully automatic quality care.
arxiv-2509-10018:
Hailong Yang and 3 co-authors design a multi-agent system that can use powerful cloud language models without leaking private data in a 2025 privacy paper. Agents that collaborate in natural language often send raw task material to servers anyone could inspect. Their system, GAMA, splits each agent's world in two: sensitive material stays in a private space, and only scrubbed, anonymised versions travel to the public side where the big models live.

Scrubbing always costs meaning, so two repair modules ride along. One restores domain knowledge from explicit rules, the other uses a disproof step to catch logical slips the anonymisation introduced. Across general question answering sets, a public leakage benchmark, and two privacy-focused custom sets, GAMA beat the existing baselines the authors compared against.
arxiv-2509-10118:
Jingyuan Zhou and 3 co-authors build stability proofs for networks of learned controllers in a 2025 control paper. Linked systems such as platoons need string stability. That is the promise that a wobble at the front fades down the line. Neural controllers perform well in such settings. They arrive as black boxes, though. So the promise had no formal backing.

Their frame joins two tools. One is a discrete-time form of scalable input-to-state stability. The other is neural network checking. Together they build certificates for the learned system. They then verify those certificates in a robust way. The check allows for gaps between true dynamics and the learned copy. Theory and methods stretch the pipeline to large systems. Fleet operators gain more than a controller. They gain a proof-shaped pledge that shocks die out.
arxiv-2509-10218:
Liangliang Yuan and Shuanggen Jin examine the faint electric field that helps ions escape from a planet's upper air in this 2025 space physics paper. That field, called ambipolar, is a key driver of atmospheric loss and shapes whether rocky planets stay habitable. Earlier comparisons between theory and measurements mostly left out the flow of heat carried by electrons.

Adding heat flow to the theory changes the picture. Matched against voltage data from the Endurance sounding rocket, the fuller theory shows the expected signs of heat-flow influence. The authors then look across rocky planets and argue that uneven ion temperatures, which strengthen the heat-flow effect, can explain the oddly large voltage drop measured in the upper air of Venus.
arxiv-2509-10418:
Błażej Ruba and Bowen Yang prove a bulk-boundary correspondence for stabilizer states in this 2025 mathematical physics paper. Stabilizer states are a structured class of quantum states central to error correction. The authors work in any spatial dimension, using modules over Laurent polynomial rings, and attach to each translation-invariant state cut by a half-space a module of boundary operators.

Those boundary modules turn out to be quasi-symplectic, objects of independent interest that force the authors into algebraic L-theory with awkward, non-projective modules. In one spatial dimension their results resolve a standing conjecture: every two-dimensional stabilizer state is captured by an abelian anyon model whose boundary can be gapped. The techniques reach beyond two dimensions too, into topics such as fractons.
arxiv-2509-10918:
Diffusion image generators are slow. Attention scales quadratically, and that is the bottleneck. Wenbo Lu and three co-authors trim the cost with ToMA, in this 2025 paper. Earlier token merging methods cut theoretical operations. They used GPU-hostile tricks, like sorting and scattered writes. Real speedups evaporated next to optimized attention libraries.

ToMA redesigns merging around the hardware. Choosing which tokens to keep becomes a submodular optimization. Diversity is what it favors. Merging and unmerging run as attention-like matrix operations. The GPU loves those. The method exploits locality in the latent image. It also exploits redundancy between steps, to skip work. On SDXL and Flux models, generation latency fell by about a quarter. Quality barely changed. Prior methods were beaten. The contribution is a bridge between efficiency on paper and efficiency on silicon.
arxiv-2509-11218:
Johann Schmidt and 3 co-authors rebuild the spatial transformer idea on modern foundations in this 2025 paper. Rotated or scaled objects hide the shape cues a classifier needs. A model for high-stakes use should resist such changes, explain any correction it makes, and admit when an input is ambiguous. Strictly symmetric architectures guarantee some of this but limit flexibility and cost heavily.

Their framework uses a transformer to estimate the affine change applied to an input image. The change is broken into readable parts and fitted under adjustable geometric limits, which avoids the degenerate warps that used to destabilize training. Sharing weights with the classifier keeps the cost low. Tests on insect and medical images beat rivals under varied transformations.
arxiv-2509-11418:
Runming Li, Yue Yao, and Robert Harper report a machine-checked formalization. This 2025 programming languages paper covers synthetic Tait computability. That method proves facts about type theories, like canonicity and normalization. It does so by placing gluing constructions inside a modal type theory.

The team mechanized the method in Istari, a proof assistant. Istari's equality reflection spares much transport bookkeeping. The team built a reusable library for phase distinction. Modalities are in it. Extension types and strict glue types are in it too. Two case studies use the library. One builds a canonicity model for dependent type theory. The other builds a Kripke-style model for a cost-aware framework. The paper proofs carried over nearly as written, now machine-checked.
arxiv-2509-11518:
Martin Kološ and David Kofroň study charged particles around a black hole with a magnetic field. This 2025 general relativity paper uses a toroidal current loop as the field's source. The loop lies in the equatorial plane. The black hole is a non-rotating Schwarzschild one. An exact relativistic solution describes the field.

The authors map stable and unstable orbits, by analysis and by computer. In the attracting setup, particles pile up near the loop. Their shared currents oppose the loop's own field. Toroidal belts form, much like planetary radiation belts. General relativity sets a floor for where belts can form. The innermost stable circular orbit marks it. A loop of zero width would create an unphysical blowup, so real models need finite width.
arxiv-2509-11818:
Taichi Aida and Danushka Bollegala make word meanings both readable and measurable. This 2025 natural language processing paper treats semantic change detection. The task tracks how a word's meaning shifts between corpora. Interpretable embedding axes tend to perform worse. Strong performers tend to be opaque.

Their method is SCDTour. It tours an embedding's interpretable axes in a chosen order. Axes get merged along the way. Two things are weighed. One is how similar axes are. The other is how much each axis adds to semantic change. The merged set keeps detection performance high. Interpretability stays high too. It matched or beat the full-dimensional embeddings in tests. Fewer, cleaner axes yield a more refined set of word senses.
arxiv-2509-11918:
Andreas Gsponer and 7 co-authors directly gauge how fast charge carriers drift in a silicon carbide detector material in a 2025 instrumentation paper. Silicon carbide tolerates high heat and strong fields, which makes it attractive for radiation-hard particle detectors. Its readout electronics have bottlenecked drift studies until now.

A new high-frequency readout board with very wide bandwidth was built for the work. Transient current signals from a small silicon carbide diode were recorded under ultraviolet laser, alpha particle, and high-energy proton hits. In all three cases, electron and hole drift split clearly in the signals. That split allowed drift velocities to be read off as a function of electric field, directly measured for the first time. A full simulation setup matched the measured data well.
arxiv-2509-12018:
In impulse control, a manager steps in with costly pushes at chosen moments. The pushes are discrete, not a smooth stream. Haoyang Cao and two co-authors give that problem a randomized form in 2025. The random form turns out to be softer. It can be proved sound, and it can be learned.

The solution of the randomized problem is a fixed point of an operator. That operator joins a smoothed nonlocal part with a smoothed stopping part. The solution also obeys a semi-linear Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. A parallel scheme built on a Poisson compound measure gives a verification theorem. An iterative argument then proves a solution exists. So the problem is well-defined and unique. As the randomization fades, solutions move toward the classic one. The proof's iteration doubles as an offline reinforcement learning method. It converges geometrically and is tested on a standard example.
arxiv-2509-12118:
Ben Maybee and 4 co-authors ask how patchy soil moisture affects large storms in West Africa in a 2025 paper. Mesoscale convective systems are the big storm complexes that bring much Sahel rainfall, including extremes. Earlier observations suggested that dry patches about two hundred kilometers wide can strengthen mature storms.

The team ran seventy-eight experiments with the Unified Model weather code, starting each run from soil moisture fields filtered to different spatial scales. Removing all smaller-scale variation cut peak storm counts by about a quarter. Keeping small-scale patches preserved most storm initiation, so the drop was smaller. Their analysis traces the chain from surface fluxes through the lower air layer to storm environments. Cloud-free slots letting in more sunlight also played a role before storms formed.
arxiv-2509-12218:
Fractional calculus studies derivatives of non-integer order, tools for processes whose present depends on their whole past. In a solo 2025 paper, Vasily E. Tarasov defines a parametric family of such operators, where the change in a function is measured against the change in a second, guiding function rather than against plain position.

Tarasov proves basic properties of these integrals and derivatives, shows how they are written on a finite interval, and establishes the fundamental theorems linking the two operations. Special cases recover known operators. He closes with readings of the derivatives as models for processes with memory in applied mathematics.
arxiv-2509-12318:
When a star wanders too close to a black hole in a young cluster, tides can shred it in a small-scale echo of the disruptions seen near galactic centers. Sara Rastello and three co-authors simulate these micro tidal disruptions in 2025 with direct N-body calculations of dense young star clusters.

Most events, they find, grow out of messy few-body encounters rather than clean two-body passes. The inferred cosmic rate runs to a few hundred per cubic gigaparsec per year. Upcoming sky surveys could catch tens per year, and the gravitational-wave signals peak in a frequency band targeted by planned space detectors.
arxiv-2509-12518:
Cuffless blood pressure from a wrist light sensor often fails on a new wearer. The model was trained on strangers, and the new wrist is different. Zequan Liang and six co-authors attack that gap in 2025. They use curriculum-adversarial learning on multi-wavelength pulse data. The data is split strictly by subject. No person appears in both training and testing.

Training first learns the easier job, sorting hypertension. Then it graduates to estimating the pressure values themselves. At the same time, an adversarial term hides subject identity. That forces the features to describe physiology, not persons. Fusing several wavelengths beats any single channel. Removing either training trick hurts the scores.
arxiv-2509-12818:
Maximilian Ilse, Harshita Sharma and 13 co-authors study in 2025 how more data helps image models trained for chest X-rays. Web models learn from huge sets, but medical sets are much smaller, so the gains from scale in clinics were not well known.

They kept training two known encoders on up to three and a half million chest films from one site, with fixed tests for disease signs, tubes and lines, and report writing. One encoder scaled best for disease signs, the other for tubes. Mixed training with reports and clear labels helped most, and for some tasks a small in-house set beat open models.
arxiv-2509-13118:
Yvain Bruned and Paul Laubie ask in 2025 whether a set between multi-indices and rooted trees can encode base steps for numeric schemes. Trees drive B-series for solvers and rough expansions for singular noisy equations. For scalar cases, multi-indices work with less bulk.

A negative result answers the hunt in part. No set that fits both trees and indices can encode the steps when size differs from one, aside from trees alone. The naive natural path is thus closed. The broader hunt stays open, but any new set must take a less direct form. The bound clarifies a core counting choice.
arxiv-2509-13218:
J. Cha, J. Lee and two co-authors weight training samples in 2025 for rare and skewed data with FOSSIL. Rare disease images, gene sets, and disaster data share scarcity and skew. Past fixes treat one facet alone and stay fragile.

FOSSIL joins class balance, difficulty staging, augmentation penalties, and warmup in one clear formula. Regret grounds give theory backing, unlike pure heuristics. Gains over plain, staged, and meta baselines hold on fake and real sets. No architecture change is needed. The single formula stays readable, which aids tuning in scarce-data work.
arxiv-2509-13418:
Julianne Goddard, Isaac Shlosman and Emilio Romano-Diaz model in 2025 how jetted Seyfert galaxies evolve from early times to today in zoom simulations. Mechanical and thermal black hole feedback shapes central galaxies in mid-mass halos. Paper one covered end states; this work tracks evolution.

Black holes seed early and mid epochs and drive jets along spin axes. Intake rates span wide fractions of the Eddington cap. Jets and over-pressured bubbles suppress star birth, cut gas shares, and reshape bulge to disk ratios. Outflows enrich halo gas and stir vorticity. Halo gas mixes outflow, bubbles, and cosmic inflow. Gas balance and hole growth self-limit.
arxiv-2509-13618:
Chang-geun Oh and four co-authors explore quantum geometry in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Beyond a material's energy bands, its quantum wavefunctions have a geometry, measured here by a quantum distance, and the team asks whether that hidden geometry can steer magnetism in solids.

Within a standard approximation for spin response, they split magnetic susceptibility into a plain part set by the energy bands and a geometric part set by the quantum distance. In a quadratic band-touching semimetal, tuning the geometry alone, with the spectrum held fixed, flips the system between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic order. Applied to iron pnictides and kagome lattices, the geometric part proves decisive for their known magnetic states.
arxiv-2509-13718:
Minho Cho, Seunghun Lee, and Frédéric Meunier prove colorful selection theorems in a 2025 combinatorics paper on oriented matroids, abstract structures that capture the sign patterns of geometric configurations. The colorful Carathéodory theorem says that, given several color classes of points all containing the origin in their convex hulls, one point per color can be chosen whose hull still contains it.

The team give a short proof of the conic version of that theorem for oriented matroids, a case an earlier sweeping generalization had missed. Their tool is a common generalization of Sperner's lemma and Meshulam's lemma from combinatorial topology, possibly useful elsewhere. The same approach yields a new colorful theorem about topes, the maximal sign patterns of a matroid.
arxiv-2509-13818:
Zheng-an Wang and thirteen co-authors build a hybrid quantum-classical system for credit risk in a 2025 paper. Lenders in inclusive finance often judge applicants with very few past records. That is a few-shot problem, where conventional models starve. Quantum machine learning promises new leverage. It must first survive today's noisy hardware.

Their workflow first runs an ensemble of classical models. Logistic regression, random forests, and gradient boosting engineer the features and shrink the data down. A quantum neural network then acts as the core classifier. It is trained with the parameter-shift rule. On a real credit dataset of a few hundred samples, the quantum model beat classical benchmarks in simulation. A run on a superconducting quantum processor via a cloud platform scored even better.
arxiv-2509-14218:
James Leiner, Robin Dunn and Aaditya Ramdas address inference from data gathered step by step in 2025, as in bandit systems that favour options that have paid off so far. Standard methods can fail there because early choices skew later data. A second snag is a working model that does not match reality.

Leiner and colleagues define the target cleanly as the best fit under a fixed evaluation policy, even when rewards shift over time. Their method then gives valid inference for a broad class of estimators, called M-estimators, fitted on such adaptive data with a possibly wrong model. A flexible way to steady the variance sits at the core. The result extends trustworthy confidence statements to a setting where both adaptivity and model error are present.
arxiv-2509-14318:
Ian J. M. Crossfield and ten co-authors map in 2025 where sulfur dioxide should appear in giant planet atmospheres. The James Webb Space Telescope has found sulfur chemistry on such planets. Sulfur dioxide can signal light driven chemistry, metal content and planet history.

Their model grid spans wide ranges of metal content and temperature for planet atmospheres. It charts a shoreline, the border where sulfur dioxide becomes abundant enough to detect. Abundance depends strongly on metal content, temperature and the carbon to oxygen ratio. It depends only weakly on harsh high energy light and barely on internal heat. The map tells observers which giant planets are worth targeting when hunting sulfur gases with limited telescope time.
arxiv-2509-14418:
Mark G. Orr and three co-authors argue in 2025 that attitude research should use more hard maths beside computer simulation. Attitude theory studies how beliefs and evaluations hang together and change. Its formal predictions have come mostly from running simulation models.

Using the causal attitude network model as an example, the authors show analysis and simulation as partners, not rivals. They then present graph dynamical systems as a broad maths framework for network models of attitudes. A second theory, attitudes as constraint satisfaction, illustrates how the framework generates precise testable claims. Other sciences treat proof and simulation as standard partners. The note urges psychology to do the same for sharper theory.
arxiv-2509-14618:
Sachin Ballal and Ardra A N study hypergraphs built from subgroups of the cyclic group in 2025, comparing an intersection hypergraph with a co-maximal hypergraph. A hypergraph lets one edge join many vertices at once, suiting subgroup overlap patterns. The two constructions look different at first glance.

The authors prove the intersection and co-maximal hypergraphs of a finite abelian group are isomorphic, so study can focus on one of them. Structural properties follow: diameter, girth and chromatic number are examined. Characterisations describe when the hypergraph is a hypertree or a star, and planarity results separate drawable cases from non planar ones. Subgroup combinatorics gains a compact graph language with computable invariants.
arxiv-2509-14718:
Zihao Feng and six co-authors introduce ToolSample in 2025, dual dynamic sampling with curriculum learning for reinforcement learning based tool training of language models. Easy samples flood tool training and give diminishing value as skill grows. Generic dynamic sampling ignores tool learning multi task structure and fine grained rewards.

Their DSCL framework samples by reward, favouring cases that still teach something, and orders learning as a curriculum across interdependent sub tasks. Multi valued reward functions guide which samples to keep or drop at each stage. Efficiency gains come from spending updates where marginal learning is highest. Tool using agents are only as good as their training mix, so smarter sampling is a direct lever on agent reliability.
arxiv-2509-14818:
Tomislav Terzić and Karlo Mrakovčić search for violations of Lorentz invariance with neural networks in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Lorentz invariance is a core symmetry of relativity, but some theories predict tiny breaks at very high energies. Such breaks could change how gamma rays are emitted, travel, and get detected, through several effects at once.

Earlier experiments usually tested each possible effect on its own. Terzić and Mrakovčić instead train artificial neural networks to look for traces of several effects together in a single analysis. Their paper presents the method and its first results, and places those results alongside earlier experimental searches. A combined search matters because real violations, if they exist, would likely show several signatures at the same time.
arxiv-2509-15518:
Siyang Wu and Zhewei Sun compare slang made by people with slang made by language models. Slang is informal speech that machines find hard. Models are now used to spot and explain slang, so their grasp of it matters. The pair ask whether model made slang matches real human use in style and craft.

Their frame checks three things: biases in how machines view slang, craft in new and reused coinages, and how useful model slang is as teaching examples. They compare a human slang dictionary with output from two known models. The models show clear biases in how they see slang. Still, they have caught much of slang's creative side.
arxiv-2509-15718:
Hao Zhang leads a team that cleans up and names wireless signals at once. Naming a signal's traits matters in modern networks, where receivers must cope without the sender's help. Weak signals and spread out networks make the task hard. Their frame learns both jobs together, across many sites that keep their data local.

A shared network sharpens the signal and reads it, with a block that catches long range patterns. Training uses a federated method tuned for sites whose data differ. A penalty keeps each site's updates near the shared model, which speeds convergence and adds robustness. Broad tests show the joint frame beats past approaches.
arxiv-2509-16218:
More electric cars on a campus mean more strain on its local power grid, and the strain peaks at certain hours. Mohammadreza Iranpour and five co-authors build an automated test bed to gauge that strain at a California campus. The tool links a fast computing language with a power simulator and feeds in a year of real charging data, recorded every fifteen minutes.

The setup tracks load on feeders and transformers through the day and flags worst cases. It can also test futures with more cars or new charging habits. Planners can reuse the modular design on other campuses with like problems.
arxiv-2509-16718:
Vishnu Raja and co-authors improve speech tools for people with dysarthria in a 2025 paper. This condition makes speech hard to understand, and top speech models do poorly on it. Past fixes trained a model for one speaker alone. The team test a mix: shared patterns across speakers plus traits unique to each voice.

Case studies compare the two styles of modeling. Tuning just the speech encoder, not the text side, worked best. Word errors fell from a very high level to about half that. The mix of shared and personal patterns proved key. Better tools could give people with atypical speech more control over devices and daily life.
arxiv-2509-17018:
Jan Pavšek and co-authors build a learning architecture for thermodynamic properties in a 2025 paper. Such properties depend on both a molecule's structure and its state, set by temperature, pressure, and mix. Past models often fed state in as an afterthought. Their design, deepEOSnet, captures state dependence in a more direct way.

The authors see strong potential where state data are sparse. When the output shape is similar across molecules, the design shines. The concept transfers easily to other molecular learning architectures. Better property predictions speed the screening of solvents, refrigerants, and process chemicals, where lab measures for every state are costly.
arxiv-2509-17418:
Junhong Liang and Bojun Zhang ask whether vision-language models can fix spelling errors seen in images. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that the task needs two skills at once: spot the error in the picture, then write the correction. Catching a typo is not the same as fixing it, and models may be far better at one than the other.

The pair built ReViCo, the first benchmark for real-world visual spelling correction in Chinese and English. Its errors come from real image data, not lab-made typos, and scoring runs at image and token level. Tests of open cascaded and native models, plus leading closed systems, show all of them trail human skill by a wide margin, above all at correction. Two fix strategies, a joint OCR-correction pipeline and added background facts, both helped. The gaps point to deep limits in current designs.
arxiv-2509-17718:
Shi-Yu Wang, Yu-Peng Jiao, Hong-Hao Zhang, and Giacomo Cacciapaglia chart how future colliders could catch shy axion-like particles. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies photophobic particles, which dodge the photon coupling most hunts rely on. The hunting grounds are FCC-ee and CEPC, electron-positron machines running at the Z pole.

The signal is a Z boson decaying to a photon plus the new particle, which then splits into two prompt leptons. A lone photon channel, where the particle escapes unseen, adds a second handle. An XGBoost classifier separates signal from background for muon and tau decay routes. At the planned luminosity, the lepton channels probe a wide span of the particle's energy scale, and the lone photon route reaches further still at low masses. The study gives collider planners concrete targets for a particle class built to hide.
arxiv-2509-18118:
Marcelo Ribeiro and 4 co-authors bring light training to small RISC-V edge chips. Their 2025 work deals with smart devices that lack graphics units or AI boosters. Cloud training raises privacy points and needs a steady link, so local training has clear appeal.

A light training method that ran on Arm chips is ported to RISC-V, an open chip design. A lack of float units on those chips slows the work a lot. An eight-bit form of the method cuts memory use near fourfold and more than doubles speed. Score loss from the packed form was tiny in their tests.
arxiv-2509-18218:
Kei-Sing Ng posits that likeness between things is the base frame for systems we can grasp. His 2025 paper sets out Similarity Field Theory, a maths frame for how like two entities are, scored from none to full. That score need not be symmetric, nor chain across pairs.

A system moves through a chain of such fields over time. An idea is cast as the set of things close enough to a core case. A maker step counts as smart, in his terms, if it makes new things that stay in that set. The frame recasts smartness as a shape task on likeness fields.
arxiv-2509-18618:
The isoperimetric problem asks which shape encloses a given volume with the least surface. Gioacchino Antonelli surveys how that problem interacts with lower bounds on curvature in this 2025 note. Curvature limits shape how space bends, and they can force isoperimetric answers into certain forms. The note grew out of mini-courses he taught at two geometry schools.

Antonelli gathers classic results and recent progress in one place. A modern thread treats curvature bounds in a synthetic way, through heat flow and optimal transport tools rather than smooth equations alone. The survey format suits readers entering research in differential geometry. It maps what is known, what is new, and where the open edges lie. The piece is a guide, not a new theorem, and it names its school lecture origins openly.
arxiv-2509-18718:
Cell masses that grow without bound are a known flaw of models for how cells move toward chemical signals. Shikun Cui and four co-authors study a three-dimensional system, the Patlak-Keller-Segel-Navier-Stokes system, that couples such cell motion with fluid flow in a finite channel. They ask when the system still has smooth solutions that stay bounded for all time, even when the starting cell mass is large.

Two added effects can each save the system. A strong shear flow of Couette type, paired with a small starting fluid speed, keeps solutions global and bounded when a logistic growth term is present. In that case there is no limit on the starting mass. When the logistic term is removed, the authors still prove global bounds for a stated range of finite starting masses, under the same strong-flow conditions.
arxiv-2509-19018:
Teng Xiao and two co-authors aim to give one system three skills that are usually built apart: understanding images with text, generating new content, and retrieving matches. Past designs often handle each skill alone, or train a fresh large model from scratch at great cost. Their system, OmniBridge, instead reuses ready-made large language models as its core.

A light module aligns the model's inner space for vision with its space for language, in both directions. Training runs in two stages so the skills do not fight each other. First the model is tuned for reasoning tasks, then a diffusion stage aligns the cross-modal spaces with guidance from meaning. Across a wide range of benchmarks, OmniBridge matches or beats the best prior results on all three skills. The authors credit the shared inner space for that range.
arxiv-2509-19418:
Forecasting hundreds of linked time series at once swamps methods that treat each series on its own. Daniel Peña and one co-author propose a shared frame that shrinks the data while it forecasts. Many known techniques, they show, are just special cases of this one frame. Dynamic principal components and reduced-rank autoregression both fit inside it. Two more members are new here: dynamic forms of two classic tools that link two sets of series.

Because the methods share one derivation, their meanings line up and fair comparisons get easier. The frame also builds in shrinkage, which steadies the fits when data are noisy or short. A simulated case and a real economic forecast task show the gains. The authors aim to give forecasters one language for a crowded family of shrinkage methods for time series.
arxiv-2509-19518:
Can precise quantum measurements beat the standard limit without entangled states? An earlier paper claimed yes, by tying the probes to a shared bath that is partly measured. D. Ballester, Yu. V. Arkhipov, and I. M. Tkachenko dispute that claim in this comment. They focus on the worked example: sensing a tiny change in the length of an optical cavity.

The critics argue that the earlier math clashes with how such a cavity actually glows and responds. Once that clash is fixed, the promised scaling fades. What remains is the standard limit, where precision grows with the square root of the probe count. Comments like this one test strong claims before others build on them. The dispute turns on fine points of cavity physics that readers can check in both papers.
arxiv-2509-19918:
Real software mixes programming languages, yet code models shine in a few and stumble in the rest. Micheline Bénédicte Moumoula and five co-authors build XL-CoGen, a three-stage pipeline that starts from a plain-language spec and one shared test list. First it tries direct generation, fixing the test harness as needed. When direct attempts fail, it routes through an intermediate language chosen by experiment, translating a proven solution.

A final stage diagnoses and patches the best candidate with minimal edits. The design assumes no starting code and no per-language test suites. Underrepresented languages gain the most from the transfer trick. Teams maintaining multilingual systems feel this gap daily. The pipeline treats strong languages as scaffolding for weak ones rather than retraining models per language.
arxiv-2509-20118:
Babak Naderi and Ross Cutler wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on video quality testing. Companies often ask crowds of online viewers to rate video quality. Raters can use a plain rating scale, a scale with a hidden clean reference, or a comparison scale. The paper tests which of these three methods works best in practice.

The team ran six studies that follow the P.910 standard for such tests. They used fifteen talking-head clips with flaws like blur, compression, scaling, and freezing. The plain and hidden-reference methods agreed closely at the level of whole conditions. The comparison method was more sensitive and caught gains beyond the reference. The hidden-reference method was about twice as fast and cheaper, but it squeezed the rating scale. The authors end with practical advice on picking a method for each use case.
arxiv-2509-20618:
Zeyu Jia, Yury Polyanskiy, and Alexander Rakhlin study how the size of a function class controls learning rates in a 2025 paper on statistical learning theory. Their focus is a gapped, scale-sensitive dimension, a measure that counts complexity only above a chosen gap.

The authors show these gapped dimensions control the covering numbers of every uniformly bounded class. The result covers both sequential and non-sequential settings and extends earlier work by other researchers. They also prove that the gapped dimensions give lower bounds on offset Rademacher averages. Those averages gauge how well a class can fit noise. Stronger lower bounds help show when learning rates cannot be improved.
arxiv-2509-20718:
How would two alien civilizations ever agree on when and where to signal each other? Naoki Seto proposes a hybrid answer in a 2025 paper accepted by the Astrophysical Journal. The search for extraterrestrial intelligence struggles with a vast space of possible signals.

Seto combines two shared reference points. The Galactic Center serves as a common spatial marker. A bright burst outside our galaxy serves as a common time marker. Together they could shrink the sky area worth surveying by more than a hundredfold, using data already in hand. Seto reviews supernovae, neutron star mergers, and gamma-ray bursts as candidate markers. One record-breaking gamma-ray burst stands out for its strength and sky position.
arxiv-2509-21018:
The Willmore energy measures how much a surface bends, and its minimizers model elastic membranes and cell shapes. Boris Gulyak, writing solo, studies Willmore boundary value problems for graph surfaces in a 2025 mathematics paper. The boundaries here are rough, with low regularity, and the surface is clamped at the edge.

Following the approach of Koch and Lamm, Gulyak rewrites the Willmore equation in divergence form. That form allows weighted second-order Sobolev spaces to handle the rough boundary and Dirichlet data. Solutions are then built by linearization and a fixed-point argument, requiring small boundary data. Existence and regularity results follow. The work extends geometric analysis tools to settings where the domain's edge is not smooth, as in many physical containers.
arxiv-2509-21318:
High quality image generation in a handful of steps, on a phone, is the engineering goal here. Authorship belongs to Hmrishav Bandyopadhyay and 5 co-authors. Large flow models make high quality images but are too costly for phones. Distillation trains a small model to mimic a large one in few steps. The authors reformulate distribution matching for that few step setting. Their system is called SD3.5-Flash.

Two ideas cut gradient noise and improve prompt alignment. Timestep sharing reduces noise across steps. Split timestep fine tuning sharpens prompt fit. Pipeline changes restructure the text encoder and add tuned quantization. Tests and large user studies show the system beats past few step methods. It runs on hardware from mobile phones to desktops.
arxiv-2509-21518:
Series over the nontrivial zeros of Dedekind zeta functions are the subject of a short 2025 paper by Vincent Nguyen. The extended Riemann hypothesis for those functions is a major open problem in number theory. Many statements equivalent to the classical Riemann hypothesis have been found over the past century. Nguyen adds an equivalence of that kind for the extended setting.

He presents a proof that closed forms for some infinite series hold exactly when the extended hypothesis is true. The series sum over the nontrivial zeros of Dedekind zeta functions. An if and only if result does not settle the hypothesis itself. It gives a new analytic route for testing it. Equivalences like this often guide later work on zero distributions.
arxiv-2509-21618:
Rank metric codes and q-matroids mirror classical coding theory in a richer algebraic setting. Heide Gluesing-Luerssen and Benjamin Jany study polynomial invariants of those objects in a 2025 paper. The Whitney function of a representable q-matroid is the central invariant. Higher weight enumerators of a representing code carry the matching information. The two determine each other, the authors show.

A monomial substitution converts between the Whitney function and the enumerator collection. Higher support enumerators likewise determine the q-matroid itself. The Whitney function of a q-matroid and of its projectivization also determine each other. Q-matroids with isomorphic projectivizations are characterized through lattice isomorphisms between their flats. Such pairs are called weakly isomorphic in the paper.
arxiv-2509-22018:
Emmanuel de Salis and eleven co-authors use deep learning to read the first chapter of cosmic history in this 2025 paper. Long ago, the first stars and galaxies lit up and ionized the hydrogen between them, an era called the Epoch of Reionization. The coming Square Kilometre Array Observatory will map that hydrogen. Its data will be vast, and the faint signal will be buried under foreground glow and instrument effects.

The team trains neural networks on two-dimensional power spectra, summaries of how the hydrogen signal varies across scales. The networks learn to recover the history of reionization from those summaries. That history reflects how fast early light sources grew and how well they ionized their surroundings. On average, the models recovered the history with very high accuracy scores. The authors present the work as evidence that machine learning can pull real astrophysics from the coming data flood.
arxiv-2509-22318:
Pierrick Chatillon, Julien Rabin, and David Tschumperlé present NIFTY, a method for synthesizing new texture from a single example image. Texture synthesis matters for graphics and design, where a small sample must grow into a large, natural-looking surface. Their 2025 approach is a hybrid. It borrows flow matching, a modern generative technique, but builds it on classical patch-based texture optimization, the older craft of rearranging patches of the example.

The twist is that NIFTY needs no neural network training at all. Its flow operates through non-local patch matching, comparing each region with similar regions elsewhere in the example. That avoids two chronic weaknesses of patch methods: poor starting points and visible artifacts where patches meet. Experiments compared the method against representative techniques from the literature, and the authors report it held up well. Code is available in public.
arxiv-2509-22418:
Anastasiia Filippova and 3 co-authors cut the cost of training large models across many machines. A common trick is to sync machines rarely, but each machine still updates every parameter locally. Their method freezes most parameters on each node during local steps. Each node updates only a fixed subset, while a full forward pass still uses all parameters.

That split cuts peak memory and the math load per step. It also removes the need to swap activation data between nodes. On a large language model trained across many nodes, the method matched prior quality. It did so under the same data and bandwidth budgets, with less memory and fewer operations.
arxiv-2509-22618:
A. David Christopher counts the parts inside partitions drawn from a fixed set of allowed sizes. A partition writes a number as a sum of parts, and the count of parts is a basic statistic of it. Christopher treats both ordinary partitions and those with all parts distinct. He obtains generating functions that encode these part counts.

From those functions flow recurrence identities for several known number functions. They include the count of prime divisors, the p-adic valuation, and the Hamming weight. He also handles the number of Carlitz-binary compositions. Finally, he gives an asymptotic estimate for the part count when parts come from a finite set of integers with no common factor.
arxiv-2509-22818:
Seungpil Lee and 3 co-authors test whether language models can develop gambling addiction. The study borrows its lens from human addiction research, at both behavior and circuit levels. In slot machine experiments, the models showed classic cognitive distortions: the illusion of control and loss chasing after defeats. Giving the model more autonomy over betting amounts sharply amplified irrational play and bankruptcy rates.

A sparse autoencoder analysis of internal features confirmed the pattern. Behavior was steered by abstract features tied to risk, not merely by prompt wording. The authors argue the models internalize human-like cognitive biases rather than just mimicking surface text. They frame the findings as an AI safety concern for agentic decision-making.
arxiv-2509-22918:
Nathan Whitsett and Tansu Daylan hunt for star flares that a close planet may have triggered. A gap in planet sizes hints that some worlds lose their gas envelopes. Magnetism may decide which worlds keep an atmosphere, but it is hard to measure. A planet passing near its star can spark flares at closest approach, which would betray its field.

The pair built a pipeline, named ardor, that fits a physics-based model to flare timing. Fake-flare tests mapped how small a flare they can still recover. One system, TOI-1062, showed flares at closest approach with strong support. A second candidate, Gliese 49b, showed weaker clustering and needs more data.
arxiv-2509-23518:
People with locked-in syndrome lose muscle control, and eye trackers fail once eye movement fades too. Ana Patrícia Pinto and 3 co-authors pilot a hybrid aid that pairs eye tracking with a brain-computer interface. The aim is a smooth handover: gaze carries communication early, and brain signals take over as gaze weakens. Five healthy volunteers tested a modified P300-based system.

Gaze and EEG data were processed in real time, and a fusion algorithm merged the two streams to read user intent. Early results suggest the mix can hold high accuracy. The team draws lessons for keeping communication open as patients move from locked-in to completely locked-in states.
arxiv-2509-23918:
In a huge server farm under heavy traffic, sending each job to the right server decides whether anyone waits. Xin Liu and Lei Ying study the Join-the-Fastest-Shortest-Queue policy for systems whose servers all differ in speed and buffer size. Jobs arrive as a Poisson stream scaled to the farm size, and service rates are fully heterogeneous. The policy weighs both queue length and service rate when placing a job.

The pair prove the policy achieves asymptotically zero waiting, in time and in probability, across both sub- and super-Halfin-Whitt regimes. Their bounds show how heterogeneity slows convergence. The proof uses Stein's method with a peeling argument and a ladder of Lyapunov functions.
arxiv-2509-24018: Whether a group element in a linear representation must fix some vector is a classic question with a scattered literature. Alexandre Zalesski surveys the state of the art on fixed-point-free actions: elements whose eigenvalue one never occurs, across linear groups and finite group representations. The paper is expository, mapping what is known, where the problems stand, and how the cases connect.
arxiv-2509-24118:
Health records hold long, sparse histories that are hard for models to read well. Md Mozaharul Mottalib and 2 co-authors built HyMaTE, a hybrid model that mixes a Mamba state-space block with a transformer. Transformers read such records well but cost grows fast with length. Mamba runs in linear time yet mostly mixes facts along the sequence, not across channels.

HyMaTE pairs Mamba's speed with attention that can link channels and expose what drove a prediction. On prediction tasks across several clinical data sets, it learned richer and more unified views of patient records. The authors present it as a scalable, general option for real care settings, and they share the code.
arxiv-2509-24318:
Matching the same object parts across two photos is core to vision, yet correlation methods for it can be costly. Seungwook Kim and Minsu Cho built MambaMatcher, which refines the four-dimensional correlation map between images with selective state-space models. Feature methods can miss tangled relations between parts, while full correlation processing is heavy.

Their similarity-aware scan adapts the linear-cost trick of Mamba models to this task. It keeps feature resolution and reach intact while cutting cost. On standard semantic correspondence benchmarks, MambaMatcher reached the top performance. The result shows state-space models can handle high-dimensional visual matching well.
arxiv-2509-24518:
A layered organic conductor offers the classic case of a metal turning insulator through charge order. Savita Priya and 9 co-authors tune that material by swapping some sulfur atoms for selenium in its molecules. The swap lowers the transition temperature and, more deeply, changes the mechanism itself, so the ground state departs from the charge-ordered insulator of the parent compound.

Infrared spectroscopy tracks the charge dynamics through the change. The substituted materials show no charge ordering at all. The authors instead blame strong electron-phonon coupling that localizes the moving charge carriers. One chemical tweak thus reroutes a famous phase transition.
arxiv-2509-25518:
Harry Robertshaw and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on robot help for clearing clots from brain vessels. Guiding a wire through fine, bent vessels is hard and calls for split second calls. Learning based pilots can help, but they strain to cope with new patients and long tasks. The team trains a world model pilot on ten real patient vessel maps.

The pilot learns a model of how its acts play out, then plans in that model. It took on many tasks with one agent. Its win rate far beat a top rival method. Its paths were more clean as well. Runs took more time, a trade the team flags. The work lays ground for broad use in vessel robots.
arxiv-2510-00018:
En-naoui generalizes the full classical theory of group extensions by adding topology and a symmetry constraint at the same time. Defining what he calls topo-symmetric extensions of topological groups. An extension here is a short exact sequence of topological groups equipped with a continuous action obeying a symmetry condition that ties the action of each group on the other together. So algebra and topology genuinely interact compatibly in this article.

He defines morphisms between such extensions, assembles them into a groupoid. And also proves classification results through an adapted cohomology. Paralleling the classical correspondence theorems for ordinary extensions. New invariants, dimension, stabilizer, and density, characterize the fine structure of these objects. And the theory is applied to finite groups. Compact Lie groups, and profinite groups. Closing with further conjectures on density and modular distribution of the extensions.
arxiv-2510-00118:
The CMS Collaboration at CERN published this 2025 measurement paper on rare particle collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. The team studied vector boson scattering, where two weak bosons bounce off each other. Such events probe how the electroweak force holds together and whether hidden new physics tweaks it. Its data come from proton collisions recorded during the 2016-2018 running period at CERN.

The analysts looked for a Z boson paired with another weak boson, plus two forward jets. They measured the production rate with modest significance in this channel alone. Combined with an earlier channel, the data set some of the world's tightest limits on odd quartic couplings. Those couplings are described through effective field theory terms of dimension eight. The result narrows where new physics could still hide in boson interactions.
arxiv-2510-00418:
Pierre Fayolle and six colleagues published this 2025 medical imaging paper on faking full-dose MRI contrast safely. Gadolinium contrast agents sharpen brain scans, especially for tumor care. Repeated doses raise worries about the metal lodging in brain and body tissue. Their deep learning system upgrades a low-dose scan into a virtual full-dose image.

The new ingredient is the patient's own history: a prior full-dose scan joins the inputs. A single-session model without that history served as the comparison. The longitudinal model improved image quality across several reconstruction metrics by clear margins. Tests at varied simulated dose levels confirmed the method stayed robust. Patients needing frequent monitoring, such as those with chronic disease, stand to gain most. Alternating full and low doses could cut total gadolinium exposure without losing diagnostic value.
arxiv-2510-00618:
Klara Janouskova, Cristian Gavrus, and Jiri Matas published this 2025 paper on image recognition that uses background without being fooled by it. Classifiers often cheat: they learn that water means boat, then fail on land. Deleting context entirely throws away real clues, though, like owners identifying a dog. Their framework, RCOR, first localizes the object, then fuses object and context evidence carefully.

Zero-shot localization separates the object-centric reading from the scene reading. A simple non-parametric rule merges the two judgments afterward. Tests covered both matched and shifted backgrounds, for plain classifiers and vision-language models alike. Performance improved in both regimes, with no fine-tuning required. Even complex ImageNet scenes yielded to the localize-first strategy, the authors report. Localization quality remains the main bottleneck when scenes get truly hard. The code is promised for public release on GitHub.
arxiv-2510-00818:
Campagnolo, Malis, Martinet, and Bahl introduce PhraseStereo in this 2025 arXiv paper, the first dataset for open-vocabulary phrase segmentation in stereo images. Phrase grounding links a natural language expression to the image region it names, but existing datasets use single-view photos only. That throws away depth and geometry cues that stereo pairs provide for free. The authors extend the PhraseCut dataset into the stereo domain to close the gap.

They used the GenStereo generator to synthesize the matching right-view image for each existing photo. The dataset ships stereo pairs together with aligned segmentation masks and phrase annotations, colour-coded by attributes, categories, and relationships. Models can now learn to reason jointly over language, appearance, and depth. The authors admit a weakness: generated right views sometimes hallucinate content, which breaks geometric consistency. They propose adding a stereo matching check with a disparity loss as the fix.
arxiv-2510-00918:
Seibold and three co-authors weigh cost savings against import dependence in Germany's industrial transformation, in this 2025 arXiv paper on energy systems. Steel, fertilizer, and plastics can cut emissions by switching to green hydrogen precursors, but German energy prices may make domestic production unviable. Cheaper production abroad exerts a renewables pull. The authors couple a detailed European energy model to global supply curves for hydrogen, hot briquetted iron, ammonia, and methanol.
