An inexact augmented Lagrangian method solves it without semidefinite programming. That design suits the demanding single-snapshot case especially well. Simulations confirm robust, high-resolution estimates for the array.
arxiv-2510-18118:
Teodora Reu, Sixtine Dromigny, Michael Bronstein, and Francisco Vargas show how straight-line flow training can quietly memorize its training pairs. Rectified flows learn paths meant to be straight from noise to data, enabling near one-step generation. The authors prove that low gradient variance under fixed training pushes the model to memorize arbitrary pairings, even when the pairing lines cross.

In a clean Gaussian setting they trace which fields the training favors in each regime. At test time the model then reproduces the training pairs. Generative model researchers get a named failure mode and a diagnostic signal for it.
arxiv-2510-18218:
Luxuan Li, with Xiao Wang and Chunfeng Cui, presents DualHash in a 2025 paper on deep hashing. Deep hashing, which turns long feature lists into short binary codes, helps computers search large image collections fast. The hard part is that binary codes jump between values instead of changing smoothly.

DualHash uses a primal-dual method, meaning it solves the main problem and a linked partner problem together. A duality trick, which rewrites a hard problem in a second form, gives steps with exact answers. The authors prove speed bounds for two versions and test them on three image search databases. Results show stronger search performance than earlier methods, with proof behind the gains.
arxiv-2510-18318:
Aaron Bell, with Amit Aides and fifty-eight co-authors, introduces Earth AI in a 2025 paper on geospatial analysis. Geospatial data describes places and conditions across the planet, from satellite images to population counts. Its volume, varied scales, and patchiness make thorough analysis hard.

Earth AI combines foundation models, meaning large pretrained models, for imagery, population, and environment data. A Gemini-powered reasoning engine answers multi-step questions across those models and outside data sources. Benchmarks show the combined models predict better together than apart. On a new crisis-scenario benchmark, the agent delivered timely insights that link raw data to decisions people can act on.
arxiv-2510-19118:
Eyad Gad and three co-authors combine a U-Net segmentation model with attention and federated learning to outline breast tumors in ultrasound images. Breast cancer is a leading cause of death for women, and ultrasound is a cheap, reliable detection tool, yet private medical data are hard to pool for training strong models.

Federated learning trains across hospitals without moving patient data, but uneven local datasets can hurt accuracy and boundary quality. The study applies the FedProx method to steady that training while attention helps the model focus on tumor edges. Better private segmentation could support earlier, safer diagnosis.
arxiv-2510-19418:
Mete Harun Akcay and three co-authors present a system for sharing visual data with fine-grained, machine-learning-assisted access control. As stored image and video collections grow and are shared among users with different roles, sensitive regions inside the visuals must be found and protected selectively, at scale.

Four modules detect sensitive regions automatically, correct the detection, manage keys, and enforce policy-based access. Protection mixes fast symmetric encryption with attribute-based encryption, so only viewers whose attributes satisfy the policy can open protected regions. The design aims for trusted sharing where privacy follows the content, not just the file.
arxiv-2510-19618:
Junfei Zhou and five co-authors address a practical obstacle in collaborative perception, where vehicles and robots share sensor information to see more than any one agent can. Fleets are heterogeneous: different sensors and models create domain gaps that break naive sharing. Earlier fixes retrained parts of each agent's network, which is intrusive and costly when new agents join.

Their mechanism, GenComm, instead has each collaborator send a compact spatial message. A conditional diffusion model then generates features matching the receiving agent's own representation space, and a channel enhancer refines them before fusion. On three vehicle-to-everything datasets GenComm beat leading methods, and adding a new agent cost about eighty percent less computing and fewer parameters.
arxiv-2510-19818:
Jacob Berg and four co-authors argue that robot world models should predict meaning, not pixels. Conventional world models forecast future camera frames, but faithful pixel reconstruction does not guarantee good planning decisions. Their semantic world models instead answer questions about the task-relevant content of future frames, turning prediction into a visual question answering problem.

That reframing lets a pretrained vision-language model be fine-tuned into a world model on image, action, and text data, inheriting the model's generalization and robustness. Used for policy improvement on open-ended robotics tasks, the semantic approach generalized far better than reconstruction-based action-conditional models. The paper suggests planning needs the future described, not repainted.
arxiv-2510-20218:
Qinyu Xu and three co-authors propose Continued Fraction Q-Learning, a value decomposition method for multi-agent reinforcement learning that can model high-order interactions between agents. Knowing how agents interact is central to coordination, but earlier methods either hit a combinatorial explosion or hid the interactions inside opaque networks. Their framework captures interactions of arbitrary order with cost that grows only linearly in the number of agents.

A variational information bottleneck extracts latent information used to assign credit to each agent. That step filters out noisy interactions, which improves both cooperation and interpretability at once. Extensive experiments show consistently better performance than rivals, and the explanations the method gives line up with the authors theoretical analysis of the interactions.
arxiv-2510-20518:
Mohamed Seif and three co-authors guard AI sense work at the edge of a radio net from spies. Sense gear and model hosts sit in split spots in such nets. So traits drawn from sense data must be sent by radio for the call. A spy who takes those traits may rebuild raw facts about a person. Stock privacy tools guard whole data sets, not one trait set.

Their frame has each gear twist its traits first, then send them to the model host. The twist cuts what a spy who knows the scheme can get back. The work aims at sight and sense tasks such as self-drive cars and site watch nets. One-trait guard is the key gap they fill.
arxiv-2510-20618:
Jesús Fernández, Loïc Vanel, and Antoine Bérut demonstrate aging in the flow of dense suspensions made of contactless silica microparticles. In rotating drum experiments, piles that rested longer before flowing start later and flow more slowly, with both effects growing logarithmically in the resting time. The packing fraction does not change during rest, so the aging is not simple compaction of the pile.

The effects are strongest for thermally driven creep in piles tilted below the athermal angle of repose, while gravity-driven flows above that angle gradually erase them. Aging appears in both uniform and mixed particle size piles, so crystallization is not required. Vigorous agitation fully restores the initial state, placing this aging between colloidal and granular behavior.
arxiv-2510-20818:
Mateo Guaman Castro leads eleven co-authors on VAMOS, a layered vision language action model that lets one navigation planner serve robots with very different bodies. A wheeled rover and a legged robot face different limits, since only one can climb stairs, yet both need the same sense of where to go.

VAMOS splits the job, a general planner trained on wide open world data proposes paths drawn in image space. A small specialist model learned in cheap simulation scores those paths against the real body limits and re ranks them. Real world trials indoors and outdoors beat strong baselines, and the same planner drives both legged and wheeled robots. Plain language steering also works, showing the split is both portable and easy to direct.
arxiv-2510-21118:
Qiang Ding leads three co-authors on the gray zone of loyalty in summary checking, where judges disagree because the boundary of allowed outside knowledge was never defined. Common sense additions are often labeled faithful, yet nobody states how much outside knowledge is allowed, so labels drift.

Their labeling framework inserts an middle category between faithful and unfaithful, capturing the ambiguous middle honestly. Cleaner labels should train and measure unfaithfulness detectors more fairly. Faithful summarization is a deployment requirement in law, medicine, and news, so resolving label ambiguity has practical weight.
arxiv-2510-21218:
Miroslav Bulíček, Petr Kaplický, and Lucie Wintrová study a heat-conducting fluid that does not flow like water, inside a flat bounded region. The fluid cannot be compressed, its stress follows a power law, and both velocity and temperature are fixed at the boundary.

For a power-law exponent of at least two and starting data with finite energy, they prove that a global weak solution exists and satisfies an entropy equality, an exact balance law. Their main new step is proving that the temperature changes continuously in time in a suitable sense, a fact not shown before in this setting. A related result covers the entropy equation in any number of spatial dimensions.
arxiv-2510-21418:
Lukas Bierling and three co-authors extend DreamerV3, a reinforcement learning agent that plans inside a learned model of its world, so that the agent explores more cleverly. Plain versions can waste effort in games where rewards are rare and the most informative experiences hide among dull ones.

Two additions drive the gains. A prioritized replay buffer stores past episodes ranked by reward, reconstruction error, and value error, so useful experience gets replayed more often. An intrinsic reward, paid when an ensemble of world models disagrees about the next reward, pushes the agent toward uncertain spots. On subsets of the Atari100k games and a visual control suite, the extended agent learns faster and models its world more accurately than the original, above all where rewards are sparse.
arxiv-2510-21518:
Lorenzo Basile and four co-authors hunt for specialists inside the attention layers of large language and vision-language models. Individual attention heads, the parallel readers inside a transformer, seem to favor particular meanings or visual traits. The team adapts a probing method to rank heads by their tie to a chosen concept.

Viewing the probe through a signal processing lens lets them pool evidence across many samples in a principled way. Specialization patterns turn out consistent across text-only and multimodal models alike. The striking part is control: editing as few as one percent of the heads, chosen by their ranking, can reliably dial a target concept up or down in the model's output. Checks span question answering, toxicity reduction, image classification, and captioning, offering simple tools for steering big generative models.
arxiv-2510-21718:
Ishaan Masilamony tests generative AI in high school physics classrooms with an experiment rather than speculation. Tools like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot arrived in schools amid loud debate. But most earlier writing about their effects leaned on trends from older classroom technology and on guesses about what these systems do well or badly.

Students in the study learned physics with generative AI available, and their performance and engagement were compared against expectations from that earlier literature. In line with most prior findings, the tools did lift student performance somewhat. The standout effect, though, was motivational: the largest gain appeared in how engaged students became with the subject itself. The author presents the result as early experimental evidence in a debate that has run mostly on opinion.
arxiv-2510-21818:
Marc Bernacki reviews numerical methods that track how the internal grain structure of a solid material changes over time, a process that shapes strength and other properties. Modelers work at an in-between scale and choose between two broad styles. Methods that follow boundaries indirectly through changing fields, and methods that draw the boundaries themselves as connected lines or surfaces.

The review concentrates on the second family, especially vertex models, which describe a network of grains through the points where several boundaries meet and let those points move. Bernacki explains how these front-tracking methods borrow mesh tools from finite element practice to stay accurate in two and three dimensions. They suit problems where what happens at the boundary itself, such as its energy or mobility, drives the change.
arxiv-2510-21918:
D. Eckert leads a nine-author team using the XRISM space telescope to read the swirling motions of hot gas inside the Coma galaxy cluster. Those motions carry clues about how infalling material settles, how black hole energy spreads, and whether common mass estimates rest on shaky assumptions.

Instead of reading the swirl pattern off directly, the team simulates it. They generate random velocity fields from a trial pattern, fold in real observing effects such as projection and instrument blur. Train a neural network to map data back to the pattern's settings. With a three-setting model covering large-scale energy input and the cascade to smaller scales, they find that just two pointings of the telescope's high-resolution instrument can recover the pattern accurately.
arxiv-2510-22018:
Johannes Feldl leads an eight-author team dissecting the vibrations of indium oxide, a wide-bandgap semiconductor used in transparent electronics. The team set out to learn which atoms move in each Raman-active vibration mode of the crystal's cubic bixbyite structure. How those modes shift when oxygen atoms are swapped for a heavier isotope.

Computer calculations of the lattice dynamics covered every mix of the two oxygen isotopes. Heavier oxygen pulled all mode frequencies downward; most high-energy modes shifted by about five and a half percent, the lowest seven by under one percent. Every mode mixed indium and oxygen motion except one pure oxygen mode. Raman measurements on real crystals, including a bulk single crystal, matched the predictions closely.
arxiv-2510-22218:
Chengrui Yang, Weixin Cai, and Taotao Qiu work on an embarrassment in early-universe cosmology. Nanohertz gravitational waves reported by pulsar timing arrays in twenty twenty-three could come from ripples amplified at the end of inflation. That same amplification would forge far too many primordial black holes, more than the universe allows.

The team asks whether a modified dispersion relation, a change in how primordial ripples of different sizes propagate, can soften the clash. Fitting the timing data, they find a version where the higher-order term grows important late produces a broken power-law spectrum that eases the overproduction nearly to the two-sigma level. Reaching full comfort still takes a touch of negative non-Gaussianity, a specific skew in the ripples. The study maps how much exotic physics the black hole problem actually demands.
arxiv-2510-22518:
Health policy rewards can shape how whole care systems perform, not just single patients. Jinho Cha, with four co-authors, presents a 2025 framework that works backward from observed results to infer how people respond to incentives tied to quality adjusted life years.

Their method recovers hidden sensitivities to efficiency, fairness, and speed of response from trade offs in data from OECD and WHO sources. A new System Impact Index links those responses to national efficiency and equity. The results suggest modern systems sit near an efficiency limit, where fairness changes help stability but bring shrinking gains, and small behavior shifts can affect resilience.
arxiv-2510-22818:
Air quality in large Indian cities can spike without warning. Soham Pahari and Sandeep Chand Kumain build a forecasting frame in 2025. It targets Delhi, Kolkata, and Mumbai. The frame mixes three methods. LOESS splits the series into parts. ARIMA models the smooth parts.

A deep network handles the rough residual part. It uses multi scale convolution and bidirectional memory. An attention gate filters residual signals. A metaheuristic optimizer tunes the settings. Data cover 2021 to 2023 from a national board. Tests span four pollutants. The frame beats statistical and deep baselines. Error fell by several percent across cities.
arxiv-2510-22918:
Dian Wu and seven co-authors report a lab test for spotting entanglement shared among many particles. Entanglement links particles so that measuring one affects the rest, and it powers tasks like secret sharing and fine sensing. The usual check measures all particles at once, which grows fragile as numbers rise.

The team shows that small groups of linked results can still prove true many-particle entanglement. Their setup also held up when measurement tools were slightly off target. The work points to a more practical way to certify large quantum states without perfect control of every part.
arxiv-2510-23018:
JaeEun Lim and five co-authors describe EAR-MP, their entry for a multilingual product search contest at CIKM 2025. Online shoppers write noisy queries in many languages, which makes matching the right products hard. The contest asked for relevance scores for both query-to-category and query-to-item pairs.

The team translated all text into English and cleaned the data heavily to cut noise and fix errors. They fine-tuned a DeBERTa model with label smoothing, self-distillation, and dropout for stability. Extra steps improved ranking further. Their write-up gives a practical recipe for search teams facing messy, multilingual catalogs in daily use.
arxiv-2510-23218:
P F L Maxted and five co-authors measure fundamental temperatures for the eclipsing binary BEBOP-3, which hosts a circumbinary planet. The system pairs a bright F9V star with a faint M dwarf eclipsed every thirteen point two days, while a planet orbits both with a period near five hundred fifty days. Spectra that found the planet also gave direct stellar masses.

Combining TESS light curves with those masses yields direct radii and surface gravities. From them the team derives effective temperatures on a fundamental scale. Such benchmarks anchor temperature scales used across stellar and exoplanet science.
arxiv-2510-23318:
Dominik Kirstein and Christian Kremer introduce a new kind of space for use in equivariant topology, the study of shapes with symmetry. Their semifree isovariant Poincaré space was introduced in 2025. It sits between smooth closed spaces with group action and the equivariant Poincaré spaces of recent work.A group, written G, acts on the space, and the action is semifree, meaning each point is either fixed or moves freely.

The notion also carries an equivariant embedding of the fixed points, built to respect the Poincaré structure. The pair then impose gap conditions, which demand enough codimension, meaning enough room around the fixed set. Under those conditions, the space of such structures on these spaces is highly connected, when the group is finite and periodic. That result gives a useful tool for putting manifold structures onto equivariant Poincaré spaces.
arxiv-2510-23618:
Sayak Guha Roy and five co-authors find a surprising way to bind particles together: repulsion. They work in a Z2 lattice gauge theory, a standard model where gauge fields glue pairs of particles into mesons, echoing how quarks bind in strong-force physics. Without extra attraction, two mesons were not known to stick together in this model at all.

Adding resonant pair-production terms opens two routes to stable two-meson bound states, which the authors call hadrons. One route works through an effective attraction, as intuition expects. The second is new: an effective repulsion binds the pair, because the state sits at high energy, cut off from the two-meson continuum by fluctuations of the gauge fields. Simulations with matrix product states track the bound state forming from local excitations, and a simpler model explains the mechanism. The effect should be visible on current quantum hardware.
arxiv-2510-23718:
Aiden Sheckler points out a broader kind of instanton symmetry in five-dimensional gauge theories with nonabelian forces, seen in their Coulomb phase. The wider symmetry can read more kinds of topological charge carried by monopole strings than the standard one. On closed spacetimes it acts in an invertible way, but with a boundary present it turns non-invertible, a newer and subtler kind.

For the case with the most supersymmetry, Sheckler traces where it comes from: a six-dimensional theory, reduced by one dimension. Extending the recipe to any ADE gauge group gives a broad new family of homotopy invariants, supplied by the boundary defects. The work ties boundary physics, these wider symmetry ideas, and topology into one construction. It also suggests monopole strings carry more readable information than physicists had assumed.
arxiv-2510-23818:
Yilang Zhang and three co-authors improve LoRA, the popular trick for fine-tuning huge language models by training only small low-rank update matrices. LoRA is cheap, but confining updates to a low-dimensional subspace can blunt quality and slow convergence. Their method, ScaLoRA, stacks up a high-rank update from a sequence of low-rank steps instead of settling for one.

At each step, the best low-rank matrix is chosen to minimize the loss and mimic full fine-tuning. The trick is that this optimal step comes from rescaling the columns of the original LoRA matrix, so optimization continues seamlessly with no restart. The authors prove the right scaling can be computed in closed form, with rigorous performance guarantees. Tests on models up to twelve billion parameters show steady gains and faster convergence than leading LoRA variants, across language understanding, commonsense reasoning, and math problem solving.
arxiv-2510-23918:
Emmanuel Sansusthy Tardio and two co-authors build a continuum model for auxetic surfaces that snap between two stable shapes. The surfaces are periodic sheets of hexagonal cells, each made of six rotating triangles with two resting states. Auxetic materials widen when stretched, and bistable ones add a click between states, making the sheet's response hard to predict from the cell behavior alone.

Their macro-model derives a stress-strain law from a free energy written in terms of logarithmic strain. The energy's double-well shape causes numerical trouble, including mesh sensitivity. Two regularizations are introduced: a gradient term on the first strain invariant, and an artificial rate dependence. The first calms the mesh problems; the second smooths the snap-through in time and helps the solver converge. Implemented in the ABAQUS finite element suite with membrane, shell, and continuum elements, the model reproduces the surfaces' deformation.
arxiv-2510-24318:
Prajit Bhaskaran and Tom Viering present Cluster-PFN, a transformer model that performs Bayesian clustering and handles missing data with proper uncertainty. Bayesian clustering accounts for uncertainty but is costly at scale, and simple filling of missing values ignores the doubt those values carry. Cluster-PFN extends prior data fitted networks to this unsupervised task.

Trained only on synthetic datasets drawn from a finite Gaussian mixture prior, the model learns to estimate the posterior over both the number of clusters and each point's assignment. It estimates cluster counts more accurately than classic criteria like AIC and BIC and variational inference, while matching or beating their clustering quality, including on data with missing entries.
arxiv-2510-24518:
Romain Poletti and four co-authors characterize and extend a rigid body dynamics solver coupled with OpenFOAM for flapping wing drone flight analysis. The agility of hummingbirds and insects inspires these drones, and coupled flow and body simulations are essential to design them. OpenFOAM tools for such multiphysics work lacked thorough verification, and wing motion control relied on torque inputs that suit parametric studies poorly.

The developments are tested on flapping wing drones with four and five degrees of freedom and a rigid, semi elliptical wing. Ascending flight motions are among the cases examined. The work gives engineers a better verified, more controllable simulation path for flapping flight performance.
arxiv-2510-24718:
Chonghyuk Song, Michal Stary, Boyuan Chen, George Kopanas, and Vincent Sitzmann fix a flaw in video models that build a film step by step. Such models can not use facts from the future of a set camera path. So the fake scene can block the path, and the film then falls apart.

Their method, called GVS, draws the whole film at once so each part fits the full camera path. It joins short chunks with a stitch rule first used for robot plans. No special training is needed for the base video model. A guide step that looks both ways in time helps keep the chunks in line.
arxiv-2510-24918:
Biyi Fang, Truong Vo, Kripa Rajshekhar, and Diego Klabjan add side facts to topic models, the tools that find hid themes in a text set. Classic topic tools are poor at use of side facts like tags, user traits, or class marks. That lack trims their range, fit to a user, and ease of read.

Their tool, nnLDA, lets a small net set the theme mix prior for each text from its side facts. That lets side facts sway themes in curved ways a fixed prior can not catch. A chance based tune loop trains the net and the theme parts as one. On a few bench sets, nnLDA beat the classic tool and its kin by a steady gap.
arxiv-2510-25418:
Timon J Vreman leads three co-authors on photonic crystals. Melissa J Goodwin, Ad Lagendijk, and Willem L Vos join. 2D photonic crystals control light propagation strongly. Theory for their band form is well established. Crystals are homogeneous in the third dimension ideally. Experimental verification remains scarce, especially at telecom wavelengths.

Real crystals cannot be perfectly homogeneous in thickness. Their crystals were periodic in two dimensions only. Thickness was homogeneous over five micrometers there. Fourier spectroscopy selected wave vectors in the plane. Tests agreed excellently with 2D band calculations. Finite-difference runs also matched their readings well. That confirms methods truly probe 2D nanophotonics. Results bridge theory and test robustly here. Techniques can extend to other 2D forms. Functional defects in crystals could be studied similarly. Such extensions broaden the value of the method.
arxiv-2510-25918:
Brandon P. Ashley and Michael T. Schultz connect the geometry of surfaces in projective space with distributions on five dimensional spaces. They study rank three vector bundles over a surface, meaning three dimensional vector spaces attached at each point, equipped with a connection that defines horizontal directions. Removing the zero section leaves a five dimensional total space with a field of two dimensional planes.

Ashley and Schultz show that any surface in three dimensional projective space can be tied to such a structure. They build a dictionary that translates features of the surface, in the language of projective differential geometry, into the growth pattern of the plane field. The growth pattern records how repeated brackets of allowed motions fill new directions.
arxiv-2510-26018:
Petr Stibinger leads seven co-authors in a system that lets small flying robots cooperate to find a radioactive source. Each micro aerial vehicle carries a Compton camera, a detector that senses ionizing radiation and infers its direction, in a new single detector design that weighs only forty grams. That light weight makes it possible to fly several detectors at once on agile aircraft.

Stibinger and the team fuse the sparse camera readings in real time to estimate the source position, with processing done on board each vehicle. The estimate feeds back into flight control, so the swarm tightens its formation to gain information, locates the source quickly, and can even track a moving source in their design.
arxiv-2510-26218:
Jia-Rou Liou, Alvina Y. L. On, H. -Y. Karen Yang, and J. A. ZuHone use simulations to explain polarized radio signals seen behind merging galaxy clusters. Observations of the Fornax cluster show depolarization on megaparsec scales, possibly tied to shocks or sloshing motions during a merger. Rotation measure, which tracks how polarization rotates as radio waves cross magnetized gas, can separate the causes.

With analytic work and full polarized radiative transfer on a simulated merger, Liou and the team find a local rotation measure boost behind the shock front from compressed gas and field lines. Behind a sloshing cold front, the measure drops as tangled fields cancel. Beam depolarization grows in both settings, a sign of stronger field fluctuations.
arxiv-2510-26518:
Rishub Jain, with five co-authors, studies how people and AI can check each other's work. Human feedback steers AI toward human values, but as AI takes on harder tasks, judging its output gets harder for people alone. The team focuses on fact-checking AI answers, a safety task that already strains human reviewers.

Jain and the team find that blending AI ratings with human ratings, weighted by the AI's confidence, beats either one alone. Giving people an AI fact-checking assistant raised their accuracy too, but the form of help mattered. Showing the AI's explanations, confidence, and labels led people to lean on it too much. Just showing search results and evidence led to better-placed trust. The work speaks to amplified oversight, the task of supervising AI as it grows past human skill.
arxiv-2510-26918:
Oindrila Ghosh, with four co-authors, asks whether magnetic fields made inside galaxies can spread out to fill cosmic voids. Blazar observations imply voids are magnetised at a tiny level on megaparsec scales. Where that field came from is unsettled, and one candidate is diffusion of galactic fields into the voids.

Ghosh and the team show an electrically conducting plasma is present in the voids. Because of it, diffusion of dynamo-generated galactic fields is far too slow to explain today's void magnetisation. Even with turbulence in the voids, such fields reach only two to four hundred kiloparsecs from a galaxy. Meeting the required volume filling factor is therefore hard. The authors conclude a primordial origin, a field born with the universe, remains the most natural explanation.
arxiv-2510-27118:
Andy Yang leads six co-authors in characterizing which probability distributions transformer language models can express. Most theory treats transformers as recognizers that accept or reject strings. In practice they generate text step by step, sampling each next token from a distribution, a very different mode of use.

The team shows that making recognizers autoregressive, meaning they build output left to right, can sometimes increase expressive power. Making them probabilistic can also break equivalences that hold in the non-probabilistic case. By separating these effects, the study clarifies what functions transformers can represent in their most common role. The results give theorists a sharper picture of language model capacity and guide where architectural changes might genuinely add power.
arxiv-2510-27318:
Wenfeng Huang, Xiangyun Liao, and five other co-authors work on rebuilding moving tissue from surgery video, in a 2025 paper. Surgeons use endoscopes, thin cameras inside the body, to guide robot tools. Turning that video into a live three-dimensional view is hard, since tissue stretches and shifts. Fast new rendering methods often leave blur and ghost edges.

Their method, SAGS, builds the view from many soft three-dimensional blobs, a trick called Gaussian splatting. Extra smoothing steps, in space and across the image, fight the blur from motion. A decoder, a small network that predicts shape change, weighs each frame's cues by importance. On two public surgery data sets, SAGS beat prior methods on all quality scores they report. It also rendered cleaner views of fine tissue detail.
arxiv-2510-27518:
Antoine Bret, Audrey DeVault, Skylar Dannhoff, Maria Gatu Johnson, Chikang Li, and Johan Frenje analyze the linear Rayleigh-Taylor instability when a foam layer is present. The instability grows where a heavy fluid is supported by a lighter one, and foams appear in inertial confinement fusion capsules and hohlraum linings. Foam passes through elastic, then plastic, then fracture phases as stress rises, and only the first two admit linear analysis.

Growth rates are computed analytically in both phases from foam microstructure. In the elastic phase the instability can be stabilized at some wavelengths, and a homogeneous foam model overestimates growth by ignoring elasticity. Although derived for a simplified foam, the result likely holds broadly, with relevance beyond fusion to other foam-bearing flows.
arxiv-2511-00118:
Stanislav Selitskiy offers a lightweight spam filter based on bags of synthetic syllables, designed for the front line of high-volume email services. Deep learning filters are accurate but resource hungry and too slow for first-pass filtering, while most incoming spam is unsophisticated. Using subject lines and short text fields, the simple algorithm screens the bulk cheaply in real time with zero footprint.

The small fraction of clever, mutable spam still passes to deeper models, whose load is unloaded by the cheap first stage. Email infrastructure readers get a tiered defense argument. Matching filter cost to spam sophistication keeps high availability under attack.
arxiv-2511-00218:
Rajatsubhra Chakraborty and four co-authors tackle a practical imaging problem: how to outline single cells in pictures from a fast phase microscope. Older threshold methods break down when noise is high or cells sit close together. Simple deep learning tools also waste information, because they just stack two kinds of images together.

Their network, DM-QPMNet, reads the two image types in separate streams, one for light intensity and one for phase. An attention step then lets the streams share what each one sees best, such as edges and texture. Tests show clear gains over single-stream and simple stacking baselines, with stable training and little extra cost.
arxiv-2511-00318:
Dana Kim, Yichen Xu, and Tiffany Lin explore a trap in synthetic data: fake tables can predict well yet give wrong causal answers. A generator may match patterns in medical or social data while badly misjudging the average effect of a treatment. The authors first show that leading generators, both GAN-based and language-model-based, fall into exactly this trap.

Their hybrid fix builds covariates with a monitored model, then learns the treatment assignment and outcome parts separately, so cause-and-effect structure survives. A pairing trick eases cases where some groups rarely get treated. With unlimited synthetic samples, they benchmark standard causal estimators under complex data patterns. The work lays groundwork for safer synthetic data pipelines.
arxiv-2511-00618:
Jeffrey Carpenter solves how long surface gravity waves get excited in a flow whose speed varies with depth, a sheared current. Standard theory leans on normal modes, tidy wave patterns with definite speeds. Carpenter finds a second ingredient beside them: a continuous spectrum, a smear of responses tied to speeds inside the shear profile itself.

For an impulse at the surface, he derives an analytical similarity solution for the free surface displacement contributed by the continuous spectrum. That contribution can be a significant share of the total response, and for Froude numbers near unity it can exceed the upstream gravity wave mode. A Landau-damped mode description ties the spectrum to dispersion-based methods and covers shear profiles that admit no normal modes in that speed range at all.
arxiv-2511-00918:
The IceCube Collaboration reports a search for dark matter signals in neutrinos from the center of our galaxy. Many dark matter models predict that particles annihilating or decaying there would produce neutrinos, and the galactic center is dense with dark matter, making it a prime target.

About nine years of data from IceCube-DeepCore, the dense core of the Antarctic IceCube detector, were scanned for neutrinos between fifteen and two hundred gigaelectronvolts. Several annihilation and decay channels and masses up to eight teraelectronvolts were tested. No significant excess over atmospheric background appeared. The team sets upper limits on annihilation rates and lower limits on decay lifetimes, the strongest dark matter constraints yet from any neutrino telescope at these masses.
arxiv-2511-01618:
Xiaoyu Zhan and thirteen colleagues probe whether multimodal large language models, systems that read images and text, truly understand three-dimensional space. Two-dimensional image skill does not guarantee cross-view consistency: knowing how a scene looks from another angle. That gap is what their Viewpoint Learning task is built to measure and fix.

They release Viewpoint-100K, a dataset of 100,000 object-centered image pairs from diverse viewpoints with question-answer pairs. Training runs in two stages. First, supervised fine-tuning on the dataset injects viewpoint knowledge. Then reinforcement learning, with group relative policy optimization, broadens it to wider questions. A hybrid cold-start scheme keeps the reasoning coherent. The result is a marked activation of the baseline model's spatial reasoning across several tasks.
arxiv-2511-01818:
Xiang Gao, Swagato Mukherjee, Qi Shi, Fei Yao, and Yong Zhao compute, on a lattice, how the pion's internal momentum is shared among its quarks. The relevant object is the pion's generalized parton distribution. Its Mellin moments summarize the sharing. The odd moments up to fifth order are the targets here. So is their dependence on skewness, the imbalance between incoming and outgoing momentum.

The calculations use nonlocal quark-bilinear correlators, expanded through the operator product expansion. The ensemble has a fine lattice spacing and a pion mass of 300 MeV. Boosted pions reach momenta of about 2.4 GeV there. Renormalization in the ratio scheme and resummed perturbative matching connect lattice results to continuum quantities. At zero skewness the moments agree with earlier lattice studies, and combining many skewness and momentum-transfer values lets polynomiality-constrained fits extract the full skewness dependence.
arxiv-2511-01918:
Ahmet Erdem Pamuk, Emir Kaan Özdemir, and Şuayp Talha Kocabay propose an optimizer for neural networks borrowed from quantum mechanics. Training large language models usually runs on classical optimizers such as AdamW. Their Superpositional Gradient Descent works differently. It injects perturbations from quantum circuits into the gradient updates. Each step is tied to the idea of superposition.

The authors present the mathematical framework and implement hybrid quantum-classical circuits in PyTorch and Qiskit. On synthetic sequence classification and on large-scale language model fine-tuning, their optimizer converged faster and reached lower final loss than AdamW. They are candid about the limits: scalability and today's quantum hardware constrain adoption. The work is offered as evidence that quantum principles can steer classical training in useful ways, not only as a future hardware promise.
arxiv-2511-02018:
Jinchen He, Xiao-Yong Jin, James Osborn, and Yong Zhao study how to design the neural networks that are now used to speed up lattice gauge theory simulations. Hybrid Monte Carlo, the field's sampling workhorse, suffers critical slowing down near the continuum limit, crawling through configuration space. Bending the sampled landscape with a neural field transformation helps, but which architectures help most was unstudied.

Working on a two-dimensional U(1) gauge theory, the authors compare neural transformation designs under controlled conditions, tracking how efficiency scales and transfers to larger volumes and finer lattices. Good designs cut autocorrelation and boosted tunneling between topological sectors while keeping favorable scaling. Emerging design rules include wider receptive fields and channel-dependent activations. The study is aimed at systematizing the approach before its extension to four-dimensional SU(3) gauge theory, the theory of the strong nuclear force.
arxiv-2511-02118:
Lucas Pereira de Souza computes, in closed form, how quantum vacuum effects change. The setting is fermions interacting with both usual electromagnetic fields and hypothetical axial vector fields. The Euler-Heisenberg action summarises these one-loop effects, but adding a massive pseudo-vector background alongside the photon field had left open questions about whether the calculation is even well-defined and stable.

By fully diagonalising the functional Hessian, de Souza maps the parameter space into sectors with distinct stability and spectral behaviour. The sectors include regimes where propagating axial fields are physically viable, plus a striking sector with chirality-asymmetric instability. The resulting actions yield new nonperturbative pair-production rates, with a pronounced stabilisation of the vacuum, plus contributions to the chiral current that allow dynamical chiral symmetry breaking. A cosmological toy model tests whether an axial field could drive baryogenesis.
arxiv-2511-02518:
Paulin Aubert, Etienne Chevalier, and Vathana Ly Vath model a feedback loop that options traders create without noticing. An option market maker quotes prices and then hedges the resulting exposure by trading the underlying asset. When many options change hands, that hedging flow is large enough to move the underlying's price, which in turn changes the options' values. Their model makes option demand a random flow whose intensity depends on the underlying's state and on the maker's own quotes.

The coupled system joins stochastic demand with permanent and transient price impact, so inventory and price evolve together. The authors first examine whether manipulation or arbitrage can arise from the feedback, then prove the mixed control problem, continuous quoting plus impulsive hedging trades, is well-posed. A numerical method based on policy optimisation approximates the optimal strategy and displays how liquidity, inventory risk, and impact trade off.
arxiv-2511-03218:
Sujoy Majumder, Nabadwip Sarkar, and Molla Basir Ahamed work on sharp size limits inside two special families of smooth complex functions. The families gather starlike and convex shapes tied to the exponential curve. Their focus falls on a set of derived numbers, called logarithmic coefficients, that encode how such functions bend and grow.

Beyond those numbers, the authors bound a determinant built from them and test two named guesses about coefficient size. Every bound they report is shown to be best possible, with cases that reach it exactly. Results of this kind tighten what analysts can claim about whole families at once. They also give clean benchmarks for later work on related shape classes.
arxiv-2511-03318:
Shouvik Sadhukhan and C S Narayanamurthy model how light flickers as it passes through plastic rods under air turbulence. Their picture treats tiny dipoles inside the material as linked oscillators with nonlinear springs. Extra forces from uneven fields and from the light itself enter through a classic mechanics rule, yielding an effective inertia that resists fast change.

When the dipoles swing in step, that shared motion can offset some of the wavefront warping that turbulence causes. The team works through the usual statistics of scintillation, the rapid brightness flicker seen in such beams. Linked-dipole thinking may help explain odd flicker patterns and guide optics that must hold steady through rough air or warm, shifting media.
arxiv-2511-03518:
Axel Potier and colleagues validate a coherent imaging method for spotting faint extended sources beside bright stars with the SPHERE instrument. Coronagraphs and adaptive optics dim starlight, yet leftover aberrations between sensing and science paths cap performance. Standard post-processing loses signal to self-subtraction, especially close to the star.

Coherent differential imaging modulates the speckles so true coherent starlight can be isolated and subtracted. Earlier sky tests showed promise, and this work checks the method on real observations of extended sources. Cleaner subtraction near the star opens room for disks and faint companions that older routes erase. Direct imaging of young planetary systems stands to gain most from the sharper view.
arxiv-2511-03718:
Nan Li, Albert Gatt, and Massimo Poesio build an annotation scheme that tracks what each speaker in a dialogue thinks a phrase refers to. In the MapTask corpus, partners guide each other by landmarks on maps that do not quite match. Partners can believe they agree while picturing different places, a grounded misunderstanding.

Separate labels for speaker and listener readings let analysts trace how understanding grows, splits, and gets repaired. A constrained language model pipeline produced thirteen thousand labeled references with reliability scores. Full misunderstandings turn out rare once wording variants are unified. Count mismatches between partners, though, reliably seed divergence, showing how apparent agreement can hide a split reference.
arxiv-2511-04218:
Michael J Williams, writing alone, presents ASPIRE, a method that updates gravitational-wave Bayesian results when the model changes, without redoing the full analysis. Events are reanalysed again and again under new waveform models or added physics, and each rerun is costly, a growing burden as catalogues expand.

Normalizing flows join a general sequential Monte Carlo scheme to transform existing posterior samples and evidence estimates into unbiased results under a different model. Likelihood counts fell by factors up to about six and wall times similarly in its tests. Switching waveform models and adding spin precession or eccentricity matched full analyses well, enabling ordered studies across large event catalogues.
arxiv-2511-04518:
Obed Amo leads five authors benchmarking a Gaussian process surrogate against finite elements. The test problem is the two-dimensional wave equation with zero values fixed at the boundary. Their surrogate builds the physics and boundary rules in exactly, using special exponential-polynomial bases.

Fairness comes from a protocol that matches degrees of freedom across both methods. Under that match, the surrogate reaches far lower errors than Crank-Nicolson finite elements. Gains run to roughly two orders of magnitude in space-time error measures. The study shows how exact constraint handling can pay off when surrogate and classic methods get equal resources.
arxiv-2511-05018:
Prasoon Varshney and co-authors present PB Suite, a test suite that checks if language models stick to custom behavior rules over long chats. Most models are tuned to one broad set of public norms, yet firms must follow their own brand, legal, and ethics rules.

The suite holds 300 realistic behavior policies drawn from 30 fields of work. Its live test frame stresses how well a model holds those rules turn after turn in a chat. The work gives a shared way to grade fit with local values, not just global safety norms.
arxiv-2511-05218:
Wenchong Chen and co-authors study color gaps in spanning trees of random graphs. Take a random graph just past the point where it joins into one piece, paint each edge one of two colors, and ask if a biased tree must exist.

They prove that, with high chance, some spanning tree has many leaves and a clear surplus of one color, more than half its edges by a fixed margin. They extend the result to dense graphs with a few random edges added. The work ties tree shape to forced color imbalance.
arxiv-2511-05418:
Luca Santosuosso and co-authors build a decomposition method, with a performance guarantee, for joint bidding by cascaded hydropower dams plus wind and solar units in the day-ahead market. Water power can flex to cover the swings of wind and sun, but joint bidding is a hard, coupled task.

Their split works along two axes at once: scenarios for the unknown weather, and space across the dam chain. That lets a distributed method run the parts in parallel. Non-convex physics makes the final method a heuristic, yet they still give a bound on how far it can stray.
arxiv-2511-05518:
Myeongseob Ko and co-authors show how large language models can be pushed to spill text they memorized in training. Such leaks raise privacy and copyright risks. Older attacks forced models off track in rough ways and gave little insight into why text comes out.

Their method, called Confusion-Inducing Attacks, raises the model's uncertainty on purpose. The team found that a long spike in prediction doubt comes just before memorized text appears. By shaping inputs to cause that state, they drew out exact or near-exact training text from many models. The work gives a clearer way to test how much a model truly remembers.
arxiv-2511-05918:
J Bartel and co-authors search for shape isomers, excited states of atomic nuclei trapped in a second shape, among platinum, mercury, and lead isotopes. They compute potential energy surfaces for nine even-even isotopes near platinum-186. The model blends a liquid-drop style energy with microscopic shell and pairing corrections.

A fast-converging shape description lets them test whether the isomeric states survive wobbles into non-axial and higher-order shapes. Orientation of the three-axis shape turns out to need care. In mercury-186 they found three prolate shape-isomeric states. Its energy surface closely matches a far heavier Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov calculation with a known force, which supports the lighter model's reliability in this region.
arxiv-2511-06018:
Alexander Zakharov recalls nearly forgotten turns in the history of cosmology, the study of the universe as a whole. He starts with Einstein's theory of gravity and his first, static model of the cosmos, soon shown to be unstable. Friedmann then found expanding solutions, and Lemaître reached like results plus the growth law that Hubble found in the sky.

Zakharov stresses how Soviet science long treated Friedmann's models as pure math with no cosmic meaning. He credits Lemaître's primeval atom idea with foreseeing a faint background glow. He also notes a Soviet reading of that glow years before Penzias and Wilson, and Gliner's early vacuum-like matter idea, which came before inflation theory. The essay says the standard history skips real work, above all from Soviet-era names.
arxiv-2511-06118:
Reza Rastegar offers a new proof of the Stanley-Wilf conjecture on pattern-avoiding permutations, and labels the work in progress. The conjecture, proved by Marcus and Tardos, bounds how fast the count of permutations avoiding a fixed pattern can grow. Their proof detoured through an extremal problem on zero-one matrices.

Rastegar's route stays inside the counting side of the field. Permutations are grown by adding new entries on the right, while a pruned frontier tracks partial pattern matches, each with a banned rank range. The adding step becomes a transfer operator on a weighted function space. A quadratic penalty makes that operator bounded, and a series argument then gives a smooth growth series. The payoff is finite growth of exponential type, with pattern counting cleanly split from operator theory.
arxiv-2511-06418:
Sunil Mohan and Theofanis Karaletsos build a test of whether language models truly understand how drugs work. Drug development and personalized medicine both need models that recall mechanism facts and reason with them in new situations. A drug's mechanism is a chain of interactions running from the drug to the disease it targets.

Their dataset probes stored knowledge and fresh reasoning side by side, using counterfactual twists the models are unlikely to have memorized. One leading small model matched or beat bigger rivals, and a compact reasoning model came close behind. Reasoning with knowledge supplied in the prompt proved easier than recalling it, and twists inside the chain were hardest.
arxiv-2511-06518:
Salam Afiouni, Jakub Cerny, Chun Kai Ling, and Christian Kroer generalize the Colonel Blotto game, the classic contest of splitting forces across battlefields. In their version, each battlefield then hosts its own normal-form game whose payoffs depend on how many soldiers each side committed there. Winning a field is no longer just a matter of outnumbering the opponent.

Discrete and continuous troop allocations are both studied, under two ways of totaling the outcome: adding field values or counting only the worst field. The general game lacks the convex shape that makes equilibria easy to find. Several settings, though, admit reformulations that restore that shape, and tests on synthetic and security-inspired cases scaled well.
arxiv-2511-06818:
Dhananjay Ram, Wei Xia, and Stefano Soatto propose a small change to the attention mechanism at the heart of transformer models. Standard softmax attention often spreads its focus too thinly, producing noisy distributions that blur feature selection, especially over long contexts. Their Focal Attention sharpens that distribution by adjusting the softmax temperature.

The temperature can be fixed in advance or learned during training, letting the model concentrate on relevant tokens and suppress the rest. Across benchmarks, models with Focal Attention matched standard transformers using up to 42 percent fewer parameters or a third less training data. On long-context tasks it delivered relative gains between 17 and 82 percent.
arxiv-2511-06918:
Gilles Audemard, Christophe Lecoutre, and Emmanuel Lonca edit the proceedings of the 2025 XCSP3 Competition, an annual contest among constraint solvers. Constraint solvers are programs that find values satisfying a set of stated constraints. XCSP3 is the shared format in which the competition's benchmark problems are written, letting very different solvers compete on identical tasks. The document records how the 2025 edition turned out.

The results were presented at CP'25, the thirty-first International Conference on Principles and Practice of Constraint Programming. As proceedings, the document serves as the official record of which solvers entered, how they performed across the benchmark set, and where the state of the art in constraint solving now stands. It is a reference for researchers comparing solvers and for organizers of future editions.
arxiv-2511-07018:
Sean Eberhard and Elena Maini prove a growth theorem for residually soluble groups, classes of symmetries whose structure can be probed through soluble quotients. The question is how fast the number of elements within a given word-length grows, and what that rate reveals. Building on work of Wilson, they show that if the growth function grows slower than a certain subexponential bound, the group must be virtually nilpotent, a highly restricted class.

Concretely, the condition is that the logarithm of the growth function, divided by the fourth root of the length, tends to zero. The result proves Grigorchuk's Gap Conjecture for all exponents below one quarter within residually soluble groups, improving Wilson's earlier exponent of one sixth. Stronger versions of the conjecture are also discussed.
arxiv-2511-07218:
Masaya Nishihata studies a dilemma every organization faces: give scarce, valuable tasks to proven performers, or spread them to discover unknown talent? Temporary injuries to star Major League Baseball players create natural tests, suddenly reallocating playing time to teammates at the same position. Nishihata tracks allocation and performance before, during, and after these absences to separate learning effects from information effects.

Crowd-out is clear: when a star is out, same-position teammates receive greatly more opportunities. Yet the extra experience barely raises their batting productivity, during the absence or after, so learning by doing is not the main benefit. Instead, performance surprises during the window predict later employment and playing time, meaning teams use the revealed information in future decisions. Counterfactuals suggest that information can partly offset the short-run production loss.
arxiv-2511-07318:
Shaowen Wang and six co-authors show that some language model hallucinations are built by the data's spurious correlations, and that standard detectors cannot see them. Superficial but statistically strong associations in training data, like surnames correlating with nationality, teach models to answer confidently and wrongly. These hallucinations survive model scaling and refusal fine-tuning, because the model believes its own statistical lesson.

Through controlled synthetic tests and tests on leading open and proprietary models, including GPT-5, the team shows confidence-based filtering and inner-state probing fundamentally fail on such cases. Their theoretical analysis explains why: the bias sits in the same statistics the detectors trust. The authors call for detection methods built specifically for correlation-driven hallucination, a class they argue has been underexplored relative to its danger.
arxiv-2511-07618:
Pal, Woods, and Persson use magnetic fluids to tune the faint Casimir forces between tiny rods. At nanoscale, dispersion forces pull particles together and cause clumping that ruins devices. Pairs of dielectric nanorods, polystyrene and zinc oxide, sit in a toluene host loaded with gold-coated magnetite particles.

Semi-classical quantum theory predicts ground state forces and magnetic parts of excited state forces. Changing magnetic permeability flips the interaction between attraction and repulsion. That switch could keep nanoparticles dispersed or let them assemble on command. Tunable Casimir forces would give engineers a dial for sticking and releasing parts without contact.
arxiv-2511-07918:
Jung-Sun Lee, Ha-Na Jo, and Eunyeong Ko compare brain synchrony across four ways of using speech: hearing it, speaking it, whispering it, and imagining it. Theta-band coordination links language, attention, and inner speech, but studies usually isolate one mode. An integrated comparison can separate shared machinery from mode-specific circuits.

Connectivity measures show overt and whispered speech engage broader, stronger theta networks than the quieter modes. Region-by-region differences map where each mode leans on shared systems. Such maps guide brain-computer interfaces that decode imagined speech, since knowing how imagination differs from speaking tells engineers what signals to expect.
arxiv-2511-08218:
John Beirne, Haroon Mumtaz, Donghyun Park, and Gazi Salah Uddin ask who gains when military spending rises, using data across many advanced and emerging economies. News shocks about future defense budgets let them trace effects on output, productivity, and household distribution over time. Earlier work found lasting rises in output and total factor productivity after such shocks.

The distributional picture splits in two. Income inequality falls, because gains are larger at the lower end, driven by labour income and industrial employment. Wealth inequality rises instead, especially in rich countries, as the top tenth gains share through business asset holdings. Defense expansions therefore help poorer workers while enriching wealthy owners.
arxiv-2511-08318: Barnabas Deme and Jean-Baptiste Fouvry show a thermodynamic blocking effect in self gravitating systems held in hydrostatic equilibrium with uniform density. Building on a thermodynamic formalism, they prove such systems are maximum entropy states when perturbations act slowly compared with the dynamical timescale. The authors name the effect thermodynamic blocking for its likeness to kinetic blocking, and argue the result shows why thermodynamic reasoning stays useful exactly where kinetic equations break down.
arxiv-2511-08418:
Hannah Lydon, Milad Kazemi, Martin Bishop, and Nicola Paoletti apply physics informed neural operators to cardiac electrophysiology, the simulation of voltage waves through heart tissue. Traditional solvers are expensive and sensitive to grid choices, while usual deep learning needs much data and struggles with chaotic, long term conduct. Physics informed networks add equation constraints but stay tied to mesh resolution and lose stability over long rollouts.

Neural operators learn maps between function spaces, so one model serves many resolutions and starting settings. Their operator reproduces cardiac dynamics over long horizons and across propagation scenarios, including zero shot cases never trained on. Predictions stay exact when fed back recursively, resolution can scale tenfold, and run time drops sharply.
arxiv-2511-08518: Jose Burillo and Marc Felipe improve, in a short note, the known bound on the word metric for Thompson group V, a classic group of homeomorphisms studied in geometric group theory. A bound given by Birget in 2004 is sharpened to a new estimate. The improved bound agrees with the previously known bounds for the related Thompson groups F and T, placing the three groups on the same footing for this metric question.
arxiv-2511-08818:
Andrew Rothstein and nine co-authors describe PACMAN, the control system that lets machine learning run a fusion experiment on the DIII-D tokamak. Learned predictors and controllers have reached regimes where traditional control fails, including plasmas free of tearing modes and edge bursts. Wiring them into a live machine end to end is its own challenge.

The architecture carries signals from diagnostic processing all the way to actuation commands in real time. Several successful experiments ran through it. They include a reinforcement learning controller for advanced non-inductive plasmas, a predictor for a wide-pedestal quiet regime, and an Alfvén eigenmode controller. A model predictive profile controller and a tearing mode predictor-controller also ran through it. The authors also distill design principles for real-time learned control on complex machines.
arxiv-2511-08918:
Kai Hu and five co-authors compress images unevenly on purpose, spending bits where the eye cares and saving them in the background, but without the hard masks that older region-of-interest methods used. Hard gating before quantization distorts the statistics the entropy model expects, and that quietly caps coding quality.

The proposed model allocates bits implicitly. A mask-guided feature enhancement module, built from region-adaptive attention and a frequency-spatial attention block, steers capacity toward the important region while strengthening features everywhere. Two decoders then rebuild foreground and background separately, letting the network balance sharpness against background quality from data. On the COCO2017 dataset the method beats explicit-allocation rivals on rate-distortion performance while keeping backgrounds visually satisfactory. The authors claim the first use of implicit bit allocation for region-adaptive coding.
arxiv-2511-09118:
Pietro Cappelli and four co-authors validate generative models the way physicists test theories: with a goodness-of-fit machine that learns where the model fails. Generative networks now sit inside scientific pipelines, but certifying them on high-dimensional data defeats classic tests, which lose power, scale, or interpretability.

The New Physics Learning Machine adapts the Neyman-Pearson construction into a trainable tester. Two benchmarks demonstrate it: generative models trained on Gaussian mixtures of growing dimension, and FlowSim, a public end-to-end model that generates high-energy physics collision events. In both, the method certifies or rejects the generator and, crucially, points at the regions of the data space the generator models worst. That diagnostic feedback turns validation from a verdict into a repair guide for model builders.
arxiv-2511-09218:
Oishik Kar and Aswath Babu H combine photonics with quantum reservoir computing to forecast time series quickly and cheaply. Reservoir computing trains only a readout layer while a fixed dynamic system does the heavy lifting. Their hybrid design pairs fast, parallel light-based hardware with a quantum reservoir that models complex nonlinear dynamics.

The authors target bottlenecks in existing reservoir models: slow computation, high energy use, and sensitivity to noise. In simulations, their system predicts more accurately and faster than both classical and quantum-only models, they report. It also stays robust in noisy settings and scales to large data sets. Proposed uses include financial forecasting, industrial automation, smart sensor networks, and edge computing.
arxiv-2511-09618:
Seunghwan Lim and four co-authors use the FLAMINGO simulations to study cosmic variance. They ask how much it can mislead JWST surveys of early galaxies. Their simulation volume is a cubic gigaparsec, big enough to carve out over a thousand independent survey-sized fields. That statistical power lets them characterize the extremes of field-to-field variation at high redshift.

Around redshift six, halo counts in a field vary two to three times more than simple Poisson statistics predict, they find. They also uncover large-scale conformity: fields whose biggest galaxy is unusually massive show elevated star formation efficiency throughout the whole volume. The brightest galaxy in a field predicts that efficiency better than raw counts do. Survey footprints themselves amplify the detectable conformity signal.
arxiv-2511-09818:
Hanzhou Liu, Peng Jiang, Jia Huang, and Mi Lu propose Lumos3D, a framework for restoring three-dimensional scenes photographed in low light. Most earlier methods need camera poses computed in advance and optimize each scene separately, which limits real-world use. Lumos3D instead works in a single forward pass, taking unposed low-light images from several views and returning a brightened, structured scene.

A cross-illumination distillation scheme trains the model: a frozen teacher sees normal-light ground truth images and passes geometric knowledge to the student. A dedicated Lumos loss further improves quality inside the reconstructed Gaussian scene. Trained on one dataset, the system matched scene-specific methods on real-world data without any per-scene retraining, and its code is public.
arxiv-2511-10218:
Haolong Xiang and seven co-authors profile urban traffic by looking at the same sensor signals in three forms at once. Most traffic models use only the raw numerical readings, missing semantic structure that other views expose. Their framework, MTP, augments each signal into frequency and periodicity images for a visual branch, and into descriptive text for a language branch, alongside the numeric original.

Frequency-domain perceptrons learn from the numeric stream, while image and text branches add their own features. A hierarchical contrastive learning scheme then fuses the three branches' spectra into one representation. Across six real-world datasets the multimodal system beat state-of-the-art approaches at traffic prediction tasks, supporting the claim that cities are easier to read in several modalities at once.
arxiv-2511-10318:
Surangana Sengupta, Björn Kubala, Joachim Ankerhold, and Ciprian Padurariu lift a hard floor that has capped the cooling of tiny moving parts coupled to light. The standard sideband method cools such parts toward the quantum ground state, but backaction heat sets a lowest phonon count that no drive strength can beat. The team widens the standard semi-classical model to cover cavity systems with both passive and active nonlinear parts.

Their test case is a circuit system whose active drive comes from a Josephson junction. In that setup, they show, the leftover backaction heat can be wiped out in full, a result that beats schemes based on passive parts alone. Beating the floor would open a new level of quantum control over small moving systems, and the team argues the method can be built in the lab.
arxiv-2511-10418:
Yaqiao Zhu, Hongkai Wen, Mark Birkin, and Man Luo introduce CityVerse, a platform for testing large language models on city problems. Urban tasks range from spatial reasoning to forecasting, but scattered data sources and mismatched task definitions make fair testing hard. CityVerse pulls the data and tasks into one system for consistent evaluation.

Its data service unifies ten kinds of urban data, from maps and demographics to images, holding over thirty-eight million curated records. Forty-three tasks are organized into four levels, from basic perception up to decision making and interaction. A visual front end lets users fetch data in real time, stack map layers, and replay simulations, supporting repeatable and systematic testing.
arxiv-2511-10618:
Benjamin L. Badger and Matthew Neligeorge ask how close language models can get to a hard limit: the entropy intrinsic to language itself, which caps prediction accuracy and sets a floor for compression. Today's best compressors are large language models, but using them to estimate that entropy directly is computationally infeasible.

The authors introduce encoder-augmented causal decoder architectures that train more efficiently and compress better than causal transformers, even on modest hardware. Their models yield entropy estimates for each token. They also show that a model trained to approach its data's entropy, but not push past it, necessarily generalizes better than one trained to keep minimizing loss. Their experiments confirm that entropy-aware training improves generalization.
arxiv-2511-10918:
Arian Nadjimzadah proves a link between two hard problems about tube patterns in space. One problem deals with curved tubes tied to wave-like sums whose phase meets a test set by Bourgain. The other is the classic Kakeya problem about straight tubes that point in many directions. Both are studied here in three or more dimensions.

He shows that the sticky case for the curved problem reduces to the sticky case for the straight one. The proof rests on a new shape-based view of Bourgain's test, in terms of straightening curved tubes. He also builds examples where that straightening fails at larger scale, giving fresh tests for future work.
arxiv-2511-11018:
Xiaokun Luan, Zeming Wei, and their colleagues address a weakness in how language models produce structured output such as code or data records. Rule-based steering can force valid output, but the results often look alike, which limits testing and other uses where range matters. The authors first confirm that lack of range in a pilot study.

Their method tracks the path taken through the rule machine and steers the model toward fresh structural patterns it has not used yet. Tests show clear gains in both structural and content range at like cost. A case study on building varied test cases for open-source libraries shows the practical value.
arxiv-2511-11118:
Gerard Pons, Besim Bilalli, and Anna Queralt address how knowledge graph embeddings, the vector forms that let software reason over fact graphs, keep up as graphs gain new entries. Each update needs starting vectors for the new entries, and that start can sway both accuracy and training time. Small, frequent updates make the start choice matter even more.

Their informed start uses the graph's schema and the vectors learned so far, seeding each new entry from the classes it belongs to. The method drops into existing continual learning tools without change. Wide tests show better forecasts, stronger retention of old knowledge, and faster uptake of new facts.
arxiv-2511-11418:
Dara Varam, Diaa Abuhani, and their colleagues adapt optimal transport quantization to flow matching generative models, which learn to turn noise into data along straight paths. Such models train without simulation and sample deterministically, but they demand high-precision weights, which blocks use on small devices. Quantization shrinks weights to few bits, and the transport-based variant chooses the shrunken values to stay closest to the original weight spread.

Theory bounds how much generation quality can degrade, and tests on five data sets show the transport method keeps visual quality and latent stability down to two or three bits per weight. Rival uniform, piecewise, and logarithmic schemes fail at that level.
arxiv-2511-11718:
Sanjana Cheerla and three co-authors mine app reviews to map how social apps get used as weapons for harassment. Treating apps as sociotechnical systems, not neutral tools, they built a dataset of more than three million reviews covering eighteen hundred apps, where users often describe abuse in plain words.

Two patterns dominate: menacing, direct threats and intimidation, and profiling, gathering personal details to target someone. A computational model flags reviews describing each pattern with high recall. Further analysis explores who the reported abusers are and what separates predatory apps' review trails from ordinary complaints, giving platform designers concrete signals for intervention.
arxiv-2511-11818:
Steven Giacalone and five co-authors locate the mass where giant planets give way to brown dwarfs. The fingerprint is the metal content of host stars. Planets built bottom-up, by a core gathering gas, prefer metal-rich stars. Brown dwarfs formed top-down, by direct collapse, barely care about metals.

A hierarchical Bayesian model is applied to survey data. The data come from the California Legacy Survey, a uniform radial velocity survey. The host metal pattern shifts at a companion mass near twenty-seven Jupiter masses. The companions sit one to five astronomical units out. That transition mass shows where formation physics changes character. It is a key calibration point for theories of planets and brown dwarfs.
arxiv-2511-11918:
Wieger Wesselink and four co-authors write down the full math of multilayer perceptrons in batch matrix form. That is the way practitioners actually compute. Textbooks rarely state it in full. Most give gradients sample by sample. Or they defer to automatic differentiation, leaving the structure implicit.

Forward and backward equations are derived for all standard layers. Advanced layers, including batch normalization and softmax, are covered too. The result is a rigorous, implementation-ready specification. Explicit batch form matters where structure must be analyzed by hand. Sparse neural networks are the model case. The reference lets a careful implementer check each index and transpose.
arxiv-2511-12218:
Lazaros Kanellopoulos investigates how stable the ruin probability is in the classic insurance risk model, where ruin means a firm's reserves fall below zero. Small changes in the model should not cause wild jumps in key quantities if the model is to be trusted. He studies continuity for ruin probability and for the deficit at the moment of ruin.

The proofs use properties of contractive integral operators. Results are then applied to a version of the surplus process with added diffusion, where ruin probability involves a compound geometric distribution mixed with a diffusion term. A continuity bound for that distribution and an iterative way to approximate it are given, with numerical examples.
arxiv-2511-12318:
Ilias Cherkaoui and Indrakshi Dey propose adding a quantum nonlocality check to Kyber, a lattice-based key exchange method meant to resist quantum attacks. Kyber's safety rests on a hard lattice problem, but the authors argue that computational hardness alone may face hybrid classical-quantum attacks. Purely quantum schemes, meanwhile, remain impractical at scale.

Their design embeds a CHSH entanglement test, using shared particle pairs, directly into the key exchange phase. Formal arguments claim an attacker must either solve the underlying lattice problem or a hard quantum complexity problem. Readers should note this is a proposed construction with stated proofs, presented by the authors as a first of its kind.
arxiv-2511-12518:
Zhongchao Yi and seven co-authors present DualGR, a generative retrieval system for large-scale short-video recommendation, where candidates must be picked from a massive catalogue under strict time limits. Generative retrieval encodes items as tokens and decodes candidates step by step. In live feeds it is hurt by clashes between long- and short-term interests, noise in token generation, and ignored feedback from items shown but not clicked.

DualGR routes long- and short-term interests through separate branches with selective activation. Its decoder constrains fine-level choices inside the current coarse group for speed and noise control. A new loss also treats unclicked exposures as negatives at the coarse level, so stale interests fade in time.
arxiv-2511-12718:
Yaniv Fogel and Meir Feder study batch learning when the data sequence is fixed, not random, using log-loss as the score. In this individual setting, sample statistics do not apply, and regret guarantees have been hard to obtain. The authors propose leave-one-out regret as the yardstick: how much worse a learner does than the best hypothesis that has seen every outcome except one. They then compute the best possible value of that regret for several hypothesis classes.

For simple multinomial models, the minimal regret has a clean leading term, about twice the size of the random-data counterpart. More broadly, every class of finite VC dimension is learnable in this setting, with regret that shrinks as data grows, and matching lower bounds hold for some classes. The results are the first showing universal batch learning with log-loss is possible without randomness in the data.
arxiv-2511-12818:
Brianna N Ryan and three co-authors test an unusual idea for nuclear security: using neutrinos to find smuggled radioactive material. Neutrinos pour out of radioactive sources but almost never interact, which has long made them seem useless for detection. A newly observed interaction, coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering, has a much larger cross-section than other neutrino channels. The authors ask whether superconducting detectors using that channel could spot trafficked sources, computing the smallest detectable activity under ideal, background-free conditions at high confidence.

They run the numbers for four commonly smuggled isotopes. Only cesium-137 sources above the petabecquerel level would be findable this way; the method does not reach the other three. The verdict is narrow but real: one important isotope is within reach. The same framework can evaluate other nuclear security problems.
arxiv-2511-13018:
S. Sairam, Sara Girdhar, and Shivam Soni take apart the R-learner, a popular method for estimating who benefits from a treatment, and find its last stage is where network applications live or die.
