The R-learner is prized because errors in its preliminary nuisance models do little damage, but it assumes the final model that predicts treatment effects is well chosen. On graph data, where a person's effect depends on their position in a network, the authors ran a large empirical dissection varying both stages.

The verdict is stark. A final stage that ignores the graph fails completely, with large errors at overwhelming statistical significance, no matter how powerful the graph neural networks used earlier. Their end-to-end Graph R-Learner succeeds and beats a strong graph-based baseline. They also trace a subtler bottleneck to information being squashed through hub nodes.
arxiv-2511-13218:
Xiaodong He, Xiao Wang, and Jianda Wu improve a computational method for lattice models that have been deformed away from exact solvability. Hamiltonian truncation studies a quantum system in a finite basis drawn from a solvable relative, but brute-force truncation wastes basis states and accrues error. Their hybrid integrates the numerical renormalization group with a truncated integrable spectrum: the renormalization group folds high-energy states into the basis in a controlled way. The hybrid extends it more effectively and cuts errors significantly.

They demonstrate on two standard models, an Ising chain in a magnetic field and a quantum Ising ladder. The computed dynamical structure factors capture the essential low-energy physics, including the famous E8 excitation spectrum of the field-driven Ising chain and the corresponding excitations of the ladder.
arxiv-2511-13318:
Peihao Li introduces LinkXplore, an open framework for gathering blockchain data without paying steep provider fees. Large studies often need enhanced provider interfaces sold at high tiers, which shuts out groups with small budgets. There was also no shared, flexible system for adding new kinds of on-chain analysis.

LinkXplore reads raw data straight from chain queries and streams, then processes it through a simple interface and backend. Any chain data type can be plugged into the framework in the same way. Code and the dataset used in the project are public, giving researchers and builders a low-cost path to high-quality chain data.
arxiv-2511-13418:
Allaa Boutaleb and 3 co-authors frame multi-table search over data lakes as an iterative process and propose a fast greedy method for it. Answering open questions often needs facts joined across several tables, so results must be both relevant and joinable. Exact optimization guarantees coherence but costs too much on large lakes.

Their Greedy Join-Aware Retrieval method balances relevance, coverage, and joinability at each step. Across five standard question-to-SQL benchmarks it matched the exact method's retrieval quality while running from four to four hundred times faster, depending on the setup. The authors argue iterative heuristics offer a practical, clear, and flexible path for large-scale table search.
arxiv-2511-13718:
Philip Boyle Smith and Joe Davighi introduce bosonisation cohomology, a tool that separates two operations often treated as one: gauging fermion parity and summing over spin structures. A theory can be free of parity anomalies yet still fail under spin summation, and no standard group marked that gap. Their new groups are built to hold exactly those cases.

A sequence of cobordism groups measures the failure, and for a point target they compute the groups in every dimension. Nontrivial values appear only in dimensions two past a multiple of four, driven by gravitational anomalies, with the first cases computed explicitly. A general formula covers all dimensions, and a supergravity example shows one class being trivialized.
arxiv-2511-14118:
Md Mosharaf Hossan, Rifat Ara Tasnim, and Farjana Z Eishita test a gamified virtual reality treatment idea for mysophobia, the fear of germs. Exposure therapy works by facing the feared thing in controlled doses, and VR can stage contamination scenes safely. The team built a VR game with a simulated sneeze as the key exposure event.

Seven participants played a baseline version and a sneeze version, with mood and anxiety measured by standard questionnaires. The sneeze version slightly raised negative affect and anxiety and lowered positive affect, but none of the changes reached statistical significance. Small samples and non-clinical players likely explain that. The authors frame the study as groundwork for larger trials.
arxiv-2511-14918:
Zefan Yang, Ge Wang, and three co-authors build X-WIN, a chest X-ray model that learns three-dimensional anatomy from a flat image. Chest radiographs are cheap and common, but a two-dimensional projection stacks structures on top of each other, which hides depth cues. The team teaches the model using chest CT scans, which do carry full volume information.

The model learns to predict X-ray views of the same chest from new angles, inside a learned latent space. A guided contrastive loss ties together views that belong to the same patient, so shared anatomy is captured. A model that has internalized body structure this way should read ordinary X-rays more reliably for diagnosis.
arxiv-2511-15218:
Byoung-Hee Kwon develops deep learning systems that decode complex imagined movements from scalp brain waves, aiming at richer brain-computer links. The work proposes complex visual imagery as the mental task. Instead of imagining one simple motion, the user pictures detailed upper limb movements. Richer imagery should carry more distinct signals for a control system to read.

Kwon's design fuses measures of how brain regions work together with a combined network tuned for EEG signals. It targets robust decoding of the imagined movements from recordings taken outside the skull. Success would stretch EEG systems toward tasks such as guiding a robotic arm by thought alone.
arxiv-2511-15318:
Plouton Grammatikos, Ali Mohamed Ali, and Fabrizio Sossan compute price signals that nudge flexible electricity users to protect their local grid. Homes and firms that both consume and produce power, called prosumers, can shift their usage, but only an incentive will make them shift at the right moments. The grid operator needs prices that prevent voltage violations and line congestion without demanding everyone's private data.

The method reads prices out of a distributed optimization algorithm, so coordination happens while sensitive details stay local. The operator can reshape an existing flat or time-of-use tariff dynamically instead of inventing a new one. Hardware tests on a small low-voltage network validate the scheme in practice, not just in simulation.
arxiv-2511-15418:
Arjun Gangwar, Kaousheik Jayakumar, and S. Umesh describe multilingual speech recognition systems for Indian languages built for a shared challenge. Systems must predict both the language and dialect of each utterance among eight languages and thirty-three dialects. Both challenge tracks restrict extra data, requiring largely from scratch systems in one track. Their core idea uses a multi decoder design.

A phonemic common label set serves as an intermediate representation between audio and text. That step improves performance in phonemic space over the baseline. Further methods preserve the gain when converting back to normal scripts. Their systems beat the baseline for three languages on error rates. They also achieve the highest language and dialect identification accuracy among all participants.
arxiv-2511-15518:
C. Katsavrias and four co-authors statistically study periodic density structures in the solar wind using Solar Orbiter data closer to the Sun. These structures are trains of density variations lasting minutes to hours. They have been well studied near Earth, but their behavior nearer the Sun was largely unknown. The team build a public list of events between a third and the full Earth Sun distance.

Detection combines multitaper and wavelet methods under an established procedure. Results show how radial length scales are distributed and how they shift with distance. The structures travel outward with the ambient slow wind in the studied sample. A public catalog plus radial trends help theorists explain how mesoscale solar wind structure forms and evolves.
arxiv-2511-15718:
Chen Yang, Ran Le, and six co-authors release ToolMind, a large data set for training language model agents to use external tools. Such agents solve real tasks through software tools, but strong training trajectories are scarce. Most synthetic dialogue data are checked only as whole trajectories, so single bad steps slip through and teach errors that compound during training.

ToolMind combines many synthetic instances built from over twenty thousand tools with augmented open-source data. A function graph based on parameter links guides realistic simulated conversations among user, assistant, and tools. Fine-grained filtering then removes faulty steps at the turn level while keeping self-correction signals. Models fine-tuned on ToolMind improved significantly over baselines on several benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-15918:
Indrila Ganguly and Ying Huang design a sequential test to judge whether a new cancer biomarker adds value to an old one. Added value is often a gain in sensitivity at a fixed specificity, key for early detection. Their setting uses a central biorepository with limited specimens, shared across labs to validate many candidate markers, so wasting samples is costly.

Their two-stage group sequential design allows early stopping for futility or success, saving specimens. Theory built on a logistic working model stays valid even if that model is wrong, keeping the method robust. A rotating group plan supports checks across labs. Tests confirm error control and lean sample use, and a use case draws on multicenter pancreatic cancer data.
arxiv-2511-16018:
Emanuel Silva and five co-authors propose SpellForger, a game where players create custom spells by writing natural language prompts. AI in games usually generates content behind the scenes. Here generation is the core co creation mechanic itself. A supervised BERT model interprets each prompt and maps it to a spell template.

Spell parameters like damage, cost, and effects are balanced automatically to preserve competitive integrity. The game runs in a common engine with a Python AI backend. The expected outcome is a functional prototype with real time spell generation. Player creativity sits at the center of the gameplay loop. The project tests whether language driven creation can stay fun without breaking game balance.
arxiv-2511-16218:
Joana Reuss, Ekaterina Gikalo, and Marco Körner tackle a mismatch that hurts crop mapping from few examples. Real farm data follow a long tail, with a few common crops and many rare ones, yet training sets are often built evenly balanced. A model trained that way meets a shifted label mix in the field and loses accuracy.

Their answer is Dirichlet Prior Augmentation, which trains the model under random label skews drawn from a Dirichlet distribution, mimicking the unknown real mix in advance. Tests show the method moves the decision boundary in the right way and steadies training. It acts like a dynamic feature regularizer and improves how few-shot crop classifiers handle real conditions.
arxiv-2511-16518:
Xiaoshuai Hao and 43 co-authors release MiMo-Embodied, an open foundation model built to serve both autonomous driving and embodied AI, the two fields that put learned models in physical motion. Most models specialize in one domain; this report tests whether a single model can lead in both at once.

MiMo-Embodied sets new records on 17 embodied AI benchmarks covering task planning, affordance prediction, and spatial understanding, and also leads on 12 driving benchmarks spanning perception, status prediction, and planning. The authors credit multi-stage training, curated data, and chain-of-thought plus reinforcement fine-tuning. They argue the two domains transfer positively to each other, and they publish the model, code, and a detailed account of the design for others to build on.
arxiv-2511-16918:
Yuichi Yoshida and Zihan Zhang study maximum matching, the task of pairing up as many vertices of a graph as possible, through a new lens: sensitivity. Sensitivity measures how much an algorithm's output can change when a single edge is deleted. A low-sensitivity algorithm gives nearly the same answer on nearly the same graph, which matters when graphs change over time or data must stay private.

By sampling matchings from a Gibbs distribution, the authors build a fast approximation algorithm whose sensitivity depends only on the graph's maximum degree. They then give still faster versions for planar and bipartite graphs. For graphs with no degree limit, their method beats the best earlier sensitivity bound. The work links sampling methods to stable, change-resistant algorithms.
arxiv-2511-17518:
Siddharth Agarwal, Maria A Rodriguez, and Rajkumar Buyya present Serv-Drishti, an open-source simulator that shows how a serverless computing platform handles requests. Serverless systems hide their machinery, so cold starts, scaling, and routing choices can be hard to grasp. The tool follows a request from the entry gateway through a dispatcher to running function copies on machines with limited room.

Users can change platform settings, swap routing and placement plans, and inject failures to see how the system answers under load or faults. That makes the tool suited to side-by-side comparison, not just display. For students and platform teams alike, it turns hidden behaviour into something that can be watched, measured, and debated before real systems are changed.
arxiv-2511-17718:
Nazanin Mirhosseini and Jie Luo study error in a shared channel where two users send messages without telling each other, or the receiver, which code they picked for each message. The receiver mainly wants the first user's message but may decode both when that helps.

They treat timed and untimed sending in a unified way, using groups of sub decoders that sort each case as normal, borderline, or a collision. For both settings they derive upper bounds on a combined error measure that mixes wrong decoding, collisions, and missed detection. The bounds give a shared yardstick for random access design.
arxiv-2511-17818:
Aishwarya Mandyam, Kalyani Limaye, Barbara E Engelhardt, and Emily Alsentzer propose using language models to strengthen off-policy evaluation. The practice of grading a treatment policy from past records before it is ever used. In high-stakes fields like medicine, such grading is a safety gate, but it is limited by how much of the space of past decisions the records cover. Expert labels for what might have happened under other treatments could widen that cover, yet they cost too much to gather at scale.

Their method, APRIL, guides a language model with domain knowledge to predict how key clinical features would evolve under alternate treatments. Known reward rules then turn those predicted features into counterfactual notes. The team first tests how well several models predict clinical features in two patient groups.
arxiv-2511-18018:
Hanwen Zhang and three co-authors model blisters that form under ice sheets when a lake on the surface drains rapidly downward. The water lifts the ice elastically and briefly changes its speed, but standard drainage models, built on cavities and channels, cannot capture such fast events.

Their unified framework couples blister evolution directly with the subglacial drainage system. Simulations motivated by winter drainage observations show seasonal contrast. Summer drainages make short lived blisters that leak into existing channels, while winter drainages make lasting blisters that creep and carry most of the water. Viscosity and a leakage length govern the behavior.
arxiv-2511-18618:
Mirza Raquib and seven co-authors sort Bangla news headlines by topic and by feeling in one joint model. A headline tells both what a story covers, politics or sports and so on, and its tone, glad, sad, or flat. Sorting both at once helps readers scan a flood of news fast.

Their hybrid stacks three parts: a BERT base that reads context, a convolutional layer that spots local cues, and a two way recurrent layer that tracks order. Tests run on a set of about nine thousand Bangla headlines, the first set used for both tasks at once, the team note. The joint build is pitched as state of the art for this pair. Bangla tools lag English ones, so gains here widen access.
arxiv-2511-18718:
Omar Garib, Jayaprakash Kambhampaty, Olivia Pinon Fischer, and Dimitri Mavris introduce AIRHILT, a simulation testbed for aviation conflict detection that keeps pilots and controllers in the loop. It brings together radio communications, camera views, and transponder data in one lightweight platform built on an open game engine.

Cases cover terminal and en route conflicts, including communication and procedural errors, and standard links let researchers swap speech, vision, and thinking models easily. A reference pipeline combining tuned speech recognition, visual detection, conflict logic, and a language model warns of runway overlaps in under eight seconds on average. The environment and cases are openly shared.
arxiv-2511-18818: Georgi Bebrov proposes combining quantum key distribution with systematic polar coding. Quantum key distribution lets several parties establish a shared cryptographic key using quantum signals, while polar coding corrects errors in the exchange. Bebrov works in the finite-size regime, where the key is built from a limited number of signals rather than an endless stream. He reports that, with a lower-error-rate quantum channel, the combined method obtains key rates greater than those of the standard BB84 protocol and its efficient version.
arxiv-2511-18918:
Qingchao Shen and seven co-authors generate tests that stress the optimization stage of deep learning compilers. Compilers tune a model graph for each chip, and that tuning is their core act. Past test tools miss it, since a test that truly triggers a set optimization path is hard to craft.

OATest mines patterns from documented optimization tests and grafts them into seed graphs. An edge reuse trick welds pattern and context tight, so the optimization path must fire. The tests then roam more paths than seeds alone reach. Compiler bugs hide in rare path blends, so coverage of paths is the point. Sound compilers guard every deployed model downstream.
arxiv-2511-19118:
Juan-Jose Guzman-Landa, Jesus Vazquez-Osorio, Juan-Manuel Torres-Moreno, and six co-authors build a symbolic algorithm, written in Perl, that unifies the varied spellings of Nahuatl. Nahuatl is an Indigenous language of Mexico written in several competing orthographies. Consistent spelling matters for building and searching text collections in the language.

Their model encodes linguistic rules as symbolic regular expressions, building on their earlier sentence analysis tools and a corpus of texts in multiple spellings. A manual evaluation protocol tests the unified sentences in a semantic task, judging whether meaning survives unification. Evaluators gave encouraging results for most of the features the team hoped the unified text would keep.
arxiv-2511-19218:
Xurui Li and four co-authors let attack and defense models for language model safety train against each other. Jailbreak attacks evolve quickly, while defenses are often static, so the two sides rarely improve together. Their framework, ACE-Safety, optimizes both models in one loop.

A group-aware tree search explores jailbreak strategies and produces varied adversarial examples that expose weak points. A second method then trains the attack and defense models on those hard cases through a curriculum of rising difficulty. Across several benchmarks the paired approach beats existing attack and defense methods, and the authors present it as a path toward safety that keeps pace with new threats.
arxiv-2511-19518:
Zhaoqi Xu and five co-authors shrink vision-language models with a pruning method grounded in information theory. These models keep growing, which strains deployment, and most compression relies on rough importance scores with no promise that key information survives. Their framework, InfoPrune, frames pruning as a trade-off from the information bottleneck principle.

Each attention head is scored by an entropy-based effective rank, and a statistical distance measures how far the pruned structure drifts from the original. Two schemes follow: trained head pruning guided by an information loss goal, and a training-free variant. The unified rule weighs sparsity against keeping task-relevant meaning.
arxiv-2511-20018:
Sian Heesom-Green, Jonathan Shock, and Geoff Nitschke test what energy costs do to the evolution of neural complexity. The cognitive buffer idea says larger brains evolved to cope with changing conditions, but big brains are costly to run. The authors evolve artificial neural networks for reinforcement learning agents under varying seasons and energy prices.

Under energy limits, stronger seasonality led to smaller networks, which fits the expensive brain idea better than the buffer idea: seasonal swings cut net energy intake and so capped brain size. Structural complexity mostly followed size, while energy costs pushed evolution toward more efficient networks. The simulation results back energy-aware design for both biology and robots.
arxiv-2511-20118:
Degenne, Ledvinka, Marion, and Pfaffelhuber rebuild Brownian motion inside a proof assistant. Their 2025 paper formalizes the process in Lean. Brownian motion underpins modern probability theory everywhere. Every proof step is machine-checked in full. Lean's library, Mathlib, supplied the measure theory base.

Several major theorems had to be built first. The Carathéodory extension theorem constructs measures from simpler data. The Kolmogorov extension theorem assembles processes from finite pieces. Gaussian measures on Banach spaces were developed too. Path continuity comes via the Kolmogorov-Chentsov theorem. Together these pieces yield a checked Brownian motion. The definition demands continuous paths almost surely. Finite-dimensional distributions must match Gaussian laws exactly. The work extends Mathlib's probability infrastructure greatly. Future work can build on checked foundations. Formalized mathematics gains one of its central objects. Errors in foundational proofs become machine-detectable here.
arxiv-2511-20618:
Yosri, Gavinsky, and Maslov shrink the quantum circuits behind finite-field arithmetic. Their 2025 paper optimizes multiplication and division in GF(2^m) fields. Such operations underpin quantum algorithms from factoring to proofs of quantumness. Older circuits needed gate counts growing with m squared. Their new multiplier needs no extra ancilla qubits at all.

The key step multiplies by one fixed polynomial cheaply. A linear-size circuit for that step unlocks the whole speedup. Constant multiplication CNOT counts drop by over one hundred times. That holds at field sizes used in real cryptography. Division also gets faster through clever polynomial choice. Irreducible polynomials are picked to make squaring cheap as well. Toffoli counts fall alongside CNOT counts in their tests. A side result warns about square roots of reversible circuits. A root can demand deeper circuits than the original map. Asymptotic gains and practical wins arrive together here.
arxiv-2511-20718:
Chenliang Li and a large team diagnose in 2025 why a training method keeps collapsing when it teaches language models to act over many turns. The method, proximal policy optimisation, trains models token by token, yet multi-turn tasks unfold stage by stage, one turn at a time. Li's team pins the instability on two mismatches: token-level importance sampling, correcting reused data at the wrong grain, and faulty advantage scores for rarely visited state-action pairs, producing wild updates.

Turn-level importance sampling scores whole turns instead of tokens, and clipping-bias correction downweights the unreliable off-policy samples that poison gradients. Combining both gives ST-PPO; using the correction alone gives S-PPO. On multi-turn search tasks spanning general, multi-hop, and medical multiple-choice questions, both variants prevented the collapses seen in large-model training, kept clipping ratios lower, and beat standard token-level training.
arxiv-2511-20818:
Arpita Mitra, Debangshu Mukherjee, and Tung Tran construct in 2025 a non-relativistic version of chiral higher-spin gravity, a theory of massless fields. Starting from the four-dimensional anti-de Sitter theory, they apply a Lifshitz deformation, an anisotropic rescaling of space and time, then a null reduction along a light-cone direction. The result is a massive higher-spin theory in deformed three-dimensional anti-de Sitter space.

Curiously, the new theory's interaction vertices are less constrained than the original's: too few generators remain to fix the couplings. Expecting high-spin interactions to fade, they propose an approximate mass-spin relation bridging both regimes, and confirm suppression at large spin. They conjecture the holographic dual is a 2D Landau-Ginzburg theory in light-cone gauge. It would describe a two-fluid system, confined to one spatial dimension, with a lambda point as in superfluid helium.
arxiv-2511-20918:
Pabitra Ray, with a co-author, extends in 2025 the classical soft photon theorems to every order, for scatterings that involve magnetic as well as electric charges. When charged or dyonic particles scatter, the emitted waveform at late and early times follows universal rules set only by the momenta and charges of the particles involved. Earlier work fixed the constant term and the first falling corrections. Using electric and magnetic potentials, the authors compute the tower of subleading terms.

They give step-by-step formulas for the trajectory coefficients and for both the electric and magnetic waveforms. The expansion is covariant under electric-magnetic duality: the two waveforms rotate into each other as an SO(2) doublet, a stiff check on the formalism. For two-body scattering they resum the series into closed expressions in both the time and frequency domains. The results complete the classical picture of soft radiation with monopoles.
arxiv-2511-21018:
Antonis Psistakis's master's thesis, submitted at the University of Crete in 2019, makes remote memory access survive its own page faults. In cluster computing, RDMA engines copy data between machines without the operating system, for speed. Standard engines dodge faults by pinning memory in place, which complicates programming and still fails under features like transparent huge pages. Working in the ExaNeSt supercomputing project, Psistakis built a fault-handling mechanism for its DMA engine instead.

When the ARM system memory unit detects a fault, the hardware-software system resolves it, then requests retransmission if needed. The fix touched the Linux SMMU driver, a new software library, the DMA engine's hardware, and its transfer scheduler. Tests ran on the project's Quad-FPGA daughter board carrying Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ chips. The thesis compares the mechanism with pinning and pre-faulting alternatives and argues fault tolerance frees programmers from pinning bookkeeping altogether.
arxiv-2511-21118:
Pius Onobhayedo and Paul Osemudiame Oamen design in 2025 an architecture for federated learning that needs no trusted coordinator. Billions of edge devices could train shared models on private data. But today's aggregators merge updates with no accountability, rewards invite gaming, coordination serialises state changes, and governance can be rewritten later. Storing weights on-chain is no fix either: Bitcoin clears about 7 transactions per second and Ethereum only 15 to 30, far below edge scale.

Four mechanisms answer the four gaps. Crypto receipts prove each aggregation was computed correctly. A geometric novelty measure pays contributors for genuinely new information, blunting incentive gaming. Parallel object ownership lets updates proceed concurrently, giving linear scalability. Time-locked policies stop after-the-fact rule changes. The authors are candid that the work is a design, not an implementation: a blueprint for verifiable, incentive-aligned collaborative intelligence, offered for others to build.
arxiv-2511-21218:
Steven Wang, Kyle Hunt, Shaojie Tang, and Kenneth Joseph ask in 2025 whether a large language model can stand in for human survey subjects after training on just a small pilot sample. Models used raw tend to flatten human diversity, misjudge minority subgroups, and state beliefs their actions do not match. The team tested finetuning as a fix, using a behavioral experiment about disclosing personal information.

Wang and his coauthors find that finetuning on the small human sample improves variety, subgroup alignment, and belief-action coherence compared with the base model. Yet even the best finetuned model failed to reproduce the original study's regression coefficients, the numbers summarizing how causes link to outcomes. The authors conclude that simulated subjects suit early prototyping, like testing survey drafts, but cannot replace human participants in formal statistical analysis.
arxiv-2511-21818:
Pacuraru and colleagues study what happens to a star's magnetic field when the star is torn apart by a supermassive black hole, an event called a tidal disruption. The shredded star forms a long stream of gas, half escaping and half falling back. Using simulations plus a simpler analytic model, they track how the inherited field stretches along the stream.

They find that if the star's field starts stronger than 10,000 gauss, magnetic pressure becomes important in a share of the stream within a year and makes the stream puff up. In that phase the stream's thickness grows with distance from the black hole following a simple power law. Widths can end up ten to a hundred times larger than in models without magnetism. A thicker stream could brighten radio emission from the escaping tail and change later shocks.
arxiv-2511-22118:
Dai, Bouras, Jia, and Mechtaev, computer scientists, fix a subtle flaw in caching large language model responses. Caching saves money and time, but a naive cache returns the same response to a repeated prompt, destroying the statistical independence that metrics like Pass@k, uncertainty estimates. Program-repair loops depend on, since those methods need genuinely fresh samples each time they ask the same question of the model.

Their design pattern, Mnimi, encodes the independence requirement in the type of the model reference itself: repeatable references replay identical response sequences, while independent references yield fresh ones. Users can transform between the types as an algorithm's scope demands. Implemented in Python with decorators and iterators, it is demonstrated on SpecFix. An automated program specification repair tool, where it improved reproducibility and debugging while cutting time and cost without breaking statistical correctness.
arxiv-2511-22418:
Han, Alsusa, and Al-Dweik analyse a wireless system where drones communicate with a base station and reveal their positions through the same signals. In this setup, the station estimates each drone's location from pilot symbols, rebuilds the channel from those estimates, and decodes data with a zero-forcing or minimum mean-square error receiver. Since the channel is rebuilt from estimated positions, location errors leak into communication quality, measured by the symbol error rate.

Exact error-rate formulas are out of reach, so the authors derive approximations combining Neumann and Taylor expansions. One drone's error rate, they show, is affected by every drone's location errors, not just its. Zero-forcing is unaffected by range estimation errors, while the mean-square error receiver is not, and both are most sensitive to angle errors. Under large errors, zero-forcing can perform worse than maximal-ratio combining. Simulations confirm the formulas.
arxiv-2511-22718:
Abarca-Ramírez and colleagues make distant optical waveguides talk to each other through an intermediary. Evanescent coupling between waveguides normally dies exponentially with distance, capping how far apart components on a photonic chip can sit. The team instead couples single-mode waveguides resonantly to photonic molecules, extended multi-waveguide structures whose higher-order states are hard to excite in individual guides, all written with femtosecond lasers in glass.

Tuning geometry, wavelength, and propagation distance, they achieve efficient resonant excitation of the molecules' higher-orbital states. The molecules relay the coupling: strong coupling is demonstrated between waveguides 127 micrometres apart, very distant by photonic standards. Long photonic molecules are proposed as long-distance links for fibre-based chips. Applied to a one-dimensional lattice, the long-range interaction produces topological edge states arising from third-order next-neighbour coupling, physics normally out of reach in evanescent systems.
arxiv-2511-22818:
Kumar, Rajawat, and Ntoutsi test whether language models can faithfully summarise therapy sessions without drifting off meaning. Mental health is a low-resource domain where models hallucinate, contradict themselves, and flatten nuance, a failure mode the authors call semantic drift. They focus on motivational interviewing, a counselling style with an integrity framework, MITI, scoring evocation, collaboration, autonomy, direction, empathy, and non-judgmental attitude.

Using expert-annotated dialogues as ground truth, three models, DeepSeek, ChatGPT, and Gemini, generate summaries and annotate sessions along those six dimensions, as multi-class classification under zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting. ChatGPT one-shot aligned closest with expert ground truth, while Gemini one-shot deviated most overall. Beyond the rankings, the study contributes a two-stage annotation scheme and an annotated dataset for a field short on both. It also gives guidance on prompting strategies keeping summaries anchored to what was actually said.
arxiv-2511-23018:
Yama and colleagues measured the chemistry of Luhman 16AB, the nearest brown dwarf binary, a pair of failed stars whose atmospheres can be studied in fine detail. Using high-resolution spectra from the CRIRES instrument on the Very Large Telescope, they ran atmospheric retrievals, fitting model atmospheres to the data to extract element abundances and the temperature profile with height.

For both dwarfs they find a carbon-to-oxygen ratio of about 0.67, modestly above the solar value of 0.59 quoted in their comparison. And they stress-test the result against the main systematic errors. The choice among three carbon monoxide line lists, the catalogues of spectral lines used in the fit, shifted answers by about 7 percent and dominated the uncertainty. A flexible Gaussian-process temperature profile and the dwarfs' known brightness variability mattered less. This makes the pair a firmer anchor for comparing brown dwarfs with giant exoplanets.
arxiv-2511-23218:
Ray and colleagues build a systematic recipe for lattices whose every energy band is perfectly flat while time-reversal symmetry is explicitly broken. That combination had not been systematized by flat-band research. Flat bands trap particles in compact localized states through destructive interference. And adding broken time symmetry lets those trapped states carry circulating currents, which ordinary flat-band constructions cannot produce.

Starting from disconnected polygonal plaquettes threaded by magnetic flux, they apply local entangling unitary transformations that preserve the flux pattern. They generate genuine all-bands-flat lattices with nontrivial hopping in one, two, and three dimensions. The compact localized states spread over both the plaquettes and the auxiliary sites the transformation introduces. And they host localized circulatory currents whose size grows with the applied flux. An extension of the framework also covers lattices mixing flat and dispersive bands with orthogonal or non-orthogonal localized states.
arxiv-2511-23318:
Zhang rethinks how to measure a signal built from many overlapping complex exponentials. He argues that engineers often need global summaries rather than every component's amplitude, frequency, and phase. Estimating all components invites permutation ambiguity, model-order headaches, and Fisher matrix inversions that become prohibitive beyond about fifty components. He defines a few sum-parameters instead: total amplitude, a power-weighted frequency, and a composite phase quantity.

For these quantities he derives exact closed-form Cramér-Rao bounds, the lowest variance any unbiased estimator can reach, under both deterministic and stochastic signal models. He shows the frequency sum-parameter automatically pools power across all components. His Efficient Global Estimation Method runs in time independent of the component count and beat Zoom-Interpolated FFT and Root-MUSIC in simulations across signal-to-noise ratios. In 2,000 Monte Carlo trials, it hugs the theoretical bounds even with only 250 observations.
arxiv-2511-23418:
Wolski and colleagues analyze the semiclassical limit of the derivative nonlinear Schrödinger equation. A wave equation used for Alfvén waves in plasmas and in nonlinear optics, when the starting wave is periodic rather than localized. For a class of periodic single-lobe initial conditions they compute the spectrum of the associated scattering problem numerically and jointly build a formal WKB expansion. The standard semiclassical approximation, for its eigenfunctions.

As the semiclassical parameter shrinks, the spectrum becomes confined to the real and imaginary axes. And the number of spectral bands in the key interval grows like one over that parameter while each band shrinks toward a point. The conclusion is that every excitation becomes an effective soliton in the limit. And direct numerical simulations plus independent spectrum calculations agree excellently with the analytical predictions for band locations and sizes in the paper.
arxiv-2512-00018:
Arthur Ji Sung Baek and Geoffrey Martin present X-SYCON, a swarm design inspired by xylem, the water channels in plants. Their multi-agent system coordinates without planning or communication between agents. Instead, incidents and hazards write into scalar fields that spread and fade over time.

Agents simply climb a local utility built from those fields, with light rules against crowding. Coordination emerges from the passive field dynamics, aimed at dynamic disaster environments. Communication-free control is valuable exactly when networks fail during a crisis. Light anti-congestion and separation rules keep agents from piling onto the same spot once the fields draw them in.
arxiv-2512-00218:
Language models that show their chain of thought give safety monitors something to watch. Matt MacDermott, Qiyao Wei, Rada Djoneva, and Francis Rhys Ward study how training incentives affect that monitorability in 2025. Visible reasoning could reveal undesirable goals, such as pursuing harmful objectives.

How faithfully the written reasoning reflects the model's real process may depend on training choices. Incentives that reward certain outputs could teach models to hide or sanitize their reasoning. The study is AI safety research: it asks whether a promising oversight tool stays trustworthy once training pressure is applied. Monitorability is valuable only while the visible reasoning stays connected to the real process.
arxiv-2512-00518:
The Hydra I galaxy cluster, also called Abell 1060, is a nearby cluster that sits between types. Alpish Srivastava and co-authors present results from the SRG/eROSITA all-sky survey in 2025, studying the cluster's hot gas. Hydra I shows properties between cool core and non-cool core clusters.

Little was known about its gas properties and large-scale structure beyond its inner region. All-sky X-ray survey data let the team trace the cluster's faint outskirts, where it merges with the cosmic web. Such outskirts record how clusters keep growing today, making Hydra I a useful nearby laboratory. eROSITA's all-sky coverage is what brings a nearby cluster's faint outskirts into view.
arxiv-2512-00618:
Graph indices compress a network's shape into a single number that predicts chemical or structural properties. Kinkar Chandra Das and Akbar Ali study the augmented Sombor index of graphs in 2025. The index is built from vertex degrees across the graph's edges.

For a connected graph with more than two vertices, each edge contributes a term involving the degrees of its endpoints. Bounding such an index tells chemists which molecular structures maximize or minimize it. Degree-based indices are cheap to compute, so sharp bounds guide screening of large compound libraries before costly experiments. Sombor-type indices weight edges by the degrees at both ends. Connected graphs are the natural domain, since isolated pieces would trivialize the index.
arxiv-2512-00818:
Haozhen Gong and a large team introduce Med-CMR in a 2025 paper on medical AI. Large multimodal models are entering clinical work, where they must reason over images, text, and patient facts together. How well they handle complex medical reasoning is still unclear.

Med-CMR is a benchmark built to test that reasoning in fine detail. It joins visual evidence from medical images with clinical logic, the chain of thinking a doctor follows. A fine-grained test can show where a model reasons soundly and where it guesses. Hospitals and builders can use such results before trusting these systems near patients.
arxiv-2512-01118:
Jaimie Krankel, Guowei Wayne Tu, and Evgueni Filipov study woven columns in a 2025 engineering paper. Woven shell structures are attractive where light weight, damage resilience, and tunable design matter, such as wearables, soft robotics, and aerospace systems. The woven column is a basic building block of such structures.

Full finite element simulations can predict a woven column's stiffness and buckling, but they are computationally expensive. They also do not explain the mechanics behind the scaling relationships engineers need. The authors work toward understanding stiffness and buckling behavior directly. Clear scaling rules would let designers size woven columns without heavy simulation.
arxiv-2512-01518:
Abdo Abouelrous and co-authors learn routes for delivery vans under doubt. Their task mixes random travel times with more than one goal. Goals can clash, like cost versus late drops. Real dispatch must weigh those clashes daily.

Their method learns end to end with deep reinforcement learning. It faces travel time doubt head on. The policy adapts routes as conditions shift. It gives dispatchers a front of trade-off choices, not one fixed plan. Learned routing could cut cost and late rates for fleets in busy cities. Multiple goals are kept visible in the output, so a human dispatcher still makes the final call on cost, time, and fairness trade-offs.
arxiv-2512-01618:
Tetsuji Kato, Hideo Sugama, and Mitsuru Honda study turbulent energy swaps in plasma. Small-scale churn moves heat and particles. It also moves energy between electrons and ions. In weak-collision plasma, that swap can beat direct collision swaps.

Past local studies showed ion heating can be hindered by such churn. The team asks how the swap shapes global temperature profiles. Profiles set fusion reactor performance. If churn steals heat from ions, reactor plans must account for it. Their work links micro churn to macro reactor outcomes. Global profiles link to alpha heating in burning plasma, the very heat source a fusion reactor must keep inside its ion core.
arxiv-2512-01918:
When two black holes spiral together, each one's gravity stretches the other, and the amount of stretch is summed up in numbers called tidal Love numbers. Classical general relativity says these numbers are exactly zero for black holes in vacuum. A 2025 paper uses the gravitational-wave event GW250114 to test that claim.

The event was recorded with an unmatched signal-to-noise ratio, giving an unusually clean test. If the numbers came out nonzero, the cause could be exotic matter nearby or a failure of general relativity itself. The authors derive the tightest constraints yet on black hole Love numbers, sharpening a precise probe of fundamental physics.
arxiv-2512-02118:
Faint dwarf galaxies are easy to miss and hard to find, yet they record how the smallest galaxies evolve. Catherine Fielder and a large team report in 2025 on four such galaxies found by SEAMLESS, a semi-automated machine learning search for semi-resolved galaxies in the nearby universe.

The four, named Hydrus A, LEDA 486718, Cetus B, and Sculptor 26, span a wide range of environments and evolutionary states, and one is reported here for the first time. Comparing dwarfs across settings shows how surroundings shape small galaxies. Each new nearby dwarf is a close-up laboratory for processes also at work, unseen, in the distant universe.
arxiv-2512-02418:
Stablecoins promise a digital dollar backed by reserves, but the proof is split: coin movements are public on the blockchain while reserve reports sit in unstructured documents. Yuexin Xiang and six co-authors work in 2025 on bridging that on-chain and off-chain transparency gap with large language models.

Coins like USDT and USDC couple issuance controls with reserve attestations, yet the two records are unconnected in practice. Language models can read the off-chain disclosures and line them up against the verifiable on-chain traces. Joining the halves would let auditors and users check a stablecoin's backing continuously instead of trusting periodic summaries.
arxiv-2512-02718:
Dražen Adamović and Veronika Pedić Tomić examine a family of algebraic modules built in recent work by others. The modules belong to an affine Lie algebra and are claimed to be smooth and irreducible, meaning they cannot be split into smaller pieces. Wakimoto modules are a classic explicit form of such objects.

The authors show the new modules admit a Wakimoto type realization at critical and noncritical levels. At the critical level, simple quotients match Wakimoto modules already known to be irreducible. Confirming these links strengthens the toolkit used to classify representations in conformal field theory. Firm ground here lets peers cite these modules with trust in proofs that build on them down the line.
arxiv-2512-03018:
Xiang Xu and five co-authors generate computer aided design solids directly, with exact geometry and closed surfaces. The boundary representation is the standard structure CAD uses to define solid models. Direct end to end generation with watertight topology has remained a challenge for learning models.

AutoBrep is a transformer that writes boundary representations autoregressively, one piece at a time. It aims for high quality and validity in the solids it produces. Reliable generated solids could speed product design, letting engineers start from an AI draft that CAD tools accept without repair. Drafts that open clean in CAD cut the fix up stage. That stage eats half the time in shops that turn AI draws into real parts for sale.
arxiv-2512-03118:
Tiny black holes from the early universe may still be out there. Paul Halpern and co-authors hunt for signs of them in this 2025 work. Such objects, called primordial black holes, could show up in data gathered for other aims.

The team sifted data from searches for planets outside our solar system. Those searches use two methods, radial velocity and gravitational microlensing. The authors looked for odd signs that a tiny black hole caused. Even a null result helps set limits on how many such objects exist. That feeds the wider quest to learn what dark matter is. Planet search archives are vast, so careful sifting can still yield fresh limits from old data.
arxiv-2512-03218:
Thin rubber capsules can be made with walls of even thickness. A. Eddi, S. Perrard, and J. Zhang show how in this 2025 work. Their capsules are about a centimeter wide, made from silicone, and bend very easily.

The team can tune wall thickness during making. Once filled and placed in water, the capsules can be inflated to set pressure and stress. Such soft drops serve as models for cells, bubbles, and soft materials. Controlled capsules help labs test how thin shells stretch, buckle, and flow. Uniform walls matter, since thin spots would burst or sag under pressure changes.
arxiv-2512-03318:
AI agents are entering social settings with humans and other agents. Chandler Smith and a large team test how well they generalize there in this 2025 work. They use Concordia, a framework for mixed-motive scenarios where interests partly align and partly clash.

Old evaluation methods fail to show if social skills transfer to new situations. The team measures that transfer for language model agents. Sound tests matter before agents negotiate, trade, or cooperate on our behalf. The work helps set standards for social AI. Novel social settings test whether agent skills are real or memorized from training scenes.
arxiv-2512-04118:
AI scribes that listen to medical visits and draft the notes are spreading through hospitals faster than their safety record is being studied. Jessica Dai and a large team mine feedback from clinicians who use one such system, in a 2025 preprint. Their mixed-methods study draws on reports from a large United States hospital system.

Quantitative counts and qualitative reading point the same way: transcription errors can create genuine patient safety risks. The most significant dangers cluster around medication and treatment details, where a wrong word matters most. The authors are careful about scale: feedback alone cannot establish how large the absolute risk is. The paper's contribution is an early-warning signal, cataloguing the errors end users actually catch.
arxiv-2512-04218:
Eric Foxall and Clément Soubrier study how long a crowded line of points can go before a large empty gap first opens. Points pop in at random spots along a unit segment and drop out on their own. New points arrive at one set rate while each old point leaves at another. The 2025 arXiv paper treats this birth-and-death flow as a Poisson point process and asks when a gap of a set size first appears.

When the target gap is a fair bit larger than the typical largest gap, a clean pattern emerges. Scaled by its mean, the waiting time settles into an exponential law with mean one. The team gives the start conditions this needs: dense local packing but not too many points in total. They also pin down how the mean wait grows as arrival rates climb, which closes the question for fast-arrival cases.
arxiv-2512-04318:
Nicolò Bragagnolo and S. Prem Kumar use a toy model of a black hole to ask how information moves as the hole evaporates. The model is the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev system, a set of fermions with random links that mimics black hole chaos. They couple it weakly to a bath, a second such system that stands in for escaping radiation. Their 2025 arXiv paper follows modular flow, an internal time set by the system's own state.

The pair track how fermion correlations change as modular flow runs. At late times, the flowed correlations grow sharp singular points. Past a threshold called the modular scrambling time, the pattern shifts: links appear to pass from one side of the setup to the other. The math uses the replica trick in imaginary time, then continues back to real time. The results give a new lens on how an evaporating hole may share its secrets.
arxiv-2512-04518:
Tianmai Zhang, Zhaoyi Sun, Sihang Zeng, and co-authors describe their entry to ChemoTimelines 2025, a shared task that builds chemotherapy timelines from hospital records. Such timelines map when each patient got which cancer drugs. Doctors and researchers need them tidy, yet they hide inside piles of free-text clinical notes. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests several language model strategies for pulling the facts out.

Every approach ran in two steps. A language model first pulled chemo events from single notes. A second stage then cleaned, matched, and merged events into one timeline per patient. The team compared chain-of-thought prompting, supervised fine-tuning, preference tuning, and dictionary lookup. A fine-tuned mid-size model ranked near the top of the test leaderboard. The findings show which mixes of reasoning and tuning best turn messy notes into reliable treatment histories.
arxiv-2512-04818:
Jun Maillard and Jan Šťovíček study two mirror-image families inside tensor-triangulated categories: objects that are torsion and objects that are complete. These categories, drawn from algebra and geometry, carry a tensor product and a triangulated structure at once. A graded commutative Noetherian ring acts at their center. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks how the dualizable members of the two families are built and how they can be recovered from smaller data.

The authors show both families carry a natural action of the completed ring. Each family can be rebuilt, as a category in its own right, from the compact torsion objects with their matching structure. When the compact objects admit a strong generator, its reflections generate the dualizable families. The results pin down how torsion and completion, two basic ways to localize information, interact with duality in very general settings.
arxiv-2512-05018:
Samuele Grossi, Xu Li, Lorenzo Rolla, and Riccardo Torre lay out a strategy for catching a subtle class of possible new physics. The setting is Drell-Yan events, where a quark and antiquark in colliding protons produce a lepton pair. Most searches lean on signals that grow with energy through interference with known processes, within an effective theory of unknown effects. The operators here do not interfere; their effects appear only squared, which makes them easy to miss and confuse with others.

The team's handle is the angular pattern of the lepton pair, together with a known relation, the Lam-Tung relation, that these operators break. Different operator classes leave different fingerprints across momentum and mass, letting the authors tell them apart. With estimates of the known background, they project what current and upgraded colliders could see, arguing angles offer a clean probe exactly where the standard contribution is small.
arxiv-2512-05118:
Davide Guerra and five co-authors ask how much the treatment of heat matters in simulations of colliding neutron stars. After two such stars merge, the hot, hypermassive remnant rings and sheds gravitational waves. Their tones depend on the equation of state — the rulebook linking pressure, density, and temperature. Modelers use a simplified hybrid rulebook; this study runs simulations with both that and the full temperature-aware tables, and compares them.

Running well past the merger, the simulations show the gravitational-wave tone's evolution diverges between the two treatments at late times, enough to break the universal relations modelers rely on. The remnant also proves unstable to convection: layered rotation and heat stratification sustain churning patterns that excite slower inertial wobbles, within reach of future detectors. Because the full tables confirm effects first seen with the hybrid shortcut, the late-time mode excitation now rests on firmer ground.
arxiv-2512-05218:
Daniel Skorohod and Ofek Birnholtz propose a two-step plan for catching the flash of light that follows a gravitational-wave detection. When two neutron stars merge, telescopes race to find the fading glow, but the gravitational-wave sky map is large and early searches are poorly coordinated. Their protocol pairs two telescopes of different strengths and has them work from the same evolving map in real time.

A wide-field auxiliary telescope scans, since its big view gives it the best chance of spotting emission. The moment it registers a candidate, a narrow-field main telescope slews to that spot for sharp follow-up. In simulations with telescopes, signal-weighted maps, and live map updates, the coordinated strategy cuts the median time to detection compared with uncoordinated benchmarks. The authors add that the biggest future gains would come from faster-slewing telescopes and a truly wide, deep auxiliary.
arxiv-2512-05318:
Vignesh Kothapalli and three co-authors find that teaching a model to reason can backfire when the teaching leans too hard on worked reasoning examples. Few-shot prompting with chain-of-thought examples unlocks reasoning in large models, but on novel tasks, where pretraining knowledge runs out, examples alone fail. The authors study meta-training — training models to learn new abstract tasks in context — in a controlled framework.

They observe that flooding meta-training with chain-of-thought examples degrades performance when supervision is scarce at test time. Their remedy, CoT-Recipe, modulates the mix of reasoning and non-reasoning examples in the training sequences. With the mix tuned, accuracy on novel tasks rises — in some settings several-fold — even when no reasoning examples are in context. Applied to pretrained models on symbolic reasoning, the techniques yield gains, a lesson for fine-tuners: more demonstration is not always better.
arxiv-2512-05418:
Yida Lin and four co-authors benchmark learning methods for segmenting tree branches in drone imagery, a perception task that forestry systems depend on for safe navigation and pruning. The right model depends on the image resolution the drone can afford. So the team evaluates twenty-two configurations of segmentation networks at three resolutions, from small to large, on a street-tree dataset. Their metrics go beyond the overlap scores to include thin-structure accuracy and connectivity preservation — the qualities that matter when the target is a twig, not a blob.

Winners emerge at each scale: one transformer-backed U-Net leads at low and middle resolutions, another variant at the highest, with a nested design best on boundary quality. The most efficient option trails on accuracy by margins at every scale. The results give engineers a multi-resolution map of the accuracy-versus-computing tradeoff for deployment.
arxiv-2512-05518:
Jason Vega and Gagandeep Singh show that a celebrated defence of open language models has a hole in it, then patch the hole. The prefilling attack slips past safety training by starting the model's answer with an agreeable prefix. A recent defence retrains models to refuse immediately after such prefixes — deep alignment. But the authors' generalized attack simply picks, at each step, low-probability harmful tokens from among the model's top candidates. It steps around the refusals entirely.

Their fix starts from a new perspective: the defence's training data should match not just the probabilities of target tokens but their ranks. The resulting method, PRESTO, regularizes the attention the model pays to harmful prefill tokens. Against the rank-assisted attack, it improves safety several-fold over data augmentation alone. The work is a reminder that alignment measured against yesterday's attack is a promise tomorrow's attack may not keep.
arxiv-2512-05818:
Hendrik Ehrich, Marvin May, and Stefan Eder automate a bottleneck in the study of friction at the atomic scale. Molecular dynamics simulations show how alloys deform under rubbing. Turning the flood of output into readable maps of deformation patterns has been slow, expert, manual work. Their workflow teaches machines to read the pictures: images colored by grain orientation, taken from simulations of a copper nickel alloy.

An autoencoder first compresses each image into a short feature vector. Reconstructions kept the essential motifs: grain boundaries, stacking faults, twins, and partial lattice rotations. Those features, joined with simulation settings like composition and load, train a hybrid network to name the dominant deformation pattern. It proved right about ninety six times in a hundred on validation data. A tougher test, holding out a whole region of grains, still supported it. The work points toward automatic tribology maps and fewer giant simulation campaigns.
arxiv-2512-06418:
Wen Zhou and four co authors sharpen the rules that govern how quantum entanglement can be shared. Entanglement links particles so that measuring one steers what can be known about another. A rule called monogamy says a particle deeply linked to one partner cannot be equally linked to a third; the link is a budget, not a free good.

Most past rules state this budget as a sum. Zhou and team state it as a product instead, for powers of a standard link measure called concurrence. They show by worked examples that the product form binds more tightly than the older sum rules. They then build still tighter product rules from a second measure, negativity, and show these hold even for larger systems where a famous older rule can fail. Tighter sharing rules help theorists map what multi particle quantum states can and cannot do.
arxiv-2512-06518:
Zongrui Pei surveys a two way street between physics and machine learning, in a perspective piece shaped by a recent Nobel Prize. The prize honored work that grew neural networks out of spin glass physics, the study of magnets with frozen, disordered patterns. The two fields share deep structure: a neural network and an Ising style magnet can be written in near matching forms, letting tools cross over.

Pei walks through what glassy, disordered systems teach about how networks store patterns, settle into states, and fail. He also marks where the two fields part ways, and what each still owes the other. Open problems in the physics of networks get special weight, from how learning reshapes the energy landscape to why some networks generalize. Quantum computing enters at the end as a possible lever on the hardest of these problems. The piece maps a shared frontier.
arxiv-2512-06718:
Zecheng Shen and four co authors devise a way to witness entanglement between spin and orbital motion inside a material, using an X ray experiment. Entanglement between these two faces of an electron is central to quantum devices, but proving it is present in a bulk material is hard. Their probe is resonant inelastic X ray scattering, where X rays bounce off a sample and lose energy in ways that fingerprint its inner states.

From the measured spectra they build a mathematical generator, an observable whose statistics yield the quantum Fisher information for the spin orbital system. That quantity caps how entangled broad classes of states can be, so passing the cap witnesses real spin orbital entanglement. The team also loosens the bounds for real experiments that cannot resolve every polarization of the scattered light. The protocol turns a standard beamline measurement into an entanglement test for quantum materials.
arxiv-2512-06818:
Jan Held and co-authors present MeshSplatting, a way to rebuild three-dimensional scenes as solid meshes that computers can render from new viewpoints. Popular recent methods build scenes from fuzzy points or blobs, which render fast but clash with the mesh-based tools used in games and virtual reality. MeshSplatting instead optimizes shape and surface appearance together through rendering that can be tuned step by step, much like training a neural network.

A restricted triangulation method keeps the surface connected and smooth while it learns. On a standard benchmark of real indoor and outdoor scenes, the meshes beat the previous best mesh method on image quality. They also trained in about half the time and used about half the memory. The result points toward neural scene capture that drops straight into ordinary real-time graphics engines without a translation step.
arxiv-2512-06918:
Da Xu proves a sharpened version of the Penrose inequality, a landmark statement linking a black hole's size to the total mass of the space around it. The classic version bounds mass from below using the horizon's area alone. Xu adds spin: for flattened, symmetric vacuum data holding a stable trapped surface, mass must also account for angular momentum. Equality holds only for slices of the spinning Kerr solution, the exact model of a rotating black hole.

The proof blends two heavy tools. One is the Jang equation, a standard device for reshaping such problems. The other is a level-set method built on a family of harmonic-type functions. Between them sits a modified Hawking mass that grows steadily along the flow while carrying the spin term. A separate rigidity argument pins down the equality case.
arxiv-2512-07018:
Yi Lin and Moshe Y Vardi tackle boolean synthesis. The problem of building a function that meets a stated logical specification, a core task behind circuit design and quantified logic puzzles. Solvers often work through decision diagrams, compact maps of a function's choices. The industry standard map is the binary decision diagram, but a newer cousin, the zero-suppressed diagram, wins on different kinds of problems and has been less explored for synthesis.

Lin and Vardi build a synthesis framework on the newer diagram type, driven by dynamic programming. They solve the theoretical snags that come with the switch and deliver a working tool, then test its performance against expectations. A further idea, a so-called magic number, caps the planning phase and relates to the problem's treewidth, framing the trade-off between exploring options and committing.
arxiv-2512-07318:
Carey M Lisse and a large team report what a space telescope saw when it looked at 3I/ATLAS, only the third known visitor from interstellar space. Over two weeks in August twenty twenty-five, the SPHEREx spacecraft gathered spectra, light curves, and images before the object reached its closest pass to the Sun. The light carries clear fingerprints of water vapor and carbon dioxide gas streaming off the body, with tentative signs of heavier carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide as well.

The carbon dioxide atmosphere is enormous, reaching hundreds of thousands of kilometers, while the water coma hugs closer in. The solid nucleus itself appears small, under a few kilometers across, drowned in a coma a hundred times brighter, rich in large icy chunks.
arxiv-2512-07718:
Vakhtang Chulukhadze and ten co-authors wrote this 2025 engineering paper on tiny ultrasound devices. Piezoelectric micromachined transducers serve where toughness, heat tolerance, and small size matter. Single-crystal lithium niobate has emerged as a promising material for them.

The material couples electricity and motion strongly, and it works in both directions. New film transfer methods now yield periodically poled films of high quality. Those films allow a bimorph stack with no electrodes in between. The team builds such a transducer on a robust active layer. They first argue the material choice through a broad comparison. Membrane geometry is then optimized to lift the coupling further. Their device runs in a flexural mode with strong transmit efficiency. The striking result is survival under extreme heat. Operation stays stable at temperatures that would kill most micro-devices. The work makes lithium niobate a serious platform for harsh settings.
arxiv-2512-07818:
Xinyuan Cao and Santosh Vempala wrote this 2025 machine learning theory paper on a puzzle. Language models are trained only to predict the next token. Yet their output reads coherently across whole documents, with long-range structure intact.

The authors prove that next-token prediction is powerful enough to explain that. Their setting is optimization over a recurrent neural network architecture. The trained model ends up close to the true training distribution. Closeness is made precise through a distinguishing test. Take any bounded algorithm that inspects only the next block of tokens. It cannot tell model text from real text after the same prefix. That holds for blocks of any size the test cares to choose. The model size needed grows only polynomially in that block size. Document length does not enter the bound at all. Long-range coherence, a seeming mystery, gets a complexity-theoretic account.
arxiv-2512-08218:
Ye Qin, Jingchao Wang, Yang Shi, and colleagues posted a methods paper on arXiv in December 2025 introducing PR CapsNet, a capsule network for learning from graph data. Capsule networks route information dynamically and keep features as vectors, which suits layered graph structure. Their weakness is geometry: they work in flat space with fixed curvature, while real graphs bend in mixed ways and can split into disconnected pieces.

PR CapsNet moves capsule routing into pseudo Riemannian spaces whose curvature adapts during learning. Its routing step splits capsule states into spherical temporal and Euclidean spatial parts, linked by smooth transformations. An adaptive curvature routing stage then fuses features from different curvature spaces, guided by local geometry through a learnable tensor and attention. A matching classifier keeps the geometric structure when labeling embeddings. In tests on node and graph classification benchmarks, PR CapsNet beat leading models.
arxiv-2512-08518:
Nadezhda Kushina, Ko Watanabe, Aarthi Kannan, and colleagues, researchers in human robot interaction, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Social robots must respect personal space, or people feel uneasy and disengage. The team tested whether eye tracking can measure that comfort during interaction with a humanoid robot named Ameca.

Nineteen participants faced the robot at four controlled distances, from half a meter to two meters, wearing mobile eye trackers and reporting their comfort. Several learning models then estimated comfort from gaze features alone. A simple decision tree won, beating the transformer models that lead in human to human studies. The strongest signal was minimum pupil diameter, a physiological marker. The authors conclude that comfort thresholds with robots follow their own rules, different from human dynamics, and that plain, readable models can capture them.
arxiv-2512-08618:
Stefano Mocatti and coauthors build a first principles framework for what happens in semiconductors right after a flash of light. The flash creates excited charge carriers and lattice vibrations, called phonons, that interact in complex ways. Their method includes light matter coupling from first principles and collision terms for three kinds of scattering: carrier with carrier, carrier with phonon, and phonon with phonon.

The equations are solved in a localized basis that allows very dense sampling and direct comparison with pump probe experiments. Tests on two monolayer materials show the power of the approach. One case tracks fast carrier cooling, hot phonon behavior, and coherent atomic motion. The results show that carrier carrier scattering is vital for realistic timing, and that phonon phonon scattering matters for long time heating and damping. The method can also link to models of light driven structural change.
arxiv-2512-08918:
Miranda Christ and coauthors construct improved random like codes, which act as watermarks for AI content with strong guarantees. A random like code is an encryption like scheme whose decoding tolerates a high rate of errors. Random like quality preserves content quality, while error tolerance lets a watermark survive edits.

Recent constructions share weaknesses. They fall to fast spotting attacks, lack strength against edits over a small symbol set, and fail when a foe knows the checking key. The new construction achieves all three missing traits at once. It has strong random like quality and strength against worst case edits over a binary symbol set. It also holds against unbounded foes holding the checking key. Security rests on a new assumption about permuted noisy codewords, stated as a formal claim. That claim follows from an earlier permuted puzzles claim, and it holds against a broad class of simple distinguishers.
arxiv-2512-09018:
Luca Ciambelli, Temple He, and Kathryn Zurek show that the soft sector of gravity in asymptotically flat spacetime can be matched to the physics of a finite causal diamond in flat spacetime. The soft sector captures long wavelength gravitational modes at infinity. A causal diamond is the region reachable and observable between two points in spacetime, here taken with spherical symmetry.

The leading soft graviton mode is identified geometrically with changes in the radial size of the diamond. The Goldstone mode involves both that radial change and its symplectic partner variable. That identification lets the authors relate radial fluctuations of the diamond to transverse fluctuations at infinity that are parametrized by the soft modes. The result gives a finite, concrete home for degrees of freedom that are usually described at infinity. It may help connect asymptotic symmetries in gravity with local, finite region physics in a precise way.
arxiv-2512-09518:
Haijun Zhao and colleagues show how mechanical strain can steer lattices of magnetic skyrmions, tiny whirlpool-like spin textures pursued for memory and computing devices. Steering skyrmions in three dimensions, where they extend as strings through the solid, has been hard. The team combines methods to build a picture of strain control.

Analytical modeling predicts that strain stretches skyrmion strings and tilts them in two directions, and micromagnetic simulations agree. The simulations add that strain can merge multi-domain states into a single domain and can snap strings by forming bobber structures at critical strain levels. How the lattice collapses changes with temperature, shifting character near the critical temperature, and thinner samples need more strain to annihilate skyrmions because tilting is suppressed. Experiments on a cobalt-zinc-manganese sample, watched under an electron microscope, confirmed the stretching and collapse, and pointed to strain-tuned magnetic interactions as the mechanism.
arxiv-2512-09618:
Job Daisie Rock and Hugh Thomas introduce a continuous version of preprojective algebras of type A, a family organizing the representation theory of the Dynkin diagram, a line of nodes. Instead of a finite quiver, their preprojective category lives over an interval of the line, giving a continuum of objects where the classical theory has finitely many.

They study the representable projective modules and define decorous modules, a class of submodules and quotient modules. Decorous modules turn out to be described by a function on the interval's closure whose slopes are nowhere too steep. With those in hand, they define permuton ideals, continuous versions of the support tau-tilting ideals of finite type A preprojective algebras. They show the classical permutation ideals can be recovered from them. Permuton ideals share the tau-rigidity property of their finite counterparts. The authors classify the brick modules of the category.
arxiv-2512-09818: Marie Abadie proves a boundedness result about ways of cutting hyperbolic surfaces into ideal triangles. A triangulation of a surface carries shear parameters, numbers that measure how neighboring triangles slide against each other along shared edges. Abadie shows that every hyperbolic surface admits such a triangulation in which all the shears stay bounded. The bound is not uniform across surfaces, but it grows only logarithmically with the topology of the surface, which is a slow and well controlled rate.
arxiv-2512-10018:
Heiko Gimperlein and Magnus Goffeng prove a sharp mapping theorem for Poisson transforms on rank one Lie groups, with a famous conjecture as the prize. Poisson transforms build functions on a symmetric space from data on its boundary. Helgason's conjecture describes their range. The authors prove a quantitative, distributional version for the transform studied by Knapp and Wallach. A certain Sobolev space on the boundary maps boundedly, with closed range, into a square integrable space on the group. The right Sobolev spaces come from a Heisenberg calculus developed by van Erp and Yuncken.

The proof goes further, showing that commutators of this transform with smooth functions on a natural compactification are compact operators. That compactness settles the last open conjecture in Julg's program toward the Baum-Connes conjecture for closed subgroups of rank one semisimple Lie groups.
arxiv-2512-10318:
Aniruddh Mishra, Benjamin Oommen, and Jimmy Liang design and build an open source Layer 2 Ethernet switch in silicon terms. Switches are the plumbing of every local network, forwarding packets between ports by destination hardware address. They must juggle parallel streams on all ports at once, prioritizing throughput, efficiency, and packet integrity. Despite that foundational role, open implementations of switching fabrics are rare, because the networking industry treats its designs as confidential. The authors propose a complete open design for a switch that ingests data from a standard media independent interface and forwards it to the right output port.

They also report the design's power, performance, and area tradeoffs. That documentation is much of the contribution: students and small teams can see not just a working switch but why it is shaped as it is, and what each choice costs.
arxiv-2512-10518:
Leonardo de la Cruz, Pavel Novichkov, and Pierre Vanhove classify special polytopes that hide inside Feynman integrals, the workhorse calculations of particle physics. To each integral they attach Newton polytopes built from its Symanzik graph polynomials. They add the polytopes together. Then they ask which of the resulting shapes are Fano or reflexive. Those are two classes prized in geometry.

For one-loop graphs and multi-loop sunset graphs they count interior points through Ehrhart polynomials to decide each case. A broader direct search covered all Feynman graphs up to ten edges and nine loops. And the finds were remarkably sparse: only a handful of reflexive and Fano examples in two and three dimensions. Some shapes even encode degenerate Calabi-Yau spaces, tying these integrals to del Pezzo surfaces, K3 surfaces, and Calabi-Yau period integrals.
arxiv-2512-10718:
Sabia Asghar and co-authors build a safer numerical scheme for a model of soft living tissue. Tissue can stretch like a solid, flow slowly like a fluid. And let liquid move through its pores, all while growing or shrinking from within, as in tumour growth or skin contracting after a burn. Their morpho-visco-poroelastic model combines all of those behaviours in one framework.

Rather than proving solutions exist, the authors check the stability of the model's equilibria in both continuous and semi-discrete form, and discuss the framework's key features. The practical problem is numerical: naive finite element solutions develop fake oscillations in the pressure. Their stabilised scheme suppresses them, and simulations confirm convergence in space and time. They also measure the pressure profile's total variation against the stabilisation parameter, giving users a quantitative dial for the fix.
arxiv-2512-10918:
Yiyang Wang and co-authors put a cast of artificial companions in the room while you watch the game.
