Mostafa Atallah and five coauthors build circuits for quantum walks with less waste. Their 2026 preprint skips Pauli decomposition in the build. A continuous-time quantum walk spreads a walker on a graph. Its Hamiltonian sets how the walk flows over time.

Pauli decomposition is the usual but costly route to circuits. The new algorithm is called matching decomposition in the work. It splits the walk Hamiltonian into exactly doable parts. Each part matches a matching in the graph below. A graph compression step then merges edges to shrink the count. The method serves arbitrary simple sparse graphs, a broad class. Fewer parts mean shorter circuits on real quantum hardware.
arxiv-2601-11618:
Luis Rosario Freytes defines attention in geometric, regime-explicit terms. The 2026 preprint names the frame Geometric Attention, or GA. Transformer attention is usually given as one fixed formula. GA instead specifies a layer by four independent inputs.

The first input is a finite carrier of addressable indices. The second is an evidence-kernel rule for weights. Masked proto-scores and a link induce nonnegative weights there. The third input is a probe family of admissible observables. The fourth is an anchor and update rule for kernels. It selects which representative kernel applies and how. The split makes hidden choices in attention explicit. Designers can then vary one choice at a time.
arxiv-2601-11718:
Andrea Gnarini, Swati Ravi, Philip Kaaret, and a large team report new X-ray data on Cyg X-2. Cyg X-2 is a bright pair made of a neutron star and a low mass star that feeds it gas. The team watched it while it sat in the state known as the horizontal branch.

They used two space tools at the same time, IXPE and NuSTAR. IXPE checks how X-rays are aligned, while NuSTAR maps their energy spread. The title reports a high level of alignment found in this state. Such data help test how gas flows and glows close to a neutron star.
arxiv-2601-12118:
Christos Liaskos, Evangelos Papapetrou, Kostas Katsalis, and a broad team wrote a tutorial on control of metasurfaces from a network view. Metasurfaces are thin structures that can steer waves in real time. They could lift data rates, privacy, and energy use, and could even sense the space round them.

The tutorial treats each surface as one node in a larger net. That view helps plan how many surfaces act as one system. It links wave control to network control in plain terms. New teams gain a shared map of the field.
arxiv-2601-12218:
De-Ji-Xiang-Mao, Ai Huang, and Yifu Wang study stability in a nutrient taxis system with two degeneracies. In such a system, cells move toward food, and both cell spread and food use can vanish at set points. That double degeneracy makes the maths hard.

They show that arbitrary structures in the three-dimensional case can stabilize. Taxis models help explain how bacteria and cells form patterns round food sources. Firm stability results tell which patterns can last. The work treats a hard, singular system in full 3D.  The result holds for a range of start shapes.
arxiv-2601-12418:
A. K. Behera and a large team study sound waves that skim the surface of a layered chip. The layers pair a piezo thin film with silicon carbide. Such films trap sound in a thin zone, well below a wavelength in depth. That tight trap suits compact devices that mix and shift sound signals.

The team probe a nonlinear effect called four wave mixing in these guided waves. They work at gigahertz rates, where four waves trade energy in set ways. Effects like this can convert frequencies or process signals on a chip. The title flags a twist: cold helps. Running the device at low heat boosts the mixing, a fact of use for future phononic tools.
arxiv-2601-12818:
Minjia Shi, Jing Wang, and Patrick Sole prove nonexistence results for perfect codes in several metrics. Perfect codes are rare gems of coding theory, packing spheres with no waste. The team combine the Lloyd theorem of Sole from 1989 with the Schwartz Zippel lemma from computer science. Their proofs rest on asymptotic enumeration of integer partitions.

The results cover the Lee metric, the NRT metric, and the mixed Hamming metric. The sum rank distance is covered as well. Ruling out perfect codes saves searches for objects that cannot exist. It also steers code design toward near perfect families that can exist. Cross field proofs like this show how algebra and combinatorics reinforce each other.
arxiv-2601-13118:
Alessandro Midolo and co-authors ask what makes a good prompt when a language model must write code. Such models are now used a lot for code tasks. Past work showed that apt prompt craft can lift the code a model gives back.

Yet staff who write prompts had no clear guide set for code tasks. The team fills that gap with a study of real prompt use. They sort what prompt parts help, what parts do not, and how staff phrase them. From that sort they draw guide lines for code prompts. For dev teams, the value is plain. Better prompts mean fewer bad drafts and less time spent on fix ups.
arxiv-2601-13318:
Leonardo de Lima, Renata Del-Vecchio, Hermie Monterde, and Heber Teixeira use a shared basis to move quantum states on special graphs. A threshold graph is a graph built by add of lone or fully linked nodes, step by step. Past work showed a star and any threshold graph on the same node count share the same eigenbasis for the Laplacian matrix.

The team builds on that fact to prove two results. One marks which threshold graphs are simply structured in their terms. The shared basis then helps treat pair state transfer, the move of a state from one node to a next. Such moves are a base act for quantum nets on graphs.
arxiv-2601-13518:
Jiayi Yuan and co-authors let a pipeline design its own red team tools for AI models. Red team work hunts flaws in a model by attack in a set way. Most auto red team tools rest on flows a human set in advance. Human flows hold human bias and cost a lot to roam wide.

Their pipeline is called AgenticRed. It uses a language model's in context learn to draft and hone red team systems on its own. Each round's finds feed the next draft. No human hand steers the loop. For safety teams, a self design loop may find attack forms a fixed flow would never try.
arxiv-2601-13718:
Dinh-Long Vu, Hitomi Mori, and Patrick Rebentrost bring a classic sampling trick to quantum machines in 2026. The Box-Muller transform turns uniform random samples into Gaussian ones. Gaussian, or normal, spreads show up all over science and finance. Quantum methods can store a whole spread in the amplitudes of a quantum state.

Their Quantum Box-Muller transform builds a superposition of grid points. Those points stand for the multi-variate normal spread, with many variables at once. Fast Gaussian sampling helps Monte Carlo work and risk models. A quantum form could speed tasks that now take long runs.
arxiv-2601-13818:
Luigi Romano extends a rolling contact friction model to handle springy materials in 2026. The base frame is FrBD, Friction with Bristle Dynamics, in distributed form. Bristles stand for the small elements that bend as a tire or wheel rolls. Romano adds linear viscoelasticity, using classic Maxwell and Kelvin-Voigt models of the bristle.

The full system becomes a set of hyperbolic partial differential equations. It tracks bristle dynamics, friction forces, and inner deformation states at once. Such a model can capture relaxation effects, where grip fades or grows over time. Tire and rail engineers need that detail.
arxiv-2601-14118:
Trevor Incerti, Jonathan Elkobi, and Daniel Mattingly study foreign influencer operations on TikTok in 2026. Roughly half of TikTok users report getting news from social media influencers. Authoritarian regimes have increasingly outsourced content creation to these influencers. The team asks how such regimes strengthen global support for nondemocratic systems.

Their focus is how TikTok shapes American perceptions of China. Influencers can present a polished view in a friendly, personal style. That style may bypass the skepticism that state media faces. The work links platform design to foreign influence in daily feeds.
arxiv-2601-14518:
Jinhui Liu, Ximeng Zhang, Yanbo Ai, and Zhou Yu work on testing database agents in this 2026 paper. Evaluating Text-to-SQL agents in private business intelligence settings is hard. Realistic, domain-specific data are scarce, and private data cannot be shared. Synthetic evaluation data offer a scalable solution. Past generation methods, though, fail to capture business realism.

The missing piece is business logic: whether questions reflect real workflows and rules. The team's method is business logic-driven Text-to-SQL data synthesis. It builds test data that mirror how firms actually query their data. Readers get a way to grade business intelligence agents on tasks that look like real work.
arxiv-2601-14818:
Christian Fiedler writes on a branch of machine learning where the inputs are not single values. In his 2026 arXiv paper, each input is a full probability distribution. The work sits in statistical learning theory, the math of how models learn from data.

The catch is that the true distributions are never seen in full. The learner gets only samples drawn from them, in a two-stage setup. Fiedler links this setup to real tasks such as medical screening and causal learning. The paper builds theory for sorting such inputs into classes.
arxiv-2601-14918:
Kai Hendriks, Lorenz Zwick, Pankaj Saini, János Takátsy, and Johan Samsing study pairs of black holes that do not orbit alone. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with gravitational waves from binary black holes. A third body nearby can pull the pair off a plain two-body path.

That pull speeds the pair up or slows it down along our line of sight. The shift leaves marks in the wave signal, an effect called dephasing. The team builds a full model of that dephasing. Their model adds curve and projection effects that simpler local treatments miss.
arxiv-2601-15218:
Luigi De Pascale and Igor Pinheiro revisit an inequality in the theory of optimal transport. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with Wasserstein distances, which gauge the cost of moving one distribution into another. They ask how the largest such distance can be controlled by the smaller ones.

That control matters for both theory and numeric work. A first paper on the problem came years ago. Later work framed the same inequality for more general costs that grow with distance. The authors give a reverse form of the inequality and place it in that wider line of work.
arxiv-2601-15418:
T. J. Martz-Oberlander, B. Bulgaru, and a team of co-authors report a transistor with record-breaking electron mobility. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a three-terminal field-effect device, with source, drain, and gate. Mobility gauges how freely electrons move, and high values promise faster, cleaner electronics.

Several devices were built for the study. The best one used a symmetrically doped gallium arsenide quantum well. It hosts a two-dimensional electron gas, a flat sheet of electrons. Its mobility passes forty million in the standard units, a mark the authors report with great care.
arxiv-2601-15518:
Wenxin Zhou, Ritesh Mehta, and Anthony Miyaguchi build a search system for half-remembered things in a 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is the TREC Tip-of-the-Tongue task. In it, a user recalls a thing vaguely and asks for help finding it. The query is fuzzy by nature. Plain keyword search often fails on such requests.

Their system works in two stages. First, hybrid retrieval merges three methods: LLM-based retrieval, sparse BM25 search, and dense BGE-M3 search. Then learned reranking and LLM-based reranking sort the results. The team's name, DS@GT, marks it as a TREC entry. Anyone who has hunted for a song or film from a faint memory knows the task. The work brings modern retrieval tools to that everyday frustration.
arxiv-2601-15818:
Siyuan Chen, Mingchen Sun, and Jian Tang review muon beams for precision physics in a 2026 arXiv paper. Accelerator advances have raised muon beam quality over past decades. Better beams enable sharper experiments. Studies of the muon and of muonium, its bound state with an electron, benefit most. These systems allow precise measurements of fundamental constants. They also support searches for physics beyond the Standard Model.

The title promises progress and prospects. A review takes stock of where beam quality stands. It also maps what future beams could unlock. Muonium is a clean, purely leptonic atom, ideal for precision tests. Any deviation from theory there would be a loud signal. The paper serves physicists planning the next round of such experiments.
arxiv-2601-16018:
Özgür Uğur and a large team build language models for Turkish law in a 2026 arXiv paper. The models are the Mecellem family. Legal language is a specialized domain in any tongue. Turkish legal text adds its own terms and forms. The team trains models both from scratch and by continued pretraining. One contribution is an encoder model built from zero. It follows the ModernBERT design and trains on a Turkish-dominant corpus.

That corpus holds 112.7 billion tokens, per the abstract. The authors stress joint evaluation: pretraining choices and downstream task scores together. Domain adaptation often looks good on one axis and poor on the other. Legal tools for Turkish speakers need models that truly read their law. This work supplies candidates and a frank way to judge them.
arxiv-2601-16118:
Marco Ronzani and Cristina Silvano use web like graphs to place spike nets on brain like chips. Their 2026 preprint deals with nets that send brief spikes. Brain like chips hold many cores tied by a chip net. Each core runs a set of nerve cells. A poor place map wastes time and power as spikes cross the chip.

The pair model the net as a graph with hubs and links. Rich graphs with hubs, called hyper graphs, hold group links at once. That rich form helps find place maps with less cross talk. Good maps make spike nets run fast on small gear. The work links graph maths to chip design.
arxiv-2601-16218:
Aleix Torres-Camps and coauthors build a wide test of maths thought in pics and many tongues. Their 2026 preprint, named M3Kang, deals with vision and language models. Top models show strong thought on maths in one tongue. Their skill in many tongues at once is far less known. That gap counts for schools and tools used world wide.

M3Kang is the first test of its kind at this scale. It checks maths thought that joins pics with text in many tongues. Scores set next to human marks show the true gap. A shared test lets teams track gains tongue by tongue. The work aids fair maths tools for all users.
arxiv-2601-16618:
Jing Xu and three coauthors grow speech to speech skills in large models step by step. Their 2026 preprint, named PROST-LLM, deals with direct speech swaps. Speech to speech keeps tone and feel that text paths lose. Large models shine on text tasks but lag on speech swaps. Scant speech swap data is a main cause of that lag.

Step growth adds skills in a set order to beat scant data. Each step builds on the last with tasks of more depth. Gains would open speech swaps to more tongue pairs. They would also cut need for rare paired speech sets. The work gives a staged path for that growth.
arxiv-2601-16818:
Siyuan Hou and a team of nine co-authors use bent quasar light to test dark matter. Gravity from a galaxy can split a quasar's light into shots. In cusp sets, three shots sit close in a line. Their glow rates should match a set pattern. When they don't, small clumps of stuff may be at fault. Their 2026 preprint checks such off marks in the largest clean set yet.

That set holds seventeen cusp lens sets. The team pits the marks against three dark tales. Cold, self-touching, and fuzzy dark stuff each face the test. Fake lens sims show which tale fits the marks. Such tests can rule out whole dark tales at once.
arxiv-2601-17118:
Zixiang Jia, Fangzhou Jiang, Shubo Li, Ran Li, Jing Wang, and Ling Zhu bound how strong dark bits bump each next. Dark bits that bump can form soft cores in galaxies. Galaxy spin curves tell how those cores spread. Their 2026 preprint builds a sharp Jeans-type tool for the gauge. The tool starts from a heat-set halo form. Three upgrades make it more true to real halos.

Bump strength can shift with the bits' speed. Core fall-in, a late dense phase, gets a rule too. Firm fits sort true halo forms from false ones. SPARC spin curves give the test data. Bounds here curb whole dark tale classes.
arxiv-2601-17618:
Latent variable models study traits that cannot be seen at once, like mood or skill. Psychologists use them to link such constructs. Full one-stage fits can be hard to compute. Two-stage factor score regression is a common fallback. Stage one fits the measurement model and gets factor scores. Stage two uses those scores in regression. The record names no author for this entry.

The authors give a general two-stage solution. It is root-N consistent, a key large-sample trait. A sound shortcut matters when full fits fail. Many applied teams rely on the two-stage path daily. Proof that it can be consistent raises trust in its results. The work serves survey and test research.
arxiv-2601-17718:
Bo Zhan and three co-authors present a tree tensor network solver for quantum impurity dynamics. Impurity models place one interacting site in a broad bath. Real-time simulation of them is a classic hard problem. Their solver decomposes the bath Hamiltonian into a Cayley tree. That gives a tensor network shaped like the problem's own scales.

The tree captures multiscale entanglement in impurity-bath systems. Accuracy and speed both matter for real-time runs. Better solvers aid study of quantum dots and magnetic impurities. They also test methods for correlated materials. The work gives a solver built for the structure at hand. Generic networks waste effort that the tree saves.
arxiv-2601-18218:
Meziah Ruby Cristobal and co-authors explore AI help for turning papers into short videos. Their 2026 preprint deals with research communication. Sharing results matters, yet researchers often lack the time and skills to make engaging short-form video. Such videos are now a main way the public meets science. The team studies how generative AI can help scholars turn their papers into clear, watchable clips.

The study looks at the process, not just the output. Where does AI help, and where does it flatten the message? Answers guide tool builders and university media teams. Done well, AI help could bring more research to public view without fake polish.
arxiv-2601-18418:
Ji Zeng and many colleagues train language models for a new kind of work: acting as agents that fix code on their own. The field has moved past one-shot code writing. A strong model must now roam a whole code base, change files, and run tests to check its own work. That kind of skill takes more than plain pre-training on text and code.

Their work adds a mid-stage of training built for agent work. In that stage the model learns from tasks that look like real software jobs. It learns to plan steps, to use tools, and to fix its own slips. The aim is a model that can take a bug report and work it through to a tested fix. Such skill would cut the hand work in large software teams.
arxiv-2601-18518:
Parvendra Kumar studies a light source built to send keys in a quantum safe way. Such keys are shared by a stream of lone bits of light. The share fails if a pulse holds two bits when it should hold one. The source here is a tiny dot with one spare charge, set in a small post of glass-like stuff that traps light.

Kumar tests two ways to wake the dot so it gives off one bit of light at a time. One way shines light that hums in tune with the dot. The next way sweeps the tune in a smooth path. He weighs which way gives a bright stream with the least double hits. A bright, clean source could make quantum key links work at a real scale.
arxiv-2601-18918:
Bram Lentjes and three co-authors build tools to study sudden shifts in delayed systems. Delay equations, where the present rate leans on past states, show up in control, biology, and climate work. When a slow forcing repeats in time, steady states can split or flip as knobs change.

The team first proves a smooth, low dimensional surface exists near a steady state that is on the edge of change. On that surface, the full system shrinks to a small normal form that is far easier to study. Their frame uses sun-star calculus to keep the proof strict.
arxiv-2601-19018:
Sahana Kumar and a large team study a rare, fast fading supernova named SN 2025coe. Its class, calcium strong transients, shines faintly, fades fast, and shows strong calcium lines with oddly weak oxygen. Some traits match exploding white dwarfs, while others match the collapse of huge stars, so the class's origin stays in doubt.

The team watched this event in X-rays, near infrared light, and radio waves. Each band adds a clue about the blast's energy, speed, and setting. More well watched cases like this one should settle what kind of star dies in this calcium rich way.
arxiv-2601-19518:
Andreas Angelou, Pourya Behmandpoor, and Marc Moonen study a design for future wireless networks. In a cell-free massive MIMO network, many access points are spread across an area. They serve all users together, rather than tying each user to one tower. When users send data up to the network, the work can be run in one central place or shared out among the access points.

Central control can give strong results but needs heavy data traffic between points. Sharing the work out cuts that traffic but can lose coordination. The authors propose a master-assisted design, where a lead unit helps the distributed points work together. Their aim is to keep most of the gains of central control while spreading the load. The work matters for building dense, fast networks that stay practical to run.
arxiv-2601-19618:
Soroosh Tayebi Arasteh and colleagues study a trade-off in medical AI: privacy versus accuracy. Differential privacy limits how much any single training image can sway a model. That protection usually costs diagnostic accuracy. Starting from pretrained weights softens the loss. The open question is which matters more: what the model was pretrained to do, or what data it was pretrained on.

The team trains chest X-ray classifiers under differential privacy from five different starting points. Their data covers close to six hundred thousand radiographs from five datasets. Comparing the runs separates the effect of the pretraining objective from the effect of the domain. The answer guides hospitals that must train on private scans. It shows where to invest effort before privacy is even applied.
arxiv-2601-19718:
Kaifeng Zhang, Kai Ming Ting, Tianrun Liang, and Qiuran Zhao rethink a classic data analysis method. Hierarchical clustering groups data into a tree of nested clusters. Divisive methods start with everything in one group and split it step by step. The authors show that current objective-based divisive methods produce trees missing three properties users would expect.

A good tree should not split groups without warrant. It should keep similar clusters together in the same branch. And its groups should correspond to the true groups in the data. The authors trace the failures to how splitting is judged, one set at a time. Their distributional viewpoint suggests a different criterion. The work aims at cluster trees that analysts can actually trust.
arxiv-2601-20118:
David Kin Wai Ho and three colleagues work on polar codes, a family of error-correcting codes planned for future 6G networks. A polar code needs a fixed order that says which positions in the code carry data. Finding a good order for each channel and decoder is a hard design task. The authors use reinforcement learning to build that order.

Their method is meant to be universal, so it can adapt to many channel conditions and decoding styles. It also scales to code lengths up to about two thousand, which suits real standards work. A single learned design tool could cut the effort of tuning codes by hand for each new setting.
arxiv-2601-20318:
Jiyuan Xu and five colleagues present CPiRi, a method for forecasting many related time series at once. Existing methods split into two camps. Channel-dependent models learn links between series but can overfit their order, so they adapt poorly when channels are added or shuffled. Channel-independent models treat each series alone, which is flexible but misses cross-links.

CPiRi is built to be invariant to channel permutation while still modeling relational interaction between channels. That pairing aims at both flexibility and accuracy. It matters for sensor networks and finance feeds, where the set and order of series change often.
arxiv-2601-20418:
Coralia Cartis and Wenqi Zhu study when nonnegative quartic polynomials can be written as sums of squares. Hilbert's seventeenth problem showed that not all nonnegative polynomials have such a representation, though he found classes where the two notions agree. The authors extend that equivalence to new subclasses of multivariate polynomials with quartic regularization.

They also characterize where these structured problems sit relative to the NP-hardness boundary. Sum-of-squares methods power a large family of optimization tools. Knowing exactly which polynomial classes are tractable tells users when those tools are guaranteed to work.
arxiv-2601-20718:
Julia Chuzhoy and Merav Parter keep sparse network stand-ins up to date while the network itself keeps changing. Their 2026 paper studies fully dynamic algorithms for graph spanners. A spanner is a sparse subgraph that preserves distances between all vertex pairs. The distances may stretch by a factor called t, the stretch. Sparsity is the point: far fewer edges than the full graph. Roads, networks, and data all use such stand-ins.

Fully dynamic means edges arrive and vanish over time. The algorithm must repair the spanner after each change, fast. Their route uses low-diameter router decomposition. The graph is broken into clusters that act as routers. A preliminary version appeared at SODA 2025. The work serves any system whose map changes while it is being used.
arxiv-2601-20818:
Quantum memory that looks after itself is the goal of Gesa Dünnweber, Georgios Styliaris, and Rahul Trivedi. Their 2026 paper presents a method for autonomous quantum error correction in two spatial dimensions. Standard correction needs active upkeep: constant measurements plus classical processing. Passive correction would avoid that burden. Until now it was only known to work in an unphysical number of dimensions.

The team's method is framed as a quantum cellular automaton. Each cell updates by a fixed, local rule that never changes across the grid. No outside controller steps in to measure or decide. The paper shows this simple setup can protect quantum memory on a flat grid. That is a notable step for quantum hardware. Self-correcting memory would cut the cost of keeping quantum data alive.
arxiv-2601-21118:
Jason Block measures how complex the models of a simple arithmetic can be. His 2026 paper classifies countable models of Presburger arithmetic. Presburger arithmetic is arithmetic with addition but no multiplication. It is weak enough to be fully decidable. Yet its models can still vary in rich ways. Block takes two approaches to that variety. They are Scott analysis and degree spectra, two tools from logic.

Scott analysis assigns each model a complexity rank. Degree spectra record which computers could rebuild the model. Block investigates which ranks and spectra actually occur. Many results come from one construction trick. Given a linear order, he builds a Presburger group that keeps much of its structure. That bridge imports hard questions from order theory. The paper maps the landscape of models for a tame arithmetic.
arxiv-2601-21318:
Zirui Zhu and Xiangyang Li build a quantum learning system that keeps spotting network attacks as attack styles change. A detector must learn new attack stages without forgetting old ones. It also faces tight limits on computing power and rules that bar storing raw traffic for long.

Their framework pairs stability tricks with rehearsal that respects privacy. A fidelity anchor keeps old skills from drifting away. Synthetic replay refreshes old attack types without keeping the real data. The design is aimed at near-term quantum hardware, where qubits are few and noisy.
arxiv-2601-21518:
Xinyi Zhang and eight co-authors study how parents and teens think adults should respond to online grooming attempts. This form of abuse harms teens' mental health and physical safety. Most past work focused on spotting the offender's behavior, not on how a teen can answer.

The authors gather views from both parents and teens on unwanted advances. Their angle fills a gap: the targets' own perspective on what helps. Knowing which responses teens would actually use shapes better safety tools and guidance. The work aims at support that families can act on before harm is done.
arxiv-2601-21618:
Martiño Ríos-García, Nawaf Alampara, and Kevin Maik Jablonka test a basic sanity property of algorithms: the answer should not depend on what is being counted. Counting items is counting items, whatever the items are. More broadly, a method's behavior should stay fixed when only the meaning of its inputs changes.

Their test, WhatCounts, isolates that property cleanly. It asks for counts of clear lists with no traps, duplicates, or reasoning steps, across different semantic types. Earlier tests mixed this property with hard reasoning and prompt quirks. A clean failure here shows a model reacting to meaning where meaning should not matter.
arxiv-2601-21918:
Alessandro Nicola Nardi and Morgane Vacher simulate a molecule that rearranges itself when it absorbs light. In 3-hydroxychromone, excitation can trigger a proton to jump within the molecule, a process used by many fluorescent probes and sunscreens. The title frames the study around proton transfer between molecules and the paths that compete with it.

The authors use non-adiabatic dynamics, a simulation method that follows molecules as they hop between energy states after excitation. Tracking the competing pathways shows which motions win and which fade. Their 2026 study helps chemists design molecules whose light-driven behavior is predictable, a need in sensors, imaging dyes, and materials that must survive sunlight.
arxiv-2601-22018:
Jinhao Zhang and co-authors shrink the networks that turn three-dimensional vision into robot action. Diffusion policies based on 3D vision learn complex manipulation skills well. But they share an odd mismatch: a tiny, efficient point-cloud encoder feeds a massive decoder that produces the actions.

Given such a compact scene summary, the authors argue, the huge decoder wastes parameters. Their 2026 preprint presents PocketDP3, a pocket-scale 3D visuomotor policy sized to match its input. Lean policies matter on real robots, where compute is limited, batteries drain, and slow reactions can mean failed grasps. A policy that does the same work with far fewer parameters is easier to deploy outside the lab.
arxiv-2601-22118:
Johann Christensen and co-authors face a blind spot in the safe use of AI. A system that works in a plant, a ward, or a plane must first be cleared for use. The clear form must state the world the system will face: the places, loads, and edge cases. For real plants and wards, that form is too short.

Rich logs of past work exist, but the terms of safe use still must be drawn from them. The team shows how to draw those terms from the logs. Watchdogs in flight, health, and road use ask for such terms more and more. A system cleared for the wrong world is a risk with a stamp on it. Ground terms in real logs, and the stamp means more.
arxiv-2601-22718:
Shiye Lei, Zhihao Cheng, and Dacheng Tao steady policy training for reasoning models by weighing the prefix of each try. RL post-training coaxes reasoning from models, but rollouts come from an older policy than the one being updated. Their 2026 preprint notes that this off-policy gap can shake training.

Their prefix importance ratio reweights each rollout by its early tokens. A steadier update should keep gains and cut collapses. The work targets the costly heart of modern model training. Small stability wins there pay off at scale. It is a focused fix, well placed.
arxiv-2601-22818:
Charles Westphal, Keivan Navaie, and Fernando E. Rosas study how language models can hide secrets in plain text. A tuned model can encode a hidden message into its outputs, a trick called steganography. Earlier schemes hid data in ways that were easy to recover once spotted.

The authors define how recoverable a hidden payload is, then build a scheme that is much harder to undo. Their hiding method draws on the geometry of embedding space, where words sit as points. The work warns defenders what to watch for, and shows a stronger attack to test against.
arxiv-2601-22918:
Rubén Calvo and five co-authors study patterns in the microbes that live in and on us. New gene-reading tools have revealed steady statistical patterns across microbial communities. Simple models that treat species as loners, like gases, match many single-species patterns but miss how pairs of species move together.

The authors link the diversity of those pair links to how close a community sits to instability. Near that edge, small shocks can tip the whole system. The idea could help predict when a gut or soil community is about to change sharply.
arxiv-2601-23018:
Sandra Loop, Erik Bertram, Sebastian Juhl, and Martin Schrepp speed up the study of user feedback for software. Product teams pair survey scores with open-ended comments, which explain the scores. Reading thousands of comments by hand is slow, so many insights stay buried.

Their approach joins multi-label classification with generative AI to sort comments at scale. Each comment can carry several labels at once, matching how users mix praise, bugs, and wishes. Faster, faithful sorting helps teams fix what users actually complain about. Open-ended comments are the hard part at scale, because they mix topics freely and resist simple counting methods.
arxiv-2602-00218: Bob Junyi Zou and Lu Tian propose GRIP2, a deep knockoff method for feature selection with strict false discovery control. Picking truly predictive traits is hard when traits correlate strongly, signals are weak, and noise is high. GRIP2 builds a feature importance statistic by adding up first layer activity over a two dimensional regularization surface. Block stochastic sampling approximates that integral in one training run. The statistics are built to be antisymmetric, giving finite sample FDR control, and tests show they hold up under correlation and noise.
arxiv-2602-00618: Yian Zhao and colleagues introduce Tune-Your-Style, letting users tune style intensity in 3D style transfer instead of accepting one fixed output. Gaussian neurons model style strength explicitly, with a learnable style tuner controlling injection. Tunable stylization guidance draws stylized views from diffusion models that agree across views via cross-view alignment, then runs two-stage optimisation balancing full-style guidance against zero-style guidance from the initial rendering. Tests show visually appealing results with flexible customisability for 3D style transfer.
arxiv-2602-00718: Noorain Mukhtiar and colleagues survey fairness in federated learning, where varied client limits and balanced results across cases make fairness critical. They classify fairness-aware methods from a many-sided view, splitting performance-led and capacity-led methods. They provide a framework for sorting and tackling fairness concerns and related technical points, checking how well each method weighs equity and results. The survey also checks metrics used to measure fairness. Finally, it explores open directions and proposes future fixes for fairness in federated learning.
arxiv-2602-00918: Aurélien Renault and colleagues adapt early classification to online learning, updating only the trigger model while keeping the classifier fixed. They study early classification of time series under cost non-stationarity. Most methods assume decision costs are known, fixed, and right, but training and deployment objectives then mismatch. They cover two cost non-stationarity forms: drift in the error-versus-delay balance, and random cost cases deviating from the nominal model. They propose online updates and baselines, with bandit-based and RL-based variants.
arxiv-2602-01018: Chongyu Zhu and co-authors teach robots to find reusable skills from long mixed-task demo tapes with no rewards or marks. A first pass cuts tapes into rough chunks with a codebook net steered by weak tags. A second pass sharpens those cuts before grouping locks in skill edges. A third pass builds a layered control plan on those skills, with a learned stop rule. The skills read as real actions to people, and the robot strung them in a new order for a fresh task.
arxiv-2602-01418: Christoffer Koo Øhrstrøm and co-authors propose PaPE, a parabola-based position encoding for tokens. Tokens from videos, event streams, images, or clouds get positions from PaPE with vision traits in mind. Earlier work mostly stretched language encodings onto vision structures, capturing traits only partly. PaPE follows rules: translation invariance, rotation invariance, distance decay, directionality, and context awareness. ImageNet-1K tests show PaPE beating the next-best encoding by up to 10.5% in absolute terms. Broader tests across 8 datasets and 4 modalities find PaPE matching the best on 5, topping all on 2.
arxiv-2602-01518: Jongseok Park and co-authors propose Qrita, an efficient GPU sampler for Top-k and Top-p via pivot-based truncation and selection. Sorting burdens GPUs, while stochastic methods alter outputs. Qrita searches by pivots for Top-k and Top-p, using Gaussian sigma-truncation to shrink vocabulary search. Quaternary pivot search handling duplicates halves iterations and guarantees determinism. Built in Triton, tested against SGLang and FlashInfer, it lifts serving throughput up to 1.4 times, halving memory, matching sorting. Qrita is now vLLM's default Top-k and Top-p sampler.
arxiv-2602-01718: Sora Nakai and colleagues revisit generalization measures for models under corruptions and perturbations beyond the identically distributed settings of benchmarks. On CIFAR-10-C/P, where labels stay fixed while inputs degrade, they test whether measures rank models well. Value proves regime tied: sharpness and input gradient measures lead among signals, while family results stay close and architecture tied. Tuning measures, info criteria and sharpness measures add regime tied signals. Model choice should not rest on IID favored measures, but should treat measures as signals for the corruption or shift setting.
arxiv-2602-01818: Mark de Jong and colleagues show how skyrmion nucleation in an Ir, Co and Pt multilayer changes with a different DMI sign per layer. In a stack the bottom half is positive DMI and the top half negative DMI. That aligns the dipolar field with the DMI field, enhancing effective DMI. It eases nucleation and stability under current and laser nucleation, with skyrmion density up to twenty times greater and visibility in stronger fields. Nucleation depends on effective DMI, and the dipolar field steers effective DMI and chiral textures.
arxiv-2602-01918: Alessandro Silacci and colleagues run a six month randomized controlled trial with 280 people, comparing solo exercise, a human peer, and a language model driven simulated exercising peer. Human peers brought stronger social presence, while AI peers gave steadier cheer and stronger working alliances. Humans motivated through real comparison, while AI peers gave consistent low stakes support. The partnership paradox shows complementary strengths: AI agents should augment human authenticity with reliability, not mimic it. Findings suggest hybrid designs joining human presence with AI support to sustain physical activity.
arxiv-2602-02218: Daniel Gratzer and others complete a build in simplicial type theory, building the infinity-category of infinity-kinds. Riehl and Shulman presented the theory to prove higher-category results with homotopy type theory. Early work stayed formal, with no nontrivial cases constructible inside it. More recent work applied cubical methods to construct the infinity-category of spaces.
arxiv-2602-02518:
Yuyang Bai and 4 co-authors teach language models to explore knowledge graphs through a difficulty-graded curriculum, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Much real-world knowledge lives in heterogeneous graphs, not plain text. Reasoning over them requires following schema-defined relations through precise function calls and aggregating evidence across several rounds.

GraphDancer interleaves natural-language reasoning with graph function execution during post-training. The first stage teaches basic interaction under rule-based rewards. The second stage rewards more grounded and efficient trajectories. Both stages are organized by the structural complexity of the information-seeking path, so difficulty rises progressively. Trained on one domain only, the model was tested on unseen domains and new question types. Despite a small three-billion-parameter backbone, it beat baselines using larger, stronger models. The graph skills transferred across domains robustly.
arxiv-2602-02618:
Fatemeh Karimi Nejadasl and 2 co-authors hunt for entirely new animal behaviors hiding in unlabeled sensor data, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Gulls wearing motion sensors produce short multivariate snippets combining three-axis acceleration and GPS speed. Expert labels cover nine behavior categories, but labels are scarce, classes are imbalanced, and some behaviors may be missing from the list.

Their semi-supervised pipeline first learns an embedding from the labeled subset. Label-guided clustering then groups labeled and unlabeled snippets into candidate behavior clusters. A containment score decides whether a cluster is truly novel. The score uses density estimation with highest-density regions to measure how much a discovered cluster overlaps each known class. When a whole behavior was withheld from supervision, the method recovered it as a distinct cluster flagged by low overlap. A negative control with nothing novel produced consistently higher overlaps.
arxiv-2602-02718:
Jiamu Bai and 4 co-authors fix a fatal flaw in Pufferfish privacy in a 2026 paper: its guarantees can vanish when an algorithm runs twice. Pufferfish is a privacy definition built on inference, appealing for correlated data where one person's record leaks another's. Some mechanisms leak nothing in one run yet reveal the whole data set across repeated runs.

The authors prove necessary and sufficient extra conditions for linear composition, meaning privacy loss that adds up in a predictable way across runs. The conditions turn out to be differential-privacy-style inequalities. Bridging the two worlds is a tool called the influence curve, which turns many current differentially private algorithms into composable Pufferfish ones. Composable algorithms for Markov chain data beat prior work by a wide margin. The paper shows clear semantics for correlated data and safe repetition no longer trade off against each other.
arxiv-2602-03018:
Outlier detection with no labeled examples is advanced by Xueying Ding and 3 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Choosing an algorithm and its settings for a new task is notoriously hard without labels. Foundation models have begun changing that, and the authors build on the first such model for outlier detection with their system, OUTFORMER.

OUTFORMER is pretrained only on synthetic labeled datasets with mixed priors. A self-evolving curriculum shapes its training. At test time, it uses the new task's own data as in-context input and needs only a forward pass. No model training or selection is required. Tests include a prominent benchmark and two new large benchmark suites the authors introduce. Performance reached state-of-the-art levels with fast inference throughout.
arxiv-2602-03518:
A superfluid flowing past an obstacle sheds vortices in patterns that echo classical fluids, but a penetrable obstacle complicates the picture. Junhwan Kwon and Y. Shin study that case in simulations in a 2026 paper. Unlike a solid object, a penetrable obstacle only partly depletes the fluid, so its true size is unclear.

The authors define an effective width from the boundary where the averaged flow turns supersonic, the region where quantized vortices are born. A superfluid Reynolds number built from that length organizes everything. Wake behavior changes around a value of two, and Strouhal numbers and drag coefficients fall on universal curves. The work extends dynamic similarity in superfluids beyond solid obstacles.
arxiv-2602-03918:
Some layers of a vision transformer may be dead weight. Peihao Xiang and 2 co-authors show how to spot them without any data in a 2026 paper. Their clue is the information entropy of a block's pretrained weights, which tracks how much performance drops when that block is removed.

Their pruning principle, Gardener, ranks blocks by entropy and cuts the weakest in one shot. On a video transformer, it matched or beat other data-free pruning methods. Even after removing most blocks, transfer performance stayed competitive. The result exposes deep redundancy in masked self-supervised models and offers cheap compression.
arxiv-2602-04018:
The brain's rhythms interact nonlinearly when a hand reaches to grasp. Sima Ghafoori and 7 co-authors measure those interactions with bispectral EEG analysis in a 2026 paper. Standard decoding uses linear spectral features, which miss cross-frequency coupling. Volunteers performed precision and power grips in a cued task.

Execution showed far stronger nonlinear coupling than planning, led by beta and gamma rhythm interactions. Grip type, by contrast, decoded about equally well in both stages. Features came from bicoherence matrices linking pairs of bands. Shuffle tests picked the useful ones. Finer neural signatures could sharpen brain-controlled artificial limbs and rehab tools.
arxiv-2602-04118:
Thirteen numbers can teach an eight-billion-parameter model to reason. John X. Morris and 3 co-authors report that startling result in a 2026 paper on TinyLoRA. Low-rank adapters normally still need thousands of parameters. Their parametrization shrinks updates to as few as one learned number.

With thirteen trained parameters, the model reached high accuracy on grade-school math problems. Across harder benchmarks, the method recovered most of the gain of full fine-tuning with a thousand times fewer parameters. Crucially, only reinforcement learning achieved this; supervised training needed far larger updates. Reasoning, the result hints, may be a low-dimensional skill hiding inside pretrained models.
arxiv-2602-04418:
Smart contract audits become a team sport in SPEAR. Indraveni Chebolu and 2 co-authors present a multi-agent coordination framework for auditing in a 2026 engineering case study. Specialized agents divide the mission: one plans and prioritizes contracts by risk, one allocates work, one repairs brittle artifacts.

Agents keep local beliefs revised by formal rules, and coordinate through negotiation and auction protocols drawn from multi-agent systems research. Plans revise as new information arrives. An empirical study compares the design with centralized and pipeline alternatives under controlled failures, focusing on coordination, recovery behavior, and resource use. The case study tests whether agent patterns survive real security workflows.
arxiv-2602-04518:
Andrés Holgado-Sánchez and 3 co-authors study how software agents could learn what their users value, in a 2026 paper on agreement technologies. These are open systems where autonomous agents negotiate on behalf of people and must reach acceptable deals.

Different people weigh moral values differently, and stating a value's exact meaning in code is hard. The authors define the value system learning problem formally. They build methods based on preference learning and inverse reinforcement learning, which infers goals from observed behavior. Their setting uses multi-objective decision processes, where several goals compete. Two simulated cases illustrate and test the approach. The goal is agreements that stay aligned with human values.
arxiv-2602-04618:
Andreas Erik Gejl Madsen reports an industrial doctoral project in a 2026 paper on counting white blood cell types with digital holographic microscopy. Such counts help acute care, and a point-of-care device could deliver them quickly outside a central laboratory.

Two prototypes were built with Radiometer Medical and a university photonics center. A lens-based system came first, then a simpler lensless design with a wider field of view. Neural networks classified the cells, reaching strong accuracy on three-part and five-part counts. The lensless system also derived a sepsis biomarker from monocyte sizes. Extra imaging tricks and a physics-informed reconstruction network were explored. The project lays groundwork for future devices.
arxiv-2602-04718:
Moritz Miller, Florent Draye, and Bernhard Schölkopf ask how to make features inside language models more separate in a 2026 interpretability paper. Researchers often treat concepts as linear paths in activation space. Acting on one path, though, can disturb others because features are tangled.

Inspired by a principle about separate causal mechanisms, the authors force features to be almost orthogonal, meaning nearly at right angles and thus less prone to clash. They formalize the gap between an ideal lone action and its real effect. A bound ties that gap to the dictionary's self-coherence, and they turn it into a direct penalty term. Tests on math reasoning concepts showed cleaner actions while model skill was preserved.
arxiv-2602-05018:
Hongbang Wu and 5 co-authors built a tool for counting the carbon cost of a promising memory technology in this 2026 computer architecture paper. The device is a ferroelectric transistor memory made with hafnium zirconium oxide, a candidate for energy-saving computing. Its full footprint, from factory to daily use, had not been measured end to end.

Their framework, COFFEE, draws on real fabrication data to estimate manufacturing emissions and on design tools for running energy. At a two-megabyte size, making the new memory cost up to 11 percent more carbon per area than standard CMOS, yet per megabyte it stayed about 4.3 times lower than SRAM. In an edge AI accelerator case study, swapping the memory cut embodied carbon by about 42 percent and running carbon by up to 70 percent.
arxiv-2602-05218:
The Segment Anything Model can cut out objects from a few point prompts, which makes it attractive for few-shot segmentation. Jiahao Nie and 8 co-authors find a flaw in that recipe when the target images come from a different domain, such as medicine or satellites, in this 2026 computer vision paper. Dense clouds of matched points, the usual prompting style, perform poorly across domains.

The authors trace the failure to domain shift disrupting how points interact with image features, and show point density itself is a key variable. Their fix, Conditional Point Sparsification, is training-free: the reference examples, whose true masks are known, guide how the dense matched points should be thinned for each target image. The sparser, better-chosen prompts restore SAM's accuracy. Across varied cross-domain few-shot datasets, the method outperformed existing training-free SAM-based approaches.
arxiv-2602-05618:
Operator algebras attach algebras of operators to groups, and a deep question is how much of the group can be recovered from its algebra. Jakub Curda and Daniel Drimbe provide a new large class of amalgamated free product groups for which a known product rigidity result holds. In plain terms, if the algebra of a product of such groups matches the algebra of some other group, that other group must split as a matching product.

The new class contains the superrigid groups identified in earlier work by other authors. As a consequence, the paper produces examples of product groups that are rigid in both the von Neumann algebra sense and the C*-algebra sense at once. Such examples are valuable test cases for rigidity theory. The paper extends earlier rigidity results to a broader family built from free products with amalgamation.
arxiv-2602-05718:
Locating actions in long untrimmed video is costly to teach, since annotators must mark start and end times for every instance. Point level supervision cuts that cost by labeling a single frame per action, but models trained that way may never learn how an action unfolds over time. Yunchuan Ma, Laiyun Qing, and 4 co-authors design a multi task framework that builds temporal understanding from those sparse points.

Three self supervised tasks do the teaching: action completion, action order understanding, and action regularity understanding. Together they help the model grasp the temporal consistency of an action across videos. The authors say this is the first work to explore temporal consistency explicitly for point supervised localization. Extensive experiments on four benchmark data sets show the method beats several state of the art approaches. The result matters for video analysis teams whose labeling budgets rule out full annotation.
arxiv-2602-05918:
Photonic chips that compute like neurons need compact nonlinear nodes, and Giovanni Donati, Stefano Biasi, Lorenzo Pavesi, and Antonio Hurtado propose one built from three coupled silicon microrings. The structure, called a SCISSOR, is passive, yet its internal feedback produces analogue, spiking, and bistable responses. Tuning injection power and wavelength selects among those regimes.

Used as a single node in a time multiplexed reservoir computer, the device classified the Iris data set without error. On a sonar task it scored above ninety seven percent accuracy, with one hundred fifty virtual nodes. In the digital scheme, spiking dynamics naturally yield sparse states, enabling classification with even a single spike. The best operating points sat at sharp transitions in dynamical complexity or output power. Performance stayed high at low injected powers, helped by spiking and thermal bistability. The authors suggest coupled microrings as building blocks for scalable on chip neuromorphic photonics.
arxiv-2602-06118:
Networks of thin conducting wires laid out in a honeycomb pattern can trap electrons in states that barely move. Chunxiao Liu and 2 co-authors show that such networks naturally host flat bands, energy ranges where waves spread across the whole pattern without dispersing. The effect holds across the entire zone of allowed momenta.

Local threefold symmetry at each junction, plus the repeating lattice, forces these flat bands to appear. They come in a fixed ratio with normal bands and survive messy details at the junctions. The team also built trapped states confined to small patches. Realistic drilled lattices keep the effect, which suits gated electron gases and patterned metal surfaces.
arxiv-2602-06318:
Stacking two sheets of molybdenum disulfide with a tiny twist creates moiré patterns whose electronic bands can be tuned. Pablo Reséndiz-Vázquez and 10 co-authors probe how random electric disorder reshapes those bands at a twist of about one degree. They use scanning tunneling spectroscopy to read band edges region by region.

Two stacking regions showed band onsets offset by a small energy gap, which symmetry arguments did not predict. The offsets varied across the sample in step with a background of random charge. Continuum calculations matched the data only when both an electric field effect and structural relaxation were included. Disorder, the authors conclude, is a central player in moiré electronics at small scales.
arxiv-2602-06418:
Turning a protein's three-dimensional shape into tokens, the chunks a model reads, is a key step toward models that grasp sequence, structure, and function together. Rohit Dilip and 2 co-authors present a global tokenization method. Older tokenizers pool local neighborhoods, so each token knows only its patch of the protein.

Here, each new token adds detail to a whole-protein picture, from coarse to fine. That ordering limits error pile-up during generation, avoids shrinking the sequence, and lets tasks draw only the level of detail they need. Tests on rebuilding, generating, and representing proteins matched or beat local methods. Token information content even guided inference toward more designable proteins, and classification probing beat rival representations.
arxiv-2602-06518:
Checking that an algorithm truly protects privacy, rather than just claiming to, is the job of empirical privacy auditors. Tim Kutta and 3 co-authors build new auditors for f-differential privacy, a richer notion that captures the whole privacy trade-off curve instead of a single pair of numbers. Most existing auditors work in batches and target the older, simpler notion.

Their auditors spot violations across the whole privacy range with statistical guarantees, backed by theory and simulations. Unlike prior tools, they need no user-supplied sample size: they adaptively find a near-optimal number of samples to reach a decision. That thrift matters most for expensive training runs like differentially private gradient descent. Both white-box and black-box settings are supported.
arxiv-2602-06618:
António Bernardes, Jasan Zughaibi, Michael Muehlebach, and Bradley J. Nelson work on magnetic navigation systems that steer small devices inside the body with coils. Precise field models are needed for control, but the standard physics model assumes tidy coil shapes and needs careful calibration. Real systems with odd coil layouts strain those assumptions.

The team trains neural networks that learn the field from data while keeping one key physical trait: the field must grow in a straight-line way with coil current. That trait allows fast, closed-form control calculations in about a millisecond. Trained on dense data from two real systems, the learned models matched the standard model's accuracy and ran in a live tracking test at 100 cycles per second. Code and data are released openly.
arxiv-2602-06818:
Anirudh Chari and Neil Pattanaik study how people learn concepts by asking questions, and what that reveals about a famous human bias. Their learner is neuro-symbolic and Bayesian: a language model proposes candidate rules as executable programs, and Bayesian updating reweights them as answers arrive. They compare two questioning styles: a rational strategy that maximizes expected information gain, and the human-like habit of testing cases the current best rule predicts as positive.

The information-maximizing strategy wins when rules are complex or exception-ridden, but loses on simple concepts. The reason is a support mismatch: sharply diagnostic questions push the learner toward regions where the language model produces invalid or overly narrow programs. The human-like strategy, though information-poor, keeps proposals valid and converges faster on simple rules. The authors suggest confirmation bias may be a rational adaptation, not a flaw.
arxiv-2602-07018:
Murad Farzulla tests whether extreme readings of the Crypto Fear and Greed Index predict wider daily price ranges for Bitcoin. The sample covers 2,896 daily observations from early 2018 to early 2026. The raw gap between extreme and neutral days is about 62 basis points, but it shrinks and loses statistical robustness once volatility controls are added.

After adjusting for realized volatility quintiles the gap falls to about 25 basis points, with none of the five separate contrasts surviving multiple-testing correction. With stricter controls the estimate is about 12 basis points with a confidence interval spanning zero. A different stratification gives about 20 basis points with marginal significance. The author concludes the pattern is descriptive and specification-dependent, and does not establish a stable or causal liquidity premium.
arxiv-2602-07218:
Fine-tuning a large model for a new task usually needs scarce labeled data, but similar tasks can help each other.  Gagik Magakyan and four co-authors propose Collaborative Low-Rank Adaptation, or CoLoRA, which exploits task similarity across users to fine-tune personalized models more efficiently.

CoLoRA trains one shared adapter that captures what tasks have in common, alongside personal adapters tuned to each user's task. The paper studies the method theoretically as well as empirically.  The idea is simple and appealing: users with similar jobs pool their effective data without pooling their models.  Users short on labels get a collaborative route to adaptation that respects personalization.
arxiv-2602-07518:
Kolmogorov-Arnold networks move nonlinearity onto network edges, but building those learnable edge functions in hardware is an open problem. Manuel Escudero and four co-authors realize them as devices with reconfigurable nonlinear-processing units, multi-ended nanoscale silicon devices tuned by control voltages.

Joining units into edge blocks and linking them into a tunable analogue network with mixed-signal links yields a real system-level build for compact regression and classification. Tests with calibrated device models and hardware measurements show exact function fitting. Hardware AI teams get a credible path from that theory to such chips.
arxiv-2602-07618:
Universal approximation theorems say large networks can approximate any continuous function, but only without restrictions on weights. Levi Rauchwerger and two co-authors show that dense neural networks, with natural constraints framing dense links, do not share that universality.

Combining a model compression argument, the weak regularity lemma, and a view of feedforward networks as message-passing graph networks, they exhibit Lipschitz functions that dense ReLU networks cannot match. The result highlights an intrinsic limitation of dense layers and motivates sparse connectivity as a necessary ingredient for true breadth. Network theorists get a precise boundary for what dense architectures can express.
arxiv-2602-07718:
Computer-drawn surfaces are only useful if one can prove the drawing is close to the true surface. Michael Burr and two co-authors generalize a classic interval-arithmetic check, the Krawczyk test, so it can certify approximations of surfaces rather than just isolated points.

The original test confirms a solution exists and is unique inside a region; the new version handles systems with more equations than unknowns and higher-dimensional shapes. A prototype implementation demonstrates the method on several examples. The paper matters for rigorous computing, where a picture or mesh must come with a guarantee, not just a plausible guess.
arxiv-2602-07918:
Tool-using AI agents can be seized by hostile orders hidden in web pages, files, or tool outputs, a threat called hidden prompt insert. Minbeom Kim and seven co-authors propose CausalArmor, a defense built on causal credit rather than always-on cleaning, which harms use even when nothing is wrong.

The key mark is a control shift: at a key choice, the user's request stops being the key support for the action, while an shady segment gives disproportionate influence. CausalArmor computes lightweight leave-one-out attributions at those choice points and sanitizes only when an shady segment dominates. Security-minded agent builders gain a selective guardrail that spends its cost only where an attack actually shows up.
arxiv-2602-08218:
Merging fine-tuned models vows mixed powers, but naive mean often harms them. Huan Zhang and four co-authors propose thinness-aware change for model merging, using step-by-step pruning-merging cycles as a tweak tool and folding thinness into the changing score.

Contest for thinness creates an odd mix: where one rival has zeros, the other's nonzero weights occupy those places, even as the sparser model wins abroad. Tested across large-scale language-model benchmarks, the line improves merging reliability and composes easily with other methods. Model-merging users gain a simple, orthogonal method that treats thinness as a feature of good merges, not a side effect.
arxiv-2602-08318:
Flow matching has become a popular way to generate time series, but it is unclear whether it truly learns the rules behind the data or just replays old paths. Soon Hoe Lim and three co-authors work out the exact target that the standard training method aims at for sequential data. Their 2026 arXiv paper gives that target in closed form for the usual Gaussian setups.

The result reads as a memory-augmented dynamical system: the sampler follows a velocity field built as a weighted mix of speeds seen in past transitions. That reading leads to FreeFM, a version that needs no training at all and still gives sensible probabilistic forecasts straight from history. Readers get a transparent reference point for judging neural flow models, plus a simple tool for forecasting when training is overkill.
arxiv-2602-08418:
Grover's search offers a quadratic speedup, but that alone cannot tame an exponentially large optimization space. Maximilian Hess and seven co-authors pair adaptive Grover search with problem-specific state preparation for the traveling salesperson problem. Their arXiv paper builds on earlier work by Baertschi and Eidenbenz, mimicking the classical Lin-Kernighan heuristic in quantum form.

The prepared states boost the amplitudes of promising tours, so a polynomial number of Grover steps can reach a reasonable approximation. The authors also compare stopping rules and iteration choices when the number of good solutions is unknown. Readers get a concrete recipe for turning a textbook quantum speedup into a practical heuristic for hard routing problems.
arxiv-2602-08618:
Gradient descent on a function with no lower bound diverges, and that divergence itself carries information. Keiya Sakabe studies first-order methods on lower-unbounded convex functions, where trajectories of gradient descent and Nesterov's accelerated method both run away. His arXiv paper quantifies their speeds and directions of escape, with implications for judging unboundedness.

The key is a dual norm-minimization problem, solvable by mirror descent with the conjugate function as its distance generator. Gradient descent on the original problem coincides with mirror descent on the dual, solving both at a one-over-k rate. Nesterov's method, unmodified, accelerates both to a one-over-k-squared rate. Readers get a precise account of divergence as dual optimization in disguise.
arxiv-2602-08918:
Testing new MRI reconstruction methods needs ground truth, which live scans rarely provide. Max H. C. van Riel and four co-authors release a public data set of moving thigh muscle, captured in vivo from nine healthy volunteers. A pneumatic cuff squeezes the leg in controlled, repeatable ways across four deformation patterns, yielding both sparse dynamic data and fully sampled check images.

The release includes multichannel k-space data, anatomical reference scans, and muscle segmentation masks for each subject. A binning-based reconstruction from six dynamic repeats matches the fully sampled images well, showing the validation route works. The data set aims to speed progress on fast, time-resolved volumetric MRI for heart, muscle, and lung imaging.
arxiv-2602-09418:
Mickaya A. Razanaparany's single-author 2026 paper works out one-loop results for the electron self-energy and vertex correction in quantum electrodynamics. The calculation uses denominator regularization, a recently proposed scheme, helped by its link with dimensional regularization to fix the needed numbers that the approach requires. The paper works out both results in closed form rather than by number-crunching.

The key check follows: the two amplitudes obey the Ward-Takahashi identity, the relation that ties vertex and self-energy together. Obeying that identity ensures gauge symmetry survives regularization, a hard rule for any scheme claiming to handle quantum electrodynamics correctly. The paper thus backs the scheme at one loop by showing it preserves the theory's central symmetry.
arxiv-2602-09618:
Sharing on short-video platforms entangles three parties: the sharer, the video, and the receiver. Caimeng Wang and four co-authors note that industrial systems usually split sharing into video recommendation and receiver recommendation, modeling each alone and wasting shared information. Their 2026 framework, UniShare, predicts both jointly, treating sharing as one ternary interaction.

Share probability flows through an enhanced representation module combining pretrained graph neural networks and multimodal embeddings with explicit bilateral interest and relationship matching. Joint training lets each task's signals strengthen the other, easing data sparsity and improving satisfaction on both sides. A large real-world dataset from Kuaishou platform logs supports the research. Offline tests beat strong baselines on both tasks, and live A/B testing confirms gains, with shares rising nearly two percent and receiver replies rising about half a percent.
arxiv-2602-09718:
Quantum machine learning joins quantum computing with machine learning, yet the field lacks full theory for how expressive quantum neural nets can be. Jialiang Tang and two co-authors offer a constructive quantum neural model in their 2026 paper. They show it holds the universal approximation property: it can approximate any square-integrable function to any accuracy. Switching function bases is supported, fitting the model to varied numerical approximation and machine learning cases.

The model holds asymptotic advantages over the best classical feed-forward neural nets in circuit size. It also reaches optimal parameter complexity when approximating Sobolev functions under the L2 norm. SAQNN thus gives the field a proven footing: a quantum neural net shown to approximate broadly, with size and parameter efficiency beating classical feed-forward rivals in the regimes studied.
arxiv-2602-10018:
Prediction sets are easy to trust when the test case was chosen blindly, but selection changes the odds. A 2026 paper by Mingyi Zheng and Ying Jin studies selective conformal prediction online, where data arrives in sequence and later choices depend on earlier ones. Existing offline methods assume selection treats labeled data symmetrically, an assumption online selection breaks.

The authors propose PEMI, a permutation-based framework that works for arbitrary asymmetric selection rules. It finds every reordering of the data that preserves the selection event, then calibrates the prediction set on that reference set. Under standard exchangeability, the sets achieve exact finite-sample coverage conditional on selection. Tests on a drug discovery data set and in simulation support the method.
arxiv-2602-10218:
Hardware design automation splits into two camps: focused RTL models that take in hardware meaning, and agent systems that steer frontier models with simulation feedback. A 2026 paper led by Chenhui Deng, with five co-authors, joins both directions in ACE-RTL through Agentic Context Evolution. An RTL-focused model trained on over one and a half million RTL samples joins a frontier thought model via three parts: generator, reflector, and coordinator.

The parts refine RTL code step by step toward working correctness, while parallel scaling tries varied debugging paths at once to cut wall-clock rounds to first success. On the CVDP benchmark, ACE-RTL lifts pass rates by about forty-one percent over fourteen rival baselines.
arxiv-2602-10418:
Large language models now anchor software development, yet securing their code remains challenging. A 2026 paper led by Weichen Yu, with six co-authors, proposes SecCodePRM, a reward model scoring each step of a code path for security. Existing pipelines use static tools or checkers trained on coarse whole-program signals. Both families need complete context, give sparse end feedback, degrade as code length grows, and suit real-time review poorly.

SecCodePRM trains on step notes from static tools and expert notes, focusing on regions tied to flaws spanning procedures. It serves full-code detection, partial-code detection, and secure code generation. For detection it pools steps weighted toward high-risk ones. For generation it ranks next lines by total reward at inference time. It beats prior approaches in all three settings and keeps correctness, with no safety-utility trade-off.
arxiv-2602-10518:
Sharat Bhat and three co-authors benchmark how well vision-language models read real maps in a 2026 paper. Maps pack geography, demographics, infrastructure, and environmental patterns into one image, and thinking over them demands spatial, visual, and domain knowledge jointly. Current benchmarks stay narrow, domain-bound, and heavy on mock content.

Their benchmark, MapVerse, is built from real-world maps: more than eleven thousand human-authored question-answer pairs across over a thousand maps and ten diverse map types. It tests map reading, reading, and mixed thinking at a depth mock sets cannot reach. Tests of ten leading models reported in the paper show how far current systems still are from genuine geospatial grasp.
arxiv-2602-10618:
Robin Beierling and four co-authors test how virtual reality controls shape demonstration quality in a 2026 paper. VR increasingly trains people and teaches robots. But the input device and its visualization may change workload and results, degrading the very demonstrations the system collects. The study compares three shapes head to head.

People performed kitchen activities of daily living: placing objects, cutting, cleaning, and pouring. They used motion-capture gloves, controllers shown as hands, and controllers shown as controllers. User experience and task execution were measured to match shapes to task types. The findings guide designers choosing VR setups: the best input depends on what the user must do.
arxiv-2602-10718:
Yifan Zhang and seven co-authors accelerate long-context decoding for a latent-focus system in a 2026 paper. Low-sharpness focus promises speed, but integrating it into decoding for DeepSeek's multi-head latent focus faces number heterogeneity, misaligned quantization scales, and missing system support. The paper's system, SnapMLA, addresses all three with hardware-aware co-design.

Key methods include keeping the rotary-embedding portion of the key-value cache in high sharpness with per-token quantization. Scales are aligned for low-sharpness matrix multiplication, and kernels are optimized alongside recipes. The result is fast long-context decoding that keeps number fidelity where it matters and cuts sharpness where it does not. The work shows how careful quantization design unlocks speed without surrendering sharpness.
arxiv-2602-10918:
Marco Cicalese and two co-authors prove measured wobble guesses for a point isocapacitary problem in a 2026 paper. In old work, among sets of fixed size, the ball alone gives the least room. In the point case that one-ness fails: the isocapacitary problem on whole-number grids may allow many best shapes.

The paper proves wobble guesses for the point problem on subsets of whole-number grids as count grows. The approach stretches the best-shape problem with care from point to smooth, joint with sharp smooth measured isocapacitary rules. The findings show how point best shapes wobble around the smooth ideal, giving shape teams exact grip over a problem where point-ness breaks one-ness.
arxiv-2602-11018:
Learning safe robot conduct from old logs is hard when logs lack cost or reward marks. Returaj Burnwal and two co-authors propose OSIL, a method that learns safety from examples of what not to do. They call such examples non-preferred paths, since they show bad conduct without spelling out costs.

OSIL frames the task as a constrained Markov decision process. It derives a reward lower bound, and learns a cost model that scores how much a path looks non-preferred. Tests show it learns safer conduct that meets cost limits without giving up reward, beating several rivals. The method suits domains where live trial is risky and hand-written safety costs are hard to trust.
arxiv-2602-11718:
When a group acts on a symplectic variety, invariant Lagrangian subspaces descend to subspaces in the quotient. Naichung Conan Leung and two co-authors study clean meets of two such subspaces whose conormal sequence splits. They match the fiber product of the reduced pieces with a shifted cotangent bundle of the reduced meet. Under a torsion condition on a determinant bundle, they also identify extension groups with equivariant cohomology.

A generalized Kirwan surjectivity follows when the meet is proper. It relates extension groups before and after passing to the stable quotient. When the two subspaces coincide, this recovers classical Kirwan surjectivity. The result is now read as symmetry commuting with reduction in a three-dimensional B-model. Similar results hold for square roots of canonical bundles, rounding out a toolkit for reduction in derived geometry.
arxiv-2602-11818:
The inner regions of planet-forming discs, including the putative habitable zone, mix a turbulent, well-ionized active zone with a poorly ionized dead zone. Matthew Roberts and two co-authors run five three-dimensional global magnetohydrodynamic simulations of discs threaded by a large-scale poloidal net-flux field. Realistic resistivity and diffusion profiles plus a cool disc and hot corona complete the setup. This second paper focuses on the vertical-net-flux regime around the interface between zones.

Five findings stand out. The interface acts as a one-way barrier to inward magnetic flux transport, draining flux from most of the active zone. Strong variability arises from maintaining current across evolving field states. A pressure maximum at the interface spawns Rossby-wave vortices. No flux-free transition zone appears; instead multiple outflow zones span all radii. Finally, a heated corona prevents active regions from puffing up.
arxiv-2602-11918:
Language models show potential in quantitative finance by processing vast raw data to emulate human-like analysis. Current methods focus either on individual stock prediction or on portfolio allocation, often ignoring the reasoning behind market movements. Taian Guo and nine co-authors propose a logic-first view, modeling the market as a dynamic web of competing investment stories, termed Modes of Thought.

Their system, MEME, reconstructs market dynamics through changing logics. A multi-agent module turns noisy data into high-quality trading arguments, and Gaussian mixture models find latent consensus in a semantic space. A temporal evaluation mechanism tracks the lifecycle and profits of these modes. By backing lasting wisdom over passing fads, MEME guides portfolio picks with robust logic. Tests on three Chinese stock pools from 2023 to 2025 show MEME beating seven state-of-the-art baselines, with follow-up tests showing shifts with market consensus.
