Across fairness and physics-informed experiments it matches state-of-the-art methods, with per-epoch runtime largely independent of constraint count and within 1.3 times regularized Adam.
arxiv-2605-18718: Aleksandr Pustyntsev and Marc Vanderhaeghen probe, in a 2026 paper, how the new MAGIX setup at MESA could sense light beyond-Standard-Model mediators. Intense electron beams of 55 and 105 MeV strike a heavy tantalum-181 target. They make scalar, pseudoscalar, vector, and axial-vector types via Bethe-Heitler pair production. Tuning the asymmetric acceptance of the double-spectrometer setup lifts signal over background. MAGIX can thus reach couplings down to order ten to the minus four, a competitive probe of the sub-GeV dark sector.
arxiv-2605-18818: Yao Fehlis and eleven colleagues describe a system that runs document AI in production at scale. Research usually stops at new models, leaving a gap to running them on thousands of multi-page files per hour. Their design splits sorting, optical character recognition, and language-model field pulls across services, keeping graphics work apart from control work. Tests find character recognition, not language parsing, takes most of the time, and shared graphics power caps how many jobs run at once.
arxiv-2605-19118: Hamzeh Mohammadigheymasi and Jin-Oh Park image the shallow crust beneath the rupture zone of the magnitude 7.6 Noto Peninsula earthquake of January 2024, which triggered a tsunami along the Japan Sea coast. A University of Tokyo vessel collected seismic data along fourteen profiles in March 2024, and the team processed them with tomography refined by continuity measures. The resulting sections and visualisations give the first detailed pictures of the rupture zone, offering a basis for studying fault shape, rupture motion, and the region's tectonic setting.
arxiv-2605-19418: He and team propose SIGMA, a way to reason with several language-model agents without letting a wrong majority crush useful dissent. Current aggregation overlooks support, contradiction and uncertainty among answers. SIGMA builds a signed evidence graph, rechecks disputed links, groups answers into reasoning communities, and stages bounded cross-examination between their representatives. A final adjudication weighs evidence rather than head counts. Across six benchmarks and varied backbones it beats state-of-the-art baselines on accuracy and conflict resilience.
arxiv-2605-19518: Castedo and team propose BLINKG, a benchmark for judging language models that build knowledge graphs from varied sources. Making such graphs still eats much time for knowledge engineers, who must match source schema elements to ontology terms. Declarative tools helped generalize the process, but no standard test existed. BLINKG offers scenarios of rising complexity from real use cases, and leading-model trials show promise yet clear limits on hard scenarios. The authors also set requirements for semi-automated model-driven graph building.
arxiv-2605-19718: Padovani and team present CAIT, a syntactic parsing toolkit for child-adult interactions built on CHILDES for language acquisition. Using the UD-English-CHILDES treebank with gold-standard Universal Dependencies annotations, they train a dependency parser tailored to CHILDES that beats widely used English parsers including SpaCy and Stanza. Alongside the parser they release a part-of-speech tagger and a construction tagger. A detailed error analysis and a case study tracking syntactic constructions across developmental time show the toolkit's value for large-scale, reproducible language acquisition research.
arxiv-2605-19918: Ruzi and Ma rework the map of light sea quarks inside the proton from two broad fits to collision data. Both fits find more anti-up than anti-down quarks across a wide span of momentum share. They then rework the Gottfried sum from these maps and get a value far from past lab results.
arxiv-2605-20018: José Llorente and Artur Nicolau prove a version of a classical limit law for smooth functions on the upper half-space. Size conditions on the gradient, and on the gradient of the Laplacian, then yield self-improvement growth properties for such functions. The results apply even where harmonicity is absent, extending the classical law beyond harmonic settings. Those growth properties follow from the size conditions alone, without assuming the function is harmonic.
arxiv-2605-20318: Pranab J Deka and three co-workers study guide-field-mediated instabilities in relativistic reconnection. Their electron-ion plasma uses a realistic mass ratio, simulated as a particle-in-cell double Harris sheet. Low magnetization: a strong guide field curbs reconnection, cuts dissipation, and weakens tearing. Higher magnetizations: no guide field lets drift-kink activity wrinkle the sheet, but a weak guide field calms it and lifts dissipation. A strong guide field curbs reconnection, so the most dissipative cases balance drift-kink calm without blocking tearing.
arxiv-2605-20518: Daniel Jacobs sets out a general rule for judging antenna-beam maps for radio telescopes. They hunt the faint 21-centimetre glow from early hydrogen, which bright foregrounds swamp. Beam errors must therefore stay below noise, though reflections can stretch the effective antenna size far past its physical width. His method ties allowed reflection sizes to instrument noise and antenna spacing.
arxiv-2605-20618: Oleksandr Yakovenko and six colleagues present COAgents, a team of agents that learn to search vehicle-routing problems. Routing is vital yet hard at scale, and hand-built rules often fail to generalize. Their search graph treats solutions as nodes and links them by small tweaks or large jumps to new regions. Separate agents pick nodes, pick moves, and trigger jumps, cleanly splitting search control from problem-specific encoding.
arxiv-2605-20718: Erhan Bayraktar and three colleagues develop a policy gradient method for entropy-regularized mean-field control in the discounted infinite-horizon setting. They weigh randomized feedback policies and a linked representative-particle and population system, with the population law governed by a McKean-Vlasov equation. A key distinction is that, after finding the value function under a fixed policy, no extra equation must be solved to obtain the gradient. Instead, an explicit formula follows directly from the value function.
arxiv-2605-21018: Vera Uzunova and Marcin Jarzyna investigate photon efficiency in high-dimensional quantum key distribution, a secure code scheme. They focus on entanglement-based protocols under realistic satellite conditions, where performance is limited by low received signal power and background glow. Their focus is cases where each photon pair encodes multiple qubits to optimally use the weak signal. By optimizing over source intensity and encoded qubit count, they study the theoretical information limit for key distribution efficiency, the best possible rate, a hard ceiling.
arxiv-2605-21118: Wenyuan Li and colleagues build an image encryption scheme that learns its chaotic map from data instead of fixing one in advance. The key holds only starting values, while the map shape itself depends on training data, so tiny changes in that data yield wholly different ciphertexts. Tests on three chaotic systems show near-ideal entropy, weak pixel correlation, and total decryption failure after a minuscule shift in starting values.
arxiv-2605-21318: Lucheng Fu and co-authors present TextReg, a method to curb prompt overfitting in large language models. Iterative prompt rewriting often yields longer prompts with narrow sample-specific rules that generalize poorly. The authors formalize this failure as waste in how prompts encode tasks, split into capacity cost and scope narrowness, whose joint growth drives overfitting. TextReg applies a soft-penalty objective through regularized textual gradients, joining gradient purification, semantic edit control, and penalty-aware updates.
arxiv-2605-21518: Han Wang studies port fillings for primary pseudoperfect numbers, addressing an Erdős problem. Erdős asked whether infinitely many prime sets and integers m satisfy a reciprocal-sum equation. This matches the infinitude of primary pseudoperfect numbers. Butske, Jaje, and Mayernik define a squarefree n as primary pseudoperfect if one over n plus the sum over its prime divisors equals one. OEIS A054377 records initial values two, six, forty-two, and one thousand eight hundred six.
arxiv-2605-21718: Chen, Ono, and Zhang settle six of ten conjectures about sums of reciprocals of subsum polynomials tied to integer partitions. They prove the claims about coprimality and divisibility in the ordinary and binary cases. They also prove the special-value and recurrence claims in the odd and ternary cases. A Lean proof checker formalized the six proofs on its own and found a counterexample to one conjecture as first printed. The corrected form of that claim remains open.
arxiv-2605-21818: Hector Ouilhet Olmos names the humorphic partnership, a class of human-AI pairs where both partners keep evolving self-models in a substrate, the partnership itself a third object. The paper traces one AI agent and her author over four months, logging one hundred eighty-one interactions. Eighty-five percent invoke two growth-witnessing archetypes, Beatrice and Muse, so it witnesses growth rather than assisting tasks. A voice-note seed grows into a four-week arc both partners author, and the system ships open-source with a preregistered study.
arxiv-2605-22118: Turatti and Ventura study tensor spaces beyond the boundary format, asking whether the critical space equals the span of singular vector tuples. For spaces exceeding the boundary format by one, in any number of factors, they relate the span's codimension within the critical space to a cohomology kernel dimension. They also exhibit an infinite family of order-three tensors with defective behavior. There, the span achieves the maximum possible codimension rather than the expected minimum. Finally, they conjecture a classification for this regime, with a connection to Koszul cohomology.
arxiv-2605-22218: Valerio Scarani points out three ways a quantum information perspective can distort claims about physics. First, it forgets that light need not be quantized to show coherence. Second, it ignores the generators of unitary evolutions. Third, it treats nature's discovery as a fight against an adversary. Together the three cases warn against letting that perspective overreach. The argument is a caution for physicists tempted to frame every question in information terms.
arxiv-2605-22418: Magalhães and Sopena-Gilboy introduce the inflation functor, a map from cochain complexes to bicomplexes. It sends quasi-isomorphisms to pluripotential weak equivalences. The functor belongs to a Quillen adjunction, whose right adjoint is a known tool in complex geometry. That tool gives a sheaf-theoretic account of Bott-Chern and Aeppli cohomologies. The inflation functor plays a key role in Koszul duality theory for operads. It also allows construction of the infinity-category of bicomplexes.
arxiv-2605-22718: Yi and others give action conditioned video world models a persistent memory without full cache attention costs. Their training free WorldKV stores evicted cache chunks in GPU or CPU memory and retrieves scene relevant chunks by camera and action match, reinserting them without re encoding. A compression step prunes redundant tokens inside each chunk against an anchor frame, halving storage and doubling history under a fixed budget. On two world generation benchmarks, WorldKV matches or beats full cache fidelity at roughly twice the throughput, with no fine tuning.
arxiv-2605-23018: Van Zandt and fourteen coauthors present first results from GEODES, a survey vetting Gaia planet candidates before DR4 and validating them after. Combining Hipparcos and Gaia astrometry with adaptive optics imaging and precision radial velocities, they showcase three accelerating systems. HIP 18512 hosts a low-mass stellar companion at 166 AU. HIP 45839 hosts a companion of about 45 Jupiter masses at roughly 18 AU. HIP 81991 hosts a companion of about 9.5 Jupiter masses at 6.4 AU, more likely a planet than a brown dwarf.
arxiv-2605-23318: Tu and three colleagues extend rank regression, a robust fitting method that resists outliers and heavy-tailed noise, to allow non-monotonic score functions. They call the result generalized rank regression, and they derive its large-sample normal behavior plus a two-stage subgradient descent method for computing it. A multiplier bootstrap supplies inference, and the method turns out to share asymptotic variance with composite quantile regression. Simulations and a real data example show its gains.
arxiv-2605-23418: Sahoo and colleagues grow wafer-scale gallium selenide sheets by metal-organic chemical vapor deposition and test them as light sources. Most two-dimensional semiconductor work chases transition metal dichalcogenides, leaving III-VI monochalcogenides aside. A 30-minute growth gives broad, bright emission across 1.7 to 2.0 electron volts, while a 3-minute film shows narrow lines and single-photon emission. Mapping points to defect-driven light rather than intrinsic exciton recombination, marking the material as a scalable platform for classical and quantum photonics.
arxiv-2605-23618: Cirillo and colleagues benchmark Google Embeddings 2 against five open-source rivals for multilingual dense retrieval and retrieval-augmented generation. Google's Vertex-AI-hosted bi-encoder, with 2048-token context and task-type conditioning, ranks first on every task, scoring 0.638 average nDCG on BEIR and 0.282 on an Italian RAG bench. But at 231.6 milliseconds median latency it runs about 14 times slower than the fastest local models. Multilingual-E5-large nearly matches it on Italian at 31 milliseconds, while LaBSE trails badly at 0.188, and all models saturate at 32-token chunks.
arxiv-2605-23918: Sai Sathvik Vadari measures the hidden idle cost of AI models parked in GPU memory around the clock. Across eighteen days of telemetry and controlled tests on three card types, idle power stays piecewise flat. The CUDA context alone forces a costly power state jump, dwarfing any memory fill effect. The context explains over 98 percent of the parking tax on every card tested. A breakeven model shows optimal unload timing hinges on request rate and load latency, not model size.
arxiv-2605-24018: Xiong and two co-authors present EvoSci, a multi-agent tool that pairs bio-inspired evolution with knowledge-graph models to advance discovery. Role-based agents, including mentor, researcher, and critic, make, judge, and refine ideas in cycles, sharing memory and feedback to sharpen clarity and novelty. On real research topics, it topped strong rivals in structured peer review and head-to-head ranking, earning the highest overall peer-review score and leading the ranking contest. The results point to stronger ideas and ongoing discovery through joint thought.
arxiv-2605-24118: Lu and three co-authors show that using principal-component scores against factors loses power against function-on-scalar regression. The loss grows with the link between the parts and the true effect, and without many-tests fix, score method raises its alpha level and gives invalid readings for the true effect. Function-on-scalar method avoids these problems with a special mix of model tools. Tests confirm the theory, and minute-level motion data from NHANES show the real stakes.
arxiv-2605-24318: Iqbal and four co-authors present a Network Digital Twin for congestion-aware traffic routing with message-passing neural networks. Telecom traffic growth congests networks, cutting throughput and raising delay, while traditional routing reacts only after degradation. The twin mirrors network behaviour through message-passing networks in two-way communication with the physical network. Synthetic traffic with rising load is generated across topologies that scale as routers are added. The twin gathers router and link metrics, classifies edges by local behaviour, and sends routing commands per router.
arxiv-2605-24618: Yoonhyung Lee and three colleagues present FC-TTS, a 2026 zero-shot speech system that controls speaking style and speaker timbre on their own from two voice clips. Earlier systems inherit limits from pre-trained disentangled representations, but FC-TTS adds design choices, training setup, and extra goals that make attribute separation more reliable. Tests show high-quality speech that sounds natural in zero-shot use. Only this system supports steady, independent control of style and timbre from those clips.
arxiv-2605-24718: Volodymyr Ovcharov maps the hidden tokenizer tax across 25 European tongues for ten base models. The tax spans 2.5 times from English to Greek and Maltese: Romance cheapest after English, then Germanic, Slavic, and Uralic and Baltic dearest. Ukrainian pays 15 to 18 percent more than cognate Slavic kin, showing thin training data. Rankings stay nearly identical across three text types. High-fertility tokenizers shred word-part boundaries instead of preserving them. Few-shot effects across languages trace to the model itself, not the language. All numbers ship as a public dataset.
arxiv-2605-24818: Johnny Tian-Zheng Wei and co-authors propose correcting test-set contamination by spiking the training data. Past work focuses on finding, not correction. The idea deliberately spikes test examples at set rates, so spiked examples tune memorization predictors, allowing sound statistical fixes for inflated test scores. To judge fix quality, the team builds a simulation setup around Hubble models, minimal pairs where one model was spiked with many test sets while the standard model stayed clean. Estimators using memorization and correctness data beat naive raw estimation.
arxiv-2605-24918: Nataša Pavlov leads the second PUDGE study, testing whether ultra-diffuse galaxies can turn into compact dwarfs inside galaxy clusters. The two kinds sit at opposite ends of dwarf structure, yet cluster maps show an anticorrelation long read as stripped-husk origins. Tracing 112 present-day compact dwarfs in IllustrisTNG, the team finds eight whose forebears passed through a diffuse, gas-rich phase before falling in. In those eight, most stars formed after peak size in a stripping starburst. The compact core was thus built fresh, not uncovered.
arxiv-2605-25318: Abhijeet and Suman Chakravorty compare Newton's method, iLQR, and differential dynamic programming for discrete-time optimal control through one unifying lens. Each method solves a sequence of quadratic programs, the paper argues. Building on comparisons, the authors show the second method is a principled SQP approach, not merely a stripped-down approximation of the third. That status guarantees a cost-descent step and convergence to an optimum under mild assumptions. Newton's method and differential dynamic programming lack those guarantees, especially far from an optimum, and numerical examples back the analysis.
arxiv-2605-25418: Nancy Iskander builds 3D face models from sketches by combining expression detection with model generation. Because expressions reshape facial contours, her method first reads the expression in a sketch, then reproduces it on a 3D model. Convolutional networks trained on her own dataset detect the expression through facial action units. The detected expression is copied onto a parametric face model called Valley Girl. Active snake contours then compute the warps that close gaps between that model and the sketch.
arxiv-2605-25518: Xinyang Zhai, Chong Yang, and Ruizhi Zhang build a radiologist-inspired network for benign versus malignant breast ultrasound classification. A cross-stage attention ResNet-18 backbone recalibrates multi-level features to highlight key tumor traits and suppress redundancy. A three-branch mixture-of-experts block learns complementary features from whole-tumor, core, and boundary views, fused by an adaptive gating network. On 2,129 images the model reaches accuracy of 96.33 percent and AUC of 99.50 percent on average, beating the ResNet-18 baseline by several points on every metric.
arxiv-2605-25618: Wang, Wei, Zhang and Luan tackle unfaithful chain-of-thought work, where step-by-step chains look sound without being reliable. They combine language models with symbolic logic but loosen strict rules, keeping results checkable while softening brittle either-or edges. Their SSR framework also builds verifiable, human-like logic chains for training. Tests across models and benchmarks show it beating current methods on robustness and interpretability.
arxiv-2605-25718: Kumar and colleagues mix femtosecond pulses from the near- and mid-infrared in thick single-crystal lead-halide perovskites. The mix yields bright, coherent, highly collimated light across a very wide tuning range, with no phase-matching setup, angular alignment, or dispersion tuning. Time-resolved checks show the light starts near the crystal faces, where phase-matching rules relax. The large intrinsic third-order response keeps conversion efficient and directional despite the tiny interaction volume. These crystals thus suit compact ultrafast photonics.
arxiv-2605-26118: Spoczynski and seven colleagues automate Triton kernel tuning for Intel GPUs via Xe-Forge, a language-model pipeline. Porting code to new accelerators repeats low-level chores: quantisation, memory coalescing, tile tuning and hardware workarounds, each needing trial profiling. Xe-Forge applies up to nine stages to a correct kernel: algorithmic restructuring, operator fusion, block-pointer modernisation, GPU-specific tuning, plus open-ended discovery as a final stage. Each stage runs under a verify-and-refine loop. The goal is ending the manual bottleneck gating deployment on new hardware.
arxiv-2605-26418: Guilin Zhang and five colleagues ask when deep reinforcement learning truly beats a well-tuned rule in adaptive resource control. Their RLScale-Bench testbed pits six standard learning agents against a calibrated rule-based autoscaler across six workload shapes and five seeds, 240 runs in all, plus a Kubernetes deployment. The rule wins on cost in every workload, though learning agents edge ahead on bursty and flash traffic. Discrete-action agents also break limits far less often than continuous-action ones. No single algorithm leads everywhere.
arxiv-2605-27018: Zhu and four co-authors review gluon condensation as a bridge between proton structure and high-energy cosmic rays. The Zhu-Shen-Ruan equation links nonlinear evolution equations and may generate condensation. Chaotic solutions can drive gluons to pile up near a critical momentum. The resulting microstructure shows up as a broken-power-law feature in cosmic gamma-ray spectra. If confirmed, the picture offers a new window on proton structure and a fresh entry point for pion condensation research.
arxiv-2605-27118: Message and nine co-authors probe random telegraph noise with a levitated microparticle sensor driven entirely by this non-white noise. This noise, jumps between two states with Poissonian waits, is the origin of 1/f noise and affects micro-, nano-, and quantum technologies. The team observes a resonant behavior: a thousandfold increase in the sensor's fluctuations, letting them measure the noise spectrum over six decades. The work gives a way to probe random telegraph noise and a platform to study dynamics under noise, with applications from biology to society.
arxiv-2605-27518: Abdul Basit and colleagues report neutron scans on the layered cobalt magnet lithium cobalt antimony oxide. Its honeycomb planes are ferromagnetic with flipped magnetization in next-door planes, and spin-wave theory fits a wider Kitaev-Heisenberg model. That makes the material a Kitaev ferromagnet, a Kitaev A-type antiferromagnet in detail.
arxiv-2605-27618: Tomas Pereira, Joao Vitorino, Eva Maia, and Isabel Praca test local explanation scores for table-based machine learning models. They test LIME, SHAP, and feature ablation across 32 datasets on faithfulness, toughness, and explanation size, splitting samples into all-right and all-wrong groups. Explanations do not always track predictive performance; dataset complexity and feature spread drive explanation quality instead.
arxiv-2605-28018: Yang and colleagues speed up drone tracking without gutting accuracy, a common cost of slimming the backbone. Their EATrack framework teaches a light student network through two teacher-guided distillations, one for features and one for localization, plus a time-adaptive module. Across five drone benchmarks it struck a strong balance of accuracy and speed.
arxiv-2605-28118: Tang and colleagues map a cascade of quantum spin states in a honeycomb magnet under rising magnetic field. Inside and beyond a one-third magnetization plateau they find at least three distinct states with near-equal magnetization, split by abrupt transitions. Further phases crowd in before full polarization, with hints of hidden order at ultra-low temperatures.
arxiv-2605-28418: Markus Herre and three colleagues test whether dataset meta-features can explain why model families differ on tabular tasks. They use results from the 51-dataset TabArena benchmark. After strict statistical controls, no feature explains neural-versus-tree gaps. One foundation-model link fails to generalize, only one comparison helps held-out prediction, and simple baselines match the rest.
arxiv-2605-28518: Chuanshu Wu and Zijian Deng disprove a conjecture on clique immersions in direct products of graphs. Collins, Heenehan, and McDonald had conjectured a lower bound on the immersion number of a product from the immersion numbers of its factors. Wu and Deng construct an infinite family of connected bipartite counterexamples violating that bound. The result closes the conjecture in the negative, showing the proposed product formula cannot hold in general.
arxiv-2605-28918: Youting Wang and colleagues treat LLM reward design for sparse structured tasks as debugging, not one-shot generation. Auditing PPO agents on MiniGrid, with MuJoCo reaching and locomotion as stress tests, they find two recurring one-shot failures: reward flooding and semantic or API misunderstanding. Their diagnostic-driven iterative refinement, guided by training diagnostics and a failure-mode taxonomy, lifts DoorKey-8x8 success sharply. It moves from about 2 percent without shaping to about 98 percent, and KeyCorridor from about 31 percent to about 87 percent.
arxiv-2605-29118: Juha Vierinen, Pavithiran Sivasothy, and Björn Gustavsson present a cross-spectral technique for timing gaps between two light signals finer than one camera frame. Aurora study motivates it, where light from different heights should show millisecond-scale lags as electrons travel down. A test rig pulsing two lights with a known lag, filmed on a phone camera, shows the method reads lags finer than 50 microseconds. The same approach maps timing shifts across one sensor, including rolling-shutter readout, and works across synced cameras viewing the same scene.
arxiv-2605-29218: Tenghao Huang and colleagues present GTA, making long-horizon tasks for web agents with process supervision. Existing benchmarks are handmade, offering coarse start-goal notes without paths, while automatic efforts stay costly and shallow. GTA integrates crawling, search seeding, contextual generation, and quality control to produce tasks paired with ready trajectories. Decoupling crawling from generation improves efficiency, grounding tasks in the site graph enforces compositionality, and replays guide. On over 50 websites spanning shops, government, forums, and news, with multihop reach, the benchmark reveals a human-agent gap.
arxiv-2605-29318: Donglai Xiang and colleagues present FreeForm, a mesh-free reduced-order method for deformable hyperelastic objects. Existing methods use meshes, hard to obtain for complex shapes, or neural fields needing per-shape optimization. FreeForm adopts a Reproducing Kernel Particle Method representation, building skinning weights by solving a generalized eigensystem on the Hessian of the elastic energy. It yields a fortyfold training speedup over per-shape neural-field optimization and lower error against finite-element results. Results span many objects, including meshes and Gaussian splats.
arxiv-2605-29418: Doyoung Choi and Jinhyung Park work out cohomology for symmetric powers of the tautological bundle. Their setting is the Hilbert scheme of two or three points on a smooth projective complex variety, with a line bundle positive enough to embed it. Group dimensions turn out to equal the Hilbert polynomials tied to the first two secant varieties. The authors work out those polynomials in full.
arxiv-2605-29718: Shivani Kumawat, Sunil Kumar, and B. K. Mani model how group-five metals change a single layer of molybdenum disulfide. Swapping in vanadium yields a half-metal, a state that conducts for one spin type only, while niobium and tantalum swaps yield plain metal-like conduct. Strong spin-orbit coupling plus broken symmetry leaves a lasting valley split in the vanadium and tantalum cases. Since the vanadium case also shows stronger piezoelectricity, the authors flag it as a base for spin, valley, and pressure-based nano devices.
arxiv-2605-30418: Roberta Angius and Roberto Volpato build a sigma-model version of Hodge loci in the moduli space of geometric Calabi-Yau compactifications, marked by the emergence of non-trivial rational Hodge endomorphisms, using generalized symmetries. Hodge loci are identified by a non-trivial category TDL of topological defects preserving the N=(2,2) superconformal algebra. At special points on these loci, TDL gains extra arithmetic structure and admits embeddings of finite products of number fields with Complex Multiplication. They analyze elliptic curves and K3 surfaces.
arxiv-2605-31118: Opletal and colleagues study cerium sawtooth chains in CeRhSn2, with a disputed ground state. Two unlike cerium sites suggest geometric frustration. From single crystals, magnetization and resistivity tests show b-axis easy. They find three shifts: antiferromagnetic order, ferromagnetic order, and a final shift. In a field, the lowest shift is at once suppressed. Field along b merges FM and AFM shifts into one shift. Field along c suppresses FM order and lowers the AFM point. Sommerfeld gain may arise from frustration but is linked to Kondo mixing.
arxiv-2605-31318: Odrowaz-Sypniewski and colleagues model rival intent in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Older methods encode intent from a fixed clue, like the rival's next move or a future state, and use it to steer the ego agent. Those clues are not always apt, the authors show, since intent shifts with task and setting. Their task-adaptive framework learns a mix of intent views driven by payoff, plus a new view that lifts mutual information with future returns. It matches or beats leading rivals across varied tasks.
arxiv-2605-31518: Simon, Adams, and Zou trace a puzzle in sparse autoencoders, tools that split neural activations into readable features. Many learned features never fire, a waste called feature death, yet rates swing from near zero on GPT-2 to over 70 percent on AlphaFold3 under identical settings. The culprit is outlier dimensions: features misaligned with the activation mean get permanently negative pre-activations at start. A severity score predicts initial death rates across 454 model-layer pairs, and subtracting the activation mean removes outlier-driven death entirely.
arxiv-2606-00118:
Foalem and co-authors track how coders talk about logging on Stack Overflow. Logging helps teams find bugs when apps fail. Past work read code or books, but the view of working coders was thin. Their study fills that gap with a huge set of posts.

The team sorts 216,094 posts by user, tag, and time trends. A large language model sorts posts into themes, checked by hand first. They find 11 themes in all. Three themes take more than 70 percent of posts. Talks on logs in boxed apps prove the hardest to solve. Most of those posts lack a marked best reply, and waits run long.
arxiv-2606-00218:
Veronesi and co-authors face the hunt for host homes of huge paired black holes. Pulse clocks in space may soon catch such pairs one by one. Each pair sings in low waves that shake the clocks. The hard part is to name which galaxy in a vast sky patch hosts the pair.

The team sims full pair crowds that match the known wave hum. They drop the loudest pair in and run a stock search pipe. Sky patches span vast zones, with huge host counts. Gaps in sky lists hide tens of thousands of hosts. A rank scheme drops hosts whose traits clash with the wave clues. It can cut the list by near half when mass and range data exist. Odds of a clean catch rise with more years of data.
arxiv-2606-00518:
Yao builds a law frame for harm done by agent AI that plans and acts in steps. Tort law asks who pays when such a tool does harm. The harm path may be picked by no one in full. Users pick less than all of it, and builders see less than all.

Three play types split the field in Yao's frame. Lone drift, pure tool use, and joint plan work make the three. Each type maps to a known strand of tort case law. Pure tool use stays with flaw and warn rules. Joint plan work maps to hire, pro-fault, and false-tale rules. Lone drift maps to stray-from-task and strict flaw rules. The state log of each run acts as prime proof in court.
arxiv-2606-00718:
Kuang and co-authors use language models to design search rules in this 2026 paper. Their field is automated heuristic design, where software writes the rules that solve hard routing and choice tasks. Past tools grow one rule at a time. That misses tasks where two choices lock tight, like the Traveling Thief Problem.

Their system, CoEvo-AHD, grows two groups of rules side by side. One group handles routes, and one handles item choice. A joint scoring step rewards pairs that work well as a team. A shared tool library gives the rules ready-made parts, like fast local-search math, through clean call points. On the Traveling Thief and Traveling Purchaser tasks, the system finds rule pairs that team up well. The authors report results that rival classic hand-built heuristics.
arxiv-2606-00818:
Sahoo and co-authors build an eye-like optical neuron in this 2026 paper. Their device aims at fast, low-power front-end vision, in the style of a retina. It rests on a Hodgkin-Huxley model of neuron firing. A two-dimensional anti-ambipolar phototransistor, run below threshold, keeps power use low.

The neuron encodes light by wavelength and brightness as spikes. Energy per spike is 0.9 picojoules in the dark and 2 picojoules at mid wavelengths. Spike rates run from near zero to 2 kilohertz. Response times beat the human retina by a wide margin. The device mimics retinal tricks: center-surround fields, adaptation to bright scenes, and color opponency. Paired with a spiking network, it hunts camouflaged objects. The authors report accuracy gains of 4.4 to 28.4 percent over standard spiking networks across three datasets.
arxiv-2606-00918:
Porat, Klein, and Pinkas break a random number generator inside Apple's kernel in this 2026 paper. The target builds IPv6 fragment IDs in XNU, the kernel of macOS and iOS. Its pseudorandom generator has a race condition: two threads can clash and leak its state. The attack learns that state by cryptanalysis, a first for a race-based break, they say.

With the state known, future fragment IDs can be predicted. That opens IPv6 fragment spoofing by an attacker who is not on the path. They show two harms. In NFS over UDP, an off-path attacker alters a file as it is written. In HTTP over TCP, an off-path attacker alters a request in flight. Apple gave the flaw the code CVE-2024-27823. All XNU-based products were patched against the attack. The paper is a case study in how a timing flaw can undo a security primitive.
arxiv-2606-01118:
Kiran and co-authors keep crop segmentation sharp under drone motion blur in this 2026 paper. Fast UAV flights blur the fine textures that mark rare, high value crop classes. Standard networks lean on high frequency magnitude features. Blur erases those first, and minority class signals vanish with them. The loss is statistical, not just visual.

Their block, Dual Quantile Activation, swaps magnitude gating for rank based scaling. Each instance's features are normalized by their own ranks, which blur cannot reorder so easily. On Agriculture-Vision 2021, across zero shot and blur trained regimes at many severities, the block is the dominant factor, they report. Gains over ReLU hold in both regimes. Rare structural classes gain the most. At moderate blur, the zero shot version beats a distilled ReLU model. With blur training added, it leads at every severity. Rank based activation and blur domain training prove complementary cures.
arxiv-2606-01218:
Gates asks how much Shannon information collision counts can give. Collision counts note how often samples land on the same state. They are easy to count in raw data. Such counts form the base of Renyi entropies of integer order. Gates uses low-order Renyi values to approach Shannon entropy. He also treats mutual information in the same way. He maps what must be lost with few collision terms.

He derives bounds on the gap from path shape. More samples cut the noise in each estimate. They do not cut the fixed gap to Shannon values. Higher collision order shifts focus to common events. Tests weigh this trade-off against plug-in and Miller-Madow tools.
arxiv-2606-01518:
Tao and co-authors generate motion for rigged 3D shapes with SkelMo. Rigged shapes need motion to become 4D assets at scale. Template methods tie to specific topologies and fail on new forms. Per-case tuning is costly and prone to local optima. SkelMo is a diffusion frame for category-free skeletal animation. It learns from 2D video guidance alone. A large dataset of about 20,000 animations supports the training.

Each clip has full textures, skeletal rigging, and rich sequences. A structural-semantic injection bridges 2D cues and 3D skeletons. Texture and semantic traits enter the joint representations directly. The model maps visual dynamics to joint hierarchies and roles. Animations stay anatomically consistent across unseen categories. Tests beat prior methods by a clear margin.
arxiv-2606-01718:
Li and Shao squeeze more accuracy from Fourier spectral methods with singular potentials. The Schrödinger equation with rough potentials is their setting. Potentials in H to the s include the 3D Coulomb case. The 1D Dirac-delta potential also fits the class. They combine the Feshbach-Schur map with a refined perturbation argument. Sharp convergence orders for the spectral method follow. Eigenvalues converge at order 2s plus 2. Eigenfunctions converge at order s plus 1 in H1 norm.

A higher-order effect appears for projected eigenfunctions. They call that gain super-convergence in the analysis. An asymptotic-recovery post-processing exploits it fully. Eigenvalue order rises to 2s plus 2 plus 2b. The post-processing costs just linear time. Numerical experiments confirm the sharp orders.
arxiv-2606-02218:
Khan and co-authors speed up synchronous RL training by sizing groups with care. Group methods like GRPO train in a stable, reproducible way. But one slow rollout can stall the whole group. Reward computation and updates wait for that straggler. Larger groups make the stall problem more severe. Yet larger groups also bring real training benefits.

Their SAGC controller adapts group size online during training. It watches observed rollout behavior to set the size. The choice is cast as an online constrained optimization problem. Long-term straggler rates are kept under control by design. Benefits of larger groups are retained where possible. Tests span synchronous GRPO and DAPO training runs. Wall-clock gains are the practical aim of the method. Stable on-policy training is preserved throughout.
arxiv-2606-02318:
Padhyegurjar and Mukherjee study pairs of black holes that merge and send out gravitational waves. Each pair forms from stars long before it merges. The gap between birth and merger is called the delay time. The authors ask whether this gap links to traits like mass and spin. They use the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA catalog, GWTC-4.

They report the first clear sign of distinct groups in the delay times. Pairs above 45 solar masses act unlike lighter pairs. Their delays depend strongly on mass ratio and spin. Near equal masses and near zero spin, pairs wait longer. Local merger rates differ across the three groups. The rates run from about 0.6 to 12 per cubic gigaparsec per year. One shared rate for all pairs no longer fits.
arxiv-2606-02418:
Cruz-Benito and co-authors use language models to hunt for new quantum error-correcting codes. The search space for quantum LDPC codes is vast. Each candidate must also pass strict checks. Their workflow runs as evolution. Language models mutate Python programs. Those programs emit bivariate bicycle codes and perturbed variants.

Five campaigns ran about 1,650 evolution steps. They screened some 200,000 candidate codes. A staged pipeline then certifies the survivors. Checks cover rank, distance, and graph duplication. Local-Clifford equivalence tests also run. At block length up to 360, the hunt found 465 distinct candidates. Of these, 97 are CSS bicycle codes. The rest are perturbed non-CSS variants. Known top codes were recovered. New finds include an indecomposable code with parameters 288, 16, and 12. The work shows guided evolution as a practical discovery tool.
arxiv-2606-02618:
Cheng and co-authors present CLIO, an AI agent that designs battery molecules in a closed loop with chemists. The agent keeps a belief-state graph that updates as results come in. A plan-then-act loop drives its work. Its key trait is called calibrated deference. CLIO can spot when its own tools or assumptions fail. It then changes strategy and forms hypotheses to guide the next fix.

The test campaign targets a negolyte for aqueous organic redox flow batteries. CLIO led proposals and readings across three rounds. Chemists made and tested 17 candidates. One phosphonate candidate improved redox potential by 130 millivolts over the baseline. Testing then exposed poor reversibility, a flaw no predictor had flagged. CLIO traced the failure to phosphonate-potassium ion pairing. It prescribed a sulfonate replacement. The new compound kept a 90 millivolt gain with far better reversibility. The full design-make-test-redesign loop closed.
arxiv-2606-02718:
Davies and Easson revisit a stationary quantum clock to separate true delay from threshold effects. Quantum transit times carry many rival definitions. The Salecker-Wigner-Peres clock reads time from the energy derivative of the transmission phase. For one-dimensional potentials of finite range, the raw clock holds a surprise. A universal term diverging at the continuum edge appears in it. Low-energy scattering data fix its coefficient.

For the attractive square well, that singularity comes from matching at vanishing exterior momentum. It is not resonant delay. The authors derive the exact clock time for the square well. They define a threshold-subtracted clock observable. The subtraction removes the universal term and isolates the resonant part. Near isolated resonances, the new clock takes the expected Lorentzian form. Its peak grows more slowly near threshold than the unsubtracted background. Control systems confirm the split between threshold kinematics and resonant delay.
arxiv-2606-03018:
Park, Ye, and Chen shrink both sides of a high-dimensional data problem at once. Cross-modal work is hard: outcomes and predictors can each be huge, noisy, and tangled. Most screening tools cut predictors only. Outcomes stay full size, and since each outcome picks its own predictor set, the joint set stays large.

Their scheme, Graph Independence Dual Screening, cuts outcomes and predictors in one pass. Fast code feeds later selection steps, and theory backs the design. In sims it beat tools that screen predictors alone. On Alzheimer's data, it cut over 865,000 methylation marks and about 49,000 gene reads to near 9,000 and 2,000. Blocks of marks and gene reads with strong links stood out. The team reads those blocks as signs of joint gene control in the disease, which plain one-side screening had missed.
arxiv-2606-03218:
Montaruli, Oliveri, Dambra, and Balzarotti show that macOS-specific features sharpen malware detection. Most malware research targets Windows and Android, so macOS lags. The Mach-O file format and the system itself have traits that can aid classification a great deal. The team builds new static features from those traits, such as embedded certificates, entitlements, persistence tricks, and key system APIs.

A new dataset holds 41,129 samples, with 11,413 benign and 29,716 malicious files. A detector trained with the new features hit about 98.5 percent detection. It beat all past approaches, with a mean gain of 16 percent in detection rate. A feature study showed the detector leans on the new macOS traits. A fresh set of 9,000 new files tested drift over time. The detector held at about 99.5 percent and beat the prior best by half. Dropping the new features cost about 16 points, which proves their worth. The dataset is released to the research community.
arxiv-2606-03518:
Ibrahim and Li propose a governance frame for AI agents that act and delegate on their own. Older access systems assume fixed users, clear requests, and static scopes. Agentic systems break those assumptions. Agents inherit and pass on permissions, act under time limits, and coordinate through shared protocols. Current identity tools lack recursive delegation and dynamic scoping as built-in parts.

Delegation is treated here as a contract term, not a static token grant. The framework defines types of delegation and what each means for accountability. A notion of scope attenuation bounds how far an agent's access can reach. A compositional operator layers these ideas onto existing policies without rewriting them. Formal proofs and an empirical test support the design. The result aims at finance and similar domains. It offers a practical base for accountable authorization in agent systems.
arxiv-2606-04018:
Zuazua studies neural approximations of elliptic PDE solutions through a variational lens. A gap sits between parameter geometry and the physical states they give. An elliptic energy can be coercive and strictly convex in its natural space. Restricted to a neural ansatz, it may lose coercivity in parameter space. The cause is non-closed neural manifolds and neuron condensation.

Yet the state functions can stay bounded through that failure. They can converge strongly to the exact PDE solution. Zuazua proves this for Gaussian wave-packet models in the whole space. Rates come with the proof. The same state-level stability covers PINN-type and hybrid methods, he argues. Relaxation and Tikhonov regularization are also discussed for practice.
arxiv-2606-04318: T Banks rederives in 2026 the cosmological supersymmetry breaking relation. It links the gravitino mass to the size of de Sitter space, the expanding geometry held to describe our universe's vacuum state. He starts from a deformation of the Awada-Gibbons-Shaw local supersymmetry algebra. From that algebra alone, the same mass formula drops out. The short paper offers the algebra as fresh support for a relation usually argued on other grounds.
arxiv-2606-04618:
Nguyen Canh and colleagues help robots decide whether a thing they see is a new object or one already on their map, in a 2026 arXiv robotics paper. This is the data association problem. It is hard in perceptually aliased scenes, where many objects look alike. Or they recompute weights as the map grows. Or they rely on hand-tuned parameters.

A Dirichlet-process prior creates a Chinese Restaurant Process association model. Accumulated evidence favors known landmarks. A concentration parameter reserves probability for new ones. Detections pass a joint semantic-geometric gate and get association probabilities. Landmarks update in closed form as semantic Gaussians. The landmark set forms a Gaussian mixture. Its dominant component feeds the back-end. A decoupled back-end keeps noisy detections from perturbing the trajectory. In simulation and on a real indoor dataset, the system improved trajectory accuracy, mapping quality, and robustness to aliasing and classifier errors.
arxiv-2606-04818:
Seisa and colleagues fly a drone through an active underground mine with its brain in a nearby computer cluster, connected over 5G, in a 2026 arXiv paper. They present the first real-world flight of a 5G-connected aerial robot controlled by an edge-offloaded controller. The high-level controller receives the robot's state over a 5G New Radio network and returns control actions, while a human operator selects waypoints.

The controller generates smooth, collision-free paths through the mining environment. The authors conclude that the deployment demonstrates edge-controlled robotic systems for time-critical operations.
arxiv-2606-04918:
Tissino and colleagues show that analyzing gravitational waves from a Moon-based detector is fundamentally a geometry problem, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Lunar Gravitational-wave Antenna targets the deci-Hertz band and promises breakthroughs from the Moon's interior to astrophysics. The authors show that adopting a frame comoving with the solar system barycenter cuts the sampling time by an order of magnitude.

They present a post-processing procedure to find the optimal origin for any signal, and find alternative timing parametrizations barely affect parameter uncertainties. Using the binary GW250114, they show the detector would measure chirp mass to a precision of two ten-thousandths of a solar mass and localize the source within 65 square degrees. They also verify an approximation linking detector orbital area to sky localization, and conclude inference for long lunar signals must treat geometry, motion, and signal evolution jointly.
arxiv-2606-05018:
Marco Peer and co-authors examine automated checking of handwritten signature lists for Swiss popular initiatives in this 2026 arXiv paper. Initiatives and referendums sit at the center of Swiss democracy, but validating the paper signature lists is still slow manual work. The team tests whether document analysis tools, including optical character recognition and AI handwriting analysis, can support that checking.

Their pipeline joins template-based line segmentation with text recognition and writer retrieval, which matches entries by handwriting style rather than by reading them. On 443 handwritten entries from 418 writers, standard OCR struggled with names, reaching a character error rate of 29.6 percent on first names. Writer retrieval proved far more robust, with a mean average precision of 50.6 percent, and the authors conclude it can help flag likely duplicate signatures.
arxiv-2606-05218:
Bart Jacobs, Michael Johnson, and Richard Buckland argue that multisets are the right datatype for counting votes in this 2026 arXiv paper. A multiset is like a set in which elements may occur several times. An election outcome is naturally a multiset: sixty yes and forty no, with no ordering imposed on the ballots. That makes multisets a natural internal datatype for vote counting algorithms as well.

The authors put the idea to work in three different counting systems: instant-runoff, the De Borda count, and single transferable vote. Along the way they isolate the abstract properties that make multisets behave so well. They form a free commutative monoid, a functor, and a monad. The paper shows how those properties derive and express election outcomes cleanly, keeping the emphasis on the voting application rather than the category theory itself.
arxiv-2606-05318:
Samuel Skirvin and colleagues examine how opacity distorts inferred wave signals in the lower solar atmosphere in this 2026 arXiv paper. Magnetohydrodynamic waves running through small structures such as solar pores carry energy through the Sun's lower atmosphere. The team observed ten solar pores within one field of view using CRISP at the 1-metre Solar Telescope.

Applying spectral inversions at several optical depths, they tracked how line-of-sight velocity and field oscillations relate to height and temperature changes across layers. Higher-frequency waves, above six millihertz, showed strong coherence with in-phase field and height fluctuations between layers. Lower-frequency waves instead showed clear phase differences, which the authors attribute to opacity effects skewing the inversion response rather than to the waves themselves. The findings warn that opacity must be allowed for when reading these signals, relevant to upcoming high-precision diagnostics from DKIST.
arxiv-2606-05518:
Tomer Bitan and colleagues guide a code model's thinking before it writes any code, in this 2026 arXiv paper on parallel code translation. Translating programs between parallel programming models is an effective testbed for code agents. Success is behavioral: the translation must compile, run, and match the original. Yet guidance methods intervene only after complete programs exist, wasting the steps spent discovering a failure.

The authors intervene earlier, in the model's latent reasoning. They train a smaller process reward model over continuous latent prefixes, the model's internal partial reasoning, and use it to select among alternative trajectories before final code is decoded. This complements post-decoding repair without retraining the main model. On a 76-task translation benchmark, latent guidance raised the mean validation rate from just under 33 percent with unguided latent reasoning to just over 42 percent. It beat fine-tuned and vanilla baselines.
arxiv-2606-05618:
Zolman and colleagues extract the triggers behind extreme events in chaotic systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. Quakes, solar storms, and rogue waves erupt from quiet build-ups that are hard to spot. The team seeks projections, compressed views of a system's state, that highlight what an extreme outcome is sensitive to. Their tool balances that sensitivity against faithful state reconstruction. Modern automatic differentiation replaces the painful adjoint math the method once needed.

A local variant handles events confined to small regions. Three hard testbeds check the approach: turbulent bursts in a two-dimensional flow, sudden sync in coupled nerve-like oscillators, and ocean rogue waves. In each case, simple forecast models built on the projections predicted extreme events well. The exposed mechanisms also suggested control laws that suppress the events. A neural stand-in for the dynamics extends the recipe to lab systems known only from data.
arxiv-2606-05718:
Kanghui Tian and colleagues change what a teacher may peek at during training in a 2026 arXiv paper. On-policy distillation trains a student on its attempts, guided by a teacher. Multimodal versions often let the teacher see answers or worked reasons. That help never exists at test time, so students learn shortcuts. ViCuR gives the teacher visual cues instead: evidence inside the image itself.

Because the cues come from the student's own input, the student can learn to recover them. A recovery module gathers visual evidence into an inner code during setup. It leaves the test-time interface untouched and needs no extra cue losses. Seven benchmarks tested two student sizes. ViCuR beat answer-based self-distillation by over a point on average at both scales. With a stronger teacher it also topped standard baselines. Teacher privilege design, the authors conclude, matters as much as teacher strength.
arxiv-2606-06118:
Yuchen Ding and Liangxun Li study Romanoff-type sumsets in this 2026 arXiv paper in additive number theory. A sumset collects every sum formed by adding one element from each of two sets of integers. Romanoff showed that odd numbers written as a prime plus a power of two make up a positive share of all odd numbers. Chen recently conjectured a broader pattern for such prime-plus-power representations, and this note asks how far that pattern extends.

The authors generalize a 1950 result of Erdős that bounded the moments of representation functions, which count how many ways each integer can be written in the required form. Building on that generalization, they give a conditional proof of Chen's conjecture, assuming the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture about prime patterns holds. They also pose an unconditional problem about integers where both a number and its shift by two admit prime-plus-power forms.
arxiv-2606-06218:
Dongwon Son and colleagues introduce the Torque Adaptation Module in this 2026 arXiv paper on robot manipulation. A control policy tuned on one robot often stumbles on another, because payloads and dynamics differ. In contact rich tasks, small motion errors break the timing of touch and cause failure. Recalibrating per robot is slow, and randomizing training makes policies timid.

TAM sits between the controller and the robot's torque interface. A history encoder compresses recent proprioceptive data, the robot's sense of its own body, into a compact state. A torque adaptor adds residual corrections so the real robot behaves like the ideal one. TAM reads only body signals, so it needs no new task data per robot. In real robot tests it reached seventy two percent success on a contact task. That nears the seventy three point five percent ideal simulation mark and beats direct transfer by twenty two points.
arxiv-2606-06618:
Jungmin Seo and Jaesik Park stitch short trips into long journeys for offline robot navigation in this 2026 arXiv paper. An agent trained on short trajectory snippets must still plan routes that hit required waypoints in a good order and stay short. Temporal distance estimates guide short hops well but degrade over long ranges. Waypoint ordering built on them goes wrong. ChronoForest answers with a closed loop: a tree diffusion planner chains anchors locally, while a multi tree orchestrator re solves the global route online.

On the OGBench AntMaze Stitch benchmark, the system reached ninety nine point eight, ninety nine point three, and ninety nine point five percent success on the medium, large, and giant mazes. The giant score is up to thirty four point five points above prior diffusion based results. On Hamiltonian route tasks, re solving corrected poor orderings and improved route quality, far cheaper than exhaustive search.
arxiv-2606-06918:
Detectors for AI generated images keep getting fooled by the next generator to appear. Ameta and co-authors rethink detection as geometry in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system, DRIFT, builds on a frozen vision foundation model. It learns a structured invariance manifold: the set of ways a real photo can change while staying real.

Two lightweight projection heads split the representation space. The robust subspace is trained to ignore physical changes like lighting and compression. The fragile subspace stays sensitive to edit like changes. A strict ordering margin keeps the two apart. Detection then becomes a violation test against the learned manifold. Patch level drift scores also localize where an image breaks the rules, producing readable heat maps. Across unseen generators and resolutions, DRIFT beat training free robustness baselines in open world tests. Interpretability comes free with the geometry.
arxiv-2606-07018:
A chain of masses linked by springs became famous for refusing to share its energy evenly. Bambusi, Carati, and Maiocchi survey the rigorous theory of that system in this 2026 arXiv paper. The system is the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam chain, first simulated in the nineteen fifties. Energy stayed trapped in a few modes for strikingly long times.

The survey leans on a close relative, the Toda chain, which is exactly solvable. Action angle variables for Toda yield stability results for the FPU chain. Finite chains come first, then the limit of infinitely many particles. In the continuum limit, two KdV equations describe the Toda flow. A direct approach shows the FPU dynamics stays near a KdV hierarchy Hamiltonian. The second half turns to thermalization times. Slowly decaying correlations imply lower bounds on how long equilibration must take.
arxiv-2606-07618:
Lin and Wan squeeze language models into four-bit arithmetic by choosing the right magnifying scales, in this 2026 arXiv paper on ScaleSweep. The NVFP4 format stores weights in four bits with block scales that rescale small groups of numbers. Existing methods initialize those scales from the block maximum, leaving a clear gap to optimal. ScaleSweep tries candidate scales and keeps whichever minimizes reconstruction error, while theory bounds the range worth sweeping under two error measures, shrinking the search to negligible overhead.

Experiments on Llama and Qwen model families showed improvements over other initialization methods and a narrower gap to full-precision quality. Under the most aggressive setting, quantizing weights, activations, the key-value cache, and query states all at once, the method preserved more than 93 percent of full-precision performance. The authors stress the method's simplicity: no retraining, no learned components, a bounded sweep that baseline operators can absorb.
arxiv-2606-07718:
Horstmann and co-authors test general-purpose coding agents on a real neuroscience pipeline in this 2026 arXiv case study. The pipeline turns fly optogenetics data, recordings from experiments that control neurons with light, into scientific findings. Its stages normally take domain experts days to months to build, and correctness matters far more than coding style.

The agents could solve several individual pipeline stages, showing that stage-level automation is within reach. They struggled most when no pre-set criterion existed to iterate against, forcing them to judge their own scientific choices. Some tried inspecting intermediate plots, but mostly failed to interpret what they saw or to act on it sensibly. Chaining every stage into a correct end-to-end run remained beyond them. The authors also flag challenges missing from standard benchmarks, such as managing computing resources and generalising to large held-out data collections.
arxiv-2606-07818:
Potter and a large team ask whether language models that think alike also work together alike, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Among humans, similar neural responses predict social closeness and cooperative success, while novelty often comes from dissimilar partners. The team tested whether the same principles govern interactions between large language models, measuring similarity of their internal representation spaces.

In experiments, two hundred seventy-six model pairs played eight games spanning cooperation and novelty. Pairs with more similar representations cooperated significantly better, but produced less novelty and creativity. Both effects survived controls for performance gaps and model size. Similarity in the early layers showed the strongest association, ahead of middle and later layers. That hints the driver is shared lexical and semantic grounding, a common basic vocabulary. The authors argue representational similarity deserves a place in multi-agent system design.
arxiv-2606-08018:
Jianling Gao and co-authors test whether text-to-SQL models speak more than one dialect, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Text-to-SQL systems turn questions into database queries, but benchmarks lean almost entirely on SQLite. Real databases differ in syntax, functions, types, and execution semantics, so the same question needs different SQL in different systems, and SQLite skill may not transfer.

Their benchmark, UniQL, aligns one thousand five hundred thirty-four questions with executable SQL across sixteen dialects, giving twenty-four thousand five hundred forty-four dialect-specific queries. Every dialect shares the same intents, schemas, and database contents, making cross-dialect comparison controlled rather than anecdotal. Experiments on open and closed models show current systems are far from dialect-universal: performance varies substantially across database systems, and success on SQLite transfers only weakly. Dialect generality should be measured, not assumed.
arxiv-2606-08218:
Mark Kozdoba and Mannor ask how deep layered probabilistic models really behave in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their objects are compositional Gaussian processes, layered random functions where each layer is itself a Gaussian process, a distribution over smooth functions used widely in Bayesian modeling. As depth grows, the overall prior, the initial belief about the function, can degenerate into constant functions only, which is useless for modeling. Earlier work found this collapse for one popular kernel across a range of bandwidth settings.

The authors sharpen that picture in two ways. First, they pin down a sharp bandwidth threshold, growing like the square root of the input dimension, above which the deep limit is guaranteed degenerate. Second, below that threshold they show the prior converges to a genuine non-Gaussian limit distribution rather than collapsing. They characterize that limit, giving the first complete account of when deep Gaussian process priors stay informative.
arxiv-2606-08818:
Grabovsky and Truskinovsky generalize a classical energy theorem to materials that bend far beyond the linear regime, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Clapeyron's theorem says the elastic energy stored in a body at rest equals half the work done by the forces applied on its boundary. That bookkeeping holds only in the linear case. The authors derive several integral formulas that act as nonlinear analogues.

The rules flow from what they call partial variational symmetries, properties broader than plain symmetry. Scale invariance is one example. Run through Noether's classical analysis, each such symmetry yields a nonlinear Clapeyron-type rule. The new rules combine the work of physical forces with configurational forces, which act when defects or boundaries move. Worked examples show the relations checking stored energy against boundary work on different problems.
arxiv-2606-09118:
Mehta and colleagues replace one-number AI benchmarks with expert report cards, and show the grades make better training rewards, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Automatic benchmarks check surface constraints like word counts, but real instruction following involves semantic judgments. The authors study rubric-based evaluation, where experts decompose success into atomic criteria. Their dataset, ComplexConstraints, holds about 1,000 prompts, each annotated with 10 to 40 criteria capturing explicit requirements and user intent.

As reinforcement-learning rewards, rubrics improved training in two settings. On ComplexConstraints itself, mean pass rate rose by 15.5 percentage points for a 4B model and 12.2 points for a 235B model. In CoreCraft, a stateful environment, rubric-reward training transferred to unseen benchmarks: 4.5 points on BFCL, 7.4 on Tau2-Bench, and 6.8 on Toolathlon. Design choices mattered: criteria must stay atomic and intent-aware, and the AI judge must be calibrated. The results argue expert rubrics are both sharper measures and scalable rewards.
arxiv-2606-09218:
Pan and colleagues recover a camera's full motion from event data without waiting for frames, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Event cameras report brightness changes as they happen, with microsecond timing and low latency, breaking frame-based algorithms built for synced images. The target: full degree-of-freedom egomotion, jointly recovering angular and linear speeds from asynchronous flow.

The team splits the differential epipolar constraint into angular and linear parts for asynchronous data. An optimization algorithm estimates full motion from just 5 points. A first-order approximation of rotation dynamics makes the constraints polynomial, yielding the first algebraic minimal 5-point solver, plus a faster variant truncating high-order angular terms. On synthetic and real-world data, the asynchronous approach beat synchronous methods in accuracy and strength against space-time noise. The work founds continuous-time motion tracking in high-speed robotics, where frame cameras blur when motion matters most.
arxiv-2606-09318:
Sanders and colleagues revive a classical parallel computing problem, list ranking, and engineer it to scales two orders of magnitude beyond prior experiments, in this 2026 arXiv paper. List ranking asks, for each element of a linked list, its distance to the list's end, a primitive underpinning prefix sums, tree operations, and genome assembly. Parallel algorithms are old and elegant, but scaling them to modern machines had stalled for two decades. The team re-engineers Sibeyn's sparse ruling-set algorithm for distributed memory.

Indirect communication, input locality, and message coalescing do the heavy lifting. Across varied input instances, the system ranks billions of elements on up to 24,576 cores. A detailed parameter analysis guides the tuning and transfers to other discrete problems. Early tests of asynchronous communication and remote memory access show promise at low partner counts but cannot yet match the tuned synchronous design.
arxiv-2606-09718:
Xiao Li and a large team build a yardstick that grades what diffusion models learn inside, not just what they draw in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diffusion models make images by undoing noise. They also serve as fine feature extractors for other tasks. The team splits each feature into two parts: an invariant core, steady across tweaks of the same image, and a residual rest.

Their metric, the Invariant Contamination Ratio, weighs how much residue leaks into the core. On the feature side, steadiness peaked at mid-level noise. Those same noise levels gave the best scores on later sorting tasks. On the making side, the metric flagged when training tipped from true learning into rote recall. Rising residue along key directions marked the tip, read from training features alone. No outside judge or held-out set was needed. The tool thus lets teams watch a model's health as it trains.
arxiv-2606-09918:
Anthony Howell and his co-authors map the skill shape of every United States county across fifteen years in this 2026 arXiv paper. The set is built from four hundred thirty-three point six million job postings, spanning twenty ten to twenty twenty-four. It covers three thousand one hundred ninety-four counties and two hundred one measures per county-year. Post counts sit beside work style shares, like remote and intern posts, and the skill mix firms ask for.

On top sits a suite of place measures: how specialized a county is, how related its skills are, and how complex its demand runs. The same split is cut by employer kind, from firms to federal labs. Pair tools then gauge how two counties' skill sets align or gap. The team pitch the set as a base for place-based policy and study.
arxiv-2606-10918:
Kuramshin and colleagues enrich robot training data by relabeling it in this 2026 arXiv paper. Robot policies follow instructions poorly, partly because demonstration datasets pair long videos with few, plain labels. Their framework TREAD uses a vision-language model in three stages. It drafts semantic sub-tasks from the original label and first scene, cuts the video at those sub-tasks, and writes varied new instructions for each piece.

Policies trained on the relabeled data, tested on LIBERO, handle novel tasks and goals better than those trained on the raw set. Splitting long demonstrations helps planning, while the wider wording improves language following. The gains come with no new robot data collected.
arxiv-2606-11718:
Euijun Chung, Jae Hyung Ju and Hyesoon Kim speed up AI computation on multi-chiplet graphics processors in this 2026 arXiv paper. A chiplet processor packs several small chips, each near its own high-bandwidth memory. Work that reads memory attached to a distant chiplet pays extra time and energy. Matrix multiplication, called GEMM, dominates language model workloads, but its data placement clashes with fixed page-sized memory interleaving.

Their Chiplet-Contiguous Layout stores each chiplet's data in one unbroken stretch of memory. Local placement becomes compatible with ordinary page granularity, the smallest unit the system moves. No system or hardware changes are needed. On real language model workloads from Qwen and Llama models, remote memory traffic falls dramatically: roughly thirteen times lower on Qwen and over twenty times lower on Llama compared with fine interleaving. Against a coarse locality-aware placement the layout still cuts remote traffic more than threefold.
arxiv-2606-11818:
Rami Ojanen, James Fant-Male and Roel Pieters study humans and robots handling delicate sheets together in this 2026 arXiv paper. Carbon fibre plies are flexible sheets used in aircraft and car parts. They deform easily, making full automation hard, while handling them manually is tedious and strains workers. Co-manipulation, where a person and a robot carry the material jointly, promises a middle way.

The team compares control methods: a predefined trajectory, stepwise voice commands, compliant force control, wrist tracking by camera, and hybrids. The fixed trajectory is fast and voice commands feel intuitive. But compliance, where the robot yields to the operator's forces, gives greater and more stable control. Vision-based wrist tracking lets the robot be guided without pulling on the ply, protecting the material and the operator's body. The authors propose combining speech, wrist tracking and compliant force control as the best route.
arxiv-2606-11918:
Théo Uscidda and four colleagues improve spatial reasoning in AI models without any labelled data in this 2026 arXiv paper. Large reasoning models lag humans badly on tasks like relative position, depth ordering and size comparison. The authors argue the ability is often already inside the model, but needs alignment through logical coherence rather than new knowledge.

Their self-supervised reinforcement learning framework rewards consistency. Verifiers check that answers stay geometrically and semantically consistent when the image is flipped or the question's object order is swapped. A new training strategy, OT-GRPO, adapts group-based policy optimisation with a minimal-matching rule from optimal transport theory, making rewards hard to earn by luck. Label-free consistency training approaches the accuracy of models trained with ground-truth supervision. It also generalises similarly across diverse tasks and data domains, suggesting interrogating a model's own consistency can substitute for expensive annotation.
arxiv-2606-12618:
Cooney and co-authors build liars whose lies can be verified, then show lie detectors fail on them, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Testing a lie detector needs models that believe the opposite of what they say. Earlier test organisms often failed that requirement. The team trains thirteen model organisms whose beliefs are verified in their chain-of-thought and generalize to tasks.

Four detectors face the tests: a chain-of-thought judge, a logprob classifier, and two activation probes, including their follow-up probe method. On prompted lying, across thirty-one models from two billion to a trillion parameters, all detectors improve with model capability. On the trained organisms, every activation and logprob detector drops sharply; their probe keeps the most signal. Only the thought judge holds, at 0.82 balanced accuracy, partly because verification favors beliefs readable in thoughts. The verdict: detectors cannot support high-confidence claims about model beliefs.
arxiv-2606-12718:
Mondal and Sundaramoorthi bring out-of-distribution detection methods to radio-frequency fingerprinting, in this 2026 arXiv paper. RF fingerprinting identifies wireless transmitters from subtle signal quirks caused by hardware imperfections. Real deployments are open-set: unknown transmitters appear, and a closed-set classifier will confidently mislabel them as known devices, a direct security risk.

Out-of-distribution, or OOD, detectors flag inputs unlike the training data, but most need example OOD data for tuning, which is impractical to collect for radio environments. The authors present feature-shaping detectors, which modify a network's internal activations before scoring, and apply recent methods for tuning them with no OOD data at all. On the public POWDER fingerprinting dataset, detectors tuned without any OOD data match baselines that were tuned with genuine OOD data. They also greatly outperform baselines denied such data, showing open-set detection is practical for RF systems.
arxiv-2606-12818:
Owusu and colleagues trace where inside a language model an irrelevant number exerts its pull on numerical judgements, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Using a multiple-choice setup with shared answer options, the authors define a logit-difference metric comparing the correct option with the option matching the anchor. They verify it tracks behavioural anchoring.

Applying circuit localisation to 7B to 8B Qwen and Llama models, in base and instruction-tuned variants, they find a clear pattern. Edge-level methods, which score the connections between components, recover the anchor-sensitive signal more faithfully than node-level methods that score components alone. Circuits for low and high anchors transfer within a model, suggesting the pathway structure is shared across anchor direction. Transfer between base and instruction-tuned variants is less reliable, indicating post-training changes which pathways matter most.
arxiv-2606-12918:
Xu and colleagues present MAStrike, a closed-loop framework for collusive red-teaming of hierarchical multi-agent systems, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Current red-teaming picks target agents by feel and perturbs messages, leaving open which agents matter most for safety and how hacked agents could act together.

MAStrike first works out agent-level Shapley values, a game-theoretic attribution of each agent's marginal contribution to system robustness, estimated from coalition-level attack success rates. Guided by those values, a red-teaming agent selects synergy-aware coalitions of agents and creates coordinated, role-aware adversarial moves, refined in rounds through failure diagnosis. The authors also build MABench, a red-teaming benchmark spanning hierarchical topologies and domains with tunable environments for collusion risk checks. MAStrike beats heuristic baselines, reaching an attack success rate of 61.8 percent against Claude Opus 4.7 and 55.6 percent against GPT-5.5.
arxiv-2606-13318:
Wu and Yan review the search for exotic spin-dependent interactions in this 2026 arXiv paper. Several deep puzzles, including the nature of dark matter and a stubborn asymmetry in the strong nuclear force, motivate hypothetical light particles. Axions and axion-like particles are leading examples: feebly interacting, possibly light enough to form cold dark matter. Such particles would mediate new forces between ordinary matter. Many of those predicted forces depend on particle spin, the intrinsic angular momentum of electrons and nuclei, which makes them distinguishable from known forces.
