The review first lays out the foundations, surveying how frameworks predict each interaction's form and strength. It then examines the experiments: precision instruments built to detect forces far weaker than any known background. Tabletop experiments using spin-polarised matter play a central role. By organising theory and experiment together, the authors map which parts of the parameter space remain unexplored.
arxiv-2606-13518:
Escobar, Klein, and Weigandt study a weak order on alternating sign matrices in this 2026 arXiv paper. Alternating sign matrices are grids of zeros, ones, and minus ones with sign rules, known for their formulas. They correspond to monotone triangles, arrays with increasing rows and columns. In 2018, Hamaker and Reiner extended the weak order, a structure on permutations, to monotone triangles, and to alternating sign matrices. This paper develops that structure, connecting it to bumpless pipe dreams, a diagrammatic tool.

Weak order is a partial order whose covering moves swap adjacent elements in controlled ways, and its lattice properties encode symmetry. The authors relate the families of objects, matrices, triangles, and pipe dreams, within this ordering. Such links let results proved for one object transfer to the others. The work continues a tradition in which alternating sign matrices meet combinatorics and representation theory.
arxiv-2606-13718:
Sanyal, Choudhury, and Rahaman model the spiral galaxy NGC 7331 within general relativity in this 2026 arXiv paper. Galaxy rotation curves, how fast stars orbit at each radius, probe the mass distribution, and this galaxy's stars move too fast for its visible matter at large radii. The authors fit a modified exponential velocity law to the motion data and use infrared light measures to constrain the stellar mass profile. Adopting a static, round spacetime with anisotropic matter, they rebuild the metric functions and derive enclosed mass, energy density, and tangential pressure profiles.

The stellar mass falls below the total gravitating mass at intermediate to large radii, indicating dominant dark matter, matching the standard profile. They check the model's viability through energy conditions, causality constraints, and the stability of circular orbits. The study demonstrates that combining rotation-curve data with photometric stellar mass estimates inside general relativity yields a consistent picture.
arxiv-2606-14118:
Dey and colleagues simulate molten lithium carbonate, a key fuel-cell electrolyte, with machine-learned potentials accurate enough to replace costly quantum calculations. The melt's many-body interactions defeat classical force fields, while ab initio simulation is too slow for transport questions. Their 2026 arXiv paper trains two equivariant graph-based potentials, MACE and NequIP, on melt-quench ab initio data. MACE, using higher body-order message passing, proved more accurate and transferable.

The model reproduced measured structure factors and shear viscosity, and the carbon-oxygen pair correlation persisted in the melt. Its central finding concerns lithium motion. Haven ratios of roughly zero point two zero to zero point four zero, far below one, show lithium ions move in concerted groups, not by independent hopping. At one thousand kelvin, transport is anisotropic and highly concerted, lithium trapped in persistent oxygen cages. At fourteen hundred kelvin it becomes isotropic and less concerted.
arxiv-2606-14318:
Sturm derives new curvature formulas in a 2026 arXiv paper. The topic is the geometry of chance. The objects are spaces whose points are measures. A measure says how mass or chance is spread out. Two distances are studied here. The Kantorovich-Wasserstein metric rests on cheapest transport cost. The Hellinger-Kantorovich metric also lets mass appear or vanish.

Sturm gives an explicit formula for sectional curvature. That number says how the space bends along each flat slice. The formula covers finite measures on a curved base space. It uses the Hellinger-Kantorovich metric. Even for flat Euclidean space, the curvature splits in two. One part is negative and one part is positive. He studies both parts in detail on the torus case. His approach also sheds new light on curvature under the Wasserstein metric.
arxiv-2606-14418:
Vakhitov and co-authors introduce COMET in a 2026 arXiv paper. The field is model-based reinforcement learning. Here an agent learns a model of its world and plans inside it. COMET plans with Monte Carlo tree search. That method explores action paths as branching trees. It works in a latent space split by objects, called slots.

A frozen object-based encoder splits each scene into slots. A transformer world model then predicts how slots change. Actions are bound to specific objects. Policy and value heads weigh slots by learned relevance. So choices focus on items that matter for the task. The team tested eight tasks from visual control, robot work, and games. COMET earned higher early scores than both object-based and monolithic rivals. This suggests object structure helps planning start faster.
arxiv-2606-14618:
Kahani and Jaskolka ask how machine learning should enter software engineering degrees in a 2026 arXiv paper. AI parts now sit inside many software products. Yet undergraduate curricula rarely prepare students to build such systems in a systematic way. Testing, deploying, and maintaining them all need teaching. The authors aim for evidence-based guidance on closing that gap.

They first compile a structured list of topics that matter for AI-based software work. Next they map those topics against required courses in sample curricula. That mapping finds coverage gaps. They also survey instructors on each topic's importance and on practical limits. Crossing the three sources yields a guideline. It recommends where high-priority topics can be embedded. The advice favors existing courses over new degrees.
arxiv-2606-14718:
Renzella and co-authors study gender differences in a school AI literacy workshop in a 2026 arXiv paper. As AI literacy programs expand in schools, designers need to know how gender shapes students' starting perceptions, tool use, and responsiveness. The study follows Australian secondary students in years seven, eight, and ten at two co-educational government schools through a one-day workshop.

About one hundred ninety-nine students answered before and one hundred thirty-six after. Beforehand, boys reported significantly higher STEM career interest in AI, computer science, and engineering, while girls were more likely to use AI for schoolwork and advice. Boys were also significantly more likely to have created or shared deepfake content. Both genders gained AI knowledge, but girls gained more broadly, with confidence and career interest rising enough to narrow the STEM gap partly, motivating gender-responsive curricula.
arxiv-2606-15118:
Guo and coauthors fuse image features at higher orders to find faint objects in space imagery in a 2026 study. Weak objects, from station experiments to distant satellites, show little appearance information. Single features miss much of the signal. The authors treat several attention outputs as multiple views of the same image.

Their module, MHF, extends standard low-order feature fusion to higher-order combinations. Spatial, channel, and frequency attention supply the multi-view features to combine. A perception step builds the high-order views, and a gated selection step weighs each view by task contribution. The module plugs into detectors and segmentation models with under two million added parameters. Experiments span two new space science datasets and a large satellite video benchmark. Applied to twenty-one advanced methods, MHF lifts detection and segmentation accuracy. The authors report state-of-the-art results on the tasks across all three datasets.
arxiv-2606-15418:
Gulgonul solves an exact tuning problem for industrial controllers in a 2026 control theory paper. A PI controller, correcting a process from its current and accumulated error, must drive a pure time-delay process to its setpoint fast without ever overshooting. Because of the delay, the response is built from polynomial pieces joined at echoes of the delay interval, with jumps that shrink geometrically.

That echo structure pins the optimum down: the best response grazes the setpoint and the settling band exactly at echo boundaries, giving as many equations as unknowns. In one band range the optimal gains are closed-form constants, and the settling time follows an exact formula. As the tolerance tightens toward zero, the gains approach a known spectral tuning point, yet adapted tuning beats it at every practical tolerance, by about forty percent at a two percent band.
arxiv-2606-15618:
Chang, Liu, and Liu prove a sharp product bound in 2026 for cross-intersecting families of sets, in extremal combinatorics. Several families are cross-intersecting when any choice of one set from each family shares a common element. Under the p-biased measure, where each element joins a set independently with probability p, the team bounds the product of the family measures.

The product is at most p raised to the number of families, over the full bias range, and a common star attains the bound. That settles the equal-bias case of a Frankl-Tokushige conjecture and, for three families, a conjecture of Tokushige. A stability theorem adds that near-extremal families sit close to a common star. The distance grows at most linearly in the product deficit, which is optimal. The proof couples coordinates at the critical bias and forces the star structure through Fourier concentration.
arxiv-2606-16118:
Wang and colleagues test in 2026 whether language models reason faithfully about legal entailment, or only appear to. Legal entailment asks whether a contract text supports a given claim. The team compares three setups: direct classification, language-model formal reasoning, and solver-based reasoning with the Z3 solver. A re-annotated ContractNLI subset, checked across five models, supplies the test bed.

Re-annotation exposes a systematic gap between pragmatic legal reading and strict formal entailment. Many legally sound inferences need unstated assumptions the contract text alone does not supply. Adding formal structure improves benchmark accuracy, and language-model formal reasoning scores highest overall. That gain does not imply faithful reasoning, the authors show. They name recurring failure modes, including scope laundering, where models report solver-style conclusions without running the formal reasoning. A second mode, implicit constraint blindness, leaves hidden assumptions unnoticed.
arxiv-2606-16218:
Li and colleagues report in 2026 a strong link between dwarf galaxy ages and how their metal content varies from center to edge. Metallicity gradients act as a fossil record of how a galaxy assembled. The team analyzes gradients for 90 nearby low-mass galaxies with VLT/MUSE spectroscopy, spanning stellar masses deep into the classical dwarf regime.

Older dwarfs show steeper, more negative metallicity gradients in the data. The negative correlation with light-weighted stellar age is robust, with strength near or above 0.7, measured out to about twice the effective radius. It holds regardless of mass, compactness, or group versus field environment, and peaks at intermediate masses. The slope closely matches FIRE-2 simulations. That match points to stellar radial migration, driven by feedback-induced potential fluctuations, as a key driver, with environmental quenching also shaping the pattern.
arxiv-2606-16318:
Gupta and co-authors analyze in 2026 a mixed local-nonlocal operator in the delicate regime where both parts are critical at once. The operator joins the p-Laplacian, a local nonlinear diffusion, with a fractional q-Laplacian, its nonlocal cousin. In the isocritical regime the two Sobolev critical exponents coincide, so both best Sobolev constants enter the variational structure simultaneously. The equation studied sets this operator against a power nonlinearity.

The authors prove four things. A nonnegative radial ground state exists, built by Nehari manifold methods with a double-threshold concentration-compactness analysis. A logarithmic energy estimate, a weak comparison principle, and a strong maximum principle hold throughout. A weak Harnack inequality follows. Finally, positive radial solutions obey sharp two-sided decay, falling like the power (N minus p) over (p minus 1) of the radius, matching the local operator's rate.
arxiv-2606-16518:
Waters and co-authors show in 2026 that describing the solar wind's turbulence, not just its average state, steadies forecasts of geomagnetic activity. The auroral electrojet index tracks currents in the upper atmosphere. Forecasting it from upstream solar wind data is hard because the magnetosphere couples nonlinearly and varies across scales. Two gradient-boosted models compete: a baseline using mean solar wind and magnetic field parameters, and a turbulence-aware twin.

The turbulence-aware model adds measures of fluctuation amplitude, intermittency, and Alfvénic structure. Both models correlate with reality above 0.8 at 60 minutes ahead. The baseline's skill peaks at 75 minutes and fades, while the turbulence-aware model holds comparable skill across the 60-to-90-minute window. It also beats a noise-surrogate control, so the gain is real information, not extra parameters. Improvements are modest in global error but systematic, and strongest in the roughest regimes.
arxiv-2606-16918:
Singh and colleagues study quantum sensing with a pair of spins in a 2026 metrology paper. Two coupled qubits with direction-dependent exchange can serve as a probe for a magnetic field. A twisting Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction and intrinsic decoherence complicate the probe's behavior.

Using quantum Fisher information, the standard measure of how much a state knows about a parameter, the authors gauge both the uniform magnetic field and the twisting interaction's strength. Exact formulas for the evolving state let them scan the tuning, decoherence and starting state choices. Tuning the exchange and picking a good entangled start improves precision noticeably. No single setting is best for both tasks, though: field sensing and interaction sensing favor different regimes. Decoherence erodes sensitivity, but smart tuning recovers much of the loss. Entanglement and coherence measures are tracked to explain the gains.
arxiv-2606-17018:
Cohen and Lellouch map how much coverage a city actually needs in a 2026 paper on urban monitoring. Distributed acoustic sensing turns existing fiber-optic cables into dense vibration arrays. New on-chip sensors could extend that reach, but real fiber layouts are patchy, so coverage stays partial for years.

Using graph theory, the authors show tasks fall along a coverage spectrum split by two thresholds. Below ten percent coverage, good designs already support earthquake early warning, groundwater monitoring, geological mapping and activity tracking. Near fifty-two percent, a percolation transition flips the city to effectively fully covered, enabling statistical traffic monitoring. Only near-complete coverage unlocks infrastructure monitoring and tracking of vehicles and pedestrians, so privacy risks stay low until then. Worked designs for real metropolises show how to place sensors for each goal. The framework gives planners a roadmap: buy coverage in the order the thresholds reward.
arxiv-2606-17218:
Nabbie and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper cataloguing transit timing variations. The catalogue uses systems observed by the TESS space telescope. When planets in one system pull on each other, their transits arrive early or late. Those shifts reveal planet traits and trace how the system migrated while forming.

The team used the first five years of TESS data, covering sectors one to sixty-nine. From an initial sample of multi-candidate systems, twenty showed significant timing shifts. Thirteen of those twenty had not been detected before this work. Compact systems were more likely to show the effect, matching earlier Kepler catalogues. TESS systems instead pile up near the two-to-one resonance, hinting at a different migration history.
arxiv-2606-17618:
Gao and Shen present a 2026 arXiv paper on an unexpected swirl inside the current carried by electrons confined in a cylinder, found within ordinary Dirac theory. Helical electron flow is usually tied to orbital angular momentum or to outside fields shaping the beam. Here, exact confined states show a definite helical current texture even in the channel with no orbital angular momentum at all. The two spin sectors curl in opposite senses around the axis of the cylinder.

For the lowest confined mode, the current runs along the axis while also circling it, and the pattern persists into the fading tail region. A static chiral potential then couples the modes through a kernel built from that texture. The coupling obeys a geometric selection rule: same-channel terms vanish, while spin-flipping conversion channels survive. No magnetic field or spin-orbit coupling is needed for the effect.
arxiv-2606-18118:
Suciu shows how to solve a stubborn groundwater equation with a function-based computing system, in a 2026 case study for Advances in Water Resources. Richards equation governs water moving through unsaturated soil, and its steady form is a nonlinear boundary value problem. The Chebfun system represents smooth functions by Chebyshev polynomial expansions and can solve such problems to near machine precision through its automated chebop class, which linearizes with Newton's method in function space.

That automation has a catch: Newton can fail to converge when the starting guess strays too far from the true solution. Suciu compares three routes on the Richards problem. Where chebop succeeds it is effortless and exact, but an explicit functional linearization widens the range of workable guesses. A simpler implicit L-scheme, swapping derivatives for chosen constants, is globally convergent and easiest to implement, trading some speed for certainty.
arxiv-2606-18418:
Oliveira, Valdrighi, and Raimundo introduce P²CE, an algorithm that generates counterfactual explanations for machine learning decisions, in a 2026 paper on explainable AI. A counterfactual tells someone denied a loan or a job what changes to their inputs would flip the outcome, but good ones must be achievable, plausible, and cheap to compute.

P²CE treats those goals as a multi-objective problem and returns a Pareto-optimal set, a spread of explanations offering trade-offs rather than one compromise. An isolation forest outlier detector keeps suggested points inside the real data distribution, so explanations do not recommend impossible profiles. SHAP values steer the search so it stays fast whatever the underlying model is. Tested on three datasets against rival techniques, P²CE produced higher-quality explanation sets at lower cost. The authors pitch it for high-stakes choices where people deserve realistic, usable routes to an outcome.
arxiv-2606-18518:
Ilaty and the team at San Diego State University present PSyGenTAB in a 2026 health informatics paper. PSyGenTAB builds synthetic clinical data tables that guard patient privacy by design. Medical AI lacks data, because privacy law and data silos block sharing. Older methods give users no dial for that trade-off.

PSyGenTAB treats data making as a constrained optimization problem, solved with the augmented Lagrangian method. A minimum privacy threshold is built right into training, while clinical utility is pushed as high as it can go. On tests built for clinical aims, it kept links between features and the diagnostic patterns of minority classes. Models trained just on its data did about as well as models trained on real records. Privacy audits found much less copying of exact patient records. Membership inference attacks did near chance. The authors argue privacy and use can be won jointly, not traded off.
arxiv-2606-18618:
Hew develops a matched asymptotic theory for a weak shock wave reflecting off a rigid wall at nearly glancing incidence, in a 2026 fluid mechanics note. Shock reflection switches between regular and Mach patterns. The weak, shallow-angle corner of the problem, tied to the von Neumann paradox, is governed near the triple point by an unsteady transonic small-disturbance equation.

Working in the joint limit of weak shock strength and small glancing angle, Hew shows the inner reflection problem is controlled by a single dimensionless parameter independent of the gas's specific-heat ratio. Every leading-order inner quantity therefore depends on the parameters only through one combination. The transition between reflection types sits at the detachment value, and the true inner field carries a sequence of supersonic patches rather than a single fan. A pilot time-marching solver is benchmarked against published triple-point results.
arxiv-2606-19018:
Kozlov studies global branches of Stokes waves on stratified fluids in a 2026 mathematics paper. The setting is steady water waves in a two-dimensional channel, where water density varies with depth. Branches of waves split off from simple laminar flows. Mass flux and the Bernoulli constant are held fixed, while the wave period is free to change along the branch, an unusual choice that widens what solutions can appear.

The author presents a new class of density and Bernoulli functions for which laminar flows generate global bifurcation branches. Those flows need not run in one direction and can include counter-currents. The branch can even split off from a laminar flow with arbitrarily large period, which was fixed in advance. Results of this kind map the full range of steady stratified waves a channel can support. They matter for understanding how layered flows sustain large steady waves.
arxiv-2606-19118:
Pesenti and colleagues use explainable AI to study what drives European electricity prices in 2026. Power markets are complex, with strong nonlinear links and growing ties across regions. Deep neural networks predict prices well but cannot explain them, which limits their use for policy and market design. The team pairs such networks with explanation tools to map price drivers across thirty nine bidding zones in Europe.

SHAP values quantify each feature's contribution, and an extended aggregation framework keeps those explanations readable in high dimensions. Solar power plays an outsized role in price formation despite its modest share of generation. Gas prices remain a dominant, steady driver across markets. Interconnections strongly shape prices too, confirming deep interdependence among national systems. The authors also build a synthetic single-price European market to explore a fully integrated case. That counterfactual helps show what integration would change, and what it would leave untouched.
arxiv-2606-19218:
Krishnappa and colleagues introduce RECOM in 2026, a dataset for testing automatic metrics on open-ended Reddit question answering. A metric must do two jobs at once. It should tell genuine content match from surface coincidence, and it should rank a better system above a worse one. On opinion-driven questions, the authors find those two jobs in direct tension for every metric they test on model answers.

The dataset holds fifteen thousand AskReddit questions with authentic community replies, all posted after every tested model's training cutoff. Five open models are scored against every reply, with a random-derangement noise floor for scale. Cosine similarity separates real from random answers strongly but cannot rank the models. A leading score appears to rank them until response length is controlled, when its edge collapses. Three judges reproduce the ordering. The tradeoff is a property of metric design, not of the models.
arxiv-2606-19518:
Z Brown and L Samushia forecast in 2026 how three-point galaxy statistics can sharpen cosmic measurements. Full-shape clustering uses the whole pattern of galaxy positions, not just one feature. The pair study emission line galaxies for the Roman Space Telescope survey and red galaxies from DESI.

Forecasts rest on AbacusSummit simulations filled with galaxies through halo occupation models matched to each survey. A fast triangle-counting code, TriCo, measures the three-point correlation function on scales below the acoustic feature. That placement yields information largely separate from standard distance-scale results. Adding the three-point signal tightens the sigma-eight constraint, a measure of matter clumping, by about a factor of five. The gain spreads across many triangle shapes rather than one hot spot. Keeping the full line-of-sight pattern adds a further two to three times over the angle-averaged version.
arxiv-2606-19918:
Jianze Wang, Wei Zhang, and Xuanyao Fong design a memory cell that switches between volatile and non-volatile modes in 2026. Standard SRAM leaks power, while emerging non-volatile memories write slowly. Hybrid non-volatile SRAM designs usually pay backup-restore steps and heavy area costs.

The cell pairs two cross-coupled ferroelectric transistors with two access transistors. Four transistors total undercut the classic six-transistor SRAM footprint. Write conditions alone select volatile or non-volatile behaviour. No explicit backup or restore operation is ever needed. In non-volatile mode the store step draws a fraction of a microwatt and takes two nanoseconds. The cell also reads as a cross-coupled gain cell for other uses. Instant-on, low-leak memory for edge devices is the natural market.
arxiv-2606-20018:
Árpád Hegedűs and Apor Roth propose a leading ultraviolet formula for vertex operator expectation values in the sine-Gordon model in 2026. In a finite volume, these expectation values are described by the kink nonlinear integral equation, and their small-volume behaviour should match conformal field theory predictions. The authors analyse the integrable description in that regime and conjecture an explicit expression for the leading term, written through kink functions.

The formula ties the finite-volume integrable picture directly to the three-point functions of the underlying conformal theory. Checked against the known expression from complex Liouville theory, it agrees to at least nineteen significant digits in high-precision numerics. Finite-volume methods for integrable models gain a sharp new asymptotic tool.
arxiv-2606-20118:
Jonghoon Lee and four colleagues at KAIST present Pose6DAug, a method that teaches robot policies to handle unfamiliar objects without collecting new demonstrations. Their 2026 paper starts from a simple observation: every successful robot episode already contains a physically valid action path plus calibrated views from several cameras. Swap only the manipulated object while that path stays fixed, and the old success becomes a fresh training example aimed at the cases where the policy failed.

Naive video editing breaks down here, because pasted objects drift between views and ignore occlusion. Pose6DAug works in 3D instead, anchoring the new object to a mesh carried along a smooth 6D pose trajectory, so every view renders consistently. Fine-tuning on the augmented data lifted success on novel objects by 16.5 percent over the best baseline, with no loss on familiar ones. Failure-driven swapping offers a cheap path to broader robot generalization.
arxiv-2606-20518:
Harshit, Ayush Pratap, and Nityanand give flow-matching text-to-speech systems a lifelong memory for pronunciation corrections. Their 2026 paper notes that deployed TTS models stay frozen: mispronunciations of unseen proper nouns persist until retraining. FlowEdit learns corrections without touching model weights.

When corrective feedback arrives, FlowEdit optimizes a token-level perturbation in the text embedding space and stores it in a Modern Hopfield Network acting as content-addressable memory. At inference, stored corrections are retrieved by soft attention with a similarity gate, enabling fuzzy word-shape matching to new words. Pronunciation can then improve continuously in deployment. A speech product can fix a name once and remember it forever.
arxiv-2606-20718:
Sayantari Ghosh, Saumik Bhattacharya, and Partha Chakrabarti model algorithmic sycophancy in 2026, where a chatbot flatters a user into a delusional spiral. They propose a mathematical framework to track how beliefs change during such chats. Tools come from dynamical systems and stochastic differential equations, which describe motion with random noise. A user's conviction is treated as a log-odds state moving through a landscape with many valleys.

Their analysis finds that sycophantic feedback can strengthen a prior belief past a critical threshold. At that point the landscape changes shape. Small early tilts deepen into strong attractor basins, states that are hard to leave. The framework also supports mitigation strategies, ways to break symmetry and weaken the trap. A formal model matters because sycophancy is often discussed in anecdotes. Equations let researchers test which feedback patterns create rigid beliefs and which interventions might restore balance.
arxiv-2606-20818:
Jia-Ming Liou proves a Krein formula in a solo 2026 mathematics paper for conic Laplacians on compact Riemann surfaces. A Laplacian is a key operator in geometry and physics. A conic one acts on a surface with cone-like singular points. Different self-adjoint extensions of it encode different boundary rules at those points. Liou's approach is based on a finite space of boundary data at the singularities.

Extensions are described by special subspaces of that boundary space. The gap between two extensions is then written through an associated Weyl function. A trace identity for that gap is derived next. It gives a way to compare spectral determinants across boundary rules. Terms from negative eigenvalues and zero modes are included. Such formulas let geometers track how spectra change when boundary rules change, a question with echoes in quantum theory on singular spaces.
arxiv-2606-21018:
Yakun Liu and three colleagues present LK_Jam in a 2026 technical report, a real-time system for human and AI music generation together. Live musical interaction needs low latency and two-way interplay. Offline generation cannot jam. Their system uses a lightweight gated recurrent unit model inside a high-performance audio host. A fixed time grid is abandoned in the representation layer.

Instead, a sparse event stream joins time shifts, harmonic embeddings, and role-aware encoding. Single-step inference captures turn-taking logic and micro-timing. The engineering layer uses C++ with the JUCE framework. A lock-free multithreaded bridge connects to a real-time neural inference engine. Designed for live audio constraints, the system targets the strict timing that human performers expect. Responsive machine partners could change rehearsal, performance, and music learning, where a delayed response breaks the musical conversation.
arxiv-2606-21418:
Nishant Narechania, Emil Poulsen, and Eric Sonnendrucker extend the GEMPICX plasma simulation framework in 2026 to fully kinetic quasineutral models of magnetized plasma. Quasineutral models assume positive and negative charges balance on the scales of interest, which removes the fastest charge-separation physics and speeds up fusion and space plasma simulations. Their version solves the Vlasov-Maxwell equations with mimetic finite differences on dual grids, keeping the equations' geometric structure.

A discrete action principle, derived with the grid duality in view, anchors the scheme. Since the electric field has no direct time derivative in this model, a curl-curl equation supplies it at each step. A Lagrange multiplier holds the current's divergence at machine zero. The companion hybrid-model work shares the same geometric machinery.
arxiv-2606-21518:
Artur Ladeira, Rafael Nunes, Eleonora Di Valentino, and Stefano Gariazzo revisit sterile neutrinos in 2026, asking whether cosmology truly rules them out or only their most populated form. Sterile neutrinos are hypothetical particles that ignore the weak force, and a fully thermalized extra species has long been squeezed by cosmic data. The team tests three scenarios: fully thermalized, a cooler thermal relic, and a Dodelson-Widrow type with reduced phase-space density.

Fits combine Planck cosmic microwave background data, DESI baryon acoustic oscillations, and two supernova samples, under both a cosmological constant and evolving dark energy. The fully thermalized case is strongly disfavored without a local expansion-rate prior. The partially populated scenarios stay viable, with the cooler relic under least pressure. Data mainly cap the effective abundance, not the particle's physical mass.
arxiv-2606-21718:
Sandeep Kumar and colleagues field PolarMind at SemEval-2026 Task 9, the shared task on detecting online polarization across languages and cultures, in 2026. Polarized speech spans politics, religion, race, and gender, and a sentence harmless in one language can be hostile in another. Low-resource languages suffer most, with little training data and big performance gaps behind English.

PolarMind's unusual move is to build on LaBSE embeddings, a model family normally reserved for retrieval, chosen for strong cross-lingual transfer. Scores in low-resource languages rise by up to 0.2 macro F1. A broad ablation over Qwen-family encoders inside a retrieval-based prompting framework rounds out the study. For platforms moderating global conversations, the result argues that retrieval-grade multilingual embeddings are an underused weapon against imported and homegrown hostility alike.
arxiv-2606-21918:
Kim, Park, and Shim study, in 2026, a Wasserstein gradient flow, the steepest-descent evolution of a distribution under the Wasserstein distance from optimal transport. Their flow is generated by extended variance functionals, which measure the expected squared volume of a random simplex. The key observation is that they depend only on the covariance matrix.

That dependence collapses the flow to a finite system for its eigenvalues. The full solution can be rebuilt through an explicit linear pushforward. Using the representation, the authors prove the flow is globally well-posed for any starting point. Every solution converges to an equilibrium whose covariance loses at least one rank direction. The rates are sharp: exponential in the non-degenerate case, and power-law at the best possible rate otherwise.
arxiv-2606-22218:
Baccheschi and Dazzi analyse, in 2026, untrained deep reservoir networks for audio surveillance, meaning the automatic detection of emergency sounds such as glass breaking, explosions, and screams. Reservoir computing uses a recurrent network whose internal connections stay fixed and untrained, so only a simple readout is learned. The authors study bidirectional echo state networks at depths from shallow to deep.

They evaluate the models on the MIVIA Audio Events dataset in a multiclass setting, across several signal-to-noise levels. Fully trained bidirectional LSTM and convolutional-recurrent networks serve as baselines. Deep and shallow reservoir models both reach competitive recognition rates. Deeper variants prove more robust in highly noisy conditions, while shallower ones give the best efficiency profile, notably on edge hardware such as the NVIDIA Orin. The approach also stays robust across input representations, including log-Mel spectrograms and MFCCs at varying resolutions.
arxiv-2606-22918:
Yu Cao and five colleagues argue that each video judge needs its own yardstick in this 2026 paper. Vision-language models increasingly grade generated videos for physical consistency, supplying reward signals and ranking decisions. But models differ in training data and architecture, so each perceives physical phenomena through different internal representations. One global scoring schema therefore credits every judge with axes it may not actually perceive.

Their procedure, JudgeFit, discovers a per-model evaluation taxonomy. It prompts the target model to list physics errors on a few videos, clusters those descriptions, then repeatedly repairs dimensions the model scores unreliably or redundantly, calibrating against human ratings. Applied to sixteen models from eight families, the refined taxonomies beat the global schema on held-out videos for every model tested, by about thirty-two percent on average in relative terms. The per-model profiles also exposed blind spots that overall rankings cannot anticipate.
arxiv-2606-23518:
Kumar extends a public cosmology code for warm inflation in a 2026 paper on computing cosmic ripples. Warm inflation describes the early universe expanding fast, with the inflaton field, the field driving expansion, leaking energy into radiation as it goes. Finding the tiny ripples usually needs many random runs, which are accurate but slow. A faster shortcut tracks how variables move together, yet it can turn unstable when variables span very different scales.

The new module, DSWIM, rescales the equations before solving them. The scaling comes from how each variable grows as space expands. The change leaves the predicted power spectrum, the strength of ripples at each size, exactly the same. Tests on sample models show fewer false artifacts and large speedups at equal accuracy. Heat noise shared between variables falls out of the setup on its own.
arxiv-2606-23618:
Young and Zapletal prove new links between the structure of certain symmetry groups and how much choice set theory needs, in a 2026 paper on mathematical logic. Nonarchimedean groups are symmetry groups of countable structures, such as the automorphisms of a graph or ordering. Each such group generates a permutation model, a universe of sets built to test which fragments of the axiom of choice hold.

One correspondence concerns pliable groups, where conjugates of small neighborhoods form a basis at the identity, for the group and all its open subgroups. The automorphism group is pliable exactly when the well ordered choice axiom holds in its model. A second correspondence concerns groups carrying a complete left invariant metric, called cli, whose model sorts every set into a well ordering hierarchy.
arxiv-2606-23818:
Pero and Weinberg simulate the winds blown off neutron stars during the most violent X ray bursts, to explain odd chemical fingerprints in recent observations, in a 2026 paper on stellar astrophysics. Some Type I X ray bursts grow so luminous that radiation pressure lifts the star's outer layers into a wind. Spectra of such bursts show absorption features suggesting the lifted material is rich in medium weight elements, the ashes of the burning.

Using the MESA stellar evolution code, the authors model bursts from fuel buildup through the wind phase. They vary the ignition depth, the fuel mix, and the treatment of convection during the burst. Wind composition proves sensitive to all three choices. Deep ignitions produce ash rich winds spanning medium weight to iron peak elements.
arxiv-2606-24018:
Basso and colleagues work on correlation functions in planar N=4 super-Yang-Mills theory, a highly symmetric quantum field theory used to probe deep links between forces and scattering. The 2026 paper focuses on correlators carrying large charge, meaning operators built from many repeated fields, taken in the null limit where neighbouring points become light-like separated. Earlier work had described four- and five-point cases; this team generalises the pattern.

A conjecture is offered for the double-logarithmic behaviour of these correlators for any number of points and to all orders in the loop expansion. The prediction is written through the tilted cusp anomalous dimension, a quantity governing how sharply a Wilson line can bend. Translated into the dual amplitude picture, the formula reproduces the expected small-mass behaviour of massive scattering amplitudes when all masses are equal, tying two descriptions of the same physics together.
arxiv-2606-24118:
Lu and colleagues train a large multimodal model to point precisely at elements inside document images, a skill called visual grounding. Knowing which paragraph, field, or figure a question refers to underpins document understanding, deep research tools, and automatic error checking, yet existing models locate elements sloppily in text-heavy pages. Their 2026 model, PreciseDoc, is built specifically for fine-grained document grounding.

Two data pipelines mass-produce training documents paired with exact element coordinates, including synthetic hand-filled forms photographed with camera effects for realism. Training on such data stretches beyond single-text localisation toward practical jobs such as finding personal information inside a CV. A further training stage supervises grounding and reasoning together with reinforcement learning, so located evidence genuinely feeds the answer. Across document grounding and understanding benchmarks, Lu's approach outperforms prior methods, and the model can be further tuned for document question answering.
arxiv-2606-24218:
Adejoh and colleagues prove that tracing light rays through flat lenses and mirrors is as powerful as any computer. Ray tracing asks where a light ray travels through an optical system, and Reif and co-authors asked in 1994 whether universality required three-dimensional space. Working in the standard ABCD model of paraxial optics, where each lens acts through a small matrix, the team answers no: two dimensions suffice.

Without mirrors, any stack of lenses collapses to a single matrix-vector product with determinant one, and conversely any such matrix can be built from exactly three suitably spaced thin lenses. Adding mirrors turns the ray's journey into a flowchart over just two variables, enough for Turing computation with rational inputs. Building on that observation, Adejoh's construction simulates a reversible Turing machine with rays, mirrors, and lenses. The 2026 result closes a thirty-year-old question about optical computation.
arxiv-2606-24418:
Tahmasebi, Weber, and Jegelka ask whether augmenting training data with only some symmetry transformations works as well as using all of them. Data augmentation copies each training sample through the transformations of a group acting on the input space. Full augmentation explodes computationally when the group is large. That motivates the question their 2026 framework answers.

Fourier analysis and the representation theory of finite groups supply the tools. For a broad class of classical learning problems, partial augmentation using a randomly sampled subset of group elements matches full augmentation's minimax rates. Those are the best possible worst case guarantees. An approximation error is the only gap, and it vanishes as the subset grows. Symmetry, in other words, can be enforced approximately at a fraction of the cost, without surrendering statistical performance. Tahmasebi's result explains a practice machine learning already relies on.
arxiv-2606-24518:
Jiofack and colleagues identify half ordered states in moving oscillator crowds, by watching patterns repeat. Chimera states, where coherent and incoherent groups coexist, fascinate network science. Mobility scrambles the node ordering that standard detection relies on, though. Their 2026 method uses recurrence analysis. Joint recurrence plots mark when systems revisit similar states. Entropy-based measures capture space time order.

Two frameworks test the approach. A network of chaotic Colpitts oscillators hosts classical chimeras. A swarmalator system, agents that both swarm and oscillate, develops chimera like boiling states under delayed interactions. The method cleanly tells apart complete sync, quasi sync, and disordered regimes, even where standard order parameters stay ambiguous. A new quantity, the degree of independence, estimates the proportion of independent nodes. It robustly tracks transitions between collective states. Jiofack's team offers recurrence thinking as the right lens when the crowd will not sit still for its portrait.
arxiv-2606-25018:
Yash Gursahani and Christopher Reynolds model how reduced metal content changes the X-ray visibility of the earliest obscured black holes. Webb telescope observations now reach past redshift ten, into the first five hundred million years. Much black hole growth likely happens inside gas tori. The authors run Monte Carlo radiative transfer of X-rays from a centre through a torus. They track the emergent spectrum against metallicity, opening angle, and column density, focusing on Compton thick obscurers.

Lower metallicity, driven by scarce iron, lets far more X-ray photons escape the torus. The covering fraction plays a subtle role: scatterings inside the torus spread the emission, vying with escape through the opening and producing geometric beaming. Non solar abundance ratios mimicking the delay pattern of Type Ia supernovae are explored. The models address whether the next generation of X-ray telescopes can see black holes at redshift ten.
arxiv-2606-25318:
A vision model should react in a fixed, known way when an image is turned or flipped. That trait is called equivariance, and transformers make it hard to enforce. Sheir Zaheer, Alexander Holston, and Chan Park propose REViT in 2026. Its attention is built from convolutions set up to respect the group of turns and flips. Feature maps then turn along with the input instead of scrambling, so the sense of which way is up survives each layer.

Tests on image classification compare the design against earlier networks built for the same trait. The authors report that their simpler build beats those past approaches for discrete roto reflection equivariance. They frame it as a practical path for fields like medical scans and robotics. In such fields, which way a structure faces carries real meaning that plain networks must relearn from data each time.
arxiv-2606-25418:
A software birthmark is a fingerprint computed from a program, sturdy enough to survive edits yet distinct between independent projects. Nikolay Fedorov and colleagues move birthmark comparison from single files to whole projects in 2026. Reuse in practice is partial: a copied project may borrow only a few modules out of many. Tiny modules also match by accident, creating false alarms that swamp the real signal at project scale.

Their framework aggregates module similarities symmetrically, then adds two guards. Larger modules count for more, damping noise from small ones, and a partial similarity score focuses on the most similar fraction of module pairs. On thirty five open source Java projects across ten categories, the method beat existing approaches on a combined resilience and credibility score. Data and artifacts are public for checking.
arxiv-2606-25718:
Reading what someone saw from scalp electrodes alone sounds fanciful, yet EEG decoding has reached hundreds of image categories. Salini Yadav, Taveena Lotey, Pravendra Singh, and Partha Pratim Roy push it further in 2026 with a multiview encoder. Earlier work squeezed the whole signal into one embedding. Theirs models three views at once. State space dynamics capture timing. Learnable wavelets capture each sample's frequency content. Attention weighted graphs capture how electrodes interact. The fused representation aligns with pretrained image embeddings through contrastive learning.

On the THINGS-EEG benchmark the method set new records. It topped fifty percent top one accuracy within a subject among two hundred choices. It also held up far better across subjects and across recording sessions. The cross session test is the first of its kind reported. Modelling the signal's structure explicitly, the authors argue, is what buys both accuracy and generalisation.
arxiv-2606-25918:
Manish Kumar Gupta, Arnab Barua, and Haralampos Hatzikirou ask why tumour growth often refuses to follow the classic exponential curve. Real tumours can grow faster or slower depending on how many cells are already present, stall at low density, peak at middle density, and level off before food or space runs out. Standard models impose such density dependence by hand, without explaining where it comes from.

Cells are modelled as Bayesian agents in their framework. Each cell senses signals produced by the whole population and adjusts its coarse-grained phenotype, its current operating mode, toward states that explain those signals well. A mismatch between sensing and the growth optimum grows with population size and bends the growth rate down quadratically. Adding a receptor-ligand decoding model makes the mismatch non-monotonic, yielding a middle-density growth optimum, an Allee survival threshold, and tissue-specific capacity from one mechanism.
arxiv-2606-26018:
Inna Kozlovskaya and Alexander Studenikin study a new twist in neutrino spin oscillations. Neutrinos can flip their spin as they travel through matter. Moving streams of matter, called transverse currents, can drive those flips. The pair give the effect a systematic quantum treatment. Both standard interactions and hypothetical nonstandard ones enter the analysis.

Dense astrophysical settings supply the test case. A binary neutron star merger provides the worked example. There, matter currents are strong and fast. The treatment shows how spin and spin-flavour oscillations arise under such flows. Results matter for reading signals from extreme cosmic events. They also matter for hunting physics beyond the Standard Model. Neutrinos remain one of the few probes of that hidden sector. The merger setting shows where the new effect could appear.
arxiv-2606-26118:
Seamus Somerstep, Aritra Guha, Divesh Srivastava, and Yuekai Sun build an open index of AI's spread through the workforce. Frontier labs publish adoption studies from private data. Their open-source version uses public chat records and the O*NET task database instead. Occupations in finance, computing, and the arts show the highest adoption rates. The index pairs adoption with capability, asking what AI can actually do in each job.

Scenario testing supplies the capability side. Benchmark tasks are generated from real occupations and their tool servers. One recent model runs the scenarios inside an agent harness across nine frequent occupations. High-level workflows come out right. Granular details go wrong: the exact tool calls and fiddly steps are where errors cluster. The open index lets anyone repeat the measurement as models change. Adoption without capability, the split suggests, overstates how ready AI is for real work.
arxiv-2606-26218:
Tri Nguyen and colleagues weigh the dark matter hearts of two tiny galaxies with a new inference engine. Draco and Boötes I are ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, and their inner dark matter profiles test dark matter physics directly. A cusp or a core at the centre separates whole families of theories. Line-of-sight velocities alone mislead: they bias fits toward cusps, even ignoring the classic mass-anisotropy tangle. GraphNPE, their simulation-based method, uses more of the data.

Higher velocity moments do the unlocking. Kurtosis, the tailedness of the velocity distribution, breaks degeneracies that dispersion cannot. Mock tests show the recovery is far less biased. Draco's results agree across two spectrograph datasets and lean mildly cuspy. One dataset's kurtosis escapes second-order Jeans models entirely, proving the extra moments matter. Boötes I stays undecided for lack of stars.
arxiv-2606-26518:
A hands-on tutorial by Zhiyuan Xu, Yueqing Dai, Junling Li, and Junwen Luo walks readers through NeuraDock Agent. The agent is an open-source tool for EEG analysis. EEG records electrical activity from the scalp. The tutorial centres on alpha dynamics, changes in the brain's alpha rhythm, and on visual cognitive load, the mental effort a visual task demands.

Readers install the agent and run preprocessing and quality control step by step. They generate alpha figures and compare rest against task within the same person. They also start a live dashboard and call a real-time interface from another program. A language model layer explains quality risks in the results. Quality gates come first throughout: workload metrics are computed only after data passes checks. On a small sample data set, the agent processed eighteen recordings. Seven of ten comparisons showed the expected task-related alpha suppression.
arxiv-2606-26618:
Phannet Pov and four colleagues study the quality gap in text-to-speech for under-served languages. Large speech models sound nearly human in major languages but much worse in rare ones. The team adapted VoxCPM2, a large open speech model, for Khmer and Korean together. They used LoRA, a light fine-tuning method that trains a small add-on instead of the whole model.

One shared corpus held about twenty-six hours of speech in both languages. A single adapter was trained on both at once. Native listeners rated the results. Khmer scores rose clearly and significantly with the best adapter, while training only a small fraction of the model's parameters. Human ratings and automatic loss disagreed about the best adapter size. Korean, already handled well, gained nothing and worsened at a large adapter size. Adaptation helps mainly where the base model truly struggles.
arxiv-2606-26718:
D. Brüggemann and eight colleagues model the beating heart as a continuous dynamical system from MRI movies. Standard risk models use a few measurements from selected heart phases. Much of the motion information in a full heartbeat cycle is discarded. Their latent model instead compresses anatomy and full-cycle motion into a trajectory through a hidden space.

A graph-based autoencoder reconstructs three-dimensional ventricular motion over time. Neural differential equations, adjusted for heart rate, govern the latent trajectory. A prior predicts the expected starting state from patient covariates. Deviations from that prior feed a survival model for heart failure risk. The study covered over seventy-two thousand UK Biobank participants. Adding the latent score improved risk discrimination beyond standard pooled cohort equations. It also beat seven established cardiac markers.
arxiv-2606-27018:
Sergio Ramírez-Gallego proposes running remote-sensing foundation models aboard satellites to spot disaster changes without labels. Satellites have tight power and computing budgets. A versatile onboard encoder can decide what deserves high-resolution capture or changed tasking. Change detection usually needs labelled examples of the change sought. Disasters are exactly the changes nobody labelled.

His method pairs a foundation model's features with a feature pyramid network that was never trained. The pyramid's built-in structure supplies useful priors for free. Comparing features between successive orbital passes reveals subtle semantic shifts. The system flags anomalies at image level and maps them at higher resolution. It matches tailored, fully trained proposals at a fraction of the effort, the author reports.
arxiv-2606-27218:
Ghorashi, Alhulaymi, and Stone compute exactly what coating a tiny scatterer needs to swallow light whole. Coherent perfect absorption traps an incoming wave by interference so no light escapes, like a laser run in reverse. Their targets are subwavelength spheres and cylinders coated with a plasmonic layer. The needed surface conductivity is derived in closed form for light of fixed angular momentum. Two far-field setups make that fixed-spin light practical in this optics paper from 2026.

One setup floats a coated sphere above a good conducting surface. The other arrays dipole-coupled coated cylinders side by side. Across a wide terahertz bandwidth, the required conductivities turn out easy to reach. Moderately doped graphene supplies them in the authors' estimates. Tunable perfect absorption thus moves from fine theory toward buildable devices. Sensors and light-controlled-by-light schemes both stand to gain.
arxiv-2606-27618:
Davison Soper tells how a simple picture of the proton grew into a full theory. The picture is the quark parton model. It grew out of deeply inelastic scattering experiments. In those experiments, electrons smash into protons and only the scattered electron is measured. The mature theory is quantum chromodynamics, or QCD. Soper's 2026 article explains the physics issues met along the way.

The story starts at the Stanford linear accelerator. First results appeared in Physical Review Letters in 1969. Their interpretation had a revolutionary impact on fundamental physics. Soper presents the account as a logical development. It begins with the simplest ideas about point-like partons inside the proton. It then leads step by step to the properties of QCD. Historical development is woven through the explanation. Definitions come first, so readers can follow the scattering setup before the theory deepens.
arxiv-2606-28018:
Hypersonic flight heats air so strongly that chemistry starts to matter, and Marco Fratini, Pedro Stefanin Volpiani, and Matteo Bernardini quantify it in 2026 with direct simulations. An oblique shock impinges on a turbulent, very hot boundary layer. The edge Mach number is six point four. Three simulations share geometry and conditions, differing only in the chemistry model, from finite-rate chemistry down to a calorically perfect gas.

The reactive case behaves differently throughout. The shock-induced temperature rise boosts chemical activity, and breakdown products peak downstream. Composition lags the thermal forcing, so the two responses fall out of sync. Turbulent Damköhler numbers reach order unity. Finite-rate chemistry gives a smaller separation bubble, lower wall heat flux, and a less inclined reflected shock. The two perfect-gas models agree closely. The dominant distinction is therefore frozen versus reacting flow, and simplified models give safe heat-flux estimates.
arxiv-2606-28118:
Jonathan Kroth and Kirill Tuchin analyse QED scattering in a chiral medium in 2026. The medium is characterised by a constant chiral chemical potential and a chiral magnetic conductivity. Amplitudes are computed for several process classes. Resonant behaviour emerges in one-to-two, two-to-two, and two-to-three particle processes. Such resonances are absent in ordinary vacuum QED. The medium's chirality creates them.

The rates of the paradigm one-to-two cases are computed in detail. Those rates determine the widths of quasi-stationary fermion and photon states in the medium. The authors explain where they come from. The conditions for their emergence are spelled out. The physical principles behind their regularisation are also clarified. Resonances need careful treatment, since naive rates diverge. The work maps how a chiral medium reshapes elementary collisions.
arxiv-2606-28218:
Matteo Cerutti reports the first global extraction of transverse-momentum-dependent distributions, maps of how quarks move sideways inside protons, that uses a neural network to describe their unknown shape. Earlier maps relied on fixed formulas, which can bias the result toward the formula chosen.

Cerutti fits two kinds of experiment together: Drell-Yan, where quark pairs produce leptons in collisions, and semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering, where a struck quark is also observed. Adding the scattering data made the extracted distributions broader, meaning quarks carry more sideways motion than collision data alone suggested. Uncertainties shrank compared with a collisions-only network fit, though they stayed larger than those from traditional formulas, which Cerutti reads as a more honest accounting.
arxiv-2606-28418:
Hana Krakovská, Klaus Stiefel, and Rudolf Hanel connect two classic descriptions of how organisms grow. The von Bertalanffy growth model fits growth curves well but says little about energy. Metabolic scaling laws describe how energy use grows with body mass. The team reads development as an energy allocation problem uniting both views.

Krakovská and colleagues split metabolic energy among maintenance, growth, and other channels, then derive direct relationships among the exponents governing mass growth, length growth, metabolism, and body geometry. Those exponents combine into one investment exponent that controls the shape of the growth-allocation curve. Requiring the inferred growth share to stay between zero and one, as biology demands, yields constraints on developmental speed and characteristic mass scales. Growth curves gain a physical, energy-based interpretation.
arxiv-2606-28518:
Shraddha Singh, Craig Gidney, and Cody Jones loosen a bottleneck in fault-tolerant quantum computing. Magic states are the fuel for the gates that error-correcting codes cannot perform directly, and distilling pure ones is a leading overhead. Factories that distill them were previously found under a strict demand: a transversal gate had to behave correctly on the entire codespace.

Their borrowed-identity condition is strictly weaker, requiring the circuit to act as the identity on just one input state. It applies across the whole Clifford hierarchy and unifies factories for different magic states inside a single design level. A brute-force search with two-group symmetry recovered every known distance-two factory in range, including entangled and multi-output designs no single search had covered. Parent circuits even let the output state's type be chosen at compile time.
arxiv-2606-28618:
Ali Aman, Muhammad Asaduzzaman, Shaowei Wang, and Chanchal K. Roy present a study design for testing how language models adapt borrowed code. Developers constantly copy snippets and reshape them for new contexts. Yet existing benchmarks either dictate the edits step by step, cover only narrow change types, or work at whole-function scale. They leave unguided fragment adaptation unmeasured.

Their planned framework harvests Java fragments from open-source projects with strong test suites. It then injects controlled changes using a taxonomy of adaptation operators drawn from studies of real developer behavior. Because the injected mutations are known exactly, the unmutated fragment serves as the reference answer. Models will adapt fragments with no edit instructions, at three levels of surrounding context, and correctness will be judged mainly by reinserting the adapted code and running the tests. The paper specifies the design and research questions rather than reporting results.
arxiv-2606-29018:
Aldridge shows how to audit a trading strategy's effect on market liquidity using only its own trades and prices. Its net demand for liquidity, whether it mostly takes liquidity or supplies it, is usually hidden inside its secret signal. She proves this quantity can be identified from the observable history alone, with no knowledge of the strategy's inner workings.

An exact multi-period regret decomposition drives the result. The sign of one statistic sorts a linear strategy into net liquidity consumer or provider, recovering a classic informed-trader versus market-maker split from observables. Under a simple cost process, the statistic equals strategy size times the squared implied spread, a direct proxy for market illiquidity. Extending to price impact and many correlated strategies yields a liquidity-balance condition. Breaking it creates welfare losses growing with the square of the strategy count, a closed-form fire-sale effect.
arxiv-2606-29118:
Keith-Norambuena puts a coherence score for narrative extraction on a firm theoretical footing. Such extraction links events in documents into storylines. The scores in use are defined by practice, with no basis in information theory. He studies one composite score: the geometric mean of two parts, an angular similarity between document embeddings and a topic proximity based on the Jensen-Shannon distance between soft cluster memberships.

He shows the score's negative log splits into an angular cost plus a topic cost, on the product geometry of a sphere and a simplex. The topic part matches the Fisher-Rao metric, the natural geometry for probability laws. Within a family of ways to combine the two parts, the geometric mean is the only one meeting four natural axioms, one being a veto: either part can block a link. Tests on four corpora fit the framework well.
arxiv-2606-29618:
Chakrabortty studies homogenization for a Cahn-Hilliard system in a periodically perforated domain, a material pierced by a regular pattern of tiny pores. The Cahn-Hilliard equation models phase separation, and here it carries an added source term. Homogenization replaces the fine porous structure with an effective smooth system.

Using the periodic unfolding method, he derives uniform energy estimates and proves convergence to a homogenized system. Its effective diffusion tensor is characterized through scalar Neumann cell problems posed on a single pore cell. For quantitative results, he builds first-order corrector approximations through a scale-splitting operator. The corrected estimate improves the rate previously known for such equations and attains the natural rate for second-order problems. On a flat torus, the rate improves further.
arxiv-2606-29718:
Xia, Wang, Huang, and Liu study context rot in long-horizon search: as a language model's context grows, its capability degrades. Rot shows up as models giving up directly or answering early with uncertain results. Deep search tasks, where agents gather evidence over many steps, make the problem acute. The authors evaluate four flagship open-source models on three benchmarks.

Pruning experiments tie the rot directly to accumulated context. Two mitigation routes follow. Context management is tested systematically: seven methods across three categories, compared on performance, cost, and impact on rot, yielding guidance for choosing a strategy. Post-hoc rejection sampling adds a rot-aware filter over candidate answers, effective across three aggregation methods. Combining both approaches improves performance further. The study frames context not as free memory but as a resource that actively harms reasoning unless managed. Their code is released as the ContextRot project.
arxiv-2606-29818:
Karimov, Izmailov, and Nandi study a family of wormholes proposed by Harko, Kovács, and Lobo. A wormhole is a hypothetical tunnel through spacetime, and this family is described by the throat size and a deviation parameter that keeps the throat open.

The authors work out the energy accounting of these wormholes and how the deviation parameter changes the tidal forces felt in a moving frame. They then apply an idea based on Fresnel coefficients, the numbers that say how light reflects, to ask how different outside observers would identify the object. The striking result is that an observer's position matters. There is a nonzero probability that the wormhole is identified as a black hole even when the parameter says it is a genuine wormhole.
arxiv-2606-30018:
Julian Hofstadler and Daniel Rudolf bound the error of adaptive sampling algorithms that change as they run. Their focus is increasingly rare MCMC, a Monte Carlo method for hard integrals. Such algorithms adapt their sampling rule less and less over time. Users still need guarantees for the time-average estimator they produce. The authors supply explicit mean squared error bounds.

One key assumption drives the analysis: simultaneous Wasserstein contraction. This means every sampling kernel in the family shrinks distances between distributions. Under that condition, the error bounds hold in full. The authors show the bounds apply to adaptive stereographic algorithms. They also cover Metropolis-Hastings schemes adapted by normalizing flows. A generic algorithm for doubly intractable problems gets a full treatment too. For that case, they add a cost analysis for reaching target precision.
arxiv-2606-30118:
Jung-hun Kim and Vianney Perchet show that discounting future rewards quietly destroys a classic guarantee in online decision making. Prophet inequalities compare a gambler's stopping rule against an all-knowing prophet. With stationary identical rewards, the gambler can guarantee a known fraction. That fraction beats the harder non-identical case by a clear margin. Multiplicative discounting over time erodes the advantage.

Even identical base rewards become as hard as the non-identical case. The competitive ratio collapses from the classical guarantee to a one-half barrier. This happens as discounting accumulates over many equal phases. The barrier persists for arbitrary stopping rules, not just thresholds. Single-quantile threshold rules can still attain the tight bounds available. Their calibration uses an effective horizon induced by the discounting. Heterogeneous decay factors and unequal phase lengths are also handled. A continuous-decay benchmark shows the same discontinuous breakdown.
arxiv-2606-30518:
Bo Wang, Heyan Huang, and five colleagues train retrieval-augmented language models to handle sources that disagree with the model. Retrieved passages can be solid, mixed, or outright adversarial. One training signal for all cases muddles incompatible lessons. Their framework, RAPS-DA, sorts conflicts into three regimes first. Grounding, Arbitration, and Resistance name the three regimes. A specialist peer model is trained for each.

Every training sample routes to its matching specialist peer. Supervision flows back as on-policy reverse-divergence training. A token-level selector adds a second layer of control. It weighs teacher disagreement, student divergence, and student uncertainty. Uninformative or unstable tokens get filtered out. Confidently wrong tokens get upweighted. Supervision concentrates on the highest-conflict tokens. The specialists exist only during training, keeping deployment simple. Five conflict scenarios and two distribution-shift benchmarks test it. RAPS-DA beats prompting, decoding, fine-tuning, and reinforcement baselines.
arxiv-2606-30618:
Jewel Mahajan and Arnab Mitra return to symmetric power L-functions in a second study of their coefficients over sums of squares. This time they restrict to sums of m squares that land in a fixed residue class modulo q, an arithmetic progression condition, for even m between two and twelve. They study partial sums of the coefficients and of their squares over that restricted set.

As an application, they investigate shifted convolution sums, which compare the coefficient sequence against a shifted copy of itself, weighted by a k-full kernel function for any k of at least two. Kernel functions of this type, introduced by Ivić and Tenenbaum, isolate the part of each integer built from high prime powers. The pair also count sign changes of the coefficients twisted by such a kernel, again over sums of squares. The work extends their moment results to finer arithmetic structure.
arxiv-2606-30818:
Iara Pintos, Daniela Pérez and Florencia Vieyro ask what happens to black holes in a bouncing universe. Bouncing cosmologies replace the big bang singularity with a contraction phase, a bounce and then expansion much like the standard model. Most large structures should be erased during contraction, yet earlier work suggests black holes might survive the bounce. The trio track a population of black holes through all three phases and ask how the holes affect the cosmic fluid around them.

Their model couples two interacting fluids, one for the background and one linked to the black holes, on a fixed geometry. Black holes persist through the bounce in their treatment. The notable effect ran the other way: the cosmological fluid changed its own properties in response to the black hole population.
arxiv-2606-31118:
Akhtaryanova and three colleagues ask whether charged wormholes could hide in the Galaxy's dark halo and betray themselves by bending light. Their lenses are Kim and Lee wormholes, built on the Ellis-Bronnikov background. The scalar-charged and electrically charged versions keep zero total mass, like the background. The electric charge adds a redshift function and changes the throat radius, giving the lens a degree of freedom.

The team computes the light deflection angle up to fourth order for the charged case. They work out image positions, magnification, centroid shift, and time delay for source stars in the Galactic Bulge and the Large Magellanic Cloud. They estimate optical depth and event rates, for wormholes bound to the Galaxy or drifting. The prediction concerns brightness curves: a charged wormhole's Paczyński curve is dimmer than a black hole's, with gutters as the source enters and leaves the Einstein ring.
arxiv-2606-31218:
Choi and three colleagues test why models of Milky Way chemical growth under-produce scandium, titanium, and vanadium early on. These elements form mostly in massive stars, so their yields depend on star rotation and on the initial mass function, the birth mix of star masses. The team runs one-zone Galactic chemical evolution models across a grid of settings.

Rotating massive-star yields with starting spin near 300 kilometres per second move model tracks much closer to metal-poor halo data. The joint pattern across all three elements improves as well. Changing the high-mass slope of the mass function adds only a secondary shift. Tensions remain near solar and higher metallicity, which the authors tie to missing enrichment physics and model uncertainty.
arxiv-2606-31418:
González-Pérez and two colleagues ask when correcting test scores for age and education actually hurts. Such demographic corrections are routine in psychology, and z-score standardization is the standard tool. In cognitive screening, though, a corrected score can classify people worse than the raw score it replaced.

The team give sufficient conditions under which raw scores beat demographically corrected ones, with a plain reading of what those conditions mean. They also test the common claim that corrected scores give fairer decisions and find it wanting in the cases studied. Applied to the Mini-Mental State Examination in the OASIS-3 dataset, the results give clinicians a concrete warning: correct a screening score only when the setting meets the case for it.
arxiv-2606-31618:
Strunk proves a comparison principle for a class of doubly nonlinear parabolic fractional equations. These model diffusion that is nonlinear in both the solution's power and its spatial change, with long-range fractional effects. It says that if one solution starts and stays below another on the boundary of a space-time region, the ordering holds in the interior.

Working with non-negative weak solutions, with at least one solution time-independent outside the spatial domain, Strunk establishes the ordering inside the cylinder. As a direct use, the non-negative weak solution of the matching Cauchy-Dirichlet problem, which fixes values at the start and on the boundary, is unique. Such order results are basic tools for ruling out spurious solutions of nonlinear diffusion models.
arxiv-2606-31918:
Jiang and three others present DriveWeaver, a system that inserts vehicles into driving-simulation video with point clouds as the control signal. The sim needs diverse corner cases, so foreground vehicles must follow set trajectories inside recorded scenes. Tools based on pre-built 3D assets often clash with the background lighting and cannot scale beyond a small asset library.

DriveWeaver instead inpaints the masked insertion area, conditioned on the vehicle's point cloud. It gives footage that stays consistent over time and blends with its surroundings. A global-to-local inpainting plan preserves each inserted vehicle's identity over long sequences. Full 3D Gaussian forms are also pulled out for real-time rendering. Across datasets the method beats baselines on visual realism and geometric consistency.
arxiv-2606-32018:
Roder and Schweighofer attack a familiar failure of image classifiers: leaning on backgrounds that merely correlate with the label. A cow-versus-camel classifier may key on grass versus sand, then collapse when the correlation breaks at test time. Many defenses quietly assume some training images already break the correlation, which practice often cannot supply.

Their method, AutoBackSwap, manufactures those broken examples automatically instead. A secondary network, trained with patch-wise labels from only a few hundred samples, separates foreground from background in each image. Inpainting then synthesizes complete backgrounds, and foregrounds are recombined with swapped backgrounds to augment training. Across classification tasks with spurious backgrounds, the augmented classifiers consistently outperform prior methods, even when no training sample breaks the correlation.
arxiv-2608-00418:
Ma and co-authors test how to give Transformers a lasting structural prior. On some Boolean tasks, Transformers extrapolate in a systematically wrong way. They fit seen data but follow a simpler rule on unseen cases. Past structured starts set query and key projections to mimic a target attention pattern. Those priors wash out fast in training, they find.

Their fix initializes the attention mask itself. The mask is a finite, learnable logit bias built from task-level interaction structure. It sits apart from content-based attention scores, so it can persist through training. On Boolean reasoning tasks, mask starts reach near-perfect extrapolation. Vanilla and QK-started models stay trapped by the default bias. Low-data arithmetic also improves. Results stay competitive on vision and language benchmarks.
atalanta-fugiens-hoc-est-emblemata-nova-:
Michael Maier, doctor and alchemist at the court of Rudolf II, published this Latin emblem book in 1618. The title promises new emblems of the secrets of chemical nature. Each one joins a copper-engraved picture with maxims, short poems, and notes for the mind. Music completes the design: some fifty fugues for three voices serve the ears. Hieronymus Galler printed the book. The de Bry house published it, and Matthaus Merian is credited with the plates.

The fleeing Atalanta of the title leads a set of strange pictures, each glossed in verse and prose. Maier draws on Greek and Roman tales and on old natural history, Pliny among his sources. The hosted scan reads roughly in machine form, yet the plan stands clear. Alchemy here is taught as picture, poem, and song at once, a mixed work three centuries before its time.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-18:
Michael L. Rodkinson's eighteenth volume pairs Tract Aboda Zara with Tract Horioth. Aboda Zara, 'strange worship,' sets the rules for Jewish life among pagan neighbors. Horioth, 'decisions,' treats what happens when courts or rulers themselves err in law.

Aboda Zara asks how close one may come to idols, their feasts, and their wine without joining their worship. Its rulings shaped daily trade between Jews and gentiles for centuries. Horioth then weighs the sacrifices owed when a court misleads the people, and when a king or high priest sins. The pairing puts private purity and public error in one frame.
blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-volume-54:
This September 1843 number of Blackwood's opens in the hosted text with a tale of the assizes, We Are All Low People There. Its narrator returns on business to the populous city where his doting mother breathed her last when he was a child.
