A calamity like that, he reflects, leaves no half impressions; it stamps itself deep in the human heart. The scene of it becomes hallowed and beloved, or hated and avoided, for life.

Politics takes the later pages to Greece. A Morning Chronicle item is recalled that once declared and certified the king of Greece an idiot, back when the paper passed for a semi-official authority. The battle of Navarino, the writer sighs, has proved a most untoward event. In these degenerate days a revolution is less serious than a bankruptcy, and kings need more than the ordinary share of wit to keep their footing.
boethius-tractates-consolation-stewart-r:
The Loeb edition of Boethius appeared in 1918, with H F Stewart and E K Rand translating the Theological Tractates. Boethius, a Roman senator executed in 524, wrote the Consolation of Philosophy in prison. The Loeb volume pairs that famous work with his five shorter tracts on theology.

In the Consolation, Lady Philosophy visits Boethius in his cell and argues him out of despair over fortune, fame, and evil. The Stewart revision used the 1609 translation by I T for that text. The tractates treat the Trinity and related questions with strict logic. Together the works made Boethius the bridge between Roman and medieval thought for a thousand years.
browne-materials-babi-religion-1918:
Edward Granville Browne, the Cambridge orientalist, gathered Materials for the Study of the Babi Religion in 1918. The Babis were the followers of the Bab, the Persian prophet whose movement gave birth to the Baha'i faith. Browne had traveled in Persia and met believers when few Westerners had.

The volume prints Babi scriptures, histories, letters, and Browne's own notes in translation, with the Persian background explained. It preserves texts that were hard to find outside the community itself. Scholars still use Browne's source-book as a doorway into the movement's first, persecuted years. Browne's sympathy for the persecuted Babis colors every page he wrote on them.
byron-childe-harold-1818:
Lord Byron traveled through Portugal, Spain, Greece, and Albania after leaving England, and turned the trip into verse. The first cantos of Childe Harold's Pilgrimage appeared in 1812 and made him famous overnight. This text holds all four cantos, complete through the fourth, published in 1818.

Harold is a weary young nobleman drifting through lands marked by war and fallen empires. Byron mixes travel scenes with fierce reflections on freedom, tyranny, and loss. The later cantos pass through Belgium after Waterloo and down through Italy. The poem created the brooding Byronic hero and shaped Romantic poetry across Europe.
cather-my-antonia-1918:
Willa Cather published My Antonia in 1918, a novel told by Jim Burden, a lawyer looking back. Jim recalls his boyhood in Nebraska and his friend Antonia Shimerda. Antonia came from Bohemia as a girl and worked hard on her family's rough farm. Her warmth and strength mark everyone who knows her.

Jim leaves for school and a career while Antonia stays close to the land. Her life includes hardship and betrayal, yet she builds a full family and farm. Cather drew on her own Nebraska childhood and a real immigrant friend. The book is a tender hymn to pioneer women. Many readers count it her finest novel.
chekhov-wife-1918:
Garnett's 1918 Chekhov volume is named for The Wife, a tale told by an engineer named Asorin. Asorin's young wife runs famine relief in their district while their marriage cools into dislike. Watching her work among hungry peasants slowly changes his view of her and of himself.

Difficult People shows a family quarrel over a son's request for money, small in cause and deep in hurt. The Grasshopper follows a doctor's wife who worships artists and misses the worth of the quiet man at home. Each story turns on blindness inside a household. Chekhov judges no one outright, yet the verdicts land. The volume catches married life with rare honesty.
chekhov-witch-1918:
The Witch, and Other Stories came to English readers in 1918, in Constance Garnett's translation. The title tale traps a sexton and his wife in a snowbound church hut. When a lost mail driver shelters there, the wife is accused of witchcraft by her own bitter husband.

Peasants, a long story of village poverty, follows a Moscow waiter who returns sick to his home village. In the Ravine traces a peasant family torn by greed, forgery, and a shocking crime. These are among Chekhov's darkest pages on rural Russia. He writes of hunger, ignorance, and cruelty without softening them. The volume shows why his peasant tales shook Russian readers.
cia-0000008918:
An American F-105 pilot's death in Bac Thai province is recorded in a CIA report dated January 1974. Bac Thai, north of Hanoi, lay under the routes Thunderchief crews flew against the north. The report came a full year after American combat flights ended.

Deaths confirmed this late closed cases that had stayed open since wartime losses. Officials had to be sure before a missing man was declared dead. The file's care with province and aircraft type reflects that duty. It belongs to the slow postwar work of turning uncertainty into record, one airman at a time.
cia-0000009018:
An American seen working for the Viet Cong is the strange subject of a February 1972 CIA report. The file traveled with a cover memo addressed to a Bennett, a trace of its path through offices. Sightings of this kind raised hard questions: defector, prisoner under pressure, or mistaken identity?

Analysts could not ignore such reports, yet each demanded strict checking. A false claim could smear a captive; a true one changed a case entirely. The report preserves the allegation as received, with its official routing intact. It shows wartime intelligence handling its most puzzling category of sighting.
cia-0000009818:
An American pilot was captured near Stung Treng, an August 1970 report states, with enemy order of battle notes for the Stung Treng area attached. Stung Treng, in northern Cambodia, sat astride routes the Ho Chi Minh Trail used to enter South Vietnam. Pilots downed there fell into borderland captivity.

Pairing the capture with local enemy strength gave readers the setting: which units could hold or move him. Order of battle notes turned an incident into a usable file. The report shows incident reporting done whole, man and military landscape together. It belongs to the months when Cambodia's war was newly open.
cia-0000009918:
Four American pilots were captured near Ban Hang Long, in Houa Phan province, in January, an October 1967 report states. The village name matches the cave site in a companion report from the same month. Four pilots taken near one place suggests a hard season for aircraft over Sam Neua.

A capture report filed nine months after the event shows the delay built into Laos news. By October, the men's trail could already be cold or well documented elsewhere. Either way, the January date anchored their files' first chapter. The two Hang Long reports together give the cave prison a human count.
cia-0000012418:
Meeting number thirty-eight falls on October 5, 1961, deep in the final productive weeks. The colonel's autumn sittings in Paris were gathering the last full harvest. Within a year he would be arrested, tried, and shot in Moscow. None of that shadow lies on the record itself, which keeps the flat, numbered order of the sessions as they happened.

The thirty-eighth session's record continues the October run. Handlers asked, the source answered, and clerks numbered the pages. For readers, the page glows with hindsight: a great case in its final season, working at full strength.
cia-0000013618:
Brazil's prospects after its 1964 coup are weighed in a CIA paper from April 1965. The generals had taken the giant country a year before, ending a civilian government Washington had feared was drifting left. Their new regime was settling in: congress tamed, opponents jailed or exiled, and an economic team installed to remake the country's finances under military guard.

The paper assesses the coup's aftermath in the regime's first year. It reads the new order with the optimism Washington preferred at the time. For readers, it shows the dictatorship being graded early, by the ally that had welcomed its birth.
cia-0000013918: Four American soldiers of the First Air Cavalry Division were captured in Binh Dinh Province, in a CIA note dated November 5, 1967. The division fought hard in that coastal province. Losing four men from one unit in one area marked a sharp local blow. The note records their capture for the division's own grim ledger.
cia-0000015318: A letter to Sam Goudsmit from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated July 2, 1958. Strong thanks Goudsmit for his letter of August 14, the title's dates again askew. The Goudsmit thread ran through the whole Davidson affair. Even the slips show how much paper one man's claims could stir up. The Goudsmit letter is held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015418: Anyone who photographed a strange object could be handed a CIA information sheet dated January 5, 1960. The form asks for the camera and lens, the date and time, the direction faced, and the place. It also asks how the object looked and moved. Standard questions turned wild claims into reports that photo experts could compare, check, and file in a common shape.
cia-0000022318: Words about Rudolf and Helen Abel, built around a letter of thanks from Helen, fill a CIA record dated in 1962. Rudolf Abel was the Soviet spy swapped for Gary Powers that year. A thank you letter from his wife adds a family note to a state bargain. The entry shows the swap's paper trail reaching into the Abel home.
cia-0000022618: Photo comparison case number 12,770 has its results kept in a CIA record dated in 1971. No man is named in the title, so the case stays a number here. Thousands of such cases built up as pictures came out of Southeast Asia. Each result either opened a lead or closed one, and both kinds of answer mattered to the search.
cia-0000045918:
Arab nationalism stood at high tide when CIA analysts wrote about it in July 1958. Egypt and Syria had just merged into one republic under Gamal Abdel Nasser, the movement's loudest champion. The paper treats that surge of feeling as a force shaping the whole Middle East.

It weighs how pride in Arab unity pressed on kings, parties, and armies across the region. It also asks what the movement meant for Western influence and for Israel's safety. Its judgments fed the debate over how far Nasser's appeal would spread. Read now, the paper catches the moment when Washington saw Arab nationalism as a central force to reckon with.
cia-0000049018: A CIA item from 1981 lays responsibility on the Treasury Police for the killings of six members of one family in El Salvador. The Treasury Police were among the security forces most feared for death-squad work. Naming a state force as the killer, in an official file, was the kind of charge the Truth Commission later weighed.
cia-0000049118: General Jose Guillermo Garcia Merino is the named subject of a CIA item from 1986, kept with the Truth Commission records. Garcia had served as El Salvador's minister of defense in the war's bloodiest years. A file on such a man, kept this late, shows the system's long memory for its wartime commanders.
cia-0000049218: Francisco A. Moran is the named subject of a CIA item from 1992, kept with the Truth Commission records. His name echoes an earlier trace in this series, on a Francisco Antonio Moran, filed two years before. Single-name files like this one hold whatever the system gathered on a man across the war's end.
cia-0000103318:
Iraq: Reducing Foreign Labor Force is declassified CIA document 0000103318, dated August 5, 1989 in the catalog. The sample text is dated September 29, 1989, weeks later than the catalog entry. It reports Baghdad preparing to demobilize five divisions by mid-October while cutting the number of foreign workers in Iraq.

The stated aims were to free jobs for returning soldiers and to conserve hard currency for development and imports. New limits would sharply cut what foreign workers could convert and send home, halving yearly remittances to about one billion dollars. About one thousand more Egyptians were leaving than entering each day, the embassy reported.
cia-0000104918:
Mocada Barracks Anniversary Ceremony Described is declassified CIA document 0000104918, dated August 3, 1992 in the catalog. The sample is an FBIS daily report dated September 3, 1992, from Havana radio and television networks. It carries a speech by Fidel Castro at a ceremony in Cienfuegos, given live.

The ceremony marked the thirty-ninth anniversary of the attack on the Moncada Barracks. It also marked the thirty-fifth anniversary of the Cienfuegos uprising, the report header says. Castro addressed relatives of the combatants of July 26 and of September 5, in the text's opening. The item is a full speech text, not a short summary.
cia-0000107418: Dated February 3, 1983, declassified CIA document 0000107418 promises new information on South Africa's nuclear program. Its heading misspells information as Infromation and Africa as Afirca. A South African-Israeli nuclear link is named next, before the heading breaks off at Nuc. The update is presented as new in its own first word. The brief record preserves both misspellings and the broken ending as released.
cia-0000112818: Propaganda in Shanghai - Subversive Activities is the heading, with its date marked as an estimate, on declassified CIA document 0000112818, dated January 1, 1945. The title pairs propaganda and subversive activities in one wartime city, Shanghai. No person or group is named in the heading itself. The brief record preserves the estimate note with the subject as released.
cia-0000119718: From September 1956, a CIA briefing paper for the National Security Council on Soviet policy toward the satellite states. It lays out how Moscow managed its East European allies as unrest spread among them that autumn. Briefings of this rank show how the Kremlin's handling of its allies looked from Washington at a tense moment in the bloc's history.
cia-0000132418: The Caribbean through 1960 is forecast in a CIA report dated November 2, 1959. Its subject line runs the first two words together as Thesituation, a typing slip kept from the original. Written as 1959 closed, the report looks a full year ahead. The coming year would bring invasion planning against Cuba into full swing, and the report sets out the region's expected course.
cia-0000132618:
Item ten in a CIA Latin America series, dated 1960, reports anti-communist sentiment mounting on the Havana waterfront. The waterfront meant the docks, where port workers loaded and unloaded the ships Cuba lived by. A year into Fidel Castro's rule, the agency was watching for signs of working-class discontent inside Cuba, and this report says it found some among the men on the piers.

Short reports of this kind fed Washington's picture of how firm Castro's grip really was. Sentiment on the docks mattered because ports were union strongholds and pressure points in Cuba's economy. Read now, the piece is a small, dated gauge of mood in Havana at a moment when the United States was deciding how hard to push against the new government.
cia-0000135818: From 5 March 1954 comes a CIA cable, since declassified, on a reported plot against President Somoza of Nicaragua, sent as a warning to the Lincoln station. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000135918: The declassified CIA cable dated 2 May 1954 takes up why the field failed to act on a task. The wider file is PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation aimed at the Arbenz government in Guatemala before the June 1954 coup. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136118: 6 April 1954 is the date on a declassified CIA cable about an answer to a reference about a sabotage operation, the scare turning into a plan. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136318: A trip by the figure called REELFOOT is the business of this June 1954 LINCOLN cable. The station wants to learn his thinking, plant ideas with him, and keep his timing sensible on announcing a provisional government, which should clear through LINCOLN first if possible. A side trip is ruled out without further specific authority because the situation is unclear. The cable shows headquarters stage-managing the political face of the PBSUCCESS operation.
cia-0000136618: The 2506 Brigade papers include this Spanish-language item under an estimated date of 1 January 1961, the estimate flagged in the catalog. The brigade was then training in secret for Cuba. No subject is stated in the record for this document. It survives in Spanish in the CIA's declassified release, grouped with similar estimated-date records from the turn of the year in the exile force's files.
cia-0000137318: The Diaz Lanz case has aroused Castro, this CIA briefing reports. It served the 411th National Security Council meeting on 16 July 1959. Asylum and public attention for this traitor anger most Cuban officials. The case dramatizes the communist danger for the Cuban public, the briefing argues. Castro called the defection a cruel blow to the revolution. He is irritable and jumpy. But he stays determined to use any means, including force. Cuban arms missions are in Europe. President Urrutia publicly attacked communism on 13 July.
cia-06408118:
Report of Audit from the CIA Office of Inspector General, Audit Staff, examines the Agency's fund balance with Treasury. The report is marked Secret/X1, with a warning page on sources and methods. Its audit covers fiscal year 2000 financial statements, as set out in the executive summary.

Three aims are stated. The audit asked whether the fiscal 2000 statements fairly showed the fund balance under accepted accounting rules. It asked whether internal controls could catch or stop errors with a material effect. It also asked whether the Agency followed laws that bear on how the balance is shown. Background text cites the Chief Financial Officers' Act of 1990 and annual audited statements sent to the Office of Management and Budget. Tables later compare Agency ledger balances with Treasury records as of 30 September 2000.
cia-06765418:
FBIS translated text, published 26 November 1998 and marked Unclassified, carries part eight of an Iraqi commander's memoirs on missiles. The source is Amman Al-Arab Al-Yawm, in Arabic, 10 November 1998, page 12. The book is Forty-Three Missiles on the Zionist Entity, by Staff Lieutenant General Hazim Abd-al-Razzaq al-Ayyubi.

Chapter four, The Battle of Hope and Honor, reaches entries for 24 January 1991. The author records orders moving brigade 224 forces from the southern sector to the western sector again. Four batteries moved west, where three others were already working, he states. Passwords and symbols were changed and new target coordinates chosen for Tel Aviv and Haifa. The memoir claims not one launcher, item of equipment, or al-Husayn missile was hit in the whole battle, and puts casualties at only 10 wounded.
cieza-war-of-chupas-markham-1918:
Pedro Cieza de León's War of Chupas, in Markham's translation of 1918, tells how the Almagrist revolt in Peru was broken. The battle of Chupas in 1542 pitted the royal forces against the followers of Almagro the younger. Cieza, the conquest's own annalist, narrates the campaign that led to that field.

He follows the rival armies through the Andes with his usual care for ground, weather, and men. The clash at Chupas ended the first great civil war of Spanish Peru. Cieza writes as the greatest chronicler the conquistadors produced, clear-eyed about their courage and their greed. This late volume of his wars completes a matched set in Markham's translations.
commons-history-of-labour-us-vol1-1918:
John Commons and his students published the first volume of the History of Labour in the United States in 1918. The Wisconsin team worked from newspapers, union records, and government reports to build a documentary history. Nothing on this scale had been tried for American workers before.

Volume 1 runs from the colonial era to the Civil War. It covers the first workingmen's parties, the fight for the ten-hour day, and the early growth of trade unions in the young republic. The editors let the records speak, with narrative tying the evidence together. The set became the foundation work of American labor history, and later scholars have built on its archive ever since, even when they argue with its judgments.
commons-history-of-labour-us-vol2-1918:
The second volume of Commons's History of Labour in the United States appeared in 1918 alongside the first. Commons led a team of researchers at Wisconsin who treated labor's past as a subject for documents, not legend. Their history aimed to show how American workers organized, struck, and bargained their way into national life.

Volume 2 carries the story from the Civil War to the end of the nineteenth century. It covers the Knights of Labor, the Haymarket affair of 1886, and the rise of the American Federation of Labor under Samuel Gompers. The narrative shows unions turning from broad reform crusades toward practical bargaining over wages and hours. With the first volume, it remains a standard starting point for the history of American labor.
constitution-baden-1818:
The Grand Duchy of Baden, a state in southwest Germany, received this constitution in 1818. Its grand duke granted the charter rather than a popular assembly writing it, which was normal for the time. Part one covers the grand duchy and the government in general. Part two lists the civil and political rights of the citizens of Baden, a notable step for its era.

Lawmaking was shared with an Estates Assembly of two chambers, whose members' rights and duties get their own part. The text also handles state finances, the courts, churches, and local communities. Baden's charter was counted among the most liberal in the German states. It gave many men a vote and promised equal civil rights.
constitution-bangladesh-2018:
Bangladesh adopted its constitution in 1972, soon after winning independence from Pakistan, and the hosted text runs through amendments made by 2018. Part one founds the People's Republic as a unitary state. Islam is the state religion, while the republic also promises equal standing to other faiths. Dhaka is the capital, and Bangla is the state language.

Part two lists fundamental principles of state policy, and part three gives enforceable fundamental rights. A president is head of state, but executive power belongs to a prime minister and cabinet answerable to the Jatiya Sangsad, the national parliament. Later parts cover the courts, elections, the public service, and emergencies. Amendments over the years have swung the system between presidential and parliamentary rule.
constitution-burundi-2018:
Burundi gained a revised constitution in 2018 after a public vote, and that text is hosted here. Title one covers the state and the sovereignty of the people. A long charter follows, giving the rights and duties of each person, from life and liberty to health and schooling. Kirundi is the national language, and the text also works in French.

A president leads the executive, with a prime minister and ministers under the 2018 design. Parliament has two houses, a National Assembly and a Senate. Seats in both are shared by quota between Hutu and Tutsi, a guard against the ethnic strife of past decades. Later titles cover the courts, elections, parties, and the army and police.
constitution-chad-2018:
Chad adopted a fresh constitution in 2018, founding what its leaders called a fourth republic. Title one covers the state and sovereignty. Chad is a single republic, and French and Arabic are the official languages. A second title lists freedoms, basic rights, and duties, from free speech and worship to schooling and health care.

The 2018 text strengthened the president, who leads the executive without a prime minister under this design. The National Assembly is the single lawmaking house; an earlier Senate plan was dropped. Later titles cover the courts, a constitutional council in new form, local areas, and public finance. The change followed years of debate about how power should be shared.
constitution-china-2018:
China's constitution dates from 1982, and the hosted text includes the changes made in 2018. Chapter one gives general principles. The state is a socialist republic led by the working class, and all power is said to belong to the people. Chapter two lists the basic rights and duties of citizens, from voting and speech to work and schooling.

The National People's Congress is named the highest organ of state power. It chooses the president, who serves as head of state, and the State Council, the government led by a premier. Later chapters cover local congresses, the courts, and prosecutors. Changes in 2018 wrote the Communist Party's leading role into article one and lifted term limits on the president.
constitution-comoros-2018:
The Comoros, an island union in the Indian Ocean, works under a constitution recast in 2018. The union joins the islands of Grande Comore, Anjouan, and Moheli, each with its own governor and a measure of self-rule. The text opens by founding the union and stating its principles, with Islam as the state religion and the union's shared rule balanced against island autonomy.

A president of the union leads the executive. The Assembly of the Union makes federal laws, while island assemblies handle local matters. Later parts cover the courts, including a Supreme Court, public finance, and the armed forces. The 2018 vote ended the old system in which the union presidency rotated among the islands.
constitution-finland-2018:
Finland's constitution took its present form in 1999, gathering rules once spread across four acts, and the hosted text includes changes through 2018. Chapter one gives the bases of the state. Finland is a republic where power rests with the people. Chapter two protects basic rights and liberties, from equality and free speech to schooling and a clean environment.

Parliament, the Eduskunta, is a single chamber of two hundred members. A prime minister leads the government, and a president, once very strong, now shares power with a smaller role than in past decades. Later chapters cover the courts, the chancellor of justice, and state finance. Finnish and Swedish are both national languages under the text.
constitution-georgia-2018:
Georgia adopted this constitution in 1995, after the Soviet collapse and a civil war, and the hosted text runs through the deep changes of 2018. Chapter one gives general provisions. Georgia is a democratic republic, and Georgian is the state language. Chapter two protects the basic rights and freedoms of citizens, from speech and faith to property and fair trials.

Changes in 2010 and 2018 shifted real power toward a prime minister and the government. The president became a head of state chosen, under the new rules, without a direct popular vote. Parliament is a single chamber. Later chapters cover the courts, a Constitutional Court, local self-rule, and state finance. The shift aimed to end years of very strong presidents.
constitution-kiribati-2018:
Kiribati, a Pacific island nation spread across a wide stretch of ocean, gained this constitution at independence from Britain in 1979, and the hosted text includes changes through 2018. Chapter one founds the republic and names the constitution its supreme law. Chapter two protects the basic rights and freedoms of each person, from life and liberty to speech, worship, and fair trial.

The head of state and government is a president with the Kiribati title Beretitenti, chosen by the people from among members of the House of Assembly. That house, the Maneaba ni Maungatabu, makes the laws. Later chapters cover the courts, the public service, citizenship, and finance. Island councils handle much daily rule across the far-flung atolls.
constitution-latvia-2018:
Latvia's constitution, the Satversme, was adopted in 1922, set aside under Soviet rule, and fully restored in 1993; the hosted text includes changes through 2018. It is one of Europe's oldest charters still in use. Early chapters give general provisions and cover the Saeima, the hundred-member parliament. A rights chapter, added in 1998, protects the basic rights of persons.

The Saeima chooses the president, who serves as head of state. A prime minister leads the cabinet and needs the Saeima's trust. Later chapters cover the courts, the state audit office, and how the charter can change. Latvian is the state language, a point the text guards with care given the country's large Russian-speaking share.
constitution-pakistan-2018:
Pakistan's constitution dates from 1973, its third since independence, and the hosted text carries changes through 2018. Opening parts found a federal republic and name Islam the state religion. Urdu is the national language, with English used for official work. A full part protects basic rights, from life and liberty to speech and fair trial, and a second part gives principles of policy.

A president heads the state, while a prime minister, answerable to the National Assembly, holds real power. Parliament pairs that assembly with a Senate giving the provinces equal seats. Later parts cover the courts, a Federal Shariat Court, elections, and the sharing of water and taxes among provinces. Changes in 2010 moved much power from the president back to parliament.
cuvier-theory-of-earth-1818:
Georges Cuvier, the great French master of the bones of dead beasts, set out his scheme of the earth's past in this work. Robert Kerr turned it into English, and this text is from 1818. Cuvier could rebuild a whole beast from a few bones, and men took his word as law.

He held that the earth had seen a string of vast floods and new sets of life. He also held, flat, that no fossil man exists, and none would be found. The men who claimed deep age for man spent the next fifty years in work to break that word.
dalton-countrey-justice-english-1618:
Michael Dalton, a lawyer, published The Countrey Justice in 1618 as a working manual for England's local magistrates. Justices of the peace handled most crime in their counties, and Dalton's book told them how. Among its chapters stands the witchcraft section that shaped English trials for a century.

Dalton sets out the law on witches, the signs to weigh, and the procedure to follow. Generations of justices reached for his guidance when a village accused a neighbor. The chapter codified witch procedure in practical form. This handbook was the legal backbone of the English witch trials. Its calm pages show persecution running on paperwork as much as on fear.
david-beuthers-universal-und-particulari:
David Beuther's teaching on the change of base metals into gold and silver fills this Hamburg book of 1718. Samuel Heyl printed it in St John's Church there. Beuther had been mint warden to the Elector of Saxony at Dresden, and Dr Johann Christoph Sproegel of Hamburg wrote the preface.

Sproegel says copies of Beuther's writings had been sold for a thousand Thaler and more, just to be transcribed. Print, he argues, ends that shameful trade. An appendix of fine copper plates shows the art from start to end. Recipes weigh white earth, silver water, and ferment in set parts, to be ground on marble. The book is alchemy sold as a public good.
debs-canton-speech-1918:
A speech against war by Eugene V. Debs fills this pamphlet from the Socialist Party of the United States, at Chicago. Debs spoke at Nimisilla Park in Canton, Ohio, on a Sunday afternoon, June 16, 1918. The chairman calls him the best loved and most hated man in the country.

Debs argues that the master class has always declared war, and the subject class has always fought the battles. The masters, he says, had all to gain and nothing to lose; the workers had nothing to gain and all to lose, their lives among it. Cheers and applause are marked through the text. The speech is printed as spoken, slang, pauses, and all. It became the most famed American socialist address of the war years.
dostoevsky-notes-from-underground-garnet:
Fyodor Dostoevsky wrote Notes from the Underground in Russian, and Constance Garnett made this English version in 1918. Many call the short book the founding text of existentialist fiction in the West. Its speaker has no name and writes from a cellar of spite in Petersburg.

The Underground Man rails at reason, progress, and the dream of a crystal palace. He claims man will choose pain and chaos just to prove he is free. In the tale half, he humiliates himself before old school friends at dinner. He then crushes Liza, a girl who shows him love he cannot accept or return. The book's bitter voice still shocks readers with its raw, modern sting.
doyle-new-revelation-1918:
Arthur Conan Doyle steps out for the faith in The New Revelation, his book of 1918. Doyle had made Holmes, the great sleuth of cold proof. War grief and long tests turned him to the dark room. Here he tells that path in plain words and claims the dead speak, with proof that passed his own strict checks through the years.

Crowds gasped that Holmes's sire could hold such faith. His fame made the book a world event at once. It took the faith from back rooms to the front page. Doyle gave his last years to its cause.
eliot-ezra-pound-metric-poetry-1918:
Eliot published this short study of Ezra Pound in 1918, without his name on it. It examines the verse of his friend and champion, the American poet then leading London's modernist charge.

Eliot works through Pound's metrics, his handling of rhythm and line, and his debts to Provençal and Chinese poetry. The tone is technical and admiring at once: one young revolutionary explaining another's craft to a puzzled public. Pound had discovered Eliot and pushed his work into print, and this book partly returns the favor. It is a rare record of modernism's makers theorizing each other mid-revolution.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-18:
Managing the will comes first in Volume 18 of Michel de Montaigne's Essays, here in Charles Cotton's translation. Montaigne (1533-1592) argues that a person should lend help to others but keep the self in reserve. Strong feelings, he warns, can seize a mind and rule it. Calm, for him, takes practice and design.

He urges a middle path between hating pain and chasing pleasure too hard. Two shorter chapters follow, one on cripples and one on physiognomy, the claimed art of reading character from faces. Both test how fast people judge bodies and signs they barely understand. Latin tags, Roman cases, and frank reports of his own cool temper carry the argument. Readers near the end of the Essays find a practical rule here: guard your inner freedom, and spend emotion only where the cause earns it.
estonian-declaration-independence-1918:
Estonia's declaration of independence, titled a Manifesto to the Peoples of Estonia, was issued in February 1918. The hosted text is the full English version. It recalls how Estonians kept their hope of freedom alive through centuries of foreign rule. It opens with old lines of national poetry about the hero Kalev coming home to his children.

The Russian Empire was falling apart, and German armies were drawing near. In that hour, the Estonian National Council claimed the right to decide the land's fate. The manifesto declares Estonia an independent, democratic republic with neutral standing. It promises land, rights, and elections to a constituent assembly. It also pledges fair treatment to Russians, Swedes, and Germans living there. German troops seized the country within days, yet the date is still marked as Estonia's birthday.
europmc-pmc10076218:
Zhang and co-workers present a method that profiles gene activity and gene control marks in tissue at the same time and place, in a 2023 study. New spatial tools can map where genes are active inside a tissue slice. Older methods captured only one layer of that information at a time, which limited what scientists could learn.

The team's co-profiling approach captures both layers from the same tissue section. They test it on mouse and human tissues. The method lets researchers link gene control states to cell behavior in place, a step toward fuller maps of organs.
europmc-pmc10427418:
Shah led the GLOW trial in 2023, a global test of a new drug pair for stomach cancer. The drug, zolbetuximab, is an antibody that seeks a protein called CLDN18.2 on cancer cells. Patients had advanced cancer of the stomach or the joint with the food pipe. Their tumours held the target but lacked a second mark, HER2.

In all, 507 patients got the drug or a dummy drug, each with the same two chemo drugs. Shah found that the drug pair slowed growth for longer. Median time before the cancer grew was 8.21 months, versus 6.80 months. Median survival was 14.39 months, versus 12.16 months. Severe side effects were near equal in both arms.
europmc-pmc10786718:
Kim and a large global team pooled gene data on Parkinson disease across many ancestries in this 2024 study. Parkinson disease is a brain illness that affects movement and worsens over time. Past gene hunts found over 90 risk variants, meaning small DNA changes tied to higher risk. Most of those hunts, though, drew on one ancestry group at a time.

The pooled analysis covered about 49,000 cases and 2.4 million controls from four ancestry groups. It found 78 DNA regions tied to the disease, 12 of them possibly new. The team also flagged 25 genes whose activity levels track with risk. The authors say the broader mix lays groundwork for finding risk regions missed in single-group studies. That matters because drug targets found in one group may not tell the full story.
europmc-pmc11836418:
Xiong and colleagues surveyed breast cancer science in a 2025 review. Breast cancer is a lead cause of cancer death in women. Tumors differ a lot from one person to the next. Sorting them into molecular subtypes has sharpened care.

New work covers tumor stem cells, microbes inside tumors, and daily body clocks. Smart software now aids scans and diagnosis with better accuracy. Fresh drugs support care tailored to each patient and subtype. Xiong argues the best plan matches risk and tumor type. That match defines modern precision care for breast cancer.
europmc-pmc1310918:
Geiser and co-authors tracked ultrafine particles crossing lung cell membranes in 2005. Within hours of breathing them, such particles appear in liver, heart, and nervous tissue. How they cross membrane boundaries was largely unknown. Rats inhaled titanium dioxide particles of 22 nanometers median size.

Particle locations were mapped one hour and 24 hours after exposure. Electron microscopy with elemental analysis pinpointed single particles. Cultured lung cells were exposed in parallel tests. Particles entered cells without being eaten by the usual engulfing route. Geiser shows a non-eating entry path for ultrafine particles. Lung cells in dishes took up the same small bits. The bits were seen in the lung one hour and one day after the rats breathed them in.
europmc-pmc1382018:
Voight, Kudaravalli, Wen, and Pritchard mapped recent natural selection in the human genome in 2006. New genetic variants favored by selection reveal local adaptation. The scan used HapMap data across three continental groups. A new method hunted variants rising in frequency but not yet fixed.

Widespread selection signals appeared in all three groups. Most signals were specific to one region. A significant excess was shared across groups, though. The strongest signals by some measures came from the Yoruba population. That counters claims of little recent selection in sub-Saharan Africans. Selected loci should hold trait variation worth mapping.
europmc-pmc1414018:
Pearse and co-authors ran a trial in 2005 on care right after major surgery. They tested goal-directed therapy, where staff tune fluids and drugs to hit a set oxygen delivery target. Half of 122 high-risk patients got the tuned care. The rest got standard care on the ward.

The tuned group got more fluid and far more of a heart drug. Fewer of them had problems after surgery, 44 percent against 68 percent. Their hospital stay was also shorter, a median of 11 days against 14. Death rates did not differ much. Pearse argues that early tuned care can cut harm after big operations.
europmc-pmc1762318:
A working tooth grew from stem cells in a pig's jaw. Sonoyama and co-authors reported that regeneration in 2006. They isolated a new stem cell population from the root tip of human teeth, called SCAP, alongside known ligament stem cells.

Transplanted into minipigs, the two cell types built a root and ligament complex. The structure was strong enough to support a porcelain crown and serve in normal chewing. The approach blended stem cells, engineered materials, and standard dental crown methods. Sonoyama presents it as a route to biological tooth replacement rather than metal implants.
europmc-pmc1794418:
Blau and co-authors tested in 2007 whether emotion changes an early brain response to faces. The response is the N170, a voltage dip measured on the scalp about 170 milliseconds after a face appears. Older two-stage models held that the N170 only encodes face structure, with emotion handled later.

The team recorded dense-array brain signals while people viewed 16 fearful and neutral faces, matched for shape, size, and brightness. Faces were beside the point of the main task, which paired a character with a spoken word. Fear still strongly modulated the N170, and the effect held in both halves of the session, so it was not just novelty. The pattern suggests fear enlarges the N170 itself. The authors propose fast input from emotion systems reaches face processing earlier than the old model allowed.
europmc-pmc1810318:
Margolin, Califano and colleagues presented ARACNE in 2006, a method that rebuilds gene control networks in mammal cells. Earlier reverse-engineering tools worked only in simple organisms with small genomes. Co-expression links also mislead, since two genes can rise together through an indirect chain.

ARACNE uses information theory to strip out most of those indirect links. The authors prove it can rebuild a network exactly when feedback loops have negligible effect, and it held up well with many loops present. On realistic synthetic data it made very few errors and beat relevance networks and Bayesian networks. Applied to human B cell data, it recovered known control links in that immune cell type. The method was designed to scale to mammalian complexity.
europmc-pmc1853118:
Libioulle, Georges and colleagues found in 2007 a new risk region for Crohn disease, a chronic gut inflammation. They scanned the genomes of 547 patients and 928 controls at over 300,000 DNA markers. Two hits matched known risk genes, IL23R and CARD15, which validated the search.

The third hit was new: a stretch of chromosome 5, band p13.1, about 250 thousand letters long. Four markers there gave very strong signals. A follow-up set of 1,266 more patients, 559 controls, and 428 family trios confirmed the region. The stretch is a gene desert, holding no known gene, yet it controls the activity of a nearby gene, PTGER4, which codes a receptor for a lipid signal. The result shows risk can hide in DNA far from any gene.
europmc-pmc1876818:
Kress and Erickson tested in 2007 whether two DNA stretches could serve as a standard barcode for all land plants. A barcode must vary enough to separate species yet stay easy to read in any plant. Plant genomes evolve slowly, which had stalled the search that already succeeded for animals.

The pair compared nine candidate regions, alone and in pairs, across 48 plant genera with two species each. No single region separated the species in more than 79 percent of genera. Pairing the non-coding spacer trnH-psbA with a coding gene lifted success to nearly 88 percent. The gene rbcL was one of the best partners. Follow-up trials on public database sequences confirmed that the rbcL plus trnH-psbA pair identifies plants correctly at high rates.
europmc-pmc2126318:
Herbert D. Taylor, William D. Witherbee, and James B. Murphy opened a series on X-ray effects with the rays' destructive action on blood cells, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1919. They dosed animals of seven species, from mouse to pony, and counted the circulating blood cells in the days that followed.

Large doses struck the lymphocytes first, before any other circulating cell. Their count fell sharply, the drop complete within forty-eight hours, then rose once, fell again, and at last climbed back to normal for good. The selective hit on lymphocytes showed in every species tried, and animals of one species given one dose answered in close parallel. The neutrophil white cells, when affected at all, rose briefly, dipped below normal, and recovered many days before the lymphocytes did. Other blood cells followed their own slower courses.
europmc-pmc2128218:
Frederick L. Gates described a quick instrument method for standardizing bacterial suspensions, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1920. Workers using bacteria for vaccines or serum tests need to know how strong a suspension is. Older counting methods were exact but slow, and simpler ones were rough.

Gates measures a suspension's cloudiness by the length of its column needed to hide a wire loop from view. A simple formula then turns that measured cloudiness into bacteria per cubic centimeter. Suspensions of the same organism can thus be compared and matched to a set strength. He describes the measuring instrument in detail for laboratories that would build it. The method trades a little precision for a large saving in time, giving vaccine and serum work a practical everyday standard.
europmc-pmc2128418:
O. T. Avery and M. Heidelberger compared the protein of the pneumococcus with its soluble specific substance, the subject of their preceding paper. Their study appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1923, from the Rockefeller Institute hospital. The protein was thrown down from dissolved pneumococci by acetic acid and put through chemical and immune tests.

Chemically, the protein answers like nucleoprotein and mucoid. Its immune behavior is the paper's point. The soluble specific substance marks the pneumococcus type: one type's substance differs from another's. The protein, by contrast, shows species specificity, shared across pneumococcus types rather than dividing them. Two parts of one germ thus carry two different levels of identity. The finding helped sort which bacterial parts a diagnostic serum should target, type markers for sorting strains and species markers for naming the germ.
europmc-pmc2128518:
Homer F. Swift, of the Rockefeller Institute hospital, set out the two opposed ways the body answers the agent of rheumatic fever. His paper on the disease's pathogenesis appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924. One answer builds tissue; the other pours out fluid, and the two explain different faces of the illness.

The building answer forms growths around blood vessels, like an infectious granuloma, and it accounts for the drawn-out, subacute course of many patients. The fluid answer floods the tissues around joints and the joint cavities themselves, matching the acute arthritis with high fever. Drugs can clear the fluid quickly, but that clearing does not mean the built lesions have resolved. In skin they are known to persist for months, and by analogy they likely persist in other invaded tissues too. Rheumatic fever's relapses, Swift's scheme implies, live in those lasting growths.
europmc-pmc2131218:
Hans Zinsser and Takeo Tamiya published an experimental analysis of bacterial allergy in The Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1926. They asked whether the violent reactions of infected animals to bacterial products work like true protein anaphylaxis, the severe allergy to foreign protein. Guinea pigs were sensitized with whole bacteria or with bacterial protein fractions to test the link.

Their tests confirmed that bacterial allergy runs on a different mechanism from protein anaphylaxis. It grows fast and leaves the infected animal open to harm from bacterial products that barely touch a normal animal. The type-specific sugar parts of bacteria, and the antibodies against them, play no part in it. Allergy instead seems tied to the cells of the body rather than to antibodies in the blood.
europmc-pmc2140618:
Ellis Fulmer and Buchanan, at Iowa State College in Ames, published studies on toxicity in 1923. Yeast was exposed to phenol, alone and with alcohol, and the survivors over time were counted by a stain test: living cells resist methylene blue, dead ones take it. Such survivor curves were often claimed to follow a simple logarithmic law.

In general the curves did not prove logarithmic. Resemblances to monomolecular reaction curves look superficial and accidental to the authors. Any rating of disinfecting power built on that supposed law must mislead, they argue. What truly shapes the death rate is the spread of resistance among individual cells: some are tough, some weak, and that distribution is of fundamental importance.
europmc-pmc2140918:
Arthur Goulding, Henry Borsook, and Hardolph Wasteneys, at the University of Toronto, studied pepsin's self-destruction in a 1927 paper. Pepsin loses its activity for good in alkaline solution. The authors ask how that autodestruction depends on the enzyme's ionization, its split into charged form, across the acidity scale.

Their evidence makes pepsin a single-charge acid with a set ionization constant, or equally a base with its own constant. Part of the destruction is an instant, irreversible change in whichever form those constants pick out. The rest proceeds steadily by the monomolecular law at any fixed acidity and temperature. The speed of destruction rises in direct proportion to the hydroxyl ion level, slowly in one range and much faster past a marked point.
europmc-pmc2186318:
Ji and Suter reviewed in 2007 the role of p38 MAPK signalling in neuropathic pain. Neuropathic pain follows nerve injury and includes spontaneous burning pain and pain from light touch. Microglia, the spinal cord's immune cells, are now implicated in driving it. The review gathers evidence on one signalling protein inside microglia, p38 MAPK, a kinase that passes signals by adding phosphate groups.

After nerve injury, p38 becomes activated in spinal microglia. That activation contributes to both the development and the maintenance of neuropathic pain. The authors trace what switches p38 on upstream. They also trace its downstream production of inflammatory mediators, substances that sensitise pain pathways. Together the evidence makes p38 a valuable drug target for managing neuropathic pain, a condition current treatments handle poorly.
europmc-pmc2291018:
Danovaro and co-workers tested in 2008 whether sunscreens cause coral bleaching by triggering viral infection in the corals' partner algae. Bleaching, where corals expel their symbiotic algae, is rising worldwide and endangers reefs and the half-billion people they support. Experiments in the Red Sea and the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans treated coral branches with sunscreens and individual ultraviolet filters. The team checked the algae for viruses using fluorescence and electron microscopy.

Sunscreens caused hard corals to bleach rapidly and completely, even at extremely low concentrations. The organic ultraviolet filters were responsible. They switched latent viruses inside the symbiotic algae into an active, cell-killing cycle. The algae then died and the coral lost its partner. The authors conclude sunscreens may drive bleaching in reefs with heavy swimming and tourism. They urge attention to a widely used product as a reef threat.
europmc-pmc2323218:
Lyne and many colleagues presented FlyMine in 2007, a web database for fruit fly and mosquito genomics. Genomics is the study of a whole set of DNA. The database covers Drosophila, the fruit fly, and Anopheles, the mosquito that spreads malaria.

FlyMine pulls genome and protein data from many sources into one warehouse that users can search as a whole. Before it existed, a researcher had to gather and reformat data from separate databases by hand. FlyMine lets users build custom queries across data types, such as gene activity, protein links, and gene silencing screens. The authors argued that combined data supports cross-checks and new testable ideas. They planned to keep adding data types as the store grew.
europmc-pmc2397418:
Olofsson, Bertilsson, and Lidén reviewed a one-pot route to plant-based ethanol in 2008. The feedstocks are lignocellulosic materials: straw, wood, and crop waste rich in tough plant fibres. Turning them into ethanol needs enzymes to free their sugars, then yeast to ferment the sugars.

The process they review, SSF, runs both steps at once in a single vessel. Doing so stops freed sugar from piling up and stalling the enzymes, and it cuts equipment costs. The trade-offs are real: enzymes and yeast want different temperatures, with the mix usually held below 37 degrees, and recycling yeast is hard. Recent work raised solid loading and cut yeast needs. For wheat straw, they report final ethanol near 40 grams per litre at over 70% yield.
europmc-pmc2570418:
Kuller, writing for the INSIGHT SMART Study Group, investigated in 2008 why interrupting HIV treatment raised deaths in a major trial. In that trial, patients who paused antiretroviral therapy when their immune counts were high died more often than those treated continuously. The team measured six inflammation and clotting markers in stored blood samples from trial participants, including 85 who died.

Higher starting levels of interleukin-6 and D-dimer, a clotting marker, strongly predicted death. Odds ran 8.3 and 12.4 times higher in the top quarter than the bottom. The pattern held at later measurements too. One month after randomisation, both markers had risen in the interruption group. Interleukin-6 rose by 30 percent and D-dimer by 16 percent, in step with rebounding virus levels. The authors suggest treatments that calm inflammation deserve study.
europmc-pmc2634718:
Koopman and colleagues reported in 2009 on a DNA repair defect found in some colon and rectum cancers. Healthy cells fix small copying errors in DNA through mismatch repair. When that system fails, tumors behave in distinct ways, and early-stage patients often do well. Far less was known about people whose cancer had already spread.

The team checked tumor samples from a large trial of 820 patients with advanced disease. Only 18 of 515 tested patients had the defect, and most cases traced to a switched-off repair gene called MLH1. Patients with the defect lived a shorter time on average and responded less often to treatment. The authors conclude the defect is rare once this cancer spreads, which hints that such tumors spread less readily.
europmc-pmc2661018:
White, Nagarajan, and Pop presented in 2009 a statistics tool, Metastats, for comparing the microbe mixes found in body and environment samples. Such surveys read DNA from whole communities at once, producing counts for thousands of microbe types. The challenge is spotting which types truly differ between two groups, amid noise and rare counts.

Their method uses a false discovery rate control, which keeps false alarms in check when many tests run at once. For types seen only a handful of times, it switches to an exact test built for sparse data. In simulations it beat older methods, most clearly on the rare types. On real data from lean and obese human guts, it found differences the first study had missed. Infant and adult gut data, plus 85 mixed samples, gave the method further workouts.
europmc-pmc2689218:
Marambaud, Dreses-Werringloer, and Vingtdeux reviewed in 2009 the role of calcium signaling gone wrong in brain degeneration. Calcium ions are the brain's universal messenger, timing synapse firing and the laying down of memory, through effectors such as CaMK enzymes and the gene switch CREB. Cells guard calcium levels fiercely, because the same signal that teaches can also kill.

The review gathers evidence that leaky calcium control is a shared thread in Alzheimer, Parkinson, and Huntington diseases. Two clues stand out for Alzheimer disease. Presenilins, proteins mutated in its inherited form, double as calcium channel regulators. Another recently found calcium channel, CALHM1, also carries risk variants. When calcium escapes its bounds, neurons suffer selective damage and death by several routes at once. Drugs that steady calcium, the authors suggest, deserve a place in the search for treatments.
europmc-pmc2706318:
Jahn and Radford reviewed in 2008 how a protein chain chooses between folding into its working shape and clumping into harmful aggregates. Aggregates called amyloid, stiff fiber-like clumps, cause several human diseases. The same tools used to study normal folding now let scientists track the misfolded states that lead toward clumps.

Their review explains how short-lived middle states on a complex energy landscape, a map of possible shapes, steer a chain toward folding or toward clumping. Traits built into the chain itself, plus help from the cell, tilt that choice toward the safe shape. Joining lab, computer, and cell work is now revealing shared rules behind that split.
europmc-pmc2721818:
Qian and co-authors showed in 2009 that a distinct group of macrophages, large immune cells, is required for breast cancer to seed and grow in the lung. Macrophages in a primary tumor were known to affect its spread, but their role at the distant site was unclear. The team used mouse models of breast cancer spread to the lung.

A macrophage group with a distinct surface profile gathered at tumor cells as they exited blood vessels into lung tissue. Removing that group by genetic or chemical means cut seeding and growth sharply, and even slowed growth that was already established. Imaging showed the cells help tumor cells cross the vessel wall, survive, and then expand.
europmc-pmc2759918:
Asharani, Hande, and Valiyaveettil tested in 2009 the anti-proliferative activity of silver nanoparticles, tiny silver particles widely sold in cosmetics, household products, and therapeutic agents for their antimicrobial action. Safety rules for these materials were lacking, and their cell uptake and toxicity paths were unanswered. They exposed normal human lung fibroblasts and human glioblastoma cancer cells to varied doses.

Cells took particles in mainly through two engulfing routes, and particles spread through cytoplasm and nucleus. Treated cells showed chromosome instability and mitotic arrest, a halt in division. Normal fibroblasts recovered from arrest efficiently, while cancer cells ceased to proliferate. Toxicity ran through calcium spikes inside cells, shape changes, and loss of a key actin-binding protein called filamin. The stress response also switched on two protective genes in the treated cells.
europmc-pmc2776018:
Teste, Duquenne, François, and Parrou validated in 2009 reference genes for measuring gene expression by real-time RT-PCR in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Such studies must normalize against genes assumed constant, yet single favorites like ACT1 in fact vary. They mined public microarray data for genes steady during long growth on glucose, then tested candidates with the geNorm algorithm across conditions and strains.

Four genes, ALG9, TAF10, TFC1, and UBC6, stayed stable in every condition and strain background tried. Averaging any three of the six best genes gave consistent results. Normalizing with ACT1 alone, by contrast, gave inconsistent answers between samples. Applying the multi-gene method, they measured a hundred-fold switch-on of one glycogen gene at the diauxic shift, the switch from sugar burning to other fuels. They advise dropping ACT1 and other common controls for this yeast.
europmc-pmc2820518:
Hazkani-Covo, Zeller, and Martin reviewed in 2010 the stray copies of mitochondrial DNA lodged inside cell nuclei, nicknamed numts. Mitochondria are the cell's energy units, with their own small genome. Over evolution, chunks of that genome keep slipping into the main nuclear genome and staying there.

Across eighty-five sequenced genomes of complex-celled life, the number of numts rose with genome size, which hints that insertion is limited by how often nuclear DNA breaks. Five human numts cause genetic disease, and a dozen spots vary between people in whether a numt is present. The copies confuse disease studies by masquerading as mitochondrial mutations, yet they also link maternal lineages to nuclear markers across time.
europmc-pmc2871118:
D'Archivio, Filesi, Varì, Scazzocchio, and Masella examined in 2010 how much of the plant compounds called polyphenols actually get into the body. Polyphenols give many fruits and drinks their color and bite, and population studies link them to lower disease rates. But eating a compound is not the same as absorbing it, and the absorbed share is called its bioavailability.

The review shows the absorbed share differs hugely from one polyphenol to another. The most common ones in the diet are often not the best absorbed, so intake tables can mislead. Gut microbes, food makeup, and the compound's own structure all shift the result. The authors close by sorting out the disputes and method flaws that make studies disagree, so future trials can rest on firmer ground.
europmc-pmc2875518:
Cuthbertson, Roughton, Jenkinson, Maclennan, and Vale followed three hundred intensive care survivors in a British university hospital for five years to chart their quality of life. Little was known past the two-year mark. Patients rated their health before admission and repeatedly afterward, and the team converted the ratings into quality-adjusted life years, a measure that combines length and quality of life.

Physical quality dipped sharply by three months, recovered to pre-illness levels by one year, then slid again between two and a half and five years. Mental scores, by contrast, matched general population norms after six months. Even so, physical scores stayed below the norm at every check, and total quality-adjusted years fell well short of what peers without intensive care would expect.
europmc-pmc2891718:
Puinean and colleagues pinpointed in 2010 how the peach-potato aphid, a global crop pest, had begun defeating neonicotinoid insecticides, the class long used as a last reliable weapon. Lab tests on a resistant clone pointed first at detoxification enzymes called P450s, which break down poisons. A gene chip covering every known detox gene found exactly one screaming outlier.

The gene, CYP6CY3, ran at twenty-two times its normal level in the resistant aphids. Counting gene copies showed why: the gene had been duplicated over and over in the genome, a mechanism called amplification. This was the first documented case of a P450 gene amplifying behind insecticide resistance in a major farm pest. Knowing the trick lets monitors watch for the extra copies before control fails in the field.
europmc-pmc2994918:
Currie, Ward, and Cheng summarised twenty years of melioidosis cases from Darwin, Australia, in a 2010 study of over five hundred patients. The soil bacterium behind the disease thrives in the tropics, and this long-running record is a reference for its behaviour.

Pneumonia led the presentations, followed by urinary, skin, and blood infections, with most cases arriving in the wet season. Diabetes and heavy alcohol use were common risk factors, though a fifth of patients had none. Deaths fell sharply across the study years as care improved. Recurrences mostly traced to patients stopping long antibiotic courses early.
europmc-pmc3042718:
D'Ambrosio, Clugston, and Blaner updated in 2011 the science of how the body handles vitamin A and its chemical relatives. These compounds, called retinoids, are needed for growth, vision, immunity, reproduction, and healthy skin. One form provides the light sensing pigment in the eye, and another switches on hundreds of genes. Humans cannot make them, so all must come from food.

The review traces how the vitamin is absorbed, carried in blood, stored, and converted between its many forms. Dozens of carrier proteins and enzymes take part, and some also handle fats and cholesterol. The authors gather the main advances of the previous ten to fifteen years. Their map helps explain both deficiency, which blinds children worldwide, and the risks of excess, and it guides work on related medicines.
europmc-pmc3140518:
Alexander Mellmann and colleagues read the genome of a deadly foodborne germ during a live outbreak in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. The 2011 German outbreak caused hundreds of cases of kidney failure and dozens of deaths, from a rare strain never found in animals. Working while the outbreak ran, the team sequenced one outbreak strain and a similar case from a decade earlier within days.

Both strains mixed genes from two normally separate disease-causing types, one clumping in the gut and one producing a potent toxin. Family analysis placed them near a known gut strain rather than the usual toxin producers. The outbreak strain differed from its older cousin in carried side DNA and surface genes. The authors show fast sequencing can profile a new threat in real time.
europmc-pmc3219018:
Omar Alkandari and colleagues studied acute kidney injury in critically ill children treated at two Montreal intensive care units, in this 2011 paper in Critical Care. Small rises in the blood marker creatinine predict death in adults, but pediatric evidence was thinner. The team also tested whether different ways of estimating a child's baseline creatinine changed the conclusions.

Among more than two thousand admissions, roughly one child in six developed kidney injury. Higher illness severity, mechanical ventilation, infection, and having a baseline measurement predicted it. Injured children were several times more likely to die, stayed longer, and needed ventilation longer, whichever baseline method was used. In children without injury on arrival, the size of the first creatinine rise helped predict who would develop it.
europmc-pmc3239318:
Omid Hamid and colleagues ran a prospective phase II trial hunting for tumor biomarkers. They wanted markers that predict response to the melanoma drug ipilimumab. The trial was reported in the Journal of Translational Medicine in 2011. The drug releases a brake on the immune system and had extended survival in advanced melanoma. Eighty-two patients with inoperable disease received it, with biopsies taken before treatment and shortly after the second dose.

Response rates and safety matched earlier trials, and inherited gene variants showed no link to benefit. Two features of the pretreatment tumor did: high levels of the immune marker FoxP3 and of an enzyme called indoleamine dioxygenase. Tumors that gained more infiltrating immune cells after treatment also tended to respond. The authors say these markers may help select patients, pending larger studies.
europmc-pmc3241518:
Zoë Morris, Steven Wooding, and Jonathan Grant examined a famous claim about medical research. The claim says findings take seventeen years to reach patients. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine in 2011. They reviewed studies that actually measured time lags in turning health research into interventions, expecting to learn where the delays sit.

Only twenty-three papers qualified, and they were barely comparable: each measured different things, in different ways, at different points in the pipeline. The authors conclude that knowledge of time lags is too patchy to guide those who fund research or move it into practice, effectively blindfolding investment decisions. Before lags can be shortened, the field needs shared models, definitions, and measures that can be applied consistently in practice.
europmc-pmc3260318:
Daniel Sloan and colleagues reported an extreme case of genome evolution in flowering plants in this 2012 paper in PLoS Biology. Plant mitochondria carry their own small genomes, and their size and stability vary. The team examined two species in the genus Silene, a group of flowering plants that includes campions.

The pair turned out to hold the largest mitochondrial genomes known in any organism. Their size did not grow slowly and steadily. It coincided with extreme shifts in DNA mutation rate and recombination activity. The genome's structure changed too, split across many chromosomes rather than the usual single circle. The authors present the pair as evidence that plant mitochondrial genomes can transform rapidly and radically, overturning assumptions that they evolve at a stately pace.
europmc-pmc3276118:
Devin Scannell and colleagues delivered improved genome sequences and laboratory strains for three yeast species, in this 2011 paper in G3. The Saccharomyces group includes the baker's yeast that anchors genetics, plus close relatives ideal for studying evolution, but their draft genomes were gappy and their strains hard to manipulate. The team resequenced three relatives, combining millions of short reads with older long-read data.

The new assemblies have far greater continuity and far fewer gaps than before. Comparing five species defined a shared set of just over five thousand protein-coding genes. That let the authors re-examine the pace and pattern of gene evolution. They could pinpoint gains, losses, and candidate genes under positive selection. They also derived stable haploid strains, each carrying genetic markers, for all three species. The resources, freely posted online, aim to make this genus the most experimentally tractable of its kind.
europmc-pmc3338918:
Papadopoulos and colleagues compared three drugs that block a vessel growth signal, measuring how tightly each grabs its target, in a 2012 study. The signal, VEGF, drives the leaky new blood vessels behind several cancers and blinding eye diseases. Two of the drugs are antibodies, while the third, called VEGF Trap, is a decoy receptor built to bait the signal away.

The trap bound every tested form of the main signal with far greater tightness than either antibody, and latched on much faster. In cell tests it shut down vessel cell activation, movement, and internal signaling more potently. It was also the only drug to catch two related signals, which the antibodies ignore. The authors say these differences set the trap apart and may explain differing performance in patients.
europmc-pmc3372318:
Arcidiacono and co-authors reviewed in 2012 why people whose bodies resist insulin face higher cancer risk. Insulin resistance is common in obesity and type 2 diabetes, and blood insulin often runs high. Studies link the condition to cancers of the breast, bowel, liver, and pancreas.

The review lays out several routes that may connect the two. High insulin and a related growth factor can push cells to multiply and resist death. Insulin also shifts sex hormone levels, while fat tissue inflammation and reactive oxygen species can damage DNA. Sorting these routes matters because each suggests a different way to cut the extra risk.
europmc-pmc3374618:
Aagaard and a large team charted the vaginal microbiome in pregnancy in 2012, a topic national microbiome projects had left open. They sampled three vaginal sites in healthy pregnant women across the second and third trimesters. Their comparison group was several hundred samples from non-pregnant women.

Pregnancy brought a distinct vaginal signature, confirmed by several kinds of analysis. Overall variety and richness fell, and Lactobacillus species took a stronger hold. The mix also shifted with the exact site sampled and with how far the pregnancy had advanced. The work gives a baseline for judging what counts as normal during pregnancy.
europmc-pmc3462118:
Du and colleagues published a genome-wide survey of the MYB gene family in soybean in BMC Plant Biology in 2012. MYB proteins help switch other genes on and off in plants, yet no one had mapped the whole family in a legume before. The team searched the soybean genome and sorted what they found by structure and family history.

They counted well over two hundred R2R3-MYB genes and grouped them into dozens of subfamilies. Duplication of whole genome segments helped the family grow so large. The authors argue some members may serve roles tied to the root nodules legumes form. Their catalog gives breeders and plant biologists a base for later work on single genes.
europmc-pmc3464218:
Aguirre and colleagues reported in PLoS Pathogens in 2012 how dengue virus weakens the alarm system of human cells it infects. Infected cells should release type I interferon, a signal that warns nearby cells, but the virus blocks that signal. The team traced the block to a virus protease, a protein-cutting enzyme complex named NS2B3.

They found that the protease cuts a human adaptor protein called STING, which the alarm pathway needs. Cells lacking STING let the virus grow more freely, while a form of STING that resists cutting restored stronger interferon output. Mouse STING cannot be cut by the protease. Aguirre's team argues this helps explain why dengue grows poorly in mice.
europmc-pmc3488318:
Genes of complex organisms are split by introns, stretches cut out before a protein is built, and Igor B. Rogozin, Liran Carmel, Miklos Csuros, and Eugene V. Koonin review a thirty-year argument over their origin in 2012. One camp held introns came first and shaped early proteins; the other held they arrived late, only in eukaryotes.

Genome comparisons changed the balance. Matching intron positions appear in matching genes across animals, plants, and even protists, pointing to many introns surviving from the last eukaryotic common ancestor. Reconstructions of gains and losses suggest that ancestor, and each supergroup ancestor after it, started with intron-rich genes. Later lineages mostly trimmed them.
europmc-pmc3547818:
Plants burn their own damaged proteins under stress, and Jie Zhou and seven colleagues identify the cargo selector NBR1 in 2013. Autophagy in plants delays aging, recycles nutrients, and answers stress, but research had focused on the machinery that builds the disposal sacs, not on how cargo is chosen.

Arabidopsis plants lacking NBR1 suffer under heat, oxidation, salt, and drought, like core autophagy mutants, and NBR1's protection requires binding ATG8, a sac protein. Yet NBR1 is unnecessary for aging-related senescence and for resisting a tissue-killing pathogen. Its cargo is insoluble ubiquitin-tagged protein aggregates. Selective autophagy, the study shows, is a targeted stress tool, not a general cleanup.
europmc-pmc3597518:
Asier Sáez-Cirión and colleagues reported a rare group of HIV patients in PLoS Pathogens in 2013, from the French VISCONTI study. Antiretroviral therapy suppresses HIV but cannot cure it, so stopping means the virus usually rebounds. Fourteen patients broke that rule. All had started long therapy very early, during the first infection, and after stopping, their virus stayed controlled for years without drugs, a state the authors call post-treatment control.

Unlike people who control HIV naturally, most of these patients lacked the protective gene variants such controllers usually carry. Theirs skewed toward risk variants, and their early infections had been harsher, with weaker killer-cell responses. Off therapy, their hidden virus stores stayed extremely low and sometimes shrank further, partly because long-lived resting cells were seldom infected. The cases suggest early, sustained treatment can hand even an unfavorable immune hand a durable win.
europmc-pmc3608918:
Marlon Cerf, writing alone in Frontiers in Endocrinology in 2013, sorted out two failing systems in diabetes. Blood sugar stays high when the pancreas's beta cells release too little insulin, and also when body tissues stop answering insulin properly, the state called insulin resistance. Each fault raises sugar, which raises insulin demand, so the two drive each other in a loop. Which one truly starts type 2 diabetes was the question under review.

Genetic evidence at the time pointed to the beta cell: most inherited risk variants act by weakening insulin release rather than insulin response. On that basis the review ranks beta cell failure as the senior partner in starting the disease, with resistance a powerful accomplice. Keeping beta cells working, and insulin signaling alive in both beta cells and target tissues, is named the way to hold blood sugar steady.
europmc-pmc3631218:
Ezequiel Gleichgerrcht and Jean Decety surveyed empathy and exhaustion across 7,584 practicing physicians in PLoS ONE in 2013. Clinical empathy improves care, but feeling with patients can also wear doctors down. Their online battery measured kinds of empathy, distress, burnout, altruism, and emotional awareness, letting them ask which traits travel with satisfaction and which with fatigue.

Satisfaction with compassion rode with empathic concern, perspective taking, and altruism. Fatigue, meaning burnout plus stress absorbed from patients' trauma, rode instead with personal distress and alexithymia, the difficulty naming one's own feelings. Women scored higher on empathic concern. Years of experience alone shifted little once age and sex were accounted for. Doctors worst off combined high fatigue with low satisfaction and the weakest emotion regulation. Training emotional self-awareness is the authors' practical suggestion.
europmc-pmc3636318:
What young adults want from health apps is the question behind a 2013 qualitative study in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Laura Dennison, Leanne Morrison, Gemma Conway and Lucy Yardley ran the work with students and staff at a university in the United Kingdom. Health apps were spreading fast, yet little was known about what users liked or feared in them.

Four focus groups with 19 people, most of them in their early twenties, talked through their use of apps for a healthy life. Tracking acts and goals and getting advice on the move scored well. Doubts centred on truth and safety of the data, the effort an app asks for, and how it leaves mood. Tools that sense context and social media links put people off, a warning the group passes to app makers.
europmc-pmc3646718:
Partner violence and low mood feed each other over time, Devries and seven colleagues report in a 2013 systematic review in PLoS Medicine. Cross-section studies had long linked abuse by a partner with depression and suicide bids in women. Snapshots cannot show which came first. The team turned to long-run studies that tracked the same people over years, for women and for men.

The pooled proof shows that abuse raises the odds of later depressive symptoms and suicide bids in women. It also shows the reverse path: depressive symptoms raise the odds of later abuse in women.
