For men, far fewer studies existed; they hinted at a link with depressive symptoms but gave no clear tie to suicide bids. Weak control of shared risks, such as drink and childhood harm, limits the claims.
europmc-pmc3684618:
Eren and colleagues present a filtering method that cleans up DNA sequence reads before they are clustered into microbial groups. Marker-gene studies often inflate diversity because sequencing errors create false groups. The method uses the overlap between paired-end reads to spot positions where errors are likely, so suspect data can be removed.

Tested on Illumina data and run within the QIIME analysis pipeline, the filter cut the number of spurious groups while keeping real biological signal. The authors offer it as a practical preprocessing step for studies that count microbes from short gene fragments, where read errors otherwise blur the difference between rare species and noise.
europmc-pmc3723318:
Angela Pirillo, Giuseppe Norata, and Alberico Catapano wrote a review in Mediators of Inflammation in 2013 on LOX-1. LOX-1 is a receptor that takes up oxidized LDL, the altered form of a blood fat that helps build artery plaques. LOX-1 sits mainly on the cells lining blood vessels, and also on macrophages and smooth muscle cells in the vessel wall.

In a healthy vessel LOX-1 is barely present, but inflammation and other plaque-promoting signals switch it on, and it shows up in plaques in animals and people. Mice without LOX-1 had thinner vessel linings and less inflammation, while mice with extra LOX-1 built plaques faster. Certain gene variants in people are tied to higher heart attack risk. Blocking the receptor is being tested as a way to control these effects.
europmc-pmc3798618:
Hiroshi Murayama, Yoshinori Fujiwara, and Ichiro Kawachi wrote a review in the Journal of Epidemiology in 2012 on social capital and health. Social capital, the resources people draw from social networks and community trust, has been proposed to explain why similar health programs fare differently in different places. The team looked for the strongest study design: prospective studies that analyze people and their areas together.

They found only 13 articles that qualified, mostly from Western countries. Both personal social capital and area or workplace social capital generally showed positive effects on health, across designs, settings, follow-up lengths, and outcomes. No prospective multilevel studies came from Asia, though snapshot studies exist there, including in Japan. The authors call for more such evidence and for tests of interventions that build social capital.
europmc-pmc3909918:
Trevor Bedford and nine colleagues present a new way to track flu evolution in eLife in 2014. Flu viruses keep changing their surface so they can dodge immunity built against earlier strains. Labs usually measure that change with antibody tests between pairs of strains, kept separate from the family trees built from gene sequences.

Their model joins the two approaches, letting antigenic change spread along a shared family tree. Applied to four flu lineages, it shows that A/H3N2 changes faster and in sharper jumps than the others. Year-to-year antigenic drift also matched rises and falls in case numbers within each lineage. The method can be reused for other fast-changing pathogens.
europmc-pmc3919818:
Zengcai V. Guo and colleagues lay out lab procedures for behavior tests in head-fixed mice in PLoS ONE in 2014. Mice are now a main model for studying brain circuits, but linking circuit activity to behavior needs tight control of stimuli and exact measures of movement. Fixing the head gently in place, long used in primates, gives that control and allows clean neural recording.

The protocol covers the fixation surgery, water restriction used to motivate the animals, and training steps. On about one milliliter of water a day, body weight settled near 80 percent of the starting weight after ten days. Mice then learned whisker-based touch tasks, reporting what they felt by licking in go and no-go choices, giving labs a shared recipe for decision experiments.
europmc-pmc3926818:
Purvaba J. Sarvaiya, Donna Guo, Ilya Ulasov, Patrik Gabikian, and Maciej S. Lesniak review chemokines in cancer in Oncotarget in 2013. Chemokines are small proteins that normally steer immune cells around the body, guiding inflammation and surveillance. Tumors twist that guidance system: the amounts of chemokines and their receptors change in many cancers, and the faulty signaling feeds the disease.

The review follows chemokines through the steps that let a tumor advance. They help cancer cells multiply, grow new blood vessels, change into a more mobile form, dodge the immune system, and spread to distant organs. Cancers named include breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and lung tumors, melanoma, and several blood cancers. Because so many steps depend on chemokine signals, the authors treat the system as a promising set of drug targets.
europmc-pmc3945918:
Steven A. Carr and a very large group of proteomics experts set best practices for targeted peptide measurement in Molecular and Cellular Proteomics in 2014. Targeted mass spectrometry, which watches for chosen protein fragments rather than scanning everything, is spreading through biology and medicine. Yet labs were using wildly different standards to declare an assay valid, and papers often lacked the detail others need to trust or reuse the test.

The authors lay out a fit-for-purpose framework: the proof an assay needs depends on what it will be used for, from exploratory research to clinical decisions. They specify what to measure, what to report, and how to show a peptide is identified uniquely and counted reliably. The goal is assays that many labs worldwide can adopt with confidence.
europmc-pmc4008818:
Paul M. Thompson and a very large group of co-authors describe a global team effort linking brain scans to genes, in Brain Imaging and Behavior in 2014. The group, called ENIGMA, pools scan and gene data from seventy sites around the world. Single-site studies are too small to catch the faint gene effects that shape the brain.

By merging results across sites, the team found gene variants tied to the size of the hippocampus, a memory centre, and to total head volume. Later work targets smaller deep-brain parts and the wiring that joins brain areas. Other groups in the network study how schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression, and attention disorders change the brain. In all, the merged sets cover close to twenty-five thousand people. The review sums up progress, snags, and surprise finds so far.
europmc-pmc4044318:
Glyn Elwyn and ten colleagues review why proven patient decision aids so rarely enter routine care, in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making in 2013. Twenty years of trials show the aids raise knowledge and decision confidence. Yet clinics have not widely adopted them.

The team screened thousands of abstracts and kept seventeen studies of real implementation attempts. Every study used the same referral model: clinic staff pointed eligible patients to the aid. The model kept failing in the same ways. Clinicians showed marked indifference. Many doubted the content of the aids. Others feared disruption to set workflows. Together these bred inertia across whole organisations. The authors judge the evidence too thin for firm recipes, since all attempts leaned on one model. They call for trials of other routes, such as embedding aids in the visit itself, before conclusions can harden.
europmc-pmc4182618:
Frederic Brosseron, Michael T. Heneka, and two co-authors surveyed inflammation proteins in Alzheimer's disease in Molecular Neurobiology in 2014. Cytokines are signal proteins of the immune system, and their levels in blood or spinal fluid might track the brain inflammation that comes with Alzheimer's and its mild early stage.

The overview gathers studies that measured cytokines in patients with mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's, in blood, serum, and spinal fluid. Some proteins clearly shift with the disease and may rise as mild impairment tips into dementia, hinting at use as warning markers. But results for the most studied proteins, such as TNF-alpha and interleukin-6, clash between studies. The authors blame uneven methods and poorly matched patient groups, and they call for standard tests and sampling over many years.
europmc-pmc4219118:
Meredith A. Shafto, Richard N. Henson, and ten co-authors published the design of a lifespan ageing study in BMC Neurology in 2014. The Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience, or Cam-CAN, set out to learn how healthy brains change from 18 to old age. It also asks how older adults flexibly recruit brain regions to stay sharp.

Stage 1 interviews 3,000 adults on health, lifestyle, and lifetime experience, with a core test of thinking skills. From them, 700 people, 100 per decade of age, go on to brain scans and fuller cognitive testing across attention, language, memory, emotion, and learning. A subset of 280 returns for deep imaging experiments. The protocol paper fixes the design so later findings can be judged against it.
europmc-pmc4235718:
David Lebeaux, Christophe Beloin, and two co-authors reviewed models of biofilm infection in Pathogens in 2013. Bacteria living in biofilms, slimy cities stuck to tissue or implants, cause many stubborn infections that resist antibiotics and immunity. Thirty to forty years of study still left the field without a model that copies these infections faithfully.

The review walks from simple dish systems through cell cultures to animal models of device and tissue infection, judging what each taught and where each misleads. Dish models expose the chemistry of film growth cheaply, while animal models capture the immune fight but vary widely. The authors see progress in blending classic setups with new imaging and genetics, and they mark the gaps a better model must close.
europmc-pmc4248318:
Ilari Scheinin, Pieter Wesseling, and nine co-authors presented a cheap genome scanning method in Genome Research in 2014. Counting DNA copies across the genome spots the gains and losses that drive cancer. Hospital archives hold millions of tumours fixed in paraffin, but their DNA is degraded and hard to read, and matched healthy samples are often missing.

Their method reads the genome shallowly, at about a tenth of normal depth, which keeps costs low. It corrects for two known distortions, how mappable each stretch is and its GC content. Using public genome data, the team also built a blacklist of unreliable genome regions, most of them never flagged before. The pipeline, QDNAseq, was proven on over 1,000 samples from more than 25 institutions, giving clean copy profiles for most archive specimens.
europmc-pmc4296918:
Laura Zannini, Domenico Delia, and Giacomo Buscemi review CHK2, a kinase that helps cells answer DNA damage. Their review appeared in the Journal of Molecular Cell Biology in 2014. When DNA breaks, CHK2 switches on and tags more than twenty other proteins, steering the cell toward pause, repair, death, or endurance depending on the harm.

Recent work also places CHK2 in jobs that run without any damage at all, in DNA structure control and in the normal cell cycle. The review weighs these wider roles against the kinase's links to cancer, since loss or change of CHK2 can favor tumor growth. That dual picture frames CHK2 as both a guardian and a possible drug target.
europmc-pmc4303918:
Jane P Messina and six co-authors produced the first full world survey of hepatitis C virus genotypes. Their study appeared in Hepatology in 2015. The virus comes in several genotypes whose spread differs by region, and that patchwork complicates work on vaccines and on treatments meant to work against every type.

The team reviewed genotype studies published from 1989 to 2013 and combined them with overall infection estimates from the Global Burden of Disease project. For countries with no genotype data, values were inferred from neighbors and patterns. The resulting maps show which genotypes dominate each region and where data are missing, a base for planning treatment programs.
europmc-pmc4308618:
Catalin Chimerel, Edward Emery, David K Summers, Ulrich Keyser, Fiona M Gribble, and Frank Reimann found that indole, a chemical made by gut bacteria, steers hormone release from gut L cells. Their study appeared in Cell Reports in 2014. L cells release GLP-1, a hormone that helps control blood sugar, and bacterial products were long suspected of influencing that release.

Indole had two opposite effects split by time. Brief contact boosted GLP-1 output by widening the cell's electrical pulses and letting in more calcium. Longer contact slowed the cell's energy production and cut release. The double action makes indole a true signal between gut microbes and host metabolism, with possible bearing on diabetes research.
europmc-pmc4336318:
Shuai Gong and eight co-authors tracked two stress hormones in mouse blood across the day, the fertility cycle, and varied stress. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE in 2015. Corticosterone is treated as the main rodent stress hormone, while cortisol, the human one, also circulates in mice and its value as a stress readout was unclear.

The two hormones moved together closely under almost every condition tested, with correlation values staying strong through cycles, rhythms, and acute or repeated stress. They parted ways only late in long stress, when cortisol held steady while corticosterone drifted. The results support using cortisol alongside corticosterone in mouse stress work, with care about timing.
europmc-pmc4337318:
Philipp Stiefel, Sabrina Schmidt-Emrich, Katharina Maniura-Weber, and Qun Ren stress tested a popular pair of dyes used to judge whether bacteria are alive. Their study appeared in BMC Microbiology in 2015. The green dye SYTO9 and the red dye propidium iodide are sold as a live-dead kit, yet results are often taken on faith.

Using Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the team found traps: with the green dye alone, live and dead staph cells glowed alike, while dead Pseudomonas glowed far brighter than live ones. The red counterstain did not fully fix the bias. Settings such as dye ratios and timing shifted answers further. The paper is a caution that viability counts need validation for each organism.
europmc-pmc4380918:
Qiuzhi Chang, Weike Wang, Gili Regev-Yochay, Marc Lipsitch, and William Hanage asked how much farm antibiotic use endangers human health, in Evolutionary Applications in 2015. Farm use is often blamed for drug-resistant disease in clinics, yet hard numbers on the size of that route were missing. The authors set out three routes by which farm use could cause human harm, and judged each against case studies of real resistant strains.

The first route, direct infection from animals, is the easiest to size and looks small next to the total burden of resistant disease. The second, animal strains that breach into humans and then spread, has known cases, including resistant Staphylococcus aureus, though direction of spread is hard to prove. The third, resistance genes moving from farm bacteria into human pathogens, is hardest to measure and may matter most.
europmc-pmc4384018:
Ian Sillitoe and co-authors updated CATH, a protein structure classification resource, in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. CATH groups protein domains by shape and evolution, and its Gene3D side projects those groupings onto genome sequences. Version 4.0 gave annotations for more than 235,000 domain structures and 25 million predicted domains in sequences. Two years of work went mainly into sharper function prediction and cleaner data sets.

The functional families inside each group, called FunFams, gained predictive power, helping guess a new protein's job from its relatives. A rolling release, CATH-B, now publishes current domain assignments without waiting for a formal version. A strictly non-redundant benchmark set, CATH-40, supports fair tests of similarity methods. Web pages were also improved. Structure-based grouping can spot kinship that raw sequences no longer show.
europmc-pmc4421818:
Cheng Zhu and six colleagues described a new kind of graphene sponge in Nature Communications in 2015. Graphene sheets are light, strong, conduct electricity well, and offer a large surface area. Earlier bulk graphene foams, though, had random pores, which limited how well their structure could be tuned for a given task.

Using direct ink writing, a form of three-dimensional printing, the team built regular lattice foams with a planned pattern. The printed material stayed light and conductive, had large surface area, and could be squeezed to a small part of its size and spring back. Its stiffness beat that of random graphene foams of like density by about tenfold, opening paths to custom sensors, electrodes, and cushions.
europmc-pmc4461318:
Leonard Freedman, Iain Cockburn, and Timothy Simcoe put a price on irreproducible early drug research in PLoS Biology in 2015. Many preclinical studies, the lab work done before human trials, cannot be repeated by other groups. That weakness slows the building of shared knowledge and delays and inflates the cost of developing new therapies for patients.

Reviewing past analyses, the authors estimate that more than half of preclinical research is irreproducible, wasting tens of billions of dollars each year in the United States alone. Flawed early studies also raise false hope and send drug programs down blind alleys. The article lays out a framework of fixes. They range from better study design and reporting to changed incentives for labs, journals, and funders. A long-term plan to raise repeat rates across the life sciences completes it.
europmc-pmc4547618:
Kathrin P. Aßhauer, Bernd Wemheuer, Rolf Daniel, and Peter Meinicke present software that guesses what a microbe community can do, in Bioinformatics in 2015. Sequencing the 16S rRNA marker gene names the microbes in a sample cheaply, but says nothing direct about their abilities. Full metagenome sequencing answers that, at far higher cost.

Their package, Tax4Fun, predicts a community's functional profile from 16S data alone. Tested on paired datasets where both kinds of sequencing existed, its profiles came close to the shotgun results. The tool is an open-source R package that works with standard analysis outputs. For broad surveys with many samples, it offers function-level insight at marker-gene prices.
europmc-pmc4557018:
Randy Chi Fai Cheung and four co-authors update the medical uses of chitosan, in Marine Drugs in 2015. Chitosan is a natural chain molecule derived from chitin, the shell material of crabs and shrimp and the second most plentiful natural polymer. It harms few tissues, breaks down in the body, and rarely triggers allergy, which makes it attractive for medicine.

Its weak spot is poor solubility in neutral or alkaline water. Chemists work around that by modifying it or blending it into gels and composites, unlocking new functions. The review surveys recent research and prospects, with special attention to drug delivery, wound care, and other pharmaceutical and biomedical uses where its friendliness to living tissue counts most.
europmc-pmc4579518:
Paul L. Plener, Teresa S. Schumacher, Lara M. Munz, and Rebecca C. Groschwitz review the long-term course of self-injury, in Borderline Personality Disorder and Emotion Dysregulation in 2015. Non-suicidal self-injury, deliberately hurting oneself without intent to die, was newly listed in the DSM-5 diagnostic manual as a condition needing study. Its path over years was poorly known, and it seemed to flicker on and off.

To widen the picture, the review also included studies framed as deliberate self-harm. Thirty-two longitudinal studies qualified. Rates rose through adolescence and fell in young adulthood. Depressive symptoms and female sex repeatedly predicted who would self-injure. The synthesis gives clinicians and researchers a firmer map of who is at risk and when.
europmc-pmc4595218:
Eric I. Benchimol and colleagues, with the RECORD Working Committee, published a 2015 statement on reporting studies that use routinely collected health data. Such data come from care and billing records rather than from studies planned in advance. Existing reporting guidance did not cover issues these data raise. The statement extends the STROBE guidance for observational studies.

RECORD is a checklist of 13 items covering the title, abstract, methods, results, and discussion of a study. The paper explains each item and gives examples of good reporting. A companion website supports discussion and updates. By following the checklist, authors, editors, and reviewers can make record-based studies clearer about where their data came from and how they were used.
europmc-pmc4643218:
In 2015, a mouse study linking the gut bacterium Akkermansia muciniphila to the onset of obesity was published by Marc Schneeberger and colleagues. Obese animals show changed gut communities and inflamed fat tissue, but the chain of events was unclear. The team fed mice a high-fat diet over different periods and tracked microbes and metabolism. The work appeared in Scientific Reports.

Akkermansia levels fell sharply with age and high-fat feeding, while one other species rose slightly. Statistical analyses tied Akkermansia loss to fat tissue inflammation markers, lipid handling genes, and blood measures such as glucose, insulin, and leptin. The tight inverse link supports the view that this mucus-loving bacterium helps keep metabolism steady, and its decline may be an early sign of diet-driven obesity.
europmc-pmc4731918:
Matt Jackson, Ian B. Jeffery, Michelle Beaumont, and six colleagues linked early frailty to gut microbe patterns in Genome Medicine in 2016. Frailty, the loss of reserve that makes older people fragile, had been tied to gut microbes only in elderly and care-dependent groups. The team looked earlier in life, analyzing stool gene data from 728 female twins in the community and scoring each woman's frailty with a standard index. Findings were checked against a separate elderly cohort.

Frailty rose as gut diversity fell, a striking and consistent link. Hundreds of microbe types tracked with the frailty score; some, like Eubacterium dolichum, grew commoner with frailty, while a Faecalibacterium type grew rarer and held up in comparisons between twins. Sixty associations repeated in the second cohort. Whether microbes drive frailty or mirror it is unknown, the authors note, but the named species are now targets for tests and possible interventions.
europmc-pmc4738418:
Collins, Ogundimu, and Altman tackle a practical gap in medical prediction research: nobody knows how large an external validation study must be. Prognostic models are often published but rarely tested on fresh patients, and small validations give shaky verdicts. Using a large real dataset, they resample patients and watch how six published models' measured performance wobbles with sample size.

Precise, unbiased estimates of discrimination and calibration need a floor of about 100 outcome events, and 200 or more events are preferable. Below that, apparent model failures or successes may be noise. The authors offer the numbers as design guidance for anyone planning a validation study.
europmc-pmc4773118:
Leay-Kiaw Er leads eight authors in PLoS ONE in 2016 testing a simple index for insulin resistance. When the body stops answering insulin well, diabetes and heart disease follow, yet the lab tests that prove resistance are too involved for routine screening. The team compared many cheap blood and body measures to find one that flags resistance early.

From 511 adults in Taiwan without diabetes, they scored fat and sugar measures against a standard resistance index. A combined score, blood fats times fasting sugar times body mass index, tracked resistance strongly and sorted people well. A hormone ratio did as well but costs more to run. The authors present the combined score as a clinic-ready screen built from three routine numbers.
europmc-pmc4792418:
Sandra M. Eldridge leads eight authors in PLoS ONE in 2016 sorting out two tangled terms: pilot studies and feasibility studies. Both are small studies run before a big trial, and the health literature uses the labels loosely, which hampers searching and judging them. The team built a shared frame from a survey of experts, an open meeting, usage outside health research, and a read of 27 real studies.

Their frame nests one term inside the other. A feasibility study asks whether a future trial can be done, should be done, and how. A pilot study asks the same, but with a defining extra: it runs the future trial, or part of it, in miniature. The authors urge researchers to label such studies plainly and to state their goals, so the prep work for trials can be found and trusted.
europmc-pmc4820618:
Chi Lam Au Yeung leads a wide author team in Nature Communications in 2016 on how ovarian tumors borrow drug resistance from their neighbors. Advanced ovarian cancer spreads to the belly fat, where support cells wrap the tumor. Sequencing found those support cells, fat cells and fibroblasts alike, rich in a small RNA, miR21, far above the cancer cells' own level, and shipping it out in tiny exosome parcels.

The parcels delivered miR21 into cancer cells, where it blocked a death-switch protein called APAF1. Shielded cells survived the chemotherapy drug paclitaxel that should have killed them. Resistance, in short, can be imported. The authors propose cutting the transfer, or the RNA itself, as a treatment route for the metastatic and returning disease that makes this cancer so lethal.
europmc-pmc4872618:
Susan E. Collins, writing solo, reviewed links between social and economic status and alcohol outcomes in 2016. The pattern holds a puzzle: people with higher status drink as much as, or more than, poorer people, yet poorer people suffer far more alcohol harm. Race, ethnicity, and gender reshape the link further.

Among low-status groups, racial and ethnic minorities and homeless people bear the heaviest harm. Same drinking, unlike damage points to unsafe settings, less care access, and added stress. The review calls for work on the steps between status and harm. Fair policy needs that chain made plain, so help lands where damage concentrates.
europmc-pmc4931018:
Bo Wang and nine co-authors use long read sequencing to reveal how complex the maize transcriptome really is. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Maize is a major crop and a model for plant gene research. Short sequencing reads, though, piece transcripts together poorly, so the full set of RNA forms stayed unclear. The team read single RNA molecules end to end across six maize tissues.

They captured 111,151 transcripts covering about 70 percent of known maize genes. More than half were new isoforms, alternate forms of known genes, and some appeared in only one tissue. About 3 percent came from gene sites not known before. They also found many long noncoding RNAs and fusion transcripts, and showed DNA methylation helps create the variety. The authors conclude that maize gene activity is far richer than gene lists alone suggest.
europmc-pmc4934518:
Yunshun Chen, Aaron T. L. Lun, and Gordon K. Smyth walk through a full RNA sequencing analysis using free R tools. Their workflow article appeared in F1000Research in 2016. RNA sequencing profiles which genes are active in a sample. A common goal is to find genes or pathways whose activity differs between conditions. The authors show each step on a real dataset from mouse mammary gland cells.

The pipeline starts with aligning reads to the genome using the Rsubread package. It then explores the data, filters weak signals, and normalizes counts. Gene testing runs in the edgeR package with its quasi-likelihood method, which handles noisy counts with care. Plots and pathway tests close the loop from raw reads to biological claims. The authors aim for a workflow that other labs can run, adapt, and trust.
europmc-pmc4971518:
Zhenyu Zhong, Mengxin Lv, and Junxia Chen map circular RNAs in bladder cancer and trace one ring's role in tumor growth. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2016. Circular RNAs are non-coding rings that can sponge up microRNAs and free their target genes. The team screened bladder tumor and normal tissue with a microarray. They found hundreds of dysregulated circles, then confirmed six with strong differences by a second method.

One circle, circTCF25, stood out. Models predicted it binds two microRNAs, miR-103a-3p and miR-107, which restrain the cell cycle gene CDK6. Forcing circTCF25 higher in bladder cancer cells lowered those microRNAs, raised CDK6, and sped growth and migration in dishes and in animals. The authors present the pathway as the first worked example of a circular RNA circuit in this cancer.
europmc-pmc4976518:
Mehrbod Estaki and eight co-authors test whether physical fitness predicts the diversity of gut microbes. Their study appeared in Microbiome in 2016. Low gut diversity links to diabetes, colorectal cancer, and bowel inflammation. Whether fitness itself shapes the flora was unknown. The team sequenced stool microbes from thirty-nine healthy adults of similar age, body mass, and diet, but with fitness levels that varied widely. Fitness was measured as peak oxygen uptake, the standard test.

Fitness explained more than a fifth of the variation in species richness after diet and other factors were counted. Fit people also carried microbes whose predicted genes favored movement, chemical sensing, and fat building. Their stool held more butyrate, a fatty acid tied to gut health. Extra dietary protein moderated the pattern. The authors stress the study is correlative, but it ties aerobic fitness to a richer, butyrate leaning gut community.
europmc-pmc5019418:
Kellie S. Gross and five co-authors compare two related receptors in the brain's reward hub, in PLoS ONE in 2016. The receptors, mGluR1a and mGluR5, both answer the signal chemical glutamate and shape how nerve cells change. Drugs aimed at them are being weighed for addiction care, so knowing each one's separate effect matters. The team boosted each receptor in turn and counted dendritic spines, the tiny knobs where nerve cells receive signals, in the nucleus accumbens.

The two boosts pulled in opposite directions. Turning up mGluR5 lowered spine counts in both parts of the nucleus accumbens, while turning up mGluR1a raised them. Neither changed the dorsal striatum nearby. Injecting an mGluR5 activator straight into the nucleus copied the drop. The findings warn that sister receptors in one drug family can reshape brain wiring in opposing ways.
europmc-pmc5037318:
Rafael Di Marco Barros and a wide team of co-authors report in Cell in 2016 on how surface tissues pick their resident T cells. Many body surfaces host their own sets of gamma-delta T cells, a rarer kind that guards tissue health. In mouse skin, a molecule called Skint1, made by skin and thymus cells, selects the local set. But neither Skint1 nor that skin set exists in the same form across species, leaving the general rule unclear.

The team shows that gut lining cells in mice use a sister molecule, Btnl1, joined by Btnl6, to select the gut's Vgamma7-positive T cells, with no input from microbes or food. Human gut lining cells do the same job with two molecules, BTNL3 and BTNL8, which selectively answer the gut's Vgamma4-positive cells. A conserved pattern emerges: each surface uses its own butyrophilin-like molecules to shape its resident T cell set.
europmc-pmc5062618:
Panagiotis Kotsantis and six co-authors find a new source of DNA damage in cancer in Nature Communications in 2016. Cancer-driving genes force cells to multiply, and the copying machinery stalls and breaks DNA in the process, a burden called replication stress. How a growth gene creates that stress was partly mysterious. The team followed the activated HRAS oncogene, which also cranks up the cell's RNA-making apparatus.

Raising one general transcription factor, TBP, was enough: RNA output climbed, R-loops accumulated where RNA sticks to DNA, copying forks slowed, and DNA damage and cell aging followed. TBP alone, with no oncogene, reproduced the full picture, and the HRAS effect ran through TBP. Since cancer cells often deregulate their transcription machinery, the authors argue that excess transcription itself may be a general engine of the genome instability that drives tumors.
europmc-pmc5099918:
Steffi Bosch and seven co-authors reported a storage study in Scientific Reports in 2016 on exosomes, tiny sacs that cells release to send proteins, fats, and RNA to other cells. Standard ways of collecting exosomes clump them together, and freezing can damage them, which makes experiments hard to repeat.

Adding trehalose, a natural sugar used to protect foods and drugs, to the storage fluid kept the vesicles separate and more uniform in size. Freeze-thaw cycles spoiled samples kept in plain salt solution but not those with trehalose, and microscope images showed no burst vesicles. Vesicles from pancreas beta cells kept in trehalose also triggered a stronger immune signal in test cells, suggesting their activity survived storage better.
europmc-pmc5114218:
Xavier Monnet, Paul E. Marik, and Jean-Louis Teboul updated guidance on predicting fluid response in Annals of Intensive Care in 2016. Patients with failing circulation often get extra fluid, but too much is harmful and the heart does not always pump more in reply. Doctors need a test before, not after, giving fluid.

Old static measures such as central venous pressure proved unreliable and should be dropped, the authors argue. Newer dynamic tests briefly shift blood volume, by lifting the legs, pausing the ventilator, or using heart-lung interaction, and watch the heart's output reply. Pulse and stroke volume swings work only under strict conditions. The leg raise test has the strongest backing, and the tests complement each other depending on the patient and monitors at hand.
europmc-pmc5115318:
Xiandi Wang, Lin Dong, Hanlu Zhang, Ruomeng Yu, Caofeng Pan, and Zhong Lin Wang reviewed electronic skin in Advanced Science in 2015. Human skin senses pressure, heat, and moisture, and engineers want flexible sheets that can do the same for robots, artificial intelligence, and human-machine interfaces.

The review covers pressure sensor arrays built on several sensing principles that can map touch with finer detail and faster response than human skin. Newer versions also detect heat and humidity, tell apart different kinds of force, and even heal themselves. Recent work adds dense flexible circuits, wireless links, and designs that harvest their own power. The authors look ahead to skins that not only sense their surroundings but react to them.
europmc-pmc5159618:
Martin J. Boeree and a large PanACEA consortium team ran a tuberculosis drug trial in The Lancet Infectious Diseases, with the hosted text dated 2017. Tuberculosis is the world's leading infectious killer, and the team sought shorter, safer drug combinations in a multi-arm, multi-stage randomized trial at seven sites in South Africa and Tanzania.

They enrolled 365 patients with new, drug-sensitive lung tuberculosis between May 2013 and March 2014. Arms tested higher doses of rifampicin, the backbone drug, with or without moxifloxacin or the experimental compound SQ109, against the standard four-drug course. Treatment ran twelve weeks in the test phase, followed by a standard continuation. The main measure was how fast sputum cultures cleared within twelve weeks, an early sign of a regimen's killing power.
europmc-pmc5241818:
Grace X. Y. Zheng and a large team presented a droplet system for profiling single cells in Nature Communications in 2017. Reading the active genes of single cells reveals cell types that bulk tests blur together, but earlier methods handled only limited cell numbers or needed laborious sorting. Their system counts messenger RNA from the tail end of each message, cell by cell, at very large scale.

Cells are sealed into droplets, up to eight samples at once in about six minutes, with roughly half the loaded cells captured. Across tests, the team gathered data from about 250,000 single cells in 29 samples, checked the system's sensitivity with cell lines and synthetic RNA, and profiled 68,000 blood immune cells. In marrow from transplant patients, natural sequence differences in the RNA let them tell host cells from donor cells one cell at a time, exposing leftover disease that routine tests missed.
europmc-pmc5243918:
Daniele Caligiore and colleagues wrote a consensus paper on cerebellar function in the journal Cerebellum in 2017. The cerebellum, long treated as a motor specialist working in its own loops, in fact exchanges signals with the cortex and the basal ganglia in one large system. The paper gathers recent views from theory and experiment on how those three partners interact.

Topics covered include the two-way traffic between the regions during movement and thought, their shared roles in learning and control, and what the cerebellum may contribute to basal ganglia movement disorders. All contributors agree that treating the three as an integrated system changes how each one's function is understood, in motor and non-motor work alike. They also agree that far more experiment and modeling is needed, and the paper marks where consensus holds, where it fails, and which questions stay open.
europmc-pmc5297918:
Dorothee Liebschner, Pavel V. Afonine, Nigel W. Moriarty, Billy K. Poon, Oleg V. Sobolev, Thomas C. Terwilliger, and Paul D. Adams introduced polder maps in Acta Crystallographica Section D in 2017. An OMIT map tests whether a doubtful feature, such as a drug molecule, is really supported by the data: the feature is deleted from the model and the map redrawn. If density remains, the feature is real.

The catch is the solvent model. Standard software fills every unmodeled space with flat bulk solvent, so deleting a ligand floods its pocket with fake solvent density that can drown the weak real signal. Polder maps, named for reclaimed land held back from the sea, keep the solvent mask out of the omitted region while atoms are excluded. The tool, phenix.polder in the PHENIX suite, yields less biased maps, with examples showing weak ligand density that ordinary OMIT maps wash away.
europmc-pmc5336618:
Shinichi Nakagawa, Daniel W. A. Noble, Alistair M. Senior, and Malgorzata Lagisz wrote a guide to judging pooled studies in BMC Biology in 2017. A meta-analysis merges data from many studies into one overall effect. In biology, the method now serves fields from ecology to body function. Its verdicts can sum up a field neatly, but they stand or fall on the care of the pooling.

The authors pose ten questions a reader can ask of any such study in biology. The checks run from how studies were found and picked, to how spread and bias were handled, to whether the work can be repeated. The same list doubles as a plain guide for those who write pooled studies. A good one earns what they call mega-enlightenment. A sloppy one is a mega-mistake. The ten questions help a reader tell which is which.
europmc-pmc5451818:
Beneke and co-authors build a CRISPR toolkit for fast gene editing in kinetoplastid parasites. Their methods article appeared in Royal Society Open Science. These parasites cause grave neglected diseases. They include Leishmania and trypanosomes. Gene knockout there was slow work. Most Leishmania lack the RNA interference path. Long DNA arms and cloning steps blocked scale. CRISPR promised a shortcut, if packaged well.

The toolkit needs no cloning by the user. Guide RNAs come from PCR-made templates. A T7 polymerase writes them inside the cell. An online tool designs the primers on its own. Plasmid sets yield transfection constructs in a few hours. Tags can be added at either end of a protein. The tags span glow proteins, luciferase, and small labels. Null mutants arose in one transfection round. Deleted genes vanished even before cloning single cells. Large knockout screens are now feasible in these species.
europmc-pmc5457518:
Wani and co-authors build a light-driven artificial flytrap that senses and grips objects on its own. Their device report appeared in Nature Communications. The Venus flytrap snaps shut without a brain. It also tells prey from random debris. Copying such autonomy in tiny robots is hard. Electronics and batteries resist miniaturization. The team used soft materials instead. A light-responsive liquid-crystal elastomer does the moving.

The elastomer sits on an optical fiber tip. The fiber supplies power as light. It also probes the environment without contact. Light feedback closes the loop. When an object enters range, actuation triggers. The grip closes autonomously, like the real plant. The device can distinguish different targets. Self-regulation happens inside a fiber-sized frame. No external computer directs the action. The authors see a path to small autonomous soft devices.
europmc-pmc5460018:
Lawson and co-authors map how microbes share work inside granules that clean wastewater. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. The granules host a process called anammox. It removes nitrogen from wastewater with little energy. Special bacteria turn ammonium into nitrogen gas without oxygen. Other bacteria live beside them in the same granules. What those neighbors do was largely unknown.

The team read DNA from a lab reactor and rebuilt 17 draft genomes. Some belonged to anammox bacteria, others to their neighbors. They paired the genomes with gene activity data. One neighbor group, kin to Chlorobi, broke down stray proteins for food. It also recycled nitrate back to nitrite, which anammox bacteria use. Other neighbors scavenged debris and dead cell matter. Some could live on hydrogen, acetate, or formate instead. The study gives a first clear view of who does what in these granules.
europmc-pmc5465318:
Duan and co-authors grow ultrathin sheets of a porous crystal on supports to split water with power. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The crystals are called metal-organic frameworks. They offer many metal sites for reactions. Poor conductivity usually wastes those sites. Tiny pores also slow the flow of materials. Most work uses bulk powders instead. The team grew sheet arrays directly on a base. One chemical bath step completes the growth.

Thin sheets expose far more active sites. Conductivity improved with the new shape. Pores at several scales aid transport. The nickel-iron array excelled at releasing oxygen. It needed only 240 millivolts of extra voltage. That held at a standard test current. It ran 20,000 seconds with no decay. Each site cycled nearly four times per second. The same platform also released hydrogen well. Full water splitting worked on it too.
europmc-pmc5486318:
Alshannaq and Yu present a review in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health on mycotoxins in food. Mycotoxins are poisons made by molds that grow on crops. They slip into food in the field and in storage. About a quarter of the world's harvest is tainted each year. Three mold genera produce most of the trouble.

Over 300 mycotoxins are known, but six groups recur in food. Aflatoxins rank as the most toxic of them. The review sets out each group's health effects and usual host foods. Detection methods range from lab chromatography to quick strip tests. Carry-over into milk, meat, and eggs adds a second risk path.
europmc-pmc5489418:
Griffanti and co-authors present a practical how-to guide in NeuroImage on cleaning fMRI data. A method called ICA splits each brain scan into separate components. Some components hold real brain signal, and others hold structured noise. Telling them apart by hand is a key step before cleanup. Trained staff also need clear rules to label training data.

The guide describes the spatial and time features of each component type. Worked examples come from varied datasets, including UK Biobank and Human Connectome Project scans. Both 3T and 7T data are covered. Tricky cases get special attention at the end. Data quality and preprocessing choices can shift what components look like.
europmc-pmc5490618:
West presents a broad review in Psychology & Health on tobacco smoking. Smoking remains a top preventable cause of illness and early death worldwide. Rates have fallen, yet the habit persists for many people. The review covers the harms, the gains from quitting, and what drives uptake. It also judges the tools used to fight smoking.

Nicotine's fast, pleasant delivery keeps the habit going, West argues. Its harms feel distant, so they rarely deter use. Taxes, media campaigns, and brief doctor advice spur more quit tries. Support with counseling and drugs raises success rates. National programs that combine these parts cut both smoking and deaths, he concludes.
europmc-pmc5496518:
McKeith and co-authors present the fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium in Neurology. It updates advice on diagnosing and managing dementia with Lewy bodies. The prior report guided practice for a decade. Many cases are still missed or misread as Alzheimer's disease, though. The new criteria split clinical features from diagnostic biomarkers more clearly.

REM sleep behavior disorder gains more diagnostic weight in this revision. A heart scan method, MIBG scintigraphy, also gains weight. Guidance covers brain imaging, lab tests, and brain tissue checks after death. Management advice rests mostly on expert opinion, since trials are few. The authors call for trials of symptom and disease-modifying drugs.
europmc-pmc5520018:
Langefeld and a large consortium report a genetics study in Nature Communications on lupus. Lupus strikes women and non-European groups hardest. Most gene hunts so far covered Europeans only. This study genotyped 27,574 people across three ancestries. Their samples span European, African, and Hispanic Amerindian roots.

Dozens of risk regions emerged in each group, they report. Twenty-four regions were new to science. Risk rose faster than the sum of single effects as risk alleles piled up. The authors call this a cumulative hit pattern. Some effects were shared across ancestries, others were not. The map sharpens the picture of lupus's ethnic gaps.
europmc-pmc5530518:
Brazendale and co-authors present a hypothesis paper in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity on childhood weight gain. Children gain weight faster over summer break than during school. Fitness also slips over the break. The authors blame the loss of daily structure. School days impose fixed meals, activity, and bedtimes.

Weekend data back the idea, they report. Some 155 of 190 studies found worse habits on unstructured days. Screen time rises, sleep drifts, snacks multiply. Summer behaves like one long weekend. Prevention programs should target the break itself, they urge. Structured summer options could protect vulnerable children.
europmc-pmc5589418:
Muir and co-authors report a cancer metabolism study in eLife. Many cancer cells lean hard on the amino acid glutamine to grow. Yet some of those cells need it less inside a body. The team hunted for the food difference behind that shift.

Cells grown in adult bovine serum used less glutamine. That serum mimics nutrients in the body better than standard lab media. One nutrient explained the gap: cystine. High cystine forced cells to burn more glutamine. The effect ran through a transporter called xCT, or SLC7A11. Together, cystine levels and that transporter set glutamine need. They also set how well glutaminase-blocking drugs can work. Readers get a clear lesson on lab conditions shaping results.
europmc-pmc5623518:
Iba and co-authors propose new criteria for sepsis-induced coagulopathy in BMJ Open. Sepsis often tangles the blood's clotting system. Anticoagulant drugs may help only the right subgroup. A recent redefinition of sepsis left old scores mismatched.

The team reanalyzed a nationwide Japanese survey. It held 1,498 sepsis patients with clotting problems. All had received recombinant thrombomodulin. Three measures predicted death within 28 days. Platelet count, prothrombin time ratio, and total SOFA score carried the signal. The new SIC score combines just those three. A score of four or more flagged higher risk. Its mortality split beat the older Japanese DIC score. The inputs are routine and the math is simple. Readers get a bedside tool, plus a candidate rule for choosing anticoagulant treatment.
europmc-pmc5651218:
Bonev and co-authors mapped how the 3D genome rewires during mouse neural development. Their research article appeared in Cell. The team built high-resolution Hi-C maps. They tracked chromatin folding in cultured cells. They also tracked it in living tissue. The maps were the sharpest available at the time.

Transcription tracked with chromatin insulation. It also tracked with long-range contacts. Forced gene activation alone could not create new domain borders. Active gene bodies contacted each other across cell types. During differentiation, active domains interacted less. Inactive domains interacted more strongly. A Polycomb network in stem cells broke apart. New contacts between enhancers and promoters formed. Those contacts matched gene expression changes.
europmc-pmc5655818:
Iorga and co-authors review how estrogen guards the heart and blood vessels. Their review appeared in Biology of Sex Differences. Women before menopause get less heart disease than men. Rates rise once menopause passes. The authors credit estrogen and its receptors. Three receptor types are covered.

The review explains the protective steps in detail. Less oxidative stress is one gain. Less scarring and better vessel tone also help. Effects differ between the sexes. Receptor roles differ by sex too. Giving estrogen as a drug stays in dispute. Risks include blood clots and some cancers. The body can make estrogen locally. An enzyme builds it from testosterone. The authors suggest drugs aimed at one receptor. That route might prove safer.
europmc-pmc5658418:
Huerta and co-authors report a field study in Scientific Reports. It traces plastic debris through a land food chain. The setting was traditional Mayan home gardens in southeast Mexico. Waste handling there is poor, and plastic litter is common. The team sampled soil, earthworm casts, and chicken feces. They also checked chicken crops and gizzards, which people eat.

Microplastic counts rose at each step of the chain. Soil held the lowest counts per gram. Earthworm casts held far more, and chicken feces held the most. Gizzards contained microplastic particles, while crops held none. Macroplastic pieces were also common in gizzards and crops. The data show plastic can enter land food webs.
europmc-pmc5673918:
Adalsteinsson and co-authors report a liquid biopsy study in Nature Communications. It tests whole-exome sequencing of cell-free DNA from blood. Such sequencing could profile tumors without repeat biopsies. Agreement with tumor tissue genome-wide was still uncertain. The team built software called ichorCNA for screening. It estimates tumor content from very low coverage genome data. No prior knowledge of tumor mutations is needed.

They applied it to 1,439 blood samples from 520 patients. The patients had metastatic prostate or breast cancer. About a third had enough tumor DNA for standard exome work. In 41 matched patients, blood and biopsy agreed closely. Clonal mutations matched at 88 percent. Copy number changes matched at 80 percent.
europmc-pmc5687818:
Walker and co-authors present a surveillance report in MMWR. It estimates teen vaccination coverage across the United States. Teens should routinely get Tdap and meningococcal vaccines. HPV vaccine is also advised at age eleven or twelve. The CDC analyzed the 2016 National Immunization Survey-Teen. Records covered 20,475 adolescents aged thirteen to seventeen. Provider records confirmed the vaccine histories.

Coverage rose between 2015 and 2016 on several measures. At least one Tdap dose reached 88 percent. At least one HPV dose reached about 60 percent. About 43 percent were fully up to date on HPV. Girls ran ahead of boys on HPV measures. Coverage was lowest outside metro areas.
europmc-pmc5698618:
Stapley and co-authors present a review in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B. It surveys how recombination rates vary across eukaryotes. Recombination swaps DNA between parental chromosomes in meiosis. It is a core feature of sexual reproduction. Rates differ hugely between species and genomes. Genome-wide rates can vary more than tenfold. The team analyzed linkage maps from 353 organisms. Patterns were traced across taxa, populations, and individuals.

The review then asks what drives that variation. Genome layout, sex, and surroundings all play roles. Genetic and epigenetic mechanisms are covered in depth. Shifting selection pressures matter as well. The authors close on how rate variation shapes evolution. Future modeling and field approaches are flagged.
europmc-pmc5750618:
Altemimi and co-authors review how to extract and identify active compounds from plants. Plant phenolics can act as antioxidants, microbe fighters, and cancer guards. Synthetic antioxidants in food raise health concerns, which boosts interest in natural ones. Fruits and vegetables are the prime sources studied.

The review describes a wide range of assays and methods for the work. More than 8,000 phenolic compounds have been characterized so far. It covers extraction, isolation, and measurement steps in turn. The health linked traits of phenolic products get a full section. The guide serves labs screening plants for useful compounds.
europmc-pmc5793418:
Yang and co-authors study a circular RNA, circ-ITCH, in bladder cancer. This RNA acts like a sponge for smaller regulatory RNAs. Its role in bladder cancer had not been reported. The team measured its levels in tumors and cell lines and tracked patient survival.

The circular RNA ran low in cancer tissue, they find. Patients with low levels lived shorter lives. Forcing its levels up slowed cell growth, movement, and spread in dishes and in mice. It works by soaking up two microRNAs, freeing two brake genes. The axis may serve as a marker and drug target.
europmc-pmc5807718:
Jones reports microscope findings on veins in a bat's wing. He was studying blood flow in the wing web. The veins caught his eye with an odd pulsing flow. Careful watching revealed a new vein behavior.

The wing veins squeeze and relax in rhythm, about ten times a minute. Each squeeze speeds the blood onward. Valves then block any backward slip. Jones measures the squeeze and tests pressure, current, and opium on the web. He also disputes claims that veins clamp shut for long spells. Readers get a classic piece of hands-on physiology from 1852.
europmc-pmc5809718:
Luby and co-authors report the WASH Benefits trial in rural Bangladesh. The study mirrors a sister trial in Kenya. It asks if water, sanitation, handwashing, and food aid cut diarrhea. Growth in young children is the second test.

A total of 5,551 pregnant women in 720 clusters took part. Groups got one aid, a mix, or none. Sanitation, handwashing, and food groups all saw less diarrhea. Water treatment alone did not help. Food aid made children modestly taller by age two. Adding hygiene steps to food aid gave no extra gain. Readers can compare two nations under one design.
europmc-pmc5826318:
Feng and co-authors review the gut microbiota as a moderator of body-wide health. Gut microbes talk with the brain, lung, liver, bone, and heart. Their chemical products carry many of those messages. Butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid, is a prime signal.

The review follows microbe signals into gene pathways. One path feeds into colorectal cancer growth signals. Another reaches T cell control in the brain. MicroRNAs join the exchange in both directions. That two-way traffic shapes blood vessel health and liver cancer. Readers get a map of one community influencing nearly every organ system.
europmc-pmc5848618:
Tardaguila and co-authors present SQANTI, a quality-control pipeline for long-read transcriptomes. Their paper appeared in Genome Research. Long reads now capture whole transcripts in one pass. Thousands of apparently new transcripts surface even in familiar species.

Many of those novelties are sequencing artifacts in disguise. SQANTI grades each transcript with 47 descriptors of structure and quality. A machine-learning filter then strips the fakes away. Applied to mouse brain cells, it cleans the catalog for study. Real new transcripts mostly remix known splice sites. The tool also fixes transcript counts that artifacts had skewed.
europmc-pmc5852618:
Park and co-authors review cardiac troponins, proteins that help control heart muscle contraction. The article appeared in Cardiovascular Research in 2017. Troponin was found in the 1960s, and its heart-only forms soon stood out. Forms of troponin I and T occur just in heart muscle. That trait let labs build blood tests for them.

The review covers troponin biology and how the protein reaches the blood. It explains the test's key role in ruling heart attack in or out. The authors note that levels also rise in chronic disease and after hard exercise. Such rises track with outlook, yet their causes stay unclear. Readers get a clear account of a gold-standard test and its limits.
europmc-pmc5863218:
Foulon and co-authors present new lesion mapping methods in the BCBtoolkit. Their article appeared in GigaScience. Brain lesions harm more than the spot that is damaged. They also cut links to distant, healthy regions. Standard mapping often misses those remote effects. The toolkit measures a lesion's impact on whole brain circuits. It combines structural links, functional links, and cortical thickness.

The team applied the methods to 37 patients with frontal lesions. They tested performance on a category fluency task. Directly cut regions matched areas known for word tasks. Wider networks also emerged, including a left fronto-parietal network. Its thickness tracked how well patients performed. The software is free for other researchers to use.
europmc-pmc5885018:
Silva and co-authors present chewBBACA, a suite for gene-by-gene bacterial typing. Their article appeared in Microbial Genomics. Gene-by-gene methods are rising in outbreak tracking. Yet open, scalable tools for building typing schemas were lacking. The suite helps users create whole-genome or core-genome schemas. It then calls alleles in strains of interest. Complete and draft genome assemblies both work as input.

The software runs on Python 3.4 or higher. It fits a laptop or a large computing cluster. Allele calls take seconds to minutes per strain. Parallel options handle hundreds of thousands of strains. Local use suits data that cannot leave the lab. The suite is freely shared on GitHub.
europmc-pmc5984618:
Raymond and a very large team of co-authors sequence the rose genome and trace the domestication of modern roses. Their study appeared in Nature Genetics. Roses carry high cultural and economic value. The team built a homozygous line from Rosa chinensis 'Old Blush'. Single-molecule sequencing yielded one of the most complete plant genomes yet. They also resequenced key genotypes behind rose breeding.

Diversity analysis showed the hybrid 'La France' has a mosaic origin, they report. It blends European vigour with Chinese repeat blooming. Segments of Chinese ancestry held new candidate genes for reblooming. Rebuilt pathways linked scent and flower colour control. The genome should speed rose improvement.
europmc-pmc5996218:
Luyckx, Tonelli, and Stanifer map the global burden of kidney disease against the sustainable development goals. Their paper appeared in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization. Kidney disease is called the most neglected chronic disease. Solid global estimates need more population-based studies. Risks span the whole social range, from malnutrition to obesity. Many patients lack access to any care at all. Causes and costs bear on policy in every country.

The authors map actions under all the development goals. Such actions could improve measurement, prevention, and treatment. Migration, pollution, and unsafe work may block progress. A multisectoral push is needed to cut future burden.
europmc-pmc6092118:
Guerrero-Ferreira and co-authors solve the structure of alpha-synuclein fibrils by cryo-electron microscopy. Their research article appeared in eLife. These fibrils fill the Lewy bodies seen in Parkinson's disease. The team imaged fibrils built from residues 1 to 121. Detail reached 3.4 angstroms.

Two protofilaments twist into one polar fibril. Staggered beta-strands form the spine. Residues 38 to 95 resolved clearly in the map. The stretch from 50 to 57 glues the two filaments together. Three known family mutation sites sit in that stretch. A greasy cleft at one end hints at growth mechanics. Readers get atomic detail for designing diagnosis and treatment tools.
europmc-pmc6165118:
Tungmunnithum and co-authors wrote an overview in Medicines on flavonoids and other plant compounds used in folk cures. These plant chemicals are known for fighting cell damage and for other useful effects in the body. They have long drawn interest for stopping and treating disease.

Examples from several plants are shown with their known effects. Reported gains include killing germs and slowing cancer growth. Others protect the heart, boost the immune system, and calm swelling. Skin protection from sun damage is also covered. The authors present these compounds as fresh sources for new drugs. The overview maps a wide field in short form for students and researchers.
europmc-pmc6210218:
Bache and co-authors present a new liquid chromatography system for proteomics. Proteomics measures thousands of proteins in a sample. The liquid step before mass spectrometry is often slow. It can also lack robustness. The work appeared in Molecular and Cellular Proteomics. The system is sold as Evosep One.

The design uses gradients formed in advance. Samples sit inside those ready gradients. A second trick refocuses peptides with offset gradients. The team ran more than 2,000 HeLa samples to test it. Crude plasma samples showed no cross-contamination. The system measured over 5,000 proteins per sample. Each run took just 21 minutes. The authors say this speed suits clinical work.
europmc-pmc6245118:
Gorissen and co-authors compared the protein value of plant protein powders on sale. Their study appeared in Amino Acids. Muscle building after a meal depends on the amino acids a protein gives. Plant proteins often carry less of some key building blocks than animal proteins. The team measured many products with the same lab method. Sources ranged from oat, soy, and pea to milk, whey, and egg.

Animal proteins held more essential amino acids overall. Whey reached about 43 percent, while oat and lupin held about 21 percent. Plant sources also varied a lot from each other. Corn protein was rich in leucine, while hemp was poor in it. Lysine and methionine ran low in most plant products. The authors suggest blends of plant proteins to close the gaps.
europmc-pmc6254218:
Sultana, Anwar, and Ashraf tested how extraction choices change the antioxidant strength of plant extracts. Their study appeared in Molecules. Seven medicinal plants were used, taking bark, leaves, roots, and fruit. Four solvents were compared, both pure and mixed with water. Two methods were also compared, shaking and heated reflux. Plant antioxidants matter because they may slow cell damage linked to disease.

Water mixed solvents gave higher yields and stronger extracts than pure solvents. The tested materials held good levels of phenolic compounds. Radical scavenging reached as high as about eighty-seven percent. Heated reflux gave more extract by weight. Shaking still gave richer phenolic content and stronger activity in most cases. The results guide labs that want the most active extract from a plant.
europmc-pmc6333918:
Cioni and co-authors find that late endosomes serve as protein-making platforms in axons. Their study appeared in Cell. Axons are the long fibers of nerve cells. They make some proteins locally, far from the cell body. How the needed messages reach those sites was unclear. The team studied retinal ganglion cells and their axons.

RNA bundles rode on endosomes along the axon. Those endosomes, marked by Rab7a, also carried ribosomes. Live imaging showed proteins being built right there. The endosomes often paused on mitochondria. Messages for mitochondrial proteins were translated on them. Blocking Rab7a cut local protein making sharply. It also hurt mitochondria and axon survival. Mutants tied to a human nerve disease had the same effects.
europmc-pmc6335418:
Taniguchi and co-authors find a protein that blunts a key lung cancer drug. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The drug, osimertinib, blocks faulty EGFR in lung tumors. Some patients respond poorly from the start. The team traced that resistance to a receptor called AXL. The drug itself switched AXL on, by cutting a feedback brake.

Active AXL teamed with EGFR and HER3 on the cells. That trio kept tumor cells alive under treatment. It also sped the rise of drug-tolerant cells. Blocking AXL made resistant cells die again. Adding an AXL blocker shrank tumors more in mice. Tumors with high AXL answered EGFR drugs less often in patients. The pair strategy now looks worth testing in the clinic.
europmc-pmc6347718:
Wilson introduces the harmonic mean p-value for combining dependent tests. His paper appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Big datasets invite thousands of tests at once. The usual Bonferroni fix is strict and wasteful. It over-penalizes large test counts, he argues. That discourages broad, exploratory analysis.

The new measure blends p-values by their harmonic mean. Its roots lie in Bayesian model averaging. It keeps the standard false positive rate under control. At the same time it gains statistical power. The paper lists the measure's useful properties. It applies across many kinds of study. Genetics is a prime example field. The author offers it as a new lens on large-scale testing.
europmc-pmc6352118:
Diether and Willing review how gut microbes ferment leftover dietary protein. Their review appeared in Microorganisms. Most protein is digested before the large intestine. What escapes feeds microbes living there. Their fermentation adds many compounds to the gut pool. It may also affect the body's amino acid balance.

The products are diverse and often bioactive. Some raise inflammation and loosen the gut wall. They worsen colitis in study models. Others link to obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver disease. Named suspects include hydrogen sulfide, ammonia, and p-cresol. Colorectal cancer may also be fed by them. The authors argue protein fermentation deserves more attention. It is a missing piece in diet and gut research.
europmc-pmc6376618:
Evans and co-authors ask how long a hip replacement lasts, in The Lancet. Their systematic review and meta-analysis used case series and national registry reports. All had at least fifteen years of follow-up after surgery for arthritis.

Total hip replacement is common and works well, they note. Still, every implant will fail if it stays in place long enough. Pooling the reports let them estimate survival of the whole implant construct over time. Such numbers help patients judge when a second operation may come. Surgeons and planners can also use them to compare implant types.
europmc-pmc6409418:
Wong and co-authors estimate drug trial success rates in Biostatistics. Older figures came from small, industry-kept samples that may be biased. The team instead used records on more than 21,000 compounds and 406,038 trial entries from 2000 to 2015.

They computed success rates and trial lengths overall and by feature. Cancer trials succeeded at 3.4 percent in their sample, below the often-cited 5.1 percent. Rates also varied by phase, sponsor, and use of biomarkers. Recent cancer rates had begun to recover, they note. Their figures give drug planners a broader, less filtered base.
europmc-pmc6418018:
Cycon and co-authors review antibiotics in soil in Frontiers in Microbiology. Antibiotics used in people, animals, and farms leak into soil and water. There they can harm soil microbes and breed drug resistance.

The review traces how soil holds or breaks down drug residues. Binding to soil particles and chemical decay set how long each drug lasts. Drug residues shift which microbes thrive and which genes they carry. Resistance genes in soil are a public health worry, the authors note. They call for tighter control of drug waste from farms and clinics.
europmc-pmc6544318:
Paquola and co-authors map how the brain's fine structure relates to its function, writing in PLoS Biology. Structure is said to govern function, but human proof was scarce, since tissue studies use dead brains that cannot be scanned at work. The team built a method from a full 3D tissue reconstruction of one human brain, then applied it to MRI data from many healthy adults.

Both maps showed the same broad slope: from primary sensory areas to limbic and transmodal regions, tissue layering grows less distinct. Yet the two gradients pulled apart in the transmodal zones, home to the default mode and frontoparietal networks. Those are the regions tied to flexible thought, self-generated ideas and social cognition. A looser structural grip there, the authors argue, is what lets such regions switch roles so freely.
europmc-pmc6558418:
Harjunpää and co-authors review cell adhesion molecules, the molecular Velcro of the immune system, writing in Frontiers in Immunology. Immune cells must travel to a tumor, squeeze out of blood vessels, and grip their targets to kill them. Integrins, selectins, cadherins and their kin manage every step, from rolling along vessel walls to forming the synapse with a cancer cell.

Integrins get the deepest treatment: how they switch between bent, closed states and open, gripping ones, and how that switch steers trafficking and activation. Tumors, meanwhile, abuse the same toolkit to anchor, spread and hide. The review closes with attempts to drug adhesion molecules for cancer therapy, whether by blocking tumor spread or by helping immune cells reach their targets.
europmc-pmc6627318:
Holditch and co-authors review recent advances on kidney injury from cisplatin. Their article appears in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Cisplatin treats many solid tumors and reaches 10 to 20% of cancer patients. Acute kidney injury strikes about 30% of those who receive it. That harm caps how much drug doctors can give.

The review leans on rodent models that mirror the human injury. Transporters pull cisplatin into kidney tubule cells, where it builds up. Cell death, inflammation, and oxidative stress then unfold. Standard markers such as creatinine can miss mild injury. Newer markers include NGAL, KIM-1, and cystatin C. The authors cover magnesium protection and transporter-based strategies. They also flag the dose gap between mouse studies and patient care.
europmc-pmc6637318:
Forte, Favieri, and Casagrande review links between heart rate variability and thinking skills. Their systematic review appears in Frontiers in Neuroscience. Autonomic faults may arrive before clear cognitive decline. Heart rate variability, or HRV, indexes how the autonomic system steers the heart. The team asked whether the two track together.

The authors screened studies under PRISMA rules and kept 20. Together they covered 19,431 participants without dementia or major illness. Higher sympathetic activity tracked with worse thinking scores. Lower parasympathetic activity did the same. The pattern spanned attention, memory, and executive function. Executive function drew the most study interest. The authors propose HRV as an early warning marker. They call for wider work beyond that single domain.
europmc-pmc6642318:
Vargas and co-authors work out how selective autophagy starts at its target. Their study appears in Molecular Cell. Cells recycle damaged organelles and clear invading bacteria this way. How the ULK1 kinase gets switched on at cargo was unclear. The team used chemically inducible dimerization tools. They paired these with CRISPR knockout cell lines. Placing the receptor NDP52 on mitochondria triggered autophagy there. The same worked on peroxisomes.

NDP52 acts by pulling the ULK1 complex to the cargo. The kinase TBK1 helps that link form. Tethering ULK1 directly to cargo skipped both requirements. Activation also ignored the usual AMPK and mTOR controls. The authors propose a lean model of targeted autophagosome birth.
europmc-pmc6651418:
Reyes-Farias and Carrasco-Pozo review the anti-cancer effects of quercetin on tumour metabolism. Their review appears in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Quercetin is a common dietary flavonoid in fruits and vegetables. Cancer cells reprogram their metabolism to grow fast. They favour glycolysis for building blocks over efficient energy output. That rewiring is a hallmark of malignancy. Quercetin presses on several of the control pathways. These include PI3K/Akt/mTOR and Wnt/beta-catenin signalling.

Through them it cuts cell viability and drives apoptosis. It also promotes autophagy in cancer cells. The review focuses on glucose handling and mitochondria. Those two fronts define the metabolic attack. The authors present quercetin as a low-cost adjunct candidate.
europmc-pmc6652118:
Brisse and Ly compare the virus sensors RIG-I and MDA5 side by side. Their review appears in Frontiers in Immunology. Both proteins detect viral double-stranded RNA inside cells. Detection triggers type 1 interferon production. Those interferons launch the early antiviral defence. The two sensors share much structure and signalling. They signal through the same MAVS adaptor. Yet their recognition strategies diverge in key ways.

Each prefers different RNA features and pathogens. Their behaviour also varies across host species. The review covers evolution and protein partnerships. It details how each tells viral RNA from host RNA. Viral countermeasures against both sensors get attention too. The authors aim to guide therapies that target them.
europmc-pmc6707218:
Yong and co-authors built a new drug carrier for cancer chemotherapy. Their study coats porous silicon particles with material shed by tumor cells. The coating comes from exosomes, tiny sacs that tumor cells release. The team loaded the particles with the drug doxorubicin.

Tumor cells took in the loaded particles and then pushed them back out, wrapped in their own coating. These wrapped particles gathered in tumors, slipped out of blood vessels, and sank deep into tumor tissue. They killed both bulk cancer cells and cancer stem cells in mice. Tumors shrank in skin, organ, and spread models of the disease.
europmc-pmc6723618:
Filbay and Grindem give evidence-based advice for managing a torn anterior cruciate ligament. This knee ligament tears most often in young, active people. The injury can harm both body and mood over time. Diagnosis rests on history, examination, and sometimes MRI scans.

Three main paths exist. Patients can start with rehabilitation and have surgery only if the knee stays unstable. They can have reconstruction first, then rehabilitation. Or they can train before surgery as well as after. The authors explain how to discuss the options with patients. They also set phase-by-phase rehab goals and clear criteria for a safe return to sport.
europmc-pmc6735718:
Heller and Vingron present SVIM, a tool for finding structural variants in genomes. Structural variants are changes larger than 50 base pairs. They affect more DNA than small variants and link to many diseases. Their size and ties to repeated DNA make them hard to spot with short reads. Long-read sequencing helps, but older tools left gaps.

SVIM collects, clusters, and combines variant signatures from long-read alignments. It separates five variant classes, including tandem and scattered duplications and inserted new elements. Tests show it detects variants with high sensitivity and precise positions. The tool aims to help researchers link these large changes to human diversity and disease.
europmc-pmc6752018:
Danso and co-authors review how microbes might break down the world's plastics. At least 350 to 400 million tons of plastic are made each year. Poor recycling lets millions of tons pile up on land and at sea. Microplastics, the tiny fragments, raise special health concerns. The authors survey both the environmental problem and the biology.

Some bacteria can feed on plastic breakdown products, such as nylon fragments in factory wastewater. Fully degrading intact, long-chain plastic is far harder and rarely shown. The review weighs which polymers microbes attack and how. It also judges the promise of using enzymes and bacteria as a cleanup tool. Expectations, the authors imply, should stay modest for now.
europmc-pmc6760118:
Maugeri and co-authors traced what happens to mRNA medicines after they enter cells. Lipid nanoparticles are the leading carriers for RNA drugs. After a cell swallows a particle, some mRNA escapes its compartment and makes protein. The rest of the story was unclear. The team loaded nanoparticles with mRNA for a human protein, erythropoietin.

They found escaped material repackaged into vesicles the cells then secreted. At a one-to-one lipid-to-mRNA ratio, both lipid and mRNA showed up in these vesicles. Injected into mice, the vesicles delivered working mRNA and produced the protein in blood and organs. They also raised fewer inflammatory signals than the original particles.
europmc-pmc6773718:
Ceccarani and co-authors studied the vaginal ecosystem during common genital infections. They recruited 79 women in all. One group was healthy. The others had a yeast infection, chlamydia, or bacterial vaginosis. Gene sequencing mapped the microbes in each woman. A lab method based on nuclear magnetic resonance mapped the chemicals present.

Healthy women were dominated by one microbe, Lactobacillus crispatus. In each illness, that microbe fell sharply in number. A close relative, L. iners, took its place step by step. Genera such as Gardnerella and Prevotella grew instead. Lactate, a key chemical, dropped in all the sick groups. Each state has its own pattern of microbes and chemicals.
europmc-pmc6821018:
Kelly and co-authors examine why artificial intelligence rarely reaches patients, in BMC Medicine. AI tools now match experts on many test tasks in scans and records. Few, though, are used in day-to-day care. The gap between promise and practice is the subject here.

The authors sort the barriers into three groups. Some sit inside machine learning itself, such as models that learn shortcuts in one dataset and fail in another. Others are practical, like fitting tools into clinic workflow. The rest concern trust, rules, and social change. They argue that firm trials in real clinics, with follow-up checks over time, are the missing step.
europmc-pmc6868818:
Mahmoud and co-authors review methods for finding structural variants, in Genome Biology.
