Structural variants are large changes in DNA, from chunks deleted or duplicated to whole segments flipped or moved. They shape disease risk, gene control, and the differences between peoples and species. Finding them reliably, though, remains hard.

Different techniques catch different slices of the problem. Short reads spot small events but blur large ones; long reads reach further at higher cost. The review sorts approaches by variant class, size range, and whether one or both gene copies carry the change. It covers combined methods that merge several signal types. The goal is a practical guide for designing a study.
europmc-pmc6908718:
Johnson and co-authors describe a public chest X-ray database, in Scientific Data. Chest radiographs are powerful but take specialist training to read well. Computer vision systems could help, if they have enough examples to learn from. MIMIC-CXR answers that need. It gathers imaging studies from the emergency department of Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center between 2011 and 2016.

The release holds 227,835 studies from 65,379 patients, totalling 377,110 images. Each study carries the radiologist's free-text report, lightly structured. All identifying details were stripped, and thousands of images were hand-checked to confirm nothing private remained. The authors intend the set as shared ground for training and testing reading algorithms.
europmc-pmc6939418:
Kim and co-authors review a cancer strategy that floods tumour cells with reactive oxygen. Their review appeared in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. Healthy redox balance keeps cells working properly. Cancer cells carry higher levels of reactive oxygen species, called ROS, yet survive through strong antioxidant defences.

Therapies that push ROS higher, or block those defences, can break that balance. The overload then damages cancer cells severely. The authors examine several pro-oxidant drugs, including cisplatin, doxorubicin, and imexon. Using pathway analysis and large-scale text mining, they map how each drug interacts with genes, cell processes, and disease. They also note side effects. Genetic studies, they argue, are still needed to sharpen selective killing.
europmc-pmc6957118:
Tsai and co-authors argue that stigma is a core obstacle in the United States opioid overdose crisis. Their article appeared in PLoS Medicine. The crisis is a complex public health emergency needing proven prevention and treatment at every level. Yet responses keep falling short.

The authors sort stigma into linked forms. Public stigma grows from stereotypes casting people with opioid use disorders as dangerous or morally weak. Enacted stigma shows up as discrimination and social distancing. Together they degrade care and block access to treatment and harm reduction. When written into laws and policies, stigma turns structural. People may also internalize it, or fear it, and pull away from care. Each form feeds the others, the authors argue, and all must be tackled.
europmc-pmc6978318:
Brennan and co-authors compare ways to fish tiny vesicles out of human blood serum. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. Cells release nano-sized extracellular vesicles carrying proteins and nucleic acids. Those parcels excite interest as disease markers in blood. Serum, though, is crowded with plain proteins and fat particles that contaminate any catch.

Using 200 microlitres of serum, the team tested common isolation methods alone and combined. They tracked particle size and count, how cleanly protein was removed, and how much lipoprotein came along, judged by marker proteins APOB and APOE. Method choice strongly changed both yield and purity. No single recipe won on every measure. The study gives researchers a practical map for picking a method that matches their goal.
europmc-pmc7029418:
The India State-Level Disease Burden Initiative Mental Disorders Collaborators report mental disorder burden across India in The Lancet Psychiatry. Mental disorders rank among the leading causes of non-fatal disease burden in the country. Yet state-by-state figures on prevalence and impact were not readily available. The collaborators filled that gap for the years 1990 to 2017.

Drawing on all accessible data sources within the Global Burden of Disease Study, they estimated prevalence, years lived with disability, and disability-adjusted life-years for each state. In 2017, 197.3 million people in India had mental disorders. That total included 45.7 million with depressive disorders and 44.9 million with anxiety disorders. Patterns differed widely between states, and state-level depression prevalence correlated modestly with suicide death rates.
europmc-pmc7045518:
Fu and co-authors build a data platform for immunotherapy research in Genome Medicine. Immune checkpoint blockade trials now produce large amounts of molecular data, yet judging which biomarkers truly predict response stays hard. Single studies are small, and reported markers perform unevenly across cohorts. The authors answer by reusing public data at scale.

Their web platform, TIDE, integrates omics data for over 33K samples in 188 tumour cohorts. It adds 998 tumours from 12 checkpoint blockade studies, and eight CRISPR screens that found genes shaping the anticancer immune response. Three interactive modules let users test hypotheses, refine biomarkers, and stratify patients. Scores on the platform capture T cell dysfunction and T cell exclusion, two routes of immune escape. The study shows how pooled public data can firm up conclusions that no single trial could support alone.
europmc-pmc7095418:
Zhou and co-authors identify the new coronavirus behind the Wuhan pneumonia outbreak and trace its likely bat origin, in Nature. The outbreak began on 12 December 2019 and had caused 2,794 confirmed infections, including 80 deaths, by 26 January 2020. The team sequenced full genomes of the virus from five early patients.

The five sequences were almost identical and shared 79.6% of their sequence with SARS-CoV. Across the whole genome, the new virus matched a bat coronavirus at 96%. Virus taken from a critically ill patient could be neutralised by blood serum from several patients. The team confirmed the virus enters cells through ACE2, the same door SARS-CoV used.
europmc-pmc7125218:
Janelidze and co-authors test a spinal fluid marker, p-tau217, against the established p-tau181 for diagnosing Alzheimer's disease, in Nature Communications. Both markers are forms of the tau protein altered at specific sites. The main study used the Swedish BioFINDER cohort of 194 people.

P-tau217 tracked tau brain scans more closely than p-tau181 and spotted abnormal scan results more accurately. Its yearly rise was also larger and matched amyloid burden better in both fluid and scans. It separated Alzheimer's dementia from other brain diseases more cleanly. Results held in a second cohort of 32 people and with a different test kit, suggesting p-tau217 could sharpen diagnosis.
europmc-pmc7140518:
Law, Valdes-Mora, and Gallego-Ortega review myeloid-derived suppressor cells as a cancer treatment target, in Cells. These immature immune cells accumulate in cancer and shut down T cells and natural killer cells. That suppression helps tumors grow, prepares sites for spread, and blunts immunotherapy.

Checkpoint inhibitor drugs have transformed some cancers, yet many patients gain little, and suppressor cells are one reason why. The review describes how these cells are identified, how they expand, and what they do. Current ways to attack them are surveyed, alone and combined with checkpoint therapy. Removing their brake on immunity, the authors argue, could raise the share of patients who benefit from immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc7144318:
Nie and co-authors establish and validate a safe test for measuring antibodies that neutralise SARS-CoV-2, in Emerging Microbes and Infections. Real virus work demands biosafety level 3 labs, which slows vaccine and drug development. Their assay instead uses a harmless pseudovirus dressed in the coronavirus spike, safe at level 2.

Blood serum from recovered COVID-19 patients showed strong neutralising power in the assay. Detection limits were set using 120 negative samples, with cutoff values of 30 for human and 50 for mouse serum. Repeat testing varied by about 16%, which the authors judge acceptable. They offer to share the pseudovirus and protocols with vaccine and therapy developers.
europmc-pmc7145518:
Haug and co-authors describe how MetaboLights, the public archive for metabolomics studies, has evolved with its community, in Nucleic Acids Research. The database stores raw data and descriptions from studies of small molecules in cells, tissues, and body fluids, across species and techniques. Leading journals and the ELIXIR infrastructure recommend it for data deposition.

Over two years the team refreshed the website and rebuilt the submission process to be far more user-friendly. The changes respond to rising submission volume and diversity, and to demands for reproducibility and linking with other omics data. Metabolite structures, reference spectra, and biological roles sit alongside the study data in one resource.
europmc-pmc7164518:
Zhang and co-authors determine the crystal structure of the SARS-CoV-2 main protease and improve a drug that blocks it, in Science. The protease cuts long viral polyproteins into working pieces, making it one of the best-characterised drug targets among coronaviruses. Without it, the virus cannot assemble its machinery.

They solved the enzyme's structure by X-ray crystallography and refined an alpha-ketoamide inhibitor into a potent lead compound. Structures of the inhibitor bound to the protease, at 1.95 and 2.20 angstrom resolution, show exactly how it grips the active site. The work lays a concrete basis for developing anticoronavirus drugs aimed at this enzyme.
europmc-pmc7221918:
Kerru and co-authors review recent advances in nitrogen-containing molecules and their medical uses. Their article appeared in Molecules. Ring structures holding nitrogen atoms sit inside a huge share of medicines. More than 75 percent of FDA-approved drugs on the market contain such rings. Chemists keep designing new ones with fresh biological effects.

The review gathers advances reported over the past year. New compounds target enzymes, cancer pathways, and liver scarring, among other goals. One highlighted compound blocked a growth signal and calmed activated liver cells in tests. Small changes to a ring's attachments could strengthen or kill its activity. The authors organize the flood of new structures by their effects. Medicinal chemists gain a compact survey of a very active field.
europmc-pmc7239918:
Smith and co-authors report on INO-4800, a synthetic DNA vaccine candidate against COVID-19. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. No vaccine existed yet to halt the pandemic. The team had earlier built a DNA vaccine against the MERS coronavirus spike. That construct was already in clinical testing. They adapted the same platform to the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.

The engineered DNA produced the spike protein strongly in lab cells. Mice and guinea pigs were then immunized with it. Both species mounted antigen-specific T cell responses. Antibodies against the spike were measured as well. DNA vaccines can be designed and made quickly, the authors argue. The results supported moving INO-4800 toward human trials. The study is an early record of the vaccine race.
europmc-pmc7284818:
Zabetakis and co-authors argue that COVID-19 hits hardest where the body is already inflamed, and that food and daily habits play a part. Their review looks at people with poor diet and long-term ills such as diabetes, lung disease, heart disease, and obesity. All of these states share a low, steady level of inflammation.

The team goes over drugs now in tests that aim to calm the cytokine storm of severe cases. They then turn to diet and way of life, which shape how well the immune system works. They name food groups and key nutrients that may help patients. Their point is plain: good food is a cheap aid that health plans should use next to hygiene, distance, and medical care.
europmc-pmc7285218:
Magne and co-authors question a popular claim: that the ratio of two bacterial groups in the gut marks obesity. Their review appeared in Nutrients. Several studies had reported a higher Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes ratio in obese animals and humans, and the ratio became a frequently cited hallmark of obesity and gut imbalance.

Lining up the literature, the authors find contradictory results too often for the marker to hold. Differences in how samples are processed and DNA is analyzed can bias results. Studies also describe their subjects poorly, ignoring lifestyle factors known to shape gut microbes. Their verdict is cautious: the ratio cannot currently be tied to a clear health status, let alone serve as a signature of obesity.
europmc-pmc7289118:
Wolff and co-authors review double-membrane vesicles, the compartments many viruses build inside infected cells to copy their genomes. Their review appeared in Trends in Microbiology. Positive-sense RNA viruses remodel the cell's internal membranes into protected workshops for replication. Coronaviruses, enteroviruses, noroviruses, and hepatitis C virus all form these double-walled bubbles.

Fifteen years of better imaging and molecular tools have clarified how the vesicles form, what they look like, and how they serve the virus. They concentrate the replication machinery and may hide viral RNA from the cell's immune sensors. Open questions remain about how host membranes are reshaped and how the vesicles connect with the rest of the cell. The review sums up the current picture for a structure central to many infections.
europmc-pmc7311918:
Barnes and co-authors solve the structures of human antibodies bound to the SARS-CoV-2 spike, revealing shared weak points. Their study appeared in Cell. Neutralizing antibodies mostly aim at the spike's receptor binding domain. The team studied blood antibodies from recovered COVID-19 patients, both whole antibodies and their binding fragments.

Different patients' antibodies focused on different sites, and some recognized both alpha- and beta-coronaviruses. Electron microscopy revealed attacks on two spike regions. A 3.4 angstrom structure showed one neutralizing antibody blocking the ACE2 binding site directly. Many of the best antibodies came from one recurring gene family, also seen against the earlier SARS virus. That recurrence gives vaccine makers criteria for judging whether a vaccine raises the right kind of antibody.
europmc-pmc7314918:
McMaughan, Oloruntoba and Smith review how income and access to care together shape healthy aging. Their mini-review appeared in Frontiers in Public Health. The world's older population is growing fast, and older age too often arrives with lower socioeconomic status, poorer access to care, and worse health. Evidence links each step of that chain to the next.

The authors present a framework centered on socioeconomic status, plus intervention examples from around the globe. Because money buys flexibility, drugs, transport, and time, supporting older adults' finances may be the most effective lever. They recommend grassroots programs that raise older people's resources, paired with data-driven policy and system change, rather than expecting individuals to overcome structural barriers alone.
europmc-pmc7397618:
Wang and co-authors review dendritic cell biology and cancer immunotherapy in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. Dendritic cells are the immune system's chief presenters, showing captured material to T cells to launch attacks. That makes them natural tools and targets for tumor treatment.

The review explains how these cells grab antigens through several routes, cut them into peptides, and display them to CD4 and CD8 T cells. Newer findings include dendritic cell exosomes joining presentation, hyperactive cells that turn effectors into memory cells, and cross-talk with natural killer cells. Inside tumors, the cells act as sentinels of surveillance. The authors then survey dendritic cell therapies in preclinical and clinical work. Readers get a full picture of a pivotal cell.
europmc-pmc7438418:
Hofmanninger and co-authors test what makes lung outlining on CT scans work well. Outlining the lungs is a basic step in scan analysis. Many methods exist, but they often fail on scans with varied diseases.

The team compared four deep learning methods and two ready-made tools. Method choice changed scores very little. Training data mattered far more. A standard U-net trained on a diverse routine set of 231 scans reached a Dice score of 0.98. That beat training on public sets with fewer disease types. The authors argue the core problem is data diversity, not model design. They release their trained model for free public use.
europmc-pmc7489918:
Hartenian and co-authors review the molecular virology of coronaviruses, with SARS-CoV-2 at the center. The virus drew intense global focus after its spillover into humans. It followed SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV, two other severe spillovers.

The review walks through the viral life cycle step by step. Entry into cells comes first, then the virus's complex gene expression and copying systems. The virus reshapes the inside of the host cell to suit itself. It also deploys many tricks to evade immune attack. The authors flag steps that antiviral drugs could strike. Other parts of the cycle still await discovery, they note. Firm grasp of this biology underlies vaccines and treatments now in use or in design.
europmc-pmc7553118:
Pellegrini and co-authors show SARS-CoV-2 infects the choroid plexus in brain organoids. COVID-19 can cause neurological symptoms in some patients. The cause of those symptoms was unknown.

The team used brain organoids grown from human stem cells. The viral receptor ACE2 appeared in mature choroid plexus cells. It did not appear in neurons or other cell types. Live virus infected choroid plexus epithelial cells. Neurons and glia showed little or no infection. Infection damaged the epithelial barrier in organoids. That damage caused leakage across the blood-CSF barrier. The results offer one route for brain effects in COVID-19.
europmc-pmc7643118:
Nguyen, Martens, Van Hoeck and Cuppen map homologous recombination deficiency across cancers. This fault impairs repair of double-strand DNA breaks. It is a frequent driver of tumor growth in patients.

The team built a classifier called CHORD from mutation scars. It can split BRCA1-type from BRCA2-type deficiency. A metastatic cohort held 3,504 patients for analysis. A primary tumor cohort held 1,854 patients as well. Deficiency was most frequent in ovarian and breast cancer. Pancreatic and prostate cancers followed in frequency. Two-copy loss of BRCA1, BRCA2, RAD51C or PALB2 caused most cases. Such testing may guide use of PARP inhibitor drugs. Cancer type shaped which gene fault lay behind the deficiency.
europmc-pmc7698618:
Hasanuzzaman and co-authors review how plants handle reactive oxygen under stress. Stresses such as drought and heat make plants produce excess reactive oxygen species. These molecules can damage DNA, proteins, and the machinery of photosynthesis. In small doses, though, they act as useful signals.

Plants run an antioxidant defense system to keep these molecules in balance. It mops up the excess and tunes levels for signaling. The review sets out where in the cell each type is made and how it harms or helps. It sums up recent tests and ways to boost plant defenses for stress tolerance.
europmc-pmc7812418:
Wurtzer and co-authors track SARS-CoV-2 in Paris wastewater to judge the lockdown effect. Infected people shed virus RNA in stool. Sewage levels can thus mirror virus spread in a city. The team sampled major treatment plants in Greater Paris. The study ran from March 5 to April 23, 2020.

Genome counts in raw sewage matched the rise in human cases. Virus was found before the epidemic peaked around March 8. France entered lockdown on March 17. Counts fell in step with new cases after that. The drop came 29 days after lockdown began. The authors argue sewage testing adds real value to outbreak tracking.
europmc-pmc7894518:
Hohenlohe and co-authors present a review of population genomics for wildlife conservation. Species face rising threats across the world. Over the past decade, genome tools have spread to animals and plants that are not standard lab species. The review asks how those tools can guide real conservation work.

Genome data give sharp estimates of traits that matter for survival. These include effective population size, inbreeding, and population structure. Studies can also find the exact variants behind inbreeding problems or adaptation to new conditions. That knowledge helps managers judge whether a population can adapt on its own. The authors give examples of genomics already shaping management choices. They close with advice on turning research findings into action faster and more often.
europmc-pmc7963218:
Bubar and co-authors present a modelling study of how to share scarce COVID-19 vaccine by age and prior infection. Demand for the first vaccine supplies far outran the stock. The team modelled sharing plans across countries. They varied what the vaccine can do: cut disease, block spread, or both. Age patterns in risk and in fading immunity were built into the model.

In almost all settings, cutting deaths meant giving vaccine first to those most at risk of death. That usually meant people over 60 and those with other illnesses. A weak vaccine in older adults could flip the choice toward younger groups. Doses could stretch further by favouring people with no prior infection. The study gives planners a way to match the plan to the vaccine they actually get.
europmc-pmc8033518:
Hammond and co-authors survey the delivery problem facing oligonucleotide-based therapeutics. These drugs steer gene expression, and development has sped up sharply. Eleven products built on antisense oligonucleotides, aptamers, or small interfering RNAs are already marketed. Better chemistry has improved drug properties and cut costs. But getting the molecules into target tissues remains the main hurdle.

The review covers the methods built to cross biological barriers. Conjugates and nanoparticles have changed the game for several diseases. Other targets still await their breakthrough delivery route. The authors describe the model systems used to test new carriers. Safety questions and regulatory demands on synthetic chemistries follow. The closing gap is translation: turning lab success into clinic-ready drugs.
europmc-pmc8047518:
Beck and co-authors review mRNA therapeutics in cancer immunotherapy. Synthetic mRNA can template any protein or peptide a designer chooses. Production scales fast under good manufacturing practice. That suits both shelf-ready cancer vaccines and personal neoantigen vaccines. The molecule also wakes innate immune sensors, acting as its own adjuvant.

The review covers how chemistry tunes that behavior. Nucleoside changes and cleanup of double-stranded RNA calm unwanted immune noise. Protein output then lasts longer. Nanoparticle carriers lift delivery into cells and toward lymph nodes. With them, mRNA can deliver cytokines, costimulatory receptors, or antibodies. Steady, brief production may beat recombinant proteins on safety. Even CAR-T cell therapy can borrow the trick. The authors close with the shifting clinical landscape.
europmc-pmc8080618:
Rungratanawanich and co-authors review advanced glycation end products and their kin in aging and alcohol injury. These products form when sugars bond to proteins, lipids, or DNA without enzymes. They gather in the body with age and stoke oxidative stress. Through their receptor, RAGE, they spark inflammation and cell death. Alcohol abuse, tied to more than 200 diseases, adds its own adducts to the pile.

The review first explains how glycation products form and build up. It then follows them through the diseases of aging. Diabetes, heart and vessel trouble, liver disease, and brain decay all feature. Gut-linked illness and cancer join the list. A special thread ties alcohol's breakdown products to the same chemistry. Drink and sugar damage, the authors show, converge on shared adducts. Treatment ideas drawn from that overlap close the survey.
europmc-pmc8122718:
Sawicki and co-authors review colorectal cancer from global spread to bedside diagnosis. The disease ranks among the commonest cancers on earth. By site and sex, it sits between second and fourth in incidence. It stands third in new cases and second in cancer deaths overall. Both counts climb year by year. Deaths from rectal and colon cancer are projected to jump sharply by 2035.

Genes load part of the risk, family history included. Lifestyle loads much of the rest, and that part can change. Inactivity, obesity, smoking, and alcohol all raise the odds. Red and processed meat add dietary risk. Movement, by contrast, protects with convincing evidence. The review orders the symptoms and stages in plain sequence. It then surveys current tests and coming ones. Population prevention anchors their closing plea. A cancer tied to development can be fought with development's tools: screening, habits, and early care.
europmc-pmc8155318:
Sebastiani and co-authors study how apolipoprotein E reshapes mRNA lipid nanoparticles. These particles carry mRNA that tells cells to make a protein. Their fate in blood depends in part on proteins that bind them.

Apolipoprotein E handles fat transport and binds these particles in the body. The team measured how its binding changed particle structure and makeup. Such changes can steer where particles go and which cells take them up. The work uses detailed structural methods on the particle mix. It helps explain why particle design affects delivery success. The findings bear on how such particles reach target cells.
europmc-pmc8305018:
Mosaddeghzadeh and Ahmadian explain how RHO family GTPases are regulated and signal. These switch proteins steer cell shape, movement, and growth. Faulty signalling through them recurs in human cancers.

About 20 canonical RHO GTPases sit at the centre. Three GDIs, 85 GEFs, and 66 GAPs control them. Over 70 downstream effectors carry their messages onward. All these partners bind shared sites on the GTPase surface. The review asks how specificity arises from that crowding. Structural hotspots that decide partner choice are mapped. The puzzle matters for drug design. Verified hotspots give that puzzle concrete footholds.
europmc-pmc8369118:
Churruca and co-authors survey patient-reported outcome measures, or PROMs. These are questionnaires that collect health outcomes straight from the people who live with them. The review covers both general measures and measures built for set conditions. It also tracks trends and current problems in the field.

The search found 315 generic and condition-specific PROMs. The largest groups covered general health, muscle and joint conditions, and cancers. The first PROMs dealt with mental health. Growth in new measures was strong from the 1980s to the 2000s, then slowed. The authors warn that tools built for one purpose are now often used for others. Picking a valid, fit-for-purpose tool stays hard.
europmc-pmc8479118:
Squair and co-authors confront false discoveries in single-cell gene expression analysis. Such tests reveal how cell types answer disease, injury, or lab treatments. Many statistical methods exist, but their real performance was unclear.

The team shows that success hinges on handling variation between biological replicates. Methods that ignore that variation are biased and spark false hits. The most used methods can report hundreds of changed genes where no true difference exists. A case from injured mouse spinal cord makes the point concrete. True and false finds are set side by side. The authors give clear rules for safer analysis.
europmc-pmc8509318:
Korbecki and co-authors review how low oxygen in tumors drives chronic inflammation. Tumors face two kinds of oxygen lack: steady chronic hypoxia and on-off cycling hypoxia. Both switch on two master factors, HIF-1 and NF-kappaB. Those factors then rewrite gene activity.

The review details how each factor wakes under both hypoxia types. It traces their crosstalk with each other. Reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, nitric oxide, and MAPK cascades all play parts. Cycling hypoxia also reshapes the tumor setting. It boosts vessel growth signals and calls in neutrophils and monocytes. The paper links these steps to a lasting low-grade inflammation in cancer.
europmc-pmc8674418:
Cao and co-authors review hydrogels designed to steer cell behavior for medical use. A hydrogel's traits, such as stiffness and pore size, can be tuned by design. Those traits send signals that shape cell fate. Decades of work have mapped how cells read these gels.

The review first sums up gel traits and how gels are made. It then traces how each trait changes cell acts. Topics span cell grip, skeleton shifts, and gene activity. Cell spread, movement, growth, and cell type choice all respond. The authors aim to guide the move from lab gels to clinic use. Their account links gel design to cell signals step by step.
europmc-pmc8891018:
Ma and co-authors find the direct target that lets low-dose metformin switch on a key energy pathway. Metformin is the most prescribed diabetes drug. It also shows anti-aging and anticancer hints. Its benefits run largely through AMPK, a master energy sensor. How the drug reaches AMPK was unknown. The team built a light-activated metformin probe. The probe caught a binding partner: PEN2, part of the γ-secretase complex.

Bound PEN2 teams with a lysosomal pump subunit, ATP6AP1. That pairing throttles the pump and wakes AMPK. It does so without changing cell energy levels. Removing PEN2 in mouse liver erased metformin's fat-cutting effect. Removing it in the gut blunted glucose lowering. Worms lacking the gene lost the lifespan benefit. The study gives metformin a clean molecular address.
europmc-pmc8982018:
Davis and co-authors update WormBase, the central data home for the worm Caenorhabditis elegans, in 2022. The worm is a workhorse model for human health and development. WormBase curates its genetics and genomics for the world. The resource is 22 years old. It grows new data types as the science moves. This paper surveys the current state. Data types, curation workflows, and analysis tools all feature.

Manual curation anchors the knowledge base. Semi-automatic pipelines add scale. New advances cover single-cell data handling. Text mining and visualization also improved. A community collaboration forum is new. WormBase is a founding member of a wider alliance. That alliance harmonizes model organism databases. Shared infrastructure is the long game. The authors stress open access throughout. Releases come every two months.
europmc-pmc9021018:
Iketani and co-authors tested how well antibodies hold up against BA.2 and a sister Omicron sublineage with an extra spike change. Sera from infected patients and mRNA vaccine recipients lost much of their neutralizing power against both. The drop matched the loss already seen for the original Omicron form. The authors conclude that all three sublineages sit far from the early virus in antibody terms.

That newer form also resisted 17 of the 19 monoclonal antibodies tested, including sotrovimab. Only the newly cleared bebtelovimab covered every sublineage. The results warn that current vaccines and antibody drugs face a moving target as Omicron keeps evolving.
europmc-pmc9066118:
Zhang and co-authors review how tumor heterogeneity, the diversity inside and between tumors, drives drug resistance. Diverse cell populations either alter drug targets directly or reshape the tumor surroundings. As tumors grow, mutation and selection keep reprogramming that environment in space and time. New profiling tools now let researchers watch this process in detail.

The review traces how heterogeneity affects treatment of every kind, including immunotherapy. It closes with strategies meant to beat resistance, from combination drugs to adaptive schedules. The authors frame heterogeneity as the central problem that cancer therapy must outwit.
europmc-pmc9143318:
Noor and co-authors review network pharmacology as an approach for studying medicinal plants. Plant remedies hold many active compounds that act on many targets at once. Single-target study methods miss that complexity. Network methods instead map compounds to the gene and protein webs they affect.

The review sums up active ingredients, tools, databases, and techniques used in this work. It shows how the approach serves drug discovery and development. Worked uses show how a plant's full range of effects can be probed at once. The authors hope the review will serve as a protocol for finding new compounds. Researchers get a guide to a systems method matched to traditional medicines.
europmc-pmc9311318:
Mahmud and co-authors review the gut-skin axis, the two-way link between gut microbes and skin health. Gut and skin both host rich microbe communities and immune tissue. When gut balance breaks, effects can surface on the skin. The routes of this influence are still being worked out.

The review covers microbe ecology in healthy gut and skin. Diet, prebiotics, probiotics, and antibiotics are weighed for their effects. Disease links include psoriasis, eczema, acne, rosacea, and hair loss conditions. Gut microbes may sway skin by shaping T cell choices and by their chemical products. The authors hope the map points to new skin treatments. They call for trials that test gut-targeted care for skin disease.
europmc-pmc9328018:
Bae and co-authors identify the exact molecule behind many health effects of the gut bacterium Akkermansia muciniphila. The microbe is linked to better metabolism and better cancer immunotherapy results. The active agent turned out to be a fat from its cell membrane. The team isolated it and rebuilt it by chemical synthesis to confirm the match.

The lipid signals through a TLR2-TLR1 receptor pair, an unexpected route. Its action is weaker than classic triggers of that receptor. It raises some inflammatory signals but not others. At very low doses it resets how immune cells respond later. The authors say this tuning sets the immune tone of the gut. That may explain the bacterium's wide links to health and disease. A synthetic copy works just as well.
europmc-pmc9329718:
Gómez-Virgilio and co-authors overview autophagy, the cell's self-eating recycling system, and its roles in health and disease. The pathway runs at low levels in all cells and ramps up under stress. It clears damaged organelles and clumped proteins, and frees building blocks during starvation. Neurons lean on it heavily since they cannot divide to dilute waste.

The review explains the pathway types, the molecular machinery, and what switches it on. Over 32 related ATG proteins help run the process. Its roles in development and tissue balance are covered next. Failure of the system is tied to liver, heart, brain, and cancer diseases. Links to COVID-19 are also noted. Modulator drugs that tune the pathway close the survey.
europmc-pmc9433318:
Karthikeyan and co-authors report a wastewater sequencing study that caught SARS-CoV-2 variants early. Clinical testing misses much spread and skews toward who gets tested. Virus RNA in wastewater tracks a whole community with less bias. Reading variant shares from mixed sewage samples was the hard part.

The team ran a 295-day sequencing effort on a large campus and its county. They built better virus concentration steps and new deconvolution software. The software splits mixed samples into single strain shares. Variants of concern showed up in wastewater up to 14 days before clinical finds. Some spread events never appeared in clinical data at all. The authors offer the method as a scalable watch system.
europmc-pmc9636018:
Markello and co-authors introduce neuromaps, a toolbox for reading structural and functional brain maps. Imaging now yields fine reference maps of brain form and work. Comparing new maps with these references can spark fresh finds. Maps are shared in mismatched coordinate systems, though. That spread blocks clean and fair comparison across studies.

Neuromaps gathers open brain maps into one shared home. It converts maps among four standard coordinate systems with care. Its library spans molecular and cell scale maps. Growth and function maps of the human brain sit beside them. Map similarity can be tested with proper statistics. Null models in the toolbox keep spatial patterns intact during tests. The authors show the full workflow on sample maps. They pitch the tool as a standard route for brain map work.
europmc-pmc9733018:
Fu, Xie, Wang, and Fu review treatment options once osimertinib stops working in lung cancer. Osimertinib is the standard first drug for EGFR-mutant lung cancer. It blocks the growth signal that drives those tumors. Tumors learn to dodge it in time, as with earlier drugs.

The review first traces three drug generations against EGFR. It then sorts the known routes of escape from osimertinib. Some routes run through new EGFR changes in the tumor. Others bypass EGFR through side paths like MET growth. Tumors can also switch cell type to survive the drug. For each route the authors weigh matching treatments. Older drugs, drug pairs, and new blocker designs all appear. Antibody pairs get a place in the survey too. The goal is longer survival through precise matching. The review frames resistance care as a sorting task.
europmc-pmc9771818:
Saunders and co-authors harness global genetic variety to find genes behind tobacco and alcohol use. Both habits are inherited in part and kill millions yearly. Past genome scans leaned hard on European ancestry samples. That narrow base left much of the world unmapped.

The study pooled 3,383,199 people from 60 cohorts worldwide. About a fifth of the sample had non-European roots. Bigger, broader samples sharpened both finding and fine mapping. The scan tied 3,823 variants across 2,143 loci to the habits. Most effects held steady across ancestry lines in size. Risk scores built in one ancestry still failed in others. The authors say diverse samples must keep growing. Only then can gene based risk tools serve everyone fairly.
europmc-pmc9935618:
Wang and co-authors examine epigenetic regulators as targets to beat drug resistance in cancer. Drug resistance drives most cancer recurrence and poor outcomes. Epigenetic change alters gene activity without changing the DNA code. Faulty epigenetic control helps tumors resist treatment.

The review sums up roles for DNA methylation, histone change, and non-coding RNA. It then details histone demethylase families in depth. These include lysine-specific, Jumonji C-domain, and arginine demethylases. Each family's control routes and links to resistance are covered. Treatment tactics include small-molecule blockers and small interfering RNA. The authors argue that hitting these regulators can restore drug response. Readers get a structured guide to a growing target class.
fbi-vault-rosenberg-case-william-perl-pa: Part 18 of the William Perl file, inside the Federal Bureau of Investigation record of the Julius and Ethel Rosenberg case, is an exhibit list. Its cover names the New York bulky exhibit files in the case of Julius Rosenberg and others. Page by page, the sheets log each exhibit and mark it released, denied, or withheld. The body, in the text layer, is too broken to read past those heads. This part holds no testimony a reader can use. It is the case's paper store, counted and marked.
foods-that-will-win-the-war-and-how-to-c:
Goudiss and his wife Alberta wrote this wartime cookbook around the Food Administration's saving rules. Save wheat and use more corn, save meat with fish and beans, go easy on fats, and swap sugar for syrups. The rules frame hundreds of recipes meant to keep a family fed under them.

The sweet section shows the substitutions at work. Peanut brittle is made with corn syrup instead of sugar, and popcorn balls likewise. A raisin and peanut loaf, chopped and moistened with molasses, is chilled and sliced as candy. C. Houston Goudiss brought a food expert's name to the book; the copyright is 1918, and the cause named on the poster pages is freedom.
frankenstein-1818:
Mary Shelley wrote this novel at the age of twenty, and it came out with no name on it in 1818. The first print ran in three parts, the form books took in that age. Its full title adds the words 'The Modern Prometheus' to the name Frankenstein.

Victor Frankenstein, a young man of science, builds a man from dead parts and gives it life. The being, left alone and spurned, turns to rage and grief and asks why it was made at all. The book is the first true work of science fiction, and its theme still haunts us.
freud-totem-taboo-brill-1918:
Sigmund Freud published Totem and Taboo in German in 1913. The English text here is A. A. Brill's translation of 1918. Freud brings psychoanalysis to anthropology, the study of early peoples. He compares taboos and totem rites with the fears of his neurotic patients.

His boldest claim tells of a primal horde whose sons killed and ate their father. Guilt from that deed, he argues, founded morality, religion, and social rules. Scholars of anthropology have largely rejected the story as history. As a myth of origins, it shaped much debate on culture. The book remains a daring, disputed classic of its field.
frus-1861-d118:
On 20 September 1861, William H. Seward wrote to John Lothrop Motley at his Austrian post. The letter is document 118 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Vienna took a strict view of rebellion and a cool view of the Union. Motley had to argue the Union's case in that chill air. Seward's September letter kept his historian envoy armed with the line from home. His envoy's pen was as fine as his historian's, and his letters were prized at home. Prized letters were read aloud in the cabinet more than once that year.
frus-1861-d18:
On 10 October 1861, Norman Judd sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 18 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Autumn brought no end to the war, and Europe began to plan for a long divide. Judd's October report kept Washington aware of Prussian views at that turn. Such steady reporting, dull as it may seem, was the means by which the Union held its ground abroad. Prussian goodwill, though quiet, denied the South a friend in the north of Europe. Quiet goodwill in the north kept one more door shut in the face of the South.
frus-1861-d218:
Seward wrote again on 30 July 1861, this time to Mr. Marsh. It was printed as Document 218 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d118:
One more Washington letter went abroad on 2 August 1862, addressed to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 118 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d18:
Seward wrote again on 13 February 1862, this time to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 18 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d218:
On 23 June 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Stuart, the acting head of the British legation in Washington. In a letter printed as Document 218 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Stuart, a legation secretary standing in for Lord Lyons, had to manage protests and questions his chief would normally carry. Seward wrote to him in the same brisk style he used with Lyons. Letters from late June belong to the opening of the Seven Days battles near Richmond, which soon tested foreign faith in a Union victory. Lyons also reported home on each note, so most of these papers exist in two archives.
frus-1862-d318:
Filed late in the sequence, Document 318 is a Dayton report dated 4 August 1862, sent from Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The printers grouped it with later papers in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Dayton wrote this report the same day as two others in the file, so August's Paris business arrived in Washington in a thick packet. The report belongs to the summer of French pressure for joint action on the war. Its late placement is a filing artifact; its content week is early August. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d418:
On 15 April 1862 Horace J. Perry dispatched a report from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It appears as Document 418 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

Perry served as secretary of the Madrid legation and often as its acting head, so his reports carried real weight in Washington. That spring he wrote while Spain weighed its next step in Mexico and while Shiloh's heavy cost was still news in Europe. His account of Spanish thinking helped Seward decide where to press and where to wait. That judgment served the broad effort to keep foreign powers out of the American war.
frus-1862-d518:
On 15 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. It is Document 518 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Two days before Antietam, Seward was writing to nearly every post in Europe, The Hague included, to set the line his ministers should hold. The Dutch questions remained the practical ones of ports, trade, and neutrality, but the week's real subject was resolve. A government that expected to win said so in advance, in writing, to all its agents. The instruction is a good example of Seward's preventive diplomacy: settle the story before events can be twisted by the other side.
frus-1862-d618:
On 25 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Bradford R. Wood in Copenhagen. The instruction is Document 618 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the Danish file's autumn paper.

Seward wrote eight days after Antietam and three days after the emancipation order, in the week he was informing every post in Europe of both. Denmark heard the news from Wood in due course, with Washington's reading of it. A five-month gap in the printed Danish file before this letter shows the post's quiet. The autumn order shows it being gathered back into the general effort. After September, no European court, however small, was left outside the emancipation story.
frus-1862-d718:
On 13 October 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Luis Molina, Costa Rica's envoy in Washington. The letter is document 718 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. It closes the two men's exchange in the volume.

A closing letter in a run like this one often sums up where the business stands. Seward's note ends a month of brisk letters between Washington and the Costa Rican legation. The file is a neat case of how foreign ties were kept. They were kept not by grand acts, but by short letters, sent on time, by men who knew each other's names. That is the record this volume keeps.
frus-1863p1-d118:
Washington's answer to the mid-March mail came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, dated 14 March 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 118 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, answering the Adams mail of mid-March.

Seward's answers did the steering in this exchange. They told Adams which of his reports had hit home and what line to take next with the British. This letter is a lone sheet between clusters, the kind that kept the loop tight. It shows the secretary at his steady work, one steamer behind the news and one ahead of the talks.
frus-1863p1-d18:
On 21 December 1862, William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 18 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Two letters to Adams in two days close Seward's year in the printed file.

Back-to-back sheets let the secretary add a point the last mail had missed. Seward used them to keep Adams stocked with the government's views as the war and the talks in Europe both moved. This letter is the second of the pair. With its mate, it shows the close hand Washington kept on its most key post at the turn of the year.
frus-1863p1-d218:
A dispatch dated 18 June 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 218 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d318:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 11 November 1862. The note is document 318 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For readers, the Stuart letters fill in the working level of the famous Lyons and Seward exchange. They show the legation's routine grind behind the headline crises. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d418:
Writing in Washington on 19 March 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 418 in the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Lyons knew that harsh words could push the two nations toward a fight neither wanted. His notes are firm on British rights but measured in tone. It dates from the spring when British debate over aiding the South was still live, and every note counted. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d518:
Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington sent an official note to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State on 18 May 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d618:
Document 618, dated 12 September 1863, records a letter from Britain's chargé d'affaires William Stuart to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Stuart was holding the British legation in Washington while Lord Lyons was away on leave, so the channel ran through him that season. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1918:
The 1918 annual volume opens with Wilson's address of December 2. The war is won; the files turn to settlement. Honduras and Nicaragua argue their boundary first. Nicaragua refuses the King of Spain's 1906 award. American good offices and commissioners follow. Argentina grants cable landing concessions to American firms. Brazil weighs cable rates and company rivalry.

China's political file runs long and troubled. Acting President Feng pursues conciliation. Northern troops loot in Hunan province. Sun Yat Sen resigns as southern generalissimo. Hsü Shih-ch'ang wins election as president. A June wire to Ecuador sets a hard deadline. All discussion must close by June 28, Lansing insists. The volume mixes victory with unfinished business. Borders and cables outlast the guns.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d118: Roosevelt wrote to Stalin on November 12, 1943, the day he sailed for the Mediterranean. The letter is Document 118 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A letter sent on sailing day was among the last the president could dispatch before radio silence at sea. The record gives the date and the two leaders' names. It is preserved in the Foreign Relations series, in the voyage sequence.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d18: Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek wrote to President Roosevelt on July 4, 1943, answering the president's letter of four days before. The exchange is Document 18 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. China's leader rarely let a week pass without reminding Washington of his front's needs. The catalog gives the date and the correspondents and no topic. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the run-up to Chiang's Cairo appearance.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d218:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt cabled Washington from Ankara on 14 November 1943 with a detailed account of Turkish foreign minister Numan Menemencioğlu's talks with Anthony Eden in Cairo. Marked most secret, it relays Numan's own summary, given the night before, plus his later talk with the British ambassador.

Numan's points run to eight. Turkey would rather discuss joining the war than mere air bases, since bases mean war anyway. Her army cannot attack, and without firm Allied air cover Istanbul and Izmir face ruin, railways would be wrecked, and hunger would follow. Eden named no Allied help and set a deadline of 3 December, far too soon. Yet Numan adds that Turkish hesitation would vanish if Anglo-American forces landed in the Balkans.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d318:
General John Hilldring, head of the War Department's Civil Affairs Division, sent a secret priority cable from Washington on 25 November 1943 to John McCloy at Cairo. Marked eyes only and signed Marshall, it reports the State Department's views after a conference with Secretary Hull and James Dunn.

On the Rankin C plan for a sudden German collapse, State has no preference between northern and southern zones for the United States. It does propose a joint British-American commission, answerable to the supreme commander, for French civil affairs, so every policy carries both nations' sanction. Hull also doubts the wisdom of separate spheres of responsibility at all, and wants firm declarations that no occupying power will take advantage from the zone its forces happen to hold.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d418:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent Secretary of State Hull a telegram from Moscow on 8 December 1943, number 2144, supplementing his report of 6 December. He had asked Molotov the night before how the Tass statement on the Tehran Conference came to be made.

Molotov explained two things. Reuters, from Lisbon, had predicted the meeting, and Senator Connally had announced it was going on. Tass could not ignore those reports, so it stated the truth to end rumors that were harming the allies' mutual interests. Harriman gives his own opinion plainly: the British and the Americans have more to explain to the Soviet government than the Soviets have to them. He therefore recommends that Washington not pursue the matter further with Moscow.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d518:
Clarence E. Gauss, the American ambassador in China, reported to Secretary of State Hull on December 14, 1943. Gauss served in Chungking, China's wartime capital. Weeks earlier, the Cairo Declaration had promised that lands taken by Japan would be returned to China. The State Department printed his report in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Gauss was a blunt reporter of China's troubles: inflation, military weakness, and friction between Chungking and Washington. His cables give the view from inside an ally whose strength the declarations praised but whose condition worried its friends. For readers, this report tests the fine words of Cairo against the facts as the man on the spot saw them.
frus-1944-quebec-d118:
From Caserta, Italy, on September 4, 1944, acting political adviser Carmel Offie telegraphed Washington a report from Polish commander General Sosnkowski. Sosnkowski had heard from General Bór, who led the Home Army inside Warsaw. The message reached the Allies through General Wilson, the Mediterranean commander, and it was grim.

Bór reported the Old Town lost and a serious breach in Warsaw's defenses. Food would last to September 7, bread only to September 5, and ammunition was running out. Sosnkowski appealed for large-scale air operations from Italian bases, with British crews taking part. Without material help fast, he warned, Polish endurance alone could not save the city.
frus-1944-quebec-d18:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on August 4, 1944, as the Allied breakout from Normandy gathered speed. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

August opened with the German front in France collapsing, Paris a month from liberation, and the Warsaw uprising beginning far to the east. Churchill's letters that month reached for the political meaning of the military triumph. For readers, this message belongs to the heady, dangerous weeks when the war's end came into sight and the leaders' correspondence turned increasingly to the Europe that victory would create.
frus-1944-quebec-d218:
C.C.S. 320/27, approved by the Combined Chiefs at Quebec on September 16, 1944, states the allocation of occupation zones in Germany in operational terms. British forces under a British commander would occupy Germany west of the Rhine. East of the river, they would hold the land north of a line from Koblenz. That line followed the northern border of Hessen-Nassau to the Soviet area.

American forces would occupy the land east of the Rhine south of that line. Control of Bremen and Bremerhaven, with their staging areas, was vested in the American zone commander, although both ports lay inside the British area. American forces also received access through the western and northwestern seaports and passage through British-controlled territory. Exact boundaries could be drawn later.
frus-1945-50-intel-d118:
Minutes of the fifth meeting of the National Intelligence Authority are dated 7 August 1946. Five meetings in six months show the board settling into its role as the system's court. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

The August meeting sat in the middle of the FBI and CIG dispute, and its minutes record the board at work on live business. Readers can set the minutes beside the letters of Hoover and Vandenberg from the same weeks. The letters argue; the minutes decide, or defer. That pairing is the volume's method at its best. It lets a reader follow a bureaucratic battle from first shot to ruling without leaving the printed record.
frus-1945-50-intel-d18:
G. E. Ramsey of the Budget Bureau staff wrote to Martin, the assistant director for estimates, on 24 September 1945. The paper came four days after the OSS was dissolved. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

With the order signed, the questions turned to money: what the leftover units would cost, and which budgets would carry them. Ramsey's memorandum to the estimates chief fits that turn exactly. Readers following the Budget Bureau thread can watch it shift from judging plans to pricing them. The shift is easy to miss and worth catching, because the prices set in these weeks bounded what the new intelligence system could actually do.
frus-1945-50-intel-d218: "Memorandum for the Record" bears the date 19 June 1947. It is document 218 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. A new law was about to remap the whole field: the armed services, the National Security Council, and the CIA all hung on it. Such a note often marks the end of a chain: the talk is over, the choice is made, and this page says so.
frus-1945-50-intel-d318:
Formal minutes cover the 13th Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board, held on 15 May 1947. It stands as document 318 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

The text is the meeting as the secretaries kept it, topic by topic, with the results marked as they were reached. Later fights over who agreed to what often end with a page like this one. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d418:
Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter wrote to Charles Cabell, the Air Force director of intelligence, on 6 March 1950. The letter is document 418 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Air Force was the youngest service, and air intelligence grew fast with it. Cabell later served as deputy director of the CIA itself. A letter between the two men in 1950 shows service intelligence and central intelligence learning to work side by side. Cabell's later years at the CIA make this early link between the two men read with added point.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d118:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to the President on 25 September 1944 about the Quebec plan for Germany. His memorandum answers Roosevelt's paper of 15 September, agreed with Churchill, on the postwar treatment of Germany. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Hull urges that the policy win the firm agreement of Britain and the Soviet Union before it is adopted. Up to now, he notes, every step on Germany has rested on a three-power basis. The European Advisory Commission in London exists for just that work. To move on any other footing, he warns, would add greatly to the burdens of American soldiers. It would burden American officials in the control period too.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d18: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on 5 November 1944, the day before Americans voted in the presidential election. His message is document 18 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, issued by the Department of State. The letter belongs to the steady stream of fall messages through which the two leaders managed the war and planned its final campaigns together.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d218:
Molotov handed Harriman a formal request for six billion dollars in American credit. The ambassador cabled the substance from Moscow on 4 January 1945. His report is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It gives the terms of the Soviet aide-mémoire of the day before, an approach foreshadowed since October.

The Soviet government says it can place large orders on long-term credit, up to six billion dollars. The money would buy manufactured goods: oil pipes, rails, railroad cars, locomotives, and industrial equipment. It would also cover Lend-Lease orders not delivered before the war's end. The credit would run thirty years. Repayment would begin only on the last day of the ninth year, and end on the last day of the thirtieth. American public men, Moscow notes, have often spoken of wanting such orders.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d318:
Restating the alliance's basic pledges is the business of a British Chiefs of Staff memorandum from Malta, February 1, 1945. London proposed that the chiefs renew the undertakings agreed at the Octagon conference in Quebec, with one change. The rewritten clause covers help for the forces of freed areas in Europe.

Under the new wording, freed peoples would be aided so they could play an active part against Germany or Japan. Other friendly states would get help as far as they could use it against the enemy. Supplies for freed areas would support their power to make war. The paper shows both allies tuning fine print while the big strategy held.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d418:
Approval without amendment crowns this Combined Chiefs session of February 9, 1945. The chiefs laid their final report before Roosevelt and Churchill, summing up the Argonaut military talks. Both leaders accepted it as written. Talk then ranged briefly over what might follow Germany's defeat.

The possible action of Russia at that time drew the leaders' attention. Churchill argued it would be of great value if Russia could be persuaded to join the war in the Pacific. The minutes are short, but the moment is large: the whole Allied military program for 1945, endorsed in one sitting at Yalta.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d118:
The State Department issued its revised roster for the Berlin trip on July 4, 1945. The top secret memorandum is document 118 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It replaces the tentative list of June 15 with the final team that would assist the President at the meeting of heads of government.

The list runs to more than forty people in eighteen groups. James Dunn and H. Freeman Matthews cover European affairs; Charles Bohlen, Llewellyn Thompson, and Edward Page supply Russian language skill; James Riddleberger handles German political questions and Emile Despres reparations. Specialists for the Balkans, the Near East, and China fill out the bench, with Charles Yost as secretary general of the delegation. The roster maps exactly the expertise Potsdam would demand.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d18:
Churchill dined with Harriman and his daughter Kathleen in Paris on May 22, 1945, and the ambassador reported the talk to Truman the next night. Churchill was greatly pleased with the decision to send Harry Hopkins with Harriman to Moscow. The resignation of his government that day, and the coming election in the first week of July, were much in his mind.

He was gravely concerned over developments with Russia. Going through firmly in Venezia Giulia mattered greatly, he felt. But basic issues such as Poland could not be settled until Truman and he met Stalin. He assured Harriman he would take no position on Russia without Truman's full support. The cable is summitry by dinner table.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d218:
Assistant Secretary Dunn recorded more of his July 14 talk with Sir Alexander Cadogan in extracts printed as document 218 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The two senior officials spent two hours going over the conference agenda at Potsdam, two days before the leaders' first full meeting.

On the German-Polish frontier, Cadogan opposed the Oder-Neisse line, which would put ten to twelve million Germans in line for transfer west. He thought the transfer question was bound to come up, given its effect on the rest of Germany and on the Control Council. On the Balkans, he proposed raising Russia's removals of oil equipment from Romania and Yugoslavia's failure to carry out the Tito-Šubašić agreement. The memo maps the ground the Western side meant to contest.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d318:
A companion message from Schuyler, also dated July 14, 1945, moves from grievances to remedies for Rumania's Control Commission. His first message that day had listed the difficulties that kept the American delegation from carrying its full share of duties. This one outlines the changes he judged necessary to overcome them.

Above all, Schuyler held to the demand from his June 28 message: the armistice commission had to be rebuilt on truly three-power lines. Anything less, he argued, left the United States a guest in a body it was meant to share. The War Department relayed his program to the Berlin conference delegation on July 16.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d418:
Coal for Europe's other countries is planned in an undated memorandum by the Joint Civil Affairs Committee. The coal industry of northwest Europe, Germany included, was then integrated under supreme headquarters. When that headquarters dissolved, the committee warns, the integration must continue through another agency, or the system falls apart.

Belgium and the Netherlands, it reports, produce just enough to keep their economies at the barest minimum. France, Norway, Denmark, and Italy depend on imports. British and American output will not cover even British and American needs in the coal year 1945-46. The only remaining sources to meet Europe's needs, the committee concludes, are Germany and Poland.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d518:
A British proposal on Poland's frontier is recorded in Durbrow's memorandum of a conversation in Washington on July 13, 1945. George Middleton of the British Embassy called that day and left an aide-mémoire. It outlined the British government's proposal to settle the western and northern frontiers of Poland at the Berlin conference.

Delay, the aide-mémoire argues, will only mean that the Soviet and Polish governments consolidate their position along the Oder-Neisse line. That would incorporate into Poland, by unilateral action, approximately one-fifth of pre-war German territory. London therefore seeks the American delegation's concurrence in acting on its lines upon arrival at Terminal, the conference's code name.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d618:
Acting Secretary Grew recorded a call by the Netherlands ambassador, Dr. Loudon, in a memo dated July 13, 1945. It is document 618 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Loudon came on his own, without instructions, to plead for Dutch troops.

Loudon said no steps had been taken to move Dutch troops to Australia. There they could train for the eventual freeing of the Netherlands East Indies. Even Dutch ships in the Allied pool were not being freed for the task. If U.S. and Australian forces freed the islands with no Dutch present, he warned, Holland's loss of face with the local people could never be undone. Grew answered by setting out the hard limits on ships and forces, all of which were tied to the main war effort.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1018:
Britain's delegation circulated this secret memorandum on war crimes at Potsdam on July 30, 1945. Britain had put the subject on the conference agenda. Given world interest in swift punishment of the major war criminals, London wants the three governments to place a set paragraph in the Protocol and Communiqué.

The draft paragraph notes the talks running in London among British, American, Soviet, and French representatives. Those talks seek agreement on how to try major criminals whose crimes had no single place. The three governments would reaffirm their intent to bring the men to swift and sure justice. They would urge that the trials begin at the earliest possible date.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1118:
Anthony Eden, Britain's foreign secretary, wrote to the United States Secretary of State on 17 July 1945. It was the opening day of the Potsdam Conference. Eden led Britain's foreign policy work under Churchill in the summit's first half, before the change of government in London.

A letter between the two chief envoys carried the joint business of the British and American teams. Much of the summit ran through this channel, minister to secretary. This message opens the paper trail between the two men at Potsdam. It shows the Western allies handling their shared work in their own words, at the top level.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1218:
Ambassador Harriman in Moscow wrote to the Secretary of State on 28 July 1945. Harriman was the American voice the Kremlin knew best. His cables from the Soviet capital carried weight on every question where Moscow's word mattered.

This dispatch reached the secretary in the summit's final days. Harriman watched Soviet conduct from inside while the leaders bargained in person. His reports tested the table talk against the facts of the capital. A cable from his hand is part of the record's Soviet thread. It shows the Moscow post feeding the endgame from its own vantage point.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1318:
A second Pauley message to the President bears the date 19 July 1945. The reparations envoy reported twice in a day because his file sat at the center of the summit's money fight. His mission's findings bore on every figure the leaders traded.

Pauley had seen Germany's ruins himself. His judgment on what could be taken without starving the land carried weight no paper claim could match. This message is the day's companion piece. Together the pair shows the reparations expert pressing his evidence on the president at the very hour the bargaining over Germany's bill began in earnest.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1418:
Charles Bohlen, a special assistant to the secretary of state and the department's leading Russian hand, wrote a memorandum dated 28 March 1960. The volume prints it with the Yalta papers, fifteen years after that conference. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Bohlen had served as Roosevelt's interpreter at Yalta, so his later word on the meeting carries a witness's weight. A memorandum written in 1960 shows the conference still being argued over long after its makers were gone. Readers get hindsight in primary form: a man who was in the room, setting down what he believed the record showed. It is an unusual, late voice in a volume of wartime papers.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-118: This editorial note sits among the unnumbered items after document 710 in the second Potsdam volume. Written by the historians who prepared Foreign Relations of the United States, it lends the reader a hand at a dense point. Such notes name sources, link files, and mark where papers are missing. The note's brevity is its virtue: context without clutter.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-18:
Thompson's minutes for the plenary session of July 18, 1945, open with an unusual subject: the press. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Churchill raised the question of the reporters massed outside the conference compound.

Churchill recalled that the press had found access hard at Tehran and impossible at Yalta. Here, he said, crowds of correspondents raised a great outcry over the lack of news. Stalin inquired who had let them in, and Churchill answered that they were outside the compound. He offered to speak to them himself, not about the work, but about why secrecy was needed. Truman cut the matter short with a cooler plan. Each delegation had its own press man on hand, and they should handle it. The meeting itself, he said, should stay secret as its predecessors had.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d718:
Hurley replied to the Secretary of State on July 31, 1945, in document 718. The letter came as the Potsdam Conference closed. Printed in the second Potsdam volume, it extends the China exchange across the conference's whole span. Hurley wrote from an embassy facing a fragile ally and an unfinished war.

Field replies like this one test the plans made at summits. An ambassador must turn broad lines into local action. Readers see that burden in Hurley's position. The document also shows the State Department's web at work: Potsdam deciding, Chungking reporting, each shaping the other in near-real time for 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d818:
Schoenfeld wrote from Hungary on July 25, 1945, in document 818. The representative in Budapest reported to the Acting Secretary of State. His steady flow of letters anchors the volume's Hungary file. This one entered the second Potsdam volume in the conference's second week.

Hungary's story in 1945 was one of slow, contested change. Schoenfeld's serial reports let readers follow it without leaps. The document shows a mission using the only weapon it had: accurate, regular reporting. Washington's picture of Budapest came from this desk. The summit's choices about Hungary can be judged against the facts he sent.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d918:
Collado wrote this memorandum on July 23, 1945, as a note for the Secretary's talk with Molotov. It treats the western boundaries of Poland as both a political and an economic question. At Yalta the powers agreed the final border awaited the peace settlement.

Since then, Poles backed by Soviet armies have moved the line to the Oder-Neisse. Truman called that a fifth occupying nation inside Germany. The paper urges trade deals to swap eastern food and coal for goods from the rest of Germany. It also says Soviet and Polish reparation claims should be met solely from the Soviet zone, which holds near half of Germany's wealth.
frus-1955-57v18:
Africa fills Volume XVIII of the 1955–1957 set. Regional policy leads, with French North Africa and the French lands south of the Sahara in the first blocks. Algeria's war takes the longest early run.

Ghana appears as a new state in these files. Morocco and Tunisia work out their first ties with Washington, arms included. Libya's aid, Ethiopia's value, and South Africa's apartheid fights at the UN fill the rest. The papers show a continent in fast change, with each capital's file dated by a flag not yet raised or just raised.
frus-1958-60v18:
Japan and Korea share Volume XVIII of the 1958–1960 set. Japan leads, in a single long policy run. The security treaty's revision and trade friction fill the files, toward the 1960 crisis over the pact.

Korea follows in two blocks. New dual-capable weapons and troop pullout talks fill the first. The second covers the rigged March 15 vote, the April crisis, and Rhee's fall.
