Yun's new government closes the volume. The files show two alliances tested in the same season, one in the streets. Trade fights with Tokyo fill the Japan files' second half.
frus-1961-63v18:
The Near East in 1962–1963 fills Volume XVIII of the 1961–1963 set, in a single run of Documents 1–395. The dispute with Israel runs on, with arms and water still the sore points. Yemen's war takes the Peninsula files.

Syria and Iraq pass through coups in these pages. Jordan and Lebanon draw steady aid talks. The record ends in late 1963, mid-argument. Read with Volume XVII, the pair shows three years of motion and no rest. Each capital's file closes on a promise the next volume would test. Yemen's war fills the Peninsula files to the end.
frus-1964-68v18:
Volume XVIII of the 1964-1968 series covers the Arab-Israeli dispute from 1964 through 1967. Its 418 documents run in one sequence. They cover arms sales to Israel and Arab states, water disputes on the Jordan River, and rising border clashes. U.S. officials weigh how to keep the region calm while backing Israel's security. The papers end on the eve of the 1967 war.

Cables from Tel Aviv, Cairo, and other posts fill much of the volume. Memos record talks on tank and aircraft sales and on nuclear questions. The records show a dispute heating up year by year. They form the prelude to the war volume that follows.
frus-1969-76v18:
China from 1973 to 1976 fills Volume XVIII of the 1969-1976 Foreign Relations series. The first chapter covers Kissinger's visits to Beijing and the opening of liaison offices in 1973. The next follows ties through the turmoil of Watergate and Nixon's fall. A third traces the slow move toward normal relations in 1974 and 1975. The Ford summit in Beijing, in December 1975, gets its own chapter.

The final chapter covers China's power struggles of 1976. Talk records with Chinese leaders fill much of the volume. Trade, Taiwan, and the Soviet threat recur in the talks. The volume ends with full normal ties still out of reach.
frus-1969-76v31-d18: A message from President Nixon to West German Chancellor Brandt forms document 18 in Volume XXXI of the 1969-1976 series. Nixon replies to a letter of March 22 about the currency crisis then under way. He agrees that the crisis should end fast and that current rates are sound. But he resists judging fixes only by whether they aid European unity. Any plan, he argues, must be weighed with the United States and Japan. He notes a like letter to Prime Minister Heath.
frus-1977-80v18:
Volume XVIII of the 1977-1980 Foreign Relations series covers the Middle East region and the Arabian Peninsula. Sections treat the region and the Gulf, the Indian Ocean, and Iraq. Saudi Arabia takes a long section of its own. The Yemens close the volume. A briefing paper in the Saudi section calls the kingdom a growing source of support for U.S. stands at the UN. It notes Saudi weight as guardian of Islam's two holiest places.

The papers follow oil, arms, and the shah's fall next door in Iran. Diego Garcia and Soviet naval moves drive the Indian Ocean section. The Yemen chapters treat the two states' rivalry and Saudi aid across the border.
gao-gaoreports-b-293105-18:
Under files B-293105.18 and B-293105.19, dated January 17, 2006, GAO sustained a protest by Greenleaf Construction Company, Inc. Greenleaf had lost a Department of Housing and Urban Development contract for single-family home management and marketing services in Ohio. The winner was Chapman Law Firm Company, LPA. GAO found the scoring of the winner's proposal unsound. It rested on key staff and a monitoring system that the winner knew, more than two months before award, would not be on hand. The winner never told the agency of the change.

A second ground was conflict of interest. The winner's owner would be paid by the owner of Ohio's closing agent firm, whose work the winner must oversee.
gao-gaoreports-b-299518:
Matthews Manufacturing protested a Coast Guard award to Universal Marine Services. The contract covered steel ocean buoys used as navigation aids. The buoys are built to agency plans and drawings. GAO decided B-299518 and B-299518.3 on June 11, 2007.

The terms gave technical points far more weight than price. The winner bid the higher price. But it showed deep past work on buoys just like these. That match of skill to the goods on offer counted most. GAO found the pick in line with the stated scheme. A higher price can win when merit leads by design. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299818:
Systems Research and Applications Corporation and Booz Allen Hamilton protested an Air Force award to Jacobs Technology. The contract covered engineering and technology acquisition support services. The work serves the Electronic Systems Center. GAO ruled in the B-299818 series on September 6, 2007.

One side point cleared a consultant for case access. The main plea won on the merits. The terms asked the agency to weigh how far each bid met or topped the needs. The agency failed to judge the bids' distinct paths in depth. Scores alone cannot fill that gap. A best-value review must weigh real contrasts. That missing step tainted the pick. GAO sustained the protests.
gao-gaoreports-b-299918:
Nautical Control Solutions protested a Navy call not to fund its phase I proposal. The plea arose under the Small Business Innovation Research program. The topic sought shipboard energy and fuel management tools. GAO ruled in B-299918 on October 1, 2007.

The tool would help crews tune a ship's operating profile. It would weigh fuel use with hard numbers. Rising fuel prices since 2004 gave the topic its push. GAO reviewed the scoring of the firm's bid. It found the review fair on the record. A firm that falls short in a scored round has no ground to upset the call. The funding choice stood. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-304718:
Snacks for focus group guests raised a funds question in this GAO decision, B-304718, dated November 9, 2005. The Veterans Benefits Administration runs focus groups with veterans and their kin. The groups help the office carry out its legal mission. The office asked if it could buy light meals or snacks. The aim was to draw more guests and get better input.

GAO answered yes, with care. The office may judge that food helps draw guests and yields better input. Funds may pay for such treats on that basis. But the office should set a firm written policy. The policy must keep treats to cases where they are needed and fit. The ruling guides agencies that weigh small perks to boost public input.
gao-gaoreports-b-307918:
Mileage pay for night call-outs is barred in this GAO decision, B-307918, dated December 20, 2006. Staff of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration serve on call at night. When a crisis hits, they drive from home to a warehouse. The agency asked if it could pay them back for those miles. The miles form part of a home-to-work trip.

GAO held that funds may not pay the miles back. A law at 31 U.S.C. section 1344(a)(1) bars funds for rides between home and work. The bar holds unless a law says else. Night duty for the government does not lift it. The ruling keeps a hard line on commute costs.
gao-gaoreports-b-310018:
The Protective Group, Inc. lost its protest (GAO decision B-310018, dated November 13, 2007). The U.S. Special Operations Command sought body armor plates. The plates form part of the SPEAR armor kit for its troops. The firm said the buy should be set aside for small firms. The agency chose to run an open race.

GAO denied the protest. The agency knew the armor trade well. An industry day drew views from firms in the trade. Those views showed two fit small firms were not likely to bid. A set-aside needs that fair hope of two bids. The hope was not there on this file.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-418:
Oil and Gas Development, GAO-05-418 of June 17, 2005, finds a land arm swamped by the drill rush it must both spur and guard. Fuel use climbs and fears of foreign fuel grow. The White House pushes home oil and gas, on public land too. The Bureau of Land Management grants the drill rights. It must curb the harm each well leaves on land, water, and life.

GAO sizes how the drill pace on its land has changed of late. It asks what that pace did to the arm's shield work. It lists the rule shifts the arm made and their mark. It names the tests that still press the arm.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-518:
Security upgrades on the National Mall in Washington are surveyed in GAO report GAO-05-518, dated June 14, 2005. The Mall holds some of the nation's best-known sites and draws millions of visitors a year. Agencies with buildings there have added physical security since the September 11 attacks. GAO counted what was built, what it cost, and how well safety was balanced with open access and good looks.

Agencies had committed about $132 million to upgrades by the time of the review. The National Park Service and the Smithsonian accounted for about 75 percent of that total. Work ranged from more guards to new gear, with fixed barriers against vehicle bombs still to come. Plans must pass review bodies that weigh history, design, and setting. GAO surveyed about 300 visitors. Most prized access and appearance and found the current security level acceptable. Early talks with reviewers, GAO found, smooth the path to approval.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-618:
Testing students with disabilities under the No Child Left Behind Act is examined in GAO-05-618 (July 20, 2005). In the 2003-04 school year, at least 95 percent of these students took state reading tests in 41 of the 49 states reporting. Most sat the regular test, often with extra time or like aids. Few took alternate tests. On the national NAEP test, 5 percent were shut out, with state rates from about 2 to 10 percent.

Building alternate tests proved hard: the pupils vary widely, the models are new, and teacher training is heavy. GAO told the Education Department to share know-how better and help states cut shut-outs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-818:
NASA's own passenger planes are costed in GAO-05-818, a report from August 26, 2005. The space agency has run passenger aircraft since its founding. Past audits have questioned the practice. GAO was asked to audit controls against waste. Here it compared the cost of agency planes with airline fares. It checked whether the service follows government-wide guidance. And it judged oversight of the program.

GAO found agency flights cost about five times what airline flights cost. Staff took at least 1,188 such flights in fiscal years 2003 and 2004. Reported costs neared $25 million, versus about $5 million for airline coach travel. The count even leaves out wear on planes bought for $14 million in 2001. The agency was weighing about $77 million more to upgrade and grow the fleet.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1018:
Hanford contamination and the Columbia River are revisited in GAO-06-1018, a report from August 28, 2006. The Washington State site is among North America's most contaminated nuclear sites. The river runs through about 50 miles of it. Waste from decades of defense work has seeped into groundwater that flows toward the river. GAO reported on the risk in November 2005 and returned to check progress.

Headings show movement and gaps. The Energy Department is taking steps to grasp the risk better. It has asked to extend regulatory milestones while it reworks its risk estimates. It is weighing new treatment tools to replace ones that do not work well near the river. Management weaknesses have drawn attention, but the fix is incomplete. The department has not fully put its management plan in place, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-18:
The Defense Travel System, a long-troubled software project, is audited in GAO-06-18, a report issued on January 18, 2006. The Defense Department has spent 10 years building one standard travel system. Past GAO work showed travel habits that wasted millions of dollars. The department says the new system will help fix them. GAO tested whether key functions were properly tried out. It asked whether the system will cure the old flaws, and what work remains.

GAO made ten recommendations to the Secretary of Defense. They target tighter management and oversight of the system. They also seek simpler travel steps, from how changed expenses display to how flight choices appear. The Defense Department agreed with all ten and sketched its fixes. The report continues a long GAO watch over a basic task: paying for official trips without waste. A system meant to end waste must first prove it works.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-518:
After four hurricanes in one season, the Red Cross spent heavily and sought repayment. In report GAO-06-518 (May 30, 2006), GAO audits reimbursement to the American Red Cross. The storms were Charley, Frances, Ivan, and Jeanne. The Red Cross reported $88.6 million in incurred expenses. Criteria were set for which costs could be repaid. Covered work included mass care, living and housing needs, and health needs.

The audit found controls avoided double payment from other federal funds. Expenses were generally for eligible services and were adequately supported, it said. Six reportable conditions in internal controls were still identified. Debit card support and monitoring drew findings. Readers get both the total and the flaws.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-618:
Lessons from Hurricane Katrina fill GAO-06-618, a long GAO report released on September 6, 2006. Katrina was the largest and most destructive natural disaster in the nation's history. Congress, the White House, and others probed what went wrong in the response. GAO drew on more than 30 of its own Katrina and Rita reports, plus earlier work on disasters such as Hurricane Andrew in 1992.

GAO sorted out what went well, what failed, and why each happened. GAO called for stronger leadership, better response capability, and tighter controls over relief spending. The report also flags open issues in the Gulf Coast recovery. It serves as a record of how the nation's disaster system must change.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-718:
Retirement of the baby boom generation is studied in GAO-06-718, a GAO report dated July 28, 2006. Boomers were born between 1946 and 1964. The first of them become eligible for early Social Security benefits in 2008. Some feared that boomers would sell stocks and homes en masse, driving down market returns. GAO reviewed financial evidence and spoke with researchers and industry voices.

GAO found little sign that boomer selling would cause a dramatic decline in market returns. Most researchers foresaw little to no impact on financial markets. Broader risks, though, threaten retirement security. Boomers and later generations will rely more on their own savings. That shift raises the stakes for saving rates and sound money management. The report separates a market myth from the real risks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-818:
Anti-drug ads aimed at teens are evaluated in GAO report GAO-06-818, issued on August 25, 2006. From 1998 through 2004, Congress gave over $1.2 billion to the National Youth Anti-Drug Media Campaign. The ads aimed to stop teens from starting drugs or to cut their use. In 2005, the firm Westat finished a multi-year national evaluation of the campaign. GAO reviewed the quality and findings of that study.

GAO found that Westat used sound sampling and analysis, so its evidence was credible. The findings were not kind to the campaign. Results on middle outcomes, such as teen beliefs, were mixed. The study found no effect on how closely parents monitor their youth. Most of all, the evaluation did not find that the campaign was effective in reducing youth drug use.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-918:
Leased space at the National Institutes of Health is the topic of GAO report GAO-06-918, dated September 8, 2006. The health agency's leased space more than doubled since 1996, to about 3.9 million square feet in 2005. Since 1996 it has held its own leasing power, by grant from the General Services Administration.

GAO studied 59 leases for two tests. First, did the agency score leases by budget rules, as operating or capital? Second, did it follow the process of notice to Congress for big leases? GAO found the leasing process better, but said Congress still lacked word on some leases.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1018:
U.S. aid to Mexico's drug fight is weighed in GAO report GAO-07-1018, dated August 17, 2007. Since fiscal year 2000 the United States has given about $397 million for that fight. Much of the drugs used in the United States flow through, or are made in, Mexico.

GAO tracked how Mexican drug output and trafficking changed since calendar year 2000. It set out what U.S. support has bought since fiscal year 2000. Aid has helped Mexican efforts, the title states. Yet tons of illicit drugs still reach the United States. The report gives Congress a sober balance sheet for a long aid effort.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-118:
The transport safety board has grown, but core work needs gains, GAO reports in GAO-07-118, dated November 22, 2006. The National Transportation Safety Board probes crashes, finds their causes, and issues safety advice. Its training center opened in 2003, to teach its own probers and others.

GAO asked how far the board keeps to top management practice. It weighed how the board does its safety work, from probe picks to follow-through. It asked if the training center pays its way, and how it could do so better. Headway has been made, GAO found. Yet management habits, probe aims, and center use should all improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-518:
Big Energy Department projects still drift over budget, and GAO-07-518, dated May 11, 2007, asks why reforms have not cured it. Contract management at the Department of Energy (DOE) has sat on GAO's high-risk list since 1990. Contractors build and run much of the department's cleanup, science, and weapons work. In 1999, a National Research Council panel joined GAO in urging fixes.

GAO traced the department's main repair efforts since 1999. It then judged whether project results had in fact improved. They had not, by much: cost and schedule goals were still missed at the same pace. Rules drawn from best practice were applied unevenly across sites. Tools such as certified earned value systems lagged. GAO pressed for steady use of its own rules everywhere. The report is a status check on a quarter-century problem.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-618:
Rust eats readiness and budgets alike, and GAO-07-618, dated April 30, 2007, finds the Pentagon's anti-corrosion drive leaderless. A fiscal year 2003 law told the Defense Department to name an office to lead the fight. A fiscal year 2006 law told GAO to grade the effort. GAO read strategy papers and checked corrosion plans in 51 big weapon buys.

Over 4 years on, the drive lags the law's hopes. No rule forces the services to send the lead office full data on their corrosion funds. Most services lack a named corrosion chief of their own. No action plan turns cost study data into savings. Most big programs in the sample skipped key corrosion steps at design time, when fixes are cheap. GAO joins the Defense Science Board in one charge: only top-level push, with real incentives, will make corrosion a design factor rather than a repair bill.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-718:
Trips that mix trains, trucks, planes, and ships are the subject of GAO-07-718, dated June 20, 2007. Such linked trips can ease crowding and cut freight costs. In 1991, Congress called for a national linked system. It set up an office for the work inside the Transportation Department. GAO asked what blocks linked projects. It also asked what the department has done and what more it could do. The report draws on state and local officials and past studies.

Three blocks stood out. Federal funds tend to be tied to one mode of travel, not mixed trips. Agencies split by mode work in silos, which hampers joint plans. Local planners also lack tools to prove the gains of linked projects. GAO said one office should lead the federal effort. It urged better teamwork and more guidance for planners. The department agreed to weigh the idea.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-818:
Farm payments to estates of dead farmers are faulted in GAO-07-818, dated July 9, 2007. Farmers get about $20 billion a year in federal farm aid. Estates may draw payments for two years after a death. After that, the Agriculture Department must check the estate is not kept open just for payments. GAO sampled estates and matched payment records with death records. It judged whether the Farm Service Agency followed its own rules.

The agency paid many estates past the two-year mark without the required checks. GAO found flaws in 142 of 181 estates reviewed. For 73 estates, no eligibility check was done at all from 1999 through 2005. Sixteen of those estates each got over $200,000 in payments. Four each got over $500,000. Records for other checks were often missing or vague. GAO urged yearly checks, death verification, and recovery of bad payments. The department agreed and began fixes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-18:
Weather satellite risks are flagged in GAO report GAO-08-18, issued October 23, 2007. The GOES-R series will supply the data weather forecasts need through 2028. The Commerce Department's weather agency leads the buy, with NASA's aid. The program is estimated to cost $7 billion. Its first satellite is set to be ready for launch in 2014.

GAO found real progress in early design work. The agency also split the space and ground parts into two contracts. That shift delayed the choice to build, though. Outside estimates run high. GAO warns that costs and schedules are likely to grow, and that risk controls need work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-418:
Rotational crewing of Navy ships is evaluated in GAO report GAO-08-418, dated May 29, 2008. Swapping crews lets one ship stay at sea longer, easing cost and tempo pressure. GAO checked whether the Navy leads, guides, measures, and learns from these efforts across ship types.

The Navy has led some crewing programs well, but it has no overall management approach, no named leader, and no team charged with the change. Guidance covers some ship types but no Navy-wide instruction exists, and concepts of operations treat crewing unevenly. Data work and lessons-learned sharing also lack a system. GAO recommended firm leadership, guidance, and a data plan, plus a step for Congress to weigh. The Defense Department agreed with only some of the advice, disputing five points.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-518:
GAO's report GAO-08-518 (dated May 16, 2008) covers the polar-orbiting weather satellite program. The National Polar-orbiting Operational Environmental Satellite System is run by the Commerce and Defense Departments with NASA. A June 2006 restructuring cut satellites and sensors, raised the cost estimate to $12.5 billion, and delayed the first two satellites by 3 to 5 years.

Most restructuring steps are done, and the contract has been renegotiated. But agency chiefs have not signed off key papers, including the tri-agency agreement. Poor workmanship and test delays pushed a key imaging sensor 8 months late, which also delayed a demonstration satellite by 8 months. Four climate and space weather sensors cut in 2006 still have no plan for replacement data. GAO urged the three agencies to plan jointly for that data. Officials agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-618:
Doctors and other health providers paid by Medicare owe a duty to pay their own taxes too. GAO-08-618, dated June 13, 2008, checks how many Medicare providers had unpaid federal taxes. Reviewers matched payment records from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services with tax debt records from the Internal Revenue Service.

More than 27,000 providers, about 6 percent of the total, owed more than $2 billion in taxes for 2006. A close look at 25 providers found some kept payroll taxes taken from staff pay, which is a felony when done on purpose. GAO urged tax checks before providers join Medicare and wider use of payment levies to pay old tax bills.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-918:
Lost computers at veterans' hospitals are the subject of GAO-08-918, a July 2008 follow-up report. Earlier GAO work in 2004 and 2007 found weak controls over IT equipment at Department of Veterans Affairs sites and made 18 recommendations. This audit checks progress on those fixes and tests whether current controls stop theft and loss.

VA finished 14 of the 18 recommendations, partly did 2, and is working on the last 2. Its July 2008 policy changes could fix many weaknesses, and a 2007 departmentwide count was a real step. But as of May 15, 2008, VA still could not locate about 62,800 IT items, and 9,800 of them could have held sensitive data. Since VA cannot tell what data was on them, affected people could not be warned. GAO adds five new recommendations.
govdocs-archive_org-Russian-Active-Measu:
On March 22, 2018, the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence released its report on Russian active measures. The report closed the committee's look into Russian interference operations aimed at the United States, an inquiry that drew heavy public attention and sharp partisan argument.

Inside, the committee lays out its findings on what Russian actors did, and it adds recommendations meant to guard future elections. The document is written as an official record, with the committee's conclusions stated plainly. It stands as one of the main congressional accounts of the interference campaign and of the political fight that surrounded the inquiry itself.
govdocs-archive_org-TheEarthJournalFlatE:
The Earth was a journal of the zetetic movement, the Victorian campaigners who argued that the world is flat and that readers should trust only what they can test themselves. The scan holds an issue of the journal, filed with material dated to 1895.

The surviving pages open with the journal's advertising rates and subscription terms, before its articles begin. Even those business pages are telling: they show a movement organized enough to sell ads, take subscriptions, and publish on a schedule. For historians of fringe science, such journals are the primary record of how flat-earth belief organized and spread in the 1890s.
grick-clypeum-veritatis-1618:
Friedrich Grick called his 1618 German work Clypeum veritatis, the Shield of Truth. The German subtitle calls it a short but thorough answer, and the claim fits the book. Grick wrote in the heat of the pamphlet war over the Rosicrucian manifestos, taking up the charges of F G Menapius.

Grick answers those charges at length, point by point, on behalf of the manifestos' claims. His defense ranks among the fullest printed in those years of furor. The tone is earnest: truth, he holds, needs a shield when slander strikes in print. For readers tracing the fight, Grick supplies the defense in its most complete early form.
hammer-purgstall-mysterium-baphometis-18:
Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall, the Viennese orientalist, published his Mysterium Baphometis Revelatum in 1818, in the Fundgruben des Orients. He argued, from trial records and carved stones, that the Knights Templar had secretly worshipped a Gnostic idol he called Baphomet. The memoir, in Latin with German notes, founded the modern Templar myth.

Hammer read the Templar trials as proof of an Ophite cult hidden in the order, and he saw its signs in fonts, seals, and statues across Europe. His learning was vast and his leaps were wild, and both fed the legend. Every later tale of Templar idolatry drinks from this spring. The text is the single most consequential work of Templar myth-making.
heindel-message-of-stars-1918:
Max Heindel and Augusta Foss Heindel wrote The Message of the Stars in 1918. The book is a full text of star lore from the Rosicrucian school. It teaches how to cast and read a birth chart. The Heindels ran the Rosicrucian Fellowship in California.

Signs, houses, and planets each get rules for their force on health and fate. Health takes a large place, with charts of the sick read in full. The pair hold that stars show trends, not fixed doom. The book is a base text of the new esoteric star lore.
heinrich-mann-untertan-1918:
Heinrich Mann finished Der Untertan, The Loyal Subject, in the summer of 1914, and the hosted text is the German edition of 1918. The novel follows Diederich Hessling, the soft, fearful son of a paper maker in a small town. School, army service, and student drinking corps teach him one lesson: bow to power above, and tread on everyone below.

Hessling takes over the family mill, fights his workers and rivals, and rises by flattering the Kaiser and copying his speech, dress, and strut. Mann builds him into a portrait of the loyal subject who made the German Empire run. The satire was too sharp to print while the war lasted. Once the empire fell in 1918, the book became a bestseller.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum:
Thomas Carlyle's eighteenth volume contains Book Eighteen, the Seven-Years War rises to a height, 1757 to 1759. Seldom, Carlyle opens, was such a combination seen against any man: the great powers resolve to partition Friedrich, cut him down, and enchain the general enemy of mankind. France, Austria, Russia, Sweden, and the Empire all take the field.

Rossbach and Leuthen answer them in 1757; Zorndorf and Hochkirch bloody 1758; Kunersdorf nearly finishes Friedrich in 1759. Prussian soldiers are billeted twenty and thirty to a house in the towns Carlyle's syndics describe. His narrative here is the history's military summit, exhausting and exultant, with the king's generalship and luck argued page by page.
holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-2-of-6-slice-:
Raphael Holinshed's chronicle gives this slice to Richard the First. Richard, second son of Henry the Second, began on the sixth of July 1189. He was proclaimed duke of Normandy at Rouen within the month. His first care was his father's treasure and its keepers.

Crusade, captivity, and ransom fill the famous reign. The emperor charges the delivered king with wrongs done to the Sicilians. Richard answers before the princes of the empire in set scene. Earl John's dealings with the French king darken the home pages. Holinshed tells the Lionheart's decade as pageant and warning at once.
hutchinson-historical-essay-witchcraft-e:
Francis Hutchinson, an Irish clergyman living in England, published his Historical Essay Concerning Witchcraft in 1718. It is the first history of English witchcraft, a new kind of book on the subject. Hutchinson looks back at the trials as a scholar of the Enlightenment, with the Salem cases across the Atlantic among his evidence.

He treats famous cases one by one and finds fraud, fear, and bad courts behind them. His manner is cool and his verdicts are plain. With this essay, history itself turns its eye on the persecution. The sober reckoning with the witch trials begins here. Hutchinson helped make disbelief in witchcraft respectable among educated readers.
in-the-shadow-of-the-glen-pg1618:
J M Synge's In the Shadow of the Glen, a one-act play first performed at the Molesworth Hall, Dublin, on October 8, 1903, with W G Fay as the Tramp. The cast list names Dan Burke, farmer and herd, his wife Nora, and the young herd Micheal Dara. The scene is a cottage kitchen at the top of a long Wicklow glen, a body lying sheeted on the bed.

Dan is feigning death to test Nora, whose loneliness has already drawn her eyes elsewhere; a tramp shelters from the great rain and refuses to leave a woman alone with a wake. Synge based the play on an Aran story. Its premiere scandalized Dublin nationalists and announced the Abbey Theatre's unsettling genius.
j-p-jacobsen-marie-grubbe-a-lady-of-the-:
Marie Grubbe was a real Danish noblewoman of the seventeenth century, and Jacobsen's novel, here in the 1918 English version, tells her fall. Born to rank and wealth, she throws both away for love. She ends her days as a ferryman's wife, far below her birth.

Jacobsen treats her not as a scandal but as a fierce, sensual soul. Each marriage and each loss strips away pride and safety. Her will to live on her own terms never breaks. The novel stands as a bold tale of a woman who would not be tamed by rank, church, or shame.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-18:
Fear closes in through Volume 18, from 1898, on the Hurons of 1640 and 1641. Raids strike from many sides as the Iroquois wars draw tight. Thwaites prints letters that carry the first clear notes of doom.

Priests describe burned fields, blocked rivers, and friends lost to ambush. Still the chapels fill, and still the work of teaching goes on. Courage under a growing shadow gives these reports their force. The drama of the whole series sharpens from this point on. Readers can feel the walls closing in around Huronia with each new report. Peace feels farther off with every season that passes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abarbanel-libra: The Abarbanel Library in Jerusalem was a book collection meant to serve as a national Jewish library. Dr. Joseph Chazanowicz, a Zionist leader in Russia, founded it. He spent almost his whole income on Hebrew books. By 1900 the library held more than 15,000 volumes. Nearly all had been sent from Byelostok, where he worked as a physician. A plan was then under way for a modern fire-proof building. Ephraim Cohen was director in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abel-beth-maach:
Abel-beth-maachah is a place-name found six times in the Old Testament. The entry leaves open whether Abel and Beth-maachah were two places or one. Abel alone is used for the same town in Second Samuel. That fact points to Abel as the chief town of Maachah, a small Syrian state on its own.

A matching passage in Second Chronicles gives the name as Abel-maim, Abel of the waters. That fits the modern village Abil, on a high hill in a well-watered tract, on the main road from Banias to the coast. The name may also stand in the war lists of Tiglathpileser III, among towns that king took. A late legend in Enoch, born of a mix-up of the name, has the fallen angels weeping there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abin-b-nahman-3: Abin ben Naḥman was a beloved disciple of R. Judah ben Ezekiel. That tie is the heart of this very short entry, cited from Baba Meẓi'a, page 107 a. One more role is set down for him. He is named as a transmitter of Baraitot, the early teachings kept outside the Mishnah. Two passages carry that note, in Yebamot and in Baba Batra. No ruling, saying, place, or date of Abin ben Naḥman is given in this brief notice beyond the master's name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abrahams-louis-:
Louis Barnett Abrahams was head master of the Jews' Free School in London. He was born at Swansea, South Wales, in 1842. His family moved to Manchester in 1845, and he was schooled there.

In 1854 he was bound as pupil-teacher to Moses Angel at the Jews' Free School. In 1864 he became principal instructor of English, and for twenty years he ran most of the boys' teaching staff. He was made vice-master in 1884. When Moses Angel retired in December 1897, Abrahams was elected head master, then succeeded Angel as principal in 1898. His books include a manual of Scriptural history for Jewish schools, from 1882. He also edited the Jewish Record at its start in 1868.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-guido-818: Guido Adler was an Austrian writer on music. He was born at Eibenschütz, Moravia, on November 1, 1855. His father, a doctor, died in 1857. Guido studied music in Vienna under Bruckner. He took law and thought degrees there in 1878 and 1880. In 1884 he helped found a journal of music study. In 1885 he took a chair at the German school in Prague. In 1898 he moved to the same chair in Vienna. From 1894 he has edited a set of Austrian music monuments.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aguilar-called-:
Aguilar, also called Aguilar de Campo, was a district in Valencia. The district sits in Spain. It sheltered a large Jewish congregation in the Middle Ages. Under Almohade rule, many local Jews hid their faith. For a time they pretended to embrace Islam. In 1290 the community paid heavy taxes. The sum was 8,600 maravedis.

War later brought worse harm. Don Pedro the Cruel fought his brother Don Henry. The Jews of Aguilar suffered badly in that civil war. Many of them were slain. The entry also notes two traces of the old community. One is a Hebrew tombstone from the fourteenth century. It stands above the gate of Reinosa. The other is a brass lamp from their synagogue. Samuel ben Pinhas Caro of Paredes made it. It still hung in a local church in the late sixteenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aix-or-aix-en-p:
Aix, or Aix-en-Provence, is a town in the south of France. The Romans knew it as Aquae Sextiae. For a short time it was the capital of Provence. Jews there are first named in a paper of 1283. For two pounds of pepper a year, the community could keep a synagogue and a cemetery.

Most Jews of Aix lived on the rue Venel, then called Jews' Street. They traded in spices, silks, and wax. In 1341 the town held 1,211 Jews, and 203 of them owned land. Hard rules bound them: baths only on Fridays, no work on Sundays, a yellow badge to wear. Under Robert of Anjou they found shelter for a time. In 1436 the Jew Astruc de Leon was executed on a blasphemy charge, and a massacre followed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-al-tabban-levi-:
Levi b. Jacob ibn al-Tabban was a grammarian and poet of Saragossa. He flourished at the start of the twelfth century. He was a friend and elder contemporary of Judah ha-Levi. Ha-Levi called him "King of Song," though the entry warns that love may have guided that judgment. Al-Harizi rated his verse far lower.

His grammar, written in Arabic, was called "Miftah," the Key. Only its title survives now. His liturgic poems still stand in the festival books of Tripoli, Avignon, and Algeria. They can be picked out by his usual acrostic. A sad strain runs through them, the entry notes. It points to the ruin of Saragossa's province under Alfonso VI, the Christian advance that Yusuf ibn Tashfin was called from Africa to check.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alex-ephraim-11:
Ephraim Alex founded the Jewish Board of Guardians in London. He was born in Cheltenham in 1800. He died in London on November 13, 1882. He was a successful man of business. That training fitted him for the charity work to which he gave his chief attention.

A plan like his had been urged as early as 1802, by Joshua Van Oven, and then forgotten. In 1858 Alex, as overseer of the Great Synagogue, saw how poorly outdoor relief was run. In February 1859 he issued a circular with a full scheme. It proposed a board for the relief of the foreign Jewish poor. The board grew on the exact lines he drew. He was its first president, serving until 1869. He stayed a member until the year of his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-algazi-solomon-:
Solomon Nissim Algazi, called the elder, was a rabbi in Smyrna and Jerusalem. He worked in the seventeenth century. He wrote on all parts of rabbinic letters. His best known work deals with Talmud method. It took the form of notes on an older method book. It came out at Venice in 1639.

The entry lists many more books by him. One set of sermons came out in 1642. One index tracks Bible verses quoted in a Midrash set. Other books treat Talmud tales and the Zohar. Two works give notes on the Tosafot. The list shows a very full writing life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amon-according-:
Amon was a god of Egypt, called the Hidden One. His name shows in Jeremiah and in Nahum. At first he was the town god of Thebes alone. With the eighteenth line of kings he rose to the top. He then ruled the whole set of Egyptian gods. Libyans and Ethiopians took him as their chief god. Greeks matched him with their own Zeus.

In art he wears a blue skin at times. A crown of feathers marks his head dress. At times he bears the head of a ram. That ram was his sacred beast. His name went through more than one form. Amon, Amun, and Amen all mark stages of its sound.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-angel-moses-151:
Moses Angel, born April 29, 1819, was headmaster of the London Jews' Free School, and died in London in 1898. After fine schooling and a spell as a bank clerk, he turned to teaching. In 1840 he took charge of the school's upper division, the Talmud Torah.

Soon the whole school was in his hands. The entry credits his gifts in management and teaching with changing its spirit fast. It grew into one of the largest and best-run elementary schools in the kingdom. From 1853 government inspectors praised it year after year, the entry reports, and Angel began training work beyond the school as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antoninus-pius-:
Antoninus Pius, full name Titus Aurelius Fulvus Boionius Arrius Antoninus, was a Roman emperor born in the year 86. He ruled from 138 until his death in 161. The entry calls his reign a blessing for the Jews, above all in Palestine.

Hadrian's persecutions had emptied towns and crushed Jewish learning there. Jewish envoys led by Rabbi Judah ben Shamu'a went to Rome to plead for relief. In August 138 or 139 the emperor let them bury their fallen soldiers and martyrs. Half a year later he repealed Hadrian's edicts against Jewish worship, on condition that no proselytes be received. Jews still could not enter Jerusalem, on pain of death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arba-kanfot-fou:
Arba Kanfot, the four-cornered garment, is a rectangular piece of cloth, usually wool, about three feet long and one foot wide. A hole in its center lets it pass over the head, so part hangs in front and part behind. Fringes, zizit, are tied to its four corners as on the tallit, so it is also called the small tallit.

Male Jews wear it under their outer clothes all day, in keeping with the command in Numbers and Deuteronomy to wear fringed garments. The tallit, by contrast, goes over the clothes for morning service only. The blessings for the two differ in their closing words, the entry notes. Among Ashkenazim, boys get the small garment as soon as they can dress themselves.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arragel-moses-1:
Moses Arragel, a Spanish rabbi, worked at Maqueda and Guadalfajara in Castile in the first half of the fifteenth century. His name may come from the Arabic al-Rijal or from a Hebrew word for the expert. In 1422 Don Luis de Guzman, grand master of the Order of Calatrava, asked him for a Spanish translation of the Bible with commentary, a task the rabbi at first refused.

Don Luis insisted and set a Franciscan friar to convey his wishes. The entry presents the joint Jewish and Catholic work as a sign of the tolerance then found in Castile. Arragel labored for years and presented the finished translation at Toledo on June 2, 1430, before a gathering of leading scholars. The head of the Franciscan order answered his address with high praise for the book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asher-abraham-a:
Abraham Adolf Asher, publisher and student of books, was born at Kammin in Prussia on August 23, 1800. Sent to England to train for trade, he settled as a jewelry merchant at St. Petersburg. One chance purchase, an old library, changed his course. He gave up the jewelry trade and gave himself wholly to bibliography and publishing.

In 1830 he moved to Berlin and set up as bookseller and publisher, winning the prized agency to buy foreign books for the British Museum. A London branch followed, and through him Joseph Zedner became curator of the museum's Hebrew books. His own essays treat early travel collections and German historians. As publisher he issued Benjamin of Tudela's Travels, edited with a full index of place names, in 1840. He died at Venice on September 1, 1853.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asmakta-2018:
Asmakta is a word meaning support or reliance. In one use it names a Bible verse quoted to back a rabbinical rule. In civil law it names a surety bargain. One party promises, for no payment, to bear a set loss. Or he promises to pay an outsized penalty if a stated thing happens, or fails to happen. Such a promise cannot be enforced.

An asmakta does not give title, the entry quotes, is the ruling principle. The reason is plain: a man who binds himself so is taken to have been sure the event would never come, so the law finds no true intent to be bound. The promise can still be made valid, if the intent to bind is made clear in set ways. Maimonides ties validity to how the condition is worded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-auerbach-isaac-:
Isaac Levin Auerbach was a German preacher, educator, and author. He was born at Inowraclaw, Prussia, on March 21, 1791. He died at Dessau on July 5, 1853. His father was rabbi of Inowraclaw, and his brother Baruch founded the Jewish Orphan Asylum in Berlin. Isaac joined the small band of young Berlin Jews who paved the way for reform.

Auerbach preached at the Jacobsen temple, where Zunz also spoke, and taught at the Jewish girls' school of Berlin. He then served the temple at Leipsic for more than twenty-five years. His work aimed at reforming the service itself. He argued in 1818, on rabbinic grounds, for German in place of Hebrew prayer. His printed sermons treat Israel's place among the nations, the Damascus affair, and the reform currents of his day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azmaveth-2218: Azmaveth is a name borne by three men and one town in the Bible. The first man was one of the thirty heroes of David, called the Barhumite. His sons joined David at Ziklag. The second was a Benjamite, a son of Jehoadah. The third, a son of Adiel, kept charge of King David's storehouses. The town Azmaveth stood in the land of Benjamin. Some of its people came back from captivity with Zerubbabel. In the book of Nehemiah the town is called Beth-azmaveth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bardach-julius-:
Julius Bardach, Russian writer and teacher, was born at Turijsk in Volhynia in 1828 and died in Odessa in 1897, though the date is marked uncertain. His father taught him Hebrew grammar, Bible, and Talmud. He also gained enough secular knowledge to qualify as a teacher in Hebrew and Russian. In 1851 he became instructor at the Russo-Hebrew school in Khotin, Bessarabia. In 1857 he moved to the Talmud Torah in Odessa, where he taught until 1882.

From 1871 the government made him censor of Hebrew books, an office he held until his death. He also taught Jewish religion in Odessa high schools and was named a hereditary honorary citizen. His works include "Ḥiḳre Leshon Arami" (1865), studies in Aramaic, and a catalogue of Simḥah Pinsker's Hebrew and Arabic manuscripts (1869). He translated Geiger's grammar of Mishnaic Hebrew into Russian. Three further works, including a course on Jewish religion, stayed in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bashan-or-ha-ba:
Bashan was the tract of land north of Gilead, with the Yarmuk River as its southern line. It ran east to Salchah and north to Mount Hermon. In the west it stopped short of the Jordan River.

The entry stresses rich soil, fine pasture, and strong cattle famed in the prophets. Oak woods grew in the east. It names royal cities such as Edrei and Ashtaroth and recalls the defeat of Og. Later notes follow raids and rule under Israel's kings. The name later passed into Greek as Batanaea and into Arabic in a changed form, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-basque-province:
Basque Provinces covers Guipuzcoa, Biscay, and Alava in Spain, along both sides of the Pyrenees. Old law barred Jews from Guipuzcoa and Biscay, and a visiting Jew could stay only a few days. At Vitoria, in Alava, Jews lived from the twelfth century.

The entry follows the Vitoria community's taxes, its work as money brokers, and harsh rules in the 1480s that cut Jews off from Christian neighbors. It ends with the expulsion edict of 1492 and the fate of named leaders of the community. Rich Jews named in the account include members of the Chacon family, Eleasar Tello, and Moses Balid.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bedan-2718:
Bedan is a puzzle name in Samuel's farewell speech, where Samuel lists him among judges who saved Israel. No such judge appears in the Book of Judges. The entry weighs four ways to fix the gap, from Samson to Abdon to a scribal slip.

The Greek version reads Barak, and the entry calls that the most likely answer, backed by four named scholars. A second Bedan is a Gileadite in Chronicles, son of Alam and a descendant of Machir. The two men share nothing but the name. On the whole, the entry judges, the Greek reading best fits the place Bedan holds in Samuel's list of heroes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belisario-miria: Miriam Mendes Belisario was an English author and teacher born in London about 1820. She died there in 1885, a granddaughter of Isaac Mendes Belisario. With her sisters she kept a girls' school for many years. Girls of the Sephardic community formed a large share of its pupils under her direction. She compiled a Hebrew and English vocabulary for a choice of daily prayers in 1848. Her later book of 1856 sets out talks at home on the spirit and rules of the Jewish religion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bene-berak-2918: Bene-Berak was a town assigned to the tribe of Dan, as Joshua xix. 45 records. It stood on the coastal plain southeast of Joppa, and the entry identifies it with the modern Ibn Ibrak. The Danites did not hold it for long. Sennacherib's record lists the place as belonging to Zidḳa. In later times Bene-Berak became the seat of Akiba's school, a point the entry supports with a Talmud citation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernays-isaac-k:
Isaac Bernays, known as Ḥakam Bernays, was chief rabbi in Hamburg. Born at Mayence in 1792, he died at Hamburg on May 1, 1849. He studied at Würzburg under a famed Talmudist, then worked as a private tutor and scholar. Hamburg chose him in 1821, where a strict orthodox man with modern schooling was wanted.

He took the post on firm terms, with all religious and school bodies under his own hand. From 1822 he remade the Talmud Torah school, adding German, science, geography, and history to its lessons. By 1827 it stood as a sound public elementary school.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beth-shittah-pl: Beth-Shittah means "place of acacia-trees." It was a place near Abel-meholah. The Midianites fled toward it from Gideon. Judges tells that flight in one verse. The name occurs only there in the Bible. The entry is just three short lines. It adds one plain fact. The place has not been identified.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bible-exegesis-:
Bible Exegesis is a vast survey of Bible interpretation. It begins with instruction in the Miḳra itself. Pupils learned to divide sentences and words correctly. Scribes also had to know the Targum. That Aramaic rendering made the text clear at once. Synagogues were the centers of this teaching. Public reading joined text and Targum together.

The survey follows the traditional literature onward. Mishnah and Tosefta grew from school tradition. Medieval chapters reach philosophic commentary in Spain and Provence. Levi Ben Gershon stands out as a strict Aristotelian. He summed up maxims from the Bible narrative. The closing bibliography lists modern critical introductions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blum-david-3418: David Blum was a German Talmudist. He lived in the mid-sixteenth century. He served as rabbi at Sulzburg near Freiburg. Contemporaries ranked him among Germany's best authorities. Joseph ha-Levi Ashkenazi was proud to be his pupil. Blum copied and compiled various works. Hamburg's library holds his copied "Niẓẓaḥon." It also holds his collection of legal documents. His identity remains uncertain in places. He may match David b. Moses Blumes. That man was Luria's friend in Palestine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-braham-john-sta:
John Braham, whose stage name replaced John Abraham, was an English tenor singer. He was born in London in 1774 and died there on Feb. 17, 1856. Orphaned young, he sang as a chorister in a London synagogue.

A former choir mate, Leoni, adopted and taught Braham. He made his debut at Covent Garden on April 21, 1787. Wealthy Abraham Goldsmid later became his patron. Study and singing in Italy from 1798 raised his craft. From 1801 his career was a run of triumphs at Covent Garden and elsewhere. He also composed operas, including The English Fleet in 1803. Costly theatre ventures later ruined him, and he sang on until 1852.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brindisi-hebrew: Brindisi is a seaport on the coast of Calabria, Italy. Ancient Romans embarked there for the East. Jews settled there at a very early period, the entry says without a date. The Talmud tells that four noted Mishnaic doctors, Gamaliel among them, returned home from this city. Benjamin of Tudela found ten Jewish families living there in his time. All ten families were engaged in the art of dyeing, he reports. That brief record closes with two modern source notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bulgaria-3818:
Bulgaria was a principality of southeastern Europe under Turkish suzerainty. The entry traces its Jews from early times. A first community formed at Nicopolis under Trajan. Czar Krum brought Jewish prisoners from Thessaly in 811, and Byzantine Jews settled widely in 967. Those Greek rite Jews kept customs such as picking a chief rabbi from another city.

Later chapters cover a Bulgarian kingdom founded in 1189, trade offices on the Danube, and growth under Assen II. Long sections follow the Jews under Turkish and later rule, town by town. The entry closes with a place by place count of Jewish residents. Sofia leads with 8,000, and the total given is 29,860.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caleb-3918:
Caleb, of the tribe of Judah, was one of the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan. He and Joshua alone brought back a hopeful report. For that faith, they alone of the Egypt generation lived to enter the land. After the conquest Caleb received Hebron and its region. He offered his daughter Achsah to whoever took the city, and his younger brother Othniel won her.

Rabbinic sources merge this Caleb with a son of Hezron and spin tales from his names. He prayed at the patriarchs' graves in Hebron and drew a sword to force the spies to carry fruit back. A critical view closes the entry. It calls Caleb the ancestor figure of the Calebite clan and sorts the story into layers from different writers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carasso-david-s: David Samuel Carasso was a Jewish traveler born at Salonica, in Turkey. A business trip took him to Yemen, in Arabia, in 1874. He used the trip to study how the Jews of that region lived. He crossed the whole inner country, through Sada, Aseer, and Sanaa, and gave Sanaa's community his closest care. His account came out in Judeo Spanish at Constantinople in 1875. To help Yemen's Jews he wrote to the Anglo Jewish Association and to Constantinople's chief rabbi. That appeal brought a chief rabbi out to Sanaa.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-castanho-abraha: Abraham Castanho was a Spanish poet who lived at Amsterdam in the middle of the seventeenth century. He wrote an elegy on the martyr Abraham Nuñez of Bernal. Bernal was burned at Cordova on May 3, 1655. The elegy was placed in a memorial volume honoring Bernal. That volume was probably published at Amsterdam in 1656. The short entry names no other poem or post for Castanho, and gives no dates for his own birth or death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chalphi-4218: Chalphi was the father of Judas. Judas was one of two captains who stayed at their posts when all the others under Jonathan had fled. That stand came at the battle of the plain of Nasor, as I Maccabees xi. 70 reports. Josephus also refers to Chalphi, the entry notes, but calls him Chapsios. The hosted text is only a few lines. It gives that family link, that battle detail, and that second form of the name, and no further facts about Chalphi himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cheyne-thomas-k:
Thomas Kelley Cheyne, an English Christian biblical critic, was born at London on Sept. 18, 1841. He served as Oriel professor of biblical exegesis at Oxford. Schooled at Merchant Taylors' and Worcester College, he also studied under Ewald at Göttingen. Scholarships in Hebrew marked his early promise.

For a long time Cheyne stood almost alone in England as a voice for the higher criticism. With Driver he supplied readings and renderings for the Queen's Printers' Bible of 1881. Isaiah drew his chief care, with editions and translations from 1869 to 1898. His Bampton Lectures of 1891, on the origin of the Psalter, may be his weightiest work. He wrote on Job and Solomon, and gave a history of Old Testament criticism in 1893. Of late he showed great daring in emending the biblical text, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coblenz-11118:
Coblenz, a Prussian city on the Rhine, drew Jewish settlers between 1135 and 1159, first named in Cologne's Jewish archives book. A custom-house note from about 1100 already charged Jews four denarii for each slave offered for sale. Benjamin of Tudela found a large community there between 1160 and 1173.

Hard years dominate the record. More than ten Jews died in a persecution of 1265. Attackers struck again in 1334, and in 1349 the Flagellants killed nearly all. Houses faced seizure and sale from 1352 on. Expulsion came in 1418 under Archbishop Otto. Later pages list rabbis of the renewed community, among them Jair Hayyim Bacharach from 1666 to 1669 and Jacob Kohen Poppers, whose responsa are still named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohn-ferdinand-:
Ferdinand Julius Cohn, a German botanist and zoologist, was born in Breslau on Jan. 24, 1828, and died there on June 25, 1898. He took his doctorate at Berlin in 1847 with a study of seed physiology. Back at Breslau he became a privat-docent in 1850, though as a Jew he waited a year to take the oath and teach.

Chairs followed in 1859 and 1872. The Botanical Institute he fought for opened in 1888, and the city gave him its freedom at seventy. His writing ran past 150 papers and books, on plant life, bacteria, and much else. He founded and edited a plant biology journal from 1875 until his death. The entry notes he was buried in the row of honor in the Jewish cemetery.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coney-2318:
Coney is the traditional rendering of the Hebrew shafan, a small plant-eating animal named four times in the Old Testament. Leviticus and Deuteronomy class it as unclean, chewing the cud yet lacking the split hoof. Proverbs counts the shefannim among four small yet wise things: a feeble folk that make their houses in the rocks.

The entry attacks the rendering itself. A true coney is a European animal unknown to Israelites, and it does not live in rocks. Bochart argued for the jerboa and was answered in turn. Shaw and Bruce proposed the rock hyrax, called Israel's lamb, backed by the Arabic word wabr used for shafan. The entry leaves the hyrax view standing, noting the animal's range from Abyssinia to Syria.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cowan-phineas-4: Phineas Cowan was an English merchant, volunteer officer, and alderman. He was born at Chatham in 1832. He died at Buxton on Oct. 22, 1899. He joined the Third London Rifles in 1863 with three companies of his own workmen. He rose to lieutenant-colonel before retiring in 1880. London made him sheriff in 1883 and alderman of Cordwainer ward in 1885. He sat on the council of the Anglo-Jewish Association. In 1885 he lost the Whitechapel seat to Sir Samuel Montagu.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cuthah-or-cuth-: Cuthah was one of five cities from which Sargon of Assyria brought settlers to replace the exiled Israelites. Lions attacked the newcomers. They read the attacks as a sign that their worship displeased the god of the land. Sargon sent a teacher at their request. The result was a mixed religion and a mixed people, the Cutheans, or Samaritans. Assyrian records place Cuthah near Babylon. Its men served the god Nergal, whose temple there was rebuilt by Nebuchadnezzar. The site is identified with the ruins of Tell Ibrahim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dato-mordecai-b:
Mordecai ben Judah Dato was an Italian rabbi and preacher born in 1527. He lived in various places in the territory of the house of Este and died after 1585. He studied under the cabalist Moses Cordovero and became an adept in the Cabala himself. Scholars such as Azariah de Rossi mentioned him with honor.

Dato's writings follow the Cabala of Cordovero and Luria. He added marginal notes to a compendium of his pupil Samuel Gallico's work, though editors badly misplaced them in print. His "Migdal Dawid" treated questions of the Cabala, and he also wrote notes on the Zohar. Manuscripts of his sermons, poems, and a commentary on Esther survive.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-death-angel-of-:
Angel of death is the Bible's figure for death as a messenger sent from God. The angel of the Lord smites 185,000 men in the Assyrian camp. A destroyer kills the first-born of Egypt. David sees the destroying angel over Jerusalem with a drawn sword. Later books speak of angels of death in the plural.

Rabbinic writing gives this angel a large role. He takes his orders from God, yet once allowed to destroy, he does not separate good from bad. Confession and acts of kindness can hold him off. The entry retells legends of his contests, above all the long struggle over the soul of Moses, who died, the rabbis said, by God's kiss.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dessauer-gabrie: Gabriel L. Dessauer was a Hungarian rabbi and author born at Neutra in 1805. He studied under Moses Sofer at Presburg and served forty years as rabbi at Balaton-Kojár, where he died on June 1, 1878. His books include a German translation of Job with commentary, printed at Presburg in 1838. The same year brought his work on the ritual slaughter laws of the Shulḥan Aruk. He also wrote on Talmud tales and on Genesis, and published a book of sermon sketches in 1862.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-disabilities-52:
Legal disabilities imposed on Jews in the Middle Ages form the subject here. The entry divides such laws into two groups. One group treats Jews as followers of an alien creed the state church must guard against. The other treats them as a foreign nation with no native rights.

Under the first view, Jews kept life, liberty, and property but lost many civil rights. Under the second, they held rights only by a ruler's grant and could be expelled at will. The entry traces both views through Roman, Germanic, and Muslim law. It then follows the long list of limits placed on trades and public life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dreyfus-case-l-:
The Dreyfus case centers on the trials of Captain Alfred Dreyfus, a French army officer, in 1894 and 1899. The entry calls it the best-known cause célèbre of modern times. It split France in two and drew the world's eyes. Ministries, and even presidents, rose and fell on it.

Its roots lay in rising anti-Semitism in France, fed by Drumont's La France Juive of 1886. Attacks on Jewish officers in La Libre Parole set the stage. Dreyfus was convicted on a document called the bordereau. The long entry follows the fight to clear him, the cover given to Esterhazy, and the Staff Office's tactics against men like Scheurer-Kestner.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ecija-5418:
Ecija is a Spanish city in the province of Seville. Its entry is a grim chain of charges and massacres. A ritual murder charge arose under a King Alfonso. The accused Jew was jailed on Passover eve. At the mere report, the crowd rose in fury.

Many Jews saved themselves in the houses of nobles. The archdeacon Ferrand Martinez, born at Ecija, found ready ground there. At his word the synagogue was destroyed in December 1390. The great massacre of 1391 then spread from Seville to Ecija. Most of its Jews joined the Church. Maranos were treated just as cruelly in 1473, until knights rescued a few.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elder-rebelliou:
A rebellious elder was a trained judge who defied the high court's reading of the Law. In the days of the Sanhedrin this was a capital crime. The penalty was death by strangulation. The rule rests on a passage in Deuteronomy. By Talmudic teaching it covered no common man. It covered an ordained rabbi or judge of set standing.

Most of the entry walks through the court process step by step. Three courts sat in Jerusalem at set spots by the Temple. The accused elder pled his case before the lowest court first. If that court had no tradition on the point, all went to the next court. The Great Sanhedrin then gave the ruling of the Torah. If the elder still held out and taught his view, he faced trial and death. Rabbi Akiba set the death at the next feast, when crowds were in town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-liepman: Eliezer Liepmann Brody was a cabalist of Galicia. He lived in the eighteenth century. The entry names two of his books. Both are cabalistic readings of books of the Bible. One treats the Psalms and came out at Vienna in 1792. It carries a long preface of its own. The other treats the book of Proverbs. That volume came out at Zolkiev in 1788. No facts of his life are given beyond his books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-endler-samuel-b: Samuel Benzion Endler was a Talmudist of Prague, most likely. He lived in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. His book bears the title Emunat Yisrael, Faith of Israel. It treats morals and the dogmas of the faith. It draws on Maimonides, Judah ha-Levi, and Nahmanides. Other old masters feed into its pages as well. Prague printed the work in the year 1832. The entry gives no dates or posts for the man himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-epilepsy-5818:
Epilepsy is defined here as a disease of the nervous system marked by attacks of unconsciousness, with or without convulsions. The entry links it to family weakness toward nervous illness. It also names syphilis and alcoholism in parents as factors. Marriage between close kin does not cause it, the entry says, but can make a weak tendency worse.

Most of the entry compares rates among Jews and others. At one Paris hospital, only 39 Jewish epileptics were seen in thirteen years. At the Rothschild Hospital, 77 cases appeared among 25,591 Jewish patients over twenty-five years. Figures from Moscow and New York point the same way. The entry concludes that Jews seem less liable to the disease.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-farhi-hayyim-mu:
Hayyim Farhi was minister to the pashas of Damascus and Acre, born at Damascus about the middle of the eighteenth century. He was killed in 1820. His father Saul had served as treasury minister at Damascus. The young Farhi showed such skill that Ahmad Jazzar, pasha of Acre and Damascus, raised him to minister. For over forty years he governed part of the Turkish empire, the entry says.

During Napoleon's siege of Acre in 1799, Farhi was the soul of the defense, foiling the French plans. Napoleon tried in vain to win him over. After Jazzar died in 1808, Sulaiman Pasha kept him in office. Under Sulaiman's heir Abdallah, once his own pupil, Farhi was murdered and his body thrown into the sea, despite Jewish pleas for burial.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankl-ludwig-a:
Ludwig August Frankl, Ritter von Hochwart, was an Austrian poet and writer. He was born at Chrast, Bohemia, on February 3, 1810, and died at Vienna on March 12, 1894. He studied medicine at Vienna and in Italy, taking his degree at Padua. He practised only a short time. In 1838 he became secretary and archivist of the Vienna Jewish congregation. He held that post for over forty years. His first book of ballads won him a place among Viennese writers in 1832.

Frankl greeted the Vienna revolution of 1848 with a famous poem on the university. It spread in half a million copies. He was wounded in the rising of that October. In 1856 he went to Jerusalem and helped found a Jewish school there. He also worked for an asylum for the blind. The emperor gave him his noble title in 1876, and Vienna made him a free citizen in 1880.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fulda-6418:
Fulda, a district town on the River Fulda in Hessen-Cassel, held a Jewish community by the twelfth century. Its fame rests sadly on a chain of massacres. On December 28, 1238, Crusaders and townsfolk killed 34 Jews after a blood charge over five dead boys. Further killings came in 1309 and again in 1349, at the time of the Black Death.

Jews were driven out in 1671 but soon let back in. The town produced noted Talmudists. Meir ben Baruch ha-Levi, who brought rabbinical ordination to Germany in 1379, came from the district. In 1890 Fulda counted 525 Jews among 13,125 people. By 1903 the count had risen to 650.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-garmon-nehorai-: Nehorai Garmon, rabbi of Tunis and a poet, was born at Tripoli about 1682 and died at Tunis in 1760. He came to Tunis at age twenty and studied Talmud under Isaac Lombroso. He followed Lombroso in the rabbinate. His book Yeter ha-Baz holds notes on the Talmud and on Maimonides. Eleven of his poems print with it. In his preface he tells that he lost much of his writing in an attack on the Jewish quarter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gluge-gottlieb-:
Gottlieb Gluge, also called Théophile, was a physician born at Brakel in Westphalia on June 18, 1812; he died at Nizza on Dec. 22, 1898. He took his medical degree at Berlin in 1835. Two years earlier he had written a prize essay on influenza, and the entry credits him as the first physician to describe that disease.

After study in Paris, Gluge became professor of physiology at Brussels in 1838, on the backing of Humboldt and Arago, and kept the chair until 1873. He also served for years as physician to the King of Belgium. He was among the first doctors to study diseased tissue under the microscope, and a parasite he found in the stickleback bears the name Glugea microspora.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-guastalla-enric:
Enrico Guastalla was an Italian soldier. He was born at Guastalla in 1828 and died at Milan on Sept. 28, 1903. Though raised for trade, he joined the army as a volunteer in 1848. He fought in Rome's defense and won a lieutenancy for bravery at Vascello. Suspected of revolt, he fled to London and met Mazzini. In 1859 he returned and joined Garibaldi. He was wounded at Volturno in 1860.

Guastalla served again in 1866 under Garibaldi at several towns. He retired as a major. He held the rank of knight commandant of the Order of St. Maurice and St. Lazarus. He also sat in the Italian Parliament for Varese.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ha-zebi-7418: Ha-Ẓebi was a Hebrew weekly published at Jerusalem by Eliezer Benjudah, beginning in 1876. Late in 1899 he added a Hebrew supplement on agriculture called "Ha-'Iḳḳar," but it lasted only a few months. Officials suspended the paper toward the end of 1900. It then resumed under the title "Hashḳafah," controlled by Ḥemdah, Benjudah's wife. The short entry gives no account of its contents beyond that farming supplement.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hafz-ibn-al-bir:
Ḥafẓ ibn al-Birr al-Ḳuṭi was an author of the eleventh century, or earlier. He turned the Book of Psalms into Arabic rime. Moses ibn Ezra quotes a passage from his preface, and Solomon ibn Gabirol quotes his sentences. A copy of the work, made in 1625, survives in the Escurial library.

Who he was is disputed. Steinschneider held that he was a Jew, and that Christian traces in the work came from later hands. Hammer called him a Jewish renegade, and Neubauer made him an Arab or Syrian Christian. Even his name is unsure: one reading gives al-Fuṭi, not al-Ḳuṭi. The byname may mean "the Goth," that is, the Spaniard, or it may point to Ḳuṭ in Balkh.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hama-b-bisa-bis:
Ḥama b. Bisa was an amora of the third century. He formed the middle link of a scholarly trio, outstripped by his successor as he had outstripped his predecessor. Like many students he left home and family for study, and he was gone twelve years. Coming back, he went first to the study house so as not to startle his family.

There a young man matched him in debate, and Ḥama wished such a son were his. At home the young man entered, and his wife's cry — "Does a father ever rise before a son?" — revealed Hoshaiah. Once father, son, and grandfather Bisa argued a point of civil law, and Bisa sided with the boy. The entry also sifts a tangled question: whether this Hoshaiah is Hoshaiah Rabbah, and whether the father's name has been mis-copied in one passage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanina-of-sura-: Hanina of Sura was a Babylonian scholar of the fifth century, the junior of Mar Zutra. His birth came from a family repair. His mother had so disliked his father that she would not live with him. Mar Zutra brought the couple together again. In haggadah he does not appear. In halakah he is quoted as an authority and reconciles conflicting opinions. His best-known point is plain. Since the "bitter water" test no longer exists, a man must not lightly suspect his wife. It may force a needless separation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haskalah-lit-wi:
Haskalah, a Hebrew word for wisdom, names the Jewish enlightenment movement of the late eighteenth century. Its followers, called Maskilim, urged Jews to drop their separateness. They pushed study of Hebrew and of modern subjects in place of Talmud study alone. They also backed farming and crafts for Jews.

The article starts with Moses Mendelssohn, whose fame as a German thinker showed what a cultured Jew could do. His German rendering of the Pentateuch became a bridge to wider learning. Hartwig Wessely then set out a program for Austrian Jews. Attacks on that program, the entry says, only helped the cause spread.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hebrew-language:
The Hebrew language is the tongue of the Old Testament and of most later Jewish writing. Bible writers call it the language of Canaan or the Jews' language. Later Jewish writers call it the Holy Tongue, to split it from everyday Aramaic. The name Hebrew for the language first shows in Greek-age writings.

The article places Hebrew inside the Semitic family. It stands close to the speech of Moab and Phoenicia. In sound it sits between Arabic and Aramaic. Some old sound splits are lost in its writing, which keeps one letter where Arabic keeps two. The study then runs through sounds, forms, and the tongue's long history in use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hekdesh-bet-hek: Hekdesh, short for a phrase meaning house consecrated to the needy, was the Hebrew name for an asylum or a hospital. The name turns up in many medieval Jewish documents. The entry says its origin reaches back to pre-Christian times. Readers are sent to the articles on Charity and Hospital for the fuller story. A few studies of Jewish life in France and Egypt are cited in passing. The notice is only a short paragraph. It gives no single house, town, or date of its own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hertzka-theodor:
Theodor Hertzka, born at Budapest on July 13, 1845, was an Austrian economist and journalist. He studied at Vienna and Budapest. In 1872 he joined the Neue Freie Presse in Vienna. In 1879 he founded the Wiener Allgemeine Zeitung, which he edited until 1886.

Hertzka was called the Austrian Bellamy for a social vision of the future printed in 1890. His other books treated Austrian company law, the nature of money, and trade policy. He urged a gold standard for Austria. He also proposed a cheap flat fare for railway passengers. Later works covered social development and exchange rates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hippos-7718:
Hippos was one of the cities of the Decapolis in Palestine, though its site is uncertain. In the Talmud it appears as Susita, its Hebrew name. It faced Tiberias across the lake. Merchants crossed between the two cities often.

The district around Hippos was called Hippene. Alexander Jannæus conquered it, Pompey freed it, and Augustus later gave it to Herod. After Herod's death it left Jewish rule and was counted a Greek city. At the Roman war's start, Jews under Justus ravaged it, and its people then massacred Jews. In Christian times it became a bishop's see. A coin with a horse bears its name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hubsch-adolph-7:
Adolph Hubsch was an American preacher born at Lipto-Szent-Miklos in Hungary on September 18, 1830. He died in New York on October 10, 1884. He taught at a Jewish school from 1845 and fought as an officer in the Hungarian Revolution of 1848. He then studied Talmud until 1854 and took a doctorate at Prague in 1861.

In 1866 Hubsch moved to America and led Congregation Ahawath Chesed in New York. He brought in a moderate Reform ritual, and his prayer book spread to other congregations. His school taught more than 400 children. His chief scholarly work treats the five Megilloth with a Syriac Targum. A book of Arabic sayings appeared in 1885.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-shem-tob-is: Isaac ibn Shem-Tob was a philosophical commentator of the fifteenth century. He was the younger brother of Joseph ibn Shem-Tob. Both followed Maimonides and sided against their own father, who had attacked Maimonides in his Book of Beliefs. Isaac's commentary on the Guide is known only through a quote in Moses Alashkar. He is probably the same Isaac who wrote on Ghazali's Metaphysics at Aguilar do Campo in 1459. The entry is short and rests on two named authorities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-inn-8118:
Inns begin in the Bible as "malon," the night stop of caravans: perhaps only a wall or enclosure near a well, where tents could be pitched and cattle kept from straying. Tradition put an inn built by Chimham near Bethlehem. By New Testament times real inns existed, with a named innkeeper; the good Samaritan left his patient at one, and a party of Levites left a sick comrade at another.

Medieval Jewish communities kept a communal inn, often joined to the dancing-hall, where travelers without acquaintances could stay a night or two free. Beggars slept on the ground floor and paying guests above. In eighteenth-century Paris all Jewish travelers had to stop at a special Jews' inn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-jekut:
Jacob ben Jekuthiel was a French Talmudic scholar born at Rouen who died at Arras in 1023. He is known for one errand. In 1007 King Robert of France set loose a persecution of Lorraine's Jews so fierce that women jumped into rivers to escape the mob. Jacob carried a petition to Pope John XVII, begging him to stop it.

Duke Richard seized Jacob on the road, with his wife and four sons, and he escaped death only by a miracle. He left his eldest son as a hostage and went on to Rome. His gift of seven gold marks and two hundred pounds moved the pope to send an envoy ordering Robert to stop. Jacob waited four years in Rome for the envoy's return. In 1023 Count Baldwin of Flanders invited him to settle at Arras; he came with thirty friends and died three months later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-meir-:
Jacob ben Meir Tam, called Rabbenu Tam, was the most prominent of the French tosafists. He was born at Ramerupt in 1100 and died at Troyes on June 9, 1171. His mother was Rashi's daughter Jochebed. His father, his brother Samuel (the RaSHBaM), and Joseph Tob Elem taught him. After his father's death he ran an academy at Ramerupt.

On May 8, 1147, French crusaders broke into his home, robbed him of all but his books, and gave him five wounds in the head. A passing prince saved him, for the promise of a horse worth five marks. At Troyes he led the first French rabbinical assembly in 1160. The entry honors him as head of the tosafist school. In the "Sefer ha-Yashar" he argues by chained questions; he told a pupil, my questions are their own answers. Some blame for later pilpul is laid at his door.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-japhia-he-shine: Japhia, a name glossed as meaning that he shines, covers three subjects in the Bible. First is a king of Lachish, one of five kings who joined against Joshua and were killed at Makkedah.
