Second is a son of David born in Jerusalem, placed eighth of eleven sons in one list and tenth of thirteen in another. Third is a place on the border of Zebulun, matched with Japha, a strong village of Galilee, and with the modern Yafa near Nazareth, where Robinson found about thirty houses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-johanan-ben-mer: Johanan ben Meriya was a Palestinian teacher of the fourth and fifth centuries. He appears often in the Jerusalem Talmud on both law and story matters, with story the larger share. In one debate on whether a prophet may use any high place as an altar for a time, Johanan backed the yes side with verses from Joshua and Samuel. He also passed on a story teaching from Johanan ben Nappaha. The entry is brief and names no work or post of his.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joshua-b-karha-: Joshua b. Karha was a tanna of the second century and a fellow worker of the patriarch Simeon b. Gamaliel II. Some wrongly took him for a son of Akiba. Only a few of his legal rulings survive, since most of his sayings were haggadic in kind. He was bald, and a heretic once mocked him for it; Joshua answered with quick wit. He lived to a great age. When he blessed Judah ha-Nasi, he wished him half as long a life as his own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-poki-puki: Judah Poki ben Eliezer Tshelebi was a Karaite scholar who lived at Constantinople and died before 1501. He was a nephew of Elijah Bashyazi. Judah traveled through Palestine, Egypt, Babylonia, and Persia to learn the Karaite writings kept in those lands. His book Sha'ar Yehudah treats the laws on forbidden marriages and was printed by his son Isaac in 1581. In it he quotes another work of his, on fixing the new moon. A prayer book and works on grammar and poetry are also tied to his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judo-german-148:
Judaeo-German is the language spoken by the German Jews in Russia, former Poland, Austria, and Rumania, and lately in America and South Africa. In Germany itself it was fast dying out. Before the end of the fifteenth century, Hebrew-letter German shows up only now and then in rabbis' writings. The entry finds no sign of a set Jewish dialect before printing.

Print spread Judaeo-German books widely, and by the seventeenth century scholars were sketching its grammar. They marked its old words, its many Hebrew loans, and above all its Hebrew letters. The entry weighs why the dialect arose and gives specimens of its speech from many lands and years. Later pages list handbooks and studies of the tongue for readers who want more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-julich-latin-ju: Juelich is a city of Rhenish Prussia near Aix-la-Chapelle, set on the river Ruhr. In 1227 Emperor Frederick II gave Count Wilhelm of Juelich free hand over any Jews who settled in his lands. Whether Wilhelm used that right is not known. Jewish families were surely there by the end of the thirteenth century. Like many German towns, its Jewish community was wiped out in 1349, at the time of the Black Death. In 1901 the town held 102 Jews out of 5,385 people.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kahan-abraham-9:
Abraham Kahan was a Russian Hebrew author born on Dec. 19, 1874, at Skomorochy, near Jitomir. He wrote and edited works in Hebrew on earlier Jewish scholars and on Jewish history. His books include letters of S. D. Luzzatto, put into Hebrew from the Italian, and letters of Samuel Vita Lolli with a life of Lolli.

Kahan also wrote a Hebrew life of Moses Ḥayyim Luzzatto, a history of the Jews in Rome, and a Hebrew grammar based on the work of S. D. Luzzatto. He edited a critical Hebrew commentary on the Bible and wrote the part on Genesis. The entry notes his steady work for Hebrew journals such as "Ha-Meliẓ" and "Ha-Shiloaḥ."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ki-lo-na-eh-931:
"Ki lo Na'eh" is a hymn for the home rite of Passover eve. Its name comes from its first words. It is one of the latest parts of the Seder Haggadah. The entry dates it to the fifteenth century. It was meant at first for the first night only. "Addir Hu" was its match for the second night. For more than two centuries both have been sung on each night.

The hymn is built like "Addir Hu" but with a twist. It runs to eight stanzas that stay the same but for three changing words. Those words carry the letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order. The entry notes one strong tune tied to the hymn. The catchiest form stands in Rittangel's Haggadah of 1644. A paraphrase in English is given to show the letter scheme.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kohen-zedek-ii-:
Kohen Ẓedeḳ II, Kahana ben Joseph, held the gaonate of Pumbedita from 917 to 935. On taking office he challenged how revenue was split between Sura and Pumbedita. Sura had taken two-thirds and Pumbedita one-third. He argued that Pumbedita was then larger and costlier to run, and an equal split was agreed.

Power struggles fill the rest of the account. Kohen Ẓedeḳ blocked the exilarch Mar ʿUḳba over the income from Chorazan, then refused to accept Mar ʿUḳba's nephew David ben Zakkai as exilarch. David answered by naming a rival gaon in 918. The entry sets two conflicting versions of the feud side by side, one from Nathan ha-Babli and one from Sherira Gaon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-landesmann-hein:
Heinrich Landesmann, an Austrian poet and writer born at Nikolsburg on Aug. 9, 1821, died at Brünn on Dec. 4, 1902. Sickly from childhood, he lost most sight and hearing by age fifteen and later went fully blind. Poems in journals began at sixteen. His first large work, a five-canto legend dated 1843, came at age twenty-two.

Writing as Hieronymus Lorm, a name taken to shield his family from Vienna police, Landesmann gained his public voice. A dark strain in his verse won him the label of a lyrical Schopenhauer. His first novel, dated 1855, treats a modern Jew's fight against the bias of his fellow citizens. Dozens of later novels, poems, and essays run to 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lehmann-joseph-:
Joseph Lehmann, a German journalist, was born at Glogau on Dec. 28, 1801, and died at Berlin on Feb. 19, 1873. He reached Berlin at fifteen and found work as an office boy in a bank. Self-taught study carried him into journalism instead.

From 1827 to 1842 Lehmann held an editorial post on the "Preussische Staatszeitung." In 1832 he founded the "Magazin für die Literatur des In- und Auslandes." The journal linked German readers with foreign writing in a way no rival matched. He also led the Gesellschaft der Freunde for decades. He helped found the Hochschule für die Wissenschaft des Judenthums and aided poor students at Breslau.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lewin-adolf-991: Adolf Lewin, a German rabbi and author, was born at Pinne, Posen, on Sept. 23, 1843. He studied at the Jewish Theological Seminary and at Breslau University. In 1872 he became rabbi at Kozmin, then at Coblenz. In 1886 he was called to Freiburg-im-Breisgau. His prize essay treats the religious disputation of Rabbi Jehiel. Other works cover the Maccabean rising, the Jews of Freiburg, and Judaism and non-Jews. He also wrote the section on Jewish history and travel writing in a survey of Jewish literature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lipschitz-rudol: Rudolf Lipschitz was a German mathematician born on May 14, 1832, at Königsberg, East Prussia, and he died at Bonn on Oct. 8, 1903. He took his doctorate at Königsberg in 1853 and began teaching at Bonn in 1857. He became professor at Breslau in 1862 and at Bonn in 1864. His books include a textbook of analysis from 1877 to 1880 and studies on sums of squares. He also wrote on science and the state and on theoretical mechanics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lysias-10218:
Lysias, the Syrian regent who fought the Maccabean revolt, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A statesman of royal descent, he was made regent by Antiochus Epiphanes in 166 or 165. He also served as guardian of the young heir, Antiochus V. His orders were to crush the Jewish rebellion. He died in 162.

The article weighs the two books of Maccabees against each other. After his generals lost, Lysias led a strong army into Judea himself and was beaten at Beth-Zur. He made peace with Judas Maccabeus, then returned with the boy king and won at Beth-Zechariah. A rival claimant forced him to settle with the Jews instead of finishing the siege of Jerusalem. The entry calls him a better politician than his king. He saw that Jewish religious freedom could not be taken by force.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-makshirin-predi:
Makshirin, meaning predisposings, names a Mishnah tractate described in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It is the eighth tractate of the order Tohorot, on purities. Six chapters in the Mishnah and three in the Tosefta make up the work. Its subject is how liquids make food able to contract ritual uncleanness.

The article builds the law from one verse of Leviticus. Food touched by a dead reptile stays clean unless water was first put upon the seed. The rabbis read the Hebrew verb two ways, put or one puts. From that double reading they required intention: moisture readies food only when it was wanted. Chapter one then works the rule through cases of rain, dew, and shaken trees. A striking precedent comes from Jerusalem's last war, when fig-cakes hidden underwater from robbers were ruled unaffected. The entry opens a window on the fine logic of purity law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marini-solomon-:
Solomon ben Isaac Marini, an Italian rabbi of Padua, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He died in 1670, having outlived his whole rabbinical generation. He was the only rabbi at Padua who survived the plague of 1631. That epidemic had decimated the community around him.

The article credits his gifts with the recovery that followed. His wisdom and eloquence did much to restore order after the plague. His one named work is Tikkun Olam, a commentary on Isaiah printed at Verona in 1652. He was renowned alike as scholar, teacher, and pastor. Among his pupils was Isaac Hayyim Cantarini, himself a physician and rabbi. The entry also names his brother Shabbethai, a physician who died in 1685. The short notice preserves the rabbi who held Padua together after catastrophe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mayer-sigmund-1:
Sigmund Mayer was an Austrian physician and histologist. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Bechtheim, in Rhine-Hesse, on December 27, 1842, and studied at Heidelberg, Giessen, and Tübingen, taking his medical degree in 1865. After further work at Heidelberg and Vienna, he moved to Prague in 1870 and rose through the German university there. In 1884 he became its professor of histology, the science of tissues.

The entry counts about sixty essays from his pen, scattered through Austrian and German medical journals and the great physiological handbooks of his day. He also wrote a pocket manual of histology, printed at Prague in 1887. His lasting marks are practical and observational. He was among the first to use methylene blue staining in microscopy. He also described the chromaffin cells of the sympathetic nerve and the breaking down and regrowth of nervous tissue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-memra-ma-amar-o:
Memra, the "Word" of God, is set out by Kaufmann Kohler in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The term names God's creative and directive speech. It is the power by which He acts in the world. The Targums use it in place of "the Lord." They do so wherever Scripture threatens to make God sound bodily or human.

The article builds the case in layers. In the Bible the word of the Lord is two things at once. It is the message brought to prophets. It is the force that made the heavens and melts the ice. In apocryphal and rabbinic writing that word hardens into a personified agent. God creates "by the Ma'amar" and sends His word to heal. The liturgy praises Him as the one who made the universe with His word. Kohler traces how a figure of speech became a doctrine, standing between God and the world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-ben-n:
Born at Narbonne about 1120, Meshullam ben Nathan became a French tosafist and a member of that city's rabbinical college. Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. About 1150 he signed a responsum issued at Narbonne, then settled at Melun in northern France.

At Melun he gained wide authority, held the official title of Rab, and corresponded with leading French rabbis, including those of Paris. His lenient rulings angered R. Tam, and after a sharp exchange of letters Meshullam gave way under threat of excommunication. The article closes with scholarly debate over whether he and Meshullam of Narbonne were one man or two.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mieses-10818:
Mieses was a family of German and Austrian scholars of the nineteenth century, given a joint entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by six contributors. The first and fullest sketch belongs to Fabius Mieses, a Galician writer and philosopher born at Brody in 1824. Raised on Hebrew literature alone until fifteen, he was hailed early as a genius.

At Dresden, in his father-in-law's house, Fabius met Rapoport and other Maskilim and found a philosophy teacher who conversed with him in Hebrew on daily walks. He taught himself German, French, Italian, Latin, mathematics, and astronomy, and wrote for Fürst's Orient from 1846. His 1878 Hebrew poem on faith and Darwinism, Ha-Emunah weha-Tebunah, secured his lasting place among Hebrew poets.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moriah-11018:
Moriah receives its own article in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, written by Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn. In the Bible the name points to two places. One is the land where Abraham was told to offer his son Isaac as a sacrifice. The other is the Jerusalem hill where Ornan the Jebusite had a threshing floor, and where Solomon later built the Temple.

The article gathers the rabbis' readings of the name, such as teaching place, place of fear, and place of myrrh. It tracks how old translations, from the Targums to the Septuagint, handled the word. It closes with modern scholars who placed the Isaac story near Shechem and Mount Gerizim instead. As a period reference it shows how Jewish learning around 1900 weighed tradition against new critical study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munk-eduard-112:
Eduard Munk was a German philologist born at Gross Glogau on January 14, 1803, a cousin of Salomon Munk. Isidore Singer and Isidor Warsaw wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied at Breslau and Berlin and became a favorite pupil of August Böckh. His career was spent teaching in schools and as a private tutor.

His religion barred him from the university chair his learning deserved, and the entry says so plainly. He studied on anyway, all his life, and gave the results to the world in books. They include a history of Greek literature and a history of Roman literature, both long in print. His works were translated into English, Spanish, and Russian, and he stayed a faithful, learned Jew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naphtali-b-isaa:
Naphtali ben Isaac ha-Kohen was a Polish-German rabbi born at Ostrov in 1649. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia life. Taken prisoner by Tatars as a boy, he escaped and succeeded his father as rabbi of Ostrov. His fame as a cabalist made rich German communities compete for him.

At Frankfort in 1711 a fire that began in his house destroyed the whole Jewish street. Naphtali was accused of setting it himself to test an amulet he was said to have made. He was jailed, freed only on resigning his rabbinate, and wandered on to Prague and Dresden. In 1719, setting out for Palestine, he died at Constantinople.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nicanor-11518:
Nicanor was a Syrian general sent against the Jews. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Antiochus Epiphanes sent him and Gorgias in 165 B.C. He brought a thousand slave dealers into camp. He meant to sell the captive Jews to them.

Gorgias fell to Judas Maccabeus, and Nicanor fled disguised. Four years later Demetrius sent him against the Jews again. He threatened to make the sanctuary a temple of Dionysus. Judas faced him at Adasa, near Beth-horon. On the thirteenth of Adar, 161, Nicanor was slain. Every man of his army died in that battle. Jews kept the day as Nicanor Day, before Purim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottolenghi-leon:
Leonetto Ottolenghi was an Italian giver of aid from Asti. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Asti on November 3, 1829. He died at Pisa on February 20, 1904. His gifts to his home town fill the short entry.

In 1889 Leonetto rebuilt the Jewish synagogue at Asti. Two years on, he set up a great fair there. He served as the head of that fair himself. In 1898 he spurred a second fair in the town. King Humbert the First came to both of those fairs. On March 14, 1899, the king made him a count. That count's rank was to pass to his heirs in turn. In 1903 he gave Asti a statue of the king.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pereda-12018:
Pereda was a Palestinian teacher of the second amora generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was likely a pupil of Rabbi Ammi. His patience with students became the stuff of legend.

Pereda once scolded pride in noble birth. A scholar without lineage, he said, still counts. A noble without learning deserves the fire. He reached a great age and explained it simply. He came first to the study house each day. He also never failed to honor a priest. None of his legal teachings survive today.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phinehas-12118:
Phinehas guarded the treasury of the Temple at Jerusalem. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He held his post in the Temple's last days. In 70 the city was falling to Rome.

When ruin came, Phinehas betrayed his sacred trust. He gathered the priests' linen coats and girdles. He took purple and silk meant for the curtain. He took the costly spices of the incense too. With this loot he bought his life from the Romans. The Mishnah may name him as keeper of the wardrobe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pochowitzer-puc: Judah Löb Pochowitzer was a preacher at Pinsk. Kaufmann Kohler and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked there in the late seventeenth century. He died in Palestine, whither he had gone before 1681. His Kench Hokmah holds seventeen sermons on penitence. His Derek Hokmah treats morals in thirty-two sections. A later volume joins ethics with notes on the Shulhan Aruk.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-potsdam-12318:
Potsdam is a city in the Prussian province of Brandenburg. Gotthard Deutsch and R. Kälter wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The electors of Brandenburg made their home there. In 1671 the Great Elector sealed a key pact in the city. It let fifty families of Vienna exiles settle in his lands.

The first Potsdam Jew on record is David Michel, in 1690. Jews of Potsdam show up at the Leipsic fair soon after. They are listed there in 1693 and 1694. The congregation counts its start from those years. The entry follows its growth under the Prussian kings. It names the men who led the small community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pseudonymous-li:
False names in Hebrew books are an old and common habit. Joseph Jacobs and Israel Davidson wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A writer takes a great name of the past as his own. Critics place many books of the Old Testament in this class. Later mystics loved the names of Ishmael and Akiba.

Those two were famed as the great teachers of secret lore. So their names lent weight to new mystic books. The choice of names was not always so apt, though. No one can tell why one famed book took its name. The article lists such books and weighs each claim. It asks why writers hid behind the dead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raca-reka-12518:
Raca is a noun formed from a Hebrew word for empty. Crawford Howell Toy and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It names a man with no learning and no morals. The book of Judges uses the root for worthless men. The noun itself stands in the Talmud more than once.

Its places in the Talmud are named one by one. Taanit, Berakot, and Gittin all hold the word. Its plural form stands in a midrash on Ecclesiastes. The word shows up in the New Testament as well. In Matthew it serves as a term of scorn. The article traces the word from Bible to gospel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reckendorf-herm:
Hermann Reckendorf was a German scholar born in Trebitsch in 1825. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died about 1875. He first mastered Hebrew language and literature.

The article says he then studied other Semitic languages. In 1856 he went to Leipzig to study history. Later he lectured at the University of Heidelberg. Inspired by a French novel, he planned a Jewish history in tales. His Secrets of the Jews ran to five volumes. It argued that David's line never vanished. He traced it through Hillel and the Abravanels. He also translated the Koran into Hebrew. The entry shows bold claims backed by footnoted sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-romi-joseph-128:
Joseph Romi is a name wrongly given to Joseph b. Judah Hamiz. Gotthard Deutsch and Ismar Elbogen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was a pupil of Leon of Modena. The entry corrects a mistaken identity at the start.

The article says Hamiz wrote a work called Belil Hamiz. Modena claimed he wrote an introduction for it. The work is not otherwise known, they note. Hamiz may also have written a work called Yode'e Binah. Azulai saw it partly burned and hard to read. Romi wrote a commentary to Zohar Genesis. Moses Zacuto continued that commentary after him. In 1663 he edited the Zohar Hadash at Venice. Three sources support the correction and the works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rozsay-joseph-1:
Joseph Rózsay was a Hungarian physician born at Lackenbach on March 15, 1815. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied at Pesth and Vienna and began practice at Pesth in 1843.

In 1848 Rózsay became head physician of a Hungarian military hospital. He later led Pesth's detention house and poorhouse as chief physician. The Hungarian Academy of Sciences elected him a member in 1864. He was raised to the nobility under the name Muraközi. His Hungarian works include a study of Jewish physicians in the Middle Ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salant-samuel-1:
Samuel Salant was chief rabbi of the Ashkenazic congregations in Jerusalem for decades. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Byelostok on January 2, 1816, he took his name by marriage.

Weak lungs sent Salant to a warm climate, and he reached Jerusalem in 1841. On the way he won Montefiore's friendship at Constantinople, during the Damascus affair. As an emissary he doubled the Wilna fund's gifts for the Holy Land. In 1860 he won equal sharing of funds between Sephardim and Ashkenazim. He became chief rabbi in 1878, succeeding Meïr Auerbach in office.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-juda:
Samuel ben Judah, called Meles Benjudas in Provençal, was a French physician and translator born at Marseilles in 1294. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. At eighteen he studied astronomy at Salon under Sen Astruc de Noves.

In 1322 Samuel was held prisoner with many Jews at Beaucaire, then released. He lived later at Murcia, Tarascon, Aix, and Montélimar in turn. His fame rests on turning scientific works from Arabic into Hebrew. At twenty-seven he finished Averroes' middle commentary on Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics. His Hebrew version later fed a Latin rendering by Abraham de Balmas.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sassoon-13218:
Joseph Jacobs, Goodman Lipkind, and J. Hyams wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on the Sassoon family. The family claims descent from the Ibn Shoshans of Spain. Its first great figure was David Sassoon of Bombay. His son, Sir Albert Abdallah David Sassoon, heads this part of the entry. Born at Bagdad in 1817, Albert died at Brighton in 1896.

Albert led David Sassoon & Co. after his father's death in 1864. The firm was called the Rothschilds of the East. Its Sassoon Dock was the first wet dock built in western India. Its mills gave work to large numbers of Bombay laborers. Albert gave freely to education for every class and creed. He backed the Elphinstone High School and founded scholarships. He also kept up a school for hundreds of Jewish children.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schreyer-jakob-:
Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Jakob Schreyer. He was a Hungarian jurist. Schreyer was born on February 7, 1847, at Ugra. He studied law at Nagyvarad, Debreczin, Budapest, and Vienna. He took his doctorate in 1870. Budapest admitted him to the bar in 1872.

Schreyer sits on the city's aldermanic board in 1905. He also serves the chamber of commerce and industry. In 1893 the justice minister asked him to draft new laws. One bill would revise the bankruptcy rules. The other would govern questions outside the courts. In 1896 he was made a knight of the Order of Francis Joseph. His system of legal procedure won a prize of 100 ducats. The Academy of Science at Budapest gave that award.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semon-sir-felix:
Sir Felix Semon was an English throat specialist born at Danzig on December 8, 1849. Joseph Jacobs and Frederick T. Haneman wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He studied medicine across Europe and at St. Thomas's Hospital in London. War service as an assistant surgeon broke into his training.

Settling in London in 1874, Semon rose to lead throat work at St. Thomas's. Prussia made him a professor, and Queen Victoria knighted him in 1897. He later served the king as a physician. He also founded a laryngology society and edited its journal. The entry traces a doctor who helped build a new medical field.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shebat-a-v-seba:
Shebat is the eleventh sacred and fifth civil month of the Jewish year. Cyrus Adler and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the month. It matches January and February and always holds thirty days. Zechariah and First Maccabees both mention the month by name.

Shebat holds the New Year for Trees, used in tithing rules. Shammai's school set it on the first of the month. Hillel's school set it on the fifteenth, and that view won. Most yearly rain falls before Shebat, so later blossoms count as a new year's crop. The fifteenth remains a semi-holy day. The entry adds odd folk rules about geese killed in Shebat, kept from old tradition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shuman-abraham-:
Abraham Shuman was an American merchant and philanthropist born in Prussia in 1839. Cyrus Adler and Godfrey Morse wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. As a child he crossed to the United States with his parents. The family settled at Newburgh, New York, upstate.

Young Shuman farmed and studied until age thirteen. Then he entered the clothing trade for his living. In 1859 he set up his own business at Boston. His firm became Phillips and Shuman, later A. Shuman and Company. It pioneered making and wholesaling children's clothing in America. Shuman also rose in Boston's civic and banking circles. He led the Boston City Hospital board as its president. The entry presents trade success turned toward public service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-shezuri-:
Simeon Shezuri was a tanna of the second generation and a pupil of Tarfon. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His name came from his home place, Shizur. That place is likely Saijur, west of Kafr Anan. His tomb was said to lie near there.

A few of his legal sayings survive in the Mishnah. They deal with tithes, oaths, divorce, and clean and unclean things. In practice, the law often follows his view. The entry names each Mishnah passage in turn. It helps readers trace how one sage shaped daily Jewish law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sobernheim-jose:
Joseph Friedrich Sobernheim was a German physician and medical author. Isidore Singer and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Königsberg in 1803. He settled as a physician at Berlin. He died there on January 30, 1846.

His books covered the treatment of human diseases in full. One work gave a general health teaching for all classes. His handbook of medicines in table form was revised often. He also wrote on the healing springs of Germany. Other works dealt with diagnosis, toxicology, and physiology. Several of his books were adapted from Latin works by Von Frank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-song-of-the-thr:
The Song of the Three Holy Children is a Greek insertion in Daniel. Joseph Jacobs and Crawford Howell Toy wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It stands after verse twenty-three of chapter three. Under that title two distinct pieces are in fact included. They are the Prayer of Azarias and the Hymn of the Three.

Catholics accept both pieces as canonical Scripture today. Protestants reject them as apocryphal writings instead. The prayer is a national plea confessing past sins. It professes present obedience and begs for mercy from God. The song is a doxology calling all creatures to praise. Its words are drawn largely from the canonical Psalter itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinitz-wilhel:
Wilhelm Steinitz was world chess champion from 1866 to 1894. Isidore Singer and A. Porter wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Steinitz was born at Prague on May 17, 1836. His parents wanted him to become a rabbi. He studied Talmud, but his love of mathematics won out.

Steinitz learned chess at age twelve and carved his own first pieces from wood. In 1866 he beat Anderssen in a match, eight games to six. That win made him champion of the world. He held the title for twenty-eight years. He lost it to Emanuel Lasker in 1894. Steinitz died in New York in 1900. The entry follows a poor student who ruled chess for decades.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tenczer-paul-14:
Paul Tenczer was a Hungarian author and lawmaker who worked for Jewish emancipation. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Tenczer was born in 1836 and died at Budapest in 1905. He studied law at Keszthely and Budapest.

In 1861 he helped found a society for Hungarian Jewish rights. He edited its journal, Magyar Izraelita, for five years. Voters sent him to the Diet in 1868. There he led within the Radical party. He also founded two newspapers and edited one for eighteen years. His efforts made tuition free in Budapest public schools. Few entries show civic work this broad.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tobiads-14418:
The Tobiads were a Jewish party and family of the Maccabean period. Joseph Jacobs and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Josephus and Second Maccabees supply the family story. It needs careful testing, the authors warn. The tale begins with a stubborn high priest named Onias.

Onias refused to pay Egypt a tribute of twenty talents. The king threatened to seize the Jewish land by force. Onias' nephew Joseph rebuked his uncle's selfish rule. He hosted the king's envoy with costly gifts. Then he traveled to plead before Ptolemy himself. At Memphis the king let Joseph ride in his own chariot. Joseph's wit won royal friendship on the spot. His bold tax bid reshaped the family's fortunes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trillinger-elie: Eliezer ben Joseph Yospa Trillinger was an Austrian rabbi of around 1700. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He was also called Eliezer Nin of Nikolsburg. His surname likely comes from Wassertrüdingen, called Trilling by Jews. He served several congregations in his career. In old age he set out for Palestine. Illness stopped him at Wilna, where he died. His son published his Pentateuch sermons in 1707. The book is titled Mishnat Rabbi Eliezer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-uz-14618:
Uz names three biblical men and, more famously, the land of Job. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Genesis lists an Uz among Shem's descendants. Another Uz was Abraham's nephew, eldest son of Nahor. A third belonged to the Horite line of Seir.

As a land, Uz appears three times in Scripture. Job's home is its best-known use. Jeremiah gave its rulers the cup of God's fury. Lamentations places part of Uz within Edom's bounds. Sabeans raided it from the south, Chaldeans from the north. That fixes it on Arabia's northern desert edge. Job's friend Eliphaz came from Teman in Edom. Shalmaneser received tribute from a son of Uzza.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wild-ass-14918:
The wild ass is a shy desert animal of the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. English versions render the Hebrew pere as wild ass. The word appears in Genesis, Job, and the prophets. In every passage the animal seems wild and swift. It is rarely seen in Syria today.

The Talmud classes it among wild animals for ritual law. Its flesh, uniquely, can tear either way under the muscles. Wild asses once turned grain mills. Their flesh fed lions in a king's menagerie. The entry points readers to the article on the tame ass.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-worms-gustave-h:
Gustave-Hippolyte Worms (born 1837) was a French actor of the Paris stage. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He left the Paris stage school in 1857 with top prizes. He won first prize for grave plays and second for gay ones.

In 1859 he first played at the Theatre Francais. A sharp stage chief soon gave him a lead role. His success won him a post in Saint Petersburg. He played there for years to warm crowds. In 1875 he came back to Paris in a famed sad role. Two years later the Comedie-Francaise called him home for good. He joined its core cast the next year. He left the stage in the year 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yom-kippur-kata:
Yom Kippur Katan is the Minor Day of Atonement in Jewish rite. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It falls on the day before each new moon day. Its rite is one of fast and prayer for pardon.

It is far less stern than the great Day of Atonement. The rite is new next to the old set laws. No word of it stands in the great law code. It rose in the 1500s at Safed with Moses Cordovero. Isaac Luria took it into his book of rite forms. One sage said a man must mend his ways that day. He must pay back wrongs in cash and in kind acts. Then he can greet the new month pure as a babe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ze-iri-15218:
Zeiri was a scholar of the third century born in Babylon. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He dwelt for a long time at Alexandria in Egypt. He then went to Palestine and sat with Rabbi Johanan.

In the name of Hanina he passed on a stern rule. A man who rules on law in a teacher's face is a thief. He passed on a word on the Messiah as well. That word says the Christ will not come till the proud fall. At Alexandria he once bought a mule at a fair price. Led to water, the mule turned to a bridge board at once. The spell on the beast broke in the wash of the stream. His cash was paid back to him on the spot then.
johannis-conradi-barchusen-elementa-chem:
Johann Conrad Barchusen's Elementa Chemiae is a Latin textbook of chemistry, printed at Leiden in 1718. The title page names Theodorum Haak as its publisher. Bound with the elements is a second work, Confectura Lapidis Philosophici. That addition offers a conjecture on the philosopher's stone, set out in pictures.

The pairing shows where chemistry stood in Barchusen's day. One part teaches the elements of the science in order. The other still chases the old alchemical prize, the stone that might change base metals. Barchusen, who lived from 1666 to 1723, stands between laboratory practice and alchemy. The sample's title pages, worn by scanning, still give the book's two-part plan clearly.
journal-of-discourses-vol-18:
Volume Eighteen, from 1877, records the passing of the prophet himself. Young dies in August, and the apostles take up the kingdom's lead. The first transfer of power in Mormon history unfolds in these pages.

Sermons of grief give way to calm claims of unbroken authority. The apostles preach unity and prove the work can outlive its founder. No crack shows in the kingdom's frame as the reins change hands. Readers watch a new faith pass its first great test of survival. The founder rests, the mission rolls on, and the record shows both in full.
joyce-exiles-1918:
Exiles, published in 1918, is the only play Joyce completed. He wrote it in the Ibsen manner he admired: a quiet surface, a few rooms, and a moral trap closing slowly on everyone inside.

Richard Rowan, a Dublin writer, returns home from exile with his wife Bertha and their son. His friend Robert presses his love on Bertha, and Richard, instead of forbidding it, seems to push them together in a test of freedom and trust. Nobody escapes the test unhurt. The play asks whether love can survive total honesty, and it leaves the answer painfully open.
kautsky-dictatorship-proletariat-1918:
Karl Kautsky published The Dictatorship of the Proletariat in 1918, and H J Stenning's English translation followed in 1919. Kautsky wrote in the first shock of the Russian Revolution. The old pope of Marxism, as some called him, now attacked Lenin's new regime in print.

Kautsky argued that the Bolsheviks had built a dictatorship over the workers, not of them, and that socialism without democracy must fail. Lenin answered with a furious pamphlet calling Kautsky a renegade. Their quarrel split world Marxism over a single question: can socialism come by votes and rights, or only by force? The book remains the classic democratic Marxist critique of Bolshevik rule.
keats-endymion-1818:
John Keats wrote Endymion when he was twenty-one, testing whether he could sustain a long poem. It appeared in 1818, and hostile reviewers mocked it so fiercely that legend later blamed them for his early death. The poem retells a Greek myth in four books.

Endymion, a shepherd prince, dreams of the moon goddess and leaves his home to find her. His search crosses earth, sea, and underworld, meeting sorrowful lovers from other myths along the way. Keats fills the journey with lush description and youthful energy. The poem is uneven, as Keats admitted, but it shows his gift growing at full speed.
kepler-epitome-astronomiae-copernicanae-:
Johannes Kepler published Epitome Astronomiae Copernicanae between 1618 and 1621. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands here in Latin, its 1618 opening date in the record. The Epitome was the first textbook of heliocentric astronomy, written to teach the Copernican system plainly.

In question-and-answer form, Kepler set out the Sun-centered system and extended his laws to all the planets. The third law, linking each planet's period to its distance from the Sun, first appeared in this work's line of books. Church authorities placed the Epitome on the Index of banned books. Even so, it trained the generation that made heliocentric astronomy the common view of educated Europe.
king-henry-iv-part-2-pg1518:
This edition of Shakespeare's Henry the Fourth, Part Two opens with an induction spoken by Rumour, painted full of tongues. The cast lists King Henry, his four sons, and the rebels of the north. Justice Shallow and his cousin Silence bring the comedy to Gloucestershire. Falstaff's ragged recruits, Feeble, Wart, and Shadow, stand in the list too.

The contents run from Warkworth and York to Gaultree Forest, where the rebels are tricked into disbanding. Westminster scenes follow: the king's last sickness in the Jerusalem Chamber and Hal's taking of the crown. An epilogue promises more Falstaff in the next play. The scene plan shows the play's double motion: rebellion collapsing abroad, and an old king dying at home.
lust-universal-naturopathic-encyclopedia:
Benedict Lust, the organizer of American naturopathy, packed his whole field into one fat volume in 1918. The Universal Naturopathic Encyclopedia, Directory and Buyers' Guide served as a year-book of drugless therapy. Lust gathered schools, healers, methods, and sellers of health goods between two covers.

Water cure, diet, massage, light, and air treatments all appear, along with lists of practitioners across the country. The directory pages show how wide the drugless movement had grown by the end of the First World War. For anyone tracing naturopathy's roots, the encyclopedia is a snapshot of the field at full stretch.
luzumiyat-rihani-1918:
Ameen Rihani selected and translated The Luzumiyat of Abu'l-Ala in 1918, introducing the blind Syrian poet to English readers. Abu'l-Ala al-Ma'arri, who lived from 973 to 1057, lost his sight as a child and spent his life in skeptical thought. His Luzumiyat, poems he called unnecessarily required, question fate, faith, and human pride.

Rihani, himself a bridge between Arabic and English letters, chose verses that show the poet's bite and pity. Death, vanity, and the cruelty of custom take the lash, while honest folk get tenderness. The selection remains a sharp door into one of Arabic poetry's most freethinking voices.
maier-atalanta-fugiens-1618:
Michael Maier, a German doctor at the court of Rudolf II, made this strange art book in Latin in 1618. Its title means Atalanta Fleeing, from a Greek myth of a swift maid and three gold apples. Maier was deep in the lore of alchemy and the Rosicrucian wave of his age.

The book holds fifty plates, each with a motto, a verse, a speech, and a piece of music. The songs are fugues, meant to be sung as the plates are viewed. It stands as the most famed work of art to come from the alchemist world.
mayakovsky-chelovek-man-1918:
Vladimir Mayakovsky's long poem Man, printed in Russian in 1918, lifts one man's life to a cosmic scale. The poet-hero loves, despairs, and dies, then rises again in triumph. Around him swirls the revolt that promised to remake Russia and the world.

Mayakovsky uses his bold stepped lines and loud, urgent voice throughout. Love turns to pain, pain to revolt, and revolt to a strange new faith. The poem mixes private grief with public hope. It stands as the great inner life story of Russian Futurism, one soul stretched to the size of an age.
memoirs-of-major-alexander-ramkins-1718:
Daniel Defoe's Memoirs of Major Alexander Ramkins came out in London in 1719. Ramkins was a Highland officer, then a prisoner at Avignon. R. King and W. Boreham sold the book in Paternoster Row.

The title promises twenty eight years of service in five lands. Scotland, Germany, Italy, Flanders, and Ireland make that list. Amours, gallantry, and household thrift stand among his tales. The publisher says a kinsman brought the papers from the south of France. The publisher warns Britons not to serve foreign interests blindly. One moral, he says, may be drawn from the major's hard life.
menapius-ad-responsum-1618:
F G Menapius published this short German answer, his Duplic, in 1618. The full German title calls it a brief reply to the response of Florentinus de Valentia. Valentia had defended the Rosicrucian brotherhood in a work called Rosa florescens, and Menapius refused to let the matter rest.

The pamphlet fires back point by point in the heated print war over the Rosicrucian manifestos. Each side claimed truth, and each side printed fast to hold the public ear. Menapius gives the critic's voice at full pitch in the fight of 1617 and 1618. Read beside Valentia's defense, it shows a debate held in pamphlets, not in person.
menapius-antikrisis-1618:
The Antikrisis of 1618 is F G Menapius's Latin counter to Florentinus de Valentia. Valentia had defended the Rosicrucian brotherhood in print, and Menapius answered in kind. The short title marks the work as a formal reply within a fast, sharp pamphlet exchange.

Menapius argues the critic's side of the 1618 fight over the Rosicrucian manifestos. He treats the brotherhood's claims as charges to be met, not wonders to be praised. Latin gave his answer reach among learned readers across Europe. The piece survives as one side of a two-sided quarrel, and it makes most sense read against the defense it attacks.
menapius-cento-virgilianus-1618:
F G Menapius took a strange path in 1618 with his Cento Virgilianus de Fratribus Roseae Crucis. A cento is a poem stitched from lines of an older poet, here Virgil, the great Latin epic voice. Menapius built his verses about the Brothers of the Rose Cross out of Virgil's own words.

The result carries the Rosicrucian manifesto fight into Latin verse, a form no plain pamphlet could match. Learned readers could enjoy the craft while they weighed the charge inside it. The poem stands as a rare literary fruit of the furor over the manifestos. It shows how deep that quarrel reached into the culture of its day.
michaelis-majeri-viatorium-hoc-est-de-mo:
Michael Maier published his Viatorium, or journey-book, in 1618. Its subject is the seven mountains of the planets, which are also the seven metals. Maier promises readers a guide through the vast ocean of chemical errors. He compares his treatise to Ariadne's thread in the labyrinth.

The book carries seven symbolic etchings among its pages. Maier, a physician at imperial courts, wrote in Latin for learned seekers. He maps metals onto planets in the old astrological scheme. For modern readers, the treatise shows how alchemy organized the mineral world before chemistry separated from it.
military-reminiscences-of-the-civil-war-:
Volume Two of Jacob Dolson Cox's Civil War reminiscences covers November 1863 to June 1865. Cox had commanded the Twenty-Third Army Corps for the Union. The volume opens with Grant taking supreme command and Rosecrans relieved after Chickamauga. Thomas succeeds him, and the armies regroup around Chattanooga.

Chapter summaries show Cox analyzing generals as carefully as battles. He weighs Grant's patience, judgment, and taciturn habits from personal knowledge. The siege of Knoxville and Burnside's campaign follow. Cox writes as both soldier and historian, checking memory against the official records throughout. His judgments on fellow officers are measured and fair.
mylius-opus-medico-chymicum-1618:
Johann Daniel Mylius was a Lutheran doctor whose Opus Medico-Chymicum came out in 1618. The work joins medicine and the furnace arts in three treatises. It served as his guide to the chemical remedies of the Paracelsian school.

Mylius tells the working doctor how to prepare remedies from metals and minerals, with furnaces, vessels, and doses spelled out step by step. Pictures and verses on the great work stand beside the practical recipes, in the manner of his age. The book shows how the new chemical medicine reached daily practice in the German lands. Doctors of his church and region read it as a trusted storehouse of cures.
neville-trueman-the-pioneer-preacher-a-t:
W. H. Withrow, a minister, wrote Neville Trueman, the Pioneer Preacher, and subtitled it A Tale of the War of 1812. He dedicated the story to Egerton Ryerson, for long service to his country. Withrow calls the book his story of the war, in Ryerson's honour.

His preface says he tried to show sides of Canadian life during the fight against invasion. That struggle, he writes, first stirred a shared national life in Canada. In time it grew stronger when the provinces joined in one Dominion. A pioneer preacher stands at the centre of the tale. War and faith meet in a young country finding itself.
openalex-w2007981718:
Julia Reisser, Jeremy Shaw, Gustaaf Hallegraeff and colleagues examined tiny plastics floating at sea. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Small plastic pieces are common in surface waters. Other work showed that organisms grow on them. The team asked which organisms live on these plastics near Australia.

They used a powerful microscope on dozens of plastic pieces. The pieces came from coastal and open waters around Australia. Diatoms were the most varied group of colonists. The team also found other algae, barnacles and small animals. Some marks on the plastic matched microbe shapes. That hints that living things may help break plastic down. Plastic has created a new floating habitat.
openalex-w2063022418:
Jorge Valdes, Inti Pedroso, Raquel Quatrini and colleagues described the metabolism of a microbe used in copper mining. Their paper appeared in BMC Genomics in 2008. The bacterium helps free copper from ore. Industry calls the process bioleaching. The microbe gains energy by oxidising iron and sulfur.

The team used the bacterium's genome sequence as a base. They mapped how it takes up nutrients. They traced how it fixes carbon and nitrogen. The model links genes to industrial performance. Better models may raise copper recovery rates. They may also cut costs and waste in mining. The paper serves both genome science and industry.
openalex-w2099259718:
Christian Kubicek, Alfredo Herrera-Estrella, Verena Seidl-Seiboth and colleagues compared genomes of fungi that attack other fungi. Their paper appeared in Genome Biology in 2011. Such fungus-eating fungi can protect crops. They kill fungi that cause plant disease. Trichoderma species are the best studied examples.

The team sequenced two biocontrol species' genomes. They compared them with a relative used in industry. Gene order was strongly conserved across the three. Several gene families were enlarged in the attackers. Those genes likely serve the parasitic lifestyle. Family trees placed one species as more ancestral. The shared attack genes arose in a common ancestor. Mycoparasitism seems to be the group's original lifestyle.
openalex-w2114404218:
Maria Ines Fariello, Bertrand Servin, Gwenola Tosser-Klopp and colleagues searched sheep genomes for marks of selection. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Domestic sheep vary across the whole world. Breeding and environment have shaped their genomes. A global sheep dataset made a fresh search possible.

The team reanalysed data from worldwide sheep populations. Their methods accounted for population family structure. They could separate recent from older selection marks. Several new selected regions were pinpointed. Some regions relate to modern breeding goals. Others reflect older pressures after domestication. Selected regions affect shape, colour and climate adaptation. The genome shows a broad response to human selection.
openalex-w2158911018:
Brett Forshey, Carolina Guevara, V. Alberto Laguna-Torres, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2010. They mapped which insect-borne viruses cause undifferentiated fever in western South America. These arboviruses spark major epidemics, yet their spread and impact in the region were poorly known.

Clinic-based surveillance ran at thirteen sites in Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, and Paraguay from 2000 to 2007. Febrile patients gave blood samples and background details at local clinics and hospitals. Samples were tested with antibody and genetic methods to identify the infecting viruses. The city of Iquitos, Peru, received a deeper epidemiological analysis because monitoring there ran longest, giving a detailed local picture.
openalex-w2295378318:
Thaís Chouin-Carneiro, Anubis Vega-Rúa, Marie Vazeille, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2016. They compared how well two Aedes mosquito species from the Americas can transmit Zika virus. The virus swept from Brazil through the region in 2015, and both species were suspected carriers.

Mosquitoes from the Caribbean, the southern United States, and South America were fed the circulating Asian strain. Bodies, heads, and saliva were checked over two weeks for infection, spread, and transmission. Both species infected easily but spread and transmitted the virus weakly. Populations from Guadeloupe and French Guiana spread it within their bodies best. Transmission appeared only at the last check, and at a low level.
openalex-w2973791718:
Sonja Leonhard, Melissa Mandarakas, Francisco Gondim, and colleagues published this consensus guideline in Nature Reviews Neurology in 2019. It lays out the diagnosis and care of Guillain-Barré syndrome in ten steps. The syndrome is a rare but sometimes fatal immune attack on the nerves, usually triggered by an infection.

Cases can surge during infection outbreaks, as seen with Zika in French Polynesia and Latin America. The illness varies widely between patients, and no worldwide guideline existed before this one. Built from current research and expert consensus, the ten steps cover diagnostic criteria, disease variants, and look-alike conditions first. The authors designed the guide for doctors anywhere, above all during outbreaks.
openalex-w3016136018:
Ami Sperber, Shrikant Bangdiwala, Douglas Drossman, and colleagues published this global study in Gastroenterology in 2020. It reports the Rome Foundation Global Study of functional gastrointestinal disorders. These are gut conditions, such as irritable bowel syndrome, that cause real suffering without visible organ damage.

The study surveyed adults across many countries with one shared method, using the Rome diagnostic criteria. It measured how common each disorder is and how heavily it burdens daily life, work, and health care use. Before this effort, most figures came from single countries that could not be compared cleanly. A worldwide picture helps doctors and health planners see the true scale of these often-dismissed conditions.
openalex-w3118630218:
Osval Montesinos-López, Abelardo Montesinos-López, Paulino Pérez-Rodríguez, and colleagues wrote this review in BMC Genomics in 2021. It surveys deep learning applications for genomic selection, the practice of predicting a plant's or animal's worth from its DNA. Breeders use such predictions to choose parents without years of field trials.

Classic prediction methods assume mostly additive gene effects with neat formulas. Deep learning instead learns tangled patterns straight from data, which suits complex traits. The authors gather the published trials into one picture of how well the methods perform. They explain the basics, list what good use requires, and weigh gains against older approaches. Large, high-quality training data emerge as the key requirement.
openalex-w4292800918:
Peter Walker, Stuart Siddell, Elliot Lefkowitz, and colleagues report the 2022 changes to virus taxonomy in Archives of Virology. The International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses votes each year on how viruses are classified and named. In March 2022 its members ratified one hundred seventy-four proposals. Approval required an absolute majority of the full membership, not just its executive committee.

The biggest shift concerns names. A rule from 2021 requires species names in a two-part form, genus name plus species epithet. More than six thousand species names, over sixty percent of all recognised names, now follow that format. The paper records each change, giving virologists one official reference for the current scheme.
openalex-w7127098018:
Amane Endo, Akio Nakamura, Mayu Nakagawa, and colleagues report family-centred care during a child's emergency admission. Their case report appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2026. The patient was a five-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder. He needed urgent hospital care for nephrotic syndrome.

Severe anxiety and behavioural difficulties blocked routine procedures. The team applied patient- and family-centred care. A child psychiatrist and a child life specialist joined the medical team. Together with the family, they built a personalised care plan. The plan rested on detailed knowledge of the child's needs and triggers. The case shows how partnership with families can make emergency care workable for autistic children.
openalex-w7204265718:
Rafaely Maria Ferreira da Silva and Hamilton Gomes de Santana Neto released a Portuguese-language legal paper in Brazil in 2026 on civil liability when a patient is wrongly told they have HIV. A false positive result can devastate a life, and the authors examine who must pay for that harm. The liberal professional, the hospital, or the laboratory that issued the test result. Their study works from the legal work and from judgments of Brazil's Superior Court of Justice and state courts.

Civil liability, they explain, turns on fault, actual damage, and a causal link between the professional's conduct and the harm. The paper maps how courts handle diagnostic error in sexually transmitted infections. HIV false positives at the center, and what duties of care and result delivery the law imposes on providers.
openalex-w7204280318:
Helenilda de Amorim Gomes led a Portuguese-language practice report, in Brazil in 2026, on the school garden at a municipal school in rural Petrolina, Pernambuco. The garden works as a living laboratory joining nature schooling, interdisciplinary teaching, inclusion, and student protagonism. Beds are organized by reusing PET bottles, vegetables and medicinal plants are grown, and the work involves students, teachers, specialized school support, and a nature group that also encourages reading.

Growing food lets teachers ground class content in meaningful, hands-on learning, the authors report, and harvest periods encourage students to eat more vegetables. The garden also functions as a space of citizenship formation, sustainability, and inclusion that values family farming, tying a small rural school to its community's agricultural life.
openalex-w7204641318:
Valéria Raquel Alcântara Barbosa wrote a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on sensitive listening in perinatal psychological care for pregnant and postpartum women in mental health beds. The review included eighteen research papers from 2021 to 2026 in Portuguese or English, drawn from five sources. The author organized the evidence into three themes: the meanings and functions of sensitive listening, intervention plans, and interprofessional work.

Sensitive listening, the author argues, is a structuring relational practice: a basic principle, starting point, and guiding thread of perinatal care. It takes medical, ethical, aesthetic, therapeutic, protective, and holistic forms. Ongoing training and interprofessional practice support teams in making this listening stronger for people at high risk.
openalex-w7204745618:
Fihama Beatriz Batista da Silva led a Portuguese-language questionnaire study, in Brazil in 2026, on chemistry laboratories in public schools and the role of PIBID, Brazil's teaching initiation scholarship program. Experimentation matters for building research knowledge, but poor laboratory infrastructure in Brazil's public schools can break the link between theory and practice. Supervisors of the program answered a Likert-scale questionnaire about how scholarship students' activities affect teaching practice, laboratory use, and student learning.

Supervisors found a stronger theory-practice connection, greater student engagement, renewed teaching practice, and wider understanding of research concepts, the authors find. Alternative supplies and better laboratory organization made activities more meaningful. The program supports beginning teacher training, they conclude, though its effectiveness still depends on better infrastructure.
openalex-w7208788718:
Patricia Pereira Alves leads a team that reads past work on play in quilombola towns. Such towns were set up by Afro-Brazilians who fled chains. They hold deep ties to land and to those who came first. The team's wide sweep takes in the games kids play, the toys they use, and the spots where play is held. The lens is the wild world: how play shows craft, land, and a sense of home soil.

The reads show a wide spread. Old games sit by new ones. Toys are shop-made, made by grown folk, built by the kids, or shaped from wild and reused stuff. Play spots span wild ground and built parts of the town. Kids in such towns, the team closes, weave play, craft, land, and home soil as one cloth of each day. That play is a true sign of who they are.
openalex-w7213556018:
Ana Maria Gonçalves Ferreira and co-authors present a case study on oppositional defiant disorder at school. Their 2026 work follows one fourth-year elementary pupil in Morro Reuter, Rio Grande do Sul. Classroom interactions, effects on the class, and teacher strategies were analysed.

Understanding the disorder's features in daily school life was the starting aim. From there, the team sought actions that support cognitive and emotional growth. Wider teaching practices for neurodivergent students are needed, the results suggest. Such practices can promote meaningful learning and reduce situations of suffering. An interdisciplinary, inclusive approach is recommended, so the pupil's full development is supported and schooling becomes fairer for the whole class.
openalex-w7214012918:
Mathias Cesar Assis, as in the sample byline, leads a systematic review on artificial intelligence for mammography quality. Technical quality shapes early breast cancer detection, and repeat rates mark service quality. Their 2026 review follows PRISMA guidance across seven databases and keeps thirteen primary studies.

Deep learning models dominate, above all convolutional networks and U-Net variants. They find anatomical landmarks, grade image quality, and give decision support and feedback during image capture. High accuracy in locating the pectoral muscle is reported. The share of inadequate images fell in the studies. Quality checking at the moment of capture, the authors imply, beats discovering faults later.
openalex-w7214936518: Yurika Sone led a Japanese materials team in a study published in 2026. It works on improving the hydrogen electrode of solid oxide electrolysis cells, devices that use electricity to split water and make hydrogen. Their approach builds the electrode's active layer from a nanocomposite combining nickel with a zirconia-based ceramic, aiming to raise the cell's performance. The evidence sample for this entry contains only the journal front matter, title, and author affiliations. It has no abstract or results, so the study's measured outcomes are not described here.
opus-medico-chymicum-continens-tres-trac: Johann Daniel Mylius's Opus medico-chymicum, dated 1618 in the catalog, is a Latin work in three treatises. Its title names them: a Basilica medica, a Basilica chymica, and a Basilica philosophica. The hosted sample, however, shows only damaged front matter from the scanned copy. Library stamps and a badly garbled title image leave no body text readable. This description therefore rests on the title alone and claims nothing about the treatises' arguments.
plaw-115-100-2018: Public Law 115-100 of 2018 extends a pause on permit rules for small boats. Boats shorter than 79 feet, and fishing boats, need no permit for spills that come with the normal running of the boat. The act amends a 2008 law. It strikes the end date of December 18, 2017, and puts in January 19, 2018. The pause thus runs about one month more.
plaw-115-101-2018:
Passed in 2018, Public Law 115-101 amends the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area Improvement Act. The act gives road access to some trucks that serve people who live in towns next to the recreation area.

Highway 209, a federal road inside the area, is closed to all trade trucks. Till September 30, 2021, that ban does not hold for trucks with four or fewer axles. The trucks must be owned and run by a firm inside the area or a town next to it, or be needed to serve firms or people there. The Secretary must set a fee and permit plan for such use, with a yearly fee capped per truck. Fees go to a special account to run the plan. School buses and fire and safety trucks are left out of the fee and permit rule.
plaw-115-102-2018:
400 Years of African-American History Commission Act is Public Law 115-102, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. The act sets up a named commission. The mark it serves is 400 years since Africans first came to the English colonies, at Point Comfort, Virginia, in 1619.

The commission holds 15 members. The Secretary of the Interior names them all, by the paths shown. Three come after the Secretary weighs names put forth by governors, the Governor of Virginia among them. Six come after the Secretary weighs names from civil rights groups and history groups. One must be a National Park Service worker with skill in the past and culture tied to the mark. Two more named paths begin where the sample ends.
plaw-115-103-2018:
Western Oregon Tribal Fairness Act is Public Law 115-103, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. The act gives some federal land in Oregon to be held in trust, and amends an older tribal act. Land held in trust is held by the United States for a tribe's gain.

The contents list three titles. Title I gives Cow Creek Umpqua land, with parts on terms, land to be held in trust, and map and legal facts. It also covers how the land is run, and a new class for the land. Title II gives Oregon coastal land on the same pattern. Title III amends the Coquille Restoration Act. A first term shown sets Council Creek land at about 17,519 acres.
plaw-115-104-2018:
African American Civil Rights Network Act of 2017 is Public Law 115-104, passed in 2018. The 115th Congress amended title 54 law to set up a network inside the National Park Service. The network bears the name African American Civil Rights Network in the act.

The stated aims are twofold. The act seeks to mark the weight of the African American civil rights movement, and the costs paid by the people who fought bias and forced separation by race. It also lets the Park Service join and aid federal and non-federal work to mark, honor, and teach that past. Parts named are the movement's role in the growth of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and its force for social justice and national healing.
plaw-115-105-2018: Jobs for Our Heroes Act is Public Law 115-105, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. The act eases the path by which active duty troops, reservists, and veterans gain a commercial driver's license, a license to drive large work trucks. It rewrites who counts as a qualified examiner for driver health checks. A fit examiner may be a veterans nurse, chiropractor, doctor, or like health worker, licensed in a state to give physical exams. The examiner must know the health rules for drivers and have never acted with fraud.
plaw-115-106-2018: No Human Trafficking on Our Roads Act is Public Law 115-106, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. The act amends title 49 law on truck driver bans. The Secretary must bar for life, with no way back, a person who uses a commercial motor vehicle to commit a felony that involves human trafficking. The trafficking acts meant are those listed in the Trafficking Victims Protection Act of 2000. The section heading is changed to Lifetime Disqualification Without Reinstatement to match.
plaw-115-107-2018: Sexual Assault Forensic Evidence Reporting Act of 2017, or SAFER Act of 2017, is Public Law 115-107, passed in 2018. The act renews the SAFER Act of 2013. One part widens training on forensic nurses to cover nurses for both adults and children, and stresses the need for child sexual assault nurse examiners. A second part fights the rape kit backlog. It moves a DNA backlog law year from 2017 to 2022, and the SAFER end date from 2018 to 2023.
plaw-115-108-2018: Martin Luther King, Jr. National Historical Park Act of 2017 is Public Law 115-108, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. The act renames a Georgia site. Each use of Martin Luther King, Junior, National Historic Site in the 1980 law is struck and Martin Luther King, Jr. National Historical Park is put in. Like swaps turn national historic site into national historical park. A new boundary map from June 2015 takes the place of the 1992 map. Other records that name the old site name the new park.
plaw-115-109-2018: In 2018, the 115th Congress passed Public Law 115-109, which names a mountain in California as Sky Point. The peak sits in the John Muir Wilderness of the Sierra National Forest, at set map points in Humphrey Basin. Findings honor Staff Sergeant Sky Mote, a Marine who gave his life on August 10, 2012, when he rushed to guard fellow Marines in Helmand province. He won the Navy Cross and the Purple Heart. The peak held meaning for his friends and family, who camped below it on yearly hunting trips.
plaw-115-110-2018: Mount Hood Cooper Spur Land Exchange Clarification Act is Public Law 115-110, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. The act amends a 2009 land law on a swap in the Mt. Hood Wilderness in Oregon. It cuts one parcel from 120 acres to 107 acres, and adds the word improvements next to buildings. It makes both sides pick a key party jointly within 120 days, and makes a land value study price each tax lot on its own. The sample ends mid-clause.
plaw-115-111-2018: In 2018, Public Law 115-111 was passed by the 115th Congress. It Makes one word swap for a park in Connecticut. The act aims to ease the growth of park offices at the Coltsville National Historical Park. It amends a part of Public Law 113-291 on a gift site for that park. The words East Armory are struck, and Colt Armory Complex is put in their place. That single swap is the whole act.
plaw-115-112-2018:
International Narcotics Trafficking Emergency Response by Detecting Incoming Contraband with Technology Act, or INTERDICT Act, is Public Law 115-112. Passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress, the act aims to improve how Customs and Border Protection stops fentanyl and like drugs. The drugs named are fentanyl, other man-made opioids, and other narcotics and mind-altering drugs brought in by unlawful means.

The act defines a chemical screening device in broad terms. Such a device may be a field test kit or a lab tool that reads light or mass in a sample. Its data must be able to show if such drugs are present. The agency head must raise the count of such devices held by officers, past the count on the date of the act. More devices must be given out as the head judges needful to stop the drugs.
plaw-115-113-2018:
Law Enforcement Mental Health and Wellness Act of 2017 is Public Law 115-113, passed in 2018. The 115th Congress wrote the act to back law agency work that guards the mental health and well-being of law officers.

The act orders two reports to Congress. The Attorney General, with the defense and veterans chiefs, must report on defense and veterans mental health practice. The report covers practice that law agencies at all levels could take up, and it must be made public. A policing office chief must send case studies of programs built to aid officer mental health, like a 2015 report of that office. The act also adds peer mentoring mental health pilot programs to the list of grants a 1968 crime law may fund.
plaw-115-114-2018: Connected Government Act is Public Law 115-114, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. The act requires a new or updated federal web site meant for public use to be mobile friendly. Mobile friendly means a site is set up so it can be moved through, viewed, and reached on a smartphone, tablet, or like device. The rule starts 180 days after the act, for sites made or remade from that date, as far as can be done. A report by two agency chiefs is also required.
plaw-115-115-2018: EPS Improvement Act of 2017 is Public Law 115-115, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. EPS here deals with external power supplies, the blocks that feed power to a device. The act amends the Energy Policy and Conservation Act. It leaves some gear out of the energy saving rules for such supplies. Left out are circuits, drivers, and devices made only to power light-emitting diodes or organic light-emitting diodes that give light. Ceiling fans that use direct current motors are left out as well.
plaw-115-116-2018: Public Law 115-116 of 2018 lifts a use limit on land in Rockingham County, Virginia. The land had been given to the county under a 1990 law. The act strikes one part of that law and adds a new part. The new part states that the roughly 1-acre part of the land used for a child care center is not bound by the use limit in the deed. The Secretary of the Interior must sign a paper to carry the change out.
plaw-115-117-2018: Little Rock Central High School National Historic Site Boundary Modification Act is Public Law 115-117, passed in 2018. The 115th Congress moved the line of that historic site in Little Rock, Arkansas. The new line takes in the 7 homes on South Park Street, a total of 1.47 acres, as shown on a map from August 2004. The Secretary may sign joint deals with the owners of those homes. Under such deals, funds may mark, teach, improve, and restore the homes, with skilled help for their care.
plaw-115-118-2018:
FISA Amendments Reauthorization Act of 2017 is Public Law 115-118, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. FISA is the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978. The act aims to improve how foreign facts are gathered, and the guards, answerability, and watch over that work. It also extends title VII of that act.

Title I lists the gains. Parts shown require set steps for searches of gathered facts, and rules on use and sharing. Other parts cover review by Congress of so-called abouts gathering, print of the steps used to trim gathered facts, and pay for court friends and tech experts. Later parts add reports, gains for a privacy board and privacy officers, whistleblower guards for spy agency contractors, and a watchdog report on searches by the Federal Bureau of Investigation.
plaw-115-119-2018:
Recognize, Assist, Include, Support, and Engage Family Caregivers Act of 2017, or RAISE Family Caregivers Act, is Public Law 115-119. Passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress, the act calls for a Family Caregiving Strategy to be set up and kept up.

The act defines its terms. A family caregiver is an adult family member, or a like close person. Such a person gives a broad range of help to a person with a long-term or other health state, a disability, or a limit on daily acts. The health chief must build the strategy with an advice council and with other agency heads. It must be sent to named groups in Congress and to state caregiver agencies, and posted on the health agency web site for the public.
plaw-115-120-2018:
In 2018, the 115th Congress passed Public Law 115-120, which makes further stopgap funds for the fiscal year that ends September 30, 2018. The act's heading joins that funds work with Federal Register printing savings, healthy kids, health taxes, and budget effects. The sample shows Division A in full and no more.

Division A is the Federal Register Printing Savings Act of 2017. It limits free printed copies of the Federal Register for Members of Congress and federal staff. Under rules to be set, the head of the Government Publishing Office may not give a free printed copy in a year. The bar holds unless the Member or office asks for a printed copy. The sample breaks off at that point.
plaw-115-121-2018:
Thomasina E. Jordan Indian Tribes of Virginia Federal Recognition Act of 2017 is Public Law 115-121, passed in 2018. The 115th Congress granted federal recognition to six Virginia tribes. They are the Chickahominy Indian Tribe, the Chickahominy Indian Tribe--Eastern Division, the Upper Mattaponi Tribe, the Rappahannock Tribe, Inc., the Monacan Indian Nation, and the Nansemond Indian Tribe.

The contents give each tribe its own title on the same pattern. Parts shown for the first tribes cover findings, terms, and the grant of recognition itself. Later parts cover who counts as a member and the papers that rule the tribe, the body that leads it, and the tribe's reservation. One part covers hunting, fishing, trapping, gathering, and water rights.
plaw-115-122-2018: Alex Diekmann Peak Designation Act of 2017 is Public Law 115-122, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. The act names a mountain peak in Montana. The peak has no name in the text and stands 9,765 feet high. It sits 2.2 miles west-northwest of Finger Mountain, on the west edge of the Lee Metcalf Wilderness, at set map coordinates. Under the act, the peak is known as Alex Diekmann Peak. Mentions of that peak in federal records count as mentions of Alex Diekmann Peak.
plaw-115-123-2018:
Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018 is Public Law 115-123, passed by the 115th Congress. The opening line of the sample speaks of flying the flag at half-staff when a first responder dies in the line of duty. That topic is Division A of the act, the only division the sample shows.

Division A is the Honoring Hometown Heroes Act. It amends the flag law in title 4. A governor may order the flag flown at half-staff for a first responder who works in a state, territory, or possession and dies while serving in the line of duty. First responders who work in the District of Columbia are added as well. The act defines first responder by a cite to the term public safety officer in a 1968 crime law.
plaw-115-124-2018: Continuing Appropriations Amendments Act, 2018 is Public Law 115-124, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. The catalog head line speaks of defense funds for the year that ended in 2017, but the enacted text does a newer job. It adds a new section 166 to the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2018. Staff sent home in a funds lapse that starts on or about February 9, 2018, must be paid at their standard rate for the lapse once it ends. Staff of the capital courts and defender service count as well.
plaw-115-125-2018:
Department of Homeland Security Blue Campaign Authorization Act is Public Law 115-125, passed in 2018. The 115th Congress amended the Homeland Security Act of 2002. The act requires the Secretary to issue agency-wide guides and build training as part of the Blue Campaign, the agency drive against human trafficking.

The new part sets the campaign in law inside the department, led by a Director named by the Secretary. Its aim is to join and align the work of the whole department against human trafficking. Duties shown are to issue guides to fit staff, build training for them, and align the training and work across the department. Guides and training must use trauma-aware practice, so victims gain fast access to victim aid groups, on top of the aid a 2000 trafficking law requires.
plaw-115-126-2018:
Protecting Young Victims from Sexual Abuse and Safe Sport Authorization Act of 2017 is Public Law 115-126, passed in 2018. The 115th Congress wrote the act to stop the sexual abuse of minors and amateur athletes. Its core tool is a duty to report sexual abuse fast to law officers.

The contents list two titles. Title I protects young victims. Its parts require reports of child and sexual abuse, and give a civil court path for personal harm. Title II grants power to the United States Center for Safe Sport. Its parts widen the aims of that body, name it in law, and add terms for grants of leave to hold amateur sports contests.
