General terms for youth sports groups close the list.
plaw-115-127-2018:
Kari's Law Act of 2017 is Public Law 115-127, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. The act amends the Communications Act of 1934. It deals with multi-line phone systems, the kind used in offices and hotels, and with calls to 9-1-1, the urgent help number.

A maker, importer, seller, or renter of such a system may not trade in a system unless it is set up in advance for direct dialing. When fit in place as the act requires, a user at any phone with dialing must be able to call 9-1-1 at once. No added digit, code, head or tail mark may be needed, not even a trunk code such as the digit 9, though such a code may be needed for other calls. A like duty binds those who fit, run, or work such systems.
plaw-115-128-2018: Gateway Arch National Park Designation Act is Public Law 115-128, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. The act gives a new name to a Missouri site. The Jefferson National Expansion Memorial, set up under a 1954 act, is known from the act on as the Gateway Arch National Park. Any mention of the old memorial name in a law, map, rule, or other federal record counts as a mention of the Gateway Arch National Park.
plaw-115-129-2018: Improving Rural Call Quality and Reliability Act of 2017 is Public Law 115-129, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. The act amends the Communications Act of 1934 to guard the soundness of voice calls and bar unfair gaps in call delivery by area. A middle provider that carries calls for a fee must sign up with the Commission and meet its service quality norms. A main provider may not use a middle provider that is not signed up. Norms are due one year after the act.
plaw-115-130-2018:
In 2018, Public Law 115-130 was passed by the 115th Congress. It Orders reports from the Secretary of Veterans Affairs. The reports deal with medical proof sent in to back claims for benefits under the laws the Secretary runs.

One report, due in 180 days, tracks the Acceptable Clinical Evidence drive of the department. That drive cuts the need for in-person disability exams. The report must count claims fit for the drive by fiscal year, and count how many needed a phone talk by a department examiner to fill gaps in proof. It must also tell of other drives to boost use of private medical proof and private doctor reports that are full enough to judge a claim.
plaw-115-131-2018: Veterans Care Financial Protection Act of 2017 is Public Law 115-131, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. The Secretary must post a warning on the department web site. The warning tells of dishonest, predatory, or unlawful acts that target people who can gain a higher pension due to a need for regular aid and attendance. The act also orders a study of money abuse by the Comptroller General, due in 18 months. The study weighs norms that guard weak groups and the kinds of abuse such veterans face.
plaw-115-132-2018:
Public Law 115-132 of 2018 names the health care system of the Department of Veterans Affairs in Lexington, Kentucky. Under the act, that system is the Lexington VA Health Care System, and the act makes some other namings as well. The sample shows the findings that back those other namings, and no more.

The findings tell of Private First Class Franklin Runyon Sousley of Hilltop, Kentucky. He joined the Marine Corps in 1944 and landed on Iwo Jima on February 19, 1945. On February 23, 1945, he was one of six men who raised a larger United States flag on Mount Suribachi, in the famed photo of that act. He was killed in combat by a sniper on March 21, 1945.
plaw-115-133-2018: Pearland, Texas, holds the postal building named by Public Law 115-133, passed in 2018. The building is at 2700 Cullen Boulevard in Pearland. The 115th Congress designated it the Endy Nddiobong Ekpanya Post Office Building. A reference to the Cullen Boulevard site in a law, map, or other United States record is a reference to the Ekpanya building.
plaw-115-134-2018: Public Law 115-134, passed in 2018, names a postal site in Pacific, Missouri. The site stands at 324 West Saint Louis Street in Pacific. Under the act of the 115th Congress, it is the Specialist Jeffrey L. White, Jr. Post Office. When a federal law, map, rule, or file speaks of the West Saint Louis Street site, it speaks of the White post office.
plaw-115-135-2018:
Taiwan Travel Act is Public Law 115-135, passed in 2018 by the 115th Congress. The act urges visits between the United States and Taiwan at all levels. High-level visits are its main concern.

Findings call the Taiwan Relations Act of 1979 a base stone of ties between the two sides, and an anchor for peace in the Western Pacific. They say peace there serves United States aims in politics, safety, and trade. They note that Taiwan made a vast shift to a democracy from the late 1980s and stands as a beacon of that path in Asia. They also say ties have hurt from too little high-level talk, due to limits the United States set on its own visits. The act then states that the United States should urge visits at all levels, where the sample ends.
plaw-115-136-2018: Passed in 2018, Public Law 115-136 amends title 38 law on grave marks. The Department of Veterans Affairs gives memorial headstones and markers for fit spouses and dependent children of veterans whose remains cannot be had. Two clauses in section 2306 are changed the same way. Each now states that the person must be one who dies on or after November 11, 1998. The act thus sets one shared date for who counts in both clauses.
plaw-115-137-2018: Canonsburg, Pennsylvania, is the home of the postal building named by Public Law 115-137, passed in 2018. Find it at 120 West Pike Street in Canonsburg. Congress called it the Police Officer Scott Bashioum Post Office Building. Laws, maps, or records that mention the West Pike Street site mention the Bashioum building. Nothing else about the site changes under the act.
plaw-115-138-2018: In 2018, the 115th Congress passed Public Law 115-138, which gives a group honor in Converse, Texas. The postal building at 9155 Schaefer Road, Converse, Texas, is called the Converse Veterans Post Office Building under the act. The name honors veterans as a group rather than one person. A law, map, or record that cites the Schaefer Road site cites the Converse Veterans Post Office Building.
plaw-115-139-2018: Liberty, Pennsylvania, holds the postal site named by Public Law 115-139, passed in 2018. The site is at 4514 Williamson Trail in Liberty. The 115th Congress designated it the Staff Sergeant Ryan Scott Ostrom Post Office. References to the Williamson Trail site in federal laws, maps, or records are references to the Ostrom post office.
plaw-115-140-2018: Bakersfield, California, holds the postal building named by Public Law 115-140, passed in 2018. The building is at 1730 18th Street in Bakersfield. The 115th Congress designated it the Merle Haggard Post Office Building. A citation of the 18th Street site in a law, map, rule, or other United States record is a citation of the Haggard building.
plaw-115-141-2018:
Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2018 is Public Law 115-141, passed by the 115th Congress. The opening line of the sample speaks of a State Department rewards topic, which does not match the funds contents that follow. The contents list is the guide to what the act holds.

Early parts state how cites in the act work, where the full account of funds sits, and when funds may be used. Division A funds farm, rural growth, food and drug, and linked agencies for 2018. Its titles cover farm programs, farm output and nature programs, rural growth, home food programs, aid abroad, and the food and drug agency. Division B then funds trade, justice, science, and linked agencies, starting with the Department of Commerce.
plaw-115-142-2018: Public Law 115-142, passed in 2018, names a postal building in Vallejo, California. The building stands at 2635 Napa Street in Vallejo. Under the act of the 115th Congress, it is the Janet Capello Post Office Building. Federal records that speak of the Napa Street site speak of the Capello building. The act changes the name and nothing else.
plaw-115-143-2018: Princeton, New Jersey, is the home of the postal site named by Public Law 115-143, passed in 2018. That site is at 259 Nassau Street, Suite 2, in Princeton. Congress designated it the Dr. John F. Nash, Jr. Post Office. References to the Nassau Street site in laws, maps, rules, or other records of the United States are deemed references to the Nash post office.
plaw-115-144-2018: In 2018, Public Law 115-144 was passed by the 115th Congress. It Names a postal site in Boston, Massachusetts. The site is at 25 New Chardon Street Lobby in Boston. Its name under the act is the John Fitzgerald Kennedy Post Office. Any mention of that site in a law, map, rule, or other federal record counts as a mention of it under that name.
plaw-115-145-2018: Fairview, Illinois, holds the postal site named by Public Law 115-145, passed in 2018. The site is at 520 Carter Street in Fairview. The 115th Congress called it the Sgt. Douglas J. Riney Post Office. A reference to the Carter Street site in a law, map, or other United States record is a reference to the Riney post office.
plaw-115-146-2018: Public Law 115-146, passed in 2018, assigns a name to a postal site in Raritan, New Jersey. The site, at 30 East Somerset Street in Raritan, is called the Gunnery Sergeant John Basilone Post Office under the act. When a federal law, map, rule, or paper points to the East Somerset Street site, it points to the Basilone post office.
plaw-115-147-2018: Wyncote, Pennsylvania, holds the postal building named by Public Law 115-147, passed in 2018. The building is at 207 Glenside Avenue in Wyncote. The 115th Congress designated it the Staff Sergeant Peter Taub Post Office Building. A citation of the Glenside Avenue site in a law, map, or other United States record is a citation of the Taub building.
plaw-115-148-2018: Public Law 115-148, passed in 2018, names a postal building in Chillicothe, Illinois. The building stands at 1114 North 2nd Street in Chillicothe. Under the act of the 115th Congress, it is the Sr. Chief Ryan Owens Post Office Building. Federal records that speak of the North 2nd Street site speak of the Owens building.
plaw-115-149-2018: Public Law 115-149, passed by the 115th Congress and approved on March 23, 2018, gives a new name to one post office in North Carolina. The law states that the postal facility at 225 North Main Street in Spring Lake shall be known as the Howard B. Pate, Jr. Post Office. It also says that any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-115-150-2018: A Jacksonville, Florida post office gained a new name under Public Law 115-150, approved on March 23, 2018 during the 115th Congress. The law states that the postal facility at 1100 Kings Road shall be known as the Rutledge Pearson Post Office Building. From then on, any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-115-151-2018: Public Law 115-151, approved on March 23, 2018, renames a post office building in Belmar, New Jersey. Under the law, the postal facility at 1300 Main Street shall be known as the Dr. Walter S. McAfee Post Office Building. The law also provides that any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-115-152-2018: Clermont, Georgia is the town covered by Public Law 115-152, a short law approved on March 23, 2018 in the 115th Congress. The law states that the postal facility at 430 Main Street shall be known as the Zack T. Addington Post Office. It adds that any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-115-153-2018: Public Law 115-153 gives a new name to the post office in Interlachen, Florida. Approved on March 23, 2018, the law states that the postal facility at 100 Mathe Avenue shall be known as the Robert H. Jenkins, Jr. Post Office. Any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts, under the law, as a mention of the new name.
plaw-115-154-2018: Kissimmee, Florida is home to the postal facility renamed by Public Law 115-154, approved on March 23, 2018. The law states that the facility at 1415 West Oak Street shall be known as the Borinqueneers Post Office Building. It also says that any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-115-155-2018: Public Law 115-155, approved on March 23, 2018, renames a post office building in Mullica Hill, New Jersey. The law states that the postal facility at 123 Bridgeton Pike shall be known as the James C. 'Billy' Johnson Post Office Building. Any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts, under the law, as a mention of the new name.
plaw-115-156-2018: Public Law 115-156 is the Removing Outdated Restrictions to Allow for Job Growth Act, approved on March 26, 2018. The law deals with land once given to the City of Old Town, Maine for use as a town airport. If the city asks in writing, the Secretary of Agriculture must release the federal claim on lands the city plans to pass on for growth of local jobs, with no payment required.
plaw-115-157-2018: Fargo, North Dakota is the site of the farm research center renamed by Public Law 115-157, approved on March 27, 2018. The law states that the Red River Valley Agricultural Research Center shall be known as the Edward T. Schafer Agricultural Research Center. Any mention of the center in a federal law, rule, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-115-158-2018: Public Law 115-158 is the Eliminating Government-funded Oil-painting Act, also called the EGO Act, approved on March 27, 2018. The law adds a new section to title 31 of the United States Code. It bars the use of federal funds to pay for painted portraits of federal officers and staff. The ban covers the President, the Vice President, members of Congress, and agency heads.
plaw-115-159-2018:
Public Law 115-159 is the State Veterans Home Adult Day Health Care Improvement Act of 2017, approved on March 27, 2018. The law changes title 38 of the United States Code, which covers veterans' benefits. Its subject is adult day health care, a daytime service offered through state veterans homes.

Under the law, the Secretary of Veterans Affairs must make a payment deal with each state home that offers a medical supervision model of adult day health care. The payment rate is set by rule and must fairly repay the home for the care it gives. The rate also covers needed transport costs for the veteran.
plaw-115-160-2018:
Public Law 115-160 is the Secret Service Recruitment and Retention Act of 2018, approved on April 3, 2018. The law deals with overtime pay for agents and staff of the United States Secret Service. Many of them work long protective shifts that push past normal federal pay caps.

The law extends an overtime pay exception through the end of 2018. It lets covered staff earn premium pay above the usual yearly cap for work done in 2016, 2017, and 2018. That extra pay is allowed only when Congress has set aside funds for it in a spending law.
plaw-115-161-2018: Public Law 115-161 is the Ceiling Fan Energy Conservation Harmonization Act, approved on April 3, 2018. The law concerns the energy rules for ceiling fan light kits, which were updated in a federal rule issued in January 2016. It sets January 21, 2020 as the date when makers must meet the new standards. The Secretary of Energy then has 60 days to fix any rule or guide that conflicts with that date.
plaw-115-162-2018: Atchison, Kansas gained a renamed post office under Public Law 115-162, approved on April 3, 2018. The law states that the postal facility at 621 Kansas Avenue shall be known as the Amelia Earhart Post Office Building. It adds that any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-115-163-2018:
Public Law 115-163 is the Kennedy-King National Commemorative Site Act, approved on April 4, 2018. The law names a new commemorative site in Indianapolis, Indiana. It honors the Landmark for Peace Memorial in Martin Luther King, Jr. Park.

Under the law, that memorial becomes the Kennedy-King National Commemorative Site and joins the African American Civil Rights Network. The Secretary of the Interior may make deals with public or private groups for learning programs at the site. The law is clear that the site is not a unit of the National Park System.
plaw-115-164-2018:
Public Law 115-164 is the Allow States and Victims to Fight Online Sex Trafficking Act of 2017, approved on April 11, 2018. The law changes the Communications Act of 1934. Its target is section 230, the rule that often shields websites from blame for posts made by their users.

Congress states that section 230 was never meant to shield sites that help promote prostitution or aid traffickers. The law clears the way for federal and state criminal and civil cases against sites and users tied to child sexual abuse or sex trafficking. It removes a legal defense that such sites had claimed.
plaw-115-165-2018:
Public Law 115-165 is the Strengthening Protections for Social Security Beneficiaries Act of 2018, approved on April 13, 2018. The law updates the part of the Social Security Act that covers representative payees. A payee is a person who receives and manages benefit checks for someone who cannot handle the money alone.

One title of the law calls for stronger checks on payees and better sharing of facts between agencies. A second title deals with how payees are chosen and kept fit for the role. It bars people found guilty of certain crimes from serving as payees.
plaw-115-166-2018: Public Law 115-166 is the Ashlynne Mike AMBER Alert in Indian Country Act, approved on April 13, 2018. The law changes the PROTECT Act, which funds the AMBER Alert system for missing children. It makes Indian tribes able to receive AMBER Alert grants, as states already could. The grants can build or improve alert plans and link tribal alert systems into state systems.
plaw-115-167-2018:
Public Law 115-167 is the African Growth and Opportunity Act and Millennium Challenge Act Modernization Act, approved on April 23, 2018. The law updates two United States programs that deal with Africa. One title covers trade with African nations, and the other covers the Millennium Challenge Corporation, which funds aid projects abroad.

On the trade side, the law backs open reporting and help for African nations to build trade skills. On the aid side, it changes how nations qualify as candidates for support. It also covers board rules, public notice before a funding deal is signed, and wider sharing of program facts.
plaw-115-168-2018: Public Law 115-168 is the Keep America's Refuges Operational Act, approved on April 23, 2018. The short law changes one line of the Fish and Wildlife Act of 1956. It renews the funding years for three programs of the National Wildlife Refuge System. Those programs cover volunteer help, work with local partners, and teaching about refuges, now funded for the years 2018 through 2022.
plaw-115-169-2018: Emporia, Kansas is the town named in Public Law 115-169, the National Memorial to Fallen Educators Act, approved on April 30, 2018. The law gives a formal title to the memorial to fallen educators at the National Teachers Hall of Fame. That memorial is now the National Memorial to Fallen Educators. The law states that the memorial is not a unit of the National Park System and that no federal funds may be spent on it.
plaw-115-170-2018: Public Law 115-170 is the Admiral Lloyd R. 'Joe' Vasey Pacific War Commemorative Display Establishment Act, approved on May 7, 2018. The law lets Pacific Historic Parks, a Hawaii group that works with the National Park Service, set up a display in Hawaii. The display honors members of the United States Armed Forces who served in the Pacific Theater of World War II.
plaw-115-171-2018: Public Law 115-171 is the Justice for Uncompensated Survivors Today (JUST) Act of 2017, approved on May 9, 2018. The law orders a report on Holocaust era assets and related issues. Covered countries are those that took part in the 2009 Holocaust Era Assets Conference and raise special concern. The law defines terms such as wrongfully seized or transferred, covering forced sales and takings under duress.
plaw-115-172-2018: Public Law 115-172 is a joint resolution approved on May 21, 2018, in which Congress cancels a federal rule. The rule came from the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection and dealt with indirect auto lending. It also dealt with how lenders follow the Equal Credit Opportunity Act. Under the resolution, that rule, issued as CFPB Bulletin 2013-02, has no force or effect.
plaw-115-173-2018: Public Law 115-173 is the Securely Expediting Clearances Through Reporting Transparency Act of 2018, or the SECRET Act, approved on May 22, 2018. The law deals with the backlog of security clearance checks run by the National Background Investigations Bureau. Within 90 days, and every three months for five years, the Bureau's director must report the size of that backlog to Congress.
plaw-115-174-2018:
Public Law 115-174 is the Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief, and Consumer Protection Act, approved on May 24, 2018. The law reshapes federal rules for banks and home loans. Its stated aims are growth of the economy, relief from rules that fit banks poorly, and stronger protection for buyers.

Early titles cover access to mortgage credit, with rules on home loans, rural appraisals, and credit union loans. Later titles ease capital rules for small community banks that qualify for relief. The law was one of the largest banking measures of the 115th Congress. The law also guards access to manufactured homes, as its contents list shows.
plaw-115-175-2018: Public Law 115-175 is the Black Hills National Cemetery Boundary Expansion Act, approved on May 25, 2018. The law moves about 200 acres of Bureau of Land Management land next to the Black Hills National Cemetery in Sturgis, South Dakota. Control of the land passes from the Secretary of the Interior to the Secretary of Veterans Affairs. The added land becomes part of the cemetery grounds.
plaw-115-176-2018:
Public Law 115-176 is the Trickett Wendler, Frank Mongiello, Jordan McLinn, and Matthew Bellina Right to Try Act of 2017, approved on May 30, 2018. The law amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. It deals with trial drugs that have not yet won full federal approval.

Under the law, a patient with a life-threatening illness may use such a drug in line with state law. The patient must have used up approved treatment choices first. A doctor must also confirm that the patient cannot take part in a clinical trial of the drug.
plaw-115-177-2018: Public Law 115-177, approved on June 1, 2018, changes title 38 of the United States Code on veterans' benefits. The law lets the Secretary of Veterans Affairs pay for changes to the homes of veterans in job rehabilitation programs. Help is capped at 77,307 dollars per veteran, though the Secretary may waive the cap when a program needs it. The changes must be ones the Secretary finds needed for the program.
plaw-115-178-2018: Public Law 115-178 is the Smithsonian National Zoological Park Central Parking Facility Authorization Act, approved on June 1, 2018. The law lets the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution plan, design, and build a central parking facility. The site is National Zoological Park land in the District of Columbia. The project may add restrooms and a foot bridge, and it must be paid for with non-federal funds.
plaw-115-179-2018: Public Law 115-179 is the Oregon Tribal Economic Development Act, approved on June 1, 2018. The law names seven Oregon tribal groups, among them the Klamath Tribes and the Burns Paiute Tribes. It states that these tribes may lease, sell, or transfer land they own without further approval from the United States. The law is clear that land held in trust for a tribe is not changed by the act.
plaw-115-180-2018:
Public Law 115-180 is the Childhood Cancer Survivorship, Treatment, Access, and Research Act of 2018, called the Childhood Cancer STAR Act, approved on June 5, 2018. The law seeks to speed the search for new treatments for cancer in children. It also aims to make promising treatments ready for use sooner.

One title backs research through sample banks that store tumor tissue for study. It also calls for better tracking of childhood cancer cases and a cancer board seat for a child cancer doctor. A second title turns to care, quality of life, and support for survivors and the people who care for them.
plaw-115-181-2018: Public Law 115-181, approved on June 5, 2018, gives new names to veterans clinics in Montana. The clinic at 2687 Palmer Street in Missoula becomes the David J. Thatcher VA Clinic. The clinic at 1775 Spring Creek Lane in Billings becomes the Dr. Joseph Medicine Crow VA Clinic. Any mention of either clinic in a federal law, rule, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of its new name.
plaw-115-182-2018:
Public Law 115-182 is the VA MISSION Act of 2018, approved on June 6, 2018. Its full name honors John S. McCain III, Daniel K. Akaka, and Samuel R. Johnson. The law sets up a lasting community care program for veterans who use the health system run by the Department of Veterans Affairs.

Under the law, veterans can receive care from local providers outside VA sites through one joined program. The law also sets up a panel to advise on updating or closing VA facilities. Other parts deal with VA building projects and the VA home loan program.
plaw-115-183-2018: Public Law 115-183, approved on June 15, 2018, renames a medical center in Huntington, West Virginia. The law states that the Department of Veterans Affairs medical center there shall be known as the Hershel 'Woody' Williams VA Medical Center. Any mention of that center in a federal law, rule, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-115-184-2018: Public Law 115-184 is the Veterans Cemetery Benefit Correction Act, approved on June 15, 2018. The law changes title 38 of the United States Code, which covers veterans' benefits. It requires the Secretary of the Interior to provide an outer burial receptacle for each grave in an open national cemetery run by the National Park Service. The change puts those cemeteries on the same footing as other national cemeteries.
plaw-115-185-2018:
Public Law 115-185 is the Project Safe Neighborhoods Grant Program Authorization Act of 2018, approved on June 18, 2018. The law sets up a block grant program inside the Office of Justice Programs at the Department of Justice. The Attorney General is in charge of running the program.

The stated purpose is to build and improve teamwork among federal, state, and local agencies. That teamwork includes the United States Attorney in each federal district. The law defines key terms for the program, among them firearms offenses under title 18 of the United States Code. The grants are paid as block grants to support the partnerships the program fosters.
plaw-115-186-2018: Public Law 115-186 is the National Veterans Memorial and Museum Act, approved on June 21, 2018. The law names the Veterans Memorial and Museum in Columbus, Ohio as the National Veterans Memorial and Museum. The museum stands on about seven acres on West Broad Street, by the Scioto River. As a condition, its director must report to Congress, and Congress may withdraw the title after five years if the museum falls short.
plaw-115-187-2018: Public Law 115-187 is the Small Business Investment Opportunity Act of 2017, approved on June 21, 2018. The short law changes one figure in the Small Business Investment Act of 1958. It raises the most leverage, or borrowed support, that one small business investment company may receive. The cap moves from 150 million dollars to 175 million dollars.
plaw-115-188-2018: Public Law 115-188 is the Department of Veterans Affairs Senior Executive Accountability Act of 2018, or the SEA Act, approved on June 21, 2018. The law adds a new section to title 38 of the United States Code. No senior executive at the Department may be moved to another such post unless the Secretary approves in writing. The Secretary must also report such moves to Congress twice a year.
plaw-115-189-2018: Public Law 115-189 is the Small Business 7(a) Lending Oversight Reform Act of 2018, approved on June 21, 2018. The law strengthens watch over the 7(a) loan program of the Small Business Administration. It writes the Office of Credit Risk Management into law, along with a lender oversight panel. That office supervises lenders who make 7(a) loans to small firms.
plaw-115-190-2018: Public Law 115-190, approved on June 22, 2018, swaps control of two small pieces of federal land in Virginia. About 0.342 acres along the George Washington Memorial Parkway pass from the Secretary of the Interior to the Secretary of Transportation. About 0.479 acres at the Turner-Fairbank Highway Research Center move the other way. The law orders both agencies to carry out the transfer quickly.
plaw-115-191-2018: Public Law 115-191 is the John Muir National Historic Site Expansion Act, approved on June 22, 2018. The law lets the Secretary of the Interior accept about 44 acres of donated land in Martinez, California. Once the land is received, the borders of the John Muir National Historic Site grow to include it. The new land is then run as part of the historic site.
plaw-115-192-2018: Public Law 115-192 is the Whistleblower Protection Coordination Act, approved on June 25, 2018. The law renews a post in each federal inspector general office and gives it a new name. The Whistleblower Ombudsman becomes the Whistleblower Protection Coordinator. That person teaches agency staff about their rights against payback for reporting wrongdoing, and about how to seek review of a claim.
plaw-115-193-2018: Public Law 115-193, approved on June 25, 2018, renames a veterans health center in Tallahassee, Florida. The law states that the center at 2181 Orange Avenue shall be known as the Sergeant Ernest I. 'Boots' Thomas VA Clinic. Any mention of that center in a federal law, rule, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-115-194-2018:
Public Law 115-194 is the Firefighter Cancer Registry Act of 2018, approved on July 7, 2018. The law orders the Secretary of Health and Human Services to build a voluntary registry of firefighters. The work runs through the Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Firefighters who join give health and work facts so that rates of cancer among them can be tracked. The law lists uses for the registry, starting with better data gathering across the country. It also backs joint work to watch how often cancer strikes firefighters. The registry is voluntary, and firefighters choose whether to take part.
plaw-115-195-2018: Public Law 115-195 is the All Circuit Review Act, approved on July 7, 2018. The law changes title 5 of the United States Code, which covers federal workers. It makes lasting a court review path for certain Merit Systems Protection Board rulings in whistleblower cases. Before, that path was set to last only five years. The law also states that the change counts as if passed on November 26, 2017.
plaw-115-196-2018:
Public Law 115-196 is the Supporting Grandparents Raising Grandchildren Act, approved on July 7, 2018. The law sets up a Federal Advisory Council to Support Grandparents Raising Grandchildren. Congress wrote its reasons into the law itself.

The findings state that more than two and a half million grandparents in the United States are the main caretakers of their grandchildren. The number is growing as the opioid crisis grows, the law says. It also notes that children placed with kin keep family ties and gain a steadier home than foster care with strangers. The council was formed to give those grandparents support at the federal level.
plaw-115-197-2018:
Public Law 115-197 is the American Innovation $1 Coin Act, approved on July 20, 2018. The law orders the Secretary of the Treasury to mint one-dollar coins that honor new ideas and bold first efforts. Each coin marks a person or group from one of the fifty states, the District of Columbia, or a United States territory.

Minting runs for a span of fourteen years starting on January 1, 2019. The coins bear fresh designs that praise the value of new thinking across the country. The program adds a new set of designs to the one-dollar coin line set out in title 31.
plaw-115-198-2018:
Public Law 115-198 is the North Korean Human Rights Reauthorization Act of 2017, approved on July 20, 2018. The law renews the North Korean Human Rights Act of 2004. Congress placed a long set of findings at the front of the law.

The findings cite a 2014 United Nations inquiry that called the abuses in North Korea crimes against humanity. The list covers forced hunger, torture, prison camps, and limits on free movement. The findings also fault China for sending North Korean refugees back by force, where they face camps, torture, or death. Congress first passed the North Korean Human Rights Act in 2004, and this law keeps that act in force.
plaw-115-199-2018: Barbara M. Barrett of Arizona kept her Smithsonian regent seat under Public Law 115-199, a joint resolution approved on July 20, 2018. The resolution fills the Board of Regents vacancy left when her term expired. It gives the seat back to Barrett for a fresh term of six years. The new term starts on January 11, 2019, or on the date the resolution passed, whichever is later.
plaw-115-200-2018: Public Law 115-200 is the Swan Lake Hydroelectric Project Boundary Correction Act, approved on July 20, 2018. The law deals with federal land inside the Swan Lake power project boundary in Alaska. Within eighteen months, the Secretary of the Interior must survey the tract of land marked Lost Creek on the project map. The Secretary must then grant that tract to the State of Alaska under the Alaska Statehood Act and the Federal Power Act.
plaw-115-201-2018: Public Law 115-201, approved on July 20, 2018, allows growth of the Terror Lake Hydroelectric Project in Alaska. The project, run under a federal license, gains a new part called the Upper Hidden Basin Diversion Expansion. The license holder may use up to twenty acres of federal land to build, run, and care for that expansion. No further permit from the Secretary of the Interior is needed for the work.
plaw-115-202-2018: Public Law 115-202, approved on July 23, 2018, gives more time to a hydroelectric project known by its federal license number, 12737. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission may, at the request of the license holder, stretch the deadline to start building. The stretch can run for up to three back-to-back spans of two years each. If the license has already run out, the law lets the Commission bring it back to life.
plaw-115-203-2018: Federal license number 12740 is the project covered by Public Law 115-203, approved on July 23, 2018. The law lets the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission push back the date by which building must start. The push can cover up to three back-to-back spans of two years each, if the license holder asks and gives fair notice. A license that has already run out may be brought back under the law.
plaw-115-204-2018: Public Law 115-204, approved on July 23, 2018, grants more time to the hydroelectric project with federal license number 12642. At the request of the license holder, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission may extend the deadline to begin building. The added time can reach three back-to-back spans of two years each. The law also lets the Commission restore a license that had already run out.
plaw-115-205-2018: Jennings Randolph Dam is the site named in Public Law 115-205, approved on July 23, 2018. The law deals with the hydroelectric project at that dam, which holds federal license number 12715. It lets the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission restore the license and push back the building deadline. The added time can reach three back-to-back spans of two years each, at the request of the license holder.
plaw-115-206-2018: Public Law 115-206, approved on July 23, 2018, concerns a power project at the Cannonsville Dam, licensed as federal project number 13287. The law lets the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission give the license holder more time to start building. The added time can run for up to four back-to-back spans of two years each. A license that has already run out may also be restored under the law.
plaw-115-207-2018: Los Angeles, California is the city covered by Public Law 115-207, approved on July 24, 2018. The law states that the postal facility at 3585 South Vermont Avenue shall be known as the Marvin Gaye Post Office. It adds that any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-115-208-2018: Public Law 115-208, approved on July 24, 2018, renames a post office in Pekin, Illinois. The law states that the postal facility at 514 Broadway Street shall be known as the Lance Corporal Jordan S. Bastean Post Office. Any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts, under the law, as a mention of the new name.
plaw-115-270-2018:
Public Law 115-270 is America's Water Infrastructure Act of 2018, approved on October 23, 2018. The law covers rivers and harbors across the United States. It also covers the saving and growth of water supplies and related lands, plus work to control water pollution.

The first title deals with water projects run by the Army Corps of Engineers. Its parts order studies of the Corps, a review of the Lake Okeechobee water schedule, and research on species that invade waterways. Other parts cover test work on blooms of harmful algae and a pilot program for dredging.
plaw-115-282-2018:
Public Law 115-282 is the Frank LoBiondo Coast Guard Authorization Act of 2018, approved on December 4, 2018. The law sets funding levels for the United States Coast Guard. It also rewrites the part of federal law that governs the service, title 14 of the United States Code.

The first title rebuilds title 14 chapter by chapter, from the service's duties to its staff rules. The second title grants funds and sets the allowed size of the force. It names sums for Fast Response Cutters, for shore sites, and for upgrades to aircraft. A third title in the contents turns to Coast Guard matters in more detail.
plos-pbio-0020218:
Anoop Kumar, Cristiana P. Velloso, Yutaka Imokawa, and their team studied limb regrowth in PLOS Biology in 2004. Urodeles, the salamander group, can regrow whole limbs. The team isolated muscle fibers from these animals and watched the cells change back into a flexible, stem-like state.

That reversal, called dedifferentiation, is a key step in forming the growth bud that rebuilds a limb. The study ties the process to a gene called Msx1. When Msx1 is active, muscle fibers can loosen their mature form. Mammals cannot do this, so the salamander system shows what would need to change. The work frames regrowth as a controlled return to youth by adult cells.
plos-pbio-0020418:
Stephanie M. Brandt, Marc S. Dionne, Ranjiv S. Khush, and their team studied Salmonella in fruit flies in PLOS Biology in 2004. Salmonella bacteria inject effector proteins into host cells to take control. In the fly, those effectors, plus a host signal called Eiger, which matches our TNF, drive infected cells to die.

Cell death can defend the host by removing the germ's home, or help the germ by clearing its path. This study shows both sides pushing toward death in the infected fly gut. The fly model lets researchers separate bacterial tricks from host responses with clean genetics. Lessons from it feed into the wider fight against Salmonella food poisoning.
plos-pone-0000018:
Virginia Zaleskas, Daniela Krause, Katherine Lazarides, and co-authors modeled a human blood disease in mice in 2006. A single mutation, JAK2 V617F, drives polycythemia vera, a condition where the body makes far too many red blood cells. The team gave mice the mutation and studied both how the disease develops and how it might be treated.

Their work traces the molecular pathogenesis, the chain from one faulty gene to thickened blood and its risks. They also tested therapy against the mutant pathway in the same animals. A mouse that faithfully mirrors the human illness lets researchers screen treatments before any patient is exposed, and this study built and used that mirror.
plos-pone-0000118:
Seth W. Coleman and Gil G. Rosenthal published this animal behavior study in PLOS ONE in 2006. Their subjects are swordtail fry, baby fish only days into life. The study asks how these tiny fish spot danger and find their own kind, testing whether they use chemical cues, visual cues, or both.

Young fish that fail to detect predators rarely survive long. The authors present the fry with scent and sight signals from predators and from fellow swordtails and record the responses. The work shows how early in life these senses come online, and it adds to what is known about how fish read their watery surroundings.
plos-pone-0000218:
Kirsi H. Pietiläinen, Marko Sysi-Aho, Aila Rissanen, and colleagues published this twin study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It examines identical twins where one twin had become obese and the other had not. The authors found that acquired obesity is tied to changes in the serum lipidomic profile. That profile is the pattern of fats in the blood, and the tie holds independent of genetic effects.

Because identical twins share their genes, differences between them point to lifestyle and environment. The lipid changes therefore track the obesity itself, not inherited risk. Such profiles may flag the metabolic harm of weight gain early, before diseases like diabetes take hold.
plos-pone-0000318:
Laura A. Díaz-Martínez, Juan F. Giménez-Abián, and Duncan J. Clarke published this chromosome study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cohesin is the protein ring that holds sister chromosomes together until division. Working in human cells, the authors reach a striking conclusion, stated in the title. Cohesin is dispensable for cohesion at the centromere, the chromosomes' central pinch point.

That result surprised a field that treated cohesin as the glue itself. Something else must help hold centromeres together in human cells. The paper reopened a basic question in cell division and pushed researchers to look for the missing mechanism.
plos-pone-0000418:
Patricia L.R. Brennan and colleagues compared the genitals of male and female waterfowl, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Ducks and their relatives are famous among biologists for elaborate, fast-changing genital shapes. The team tested whether male and female structures have evolved together, each shaping the other over time.

Such coevolution can arise when the sexes' interests conflict over mating and fertilization. If female structures evolve to keep control over which males succeed, male structures evolve in response. Waterfowl make the pattern visible because the anatomy is so extreme. The study is a widely noted example of how sexual conflict can drive rapid evolutionary change.
plos-pone-0000518:
Stéphanie Schrambach and colleagues mapped where two immune alarm proteins appear in the body, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The proteins, MICA and MICB, appear on stressed or infected cells and flag them for immune attack. The team described their in vivo expression pattern and its relevance to auto-immunity and cancer.

Where a flag is normally raised decides where mistaken attacks can happen. If healthy tissues display MICA or MICB, the immune system may target them, feeding autoimmune disease; tumors may raise or shed them to escape. An expression map is the reference that such disease studies need before they can claim anything is abnormal.
plos-pone-0000618:
Yinyi Huang, P. T. Tran, Snezhana Oliferenko and their team found a new genetic way to strip cells of major parts, reported in PLOS ONE in 2007. They removed both the nucleus and the spindle pole bodies, the yeast version of centrosomes. Both parts were thought to be key organizers of the cell's inner framework.

Even without them, the cells still assembled microtubules, the framework's rods, and actomyosin rings, the bands that pinch a cell in two. That result tests long-held beliefs about who runs cell organization. Cell biologists get a fresh method here, plus evidence that the framework can organize itself more than expected.
plos-pone-0000718:
Debbie Winter, Ben Vinegar, Hardeep Nahal and colleagues built a visual browser for huge biological data sets, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Exploring microarray data and other high-throughput results had become vital for generating hypotheses in post-genomic research. For specialists outside bioinformatics, though, many tools present overwhelming amounts of data in forbidding forms.

Their answer is an electronic fluorescent pictograph browser, presenting data as pictures rather than tables. Pictographs let a researcher spot patterns across thousands of genes at a glance. Tools like this decide who gets to use big data. Bench biologists gain entry too, even without programming training. Results become readable pictures instead of raw numbers.
plos-pone-0000818:
Sa'ar Mizrahi, Gal Markel, Angel Porgador and colleagues found a surface protein that sharpens natural killer cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. NK cells kill tumor and virus-infected cells without needing prior antigen stimulation. Their killing is regulated by inhibitory, lysis, and co-stimulatory receptors on the cell surface. CD100, also called Semaphorin 4D, is a 150-kilodalton transmembrane protein found on such cells.

The title reports that CD100 on NK cells enhances secretion of interferon-gamma and killing of target cells expressing CD72. A receptor pairing that boosts both alarm signals and killing could be exploited in cancer immunotherapy. It also redraws CD100's job description beyond nerve guidance, where semaphorins were first known.
plos-pone-0000918:
Lisa Denning, Jennifer Anderson, Ryan Davis and co-authors tested resequencing microarrays for a group of muscle nerve disorders, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Congenital myasthenic syndromes are inherited faults where nerves fail to drive muscles properly. Many genes can cause them, so testing one gene at a time is slow.

Resequencing arrays screen many candidate sites at once, offering an alternative to classic capillary sequencing. The team describe how their custom array performed on real cases. A faster screen means families get answers sooner, and doctors can match care to the exact fault. The paper is a practical check on whether the shortcut can be trusted.
plos-pone-0001018:
Blaise Genton, Gerd Pluschke, Lukas Degen and colleagues ran an early malaria vaccine trial using virus like carriers, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The trial used influenza virosomes, hollow virus shells that can carry other material safely. Virosomes had already proved fit for subunit vaccines, designs that use only pieces of a germ.

Two synthetic peptides, short malaria protein pieces, were mounted on the virosomes. Healthy adult volunteers received them in a randomized, placebo controlled phase one trial. The aim was proof of concept: can this carrier raise strong antibodies against malaria pieces. Early trials like this decide whether a vaccine idea earns larger tests.
plos-pone-0001118:
Annexin A2 is a protein that binds cell membranes and helps organize traffic inside the cell. Etienne Morel and Jean Gruenberg explain its workings in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The protein usually works as a four-part complex that includes a small partner chain called p11, or S100A10.

Morel and Gruenberg asked whether annexin A2 needs that partner to reach endosomes, the sorting stations that move cargo through the cell. Their title states the answer. The p11 chain is not required for annexin A2 to reach endosomes, or to do its work in endosomal transport. The result narrows down which parts of the complex truly matter.
plos-pone-0001218:
Changing the dose of a single gene often shifts the levels of hundreds of other proteins, a puzzle seen in mouse models of neurodegenerative disease. Lei Mao and colleagues investigated that ripple effect in embryonic stem cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They carried out a proteomic investigation, measuring many proteins at once.

The proteomic shifts they observed suggest the presence of balancer proteins in protein regulatory networks, proteins that absorb or compensate for changes. The idea would explain why cells stay stable despite genetic perturbations. Their work reframes gene dose effects as a network property, not just a single gene's fault.
plos-pone-0001318:
Tuberculosis is the leading cause of death worldwide from a single infectious agent. Decades of data suggest that human susceptibility to it has a genetic component. Xin Ma and colleagues resequenced all the coding regions of Toll-like receptor genes to test their contribution, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Toll-like receptors play a critical role in initiating the innate immune response to TB.

Full-exon resequencing reads every protein-coding segment, catching rare variants that chip studies miss. The authors report that Toll-like receptor variants contribute to human susceptibility to tuberculosis disease. Their results support targeted genetics for a disease usually fought at the public health level.
plos-pone-0001418:
Anne Tisserant and Harald König wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how gene messages are cut and rejoined. Cells can splice a message in more than one way, and signals from outside the cell can steer the choice. A core splicing factor must first sit on the message. The pair asked how signals change that seating.

They show that cell signals shift where and how firmly the factor binds before splicing starts. That early step helps decide which version of a protein the cell will make. The finding adds a control point to a key gene process. It may help explain how cells adapt fast when their state changes.
plos-pone-0001518:
Sarah Brosnan and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on trade in chimpanzees. Economists hold that barter lies at the root of social wealth and much of human culture. Yet how barter arose in evolution was little known. The team tested when chimps will trade goods with each other or with people.

Chimps did trade in some setups but held back in others. Their choices hinged on trust and on what each side gained. The pattern hints at what must be in place for barter to thrive. It gives a base for tests on how human trade grew from primate roots.
plos-pone-0001618:
Timothy J. Page, William F. Humphreys, and Jane M. Hughes studied a small shrimp that lives only in underground waters in Western Australia. Their 2008 PLOS ONE research article looks at Stygiocaris, a genus of cave shrimp, and asks how its species are related to each other. The shrimp belong to a rare group of animals found in coastal limestone caves where fresh water and sea water mix.

Page and his co-authors used nuclear and mitochondrial genes to trace both the large-scale and small-scale family links among these shrimp. Work of this kind helps show how cave species split apart and adapt to life in the dark. The full text gives the gene data and the family tree the team built from it. It also gives their account of what the tree says about the history of these hidden animals.
plos-pone-0001718:
Helga Schneider, Hongyan Wang, Monika Raab, and their co-authors studied a signaling adaptor in T cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The adaptor is SKAP-55, known for helping T cells stick to other cells through LFA-1 adhesion. Whether it also shapes other signaling was unknown. Adaptors act as nodes that can coordinate several jobs at once.

The team reports that SKAP-55 binds RasGRP1, an exchange factor that switches on the p21 ras protein. That binding negatively regulates the p21 ras to ERK pathway. The full text gives the binding tests and the pathway measurements. One adaptor that both aids adhesion and brakes a growth pathway shows how T cells keep activation strong but bounded.
plos-pone-0001818:
Chaoyang Lin, Jun Fang, Xiaoli Xu, and their co-authors engineered rice that can be selectively terminated in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Gene transfer improves crops and yields valuable proteins such as drugs. The unplanned spread of commercial transgenic crops by pollen and seed is a major public concern.

Their built-in containment strategy creates rice plants that farmers can kill off on demand while nearby ordinary rice is unharmed. The full text gives the genetic design and the field tests. A built-in kill switch answers a long-standing public worry about gene-altered crops grown outdoors.
plos-pone-0001918:
Meltem Muftuoglu and co-authors studied a chemical tag that tunes a DNA repair protein, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, WRN, fails in Werner syndrome, an illness that ages the body far too fast. WRN takes part in many tasks that keep DNA sound, among them base excision repair, which fixes small daily lesions in the code.

The team asked whether acetylation, a small chemical tag placed on proteins, changes what WRN can do. They report that the tag regulates WRN's work as a catalyst and shifts how well repair proceeds. Tags like this may be dials that cells use to aim repair where it is needed.
plos-pone-0002018:
Joseph Gillespie and co-authors charted the family tree of a group of bacteria that live only inside cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Rickettsia species cause human ills from epidemic typhus to Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Their genomes were being read at a fast pace, giving a rich set for comparison.

To build a sound tree, the team first sorted genes into orthologous groups, sets of genes that descend from one gene in a shared ancestor. Only then can branch order be trusted. A clean tree of these parasites helps trace how an inside-cell life evolves and trims a genome down.
plos-pone-0002118:
LaReesa Wolfenbarger and co-authors pooled field studies on how Bt crops affect other insects, in a 2008 PLOS ONE meta-analysis. Bt crops are engineered to make the insect-killing Cry proteins of the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. Uncertainty persists over their effects on arthropods they are not meant to target, from predators to pollinators.

The team performed meta-analyses on a modified public database, grouping non-target arthropods by functional guild, the job each group does in the field. Bt cotton anchors the analysis. Pooling many field studies gives a firmer answer on bystander harm than any single field season can.
plos-pone-0002218:
Chiara Marchesi and co-authors measured stem cell levels in the blood of patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Duchenne is a severe muscle-wasting disease of boys. Blood and cell markers can predict the course of many diseases, and the team asked whether certain stem cells might do the same here.

They counted subclasses of circulating progenitor cells marked by CD133. Levels of some groups matched a milder course of the disease. A blood test that hints at how fast Duchenne will progress would help families plan and help trials judge whether a treatment truly works.
plos-pone-0002318:
Tohru Nakagawa and co-authors built a tissue test to predict which prostate cancers will spread after treatment, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Many men see their PSA level rise again after initial therapy for prostate cancer. Some will develop local or distant recurrence needing more treatment, while others show no progression at all.

The team hypothesized that a panel of expression biomarkers in the tumor could separate those paths. Their panel predicts systemic progression after PSA recurrence. A test like this could spare low-risk men harsh extra therapy while catching high-risk cases early enough to act.
plos-pone-0002418:
In 2008, Kucherenko and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Mariya M. Kucherenko, Mario Pantoja, Andriy S. Yatsenko, and others. Its subject is genetic Modifier Screens Reveal New Components that Interact with the Drosophila Dystroglycan-Dystrophin Complex. The Dystroglycan-Dystrophin (Dg-Dys) complex has a capacity to transmit information from the extracellular matrix to the cytoskeleton inside the cell.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002518:
A research team led by Destouches reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Damien Destouches, Diala El Khoury, Yamina Hamma-Kourbali, and others. Its subject is suppression of Tumor Growth and Angiogenesis by a Specific Antagonist of the Cell-Surface Expressed Nucleolin. Emerging evidences suggest that nucleolin expressed on the cell surface is implicated in growth of tumor cells and angiogenesis.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002618:
Work from Sande and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Marianne van der Sande, Peter Teunis, Rob Sabel, and others. Its subject is professional and Home-Made Face Masks Reduce Exposure to Respiratory Infections among the General Population. Governments are preparing for a potential influenza pandemic.

Therefore they need data to assess the possible impact of interventions. Face-masks worn by the general population could be an accessible and affordable intervention, if effective when worn under routine circumstances. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002718:
Sara Sanz-Blasco led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was mitochondrial ca 2+ overload underlies aβ oligomers neurotoxicity providing an unexpected mechanism of neuroprotection by NSAIDs. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Sara Sanz-Blasco, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Dysregulation of intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis may underlie amyloid β peptide (Aβ) toxicity in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) but the mechanism is unknown. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002818:
Carolina Ibáñez-Ventoso led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was sequence relationships among C. elegans , D. melanogaster and human microRNAs highlight the extensive conservation of microRNAs in biology. The catalog record names Carolina Ibáñez-Ventoso first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. MicroRNAs act in a prevalent and conserved post-transcriptional gene regulatory mechanism that impacts development, homeostasis and disease. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002918:
Patrick Reynolds, Jeffrey Simms and Robert Duronio used domain swapping in fruit flies in 2008 to study protein destruction. Cullin-based ligases tag proteins for removal and help run many cell processes. Their Roc subunit holds a RING domain that grips the charged partner needed for tagging.

Drosophila has three Roc proteins with different jobs. By swapping domains between them, the team identified what decides which cullin each Roc binds. Published in PLOS ONE, the results clarify how cells assemble distinct destruction machines from similar parts, a basic question in cell control. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003018:
Armand Paauw, Martien Caspers, Frank Schuren and co-authors charted genomic diversity in the Enterobacter cloacae complex in 2008. These bacteria are increasingly found as hospital-acquired pathogens. Yet identifying them by appearance and chemistry is unreliable and hard to reproduce between labs.

Even genotyping tools of the time were being superseded for telling species apart. The PLOS ONE study uses genome-level diversity to sort the complex more soundly. Better identification matters in hospitals, where the species behind an outbreak guides infection control and antibiotic choice. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003118:
Shrimati Datta and Nora Sarvetnick studied how IL-21 limits lymphocyte numbers in 2008. IL-21 is a cytokine in the common gamma-chain family that participates in immune and inflammatory processes. The cytokine has also been linked to autoimmunity in humans and rodents, which made its normal role worth pinning down.

To investigate the mechanism, the team examined how IL-21 affects the immune system through T cell homeostatic mechanisms, the balancing systems that hold cell counts steady. IL-21 limits peripheral lymphocyte numbers that way, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, a brake on cell numbers matters for both deficiency and excess.
plos-pone-0003218:
Rune W. Berg, Susanne Ditlevsen and Jørn Hounsgaard study spike timing in spinal neurons in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In neurons, spike timing is set by integration of synaptic potentials together with intrinsic properties. Although integration time is functionally crucial, it remains elusive during network activity. Mechanisms of rapid processing are well documented in some systems but harder to capture here.

The title reports that intense synaptic activity enhances temporal resolution in spinal motoneurons. Readers see busy input sharpen, rather than blur, timing in these cells. That finding matters for motor control, where precise timing of muscle commands is essential.
plos-pone-0003318:
Damon H. Meyer and Adam M. Bailis study lost chromosome ends in yeast in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Telomerase is the complex that copies and guards telomeres, the DNA caps at chromosome ends. Cells with no telomerase lose a bit of cap DNA at each division. In time they lose viability and their genomes grow unstable.

The title reports that lack of telomerase changes how often chromosomes swap arms by homologous recombination in baker's yeast. Readers see worn ends lead to large-scale genome shuffles. Such translocations mark many cancers, so yeast work helps show how they start.
plos-pone-0003418:
Ruth Bollongino, Julia Elsner, and Jean-Denis Vigne read cattle DNA for this 2008 study. Europe's first farm cattle came from the Near East long ago. Earlier DNA work confirmed that origin but could not test male lines. The question was whether wild European bulls, called aurochs, later bred with farm herds.

The team checked Y-chromosome markers, which pass from fathers to sons. They looked at both ancient bones and modern cattle. The markers showed no sign of mixing with wild male aurochs. Farm herds and wild herds seem to have stayed apart.
plos-pone-0003518:
Valérie Kédinger and co-authors followed a shuttle protein at cell borders in this 2008 paper. TRAF4 had plenty of evidence for a key biological role. Yet how it works inside cells stayed unclear. Tight junctions are the seals that join one cell sheet to the next.

Using imaging methods, the team saw TRAF4 move in and out of those junctions. It acts as a dynamic shuttle tied to junction upkeep. That movement supports the balance of the epithelium, the body's lining tissue. One protein thus serves both signaling and structural roles.
plos-pone-0003618:
Catriona S. Bradshaw, Marcus Y. Chen, and Christopher K. Fairley followed a stubborn infection after treatment in this 2008 study. Mycoplasma genitalium causes genital infection in men and women. Patients at a Melbourne sexual health centre received azithromycin therapy. The standard course was a single one-gram dose.

The team determined clinical outcomes and cure rates after that dose. Some infections persisted following therapy, as the title records. Persistence flags a growing treatment problem for this infection. Clinicians may need new drugs or longer courses. This infection is often missed, since tests for it are not routine in clinics.
plos-pone-0003718:
Steven V. Vollmer and David I. Kline published this coral study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Disease outbreaks have done heavy damage to tropical reefs and to the corals that build them. Almost nothing was known about whether corals themselves can resist infection. The authors studied threatened staghorn corals.

They found natural variation in disease resistance among the corals. Some hosts resisted infection where others fell ill. That first evidence of coral resistance matters for reefs in crisis, since resistant stock could seed recovery and guide which corals to protect or breed.
plos-pone-0003818:
Guenter Albrecht-Buehler published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Mammalian genomes hold a strange feature: stretches longer than fifty bases made only of the letters G and A. Chance says such pure GA-sequences should be vanishingly rare. Yet they occur across many species.

The author describes the properties and distribution of these sequences in human, chimpanzee, dog, cat, rat, and mouse genomes. Their chromosomes contain far more of them than random expectation allows. The census of these odd repeats raises the question of what, if anything, they do in the genome.
plos-pone-0003918:
Taisheng Li, Yi Dai, Jiqiu Kuang, and co-authors compared three HIV drug plans in China in 2008. All three plans were built on the drug nevirapine and used generic drugs. The study enrolled adults with HIV-1 who had never taken such drugs. It ran at several centers as a forward-looking cohort.

A total of 198 patients took part across the three treatment arms. The team judged how well each plan controlled the virus and how safe each was. Real-world comparisons help clinics pick plans they can sustain. The results speak to national programs relying on low-cost generic drugs.
plos-pone-0004018:
Alexander S. Klyubin, Daniel Polani, and Chrystopher L. Nehaniv proposed an information rule for robot and animal behavior in 2008. Sensorimotor systems process information as their central resource. The authors define a measure of how well an agent senses and acts. It gauges the options an organism keeps open for its future.

Their PLOS ONE article argues agents should keep their options open. That drive can produce sensible behavior without fixed goals. The principle speaks to robotics, where simple rules must guide machines. It also offers a lens on why animals explore and play. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004118:
Amy Fulton, Sarah T. Peters, Gillian A. Perkins, and co-authors treated a horse herpesvirus with RNA interference in 2009. Equine herpesvirus type 1 spreads through nasal secretions. It causes respiratory disease, nerve disorders, and abortions in horses. Current vaccines protect only partially against it.

Their PLOS ONE article reports RNA interference treated the infection effectively. Small RNAs can be designed to silence viral genes directly. Success in this respiratory infection supports RNA therapy in veterinary medicine. It may also guide similar work on human herpesviruses. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004218:
Lisa Creary and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fetal haemoglobin, or HbF, softens the severity of sickle cell disease, so factors that raise it matter to patients. The team investigated a region on chromosome 6, called a quantitative trait locus, that earlier work had linked to HbF levels.

They tested whether variants in this region are associated with HbF and with F cells, the red cells that carry fetal haemoglobin. Their subjects were healthy people of African descent and sickle cell patients. The study checks a genetic lead that could one day guide treatments raising fetal haemoglobin.
plos-pone-0004318:
Sureshkumar Balasubramanian and colleagues published this plant genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Even when visible differences between plant strains are large, the underlying genetics are often complex. The causal regions must be found by quantitative trait locus mapping. Unfortunately, those mapping methods usually leave large confidence intervals, wide stretches of genome that might hold the gene.

The team present new advanced intercross-recombinant inbred lines of Arabidopsis thaliana for QTL mapping. Repeated crossing shuffles the genome more finely, narrowing the intervals. Better plant lines mean gene hunts end at a gene, not a neighbourhood.
plos-pone-0004418:
Separating many glowing colors inside a living brain is the problem taken up by Mathieu Ducros, Laurent Moreaux, Jonathan Bradley, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. New strains of mice can be bred to make several bright proteins at once in nerve cells. Those proteins help mark which cells are active, but their colors overlap and blur together.

The team tested a method called spectral unmixing, which pulls apart mixed color signals, deep in the smell center of the living mouse brain. They measured how well the method worked under real conditions, not just in theory. The findings guide researchers who use glowing markers to map nerve circuits and watch the brain at work.
plos-pone-0004518:
Removing a cell-cycle brake gene kills mouse embryos very early, report Yong Kim, Jim McBride, Lauren Kimlin, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene is Cdk2ap1, also called p12. Its protein restrains CDK2, an engine that pushes cells from the resting phase into copying their DNA.

The team inactivated the gene in mice. Most embryos died between the third and fifth day after conception, before implantation is complete. Timed studies of pregnancies pinpointed that window. A gene whose loss is lethal so early is plainly doing essential work in the first cell divisions. The finding also warns that drugs aimed at this pathway would need great care around early development and fertility.
plos-pone-0004618:
Thinking about yourself switches on a strip of brain called the anterior insula, show Gemma Modinos, Johan Ormel, and Andre Aleman in PLOS ONE in 2009. Functional neuroimaging studies had suggested that midline frontoparietal regions, along the brain's center seam, are at the core of self-related processes. The insula, buried deep in the side of the brain, was reported in some studies but got little attention.

The team examined anterior insula activation during self-reflection. The insula is best known for sensing the body's inner state: heartbeat, gut feelings, and pain. If self-reflection engages it, then thinking about oneself is partly a bodily act, not a purely abstract one. That matters for disorders where self-awareness goes wrong, from depression to schizophrenia.
plos-pone-0004718:
Jelle van Zweden and colleagues tested if ant queen egg marks found in the lab hold true in nature, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Lab tests can give crisp proof for a claim, but only if they match complex real life. That match is seldom checked in a direct way, the authors note.

Queen ants mark their eggs with a scent that workers can read. The team compared neat lab setups with the mess of real nests. Their check shows where simple tests mislead and where they hold. The lesson reaches past ants to all lab based claims about animal behavior.
plos-pone-0004818:
Alexandre Valin and colleagues showed that skin fibroblasts from Gorlin syndrome patients exhibit features of carcinoma linked fibroblasts, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gorlin syndrome, or nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome, causes predisposition to basal cell carcinoma, the commonest cancer in adult humans. Mutations in the tumor suppressor gene PTCH1 are responsible for this autosomal dominant syndrome with multiple developmental abnormalities and tumors.

Even healthy skin fibroblasts carried tumor like traits. Stroma may prime cancer growth in carriers. That shifts focus beyond lining cells alone. Prevention strategies might target the microenvironment. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend.
plos-pone-0004918:
Leishmaniasis is a tropical disease caused by Leishmania parasites. Its current drugs are toxic, and resistance is growing. In a 2009 PLOS ONE paper, Lívia Santos and colleagues tested a new idea. They asked whether HIV drugs that block enzymes called aspartyl peptidases could also work against Leishmania amazonensis.

The HIV drugs slowed the growth of the parasite. They also damaged its inner structure. Treated parasites had more trouble infecting macrophages, the immune cells they normally invade. Because these medicines already exist for HIV care, the results suggest a shortcut. A neglected tropical disease might gain new treatment options from drugs already on the shelf.
plos-pone-0005018:
Cervical cancer is frequently tied to HPV infection. The viral proteins E6 and E7 are key factors in its development. Abdessamad Amine and colleagues tested an antiviral drug against it. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The drug is cidofovir. They found it also blocks tumor spread.

Cidofovir silences the viral E6 and E7 proteins. It also jams two migration signals, CXCR4 and the Rho/ROCK pathway. Together these actions give it a novel anti-metastatic effect. An old antiviral becomes a candidate against metastatic cervical cancer. The study shows how much remains hidden in familiar drugs. Repurposing them could speed new treatments to patients.
plos-pone-0005118:
When cells divide, sister chromosomes are glued together by cohesin. The glue holds until the right moment for separation. Dense DNA regions, heterochromatin, were thought to attract extra cohesin. Ángel Serrano and colleagues tested that idea in human cells. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The suspected recruiter was heterochromatin protein 1, HP1.

HP1 proteins do not drive pericentromeric cohesin enrichment. The classical picture fails in human cells. A negative result like this forces a rethink. Something else must target cohesin to chromosome centers. Accurate segregation depends on that targeting. Errors cause miscarriage and birth defects. The study clears away a wrong answer. That is real progress in a precise field.
plos-pone-0005218:
When nerves are damaged, they often fail to regrow, and proteins in myelin are part of the reason. One of them, myelin-associated glycoprotein, strongly blocks new growth from sensory neurons. Wörter and colleagues mapped where that blocking power sits in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Two known receptors, NgR1 and NgR2, were thought to carry much of the block. The team found the block is largely independent of both, and traced it to two sections of the protein, its fourth and fifth Ig-like domains. A precise map of the brake helps repair researchers aim at the right part.
plos-pone-0005318:
Controlling malaria means not only curing patients but also stopping spread to mosquitoes. Drugs that kill the parasite's sexual stages, called gametocytes, can break transmission. Coulibaly and colleagues ran a randomized controlled trial of a methylene blue combination therapy in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Methylene blue is an old, blue-dyed drug with activity against malaria parasites. The trial found a strong gametocytocidal effect, as the title states, against falciparum malaria. A transmission-blocking treatment like this could support local elimination of malaria, not just treatment of the sick. A drug that stops spread, not just cures the sick, could help a town clear malaria for good. Since each cured case would no longer seed new ones by mosquito bite.
plos-pone-0005418:
Elena Rusconi and her co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how people know their own bodies. Knowing the shape and layout of one's body is often seen as a basic part of self-awareness. Yet little was known about how the brain holds a built-in map of that structure.

The team made a new two-hand version of a classic finger test. People had to judge which finger had been touched, without looking at their hands. Their answers gave proof that the brain keeps a clear structural map of the body. The work helps explain how touch and body sense fit together.
plos-pone-0005518:
Laura Dugan and co-authors studied inflammation and the aging brain in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A signal called IL-6 rises in the blood in many poor health states of later life, from heart disease to frailty. The team asked what raised IL-6 does inside the aging brain itself.

In aged mice, IL-6 harmed a class of calming brain cells in the front of the brain. It acted through an enzyme that makes harsh oxygen chemicals. Thinking scores suffered along with the cell loss. The chain points to new ways to protect the aging mind.
plos-pone-0005618:
Igor Ruvinsky and co-authors studied mice whose ribosomal protein cannot be tagged, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Ribosomes build all proteins in cells, and one of their parts, S6, is often tagged to adjust that building. Mice engineered so S6 cannot be tagged are born and breed normally at first glance.

Closer study found growth faults, low energy, and weak muscles in these mice and their cells. The faults show that a single tag on the protein machine matters for muscle strength. That insight bears on diseases of growth and metabolism.
plos-pone-0005718:
Basirudeen Kabeer and co-authors tested in 2009 how well a blood test for tuberculosis works in people who also have HIV. Finding TB fast in HIV patients is hard, and a quick, sure test is badly needed. The test they checked measures interferon gamma released by immune cells.

The team measured how often the test catches true TB cases in this group. HIV weakens the very cells the test depends on, so its accuracy was in doubt. Clear numbers on that accuracy help clinics decide when to trust the test and when to use others. In co-infected patients, a wrong call can cost lives.
plos-pone-0005818:
Lisa Kinch, Melanie Yarbrough, and Kim Orth defined a new protein domain family in 2009. A bacterial toxin called VopS attaches AMP tags to host proteins, jamming their signals. Its working piece, the fic domain, shares a sequence motif with other proteins.

The team showed that motif marks a wider family, which they named Fido, spanning Fic, Doc, and AvrB proteins. AMPylation, once thought rare, may be a broad bacterial strategy. Recognizing the family lets scientists spot the trick in new pathogens quickly. It also adds a tool bacteria use that drug design might block.
plos-pone-0005918:
Yaakov Bentov and co-authors tested in 2009 whether variants in blood-clotting genes change a woman's risk of ovarian cancer. The cause of ovarian cancer is largely unknown, making every credible lead worth checking. One hypothesis blames the slow clearing of clots and fibrin shed near the ovary each month.
