Genes of the fibrinolytic system govern that clearing. If their variants raise risk, the hypothesis gains support and a screening angle opens. The team's analysis weighs that link in real patient data. Ovarian cancer is often caught late, so risk markers carry unusual value.
plos-pone-0006018:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a germ that thrives almost anywhere and infects people whose defenses are down. Helga Mikkelsen, Geneviève Ball, Caroline Giraud and colleagues studied how it controls one set of its tools in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper covers the CupD fimbrial genes, which build hair-like parts that help the germ stick and form biofilms.

Two regulators pull those genes in opposite ways: RcsB pushes one way, while PvrR, a regulator carrying an EAL part, pushes back. A tug-of-war like this lets the germ tune its grip to the place it finds itself. Knowing the switch matters for fighting biofilm infections, which resist drugs far better than free-swimming germs do.
plos-pone-0006118:
South America had little hard data on the germs behind flu-like illness when Peru built a sentinel system. Alberto Laguna-Torres, Jorge Gómez, Víctor Ocaña and colleagues report that system in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper covers influenza-like illness sentinel surveillance set up in 2006, sampling cases at chosen clinics to learn what causes acute respiratory illness in the country.

Sentinel sites trade breadth for depth: fewer clinics, fully tested. That design can name the viruses at work where blanket reporting cannot. The Peruvian record fills a regional gap and gives health teams a base for vaccine and hospital planning when respiratory illness surges.
plos-pone-0006218:
Gene faults that harm nerves in people can sometimes soften harm from other gene faults. Gareth Banks and colleagues tested that idea in mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. In humans, faults in the GARS enzyme cause loss of motor and feeling nerves, ranging from Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease to a severe infantile form.

A mutant Gars gene eased motor neuron decline in mice bred to model ALS, as the title reports. The same gene had little effect in a different mouse strain with a dynein fault. The contrast shows that gene interactions are specific, not general rescue. Such modifiers may one day explain why the same disease strikes people unevenly.
plos-pone-0006318:
Earlier recipes for making neurons from human stem cells borrowed fluids from rodent brain cells. Tsuyoshi Okuno and colleagues present a self-contained method in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Mouse stem cells had been converted efficiently using medium conditioned by rat astrocytes, but rodent materials raise supply and safety problems for human use.

Their method induces neurons from human embryonic stem cells without that animal support. Removing animal-derived inputs is a step toward clinical-grade cell production. The neurons produced can serve research on development and disease. Cleaner recipes also make results easier to reproduce between labs.
plos-pone-0006418:
Repeated DNA stretches that expand cause many nerve and muscle diseases. Joao Paulo Tavanez and colleagues studied inclusions formed by polyalanine expansions in the protein PABPN1 in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Expansions in coding regions are translated into long runs of a single amino acid.

The nuclear inclusions sequester Hsp70 chaperones and type I PRMT enzymes, per the title. Trapped helper proteins cannot do their normal jobs elsewhere. Sequestration may be a shared damage mechanism across repeat diseases. The detailed guest list of the inclusions guides that idea. The guest list gives drug work a set of clear parts to aim at.
plos-pone-0006518:
Arkan Abadi, Elisa Glover, Robert Isfort, and colleagues measured what happens when a limb is immobilized, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Animal models and cell culture have been invaluable for explaining muscle atrophy. However, few studies had examined immobilization effects in men directly. The team studied human volunteers whose limbs were immobilized.

Their title reports a coordinate down-regulation of mitochondrial and other metabolic pathways. In other words, the resting muscle turns down its energy machinery as a set. That coordinated response helps explain why casted limbs weaken so fast. It also gives targets for keeping muscle alive during injury recovery or spaceflight.
plos-pone-0006618:
Susana Oliveira, Jorge Pinto, Gonçalo Picarote, and colleagues studied iron regulation under cell stress in PLOS ONE in 2009. Endoplasmic reticulum stress induces a complex network of pathways collectively termed the unfolded protein response. Clarification of these pathways has linked them to many diseases. The team examined how the stress-inducible factor CHOP affects expression of hepcidin, the master iron hormone.

Their title reports CHOP affects hepcidin expression by modulating C/EBP alpha activity. A stress pathway thus reaches into iron control. That link may explain anemia seen in chronic disease and inflammation. It connects two fields that rarely meet.
plos-pone-0006718:
Nicolas Pottier and co-authors linked a small RNA to a growth factor in lung cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The small RNA is microRNA-155. The growth factor is keratinocyte growth factor, made by lung fibroblasts. Fibroblasts and epithelial cells constantly exchange signals. Those exchanges build tissues in embryos and maintain them in adults. Paracrine signals, sent between neighboring cells, carry much of that traffic.

The team identified keratinocyte growth factor as a target of microRNA-155. That means the small RNA can dial the growth factor down. Dialing it changes how fibroblasts talk to epithelial cells nearby. The link matters for lung development and repair. It may also matter in diseases where that conversation goes wrong.
plos-pone-0006818:
Jesús Villar and colleagues tracked a blood marker in patients with severe sepsis in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sepsis is the body's dangerous overreaction to infection. Doctors need biomarkers that flag patients at high risk of death. The marker studied is lipopolysaccharide binding protein, or LBP. It binds a toxin from bacterial walls.

The prospective, multicenter study followed LBP levels over time. Levels predicted severity of lung injury in these patients. They also predicted mortality. A predictive marker can steer intensive care resources early. It may also help select patients for trials of new sepsis treatments.
plos-pone-0006918:
Hui Chen and his team hung a brake on gene reads on the tail of one protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene reader, RNA polymerase II, stalls at the gates of many genes. Those genes count growth guides, stress genes, and HIV's own genes. How the reader walks on is thus a control step on par with how it starts. Spt5 is the big half of the crew that runs that step.

The brake in live cells hung on the tail end of Spt5. Cut or change that tail, and the brake came off. The find pins control to one patch of one protein. A pin that fine guides crisp tests of the stall. It may count too for curbs on HIV gene use.
plos-pone-0007018:
Marjolein Smith, Windy Boyd, Grace Kissling, and colleagues modelled worm growth data in PLOS ONE in 2009. Toxicologists increasingly use the roundworm C. elegans to predict chemical harm. Their assays grow worms by the thousands and measure them with sorting machines. Standard analysis tools fit that flood of repeated measurements poorly.

The authors built a discrete time model for medium-throughput growth data. It handles repeated measures on growing worms over time. Better statistics mean fewer false alarms and fewer missed toxic effects. That supports the wider goal of testing chemicals without using large animals.
plos-pone-0007118:
James Byrne, Ha Nam Nguyen, and Renee Reijo Pera improved stem cell reprogramming in PLOS ONE in 2009. Induced pluripotent stem cells open new paths for research and cell therapy. The process, though, is inefficient and poorly understood. Only a small share of treated cells complete the change. The team worked with human fibroblasts, the usual starting cells.

They found a subpopulation of fibroblasts that reprogrammed far better. Starting from those cells raised the yield of true iPSCs. Picking the right starters could make reprogramming faster and cleaner. That matters for any future therapy that must grow patient cells at scale.
plos-pone-0007218:
Mya S. Thu, Joseph Najbauer, Stephen E. Kendall, and colleagues worked on imaging therapeutic stem cells in a brain tumor model in 2009. Glioblastoma is a highly invasive brain tumor. Treatment must reach cancer cells that have already spread into surrounding brain tissue, beyond the main tumor mass.

Neural stem cells naturally move toward tumor sites. The authors label human neural stem cells with iron and image them by MRI in mice with glioma. Their pre-clinical work tests whether doctors could track therapeutic cells after delivery. Reliable tracking is key for future stem cell treatments.
plos-pone-0007318:
Howard C. Rosenbaum, Cristina Pomilla, Martin Mendez, and colleagues mapped humpback whale populations in the Southern Hemisphere in 2009. Humpback whales are among the best-studied large whales. Yet population boundaries in southern oceans had remained largely untested, despite hunting history and ongoing recovery of whale numbers worldwide.

The authors assess population structure using well over a thousand samples. Samples came from breeding grounds in the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans, at fourteen sampling sites. Their genetic analysis tests whether breeding groups are distinct populations. Results guide conservation units for managing recovering whale stocks.
plos-pone-0007418:
Hendrik P. N. Scholl, Monika Fleckenstein, Lars G. Fritsche, and colleagues tested eye disease genes for progression effects in 2009. Age-related macular degeneration is a prevalent cause of blindness in Western societies. Variants in genes CFH, C3, and ARMS2 had repeatedly been shown to confer significant risk for the disease in earlier genetic studies.

The authors ask whether those loci also drive progression. They focus on geographic atrophy, the advanced dry form of the disease. They report the loci are significant for susceptibility but not for disease progression. That distinction matters for trials that aim to slow atrophy.
plos-pone-0007518:
Paul Davies and David Brown published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on prion diseases and the soils where their agent may linger. Prion diseases, such as scrapie in sheep, spread through an infectious protein. Sporadic cases imply an environmental source for that agent. Soil is a suspected reservoir. The team tested how the metal manganese affects prion survival in model soils, and what happens to infectivity.

Manganese helped the prion protein survive longer in the soil models. It also increased how infectious the prions were to cells. That combination makes manganese-rich environments a greater concern for disease spread. Soil chemistry, usually ignored in outbreak thinking, may shape where prions persist. The result argues for including the environment's metal content in risk assessments. It also helps explain the patchy geography of prion diseases.
plos-pone-0007618:
Anita Pepper and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the gene behind fragile X syndrome. That condition, a leading inherited cause of intellectual disability, comes from silencing the FMR1 gene. Yet too much of the gene's product is also harmful; dosage must be kept in range. How normal expression levels are maintained was unclear. The team studied a protein called Argonaute2 in fruit flies and its effect on the fly version of the gene.

Argonaute2 suppresses fragile X expression in the fly. That suppression prevents defects in nerve development and egg formation. So a small-RNA pathway protein acts as a dosage guard for this sensitive gene. Dosage guards matter where both shortage and excess cause disease. The fly work gives human fragile X research a new regulatory thread to pull. It also shows Argonaute proteins doing more than silencing targets outright.
plos-pone-0007718:
Amaresh Ranjan and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tackles a weak point of artificial blood vessels. Small synthetic grafts often fail when clots form or the wall thickens. Lining a graft with the patient's own vessel cells could prevent both problems.

The team grew endothelial progenitor cells taken from human blood vessels. Such cells can coat the inside of a small-diameter prosthesis. A living lining makes the graft act more like a natural vessel. The work is an early step toward safer bypass grafts for people with blocked heart arteries.
plos-pone-0007818:
Hilbert de Vries and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests a gene variant tied to a fungal sensor in bowel disease. The sensor, dectin-1, sits on immune cells and detects fungal cell walls. When triggered, it signals through the adaptor CARD9, much like the Crohn's-linked gene NOD2.

The authors ran a genetic association analysis on one functional variant. They also measured dectin-1 levels in gut lining from patients. Their question was whether this variant tracks with inflammatory bowel disease. The study adds one more piece to the genetics of gut inflammation.
plos-pone-0007918:
Jean-Michel Garcia and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks which flu protein draws the antibodies that can stop H5N1 bird flu. Being sick with one flu strain can leave a person with some guard against other strains. Those shared defenses might blunt a new flu that jumps from birds.

Two proteins on the virus coat were the main suspects. The team built fake viruses to test each one on its own. The guard came from antibodies aimed at haemagglutinin, the coat protein the virus uses to enter cells. That answer tells vaccine makers where to aim. A shot that raises such antibodies could soften a future outbreak.
plos-pone-0008018:
Heidi Blank and colleagues found that sulfur handling can push yeast to divide, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Yeast cells were known to need sulfur work before a new round of division can start. The open question was whether that work merely allows division or truly drives it.

Cells rich in extra DNA copies ran a longer reducing phase in their cycle and pushed more sulfur through their pathways. That push came before, and seemed to spur, the start of division. The result gives sulfur a command role in the cell cycle, not just a support job.
plos-pone-0008118:
Yongjin Park and colleagues modeled protein networks as changing over time in PLOS ONE in 2010. A network drawn once, with all links merged, hides the truth that links come and go as proteins are made and destroyed. Tissue and time both redraw the map.

Their method groups the network afresh at each stage using a layered Bayesian model, a statistics frame that weighs doubt honestly. The moving map caught shifts that a fixed map missed. Drug and disease studies that ignore the timing of links may be aiming at partners that are rarely in the room together.
plos-pone-0008218:
Frank H. Guenther and colleagues reported a wireless brain-machine interface in PLOS ONE in 2009. Such devices use electrodes placed in the cerebral cortex. They aim to restore function to people with profound paralysis. Earlier systems for communication mostly let users type slowly. This work targeted real-time speech synthesis instead.

Signals from the speech areas of the brain were sent wirelessly to a synthesizer. The system turned intended speech sounds into audible output as they occurred. Real-time voice could give paralyzed people a far more natural way to communicate. The study shows an early working step toward that goal.
plos-pone-0008318:
Laetitia Horzinski and colleagues studied a diagnostic test for brain disorders in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mutations in eIF2B genes cause a family of leukodystrophies. These disorders destroy white matter in the brain. The classic form brings childhood ataxia and vanishing white matter. The observed clinical spectrum has grown much wider in recent years.

The team evaluated eIF2B activity as a diagnostic tool. Measuring the factor's GEF activity could confirm unclear cases. A functional test helps when gene results are ambiguous. It could speed diagnosis for families facing these rare disorders.
plos-pone-0008418:
Daisuke Kawabata and colleagues studied lupus treatment effects in mice in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. A major goal in treating systemic lupus erythematosus is long-term remission. Cytotoxic therapies such as cyclophosphamide are used toward that goal. Little information existed on how they affect the rebuilding B cell repertoire. That repertoire decides which antibodies the body can make afterward.

After cyclophosphamide treatment, selection of high affinity DNA-reactive B cells was enhanced. DNA-reactive cells are exactly the kind that drive lupus. A treatment that favors their return could explain relapses. The finding guides safer use of cytotoxic therapy.
plos-pone-0008518:
Anne Wisdom and co-authors study a new cold virus group in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Human rhinoviruses are the main cause of the common cold. A species called HRV-C had only recently been described. Its frequency and clinical effects were still unclear. The team screen thousands of respiratory samples from Edinburgh. They use a test targeting the VP4 region of the virus. They also study how HRV-C interacts with other respiratory viruses.

They estimate how often HRV-C causes infection in that sample set. They link it to clinical features and seasonal patterns. Genetic analysis shows recombination shapes its diversity. The work defines HRV-C as a real clinical player, not a curiosity.
plos-pone-0008618:
Jorge Castro and co-authors study how antidepressants work in rats in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Those drugs boost new nerve cell growth in the hippocampus. That growth has been tied to many molecular paths. The role of other brain areas had got far less attention. One such area is the amygdala, which handles emotion and stress. The team test if the amygdala shapes the drug effect.

They measure new cell growth in the hippocampus and depression-like behavior. The amygdala proves needed for both drug effects. Without it, new cells and better behavior do not appear. Drug action is thus a circuit effect across brain areas.
plos-pone-0008718:
Antje Vogelgesang, Verena May, Uwe Grunwald, and colleagues checked immune cells in stroke patients. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ischemic stroke cuts blood to part of the brain and kills tissue. Soon after, patients lose many T cells from their blood. That dip raises the risk of infections like pneumonia. Counts alone do not show how well the remaining cells work.

The team tested the working state of blood T cells after stroke. Their assays measured responses that healthy cells should give. Knowing whether survivors are weak or merely fewer matters for care. It may guide steps to prevent post-stroke infections.
plos-pone-0008818:
Jerry Conway, Laura Sherwood, M. Thelma Collazo, and colleagues raised llama antibodies against botulism toxins. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The toxins that cause botulism come in seven types, all of them dangerous. A good test must tell the types apart fast. Llamas make small, tough antibodies of a special kind. Small size makes them handy for test kits used in the field.

The team raised one antibody for each of the seven toxin types. Used as a set, the seven can spot any type in a sample. Fast, sure tests matter for food safety and defense. Tough llama antibodies may beat normal ones when conditions are rough.
plos-pone-0008918:
Ethan Cerami, Emek Demir, Nikolaus Schultz, and colleagues let computers find the core pathways inside a lethal brain tumor. Their analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Glioblastoma is the most common and aggressive brain tumor in adults. The Cancer Genome Atlas had just profiled it in depth. Such data floods are hard to read gene by gene. Automated network analysis can surface the pathways that matter most across patients.

The network approach distilled core altered pathways from the genomic noise. Shared pathways suggest shared drug targets for many patients. A core map beats long lists of single-patient mutations. The work shows how to mine atlas-scale cancer data.
plos-pone-0009018:
Samantha Tracht, Sara Del Valle, and James Hyman modelled whether face masks slow a new flu, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The new virus was influenza A H1N1, declared a pandemic in June 2009. Vaccines and antiviral drugs were in short supply early on. Masks were a cheap option countries and families could use at once.

Their mathematical model tested mask use under different assumptions. It varied how many people wore masks and how well the masks filtered. The runs showed how much spread masks could cut in each case. Planners facing the next pandemic gain numbers, not just guesses, for mask advice.
plos-pone-0009118:
Xiaoyang Wan and co-authors found two proteins that put a brake on a growth signal, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The signal is Wnt4, part of a family steering development and cancer. EAF1 and EAF2 are proteins tied to both embryos and tumours. EAF2 in particular can act as a tumour suppressor in prostate tissue.

Both proteins fed back to dampen Wnt4's signalling. Negative feedback keeps the pathway from running too hot. The brake is built into the pathway's own downstream machinery. Losing it could help explain some cancers and birth defects.
plos-pone-0009218:
Patricia Fauque and co-authors published this reproduction study in PLOS ONE in 2010. More and more babies begin with in vitro fertilization, yet the method's effects are now questioned. Early embryos grow for days in lab dishes rather than in the body. At that stage, the embryo's outer cells touch the culture fluid directly, and those cells later form the placenta.

Using mice, the team compared placentas from embryos made naturally and in dishes. They read the full set of genes switched on in each placenta. Fertilization and culture in vitro strongly changed that gene pattern. The result warns that lab conditions at the very start can echo into the organ that feeds the baby.
plos-pone-0009318:
Hua-Ling Chen, Chiou-Hwa Yuh, and Kenneth Wu published this zebrafish study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nestin is a protein found in the young cells that build the brain. Scientists use it as a marker for those neural progenitor cells. What nestin itself actually does during development was unclear.

Working in zebrafish, where the gene is conserved, the team removed nestin's function. Brain and eye development suffered as a result. The cause was excess death among the progenitor cells that nestin normally protects. So the familiar marker turns out to be a working part of development, keeping young brain cells alive.
plos-pone-0009418:
Lyssia Gruaz and co-authors published this inflammation study in PLOS ONE in 2010. When T cells touch monocytes directly, the monocytes pour out inflammatory signals. That contact trigger likely fuels long-running sterile inflammation in many diseases. HDL, the so-called good cholesterol, was known to block that production.

The team used HDL to block the contact activation in human monocytes. Blocking it revealed a fresh pattern of cytokine and inflammatory genes. Patterns revealed by a blocker show which genes the contact truly controls. The result also adds an anti-inflammatory talent to HDL's known list.
plos-pone-0009518:
Elizabeth Sweeney and colleagues confirmed a link between cartilage and blood in mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. Collagen X is a protein in growing cartilage near bone ends. Earlier mice with faulty collagen X had both skeletal flaws and blood flaws. That hinted the two systems are linked. The team used congenic mice, bred to share one genetic background, to test the claim cleanly.

Even with background held constant, faulty collagen X disrupted blood formation. So the effect is real, not a side effect of other genes. The skeleton's scaffold thus helps cradle blood development in the marrow. The finding may inform care for marrow diseases.
plos-pone-0009618:
Jantina Manning and co-authors studied how cells fetch a key building part in PLOS ONE in 2010. Before a cell divides, it builds a structure called the centrosome. That structure organizes the fibers that pull chromosomes apart. A protein named gamma tubulin is a core part of it. The team showed that another protein, NEDD1, binds gamma tubulin directly.

That direct binding is how gamma tubulin is recruited to the centrosome. Without the hand off, the structure cannot form properly. Every cell division depends on this small delivery step. The work details a piece of machinery that cancer drugs already try to jam, since dividing cells need it most.
plos-pone-0009718:
Resistin is a hormone in the blood that is tied to insulin resistance. Hiroshi Onuma and colleagues studied two letter changes in its gene in Japanese adults. Their findings appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

One change sits at position minus 420 and another at position minus 358 of the gene. The highest resistin levels appeared only when both changes came together in a set pairing. Neither variant alone explained the peak levels. The study drew on the general Japanese population, not just patients. The pairing shows how gene variants can interact instead of acting separately.
plos-pone-0009818:
Rex E Jung and colleagues use brain scans in a 2010 PLOS ONE study to test a popular claim: that creativity and mental illness traits may sit on one scale. Seventy-two healthy young adults took idea-generating tests and personality measures, and four raters scored their creative work.

Scans tracked water flow along brain wiring, a sign of wiring strength called fractional anisotropy. Stronger creative scores linked to weaker wiring in a left frontal area. Openness to new experience linked to weaker wiring in a right frontal area. The authors read the overlap as support for a shared brain base, in healthy people, for creative thought and unusual traits.
plos-pone-0009918:
Judging how far away something is feels automatic, yet learning conditions can bend the judgment. Anna Oleksiak and colleagues tested how the way a scene is encoded changes distance estimates. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Encoding conditions are the circumstances under which a person first takes in a scene. Those conditions influenced how distances were later estimated. Distance cues include size, overlap, and perspective lines. The same real distance can thus be judged longer or shorter. The result matters for training drivers, pilots, and anyone who must judge space.
plos-pone-0010018:
Zhonghui Gai, Xiaoyu Wang, Xiaorui Liu, and co-workers studied pollutant-eating bacteria in PLOS ONE in 2010. Carbazole is a stubborn chemical with a dioxin-like shape, and it can damage genes and poison living things. Some bacteria survive it by gaining new genes that let them break it down for food.

In one Sphingomonas strain, the team found the genes that turn carbazole into catechol, a simpler compound. Mobile DNA chunks called IS6100 elements flank those genes on both sides. That layout suggests the clean-up trait can move between bacteria, a clue to how microbes adapt to toxic waste.
plos-pone-0010118:
Manuela Zanetti and colleagues identify a new potassium channel in a 2010 PLOS ONE study of cyanobacteria, bacteria that make food from sunlight. Potassium channels are pores that let potassium ions, charged atoms, pass through cell membranes. Few such channels in these bacteria had been tested.

Found in the genome of a model cyanobacterium, the channel rescued potassium-starved E. coli and acted as a selective potassium pore in hamster cells. Tagging showed it sitting in both the outer membrane and the inner light-harvesting membranes. A matching channel in a higher plant sits in those same inner membranes, the first such channel found there, opening new work on plant energy membranes.
plos-pone-0010218:
Antonio Salas and Jorge Amigo asked how few markers can capture mitochondrial diversity in 2010. Mitochondrial DNA varies a great deal, because it mutates faster than nuclear DNA. Its patterns differ deeply between population groups and ethnic groups worldwide. Many studies wanted a small, standard set of markers to type that diversity without sequencing everything.

The pair showed that a reduced number of mitochondrial SNPs can saturate haplotype diversity. In plain terms, a modest marker set captures nearly all the group patterns. Their PLOS ONE finding can cut cost and effort in population genetics surveys.
plos-pone-0010318:
Hakryul Jo, Fabien Loison, Hidenori Hattori and colleagues published a cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. They tested celastrol, a natural product, together with drugs that attack microtubules inside cells. Such drugs can halt cell division and then push cancer cells to die. Some tumors, though, resist them from the start or learn to resist over time.

When dividing cells stall but fail to die, treatment loses its punch. Celastrol, the team reports, weakens the tubulin pairs that microtubules are built from. That damage makes stalled cells more likely to die during division. Pairing a plant compound with standard drugs is the strategy on test here. If it holds up, resistant tumors might be beaten with a combined push.
plos-pone-0010418:
Courtney Karner and colleagues showed that a protein called Lrp4 is crucial for building kidneys, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Kidney formation starts when a small bud grows from a duct into nearby tissue. That meeting triggers the branching tubes that become the kidney. Many signals must align for the bud to start at all. The team studied mice lacking Lrp4 to see its part.

Without Lrp4, the bud's start went wrong and kidneys failed to form properly. The mouse mirrors a human syndrome with similar defects, Cenani-Lenz syndrome. Animal models that match human conditions help trace their causes. This one pins early kidney growth to a single protein's signal. It may also explain limb and bone signs seen in the syndrome.
plos-pone-0010518:
Catherine Pfister, Folker Meyer and Dionysios Antonopoulos profiled microbes living on California mussels in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mussels crowd rocky shores and filter huge amounts of water. Their feeding and waste move nitrogen through coastal food webs. A rich microbial community coats their shells. The team used shotgun metagenomics, reading all DNA in a sample at once, to catalog that community.

The catalog shows which microbes ride on mussels and what jobs they may do. Some likely help cycle carbon and nitrogen in the shore zone. A mussel bed thus acts as a hub in coastal nutrient networks. Knowing its microbes refines models of shore ecology. It also gives a baseline as oceans warm and acidify.
plos-pone-0010618:
Yuyan Zhang and colleagues studied a cancer drug target in zebrafish embryos, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme thymidylate synthase helps cells build DNA. Chemotherapy drugs like 5-FU attack it, which is why it matters in cancer care.

In the embryos, the enzyme's own message RNA appeared to bind and restrain the enzyme. Two cancer drugs changed that self-control in measurable ways. Watching the loop in a living embryo shows regulation that dish studies can miss. The finding may help explain why some tumors resist drugs aimed at this enzyme.
plos-pone-0010718:
Yun-Shiang Chang and colleagues modeled the surface armor of a shrimp virus, in PLOS ONE in 2010. White spot syndrome virus has killed farmed shrimp on a huge scale worldwide. The virus particle is large for a virus, wrapped in a membrane studded with structural proteins.

The team combined data on those proteins into a three-dimensional model of their complex. The model shows how the proteins fit together on the membrane. Knowing the armor's layout points to weak seams that vaccines or treatments could target. Shrimp farming loses billions to this virus, so even basic maps carry real economic weight.
plos-pone-0010818:
Behazine Combadière and colleagues ran an early human trial of a needle-free flu vaccine, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Standard flu shots train antibodies well but raise weak killer T cell responses. Killer CD8 cells matter most against new flu strains that antibodies miss. The skin is rich in immune sentinels, and hair follicles offer a route in.

Volunteers received inactivated flu vaccine through the skin in a randomized phase I trial. The skin route preferentially amplified CD8 effector T cells. That bias is exactly what flu vaccinology has been missing. A safe, needle-free patch that trains killer cells could change both yearly flu shots and pandemic response.
plos-pone-0010918:
Belinda Cornes, Clara Tang, Thomas Leon and co-authors published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hirschsprung's disease is a birth defect in which nerve cells are missing from parts of the gut, blocking digestion. One change in the RET gene, called R114H, shows up in roughly six or seven of every hundred Chinese patients but had never been seen in European patients.

Such clustering hints at a founder effect, where today's carriers descend from one ancestor who first carried the change. The team analyzed gene patterns in hundreds of Chinese patients, including those carrying R114H, and estimated the mutation's age with statistical methods. Cornes and colleagues test whether a single mutational event seeded this risk across a population. Founder mutations simplify screening and reveal how disease genes travel through history.
plos-pone-0011018:
Brooke Fridley, Gregory Jenkins, Matthew Deyo-Svendsen and co-authors published this genetics methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Genome-wide association studies had flagged well over a thousand DNA sites linked to diseases, but the flagged markers are rarely the causal variants themselves. Sequencing every flagged region in thousands of people was still too expensive, so the team proposed a shortcut.

Genotype imputation, which fills in unmeasured variants from reference patterns, can also augment real sequence data, letting a study sequence fewer people deeply and extend the information statistically to the rest. Fridley and colleagues lay out how to combine partial sequencing with imputation to catalogue the rare variants hiding in disease-linked regions. Their strategy aims to move association studies from signposts to the actual functional spelling changes behind disease.
plos-pone-0011118:
Huang, Su, Li and colleagues compared three Chinese groups in PLOS ONE in 2010. All three groups share an unusually high rate of cancer of the food pipe. The team read the Y chromosome, passed from father to son, to test whether the groups share paternal roots.

The evidence supported common ancestry among the three high risk groups. Shared roots raise the chance that shared genes help explain the shared cancer risk. That does not rule out food, drink or local habits, which also matter. Still, the genetic link gives cancer researchers a sharper place to look for risk factors.
plos-pone-0011218:
Shin, Pierce, Gillenwater and colleagues built a low cost microscope in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their device uses optical fibers and a consumer grade digital camera to capture glowing images of living cells inside the body. Such imaging normally demands costly specialist equipment.

The budget microscope still delivered useful cellular images in living tissue. Affordable imaging could bring cancer screening to clinics with few resources. Early cancer found by direct cell viewing can be treated far more successfully. The study demonstrates frugal innovation: smart assembly of cheap parts can match the job of pricey tools.
plos-pone-0011318:
Singhal, Ren and Kern improved a DNA lab method in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gels that sort DNA by size are a daily tool, but long fragments can bunch together and blur. The team developed gel conditions using borate compounds and related chemistry that spread those long fragments more clearly.

Sharper separation means DNA pieces can be sized and read more accurately. Labs gain the improvement without buying new equipment, since only buffer conditions change. Clearer gels aid everything from gene cloning to forensic checks. The study is a reminder that basic technique advances quietly lift a whole field.
plos-pone-0011418:
Ming-Szu Hung and co-authors reported in 2010 that an unusual copy of a growth gene helps drive lung cancer. The gene makes a protein kinase involved in cell growth, and its extra copy is streamlined, lacking the spacer sections most genes carry. Such intronless copies are often dismissed as dead leftovers, but this one is active in lung tumors.

The team found that a common variant of the streamlined gene plays a cancer-promoting role in lung cancer cells. That finding adds a new suspect to the list of lung cancer drivers and a possible marker for risk. It also challenges the habit of ignoring streamlined gene copies in genome scans. If more such copies prove active, cancer genetics may have been overlooking a whole class of contributors hiding in plain sight.
plos-pone-0011518:
Matt Cahill and co-authors explored in 2010 how the length of DNA reads decides whether a bacterial genome can be assembled cleanly. New sequencing machines read DNA in short fragments, and repetitive stretches longer than the reads tangle assembly, since the computer cannot tell which copy a fragment came from. The team tested assembly across prokaryote genomes while varying read length.

They found that read length strongly affects repeat resolution, and that longer reads crack stubborn genomes that more short reads cannot. The practical guidance is that sequencing strategy should fit the genome: sometimes longer reads, not more reads, are the answer. Labs planning a genome project can spend their budget where it counts. As sequencing gets cheaper, this kind of strategy paper keeps the savings from being wasted on the wrong kind of data.
plos-pone-0011618:
Bonnie McGill, Ariana Sutton-Grier and Justin Wright studied how plant variety affects soil nitrogen cleanup, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Through a process called denitrification, soil microbes return excess nitrogen to the air. That service protects streams and lakes from pollution that would otherwise feed harmful algal growth.

The authors asked whether having many kinds of plant traits steadies that cleanup across seasons and soil types. They found that diverse plant traits did buffer swings in the process. For land managers, the result means keeping varied plant communities can keep a vital water-cleaning service reliable year-round.
plos-pone-0011718:
Tsuyoshi Hayashi and co-authors listed the proteins of the Legionnaires' disease germ at each growth stage, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Legionella pneumophila turns harmful in response to growth state, growing most dangerous late in lab culture, after its fast growth phase ends. Which proteins change as it enters that state was the open question.

Their protein survey compared levels between growth phases. The list ties clear protein shifts to the control of the germ's harmful traits. A stage-by-stage record of a germ retooling itself as it grows gives researchers firm leads for blocking infection.
plos-pone-0011818:
Yanmin Hu and co-authors took a fresh path to finding antibiotics, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In a real infection, germs that are splitting and germs that are not live side by side. Standard drugs kill the splitters well but barely touch the quiet ones, so killing is slow or partial and infection can bounce back.

By aiming at non-splitting germs, the team's search yielded a new skin antibiotic for staph infections. A cream that hits the quiet germs strikes the pool that other drugs miss. The tactic could stretch to other stubborn infections where quiet germs ride out standard therapy in tissue.
plos-pone-0011918:
Carole Fakhry and colleagues asked in 2010 how often researchers need to sample the mouth to track HPV infection fairly. Oral HPV matters because some types can lead to throat cancers. The team worked with an HIV-positive cohort, collecting fourteen mouth rinse samples in a row from each person.

They compared what two-week sampling showed against what samples six months apart would have suggested. Wide gaps between tests can make infections look shorter or longer than they are, biasing natural history studies. The comparison gives future studies a concrete basis for picking a sampling schedule instead of copying habit.
plos-pone-0012018:
Aksana Andreyeva and co-workers reported in 2010 that a brain protein called CHL1 organizes the nerve terminal's release machinery. When a nerve ending releases its chemical message, the SNARE protein complex drives membrane fusion, changing shape drastically in the process. Shape-changing proteins risk clumping and damage, yet little was known about the chaperones guarding them.

The team found CHL1 acting as a selective organizer on the presynaptic side, chaperoning the SNARE complex. Selectivity matters: a general helper would blur the careful assembly that fast signaling needs. Knowing who guards the release machinery opens a new angle on synapse failure in brain disease.
plos-pone-0012118:
Florence Kermen, Sébastien Sultan, Joëlle Sacquet, and co-authors wrote in PLOS ONE in 2010 about smell, memory, and new brain cells. The smell center of the adult brain keeps gaining newborn neurons, and learning seems to help some of them survive. The puzzle was how the brain picks which new cells to keep for a lasting memory of a scent.

Their work points to a settling step in the smell center itself, where a fresh memory trace must be locked in. Only when that happens do the chosen new neurons survive and the memory last. The finding links a tiny brain region to the long life of a memory, and to the cells that carry it.
plos-pone-0012218:
Manfred Bohn and Dieter Heermann modeled how the genome folds inside the cell nucleus, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chromatin, the DNA-and-protein fiber, folds at many scales at once, yet its large-scale arrangement had resisted every tidy explanation. Experiments kept showing tight loops and clustered regions without a unifying cause.

Their model shows that loops formed simply as the fiber drifts and sticks can reproduce those patterns. A single simple mechanism that matches many observations is powerful: it turns a confusing catalog of structures into one process with rules. That gives experimentalists clear predictions to test about how genes find their partners in three dimensions.
plos-pone-0012318:
Michael Allan, Christina Korownyk, Kate LaSalle, and co-authors checked whether clinical trials talk about money, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Randomized controlled trials decide which treatments medicine adopts, yet health care costs, above all drug costs, dominate the budgets of the organizations that must pay for those treatments. A trial can prove a drug works while saying nothing about whether it is worth its price.

The team measured how often trial reports include costs, and what features make a trial more likely to mention them. If cost talk is rare, decision-makers are flying blind on value even when the science is clear. The paper gives medical journals and funders a baseline for demanding better.
plos-pone-0012418:
Stephen Murray, Judith Morgan, Coleen Kane and colleagues asked what sets the length of pregnancy in mice, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Early birth is a huge health problem in people, causing many infant deaths and costing billions. Twin studies hint that genes play a part, and the mouse lets scientists test that idea under controlled conditions.

By comparing mouse strains and crosses, the team showed that gestation length is strongly set by genetics, including genes of both mother and pups. A firm genetic base means mouse strains can be used to find the actual genes. Those genes may point to pathways that time birth in humans as well.
plos-pone-0012518:
Sandhya Buchanan, David Pyatt and John Carpenter freeze-dried human blood stem and progenitor cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Stem cell therapies promise much, but cells usually must ship frozen, a costly chain that many clinics cannot support. Dried cells stored on a shelf would travel anywhere, if they survived the drying alive.

The team lyophilized hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and stored them at room conditions, then checked whether the cells kept their identity and growth potential. Preservation held up surprisingly well in their tests. Shelf-stable cells could widen access to cell therapy far beyond rich hospital centers.
plos-pone-0012618:
Griffin, Cairns, Ghani and co-authors modelled a malaria prevention plan for babies. The plan gives infants a drug called sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine at set visits, even when they are not sick. Health officials support the plan where the drug still works, but parasite resistance can wear it down.

Their 2010 analysis linked how well the plan protects infants to measures of drug resistance in local parasites. That link helps officials decide where the plan still pays off and where it needs replacing. Good models of this kind save money and protect babies from needless doses.
plos-pone-0344618:
Selvi and colleagues compared three kinds of feedback for student writing in Turkey in a 2026 study. Eighty-four university students learning English wrote argument essays over ten weeks. One group used a grammar checker, one used a chat-based AI tool, and one relied only on teacher comments.

All groups grew in planning and thinking strategies over time, but the chat-based AI group gained most in self-managed learning. Its writing also improved in accuracy and content quality beyond the other groups. Gains were strongest for mid-level learners. The authors suggest smart AI feedback can lighten teacher load, though that effect was not measured directly in the trial.
plos-pone-0347018:
Heeseung Choi and a team including patient and clinician reviewers check whether a Korean translation of a shared-decision rating tool works as intended. The tool scores how well doctors and patients make treatment choices together, following a six-step model. Translators moved it into Korean through forward and back translation with checks for meaning, then doctors and several hundred patients used it in real shared decisions.

Statistical checks supported a single overall score for both the patient and doctor versions, and both scored high on internal consistency. The doctor version matched closely with an established doctor questionnaire, while the patient version aligned moderately with its partner tools. Choi and colleagues say Korean clinics can now measure shared decision quality with a tested local instrument.
plos-pone-0347118:
Youssef Zougheib and co-workers follow how fast nearsightedness worsened in Lebanese children across the COVID-19 lockdown years. Lockdown pushed children indoors onto screens, and eye doctors feared a surge. Their 2026 study tracks one hundred children seen at a Beirut medical center, joining eye records going back years with family reports of screen and outdoor time.

Worsening ran fastest during the lockdown school years, then slowed to about half that pace afterward. Screen time rose and outdoor time fell sharply during lockdown. Yet within the group, reported hours alone did not predict whose eyes worsened most. Younger children favored tablets and logged fewer screen hours. The era clearly mattered, even if single habits explain less than expected.
plos-pone-0347518:
AshaRani and colleagues catalog Singapore's programs for promoting mental health in this 2026 PLOS ONE scoping review. Searching medical and gray literature from 2000 onward, they gathered one hundred six studies describing programs that aim to build wellbeing rather than only treat illness.

Programs served many groups, with a particular concentration on older adults in hospitals and community settings, and covered people with mental disorders, physical illnesses, and developmental conditions. Each program was documented with a standard checklist so future reviews can replicate or compare them. The map exposes where provision is thick and where it is missing, giving Singapore's planners a base for systematic evaluation.
plos-pone-0347918:
Grace Chang, Rahul Malhotra, and Benjamin Seligman asked whether money and education change how much physical ability older Americans need to stay independent in daily life. Bathing, dressing, and eating without help is a defining outcome of healthy aging. Using a national retirement study, they linked walking speed and grip strength to daily-living limits, then tested whether education, income, or wealth softened that link.

Thousands of participants were followed both at one point in time and as new limits developed. If wealth buys help, equipment, and home changes, then richer adults might stay independent despite weaker bodies, while poorer adults cannot. The answer guides whether support programs should fund strength itself or fund the workarounds that money usually buys.
plos-pone-0348018:
Oak E. Milam and Gary Marsat study weakly electric fish, which sense nearby fish of their own kind through faint electric fields. Their 2026 paper asks how the fish brain knows where another fish is located. They focus on a brain area that first handles these electric signals and on the different cell types found there.

The team played an artificial signal shaped like a real fish signal and recorded from cells across the body surface map. Some cells, including deep-layer cells of one response type, carried sharp place information. Other cell groups carried much weaker place clues. The split suggests the brain sorts this signal stream into separate paths very early in processing.
plos-pone-0348118:
Ahmad Ahadi and colleagues combined two cleaning forces, electric plasma above water and bubble collapse inside water, to strip blue dye from wastewater. Each method alone makes reactive oxygen that attacks pollutants. Together in one rig, they treated dye at several strengths in distilled and tap water, with most colour gone in under five minutes.

Full clearing always arrived within fifteen minutes. Direct coupling, where plasma and bubbles act together, beat a split setup. Energy use per gram removed beat prior reports for the strongest dye mix. Light checks confirmed hydroxyl radicals, the main attackers, were present. A fast, frugal hybrid could scale to factory dye waste if costs hold.
plos-pone-0348518:
Zakir Hossion and co-authors tested whether a simple ratio from a routine blood count can forecast how pneumonia patients will fare in hospital. Costly inflammation markers are not always available in Bangladesh, where their 2026 study followed one hundred adults admitted with community-acquired pneumonia at Dhaka Medical College Hospital. The ratio compares neutrophils, first-responder cells, to lymphocytes, and a set cutoff marked it as high.

Two thirds of patients had a high ratio, and they were significantly more likely to die, need oxygen or intensive care, and stay longer in hospital. The link with a long stay was especially strong. The ratio's accuracy was moderate for predicting long stays and modest for other outcomes. The authors present it as a cheap, immediate aid for judging risk where advanced tests are scarce.
plos-pone-0349018:
Xiaosa Wang and co-workers ask whether the amount of fetal DNA floating in a pregnant person's blood early on predicts early birth or small babies. The DNA comes from the placenta and is already measured in common screening tests. Their 2026 study matches hundreds of cases with thousands of controls to balance other risk factors before comparing outcomes.

Higher fetal DNA levels went with lower risk of early birth at every level measured. For low birth weight, the link appeared only at the highest levels, like a threshold. The patterns held across most groups of mothers. If confirmed, a value already in the chart could give doctors an early warning sign at no extra testing cost.
plos-pone-0349118:
Temesgen Yaekob Ergano and Sure Pulla Rao examined finance and growth across sub-Saharan Africa in 2026. Whether deeper banking helps economies grow, or at times harms them, is a live policy question for the region.

Using a method suited to data that track countries over time, they weighed several banking and money measures against growth. Bank reserves, open trade, and broad money links looked positive, while heavy bank lending to private borrowers dragged growth down. The contrast hints that careless lending can undo the gains of a growing financial system, a caution for regulators pushing credit expansion.
plos-pone-0349218:
Naishen Qin and co-authors mined two decades of the United States adverse event database in 2026 for drugs tied to cardiovascular harm. Spontaneous reports cannot prove cause, but patterns across millions of records flag risks worth probing.

More than one and a half million heart related reports were analysed with four signal methods. Three drugs topped the list, all since withdrawn or restricted, which supports the method. Subgroup patterns differed by sex and age, and known cancer drug heart damage also appeared. The authors caution that some signals may reflect the illness treated rather than the drug, a nuance prescribers must keep.
plos-pone-0349318:
van Wijk and colleagues, in a 2026 study, compare two exam question types for telling strong medical students from struggling ones. Multiple-choice questions are efficient but invite guessing and cueing. Very short answer questions force students to produce the answer themselves. The team mined six exams from three cohorts of medical students in their first and second years.

Single short-answer items separated students more sharply than single multiple-choice items in every exam. Across exams, short-answer scores also tracked students' overall grade averages more strongly, and were better at flagging both the weakest and the strongest fifth of students. The authors argue the format earns its marking cost: used across a program, short answers can spot students who need help earlier, and confirm excellence more fairly. They place the work within a standard framework for judging whether a test measures what it should.
plos-pone-0349418:
Jia-hao Wang, Yan-ming Hao, and co-authors examined two blood measures in patients hospitalized with fractures caused by fragile bones. One measure, homocysteine, is tied to vessel damage and weak bones, while parathyroid hormone controls how bone is rebuilt. Their 2026 study covered more than two thousand fracture patients at one hospital and compared fasting blood levels taken at admission.

Higher homocysteine came with higher hormone levels, but the pattern was not a straight line. The hormone rose steadily up to a point, then climbed more sharply beyond it. The link looked stronger in patients with high blood pressure, poor kidney function, or low magnesium. The authors caution that the clinical value of homocysteine in judging risk still needs confirmation in further studies.
plos-pone-0349618:
Nicole Freene and co-authors set out to calibrate activity trackers for heart patients, whose bodies respond to exercise differently from healthy adults. Guidelines urge these patients to reach moderate-to-vigorous activity, yet the tracker thresholds in use were built on other populations. Their 2026 study fitted eighty-six patients with hip and wrist devices during rest, daily activities, and a treadmill test with measured breathing gases.

Resting energy use came out about twenty percent below the textbook value trackers assume. Hip-worn counts tracked exercise intensity strongly and gave the best thresholds for identifying moderate-to-vigorous activity, while wrist readings related weakly. A check in a separate international group of patients broadly supported the new cut-points, though individual variation stayed wide. The authors offer heart patients a fairer yardstick for their activity.
plos-pone-0350118:
Quang Tuan Rémy Nguyen and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of speech in Huntington's disease. It tests whether speech recordings can reveal psychiatric symptoms. Eighty-nine patients with confirmed disease recorded six storytelling and description tasks at a Paris hospital. Their speech was analyzed for word choice, meaning, and sound traits. Machine learning models were trained to detect symptoms rated by clinicians.

The models detected obsessive-compulsive behavior, depression, and apathy at rates well above chance. Language-based traits were the most steady performers. Sound traits added help for depression. Irritability resisted detection by every trait type. The authors present speech analysis as a promising, low-burden way to flag mental health problems. That matters in a disease where clinic visits are already demanding.
plos-pone-0350218:
Aiju Li and colleagues built a forecasting system for river runoff across China, the numbers that decide flood warnings and reservoir releases. Rivers remember at several speeds at once, quick storm pulses and slow seasonal swells, and water flows downhill through connected basins, so a model must respect both clocks and maps. Their design fuses time scales with a gating step and teaches spatial attention the true upstream-downstream links.

Tested on a national gridded benchmark built from a public global flood dataset, the method beat existing approaches overall and kept its forecasts spatially consistent with the river network. For agencies watching monsoon floods, forecasts that honor basin shape, not just local history, could mean earlier and better-placed warnings. The work is a modeling study, so its proof rests on benchmark data rather than a live season.
plos-pone-0350418:
Ngo Cao Nghia, Phan Khanh Duy, and Bao Quoc Truong-Dinh surveyed hotel guests in Vietnam and Thailand to learn how frontline staff turn satisfied customers into passionate brand advocates. Such evangelism, where guests promote a hotel unprompted, is marketing gold. Their 2026 two-wave survey of more than four hundred guests tested staff digital skill, proactive help, and relationship building, alongside brand image and customer trust.

Both image and trust carried staff behavior into advocacy, but the balance differed by country. In Vietnam, symbolic brand image dominated, while in Thailand, trust built through relationships prevailed. Loyalty programs strengthened the trust route in Thailand, and repeat visits shaped the image route differently in each place. The authors advise hotels to adapt their advocacy strategy to local culture rather than copy one playbook.
plos-pone-0350818:
Frida Torell, Michael Dimitriou, and co-authors studied how the arm's fastest reflexes change with the task at hand. When a robot tugs the arm, muscles answer in waves, from a near-instant stretch reflex to later, more flexible responses. Their 2026 study used a delayed reaching task, varying load, waiting time, tug direction, and target position while recording activity in seven arm muscles.

Shoulder muscles adjusted their responses to the task from the earliest wave, though a steady background load blunted that tuning. The latest wave showed the strongest task influence, growing when target and tug pulled in opposite ways. The results show reflexes are not fixed wiring. Even the quickest responses carry information about what the person is trying to do.
plos-pone-0350918:
Danielle Lamb and seven colleagues follow the mental health of England's health workers through the pandemic's first three years. Their 2026 cohort study, called NHS CHECK, enrolled over twenty-two thousand staff from seventeen hospital trusts. Surveys ran four times between April 2020 and March 2023. They measured common mental disorders, depression, anxiety, alcohol misuse, trauma symptoms, moral injury, and burnout. Non-clinical staff were included alongside doctors and nurses.

The burden barely budged. About half the participants met the threshold for a probable common mental disorder at every single wave. The strongest predictor of later trouble was already being unwell at the start. Clinical and non-clinical staff suffered alike, with no consistent gap. Younger, female, and lower-paid staff fared worse, as did those feeling unsupported by colleagues and managers. Sustained distress on this scale threatens staffing itself, through absence and turnover, long after the emergency wards emptied.
plos-pone-0351218:
Gene testing can fine-tune heart drugs, yet cardiologists rarely order it. Maram O Abbas and colleagues interviewed fifteen cardiologists across public and private care in the United Arab Emirates about what blocks adoption, in this 2026 PLOS One qualitative study.

Doctors voiced strong support in principle, especially for high-risk patients. Barriers sat at every level: test cost and turnaround, unclear rules, patchy lab access, and uneven doctor training. The analysis followed an established framework covering the tool, the setting, and the people involved. The authors say the mixed public and private system needs shared pathways before gene-guided prescribing can become routine heart care.
plos-pone-0351318:
HuiYing Jin and five colleagues build a skin lesion classifier designed to learn from very few examples. Their 2026 study addresses a real bottleneck in medical imaging. Rare lesions offer few training pictures, boundaries blur, and sizes vary wildly. Their network carries three cooperating modules. One adjusts its viewing window to each lesion's scale. Another blends information across resolutions, weighting the most useful channels. A third uses image gradients to sharpen attention on borders and texture.

Few-shot experiments ran on two public datasets of skin images. The system beat existing baseline models across several metrics. It also generalised promisingly between the datasets. Visual checks confirmed the model genuinely looks at the lesion, not the surrounding skin. Dermatology AI usually starves on rare conditions. A classifier built for scarcity could extend computer-aided diagnosis to the lesions doctors see least and worry about most.
plos-pone-0351418:
Cédric Gutfreund led a team of seven authors on this 2026 crystal structure study of an enzyme that copies an artificial genetic material. The material, called HNA, uses a different sugar backbone from DNA and could serve in future sensors and catalysts. Their enzyme, engineered from a heat-loving microbe's copying protein, converts HNA back into DNA.

Frozen mid-action with its template, the enzyme clamps shut much like the natural version does with DNA. One HNA building block also flips its sugar shape as the complex closes. Gutfreund says that flexibility must guide the next round of enzyme design.
plos-pone-0351518: Garcia Castillo, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on leaf-cutter ants in the tropics of the Americas. The study asks a plain question: do ant species with broad tastes cope with farm and town land use better than picky ones? Comparing wide-ranging and narrow-ranging species can show which ants survive when people reshape the land. That matters for farms and forests that depend on ants to move soil and seeds.
plos-pone-0352018:
Frisch and colleagues reviewed a liver treatment for hormone-linked tumors that had spread from elsewhere in the body in a 2026 study. The treatment sends tiny radioactive beads through blood vessels into liver tumors. Thirty patients treated over seven years at one center were checked with scans before and after care.

Tumors with richer blood flow on early scans tended to shrink more after treatment. The team also weighed scan measures against how long patients lived, which averaged close to three years. Being able to receive a follow-on targeted therapy linked most strongly to longer life. Early blood flow on scans may help doctors pick who benefits most from the bead treatment.
plos-pone-0352318:
Thurayya Eid and three colleagues study what good supervision does for nursing students on hospital placements in Saudi Arabia, in this 2026 PLOS ONE survey. One hundred and forty-five students at three teaching hospitals in Riyadh rated the support they received from supervisors, their own confidence in clinical tasks, and their satisfaction with the placement. The question matters nationally, as health reforms demand many more well-trained nurses.

Support, confidence, and satisfaction all climbed together, and statistical modelling showed supervision boosting satisfaction partly by first building confidence. The authors recommend standardising how supervisors are trained and how feedback is given, so a student's experience stops depending on which ward they land in.
plos-pone-0352418:
Dandan Xu, Kun Hu, and Linlu Cai generate advertisement images that obey a planned layout. Their 2026 study builds a two-stage framework. Layout decides where the eye lands, and with it whether the product registers. Text-to-image systems handle simple scenes well but garble complex ones. Stage one turns a written brief into a full layout plan. A transformer generator plans background and objects together, learning long-range links between words and regions. Earlier systems planned objects alone.

Stage two paints the image inside that plan. A fine-grained interaction step keeps text, layout, and pixels in constant conversation. Object fidelity, whether the product itself survives generation intact, is the named optimisation target. Advertisers cannot use a beautiful image whose bottle is warped. The framework treats layout as a contract: plan the whole scene first, then render it faithfully enough to sell.
plos-pone-0353018:
Oliver Mendoza-Cano and seven colleagues map this 2026 PLOS One analysis of Mexico's measles resurgence in 2025 and 2026, after more than twenty years without home-grown transmission. Falling vaccination coverage and pandemic disruptions had left pockets of low immunity. Using national case reports at municipal level, the team applied a scanning method that finds clusters of cases beyond what population size would predict.

More than eight thousand confirmed cases appeared across several hundred municipalities. The largest cluster sat in northern Mexico and held nearly half the cases, while a later western cluster and many brief, intense local outbreaks followed. A final faint, wide cluster suggested transmission was spreading diffusely. The authors recommend region-specific surveillance and catch-up vaccination drives to close the immunity gaps.
plos-pone-0353118:
Jafari and colleagues, in a 2026 trial, test whether pregnant women fare better when the same midwifery students care for them throughout. Continuous care from a known provider is known to help mothers, and using final-year students could extend that care where staff are scarce. No trial had checked this student-led version before.

Low-risk women in the later months of pregnancy were assigned at random to student continuity care or usual care, with both groups also getting standard services. About ninety women took part, and all were followed after birth. Women with student support reported far better birth experiences on a standard questionnaire. Their ratings of care during pregnancy, labor, and the weeks after birth were also higher, as was overall satisfaction. Cesarean births were somewhat fewer in the student group. The authors present student continuity as a practical way to give more women a known, steady caregiver.
plos-pone-0354018:
Yue Chang proposes an automated way to find and measure cracks in concrete, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Human inspectors judge small cracks inconsistently and sometimes at personal risk, while computer methods starve for labelled training images. The author's answer pairs an image-generating network, which fabricates extra realistic crack photos, with a segmentation network sharpened by attention modules to outline real cracks in new pictures.

Trained this way, the model outlined cracks with accuracy and F1 scores in the low eighties. A fractal measurement step then quantified each crack's geometry. The pipeline points toward cheaper, safer routine checks of bridges, dams, and towers, where catching a crack early prevents costly failures.
plos-pone-0354118:
Jeff Vallance and Lynn Corcoran interview in 2026 people who had a stroke linked to a small hole between heart chambers, most of whom later had it closed with a device. Such heart linked stroke may leave special worries about exercise. Talks explored what helped or blocked a return to physical activity after the event and procedure.

Fear, anxiety, and worry about the closure device formed one barrier group. Fitness change varied, with some feeling fitter and others less active than before. Lasting tiredness, leftover symptoms, and odd heart sensations also held people back. The authors call for clearer guidance and support on returning to activity.
plos-pone-0354418:
Yang and colleagues, in a 2026 study, link three simple body and blood measures to thinking decline and dementia, using the giant UK Biobank. One measure blends blood sugar and fat markers into an insulin resistance index. Another describes body shape, especially a wide waist for one's weight. The team followed more than three hundred seventy thousand people.

All three measures, including the two multiplied together, tracked with poorer scores on thinking tests. People in the highest quarter of each measure carried notably higher dementia risk than those in the lowest quarter, with the body shape index showing the strongest link. The patterns held for Alzheimer's disease and for vascular dementia as well. Because all three measures come from cheap, routine data, the authors suggest they could help flag people for earlier brain checks, while noting such links alone do not prove cause.
plos-pone-0354518:
Abera and colleagues, in a 2026 review, pool studies on vitamin D shortage in Africans with type 2 diabetes. Africa has plenty of sun, yet shortage is common and may worsen blood sugar control. Genes that shape how the body uses vitamin D could matter too. The team searched major databases for studies up to mid-2025.

Twenty-two studies with thousands of people from eleven countries were combined. About half of the patients lacked enough vitamin D, with the highest share in East Africa. People who were deficient had notably worse long-term blood sugar readings than those with enough. One well-studied gene variant showed no clear link to diabetes risk, though the estimate was very uncertain. Study results varied widely, so the authors call the pooled figures a starting point. They argue that checking vitamin D in African diabetes care deserves more attention and better local studies.
plos-pone-0354618:
Dragoș-Vasile Leordean and Eugen-Richard Ardelean published this 2026 benchmark study of artificial intelligence that finds objects in microscope images of tissue. They ran the newest YOLO detector family against several rival architectures on five histology data sets, using shared training rules and measuring accuracy, speed, and computing cost.

One mid-generation model, YOLOv11, performed strongly across most collections. The authors also add a rescoring trick that spreads confident labels to neighboring boxes, lifting results most when the base model's confidence is poorly calibrated. Their comparison aims to guide labs choosing detection software.
plos-pone-0354718:
Yuanmin Zhang led a team of six authors on this 2026 computer science paper about grouping unlabeled text into topics. Clustering short documents is hard because word features are sparse and tangled. Their model learns by contrasting similar and different texts, sharpens the signal with mutual information, invents more negative examples, and uses a newer network type built for complex patterns.

Across eight standard data sets it took top accuracy on seven. Applied to Chinese social media posts about technology, it separated themes like artificial intelligence and consumer gadgets cleanly, showing real-world promise.
plos-pone-0354818:
Fertitta and colleagues, in a 2026 methods paper, build a standard way to measure skin tumors in mice used to study neurofibromatosis type 1. People with this inherited condition often grow many small skin tumors, and no approved drug treatment exists. Testing new drugs in mice first requires measures that different labs can trust and repeat.

Their mouse model marks the tumor-forming cells with a glowing tag, so tumors can be tracked and counted in images. The team defined measures at two scales, from whole-tumor counts and glowing area down to cell makeup in tissue slices. They wrote automated image tools and checked them against careful hand counts. The automated scores matched hand work closely, showed no steady bias, and ran far faster, up to a hundred times quicker. The shared workflow should let drug studies in this model be compared more fairly.
plos-pone-0354918:
Setegn Muche Fenta and a large team mined health surveys from thirty-three Sub-Saharan African countries. The surveys covered 195,000 toddlers. The team counted how many vaccine doses children actually receive. It also looked at what drives the count up or down. Their 2026 analysis used count regression models. These handle the many children with few or no doses, while allowing communities to differ.

The average child received only about five and a half doses, far short of a full schedule. Doses rose with mothers' schooling and work. They rose with household wealth, holding a health card, and delivering in a facility. Frequent antenatal visits and vitamin A receipt helped too. Doses fell in rural areas. Each contact with the health system, the pattern suggests, is another chance to vaccinate that systems should not waste.
plos-pone-0355018:
Jackline Akello and colleagues report in 2026 on the strain felt by health workers in Uganda. Their focus is care for women who are pregnant and live with sickle cell illness. Interviews and group talks were held at referral hospitals. Doctors, midwives, and other maternity staff took part.

Workers described gaps in their own knowledge and fear when cases turned grave. Sadness ran deep when outcomes were poor. Myths in the community made the work harder still. Short supplies, missing guidelines, and no joined up specialist care added strain. The authors call for team based care, better training, and system reform.
plos-pone-0355218:
Nan Tao and co-authors studied how visitors picture three living historic neighbourhoods in Yunnan, China. These districts mix heritage protection, daily community life, and tourism in the same streets. Their 2026 study proposed a five-part lens covering people, space, setting, place, and felt atmosphere, then tested it on visitor writing.

The team mined visitor posts, measured their feelings with a text model, and weighed what mattered most against how well each site performed. All three districts blended old buildings, street life, and local routine, but they differed in how developed tourism was. Historic remains were a shared strength everywhere. Weak points included basic facilities and some visitor experiences, which the authors flag for improvement.
plos-pone-0356518:
Sai-Leung Ng, writing alone in PLOS ONE in 2026, asks what actually drives Hong Kong shoppers to buy secondhand clothing. Surveys everywhere say people love the idea; the author wanted the mechanics. An online survey of five hundred forty-five respondents fed a structural model. It extended the classic knowledge, attitude, practice chain with two situational factors: price consciousness and perceived risk. Hong Kong's cheap new clothing might erase the usual thrift motive, so both belonged in the test.

The results partly overturned the textbook chain. Environmental knowledge pushed purchases directly, and perceived risk did too, while attitude mattered only indirectly, by shaping how risky secondhand clothes felt. Price consciousness did nothing at all, neither driving nor mediating purchases. Ng credits the city's fiercely competitive, duty free retail market, where new clothes are already cheap enough to mute thrift. Green retail strategy there should sell knowledge and trust, not discounts.
plos-pone-0356818:
Daniel Martel and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It characterizes the dual functions of CK1.2, a protein from Leishmania, the parasite that causes leishmaniasis. Dual means the protein works in two arenas: inside the parasite itself and inside the macrophage, the human immune cell the parasite invades and lives within.

A protein that serves the parasite in both places is an attractive drug target, since blocking it could strike twice. Characterizing both functions carefully is the groundwork for that hope. Parasitologists and drug developers working on a neglected tropical disease are the readers for this two-sided portrait.
plos-pone-0357018:
Yun Zhang led a team of seven authors who used language models to track public opinion in China, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their market was portable energy gear, a fast-moving sector where social media chatter can signal demand shifts early. The team analyzed large sets of social media comments with large language models.

Zhang's group turned that chatter into a data-driven read on what buyers think, want, and complain about. Companies in fast markets can use such monitoring to spot problems and trends sooner than sales figures reveal them. The study also tests how well current language models handle opinion at scale. For market researchers, it is a worked example of AI listening posts done with care.
plos-pone-0357918:
Naveed Shahid led a team of six authors modeling a poultry disease in PLOS ONE in 2026. Newcastle disease can devastate flocks, and planners use epidemic models to foresee its course. Shahid's team added delayed, chance-based terms to capture how outbreaks unfold with lags and random variation.

The authors checked the model's stability and worked out approximations that make it usable. A model that reflects delay matters because control steps, like vaccination or culling, also act with lags. Veterinarians and farm officials gain sharper forecasts of when an outbreak will peak and fade. Better forecasts support faster, better-sized responses that can save flocks and limit spread between farms.
plos-pone-0358118:
Cong Liang, Hongyan Niu, and Lina Xue built a scale to measure how much care dialysis patients need, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. People on hemodialysis depend on nurses for many tasks, but no existing scale captured that dependency well. The team developed the HD-CDS scale and ran a first evaluation of how it performs.

Liang's tool lets clinics measure real dependency and staff their units to match what patients actually need. Understaffing a unit of highly dependent patients risks safety; overstaffing wastes scarce nurses. A validated scale turns staffing arguments into measurements. The preliminary testing reported here is the first step; wider use will show whether the scale holds up across different units and patient mixes.
plos-pone-0358218:
Kun He and three colleagues combine data mining with a rat model to find the genes that drive uveitis, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Uveitis, inflammation inside the eye, can blind, and its autoimmune machinery is partly mapped. The team mined a dataset of immune cells from patients and healthy donors, and crossed it with six disease gene databases.
