From the one hundred thirty-nine genes that surfaced, they built an interaction network. Hub genes were picked by their connections.

The gene set clustered in inflammation, immune response, and viral defense pathways. The hubs were then checked in rats with induced autoimmune eye inflammation, measuring their activity in eye, liver, and spleen tissue. The animal results supported the computational nominations, tying the database exercise to disease. The authors offer the hub genes as candidate markers and drug targets, in a field where diagnosis still leans on a clinician's eye and experience.
plos-pone-0359418: Pacheco and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on nursing students in Saudi Arabia. They asked whether gender changes the link between belief in one's own study skills and actual grades. That belief, called academic self-efficacy, often predicts effort. If the link differs by gender, teachers can tailor support instead of giving every student the same advice.
plos-pone-0359618: Sun and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a desktop virtual reality game for design students. The game teaches color composition, how hues are matched and balanced in basic design work. The team built the game and then tested how well it teaches. A playful, low-cost tool could help beginners grasp color rules that lectures alone make abstract.
plos-pone-0360418:
Shiwei Wu and colleagues examined in 2026 whether simple blood based scores measured before surgery can flag patients likely to develop a pancreatic fistula after distal pancreatectomy. In that operation, part of the pancreas is removed, and a fistula, a leak of pancreatic fluid, is among its most feared complications. The scores under study combine signs of inflammation and nutrition from routine preoperative tests.

The team analyzed how strongly those indices correlated with fistula risk in their patients. A cheap warning drawn from blood tests already ordered would let surgeons watch high risk patients more closely and act at the first sign of a leak. Studies of this kind aim to turn ordinary lab results into early, practical protection.
plotinus-enneads-guthrie-1918:
Plotinus wrote the tracts that his pupil Porphyry set as the Enneads. Kenneth Sylvan Guthrie gave the full set English dress in 1918. Plotinus was a Greek sage in Rome in the third century. His thought is the root of Neoplatonism and of much of the West's hid line.

Six sets of nine tracts make up the whole work. The One stands at the top, past thought and past name. Mind and Soul flow from it, and the world of sense comes last. Guthrie's full dress let English readers take the whole climb at last.
pmc-10652518:
Carlos Riera-Ruiz and Hideaki Moriyama measure how an enzyme from the western corn rootworm does its job. Their study was published in twenty twenty-three. The rootworm is a stubborn corn pest that has beaten many control methods, so its basic proteins draw interest as weak points.

The enzyme, dUTPase, clears a building block that would otherwise slip wrong letters into DNA. Blocking it can starve the cell of a needed letter and kill it. The team made the rootworm enzyme in bacteria, purified it, and confirmed it breaks down its target. They then charted its working rates and traits. The baseline data help judge whether this housekeeping enzyme could serve as a drug or insecticide target.
pmc-10674918:
Feng, Liu, Jiang, and Xu fit in twenty twenty-three two classic kinds of mass measurement into one brick-sized portable spectrometer. Quadrupole and ion trap analysers complement each other but normally need different shapes, settings, and electronics. A printed-circuit multi-electrode part lets their single analyser switch between the two modes, and two source types cover both evaporating and stubborn samples.

Quadrupole mode reads lighter ions, while trap mode reaches heavier ones and can break ions apart for deeper identification. Tests charted resolution, sensitivity, and range in both modes. The authors say the pairing gives a small instrument new reach for field analysis, where carrying two machines is not an option.
pmc-10693118:
Kanade-Mehta and five co-authors map posture-dependent resistance in the stiff post-stroke arm across its workspace, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Stroke arms resist passive movement through abnormal reflexes that vary with position and speed. A robot moves relaxed hands between sampled locations at three speeds. Forces and muscle signals are recorded during and after each move.

Controls show tiny forces at all speeds and times uniformly. Stroke arms show speed-dependent resistance during and just after movement. Velocity effects fade within two seconds of stopping. Steady forces then depend on posture alone, growing near workspace edges. Muscle patterns fit lowered stretch reflex thresholds after stroke. Maps are stable across repeated testing days.
pmc-10709418:
Eriksen and a large team studied in twenty twenty-three how gut germs get coated when a key shield protein is missing. That protein, IgA, coats germs at the gut wall to keep them in check. Folks who lack it have few ills, which hints that kin proteins step in.

They matched folks who lack IgA with kin who have it and read germ coats in stool. Two kin proteins, IgM and IgG, coated most germ groups in the lack group, though at a lower rate. One lone IgG type on germs was sparse and tied to gut strain. That lone coat may mark swelling, they say.
pmc-10709918:
Shuying Wang and fourteen co-authors test whether fluid from parasite cysts can treat bacterial sepsis in mice. Their study came out in 2023. Sepsis is a life-threatening overreaction to infection, and the parasite in question is known to calm its host's immune system.

In laboratory cultures, the cyst fluid pushed macrophages, a type of immune cell, toward their calming form and blocked the inflammatory form. In mice with induced sepsis, treatment improved survival and reduced damage to the liver, kidney, and lung. Treated animals showed more anti-inflammatory signals and fewer inflammatory ones. A key inflammatory signaling pathway was also quieter in their tissues. The authors conclude that the fluid's calming effect works largely by rebalancing these immune cells.
pmc-10720418:
Guatelli-Steinberg and five co-authors compare mangabey monkey molars under distinct diets, in work from twenty twenty-three. Fallback foods are low quality items eaten when preferred food is scarce. They are thought to shape primate teeth, even if eaten rarely.

One mangabey species eats hard seeds only in crunch times and has thick tooth enamel. Another eats hard foods all year and also has thick enamel. The study asks whether molar form differs between routine and fallback hard food regimes. If form matches despite distinct timing, the fallback story needs revision. Teeth can mislead diet guesses if timing is ignored.
pmc-10734018:
Yiyu Chen and colleagues model what happens when hydrogen is blended into natural gas for home water heaters, in this study from twenty twenty-three. Blending is pitched as a quick way to cut carbon output and give hydrogen a market. But hydrogen burns hotter and faster than methane, so heaters built for plain gas may behave oddly.

The team first shrank the chemistry of the burn to a compact set of nineteen species and sixty-seven steps, fast enough for design work. Simulations then showed that burning the mix inside a porous block helps it burn fully and cuts pollutants. A cost and impact check on a heater burning twenty percent hydrogen found fuel costs down. Carbon monoxide fell by about a quarter, and nitrogen oxides by over half. Carbon dioxide fell modestly. The authors back the blend, with the right burner design.
pmc-10736218:
Ann Pearman describes how a large city hospital system built a mental health service for older patients inside its medical clinics. The system serves over three hundred thousand people, most on public cover or uninsured. Older patients often carry several long-term illnesses plus higher risk of memory disorders, yet mental health needs are easy to miss.

A specialist in aging and mental health joined in twenty twenty-one to build the service. Care runs three ways: joint work inside clinics, placed services, and referrals. Over twelve hundred referrals have come in, many for people getting mental health care for the first time. Training posts for young doctors were added as well.
pmc-10736718:
Bruce and six co-authors tie faith acts to wit state in men of two races in this twenty twenty-three study. Black men bear more strain loads and high wit-loss risk in old age. Faith webs may serve as a cope bank for that load.

Inside, a state age bank gave men of like low cash bands for the checks. Black men bore wit loss at near half; white men at near a third. White men gained from now-and-then church meets in the math. Black men gained from lone prayer and strong faith grades most. The team calls for full faith-grade tools in next rounds.
pmc-10737518:
Ashley Kuzmik wrote this research paper, published in 2023, on hospital care for older patients who live with dementia. It looks at what helps or holds back function-focused care, an approach that keeps patients active and moving during a hospital stay.

The study used baseline data from 365 patients at ten hospitals in a larger trial. Using a statistical model, Kuzmik found that pain, thinking ability, and the quality of staff interactions shaped how much function-focused care patients took part in. Medical tethers that tie patients to beds or tubes also mattered. The paper says care should focus on treating pain, easing dementia symptoms, cutting tether use, and improving how staff interact with patients.
pmc-10737718:
Amy Powell-Versteeg, Rebekah Perkins, R. Scott Ward, Linda Edelman, and Katherine Supiano wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It describes a training model that fights ageism among health care students while building their sense of themselves as capable providers.

The model, called IMPACT, blends two forms of learning by direct experience. Third-year physical therapy students took classroom training plus a two-week Parkinson's disease boot camp with older patients. Nine students were interviewed afterward. They reported fresh insight into what their clients could do, strong working bonds with patients, and better choices made through teamwork. The authors argue that real contact with older adults, paired with focused study, can draw more students toward geriatric care.
pmc-10739218:
Bronwyn Keefe presents training to fight ageism among medical students in this 2023 paper. Age based bias in clinicians can skew care decisions for older patients. Evidence on student attitudes is mixed, with both negative and positive views reported. An interactive online module was built for fourth year students.

Students took an expectations about aging survey before and after the module. At entry, about 70 percent expected growing forgetfulness with age, among other beliefs. The session teaches how bias forms and how contact with older people counters it. Intergenerational contact is a proven companion strategy. The goal is care decisions based on the patient, not the stereotype. Results from the module are presented for educators.
pmc-10739518:
Cho, Allen, and Cheng reported in twenty twenty-three on a new survey scale for couples who juggle paid work and care for an older adult. The scale measures couple efficacy, meaning a couple's shared belief that they can handle both demands together as a team.

The team surveyed four hundred eight dual-earner couples in Taiwan who care for an older adult. Their work produced a ten-item scale with two parts. One part covers shared tasks, such as giving enough time to job and care duties. The other covers the bond itself, such as backing each other in times of stress. Tests supported the scale's soundness, linking it to life, job, and marital satisfaction.
pmc-10743618:
Nazar Shapoval and a team of co-authors trace the history of two sulphur butterflies in this twenty twenty-three study. Both were named in the late 1800s, and experts have long argued about what they are. Some treat them as forms of one species, some as sub-types of near kin, and some as full species of their own.

The team read DNA from fresh samples and from hundred-year-old museum specimens, including a key type specimen kept in Berlin. They mapped where each line lives and how the lines split over time. They also checked for a common bacterial infection that can skew butterfly family lines. The work helps settle the place of these two insects on the tree of life.
pmc-10744618:
David Gendron and Grzegorz Bubak ask if there is a shared view on the safety of carbon nanotubes and graphene in living systems. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-three. Both materials have rare traits and wide promise, in medicine, energy stores, and gas sensors. Yet their risks to health and to the wild are still in dispute.

They sum up the plus and minus points of each, and of mixes that hold them, for how they sit with living tissue and where they may poison it. Some work has set work exposure caps, but more is needed. They also scan the rules and guides now in force for such nano materials.
pmc-10745818:
Luka Morita leads an eleven-author team making stretchy wires with liquid metal cores cheaply and at speed, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-three. Liquid metal wires stretch over five times their length, ideal for wearable electronics. Production has been slow, leaky, and corrosive to connectors.

The team presents methods to produce, refine, and terminate these wires so they plug into standard prototyping connectors. Their strategies attack leakage, gallium corrosion of electrodes, metal consumption, and production rate together. Rather than showcasing one device, the paper builds the manufacturing base for a prototyping ecosystem. Think of it as bringing liquid metal wiring to the stage solderless breadboards once brought ordinary circuits: quick, cheap, and endlessly reconfigurable.
pmc-10747618:
Yu Diao and five co-authors shared a review in twenty twenty-three. It is about metal-oxide heterojunctions as artificial synapses. These are hardware parts that compute the way brains do. Conventional architectures shuttle data back and forth. They move it between memory and processor, and that wastes energy. Neuromorphic devices merge the two in one place. Layered metal oxides are leading candidates. Their interfaces can be tuned by design.

The review covers how the materials are made. It covers how their junctions mimic synaptic strengthening and weakening. It covers the device numbers that matter too. Those are power, stability, and switching behavior. New systems sense vision, touch, and even pain through such junctions. Challenges remain, from uniformity to integration. The review lists them with candidate fixes. The authors put interface engineering at the center. The deliberate design of the boundary between oxides will decide the technology.
pmc-10747918:
Liao and eight co-authors test microwave ablation power plus PD-one therapy for distant effects in liver cancer, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Ablation treats the main tumor, but effects on distant tumors were unclear. Mice carry tumors on both flanks while one side is ablated. Distant growth, immune infiltration, and blood cytokines are tracked.

Low-power ablation alone actually promotes distant tumor growth. High-power ablation plus anti-PD-one therapy reverses that pattern. Killer T cells infiltrate distant tumors while regulatory cells fall. A Th-one cytokine rises in the blood correspondingly. The combination activates a strong systemic anti-tumor response.
pmc-10750418:
Liu and co-authors hunt for a stem-like B cell group inside diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, the most common aggressive lymphoma of its class. Some patients relapse or resist standard care, and cancer stem cells may be to blame. The team read single-cell gene data from three tumors and one normal lymph sample. Software judged which B cell groups looked malignant by chromosome copy changes. A second tool estimated group shares across 230 tumor tissues.

Regulator analysis flagged the switch proteins steering each group. Contact mapping charted how groups talk to the tumor setting. One subpopulation carried stem-like traits. Finding it may explain stubborn cases and offer new targets.
pmc-10753418:
Daynes-Kearney and Gallagher review online support groups for family caregivers, in a review from twenty twenty-three. Caring for a sick relative can harm the caregiver's own health. Peer support can buffer that harm, and groups have moved online fast. Yet no one had mapped what kinds of groups exist or what helps them work.

They searched seven databases and kept nineteen studies of adult caregivers. Most groups met on public text forums and focused on one illness. Members were mostly women with degrees who wrote posts at times that suited them. Good groups felt safe and free of judgment. They paired people with shared lived experience. Trained peer or expert moderators helped groups thrive.
pmc-10754618:
Kwon and co-authors look at pulse pressure and low muscle mass in Korean adults in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Pulse pressure is the gap between the two blood pressure numbers, and it reflects stiff arteries. Low muscle mass, a sign of sarcopenia, raises the risk of heart events and death.

The team used national health survey data from two thousand eight to two thousand eleven. Adults with a high pulse pressure were older and had more high blood pressure, diabetes, and high blood fats. They also had low muscle mass more often than the low pressure group, even after other factors were taken into account. The authors suggest watching pulse pressure could help spot people at risk.
pmc-10761318:
Choi and co-authors review long-term results of widening the jaw ridge with pig bone grafts before placing implants. A ridge too narrow cannot hold an implant well. The study covered 49 graft sites with more than five years of follow-up. A deeper look covered 24 sites where pig bone was the only graft material used. Follow-up after the crown was fitted averaged 67.5 months.

Bone loss at the implant edge averaged 0.23 mm at one year. Over the full period it reached 0.40 mm on average. Two of 49 implants were lost, giving a survival rate of 95.9%. The authors judge the graft stable over the long term.
pmc-10781918:
Jianmin Wu and eleven co-authors build a scan-only score that reads liver tumor immune mix and fate with no cut. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. A tumor's immune mix drives growth, spread, and cure take, yet past reads need tissue. Three hundred one patients had MRI scans, and a tissue test scored immune marks. Five scan traits were sifted to stand for that score.

The scan score split high and low immune states with fair truth in test runs. It also guessed take to an immune drug in a fresh group. Past such models, this one adds fate guess and drug guide in one. The team pitch it for no-cut care picks.
pmc-10784818:
Huang and Tian study anesthesia drug effects in rectal cancer surgery, in work from twenty twenty-three. Rectal carcinoma is mainly treated with laparoscopic surgery. The operation can cause strong blood flow changes and weaken immune function, and opioid based anesthesia carries a risk of low blood pressure.

More than two hundred patients having rectal tumor removal were studied. The combination of remifentanil with propofol was tested for its effects on hemodynamics, meaning blood pressure and circulation stability, and on oxidative stress markers. A regimen that steadies circulation while limiting cell stress could improve recovery after major bowel surgery.
pmc-10824918: Neil Carleton and Julia Foldi report a drug side effect case in breast cancer care. Their case deals with abemaciclib, now standard added care for high risk hormone positive tumors. The patient grew a hormone fault called SIADH sans kidney harm. Real world use can show side effects that trials missed. The case tells her course in full.
pmc-10899318:
Samia Valeria Ozorio Dutra and four co-authors ask whether the gut microbes of very small newborns relate to behavior years later, in a paper published in twenty twenty-three. Babies born under fifteen hundred grams face risks to gut balance and to brain growth. Behavior problems can be subtle and hard to measure, so early signs would help.

The team followed nineteen children who had been studied as infants in intensive care. Parents filled in a standard behavior checklist when the children reached four years of age. The scores covered mood, anxiety, attention, and defiant behavior. After adjusting for birth and care factors, certain early gut bacteria tied to later scores. One bacterium linked to several behavior scales. The authors call the work preliminary and urge larger studies.
pmc-10900518:
Jackson and co-authors grade a program that spreads good practices across VA hospitals. The Diffusion of Excellence program finds local wins through Shark Tank style contests. Facility chiefs bid staff and funds to copy each winning practice. Winners get a year of outside help to set the practice up. Staff then push proven practices across the whole system.

The first eight contests drew 3,280 bids from 2016 to 2022. Judges named 88 practices as promising. Records show 1,440 cases of adoption or copying since then. Rural sites account for 180 of those cases. The review uses the RE-AIM frame to judge reach and upkeep.
pmc-10955218:
Bae, Jeong, and Huh test a cross-culture nursing course for graduate students in Korea. Nurses need skill to care well for patients of all cultures. The course was built on two classic culture care models. It covered speech, family, food, death rites, and faith.

Students at Hallym University took the course in spring 2023. Surveys before and after gauged culture skill gains. The team expected gains in most skill zones. Course satisfaction was also scored at the end. Gains would back wider use of the course design. The study gives a model for graduate nurse training.
pmc-11535118:
Vine and a large team measured in twenty twenty-four how cells use oxygen in folks with a grave diabetes crisis. In that crisis, blood sugar and acid swing far from safe, and cell power plants may fail. Two food factors help cells burn fuel with oxygen.

They took blood cells from sixty-two sick folks and forty-eight healthy folks. Sick cells used less oxygen at rest and at peak than healthy cells. Adding one or both food factors raised oxygen use in sick cells in a clear way. In healthy cells just one factor helped. The team sees a path to aid care.
pmc-11547518:
Robert Mroczka, Agnieszka Słodkowska, and Jerzy Kubacki studied drug-releasing metal wire in 2024. Nitinol wire can carry implant coatings. Heat treatment changes how those coatings behave. Surface treatment matters as well. The team tested corrosion and coating quality. They also measured ibuprofen release amounts.

One coating layer used a bone-like mineral. Another used a degradable polymer blend. Chemical cleaning plus heating worked best. That wire gave even, compact coatings. It also released the most ibuprofen. Most drug escaped within five hours. The saline test mimicked body fluid conditions. Heating near a set high temperature was optimal.
pmc-11549918:
Zou and six co-authors compared two sedative drugs in twenty twenty-four for putting older adults to sleep before surgery, watching closely for drops in blood pressure. Low pressure during induction is risky for older patients, and the standard drug, propofol, is known for it.

The trial enrolled one hundred seventeen older adults at one center, each randomly assigned and blinded. Just over a quarter of the ciprofol group suffered the defined pressure drop, against nearly half of the propofol group. Ciprofol also caused far less pain at the injection site. Every patient in both groups reached the target depth of sleep, measured by a brain monitor. Extra doses and recovery measures looked similar. Ciprofol patients showed a steadier pressure and slightly deeper sleep. The authors judge the newer drug a safe, effective choice for this group.
pmc-11569018:
Alrashdi and three colleagues test toxic metals in rice eaten in Saudi Arabia in twenty twenty-four. Local Hassawi rice and imports were digested and run through fine mass tools. Four metals plus inorganic arsenic were measured. Inorganic arsenic stood out as the worry.

Local rice carried far less inorganic arsenic than imports on average. Adult intake from imports in one city neared a since pulled world safety line. It also cleared a European cancer based caution level many times over. Other metals stayed low by contrast. The team flags import checks as the lever for public safety.
pmc-11585218:
Yingying Zhang and colleagues systematically review gene variants linked to lung scarring diseases from silica and coal dust exposure. Their 2024 meta-analysis asks why workers with similar dust exposure respond so differently.

The search covered four databases and gathered eighty-three articles spanning hundreds of individual studies and gene sites. Eight candidate genes passed rigorous evaluation for pooled analysis. Specific variants in two inflammation genes and one immune regulator gene emerged as risk factors for developing the diseases. Other commonly studied variants showed no confirmed effect. The authors conclude the confirmed variants can inform susceptibility screening for dust-exposed workers, while most candidate genes still lack solid evidence.
pmc-11586418:
Manish Sharma and co-authors design a bendable four-port antenna for millimeter-wave 5G phones, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The compact board carries four matched radiators with a shared ground. Edge tapering on the patches opened three working bands from one design.

A spacer element between radiators cut cross-talk sharply at two bands. Diversity scores stayed excellent, with near-zero signal correlation and full diversity gain. Body absorption tests stayed under safety limits at all bands. Bending tests also held up within the working range. The authors pitch the design for smart devices, defense navigation, and future 5G gear.
pmc-11590218:
Yuchen Long, Xueyan Cheng, and Jing Chen study when medical students share what they know, and when they hide it. Both habits shape learning in a class. The team surveyed 761 undergraduates at two medical schools in Wuhan, China. Scales measured the study climate, trust between students, the wish to share, and both sharing and hiding.

Sharing and hiding turned out to be only weakly linked. Trust fed sharing in every group, and it cut hiding among stronger and mid-level students. A good study climate worked through trust and intent, with little direct effect. The paper shows why trust is the lever schools should pull first.
pmc-11590618:
Huo and coauthors ask if mind-health training shifts pain drug scripts. Opioid deaths are a grave concern in the United States. Front-line doctors often say their training in pain care is thin. A year-long program trains those doctors in mind-health care.

The team used records from a public plan in Southern California. The set held near 12,000 patients and 180 doctors. Of those doctors, 38 took the training and 142 did not. Scripts per patient were tracked by quarter year. Care after training counted as the exposed group. The team weighed script rates in trained and untrained care.
pmc-11600818:
Widyandana and four co-authors compared paper and phone-based peer grading in Indonesian health training in twenty twenty-four. Students in medicine, nursing, and nutrition learn teamwork through community placements, then rank each other's performance. During the pandemic the university moved classes online and needed fair remote assessment.

Records covered four thousand seven hundred ninety students from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-two. Paper forms used a five-rank scale; a mobile app introduced in twenty nineteen used ten ranks. Average peer scores rose from about sixty-two to about eighty-two after the app arrived, and the score distribution shifted right, suggesting more objective marking. The authors say the app-based ranking was well received during and after the pandemic and can serve as a model for similar programs.
pmc-11602118:
Mizuki Okuno and colleagues reported keyhole removal of a metal fragment from a man's abdominal wall in 2024. A twenty-seven-year-old forging worker arrived with abdominal pain three hours after a fragment flew from a power hammer and pierced his lower abdomen. The piece sat embedded in the wall near the inner lining, a spot the authors say had not been reported for this approach before.

Guided in real time by X-ray imaging, surgeons removed the fragment through laparoscopic instruments successfully. Surface fragments are usually taken out through the skin, they note, but keyhole surgery deserves consideration for deep wall fragments near the lining. Principles for safe, low-impact removal close the report.
pmc-11604018:
Gerry Leisman and co-authors present a case series from two thousand twenty-four on a sound-based device for easing distress in depression and anxiety. The device feeds each ear a slightly different tone, creating a pulsing beat meant to nudge the nervous system. Users tune the sound themselves during guided sessions.

Four adults took part in the pilot. Each calibrated the pulse while recalling an experience with the target emotion, turning a knob until the tone felt uncomfortable, then canceling it with a second control, a step linked to relief. Standard scales for anxiety, pandemic stress, trauma symptoms, and depression were tracked from screening to twelve weeks after treatment. Brain-wave and other measures were also recorded. The authors frame the series as an early feasibility look.
pmc-11604918:
Gloria Solano-Aguilar and colleagues compare two diets in pigs to see how food shapes the brain's small blood vessels, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Thirty-two Ossabaw pigs ate either a Western diet, rich in refined carbs, cholesterol, and saturated fat, or a heart-healthy diet rich in fiber and unsaturated fat. Half of each group also got a statin drug.

After six months, pigs on the Western diet showed clear shifts in gene activity in brain vessels. Genes tied to inflammation, vessel growth, and cell death were more active, while the healthy-diet pigs favored genes for energy use, nerve signals, and calming inflammation. Brain chemicals differed too, with some amino acids higher on the Western diet. The statin changed none of the gene results. The team reads this as a sign that daily food choices can push the brain toward or away from damage.
pmc-11609418:
Menglei Wang and nine colleagues review how water-rich gels can be built to spur the growth of new blood vessels, in a twenty twenty-four article. New vessels are key to healing wounds and rebuilding bone and heart tissue. Gels, called hydrogels, can carry drugs, fight cell damage, and even conduct signals. Many groups now design gels for several jobs at once.

The review sorts designs by extra skill: resisting oxidation, releasing cargo, sensing triggers, self-healing, carrying current, or tracking a wound. It then shows uses in skin wounds, bone repair, and heart attacks. The authors close with future paths for such gels and fresh ideas for treating the diseases they target.
pmc-11615918:
Čerevková, Sarabeev, and Renčo published in twenty twenty-four a dataset on soil nematodes in invaded and uninvaded European ecosystems. Nematodes are tiny worms that signal soil health and food web state. The data come from Slovakia, Poland, Lithuania, and Russia. Plots invaded by alien plants were paired with uninvaded plots. Grasslands and two forest types were sampled with standard methods. Six major invasive plant species anchor the comparisons across sites.

Soil chemistry, including pH, moisture, carbon, and nitrogen, was recorded. Nematode genera were classified by feeding type and life strategy. The dataset supports comparisons of community change under invasion. Modelers can use it to predict invasion impacts on soil life. Conservation managers can gauge ecosystem resilience from the patterns. The authors present the data as a reusable public resource.
pmc-11617618:
Hohyeon Han and five co-authors build a blood brain barrier model from a brain vessel specific matrix bioink, printed as a tube that fluid can flow through. Long term brain inflammation drives diseases like Alzheimer's, and the barrier's cells govern that process. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

The ink blends matrices drawn from brain and from blood vessels. Vessel lining cells and support cells inside sorted themselves into a dual layer much like the real barrier. The grown tissue showed true barrier tasks and inflammation responses. The authors argue the vessel tuned setting guides cells to native like form and role, a base for disease models.
pmc-11624818:
Daniel Pan leads a large multi-author team setting out a plan to map COVID-19 viral loads over time, in a protocol published in two thousand twenty-four. Knowing when patients carry the most virus, and where in the airway, predicts infectiousness. Studies disagree because sampling sites and timings vary.

The protocol defines a systematic review and meta-analysis before results exist. It will gather longitudinal viral load data from nose, throat, saliva, and exhaled breath. Analyses will slice by age, sex, ethnicity, immune status, severity, vaccination, treatment, and variant. Publishing the plan first guards against cherry-picking later. The synthesis should clarify isolation guidance: who is infectious, when, and how a swab's location changes the answer.
pmc-11628318:
An-Na Li and co-authors test a skin treatment in 2024 made from fat stem cells. Skin ages from within and from sun and other outside harms, losing its firm spring. The team collected the fluid around fat stem cells, which is rich in tiny sacs called exosomes that cells use to send signals.

Tests showed the fluid helped skin cells stay alive and make more collagen, the protein that gives skin strength. Mice exposed to ultraviolet light fared better with the treatment. Their skin layer stayed thinner and healthier, with more collagen packed in. The team credits the exosomes for the gains, and sees a new path for anti-aging skin care based on cell signals.
pmc-11633018:
Daniel Hettrick and co-authors report an unusual cancer spread in a case paper from two thousand twenty-four. A rare uterine cancer often spreads before symptoms appear, most often to lungs, liver, or bones. Spread to the brain is rare, and a single brain site with no other spread is rarer still.

The patient was a woman aged sixty-five with weakness on her right side, unsteady walking, and worsening slurred speech. Scans found a lesion in the pons, a small part of the brainstem. A biopsy showed it matched her earlier uterine cancer. The authors suggest the cancer may have traveled through a vein network near the spine. They warn that this cancer can reach odd sites without other disease.
pmc-11640818:
Heekyong Bae and five co-authors chart how inflammation spreads through the body over time in mice fed a high-fat diet. Their study came out in 2024. Obesity inflames many tissues, but the order and timing of that spread were unclear.

Gene activity was tracked in brain, liver, fat, and muscle across months of feeding. The inflammatory wave started in the liver, moved to fat, and reached muscle and brain last. The brain at first held its response down more than other tissues. Around the half-year mark, pathways toward brain inflammation switched on as whole-body chronic inflammation set in. One mitochondrial measure flagged the transition from liver to the rest. Similar patterns appeared in brain data from Alzheimer's patients, hinting the sequence matters beyond obesity.
pmc-11641518:
Xiaoyu Gao and a team including Rustam Aminov test whether an antiviral drug, vidarabine, can also ease constipation. Their mouse study was published in twenty twenty-four. The drug treats viral diseases in which constipation is a common side problem, yet no one had checked its effect on the bowel.

Mice were made constipated with a standard drug. Oral vidarabine sped gut movement, softened droppings, and eased passing. It raised water channel proteins in the colon, which wets the stool. It also tuned messenger chemicals and a receptor pathway that drives gut muscle squeeze. Gut microbe shifts accompanied the effect. The authors propose a fresh use for an old drug, pending the human tests that would need to follow.
pmc-11642018:
Zolkowska and a team including Uchmanowicz study frailty in older patients with heart failure in twenty twenty-four. Frailty is common in this group and links to worse outcomes. The team examined how frailty relates to thinking problems and depression. They also asked which factors predict frailty on their own.

The study included two hundred fifty patients aged sixty or older in hospital. About sixty percent were classed as frail by a standard phenotype method. Frail patients were older and stayed in hospital longer. They also had worse scores on thinking tests and more depression. In adjusted models, age, an inflammation marker, and anxiety predicted frailty. Depression and thinking scores differed between groups but were not independent predictors. The authors note the tight links among these problems.
pmc-11647418:
Ibraheem Hamzat and co-authors present a crash patient whose hospital course stacked clots on clots, in a case report from two thousand twenty-four. The patient arrived with rib, thigh, and foot breaks after a car crash. Care hit spleen bleeding that early scans missed, plus a neck fix for spine squeeze.

Clots formed in leg and arm veins despite guards and a filter. On the planned exit day, breath crashed and pressure fell hard. Chest scans showed big clots in both lung arteries. A heart hole, named in the case title, adds stroke risk to the mix. The quiz-style report asks readers to pick the next move. Readers get a trauma course where each fix breeds the next risk.
pmc-11655818:
Salla Lahdenpohja and colleagues produce three brain scan tracers on an automated microfluidic platform. Their study from twenty twenty-four pushes toward clinical production. PET imaging reveals body processes without disturbing them. Hospitals mostly make one common tracer in large batches.

Smaller batches of varied tracers would enable personalised nuclear medicine. The palm-sized module had already made several other tracer types. This work adds three fluorine-labelled brain tracers to its record. Automated production cuts staff radiation exposure and variability. Results for each tracer are reported in the study. Compact platforms could bring rare tracers to more hospitals.
pmc-11656818:
Nakalega and coauthors test a video to teach pregnant women about malaria care. Malaria in pregnancy harms both mother and unborn child. Preventive drug doses cut that harm a great deal. Yet uptake stays low in Uganda, in part from poor knowledge.

The team made a short teaching video for clinic use. Women with and without HIV took part, as did midwives. The study ran at a public pregnancy clinic in Kampala. Talks and surveys checked if the video was clear and welcome. The team also asked if women would watch and share it. Good uptake could lift drug use in pregnancy.
pmc-11658218:
Morgan Kinsinger, Jelena Ivanisevic, and Divakar Mithal published a case report and literature review in twenty twenty-four on an unusually mild case of molybdenum cofactor deficiency type B. The rare metabolic disorder poisons the body with sulfite and usually devastates newborns with untreatable seizures. Milder, later forms follow a more varied course.

Their patient developed normally until a year old, then regressed during an illness, with brain injury visible on MRI and telltale low uric acid. Sequencing found a homozygous variant in the MOCS2 gene, in an overlapping region encoding two subunits at once. It is the first mild variant reported there, expanding what doctors should suspect.
pmc-11663918:
Marta Weinstock gives a critical review of drugs for Alzheimer's disease, the most common cause of dementia. Faulty amyloid protein sits at the center of the inherited form, which led to antibody drugs against it. Two won approval in the United States, but gains were small and side effects can be serious.

She notes that cell damage from oxygen stress and raised inflammatory signals appear in all patients and track memory loss well. Some drugs for other ills ease thinking but cannot enter the brain safely. She ends with a compound she favors, which calmed these processes and slowed memory decline in a mid-stage trial, with no more side effects than a dummy pill.
pmc-11666218:
Li Da and Kai Zhang published a 2024 study on early rehab for the lungs after severe lung failure. Their patients had acute respiratory distress syndrome and had just come off breathing machines in intensive care. The question was whether lung training begun early helps them breathe better and live longer.

Records came from a hospital in Chengdu for the years 2018 to 2022. Of 240 patients, half got standard training and half got the early program. Both groups looked alike at the start. The team compared strength, lung measures, and fitness at discharge and three months later. They also tracked survival over six months. Early training is weighed as a way to speed recovery.
pmc-11671218:
You Wu and eight colleagues review China's public strategies during the COVID-19 pandemic across five domains. The domains are infrastructure and system design, medical care, disease prevention and control, economic and social resilience, and global health engagement. The review credits a top-down command system, cross-sector coordination, legal frameworks, and community governance for the response's speed.

Medical sections highlight rapid emergency mobilization, evidence-based treatment, and planned vaccine rollout. Prevention sections cover adaptive controls, transmission interruption, and technology use. Economic sections address supply, livelihoods, and revival, while the global section covers knowledge sharing and multilateral aid. The authors draw universal lessons while acknowledging every country must tailor its approach.
pmc-11672118:
Lau and Mostafa open a twenty twenty-four review set on nuclear medicine, a field that uses small amounts of radioactive drugs to image the body. Scans of this kind show how organs work, not just how they look. They help doctors find disease, plan care, and track how well care works.

The editors note high costs, scarce gear and drugs, and safety steps as real limits on wider use. Even so, they stress steady gains when these scans join standard scans. The reviews they introduce cover stroke, low mood, and prostate cancer. They also cover drugs that can both find a tumour and treat it, a pairing that keeps drawing strong interest.
pmc-11673418: Sheila Martins and co-authors explore marker candidates that might predict rectal cancer behavior, through the molecular paths that drive the disease. The hosted text opens with the burden of bowel cancer in Europe, where it ranked second in new cases in two thousand twenty-two, behind only breast cancer. The review's stated aim is to link pathway knowledge to markers of use in care.
pmc-11674218:
Rafał Gerymski and co-authors study sexual well-being in 2024 in people with multiple sclerosis, a disease where the immune system attacks the nerves. Past work shows people with MS often pull back from sexual life and rate it as less central. The team tested whether disability level links to sexual well-being in a straight or curved pattern.

They surveyed one hundred twenty-one patients with standard scales for disability and sexual well-being. Nerve-related disability tracked with more sexual problems, and more problems tracked with lower well-being. Physical disability alone showed no clear link. No curved pattern appeared in the data. The authors stress that sexual health should not be skipped in MS care.
pmc-11674918:
Rosa Verhoeven and four co-authors use machine learning to predict a severe gut disease in premature babies in a 2024 study. The disease destroys intestinal tissue and lacks accurate early prediction, which blocks preventive treatment. The team trained models on vital signs from the first five days of life for very preterm infants, including oxygen levels in brain and gut measured by light sensors.

Among two hundred sixty seven babies, thirty two developed the disease. Two of the tested models predicted it well, clearly beating a third. Gut and brain oxygen measures contributed the most predictive features. The authors call the work a pioneering step toward early warning from routine monitoring data.
pmc-11675718:
Luca Paoletti and colleagues strengthened sugar-based gels in two thousand twenty-four. Dextran gels are gentle and body-friendly materials. Their softness limits medical use, though. The team added crosslinkers with multiple arms. Light set the gels in place. Woven dual networks were also tested. Gellan gum formed the second network in some.

Stiffness, resistance, and strength were measured carefully. More arms per crosslinker changed network density predictably. Properties could thus be tuned for different uses. Semi and full interpenetrated networks behaved distinctly. Tissue scaffolds need exactly such tunability. The strategy suits many advanced therapy materials. Polysaccharide gels gain a practical upgrade path.
pmc-11676318:
Armita Vali Sichani and co-authors test two drugs dabbed on a tooth to ease deep pulp pain when standard numbing fails, in work from twenty twenty-four. The pain comes from irreversible pulpitis, an inflamed tooth nerve. A successful nerve block sometimes still leaves the pulp awake and sore.

Forty-five patients were split by chance into three groups of fifteen. Two groups got a topical antidepressant drug, and one got a starch placebo. Pain was scored on two scales before and after each step. All three groups felt less pain, with the nortriptyline group easing most. The gap between groups was not firm by statistics. The authors suggest larger trials without a placebo arm.
pmc-11676818:
Payel Kundu leads a large team on a plant extract in a multiple sclerosis model. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with Centella asiatica. The plant is a traditional remedy for aging and dementia.

Water extracts raised antioxidant response genes in past models. They also improved cell power function and nerve health. MS shares oxidative stress and power faults with aging. The team tested the extract in an autoimmune model. Gene expression and cell breathing were measured. Disability and swelling effects were tracked as well. Brain symptoms of MS are the target benefit.
pmc-11677018:
Gabriela Fonseca-Camarillo and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-four, a selenium-linked protein in ulcerative colitis, a long-term gut illness with swelling. The protein helps the colon take up selenium, a mineral that calms the immune system. Its role in this illness was not known. The team measured gene activity for the protein in colon tissue from thirty-four patients and twenty controls.

Gene activity was lower in patients with active illness than in those in remission or in controls. High activity linked to a milder course, with long remission and mild tissue harm. Cells with the protein were found in swollen tissue layers of active patients. The authors cast the protein as a guard for the colon.
pmc-11678618:
A team including Yongjie Meng studies two genes that help soybean plants form root nodules. The nodules house bacteria that pull nitrogen from the air for the plant. Making nodules costs the plant a great deal of energy, so the count must be tuned. The two genes switch on when the bacteria arrive. The team knocked both out in soybean plants and counted what followed.

The altered plants made fewer entry threads for the bacteria and so fewer nodules. The nodules that did form worked as usual. Gene reads showed the plants failed to switch on a hormone path that starts nodule growth. The paper ties these two genes to that early hormone signal.
pmc-11678818:
Sha-Sha Jia and colleagues study a rice gene that shapes seed traits in this two thousand twenty-four paper. The gene, OsIAA19, belongs to the Aux/IAA family. These genes help run auxin signaling, a hormone system that guides plant growth. Most family members in rice had not been tested, even though grain size drives both yield and quality. The team picked OsIAA19 from computer analysis as a candidate.

They found the gene active in all tissues tested, with its protein located in the cell nucleus. They then bred mutant rice lines that lack the working gene. Comparing mutants with normal plants reveals what the gene does to grain size and other seed traits. The work adds a piece to the puzzle of breeding higher-yield rice.
pmc-11680318:
Hiroshi Kusunoki reviews whether extra COVID-19 vaccine doses still make sense in Japan. His report was published in twenty twenty-four. The disease was downgraded to a routine category in twenty twenty-three, and public concern faded.

Over half the population is estimated to carry hybrid immunity from infection plus vaccination. Antibody studies show such people keep strong, long-lasting titers. Medical societies still urge continued vaccination, yet cost, side effects, and doubt about frequent boosters breed skepticism. A newly approved self-amplifying vaccine enters the discussion. Kusunoki weighs uniform booster policy against a more targeted approach shaped by actual immunity levels.
pmc-11689418:
Jordan Lewis and Steffi Kim describe how their team shares study results back with Alaska Native towns in ways the towns themselves choose. Their talk, from two thousand twenty-four, rests on more than sixteen years of joint work.

The team held deep talks with one hundred sixty-two Elders from twenty-one towns on what aging well means. Elders named six parts, from good feelings and faith to Native ways of life and health. In place of the usual papers and slides, the team made goods such as berry buckets, mugs, and shirts that carry the findings. The talk shows how to work within grant rules while making results last past the grant.
pmc-11690618:
Lillian Agyemang, Mary Milnamow, Jason Dauenhauer, and Louanne Bakk published a 2024 study of volunteers using virtual reality with people living with dementia. Most people with dementia and their caregivers prefer to age at home. Community respite centers let caregivers drop off their loved one for a few hours while trained volunteers run engaging activities.

Few studies have tested virtual reality in such drop-in programs. The researchers held a focus group with eight volunteers, all aged 65 or older, who had delivered VR sessions at a respite center. Four main themes emerged from the discussion, beginning with motivation. The volunteers' experiences show what encourages helpers, what worries them, and what support they need to run VR well.
pmc-11690818:
Sofhia Ramos and seven co-authors published a study in 2024 on muscle composition in older adults. Low muscle volume and fat infiltration into muscle are core features of sarcopenic obesity. The researchers asked how these traits relate to mitochondrial respiration, the process by which muscle produces energy, and to walking speed.

The study tested 828 adults with an average age in the mid-seventies. Body scans sorted people by muscle volume and fat infiltration, and muscle samples were taken by biopsy. Respiration was lower in every group with poor muscle composition than in the group with normal composition. Walking speeds over both short and long distances were also slower in those groups. Lower respiration explained a large share of the slower walking. The findings tie muscle quality, not only muscle size, to how well older adults move.
pmc-11706618:
Saima Faraz and four co-authors report a rare bleeding disorder in a newborn in a 2024 case report. The disorder stops platelets from clumping, so bleeding from skin and gums can be severe. It is passed down when both parents carry the same gene change, and the baby's parents were related, with a family history of the disorder.

The baby girl was born by planned surgery and soon showed bruising, gum bleeding, and jaundice. Standard clotting tests looked normal, but platelet function was badly impaired. Gene tests found the same rare change in both copies of a key gene, with each parent carrying one copy. Care included clotting factor, platelet transfusions, and blood products, plus advice on future pregnancy risk.
pmc-11707418:
Rahul Tiwari and eight co-authors review how immunity against visceral leishmaniasis grows and endures, in a two thousand twenty-four immune-system review. Curing this disease, caused by a parasite, with drugs or on its own, usually protects for life, a fact vaccine makers want to copy.

Protection rests on CD4 helper T cells: Th1 cells switch on the phagocytes that kill resident parasites, while regulatory and Th2 cells can work against them. After healing, tissue-resident, effector, and central memory subsets guard against reinfection, maybe kept up by lingering parasites or repeat contact, so-called concomitant immunity. Looking at Indian visceral disease, the authors survey why lasting vaccine-induced protection remains still out of reach.
pmc-11713618:
Morgan Elizabeth Lambert and co-authors published this early-stage study in two thousand twenty-five on loose DNA loops inside brain cells. The loops come from retrotransposons, jumping genes that can copy themselves around the genome, and the team asked whether they stir up the cell's alarm system in tau diseases.

The team pulled circular DNA from the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease, a tau disease called progressive supranuclear palsy, and healthy controls. They also stained brain slices to see the loose DNA and a switched-on alarm protein side by side. Early results point to more alarm activity and more of these DNA loops in the diseased brains. Fruit flies served as a living model for the same process. The authors propose that stray DNA loops may help drive harmful swelling in tau diseases.
pmc-11722118:
Toh and a large team compare two forms of a post transplant lymphoma in twenty twenty-four. The disorder can arise after organ transplant when immunity is suppressed. A virus called EBV drives many cases, but some arise without it. How the two forms differ in biology was poorly known.

The team used many data types to profile tumors and immune cells. Virus positive tumors showed more activity in immune related genes. Virus negative tumors showed more activity in genes tied to DNA interaction. Virus positive cancer cells also released signals that draw in monocytes, shaping their surroundings. The study names proteins that mark each form, and one protein proved key for survival of virus positive cells. The authors see paths to more precise therapies.
pmc-11728318:
Akanksha Gautam leads a team on shrimp shell protein joined with polyphenols. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses Pacific white shrimp shells. Protein hydrolysates were made with two distinct enzymes.

Three polyphenols were joined to the hydrolysates at varied levels. A redox pair helped drive the joining in the tests. Low polyphenol levels gave the best joining rates of all. Higher levels cut the joining rate in their checks. Spectra tests proved the joins had formed as planned. One join type led in radical scavenging scores. Use in surimi gel was also tested.
pmc-11728418:
Table olives lose minerals and gain salt during curing, and Antonio López-López and a team of co-authors try to reverse that at the packing stage. They packed a traditional Spanish green olive in brine spiked with potassium, calcium, and magnesium salts while cutting the normal salt. Then they measured how the minerals split between the olives and the brine.

The fortified olives took up far more of the three added minerals, in some mixes many times the usual levels. Meanwhile sodium dropped from near twelve thousand to about six thousand seven hundred milligrams per kilogram of pulp. Math models found the best salt blends for set goals. The team says such olives could reach the market as a healthier traditional food.
pmc-11728818:
Giulia Cagnoli and colleagues published a 2024 lab study of herbal oils against dangerous gut bacteria. Three E. coli types cause severe disease in people and animals. Infected animals contaminate the environment through feces. Oregano, savory, and thyme oils were tested. A blend of all three was included.

Bacterial strains came from bird fecal samples. Tiny oil amounts stopped bacterial growth. Thyme and savory oils worked at the lowest doses. The equal blend performed comparably well. Plant oils might help disinfect farm environments. They could also reduce reliance on synthetic agents. Further tests must check safety and real-world conditions.
pmc-11794318:
Eric Yanchenko, Thomas Chappell, and Anders Huseth use a smart search method to place insect traps where they teach the most. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Trap networks watch for crop pests, yet sites are often chosen for convenience, not for information.

The target was a moth that ranks among North America's worst farm pests. Traps ran at twenty-one sites across five North Carolina counties for four years. Three years of catches trained a Bayesian optimization model, and the fourth year tested it. For any set number of traps, the method picked the sites that pinned down pest density best. The authors say the approach lets growers get more from limited traps and time.
pmc-11802518:
Jose Tantalean leads a team on Down syndrome in grave ill kids. Their study is set in a children's hospital in Lima, Peru. Data on such kids in intensive care are thin and split.

Records of kids admitted in a row were checked again. Traits, nutrition state, and outcomes were pulled from a data base. Death, stay length, and breathing machine time were key outcomes. Infections gained in care were also logged for the group. Stats models gave both raw and adjusted links. The aim is to test if Down syndrome shapes outcomes.
pmc-11839218:
Svetlana Klimanova and a large team of co-authors review melatonin-linked antidepressants in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Depression often travels with alcohol abuse, anxiety, epilepsy, or Parkinson's disease. A shared thread is broken body clocks, which these drugs target.

The review gathered twenty studies with over eighteen hundred patients in total. The two drugs examined may ease depression and anxiety together. They also improved sleep, cut alcohol cravings, and softened motor symptoms in Parkinson's cases. Evidence was drawn from English and Russian sources and checked for bias. The authors call the class promising for keeping remission steady when depression is comorbid. Bigger, cleaner trials would firm up the case.
pmc-11967518:
Park and co-authors ask if the type of drug resistance mutation changes cure rates for a common stomach germ. Helicobacter pylori can carry changes in its 23S ribosomal RNA that block clarithromycin. Two changes, A2142G and A2143G, are the most common forms of this resistance in patients.

The study used data from an earlier randomised trial of clarithromycin-based triple therapy. It compared cure rates in patients whose germs carried each mutation type. If one form cures less often, doctors could test for the type before choosing drugs. That would spare patients a course bound to fail.
pmc-12683818:
Lohrasbi and colleagues pool trial results in twenty twenty-five on stem cells from bone marrow as a treatment for worn joints. Such cells are a hopeful way to repair joint tissue and ease pain, but dose and safety were unclear. The team searched major databases and found a small set of sound trials covering over one thousand patients.

Pain and daily function showed no clear gain in the first few months after injection. Gains appeared by six months and peaked at one year. Lower cell doses worked as well as higher ones for pain relief. No serious side effects were reported in most trials. The authors urge larger, standard trials with long follow-up to pin down the best dose.
pmc-12692018:
Kamal Shaik and four co-authors ask whether adding heat ablation improves standard care for lung cancer spread to the spine. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Such spread causes pain, instability, and nerve harm, and two treatments are already standard.

The standards are radiation and kyphoplasty, a procedure that steadies the bone with cement. The added method burns tumor tissue with radio waves. Using a large health database, the team matched seven hundred three patients into fair comparison groups. One-year death rates were nearly the same with or without the added burn. Tumor return, nerve problems, and pain medicine use also matched. The authors conclude the extra step brought no clear benefit in this group.
pmc-12693918:
Wang and a team including Tian and Teng studied in twenty twenty-five a rice gene that helps the plant stand heat. The gene makes a protein kin to ones that build wood-like stuff in plant walls. Its role in heat stress was not clear at the start.

Tests showed the gene is most at work in roots and turns up when heat hits. Plants with extra gene made more wall stuff and more plant shield compounds, and stood heat better. Plants with the gene knocked out made less of those compounds and fared worse in heat. The gene could be a target to breed crops that bear heat.
pmc-12696118:
Khosla, Keenan, and Raman review new models and measures for teaching urology in twenty twenty-five. Urology covers the urinary tract and male reproductive organs. Fresh tools include augmented reality and three dimensional printing for hands on training. Online lessons let students learn at their own pace, which many prefer.

Staged frameworks grant trainees more freedom step by step without harming patient care. For students, interest groups and required skills sessions lift confidence in basic tasks. Targeted outreach helps close gaps for groups with less access. The authors call for standard, flexible training with graded freedom. AI can aid content and feedback, they add, and proof against old methods is still owed.
pmc-12700918:
Pietramale and four co-authors reported in twenty twenty-five that the working arms of microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, often lack mitochondria. Microglia constantly patrol the brain for damage or infection. Mitochondria supply cell energy, yet how they are placed inside microglia was unknown.

Using live imaging in mice and fine structural study in mouse and human tissue, the team found uneven placement. Some cell arms held several mitochondria, while others held none. The arms doing minute-to-minute watching usually had none. Arms rushing toward a lesion or first touching a dying neuron also lacked them. Mitochondria arrived later instead. Support structures and a metabolic enzyme followed the same pattern, suggesting tight links in how these cells organize energy.
pmc-12702318:
Abhishek Bhattacharya and nine co-authors set out a protocol for teaching computers to outline single cells in a new kind of surgical image. The imaging method reads tissue chemistry with light, giving surgeons stain-free views during brain operations. To read such images cell by cell, a model must first learn from hand-labeled examples. The protocol walks through labeling cells with a web tool built for the task.

It then covers training a deep learning model with a paired software library. The images come from real neurosurgical cases taken during operations. The paper aims to make single-cell spatial study of these images routine for other labs.
pmc-12707118:
Golchini and three co-authors report a survey from twenty twenty-five on how dentists in Turkey use antibiotics in mouth surgery. The team asked two hundred sixty-three dentists about their habits early in twenty twenty-five. The survey had twenty-five items on drug choice, rule use, and allergy care. Most dentists picked penicillin-type drugs first, as the results show. Far fewer said they always follow the written rules for these drugs.

Only a small share sent patients for allergy tests when allergy was in doubt. Many picked a backup drug instead, and few always warned patients of side effects. Most knew the national rules, but only a third said they apply them. The authors call for clearer rules and more training.
pmc-12711118:
Ilker Sengul and Demet Sengul write a short comment from twenty twenty-five on a plan to track plastics. The plan they discuss uses small molecules tied to plastics as chemical fingerprints. Such marks could show where a plastic has been over its life. That life runs from making and use to recycling, dumping, and wear in the open air.

The authors praise the idea as new and full of promise. They also raise hard points that must be solved before it can work well at scale. One is the sheer mix and unknown nature of many of these small molecules. Readers get both the hope in the plan and the main doubts about its use.
pmc-12716718:
Laura Bahr and a large team study two fat-cutting enzymes in the worm C elegans. Their genetics paper from twenty twenty-five links the enzymes to immunity and fertility. Reproduction and immune defence both demand heavy energy. Animals must balance those demands during infection.

A regulator called TCER-1 normally boosts fertility and suppresses immunity. It controls both lysosomal lipases studied here. One lipase supports immune defence after infection. The other lipase does not share that immune role. The immune lipase builds specific ceramide fats that aid survival. Adding those fats rescued weak immunity in mutant worms. Both enzymes also shape fertility, showing how one system splits shared resources.
pmc-12717218:
Yuxiang Peng and co-authors watch a heat-storing material at work in 2025 with X-ray imaging. Cobalt oxide can soak up heat by giving off oxygen when hot and taking it back when cooler, a cycle useful for storing solar energy. Why some batches fade with use was unclear.

The team filmed single particles during heating cycles at very high temperatures. Tiny nanoparticles swapped oxygen fast and kept their solid form. Larger grains grew inner pores as they released oxygen, and those pores stayed, slowing later cycles. The contrast shows size itself steers wear. The authors say future heat-storage materials should be built small, or designed to resist pore growth.
pmc-12717718:
Li and six colleagues tie air pollution to heart disease risk partly through DNA methylation in twenty twenty-five. A long cohort tracked pollution against new heart cases. Four pollutants each raised risk in a straight line with dose. Fine particles carried the largest share of the joint load.

Gene based tests then linked pollution tied methylation sites to heart outcomes. One site for fine particles tied to heart attack and coronary disease. Sites for nitrogen dioxide tied to heart attack and heart failure. Overlap checks backed some of the links. The study maps a path from dirty air to heart harm.
pmc-12717818:
Tzu-Ning Tseng and five co-authors study whether Chinese herbal medicine lowers the risk of early ovary failure after chemotherapy, in a 2025 study. Early ovary failure is a common late effect for young women treated for cancer. The team used population health claims data for women aged twenty to thirty nine with a new cancer diagnosis.

They matched one thousand forty women who developed ovary failure with similar women who did not. Those who added herbal medicine to standard care had much lower odds of ovary failure. Starting the herbs within the first three years after diagnosis gave the largest benefit. The authors suggest joint care planning between cancer and herbal practitioners.
pmc-12719918:
Xuanxuan Li and a team of co-authors report a 2025 study of a gene family in wheat and its kin. The WRKY genes help control how plants respond to stress and growth cues. Past work had not compared this family across the full range of wheat genomes.

The team searched one diploid, two tetraploid, and five hexaploid genomes and found 1,912 WRKY genes in total. They sorted the genes into three groups by shared features, and one group was the largest and most varied. Repeated copies side by side drove much of the family's growth. They also tracked gene loss after new wheat forms arose and checked which genes switch on under salt stress.
pmc-12728218:
Joonsik Moon and Peter Bex wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It compares the eyes' automatic tracking with conscious judgment when people watch global motion, asking which motion features each system trusts.

Vision reads two kinds of motion: the fine carrier pattern and its broader envelope. Both eye following and perceived direction leaned on the envelope, while carrier motion alone produced big direction errors and barely moved the eyes. Shorter showings hurt judged speed, by weakening signal and adding noise, but left eye responses untouched. Direction judgments and eye movements, though, shared a noise pattern, hinting at a common source. Trial by trial, judged direction trailed the eyes' direction slightly, while judged speed ignored eye speed. The authors say feedback loops link the systems for direction only.
pmc-12730418:
Ivana Bogavac and six co-authors follow a child who had a stroke around birth in this two thousand twenty-five case report. The stroke struck an artery on the left side of her brain, the side that usually hosts language. Early brain injury raises a deep question: how does language grow when its usual home is damaged? The girl has had speech therapy since age four and physical therapy since infancy. The team assessed her thinking and language at age seven.

They set the test results beside her MRI findings. Her progress shows how a young brain can reroute around early damage. Single cases like this guide therapy and family expectations. The report adds a detailed data point to a mixed evidence base on early stroke outcomes.
pmc-12732418:
Aleksandr Tkachenko and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-five on gene activity in blood from people with type two diabetes. Many past studies hunted for blood signs of the disease, but their gene lists rarely matched. The team asked what a combined look across studies could find.

They sequenced blood RNA from nine patients and nine controls, then merged the data with seven public sets. Single studies agreed poorly with each other, and few genes appeared in all. The combined analysis still found a broad set of changed genes, many of them new. The set pointed to activation and growth of a white blood cell type called neutrophils. The work also warns how hard blood markers are to pin down.
pmc-12734218:
Hunaida Tayeb and colleagues compare three-dimensional printed crown materials with milled ones for strength and hardness, in a twenty twenty-five study. Printed crowns are now used as lasting tooth repairs, not just trial pieces. The team tested three printed resins and three milled blocks made for final crowns. They measured filler share, bending strength, and two kinds of hardness.

Milled blocks bent far less easily, with much higher strength scores than printed resins. Their hardness was also two to four times higher. The printed resins all scored near the same hardness. Filler share tracked with several strength measures. The authors say milled blocks still lead on raw strength, a fact dentists should weigh when picking materials.
pmc-12737018:
Junpil Park and co-authors gauge how ultrasonic traits of aluminium alloys shift as heat changes, alloy by alloy. Their 2025 study looks at ultrasound as a choice in place of thermistors. The aim is to track heat in motors and batteries for electric vehicles.

Samples in the shape of a step wedge were made from three alloys in wide use, each in five levels of thickness. In spite of splits in what they are made of, the alloys showed ultrasonic traits that were much the same. As heat rose, attenuation rose and the speed of the waves fell. Samples with no flaws showed nonlinearity rise with heat, then level off. Samples worn by fatigue acted in a unlike way, with a more strong nonlinear response at high heat. The team says ultrasound could give a cheaper way to gauge heat and spot flaws.
pmc-12737218:
Xiaoming Wang and co-authors map thigh muscle sparks to knee moves to drive a smart fake knee by thought alone. Their pilot study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Fast, smooth help from such knees needs a true read of what the user means to do. Spark reads from leg muscles and knee bend reads were taped in flat walk.

A long-short mind net was taught to guess joint path from spark traits. It beat plain nets on truth and smooth time flow. The guess flow was then tied to a body-gear force model and a fluid drive, so the knee can shift its stiff drag on the fly. The team call the way fit and of use.
pmc-12738618:
Xuanning Luo, Chuanlei Zheng, and Qingfeng Wu pooled community diabetes trials in 2025. Staff shortages push care toward trained lay helpers. Peer support models offer another low-cost route. Whether they match professional-led care was untested at scale. The team searched eight databases for randomized trials. Thirty studies entered the analysis. Outcomes covered blood sugar, fats, and body weight. Evidence quality was graded for each outcome.

Community programs improved long-term blood sugar. Meal-time and fasting sugar also fell. Total cholesterol, triglycerides, and body mass index improved. Two cholesterol fractions did not change significantly. Professional-led programs beat lay-led ones on sugar control. Peer support programs did worse than non-peer ones there. Evidence certainty stayed low, the authors warn. Still, gains reached levels that matter clinically. They frame lay and peer models as practical second-best options. Resource-limited settings may benefit most from them.
pmc-12741318:
Hassan Jubair and three co-authors review neurofeedback, training people to steer their own brain activity in real time. Their synthesis appeared in twenty twenty-five. The method has spread from clinics into performance coaching, and the evidence needs a sober stock-take.

Sixty-five studies anchor the review. The authors trace the field's history, its techniques, and new twists like connectivity-based and combined feedback. Trials cover attention deficit disorder, trauma stress, depression, and autism, plus healthy users chasing sharper focus. Benefits appear, but methods vary wildly and placebo effects cloud the picture. The authors push for personalization and stricter designs before the method's promise can be trusted.
pmc-12747918:
Zhang and four co-authors report a rare benign lung tumor in an older patient, in work from twenty twenty-five. The tumor mixes two cell types, squamous and glandular, in one growth called a papilloma. It most often grows in the central airway of middle aged and older adults.

Because the tumor is rare, doctors often misread it at first. The report details the older patient case step by step. It then reviews past reports on older patients with the same tumor. The aim is to sharpen how doctors spot it, so patients get the right care sooner and avoid needless treatment for a cancer it is not.
pmc-12749518:
Jatinder Singh, Santosh Gudi, Peter Maughan, Rajeev Gupta, and Upinder Gill rebuilt the gene map of a wild wheat kin in twenty twenty-five, hunting leaf rust resistance. Leaf rust cuts wheat yield worldwide. The wild species Aegilops umbellulata resists many rust races. The team used short-read data with long-read transcript data to re-map one accession.

The new map holds sixty-two thousand four hundred thirty-four gene models, most of high confidence. Gene activity in resistant and susceptible plants was compared after rust infection. The resistant one replied early and strongly, within six hours, while the other lagged. Two candidate genes stood out early. One bore a repeat motif and one a kinase part. The authors call them prime picks for tests and tougher wheat breeding.
pmc-12751818:
Wenxuan Du, Abdul Pitafi, and Sobia Asher study how work social media shapes new ideas in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Tools like internal social networks may help staff cope with doubt and think in fresh ways. The authors asked which features of such tools matter. They name four: whether work can be seen by others, whether people can link up, whether posts can be edited, and whether posts stay up over time.

Survey data came from three hundred ninety-one staff who use these tools at work. Seeing others' work and linking up fed a sense of meaning and of having resources at hand, but not a sense of safety. Posts staying up fed safety alone. Editing fed all three states. All three states, meaning, resources, and safety, in turn lifted creativity. The study maps which tool features spark the inner states that help staff create.
pmc-12752318:
Witdiawati Witdiawati, Kusman Ibrahim, and three co-authors map HIV programs reshaped to fit local culture. Their scoping review, from twenty twenty-five, searches three major databases. Drugs for HIV are widely available, yet social and cultural walls still block care. Generic programs often see low uptake in minority and youth groups.

Eligible studies tailor programs with local stakeholder input. Language, values, and norms count as cultural ingredients. Settings span clinics and communities. The review follows standard scoping frameworks and reporting rules. It charts which adaptations were tried and where. The synthesis aims to guide programs that people actually use.
pmc-12755118:
Das and coauthors study tiny sacs shed by germs as drug carriers. Such sacs can carry drugs straight to sick cells. Most work so far used one broad germ class for sacs. Sacs from the other class stay far less explored.

The team used a milk germ known for safe use in food. They sought clean ways to pull its sacs out intact. They also mapped sac parts, size, and load skills. Gaps in yield and in sac checks have held back use. Full maps of sac traits could open new drug delivery routes.
pmc-12756918:
Karolina Cysneiros de Carvalho and four colleagues published an air quality study in two thousand twenty-five on the polluted Tijuana River. For a century the river has carried untreated sewage and industrial waste across the border. Its effect on air, not just water, had been overlooked.

Cheap sensor data showed gases rising from the river help form fine particles in the air. The smallest particles made up most of the fine particle mass, and levels rose when river flow ran high and air stayed still. Peaks clustered near a turbulent stretch of river, above all at night. The authors identify the river-to-air pathway as a hidden source of urban pollution with justice and health stakes.
pmc-12767218:
Lanxing Zhang and Fuxue Zhao published a student health study in two thousand twenty-five on what builds a healthy lifestyle in teenagers. Feelings skills, such as calming oneself and sensing others' moods, may shape daily habits. The pathways between them were murky.
