The team surveyed over one thousand one hundred adolescents with an average age near thirteen. Two analysis styles were combined. The first showed that emotion control, self-control, and empathy each fed body image, which then fed healthy habits. The second found several mixes of traits that all ended in strong healthy habits. Social media use strengthened the body image link rather than weakening it. The authors offer tips for families and schools.
pmc-12780218:
Nguyen Thanh Tam and colleagues published a 2025 review of fast-track drug approvals. The study covered a decade of United States approvals. Infectious disease drugs were the focus. Critics say they get less urgency than cancer drugs. The team compared development and review times across fields.

They examined nearly five hundred approved products. Records came from official drug and trial databases. Infectious products were compared with all others. Statistical tests measured delays and program use. The authors also built predictive models. Findings can guide fairer use of expedited pathways. Speed matters most when outbreaks will not wait.
pmc-12783618:
Maneli Ansari Mood wrote a solo study in two thousand twenty-five on treating a deadly cat disease with an antiviral drug. Feline infectious peritonitis is caused by a coronavirus and was long considered untreatable. The drug GS-441524 has changed that picture, though survival still depends on the form of the disease and its signs.

The study reviewed six hundred twenty-nine cats treated in Iran between late two thousand twenty and early two thousand twenty-four. Diagnosis rested on signs, lab tests, ultrasound, and response to treatment. The author tracked survival, hunted for factors that predict outcome, and followed lab and imaging changes to propose a safe protocol.
pmc-12784818:
Chen and co-authors review efforts to target support cells that surround prostate tumors. Advanced prostate cancer, in particular the castration-resistant form, remains hard to treat. The tumor setting shuts out immune attack and blunts therapy. Fibroblasts tied to the cancer shape talk between tumor and its support tissue. Yet these cells vary widely and shift form, which muddies sorting them. Wiping them out wholesale may fail or even backfire.

The review covers where these fibroblasts come from and what subtypes do. It tracks how they drive growth and drug resistance. New treatment angles that aim at fibroblasts get close attention. Careful targeting, not broad removal, is the theme.
pmc-12787818:
Hana Ivandic and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five study using machine learning to stratify sudden cardiac death risk. Implanted defibrillators prevent many such deaths, but picking who needs one relies on crude markers. Better prediction could target devices more fairly.

Patient records from a Croatian heart center combined clinical, laboratory, and device data. Several model types competed to predict device activation as a risk stand-in. Scoring favoured catching high-risk patients over avoiding false alarms. A forest model performed best. Explanation analysis confirmed known predictors and surfaced new candidates for doctors to weigh.
pmc-12803518:
HyungSub Jin, Ji-Won Kwon, and eight co-authors pool studies on ways to stop a spine surgery side effect. Their review, from twenty twenty-five, covers long spine fusions in adults with bent spines. The joint above the fusion can bend too far or fail, a pair of problems seen often after such surgery. Many tricks have been proposed to prevent them.

The team searched three databases through March of twenty twenty-five. Thirty-eight past studies entered the review. Methods under test include soft tethers, hooks, cement boosts, and rod choices. They also weigh where the top of the fusion should sit. Pooled odds give a clearer view of which tricks truly cut risk.
pmc-12804718:
Je Min Suh and eight co-authors study peak blood pressure in the first day after in-hospital cardiac arrest in the oldest ICU patients. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Patients aged ninety and up face high death rates after arrest, yet peak early pressure marks were not known. Data came from a two-land ICU base for more than two hundred such patients.

Death hit near three in five at one month and two in three at one year. Low peak marks tied to high death at both spans, with clear cut lines for each mark. Marks above those lines gave no extra shield. The team urges close early pressure watch and care in this frail group.
pmc-12817418:
Ullas Nayak and five co-authors set out a protocol for a review of work-related muscle and joint disorders in radiographers, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Imaging staff lift patients, repeat the same motions, and hold awkward postures, all of which strain the body. No pooled review of their burden yet exists.

The planned review will search six databases from their start to mid twenty twenty-five. Study quality will be graded with standard checklists for this kind of evidence. Prevalence and risk factors will be pooled with care for differences between studies. The authors expect the results to guide safer equipment, training, and workplace health programs for imaging staff.
pmc-12824518:
Hui Zhang and six co-authors charted a rodent-borne fever illness in Weifang, China, across the years twenty thirteen to twenty twenty-one, in a study from twenty twenty-five. The illness, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, harms the kidneys. Weifang logged two thousand one hundred eighteen cases in the span. The team linked case counts to weather, farm, and economic data, then built models to call future risk.

Cases followed a clear seasonal rhythm. Heat, air pressure, crop area, and output all tracked case counts closely. Two rodent species took turns as the main reservoir across the span. Rodent density showed a U-shaped link to cases, while heat showed a peak near a set threshold. Climate acted both directly and through rodent numbers. A Bayesian time-series model forecast case trends well, and the authors say such forecasts can sharpen local prevention work.
pmc-12827118:
Yu, Cheng, and Zhang present a trial from twenty twenty-five on a new teaching model for anesthesia residents. Sixty residents split evenly into new-model and traditional groups. The new model blends online and offline teaching with mind mapping. It is guided by outcome-based education goals. Theory and hands-on scores both run higher in the new-model group. Trainee satisfaction rises across teamwork, communication, and clinical thinking. Instructor ratings also favor the new-model residents.

Self-directed learning improves on every measured dimension. The authors credit the blend of structure, visuals, and mixed delivery. They recommend the model for standardized residency training. The trial offers a template for other specialty programs.
pmc-12835018:
Jinxin Zhang and five co-authors study how blockchain use relates to how concentrated a firm's supply chain is. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five, using data on one hundred and forty-seven Chinese firms that adopted blockchain between twenty nineteen and twenty twenty-three.

Supply chain concentration has two sides: reliance on few suppliers and reliance on few customers. Standard regression showed blockchain mattered for both. Spending on research, years listed, and industry type strengthened the link. A set-based method then showed no single factor alone produced high concentration. Instead, firms reached it through blends of blockchain with those other traits. The work maps several roads to the same outcome, a question past studies had not taken up.
pmc-12837218:
Fahimeh Ahmadi leads a team of eight authors engineering a smart tube to guide severed peripheral nerves back together. Their conduit electrospins a polyester mesh laced with carbon nanotubes for strength and conductivity, plus a green-tea antioxidant with anti-inflammatory effects, then fills the tube with collagen gel. Stem cell tests checked the scaffold's hospitality in the dish; in animals, severed sciatic nerves were bridged and recovery tracked.

Function was measured by walking indices and muscle electrical signals. Twelve weeks after injury, microscopy, MRI, tissue counts, and gene expression showed significant rises in neuronal markers and Schwann cell markers in the regenerated nerves. The multi-material design attacks regeneration from mechanical, electrical, and biochemical angles at once.
pmc-12844818:
Nichole Cufino, Tania Flink, and Carlos Lamoutte report a severe pregnancy hypertension case complicated by hearing voices, in a case study from twenty twenty-five. A forty-one-year-old woman with bipolar disorder and no prenatal care arrived in hypertensive crisis, with headaches and vision changes of four days. Tests showed heavy protein in her urine and failing kidneys.

An urgent cesarean followed. Her pressure stayed high afterward, and she reported auditory hallucinations, heavy urination, blurred sight, and vomiting. Brain imaging revealed an atypical swelling pattern centered on the brainstem and memory regions. A second crisis on day four was controlled with medication. The authors stress close monitoring and prenatal care for patients with bipolar disorder, and probe the link between the untreated illness and the hallucinations.
pmc-12846118:
Rasha Alharthi and seven colleagues map how parts of the amygdala connect to big brain networks in schizophrenia, in a twenty twenty-five study. The amygdala, the brain's alarm center, has distinct parts with distinct jobs. The team took resting brain scans from fifty patients and fifty healthy peers. They measured links between three amygdala parts and the main brain networks.

Patients showed stronger links from one amygdala part to the daydream and visual networks. They showed weaker links from another part to the movement network. The authors say the amygdala should be studied part by part, not as one lump, to grasp the illness.
pmc-12848118:
Lim and coauthors design a control motif that holds cell output steady and quiet. Steady output after a shock is a prized trait in living systems. A known feedback loop can hold the average output steady. That loop, though, makes single-cell output more noisy.

Their new motif senses output through pairing of output parts. Paired with the known loop, it holds noise in check too. Mean and noise both stayed near start levels after shocks. That gives true steady control at the single-cell scale. Tests in model systems backed the design in full. The motif may guide synthetic cell control work.
pmc-12853918:
Cornelia Wähner led a large team surveying men who have sex with men in Germany in a 2025 study. This group faces high rates of HPV infection, which can lead to several cancers. Adult men in this group are not covered by the national vaccine advice, unlike children. The team asked what they know and whether they accept the vaccine.

Over nine hundred men at ten clinics took an electronic survey. Most had heard of the virus, and about two thirds knew a vaccine exists. Among those aware, most were vaccinated or planned to be, but many hesitated for lack of information. Cost and missing doctor advice were the main blocks.
pmc-12855918:
Long Chen and colleagues made nickel nanosheets for acetone conversion in 2025. Turning acetone into alcohols adds value. Heat-based methods dominate that conversion now. Electric methods offer a cleaner alternative. Noble metals work but cost too much. Nickel sheets with unusual structure were tested.

The sheets held a metastable hexagonal phase. Nearly all acetone converted under current. The alcohol product was perfectly selective. Scale-up tests kept performance high. Production rates impressed at strong current. Other carbonyl compounds also converted well. Strong binding helped the reaction start. Easy product release finished it cleanly.
pmc-12860118:
Jiayin Qin and colleagues assess a combined eye surgery for acute angle-closure glaucoma in a prospective study published in 2025. The operation joins pupil reconstruction with cataract removal and lens implantation.

Patients had experienced a first acute attack and could not recover pupil function with medication or laser treatment. Imaging measured anterior chamber angle parameters before and after surgery. Average follow-up exceeded twelve months. Eye pressure fell after surgery, visual acuity improved by one year, and fewer pressure-lowering drugs were needed. Corneal cell counts stayed comparable, pupil diameter shrank, and chamber depth and volume increased. The authors evaluate both efficacy and safety indicators.
pmc-12896118:
Caihong Liu and co-authors give a set review of nafamostat mesilate, used to stop blood from clotting while blood is cleaned. Their 2025 meta-analysis sets it next to heparin, next to citrate, and next to plans that use no drug to stop clotting.

Sixteen studies took part, with over four thousand people in all. They covered renal replacement therapy and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Nafamostat showed a risk of bleeding that was far lower than the drugs it was set next to. Its risk ratio was close to one half. How long filters lasted, and other results, were also set side by side. Checks were split by the type of drug and by the way the blood was cleaned. The team gauged the quality of the studies, how firm the results were, and bias in which studies came out.
pmc-12961018:
Jessica Blank and four colleagues describe a hands-on procedure rotation for medical students, in a twenty twenty-five paper. Such rotations exist for residents but rarely for students. The multi-week elective mixed online study with supervised practice on real patients. Students took knowledge tests and surveys before and after, rating their case volume, confidence, and satisfaction.

Each student performed about eighteen procedures, most often draining belly fluid, with no major mishaps. Knowledge scores jumped from about sixty-six to eighty-seven percent. Confidence and satisfaction rose clearly as well. The authors argue early hands-on training, long thought a resident perk, safely belongs in student years too.
pmc-12993618:
A team including Yugandhar Reddy and Nagasuma Chandra profiles the skin germs of people with melasma, a condition of dark facial patches, in a twenty twenty-five study. Skin hosts a vast community of microbes that shifts in disease. Early proof hints these germs play a part in pigment problems, but melasma itself was little studied. The team compared germs on dark patches with those on nearby normal skin.

The patches showed clear changes in stress, swelling, and barrier measures in skin tests. Sequencing found less germ variety on patches and fewer links between germ types. Hundreds of germ groups were shared, while a few appeared on only one side. Germ shifts also tracked with skin measures. The work maps how the skin community changes in melasma.
pmc-13085918:
James Roll and Craig Zirbel present a tool that spots known three-dimensional shapes inside RNA sequences, in this paper from twenty twenty-six. Many working RNAs never code for protein; their jobs depend on how they fold. Loops in the fold often reuse a small set of proven shapes, called motifs, such as kink turns and T-loops.

Their program, JAR3D, compares the letters of a loop against a library of known motif shapes and reports the best matches. For this work they extended it to loops where three or four strands meet. They ran it over more than four thousand families in the Rfam database and posted the results on a public web page. Test cases outside the training set came out right. Internal loops matched known shapes far more often than hairpin loops or junctions, a pattern that tells its own story about RNA design.
pmc-13086918:
Jing Wei and eight co-authors model how a university handles a public health emergency, using game theory, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. A crisis like the COVID-19 pandemic forces choices by campus departments, students, and public opinion channels. Each side acts with partial facts and its own aims. The team built a three-sided game and ran it in simulation software.

Fair fines from government pushed departments to share facts on time. Lower costs for student complaints changed how media channels checked claims. Students' hopeful bias also shaped every side's choices. The authors advise joint governance, stronger response plans, and clearer talk between all sides. The work gives campus leaders a tested frame for the next crisis.
pmc-13132218:
Yalda Hashempour and nine co-authors watch wrapped virus stay in hospital air, surfaces, and waste water. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Such viruses, like SARS-CoV-2, can last in rooms and drains and threat ward safety. Past work was summed, plus a case run in two north Iran wards.

More than two hundred swabs from COVID wards were gene-probed. Waste water hit the top find rate, past six in ten, with air and surfaces near one fourth each. Gene finds do not prove live germs, the team note. Yet they flag spread paths that need wash and air care. Joint watch plans are urged.
pmc-13132918:
Dragan Petrovic, Friederike Schrade, Stephan Bosch, and Harald Kunstmann test whether a region can go carbon-neutral on local renewables in this two thousand twenty-six modeling study. Germany targets climate neutrality by twenty forty-five, demanding wind and solar expansion. Using GIS mapping with a siting algorithm, the authors simulated renewable growth in the Cologne planning region. Scenarios varied land-use regulation, drawing on population, carbon budgets, and electricity demand through twenty forty-five.

The verdict is stark: climate-neutral electricity cannot be achieved under the planning framework, because too little land is available. Even with flexible rules and higher-efficiency turbines, land stayed scarce. Only a modeled fifty percent cut in energy demand made the targets attainable. Every scenario reshaped the landscape. The authors see room to raise the renewable share through targeted measures, and validate their GIS-plus-siting method for regional planning.
pmc-13136518:
Muneezah Elahi and six co-authors test a natural antioxidant, carnosine, against stress-hormone damage to mood and memory in rats. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. The hormone corticosterone drives oxidative stress, a path into depression-like states.

Thirty-six female rats were split into six groups crossing hormone and two carnosine doses, all injected for two weeks. Behavior was read with a despair test and a water maze for spatial memory. Carnosine softened the hormone's harm on both behavior fronts. The team also measured oxidative damage, defense enzymes, inflammation marks, serotonin chemistry, and tissue slides. The dipeptide, made in the body from two amino acids, is a candidate shield for stress-driven brain harm.
pmc-13139918:
Marchi and a large team reviewed in twenty twenty-six how smart tools and scan traits can help spot lung harm caused by drugs. Such harm is hard to name, since its signs mimic other lung ills and germs. Late finds can let the harm grow grave in sick folks on strong drugs.

Scan trait tools pull rich counts from chest scans that the eye can not see. In drug-harm cases they may split like forms and guess if scar growth will come. Smart nets add skill at form finds and risk sorts. Wide use needs shared scan rules and large checks in many sites, they warn.
pmc-13143518:
Kusumawati and co-authors build a delivery system for black sticky rice extract and track where it goes in the body. The extract is rich in plant compounds with antioxidant and liver-protecting effects. Poor water solubility and weak stability keep its absorption low, though. The team packed the extract into a self-emulsifying system of corn oil, Tween 80, and propylene glycol. A dye label let them image the system in living animals.

The liquid mix was then dried onto a solid carrier to make a powder form. Tests checked flow, density, and moisture for handling and shelf life. Imaging in animals mapped how the dose spread through organs. The goal is better liver targeting from an oral dose.
pmc-13150818:
Julia Im leads a 2026 study of why binder glue lowers supercapacitor performance. How the binder affects the pores that store charge was unclear, so several measurement methods were combined.

More binder meant lower charge storage per gram. Gas and magnetic resonance tests showed the binder creeping into the carbon's tiny pores, shrinking pore space and blocking sodium ions from entering. A dry processing alternative reduced pore intrusion but left excess binder in gaps, which also hurt performance in water-based systems. Better formulations must keep binder out of the pores, the authors argue.
pmc-13161818:
Tania Lincoln and co-authors published a 2026 review of why delusions, fixed false beliefs, stay in place once they form. Such beliefs are defined by how hard they are to shift with evidence against them. Most earlier models look at how delusions start, not at how they persist.

The team searched the field for models of that persistence and found seventy-four. They fall into six groups, from probability-based reasoning to social life. Most groups agree on two points. Behavior that avoids clashing with the belief is rewarded, which reinforces the belief. And the belief, once formed, bends how new information is processed. The combined view, they say, tells a much fuller story of persistence than any single group.
pmc-13164618:
Chen and co-authors test phillygenin, a plant compound from Forsythia, against kidney damage in mice. The compound had shown promise in colon, lung, and diabetes studies. Chronic kidney disease brings high illness and death rates, so new options matter.

Mice with a blocked ureter got 50 milligrams per kilogram each day for fourteen days. Treated mice showed less collagen buildup and less matrix buildup in the kidney. Stress-response proteins shifted as well. In lab cells, the team triggered a fiery cell death called pyroptosis. The work probes which signals the compound calms.
pmc-13171318:
Emmanouil Karofylakis and nine colleagues track how the COVID virus evolves inside patients whose immune systems are weakened by treatment, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Such patients can carry the virus for long stretches, letting it change. The team followed twenty-six patients with rheumatic or blood diseases on strong immune-suppressing care. Virus gene reads came from airway samples over time.

Most patients were hospitalized and some died. Rare mutations appeared in the virus's copying genes and in its spike. In patients with paired samples, small variants piled up at a steady rate. The build-up rate did not differ between the two disease groups. The authors warn these hidden changes could seed escape variants.
pmc-13171818:
Oskar Pasek and a team of co-authors survey COVID-19 vaccination among Ukrainian refugees in Poland, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Their poll ran at a refugee center in Zielona Góra in twenty twenty-three. A total of 837 people took part, with a response rate above eighty percent.

Under a fifth had finished the full vaccine course. Guarding their own health was the top stated reason for getting shots. Past infection and yearly flu shots tied strongly to uptake. So did coming from a larger Ukrainian city. The authors urge focused outreach for this group.
pmc-13172118:
Steffen Brenner, Achim Schilling, Patrick Krauss, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It is an early test of whether a spinal cord stimulator that eases chronic pain also changes activity higher up in the brain.

Eleven patients with chronic back or leg pain took part. Each had a BurstDR stimulator, a device that sends pulses to the spinal cord. After three months, pain scores fell sharply, and sleep, mood, and daily function all improved. Brain scans taken while patients moved a foot showed activity in the expected motor area. No broad brain-wide change passed the study's strict cutoff. The authors treat the work as a first step toward tracking how spinal stimulation reshapes the brain's pain networks.
pmc-13176318:
Video games reach more than three point six billion people and have become a major place where people meet, team up, and form ties. Exclusion ran through how characters are shown, how communities treat members, and how the industry is set up. The team gathers the fixes already tried by developers, organizers, and rule-makers into one framework, and adds fresh ones. They argue researchers can help by joining sectors, testing what works, and spreading know-how.
pmc-13179318:
Sabry Fayed, Ali Basha, and Amira Elnagar compare how world building codes handle shear in slim concrete beams, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Slim beams save material while keeping buildings safe, but they can fail by shear, a sliding break. Each major code treats that risk in its own way. The team lined up six codes from Egypt, America, Europe, Canada, Britain, and Japan.

They compared how each code sets shear capacity, the least steel required, and service limits. The codes agreed on some points and split on others, with gaps that affect safety and cost. The authors offer steps toward a shared world approach so engineers can design slim beams with more trust.
pmc-13179918:
Emlik and colleagues report in twenty twenty-six a case of blood in the urine in a young Holstein cow in Türkiye, tied to a blood parasite. These parasites spread by insect bites and can cause real illness in cattle. The cow showed yellow skin and low red blood counts, along with the dark urine that named her problem.

Blood checks, microscope work, and gene tests confirmed the parasite as the cause. She was treated with fluids, an antibiotic, and drugs for blood loss. She died a month later, reportedly from a chest infection. The authors set out the test steps in full and call for a wide survey of this parasite in cattle. Its spread and harm are still poorly mapped.
pmc-13180618:
Chisato Umeda and six colleagues report a new disease-causing variant in a twelve-year-old Japanese girl with a rare inherited diabetes. The defect worked through simple insufficiency, since one working copy was not enough, rather than poisoning the normal protein. The twenty twenty-six case links this binding domain to the syndrome's multisystem features and widens the catalog of MODY5 mutations.
pmc-13183718:
Sean Thomas and colleagues study how a growth signal primes lung defense cells, in this paper from twenty twenty-six. pmc-13184518:

pmc-13193718:

pmc-13193918:

Over one hundred twenty webs were analyzed. Symptomatic and incidental cases were compared. Scans supplied angle, pocket, and length measures. A simple score was built from the strongest features. Discrimination testing checked its accuracy. A validated score could guide monitoring of harmless-looking webs. Surgery decisions might also become more consistent.
pmc-13195718:
Audrey Huili Lim is first author on a 2026 analysis of national antibiotic use in Malaysia from twenty nineteen to twenty twenty-three. Tracking national use helps target stewardship, efforts to use antibiotics wisely, amid resistance concerns. Two thirds of use came from primary care, and private sector use exceeded public sector use in both clinics and hospitals. Overall use and spending were broadly flat over the period. Access antibiotics, the preferred first-line group, made up fifty-six percent of use, short of the sixty percent world target, with the weakest share in private hospitals. Stewardship should target those settings, the authors say.
pmc-13197718:
Thierry Schweizer, Dariush Nikkhah, and Shadi Ghali report a breast rebuild done across the chest. Their case report, from twenty twenty-six, follows a failed first rebuild. The first flap, taken from the belly, did not survive. Radiation had also blocked the blood vessels on the same side of the chest.

The team took a flap from the thigh, fed by a deep artery branch. Its long stalk let them tunnel it across the breastbone. They joined it to vessels on the other side of the chest. A dye test showed good blood flow through the flap. The patient healed well and the rebuilt breast held a pleasing shape.
pmc-13198518:
Elisa Balboni and colleagues improve a device for transplanting insulin-making cells under the skin in a 2026 study. Islet transplantation can treat type 1 diabetes, where the body cannot make insulin. Skin sites are safer and easier to reach than the liver route, but poor blood supply kills many grafted cells.

Their device first grows a vessel-rich pocket under the skin. A printed placeholder now holds a defined cavity open during that growth phase. Removing it leaves a shaped space, so islets spread evenly instead of clumping. Results fit with kept blood supply, better spread, less inflammation, and supported cell function versus injection delivery. Spatial control may lift graft success.
pmc-13198718:
Songming Ding and colleagues present a 2026 case report on bleeding into the bile duct found during an emergency scope. Hemobilia means bleeding from the bile tree into the gut. It is rare and can be deadly, and blood-thinning drugs raise the risk, yet drug-linked cases are seldom reported.

Their patient was a 73-year-old woman with past bile duct work and long aspirin use. She had bile duct infection from stones. A planned scope after a week off aspirin became an emergency when severe belly pain struck. The scope found clots blocking the duct opening. Clearing clots, removing stones, and placing a drain settled her without vessel or open surgery.
pmc-13199618:
Shen, Qiu, and Sun analyzed the concept of psychological birth trauma in couples in twenty twenty-six. Birth trauma is usually studied in mothers alone. This analysis asks what the concept means when partners are included, to guide clinical practice.

Searching nine databases, they gathered twenty-eight papers from twenty twenty-one to twenty twenty-four. Core features of the concept were partners' subjective feelings and avoidance behavior, spanning labor through the period after birth. Causes grouped into personal, birth-related, medical, and interpersonal factors. Effects reached mental health, family relationships, and plans for another pregnancy. The authors argue trauma care must cover both parents, backed by social support, mental health services, and medical systems working together.
pmc-13199818:
Christopher Ruggiero and colleagues report an unusual prostate cancer spread pattern on a specialised scan. Their case from twenty twenty-six involves a man with returning cancer. A radioactive tracer scan lights up prostate cancer cells clearly. It found a single groin lymph node carrying the disease.

The cancer had reached rectal tissue, an uncommon finding. That involvement may explain the odd groin node route. Prior pelvic radiation could have opened a fistula path between organs. The node was the only distant site the scan detected. Standard staging might have missed this atypical spread entirely. The authors stress tracer scans in recurrent prostate cancer workups.
pmc-13200318:
Benedikt Wynands and colleagues engineered a bacterium to make a chemical building block from plant sugars in a 2026 study. Aromatics feed polymers, drugs, and materials but now come from oil. Adding a gene from a cyanobacterium sped the key step, and deleting one gene raised output further. New uptake pathways let the strain eat xylose and arabinose, sugars common in plant waste. Guided evolution and gene edits tuned those pathways. Final yields on the plant sugars beat those on glucose. Mixed-sugar tests mimicking plant waste confirmed the gain over the parent strain.
pmc-13204318:
Ten authors present a study dated two thousand twenty-six on a molecule that helps switch inflammation off. Resolvin D1 is made by the body to resolve inflammation rather than merely block it. The team tested it on human monocytes, immune cells provoked by a bacterial toxin.

Cells were treated with the toxin, the resolvin, or a control for a day. The resolvin lowered two inflammatory signals the toxin raised. Gene-readout scans found wide expression changes, and the resolvin boosted genes tied to antioxidant defense and cell survival. Two classic inflammatory pathways were checked to pin down the mechanism.
pmc-13205118:
Dhika Dharmansyah and co-authors scope the tools used to judge fall risk in older adults across Southeast Asia, and ask if those tools fit local life. Falls are the second cause of death from unintentional injury round the world, and the burden sits heaviest in poorer countries. Checking fall risk is core to prevention. But most check tools were built in the West, and it is unclear which are used, or even valid, in the 11 ASEAN nations.

The review followed standard scoping rules and searched three big databases. It mapped which tools appear in studies from the region and how they are used in clinics. It also weighed how local customs and daily habits shape fall risk in ways imported tools may miss. The aim is practical: screening in the region should measure the risks older people there in fact face.
pmc-13205418:
Mikayla Foley and six co-authors describe a five-year path to a rare diagnosis in this twenty twenty-six case paper. The disease harms small vessels in the brain and eyes, leaving calcium deposits and cysts. It is passed down in families and stems from a fault in a gene that guards chromosome ends.

The patient had a large cyst in the brain that looked strongly like a tumor. Several operations gave tissue samples that settled nothing. Only after five years, and with several specialists working together, was the true disease named. The paper also shares detailed eye scans from a strong magnet scanner, a rare record for this condition.
pmc-13207118:
Gregorio Benites-Narcizo and seven co-authors review a glow-based eye scan as a sign of cell health in eye disease. The scan reads light from proteins in the retina's power plants. When those fail, sight diseases often follow. The team gathered seventeen studies covering more than nineteen hundred eyes, mostly one-time snapshots.

Healthy eyes showed a base glow level. Glow ran higher in diabetes, in a wet form of age-related sight loss, and in an inherited retinal disease. Yet some studies found low or mixed results for the same diseases. Differing methods made studies hard to compare. The review calls for shared standards before the scan guides care.
pmc-13210318:
Logins could adapt their strictness to risk, and a 2026 study authored by K Sasikumar assembles a hybrid machine learning framework for that judgment. The proposed system scores account takeover risk from login behavior, device traits, and network signals, then maps the score to allow, challenge, or deny decisions.

An ensemble of three classifiers estimates compromise probability, while clustering seeds risk bands and a fuzzy logic layer smooths the thresholds between them. An optimization routine fine-tunes those fuzzy boundaries for consistency across the experiments reported. The authors report accuracy above ninety-seven percent on their test data and use an explanation technique to keep each decision interpretable for security teams.
pmc-13212718:
Chen Wu and co-authors present in 2026 a tiny pump for moving fluids inside lab-on-a-chip devices, driven by ultrasound rather than moving parts. The pump uses membranes made from scandium-doped aluminium nitride, a material compatible with standard chip manufacture.

Three electrical signals, each offset in phase, drive neighbouring membranes so sound pushes liquid in one direction along a soft polymer channel. The working area measures barely more than a millimetre across, and measured flow matched computer simulations. Modelling further suggests design tweaks could raise flow roughly eightfold. A pump this small suits portable analysis systems that need precise control of very small liquid volumes.
pmc-13213018:
Hyunsue Do and co-authors build in 2026 a simple score to predict kidney failure in Korean patients with a vessel-inflaming autoimmune disease. In this condition, called ANCA-associated vasculitis, kidney damage can progress quietly to the point where dialysis or transplant becomes necessary.

Working from 239 patients at one large hospital, the team found two baseline measures that independently predicted progression. Their index gives one point for each measure falling in its worst third, using a severity score and a blood kidney marker. Patients scoring two fared far worse than those scoring zero or one. A two-item score is easy to use at the bedside, though wider testing is still needed.
pmc-13213118:
Seyed Reza Hosseini and colleagues test in 2026 whether injecting botulinum toxin under the skin near the tip of the penis can delay ejaculation, a common and distressing male sexual problem. The toxin dulls nerve signalling, and the chosen site is rich in sensation.

Seven men with lifelong early ejaculation received a single injection and completed standard questionnaires before treatment and at one and six months afterwards. Scores for control, erection, and satisfaction barely moved at either check. No side effects appeared, so the approach proved safe but ineffective in this small group. Dulling sensation alone, the authors conclude, does not fix the reflex behind the condition.
pmc-13215118:
Keiran Mc Carogher and colleagues build in 2026 a sound-based platform for making polymer nanoparticles to order. Ultrasound shakes a liquid into fine droplets that harden into particles, and the team wanted rules that predict the final size instead of trial and error.

Two knobs controlled the outcome: the sound frequency and the polymer concentration. Lower frequencies made bigger cavitation bubbles that burst harder, yielding smaller droplets, while concentration fine-tuned the dried particle size. Particles spanned roughly fifty to one hundred eighty nanometres across settings. Because droplet size at a given frequency ignored concentration, a simple mass balance predicts the recipe for any target size, turning an art into a calculation.
pmc-13215518:
Béatrice Parguel and co-authors published a 2026 study on what happens when women researchers get more media visibility in management science. Women still receive less coverage than men, and the authors test how audiences react when that balance shifts.

Two laboratory experiments, one with 271 members of the public and one with 129 graduate students, varied how many women appeared in a mock science newsletter. Greater visibility narrowed the gender gap in confidence for both groups and raised women's perceived expertise among the public. Among male graduate students, though, academic careers looked less attractive. The authors draw lessons for universities and media outlets that promote research.
pmc-13216618:
Julio E. Villalón-Reina and co-authors present a 2026 brain imaging resource: the first lifespan reference charts for the microstructure of the brain's white matter. Doctors can chart a child's height against population norms; this work aims to give brain scans the same kind of yardstick.

Nineteen international diffusion MRI datasets, totalling 54,583 people aged four to ninety-one, were processed through one standardized pipeline. Hierarchical Bayesian models then produced age and sex centile curves for white matter measures in each region. The charts were road-tested by mapping deviations in mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease, and a genetic syndrome that raises schizophrenia risk. The models are released openly for the research community to extend.
pmc-13218618:
Kneeland and a team including Torrico Villanueva, Chen, and Ojeda build a method that draws mental images from brain scans in this twenty twenty-six paper. Models that rebuild seen images from brain waves must also work on images a person only holds in mind. The team first checked how well known models make that jump on a fresh data set.

Inside, some known models did well on mental images and some failed, and top scores on seen images gave no sure sign of top scores on mind images. Their new method pairs a simple core with text and image traits fed to an image maker. Human judges and scores rate it as the best yet on the test set used.
pmc-13218718:
Heyel Sodhi-Kalra and colleagues audit a cleared AI tool for lung nodules against radiologists' reports in a 2026 real-world study. More than a thousand AI products hold clearance, yet few work in clinics, partly from doubts about performance. Errors in counting or classifying nodules can push patients toward needless follow-up or, worse, miss a cancer.

The team took 650 noncontrast chest CT scans from adults, all processed by an FDA-cleared tool that detects, locates, and measures lung nodules. They set its output beside the reports of eighteen subspecialty radiologists. Their finding is frequent discordance between software and radiologists on nodule assessment. Because the tool was deployed, the study measures performance where it matters, in the flow of routine care rather than in a test set. The authors argue such real-world checks should accompany adoption of AI, since clearance testing alone does not guarantee agreement with radiologists.
pmc-13219918:
Nupur Gupta and colleagues add a home dialysis counselling station to the simulated exams used to train kidney specialists, in a 2026 letter. Home hemodialysis is uncommon in the United States, so trainee nephrologists may rarely see it and hesitate to offer it to patients. A practice conversation with a standardized patient lets fellows rehearse that counselling without risk.

Nineteen fellows from four programs, split between first and second years, each ran a consultation. The standardized patient scored their communication on a global scale, while faculty graded dialysis-specific skills with an exercise. No fellow scored unsatisfactorily, and first- and second-year fellows performed alike, even though only one program ran a home dialysis clinic. In the survey, six of seven responding fellows said the simulation increased their comfort in discussing home dialysis with a patient. The authors present the scenario as a low-risk addition to fellowship training.
pmc-13220218:
Animasahun and colleagues assess nutrition in children with heart disease seen at a major hospital clinic in Lagos, Nigeria. Malnutrition is a well-known partner of childhood heart disease. Hearts that work harder burn more energy, feeding is often difficult, and repeated illness steals appetite and growth at the same time.

Poor nutrition then feeds back into worse outcomes: weaker immunity, more infections, and higher risk around surgery. By measuring how common and how deep malnutrition is in this clinic group, the study gives local teams a baseline for action. Screening at every visit, the authors imply, should be routine care, not an extra.
pmc-13221118:
Shiru Yuan and colleagues built a two-stage CRISPR screening system in living mice, reported in 2026, to find genes governing long-term blood stem cells. Single screens can miss how clones evolve over months. Their platform recovered guide RNAs after five months, then used pooled secondary transplants to watch clonal competition unfold.

One hit dominated: loss of Nf1, a known tumor suppressor gene. The first screen reproduced a state of excess blood cell production. After secondary transplant, that state advanced toward malignant blood disease. The design lets researchers follow the step from healthy stem cell function to cancer in one system, useful for studying leukemia origins.
pmc-13222218:
Bradley J Lauck and co-authors test whether extra oral antibiotics after outpatient shoulder replacement prevent joint infection, in a 2026 matched cohort analysis. Outpatient surgery cuts the chance to give a full day of intravenous antibiotics, so extended pills became common despite thin evidence. A large health database supplied primary outpatient cases from 2015 to 2025.

Matching produced two groups of 2,647 patients each, with and without extended prophylaxis. Infection rates around the joint and wound were low and statistically similar at ninety days and at one year. Revision, wound problems, and emergency visits also matched. Extended antibiotics, the authors conclude, did not reduce infection outcomes here.
pmc-13222618:
Junfei Guo and co-authors review how to protect recovery quality when hip replacement patients go home the same day, in a 2026 narrative review. Enhanced recovery protocols, better anesthesia, and payment changes are pushing total hip arthroplasty toward same-day discharge worldwide. Early recovery quality spans pain control, function, stability, and patient-reported well-being.

The review walks through patient selection, perioperative care plans, anesthetic and pain strategies, blood management, complication prevention, and early rehabilitation. Policy and payment rules get a section as well. The authors propose a patient-focused improvement pathway that treats speed of getting back independence as the defining endpoint. Done well, same-day discharge saves beds and staff time without trading away safety.
pmc-13224018:
Dilixiati Duolikun and colleagues report a 2026 materials study aimed at healing bone defects in diabetes, where lingering inflammation slows repair. A key problem is that macrophages, the immune cells that clear dead cells, perform that cleanup poorly in diabetic tissue. The team built a gel with zinc oxide grains that generate small electric signals under ultrasound.

In diabetic-like settings, sound-driven signals switched on a sensor protein called Piezo1 and restored the cleanup work of macrophages. Swelling eased, bone-forming action rose, and bone-destroying cell growth fell. In rats with thigh-bone defects, the gel plus ultrasound sped up repair and increased collagen and bone markers.
pmc-13227818:
Mitiku Desalegn and colleagues survey a 2026 cross-sectional study of abuse during childbirth in public hospitals in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Staff asked 409 mothers who gave birth in four hospitals picked at random during November 2024 about their labour and delivery care. The study sorted experiences into forms of obstetric violence, from care given without consent to physical abuse.

Three quarters of mothers described at least one form of mistreatment. Care without consent was the most common complaint, followed by breaches of privacy and physical abuse affecting about forty percent. Induced labour more than tripled the odds of reporting violence, while caesarean delivery was linked to lower odds. The authors tie respectful maternity care directly to safer outcomes for mothers and babies.
pmc-13229218:
Jillian M. Silva and colleagues report a 2026 molecular study of neurofibromin, the protein lost in neurofibromatosis type 1, and its partner proteins SPRED1 and SPRED2. Neurofibromin is famous for switching off the growth signal RAS, yet that activity occupies only a small part of the large protein. Gene-signature analysis showed the partners jointly control programmes linked to a shift in cell type that matters in development and cancer.

Surprisingly, those shared outputs did not depend on extra RAS activation or on sustained firing of the MAPK cascade downstream. They did depend on neurofibromin's RAS-switching domain itself. The complex therefore produces noncanonical outputs that are GAP-dependent yet MAPK-independent, widening what this tumour-suppressor partnership is understood to do.
pmc-13232818:
Maja Hemberg and colleagues test in 2026 whether a signaling hub called MAVS is truly required for airway defense against flu in human tissue. Two virus sensors in airway cells pass their alarm through MAVS to trigger interferon, the early antiviral signal. Gene editing removed MAVS from donated human airway cells grown at an air surface, a close stand-in for the real lining.

Without MAVS, infected cultures failed to raise either major interferon family and missed the follow-on protective gene wave. Virus copies also grew higher, showing the hub does real defensive work rather than serving as backup. Mouse and cell-line hints now have direct proof in primary human tissue. Strengthening this alarm path could inspire flu drugs that work at the entry point.
pmc-13232918:
Peter von Dadelszen leads the author group behind a 2026 secondary analysis of blood pressure measurement in pregnancy. Accurate readings matter because high blood pressure in pregnancy can signal preeclampsia, a dangerous condition. The researchers asked whether human habits still distort readings taken with digital devices, through habits like rounding numbers or avoiding values just above a treatment threshold.

They pooled readings from the CLIP trials in India, Mozambique, Nigeria, and Pakistan and the PRECISE cohorts in the Gambia, Kenya, and Mozambique. Trained staff used two low-cost Microlife devices and entered readings by hand into a digital platform. The analysis compares repeated readings to check for digit preference and threshold avoidance. Results give trainers evidence on where measurement coaching still needs attention.
pmc-13233518:
Nawaf Salah Ayad Mohamed and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a blood filter left in the body for nine years. Inferior vena cava filters catch clots traveling toward the lungs and are meant to be removed once risk passes. A 61-year-old man came in with nerve-type back pain, and scans showed his old filter's legs had pierced in several directions.

Struts reached into a lumbar vertebra, soft tissue, bowel loops, the abdominal aorta, and the tissue holding the bowel, and one strut had broken. Earlier removal attempts had failed because the filter was tilted and its hook embedded, yet no bleeding had occurred. The authors referred him for specialist endovascular retrieval and stress structured follow-up so filters are removed on time.
pmc-13233718:
Mohamad Mourad, Layal Al Mahmasani, Noura Abbas, and Ali Shamseddine shared a review in twenty twenty-six. It asks why colorectal cancer immunotherapy works unevenly. The answer depends on where tumors spread. Before cancer cells arrive, tumors prepare target organs from afar. They turn them into welcoming niches. They use vesicles, cytokines, and adhesion molecules. Liver and lung niches turn out very different.

The liver niche is deeply tolerant. It is packed with suppressive myeloid cells and drained of T cells. Liver metastases resist checkpoint immunotherapy. The lung niche is more inflamed and reactive. Its metastases respond better, though neutrophils add some suppression. The authors argue that knowing each organ's niche is the route to organ-specific treatment strategies.
pmc-13236518:
Lydia González del Barrio and co-authors reviewed in 2026 immune cells called macrophages as targets for treating liver scarring. Fibrosis follows chronic liver injury and can end in organ failure. Macrophages sit at the centre of the scarred liver's environment, steering inflammation and repair. New research shows these cells take many more states than the classic two-type scheme suggested.

Liver scarring can reverse, and reversal tracks closely with macrophages shifting into restorative modes. Restorative cells clear dead material efficiently, quiet inflammatory signals, and break down scar matrix actively. Therapy design is moving away from simply blocking new immune cell arrivals toward reprogramming cells already in the liver. Cell-based treatments, where prepared macrophages are given to patients, are the newest direction discussed. The review maps opportunities and obstacles for each strategy in development.
pmc-13237818:
Alejandro Caballero, Thomas F. Allard, and Paloma A. Huidobro built a theory in 2026 for interface states in space-time photonic crystals, materials whose properties ripple through both space and time. Such moving modulations break the usual symmetries, which had blocked a clean topological account. The authors show a combined parity and time-reversal symmetry survives when the problem is viewed from a moving frame.

That symmetry forces a phase quantity to take discrete values, turning it into a true topological label for modulations slower or faster than light. The predicted boundary states show unusual tricks, including one-way amplification and copies of signals shifted in frequency and momentum. The scheme also covers photonic time crystals. It gives device makers a unified map for steering and boosting light.
pmc-13239618:
Faruk Tamtürk and team study freeze-drying of a nutrient-rich microalga in a 2026 food science paper. Chlorella vulgaris offers rich protein and pigments, yet it needs a shell of wall material to survive drying and storage. The team tried newer shell options next to standard ones.

Blends mixed the algae with maltodextrin, inulin, aquafaba from chickpea water, or stilled yeast cells, in varied shares. Tests covered moisture, protein, chlorophyll, carotenoids, colour, and how the powders wet and took up damp air. The maltodextrin share swayed particle size and clumping. The authors say aquafaba and yeast both show real promise as shell materials for algae goods.
pmc-13240018:
Nicoleta Balan and team mine red grape pomace, the skins and seeds left by winemaking, for health compounds in a 2026 study. With green solvents they drew out a mix rich in polyphenols. They then tested the mix against three enzymes tied to inflammation and metabolic syndrome.

Lab work named thirty-two compounds, most of them phenolic acids, with vanillic acid among the chief ones. Tests in the lab and on computers pointed to strong blocking of two starch-digesting enzymes, amylase and glucosidase, and of lipoxygenase, an inflammation enzyme. Docking work showed set compounds fitting the active sites of the enzymes. The authors present pomace as a rich source of natural blockers worth more work.
pmc-13240418:
Qingyun Chen and colleagues create stem cell lines from fetuses with an inherited blood disorder in a 2026 laboratory study. Intermediate alpha-thalassemia, also called hemoglobin H disease, varies greatly between patients, and living cell models carrying the exact gene deletions could reveal why.

Cells from amniotic fluid of six affected fetuses were reprogrammed into induced pluripotent stem cells using non-integrating carriers. Every line kept the fetus's thalassemia genotype, showed normal chromosomes, and displayed the standard markers of pluripotency. In mice the lines formed tumours containing all three basic tissue types, and in dishes they produced early blood-forming cells that grew into colonies. The lines are offered as a research resource.
pmc-13241418:
Mourits's team at UMC Utrecht checked two participation surveys for rehab patients across the country. 553 inpatients and outpatients filled in both scales again and again. One measures limits on taking part; the other, ability to join social roles. Steadiness over two weeks and change-spotting over six months were tested.

Both scales proved stable on retest and alert to change at group level. The limits scale responded better among inpatients than its rival. Key-change thresholds beat measurement noise for groups but rarely for one person. Mourits backs both for program checks, not personal goal tracking.
pmc-13241518:
Guo and co-workers at Xi'an Jiaotong University built a chip-scale sensor for measuring very strong magnetic fields. Tesla-range fields are hard to gauge because calibration drifts and responses bend. Their device packs cesium vapor into a tiny dual-chamber glass and silicon cell. Microheaters sit directly on the optical window.

Laser sidebands were aligned with split atomic lines of cesium under strong-field conditions. Sixteen transitions were resolved, letting the team read a field of about two-thirds of a tesla. Single measurements resolved a few microtesla, and repeat readings agreed within ten microtesla. The millimeter-scale sensor needs no uniform bias field, suiting compact quantum devices.
pmc-13242018:
Luanbiao Sun and co-authors present a 2026 review of nanomaterial strategies against antibiotic-resistant infections. Standard antibiotics fail in several hard settings: fast-spreading blood infections, germs hiding inside cells, and slimy biofilm communities on tissues or devices. Nanomaterials can attack through several routes at once.

The review organizes materials by the barrier they tackle, from first surface contact to biofilm growth and relapse. Functions include punching holes in bacterial membranes, draining their energy, breaking into biofilm matrix, and releasing drugs inside infected cells. Some materials kill directly, while others carry existing antibiotics or respond to triggers. The authors also weigh manufacturing consistency, safety of released particles, and regulatory steps needed before clinical use.
pmc-13242418:
Fabio Di Domenico and co-authors report what happened at the Trisomy 21 Research Society's fifth international conference. The meeting report appeared in Neuromolecular Medicine in 2026. Down syndrome, the most frequent genetic cause of intellectual disability, also brings a very high risk of early Alzheimer's disease. The society has linked researchers, doctors, families, and self-advocates since 2014.

The 2024 conference met in Rome and drew about five hundred scientists from twenty-six countries, with more than nine hundred attendees overall. Talks ranged from gene regulation and brain development to aging, medical conditions, and new therapies. Sixty fellowships supported young investigators, and childcare awards helped families take part. The proceedings show a field growing more global and more connected to the people it studies. They also mark ten years of the society.
pmc-13242518:
Laura Schwarzmann and colleagues tested whether artificial intelligence can infer the molecular subtype of endometrial cancer straight from stained tissue slides. Their study appeared in NPJ Precision Oncology in 2026. Endometrial cancers fall into four molecular groups that guide treatment, but testing is not always available. Using routine diagnostic slides of mixed quality from real practice, the team compared two foundation models that extract features from whole-slide images.

Performance varied sharply by subtype. The UNI model read the p53-abnormal group well but was much weaker on the other three, including the largest group. Results held up across different scanners, and stain correction shifted scores somewhat. Pathologists also interpreted which tissue patterns each model seemed to use. The authors frame the work as groundwork, not a finished test. It shows both the promise and the unevenness of slide-based subtyping outside clean research collections.
pmc-13242818:
Novi Irmala and co-authors offer a 2026 scoping review of non-drug interventions for symptom clusters in women with cancer. Fatigue, poor sleep, and psychological distress commonly arrive together, yet most programs chase single symptoms. The review mapped recent studies that target these problems in women.

Twenty-nine studies, mostly randomized trials, fell into five families: exercise, mind-body and relaxation methods, complementary therapies, psychosocial programs, and technology-based or nurse-led care. Exercise reliably eased fatigue, while mind-body work helped distress and sleep. Combined programs showed the broadest and most lasting gains across the cluster. Few studies, however, designed explicitly around symptom clusters. The authors call for integrated, mechanism-based models in women cancer care.
pmc-13245518:
An editorial in The Lancet Regional Health – Europe calls Eastern Europe's alcohol-related liver disease crisis preventable in 2026. The WHO European region drinks more than any other, and liver deaths run near 780 per day across it. Eastern Europe carries the heaviest share of that harm.

Liver damage from alcohol builds silently for years before it is found. Policy shapes the toll through prices, sales hours, advertising rules, and enforcement. Lithuania's reforms from 2016 to 2018 cut drinking and alcohol deaths steeply, and life expectancy rose. Where firm policies are missing, as in Romania, harm keeps climbing. The editorial urges governments to copy what has already worked.
pmc-13246018:
Divaris measured the faces of one hundred twenty aesthetic patients in three dimensions and compared anatomy with self-image, in this 2026 Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open study. Nearly everyone, over ninety-eight percent, had objectively asymmetric cheeks, with the left side wider in almost all cases, a strong directional pattern. Patients also answered a questionnaire about their preferred side, photographic habits, and how different they look in mirrors versus photos.

Preferences split almost evenly between left and right and bore no relationship to which side was actually wider. Forty percent noticed their mirror image and photographs disagree. Divaris argues the practical lesson is expectation management: because structure and self-perception are dissociated, surgeons should surface that gap in consultation before operating, to prevent postoperative misunderstanding and dissatisfaction.
pmc-13247018:
Lee, Shin, and Yu trained deep learning to identify bile-duct stents from X-ray images in this 2026 European Radiology Experimental study. When patients need a repeat procedure, doctors must know exactly which stent a previous team implanted, but vendor designs look confusingly similar on imaging. The team assembled images from one hundred eighty-five patients covering four stent types, later adding a fifth, partly covered design.

Their ResNet-50 model sorted stents by maker and specific type with high scores, though telling one stent from two overlapping ones proved harder. When the new stent type arrived, transfer learning, retraining only part of the network, absorbed it with little loss of accuracy. The authors say such updating keeps the tool useful as devices change.
pmc-13247518:
Bora, Manasa, and Alekya report a double diagnosis in this 2026 JCEM Case Reports article. Their patient, a twenty-two-year-old woman, was found to have diabetes at eighteen. She carried an antibody marking autoimmune diabetes, yet managed four years on oral tablets before needing insulin, a slow pattern called latent autoimmune diabetes in the young. Genetic sequencing then found something else as well.

Her whole-exome results showed a deletion in the CEL gene, the cause of MODY 8, a single-gene form of diabetes that often involves the pancreas's digestive side too. Having both an autoimmune diabetes and a monogenic diabetes in one young person is unusual, the authors note. The case argues for genetic testing when a young patient's diabetes does not behave like a single familiar type.
pmc-13248518:
Caterina Vizzardelli edits a 2026 editorial on restoring immune tolerance through allergen therapy. Allergy and autoimmune diseases share one root problem. The immune system attacks substances or tissues it should leave alone. The editorial introduces sixteen studies gathered in one research collection.

The collected work shows a shift toward precise, personal, and combined strategies. Food allergy trials report that many patients stayed free of reactions long after oral therapy ended. Shifts in blood immune cells marked the patients who gained the most. New delivery tricks pair allergen pieces with helper signals inside one particle. Peptide methods, cell energy rework, and lab-built cell treatments widen the toolkit further. The editor frames tolerance care as entering a more exact era.
pmc-13248918:
Phila Cara Baumann and Lennart Matthias Roesner review T cell behavior in atopic dermatitis in a 2026 survey. The skin disease flares in cycles and ranks among the most common chronic inflammatory conditions. T cells drive the inflammation once they home into the skin.

The review follows how T cells recognize targets, enter skin, and settle as resident memory cells. It weighs proof that microbes and the body's own proteins can serve as triggers beside outside allergens. Small lymphoid clusters inside skin may host part of this learning. Patient groups differ in cell patterns, which may explain uneven drug success. Finer grouping could guide tailored therapy, the authors suggest.
pmc-13249218:
Levy and Rothlisberger tested whether zinc-finding software can locate other metals in proteins, in a 2026 PLOS One study. Metal-based drugs, including promising cancer compounds, need known docking sites before they can be refined. The authors ran two predictors, Metal3D and Metal1D, on protein structures whose metal binding sites were already established experimentally, even though both tools were trained only on zinc.

For every protein tested, at least one predicted hotspot matched a real binding site. Performance wobbled with the exact pose of amino acid side chains, which the authors flag as the main weakness. They propose a pipeline where such cheap predictors scout candidate sites first, and heavier simulations refine the shortlist afterward.
pmc-13249618:
Rasic and colleagues read gene activity across stages of alcohol-related liver disease, in a 2026 study. They profiled seven hundred sixty messenger RNAs in liver biopsies from fifty adults with a history of heavy drinking, grouped by scarring: none, mild to moderate, or advanced. Two candidate proteins were then checked in tissue with staining methods.

Early scarring already showed metabolism genes switching off and matrix-building genes switching on. Advanced disease added a coordinated fibrogenic program centered on the TGF-beta pathway, while metabolism sank further. Two molecules, LGALS3 and S100A4, emerged as candidate markers of stage. The authors say the sequence of changes could guide stage-specific treatment ideas.
pmc-13249918:
Roy and colleagues built a fairer crystal ball for battery material factories, in a 2026 life cycle assessment study. Their method projects how mineral processing will actually change, switch by switch, instead of assuming smooth improvement. Seven families of change are modeled, from new processing routes and substitute feedstocks to recycling waste streams and better water handling, then applied to three battery cathode chemistries.

Full adoption of the switches cut climate impact steeply by 2060, but slow real-world adoption shrank the cumulative savings to single digits for climate. A popular forecasting premise, the authors show, paints impacts systematically too rosy for the coming decades. They recommend their granular approach for solar and wind supply chains too.
pmc-13250218:
Cho and co-authors describe a planned study of a gentler breathing support for premature babies. Their 2026 BMJ Open protocol covers NIV-NAVA, a non-invasive support that reads the baby's own breathing signals to time each breath. The study will recruit two hundred thirty preterm infants born between about twenty-seven and thirty-two weeks of pregnancy.

Babies needing breathing help in their first two days will start the new support instead of a breathing tube where possible. Researchers will track support failure, breathing tube time, lung damage, and other newborn complications. Child development will also be followed for up to three years. The authors hope to learn whether the method is practical as a first-line support and safe for fragile infants.
pmc-13250918:
Le and co-authors test whether squeezing the eyelid oil glands helps them recover in blocked-gland dry eye disease. Their 2026 Clinical Ophthalmology trial randomized sixty-four patients with mild or moderate gland dropout to lid hygiene alone, or hygiene plus gland expression every two weeks. Outcomes over twelve weeks included gland loss area, symptoms, and tear measures.

Gland dropout shrank in both groups, but recovery came faster with added expression at the four-week check. By eight to twelve weeks the groups looked similar on gland shape. The expression group still reported better symptom relief and healthier gland oil quality than controls. No adverse events appeared and pain stayed mild, supporting expression as a safe booster treatment.
pmc-13251218:
Han and a large team build tiny spheres patients swallow that set the rhythm for bone, powered by daily motion. Their 2026 Bioactive Materials study targets osteoporosis, where bone loses its natural charge rhythms and steadily weakens. The spheres carry pressure-powered grains, coated to home to bone, inside soft gel shells.

Swallowed spheres passed the stomach, opened in the gut, and reached bone far more than controls in animal tests. Daily motion then squeezed the particles, making charge pulses in step with motion that raised bone's charge signaling within a day. Bone-eating cells quieted while bone building rose, and pairing with gentle workouts boosted both effects. The authors present the closed loop as a new, surgery-free way to restore bone balance.
pmc-13251518:
Hoberman and colleagues test giving two meningococcal vaccines in the same visit to older teenagers. Their 2026 Human Vaccines and Immunotherapeutics trial randomized nine hundred forty healthy sixteen-to-eighteen-year-olds who had a quadrivalent vaccine at least four years earlier. Groups received both vaccines together, or each one alone.

Antibody responses after combined dosing matched those after separate dosing on every measure the trial set. Blood killing tests showed similar rises and similar shares of teenagers reaching protective levels. Side effects with the pair resembled those of the B vaccine given alone, with no new safety signal. The authors conclude that co-administration is well tolerated and immunologically sound, easing clinic scheduling for adolescents.
pmc-13252718:
Charumita Vasudev and colleagues document hunger coping in India during COVID-19 in this 2026 qualitative study. The pandemic's job losses and illness shocks hit food security hard, and the team asked how fragile households in two states actually got through.

Between late 2022 and early 2023 they ran 343 interviews in 86 households in Uttar Pradesh and Goa, chosen across migrant status, place, and caste. Everyday fixes came first: swapping foods, shrinking portions, pooling resources. Harder shocks brought costlier moves, mothers eating last, selling assets, debt, pulling children from school. Migrants were shut out of both food entitlements and support networks, which mattered more than income alone.
pmc-13254218:
Karrar Jasim Hamzah and colleagues study two cattle pathogens and plant compounds in a 2026 paper. Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteria and bovine herpesvirus type 1 cause costly disease in dairy cows, and drug resistance is growing. The team collected 40 milk samples from cows with mastitis and 10 nasal swabs from cattle with breathing symptoms.

The bacterium was found in 15 of 40 milk samples, and the virus in half the swabbed animals. Computer docking showed quercetin bound a bacterial protein more strongly than a standard antibiotic. Kaempferol, another plant compound, bound targets in both pathogens, so the authors urge further tests.
pmc-13254318:
Leandro Harries, Stefan Böhm, and Jia Liu test paver settings in field trials in a 2026 study. Asphalt pavers use a screed with tamper and vibratory units to pre-compact fresh pavement. Two field trials used a set paver and roller with one asphalt mix, and lab tests checked thickness, density, voids, and surface roughness.

Tamper speed clearly shaped layer thickness and compaction degree, while vibratory speed showed no real effect. Void distribution stayed highly even, above 98 percent, across pre-compacted areas. Surface roughness tended to fall as tamper speed rose. The authors advise keeping tamper changes minimal and switching vibration off for this mix.
pmc-13254718:
Noureen Rasheed and colleagues screen nanobodies for control of a stress pathway in fission yeast in a 2026 study. Yeast cell walls face constant mechanical and chemical attack, and wall sensors relay damage reports to repair pathways. The sensor protein Mtl2 is one such reporter; yeast missing it die under the antifungal drug caspofungin, making them a clean test bed.

The team built an in-vivo screening platform in the sensor-deficient strain under lethal drug conditions, hunting nanobodies, small antibody fragments, that could rescue survival. One hit, clone C, improved survival of the mutant and modulated Rgf1, an activator in the wall-integrity pathway. Computer docking suggested clone C grips Rgf1 away from the sites where it engages its partner GTPase, implying a tuning rather than blocking action. The experiments position nanobody screening inside living cells as a way to find modulators of stress signaling.
pmc-13255618:
Danieli and colleagues compared bedding behavior in nine subtropical dairy farms using bedded-pack barns, some managed for active composting and some not. Farms fell into large full-time composting, adapted full-time composting, and partial non-composting groups. The team measured bedding temperature and moisture around the clock in cold and hot seasons, plus pH, density, depth, and particle size.

Bedding ran hotter in the hot season, and adapted composting barns reached the highest temperatures, while partial barns stayed too cool for composting. Moisture dropped in the hot season for the composting groups and tracked temperature closely. Only the actively managed barns sustained conditions favorable to composting over a full day.
pmc-13255718:
Zhou and co-authors correct errors in their 2026 Animals paper on choosing reference sets for genomic prediction across cattle populations. The original study combined differentiation statistics and genetic distance to improve prediction when training and target populations differ. Mistakes had crept into two figures and the author address list.

The correction fixes spelling errors in the legends and labels of figures four and five, and revises the affiliations for all six authors. One author gains an additional affiliation at Inner Mongolia Agricultural University. The authors state the scientific conclusions are unaffected, and the academic editor approved the changes. The original article has been updated.
pmc-13256818:
Ngoc Ha Nguyen and colleagues evaluate in 2026 a skin product built around disodium adenosine monophosphate, a compound meant to restore the energy supply of aging skin cells. Aging and sunlight damage drain cellular energy and slow surface renewal, producing wrinkles, dryness, and uneven pigmentation.

Their multi-tiered program combined cell experiments, UV-exposed skin explants, and two small clinical studies in women. pmc-13262618:

pmc-13263018:

pmc-13263218:

pmc-13263318:

pmc-13263518:

pmc-13263818:

pmc-13263918:

pmc-13264018:

pmc-13264318:

pmc-13264618:

pmc-13264918:

pmc-13265018:

pmc-13265918:

pmc-13266218:

pmc-13272318:

pmc-13272918:

pmc-13273118:

pmc-13273218:

pmc-13273418:
