pmc-13274118:
Emanuele Bobbio and a large team present a 2026 systematic review of heart disease caused by faults in the FHL1 gene. This rare inherited condition often pairs heart muscle disease with skeletal muscle weakness, but its full picture was poorly defined. The reviewers gathered every published case they could find.

Searching two databases through July 2025 yielded twenty-two studies covering 114 patients, sixty-nine percent of them male, with illness starting at a median age of eighteen. Thickened heart muscle appeared in fifty-six percent and rhythm problems in fifty-one percent. Sudden cardiac death struck seven percent. Three quarters also had skeletal muscle involvement, from mild tightness to serious weakness.
pmc-13274518:
Grace M Hindmarch and co-authors wrote a 2026 perspective article reexamining the Collaborative Care Model, a team approach that embeds mental health care in primary care clinics. The model was built and proven mainly for depression. The authors drew on their trial extending it to opioid use disorder combined with trauma or depression in low-resource settings.

They argue that stretching a principle-based model to complex patients strains each principle in practice. Open questions include how much therapy community health workers acting as care managers should deliver, and whether care plans should cover social needs. Another gap is the lack of validated symptom measures for opioid use disorder. They urge joint work to sharpen the principles before further scaling.
pmc-13274618:
Taylor A Stevens and colleagues report a 2026 journal article tracing the family history of the machines that install proteins into mitochondria's outer skin. Mitochondria are the cell's power plants, and their outer membrane needs hundreds of proteins inserted correctly. The human protein MTCH2 was known to do this job, but its relatives and method were unclear.

Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team solved the structure of the thirty-three-kilodalton human MTCH2. It lost one membrane-spanning segment during evolution, opening a water-loving groove that fat can reach, the key to its inserting trick. Tuning the groove's lining dialed activity up or down. The structure also let them spot the matching insertase in plants, suggesting one universal mechanism.
pmc-13274818:
Shan Xiong and colleagues present a 2026 preliminary study on computer help for spotting rib fractures in older emergency patients. Brittle, overgrown bone in older people makes fractures easier to miss on chest CT scans. The team split 1,012 blunt chest trauma patients at age sixty and had six radiologists read scans alone and with a deep-learning aid.

Reading alone, radiologists caught 86.7 percent of fresh fractures in older patients versus 91.5 percent in younger ones. With the computer aid, older-group sensitivity rose to 92.5 percent, matching the younger group. False alarms per patient in the older group also fell to the younger group's level. An expert panel's verdict served as the reference standard.
pmc-13275218:
Venkatesh Kumaresan and co-authors used systems biology to explain why one Q fever vaccine protects mice better than another in a 2026 study. The bacterium Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever, and a killed vaccine from its virulent phase protects well while the mild phase version does not. The immune reasons were unclear.

Both vaccines were made from modern cell free cultures and kept their uneven protection in mice. The strong vaccine triggered earlier antibody of one class and lasting higher levels of another. Gene and cell analyses showed it also kept neutrophils active in the spleen for longer, with genes for granule release and metal trapping switched on. Removing neutrophils before challenge cut the vaccine's protection, which proves their role in the effect.
pmc-13275518:
M Ferrari and co-authors present a 2026 journal article tracing river chemistry along the Greve River in Tuscany, Italy, during the extreme 2022 European drought and the heavy rain that followed. The river runs from countryside into urban Florence's orbit, gathering pollution downstream. Six sampling campaigns between May and October 2022 combined chemical and isotope tracers.

Downstream water grew richer in human tracers such as nitrate, up to nine milligrams per liter, and potassium. In the driest months, isotope patterns showed strong evaporation stress. The first intense rain then flushed accumulated material downstream in a rapid, uneven pulse, with ammonium peaking in urban sectors. The authors frame tracer monitoring as a transferable way to judge river vulnerability under climate extremes.
pmc-13276118:
Mikyeong Lee and co-authors present a 2026 journal article mapping blood proteins against lung function. Breathing tests that measure how much air the lungs can push out help diagnose lung disease and predict later health. Genes alone do not explain these measures well, so the team turned to proteins, the body's working molecules.

Their meta-analysis pooled five cohorts with more than twenty thousand adults of European, African, and Asian ancestry. A lab platform measured nearly forty-seven hundred proteins in blood samples. Each cohort linked protein levels to three breathing measures, adjusting for age, sex, height, smoking, and other factors. The team then checked which protein patterns clustered into known pathways, looked up the proteins in other studies, and used a genetics method to probe which proteins might actually cause lung differences.
pmc-13276318:
Chloe Kharsa and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on using ultrasound guidance during radiation treatment inside heart arteries. In-stent restenosis, the re-narrowing of a previously stented artery, resists many standard fixes. Brachytherapy delivers focused radiation inside the artery to stop tissue regrowth, and ultrasound imaging can reveal why the stent failed.

The team reviewed two hundred twenty-one patients treated between 2016 and 2024. About sixty percent had ultrasound guidance during the procedure. Guided cases had wider vessels, more thorough lesion preparation, and slightly longer radiation times. At about two years of follow-up, deaths and heart attacks were more common without guidance. But repeat procedures on the same lesion were oddly more frequent in the guided group. The authors conclude guidance was safe but did not clearly improve long-term outcomes on its own.
pmc-13276418:
Szymon Baluszek and co-authors report a 2026 journal article sorting a rare skull base cancer into four groups by its DNA gains and losses. Chordoma grows slowly from leftover embryonic tissue but presses aggressively on nearby nerves and vessels. Copy-number changes, whole chunks of DNA gained or lost, drive the disease.

Two patient groups, one of thirty-two and one of seventy-one, were analyzed with different platforms. Clustering found the same four groups in both. One group was copy-stable; others were marked by chromosome nine loss, chromosome seven gain, or gains of both two and seven. A spot-check method confirmed the groups with high agreement. The groups explained about a third of the differences in gene activity between tumors. One group switched on a known growth pathway. The authors say this shared scheme links tumor DNA to behavior and possible drug targets.
pmc-13276518:
Lisa Budzinski and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on the gut microbe fingerprint of a rare immune disease. IgG4-related disease causes swelling and scarring in many organs, and gut microbes have been suspected in its origins but barely characterized. The team compared patients' stool microbes with healthy people's two ways.

Twenty-eight patients and twenty-four healthy controls gave frozen stool samples. Gene sequencing found lower microbe diversity in patients and a distinct species pattern, heavy in one large bacterial group. Those patterns separated patients from controls fairly well, though less well in a small validation group. A second method, flow cytometry profiling single cells, separated the groups robustly in both sets. The patient microbes were mostly low in DNA content and were not coated with the disease-linked antibody. The authors present the fingerprint as a proof of concept.
pmc-13276818:
Zhouyan Liao leads a 2026 study of kidney transplant patients who sit in a diagnostic gray zone. Small changes in kidney function or unclear ultrasound results leave doctors unsure whether a biopsy, an invasive tissue test, is needed. The team tested whether advanced MRI scans plus blood measures could sort 120 transplant patients.

Each patient had a detailed diffusion MRI, which tracks water movement in tissue, shortly before a biopsy. One scan measure and blood bicarbonate, a measure of acid balance, predicted cases where treatment needed to change. The combined model sorted patients far better than standard checks, and high-risk scores were tied to later loss of kidney function. Early results need confirmation in larger groups.
pmc-13277118:
Kaichao Hu leads a 2026 animal study of a classic Chinese herbal formula used for long-term poor blood flow to the brain. The formula, Buyang Huanwu Decoction, is traditionally made with a high dose of the herb astragalus. The team compared high-dose and low-dose versions in mice with the target condition.

The high-dose version eased memory problems and fatigue-like behavior better and improved brain connectivity on scans. It also helped star-shaped brain support cells recover and restored the matching of blood flow to nerve activity. Silencing a gene called NFIA wiped out those gains, tying the effect to that gene. The dose of astragalus is not a minor detail, the authors conclude.
pmc-13277418:
Do Kyun Kim heads the panel for part eight of the 2025 Korean resuscitation guidelines, published in 2026. Paediatric advanced life support addresses arrest care for infants and children in and out of hospital. The update shifts practice toward measured targets and brain protection after circulation returns.

Outside hospital, bag-mask ventilation is now suggested ahead of advanced airway placement for children. With an advanced airway in place, breathing rates are set by age band to avoid over- or under-ventilation. Blood pressure targets during and after resuscitation are specified by age when monitors are in place. Brain outcome prediction should combine exams, scans, and brain traces over time. Machine-supported CPR is reserved for selected cases in well-equipped hospitals.
pmc-13278018:
Darko Sarovic wrote a 2026 theory article that joins two ways of explaining why depression and anxiety are common among neurodivergent people. Neurodivergence covers trait profiles such as autism and ADHD. One view, from evolutionary psychiatry, treats these profiles as natural variation shaped by evolution, whose effects depend on fit with the setting.

A second framework, the pathogenetic triad, tracks how traits, coping capacity, burden, and demands interact in one person. Long mismatch with the setting can raise coping demands and repeatedly trigger evolved mood defenses, the article argues. Separating natural variation from the process that turns it into illness may reconcile neurodiversity and medical models of care.
pmc-13278418:
Gregory E Simon leads a 2026 study that builds prediction models for drug poisoning after mental health visits, using health records from four systems. Poisonings include both accidental overdoses and self-harm, and prevention differs for each. The team modeled visits from 2015 to 2019 in two steps: first predicting any poisoning, then separating self-harm from accidental cases.

Among more than nineteen million visits, about zero point six percent were followed by a poisoning. Models predicted any poisoning with moderate accuracy and self-harm poisoning with good accuracy. Visits flagged in the top five percent of risk accounted for about forty percent of later self-harm poisonings. Prior self-harm and past poisoning were shared predictors, while age and diagnoses sharpened the self-harm call.
pmc-13278618:
Elizabeth S Jarrett leads a 2026 survey study of a virtual rounding queue in a neonatal intensive care unit, where teams visit each baby's bedside in turn. Families and nurses often miss rounds because they cannot predict when the team will arrive. The software, called Q-rounds, sits inside the health record and tells nurses and families when to expect the team, in person or by phone.

Clinicians surveyed before and six weeks after the May 2023 launch perceived clear gains. Nurse and family presence on rounds rose sharply, as did perceived efficiency and satisfaction. Rounding duration felt unchanged. Open-ended replies matched the numbers. Better timing notice can make family-centered rounds workable, the authors conclude.
pmc-13278918:
Erica Cardamone and colleagues check a new food questionnaire for ultra-processed food intake in Italian adults, in a 2026 pilot study. Measuring what people eat is hard, and the ultra-processed concept itself is debated. Their modified NOVA questionnaire needed testing for clarity and coverage before wider use.

Fifty-two volunteers from two institutions completed the draft questionnaire, a day-long diet recall, and a structured interview. Every food in the recalls appeared in the questionnaire, showing complete coverage. Twenty items drew mostly negative feedback on the main clarity questions, marking them for revision. Participants generally found the tool clear and easy, though interviews surfaced several fixes. The team refined the food list and wording for later reliability testing.
pmc-13279018:
Anna-Theresa Pfaller and a large team report a 2026 study of a heart muscle illness in mice. The illness is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, where heart walls grow thick and stiff. It affects about one in five hundred people and is a top cause of sudden death in the young. The team tests whether a drug called pioglitazone, and its R form, can calm swelling and curb bad heart change.

Early pages set out why thick walls may stem from high energy use, worn power parts in cells and swelling that scars the heart. The study uses a mouse line that carries a common human gene fault for the illness. Those mice grow thick walls and scars by about thirty weeks of age, giving a test bed for the drug.
pmc-13279218:
Mirjam J Esser and colleagues published a 2026 review of the immune system in preterm infants, the roughly 13 million babies born before 37 weeks each year. Prematurity is the leading cause of newborn death worldwide, and infections hit this group especially hard. The review compares the phenotype and function of immune cells in preterm and full-term babies, with particular attention to adaptive immunity, the branch that builds lasting memory of infections.

At birth, both the fast innate defenses and the adaptive arm look immature in preterm infants, antibody levels run low, and some vaccine parts provoke weaker responses. Those gaps help explain poor pathogen clearance in the first weeks of life. During the first year, maturation proceeds quickly and most differences from full-term infants shrink or vanish. The authors offer it as a framework for combined strategies, from infection prevention to vaccine timing, that match how these infants actually develop.
pmc-13279318:
Minqiu Kuang and colleagues published a 2026 paper on a vision system that finds chili flowers and judges their pose so robots can pollinate them. Flowers are small, crowded, often hidden by leaves, and lit unevenly in greenhouses, which makes machine perception hard. Their framework, CFPR-YOLO, adapts a compact detection network with a stronger feature extractor and modules tuned for tiny and partly hidden targets.

On their own and outside test sets the system reached a precision of 92.6 percent and a detection score of 92.1 percent with only 7.26 million parameters, small enough for field hardware. Running on a Jetson edge computer it processed 39.5 frames per second, fast enough for a moving robot. In indoor trials it supported simulated pollination with a success rate of 90 percent on upward-facing flowers. The authors see it as a building block for precision pollination and fruit-set management.
pmc-13279418:
Weizhong Chu and colleagues published a 2026 analysis of silica dust monitoring across industrial and mining workplaces in Sichuan Province, China, from 2021 to 2025. Overall, 82.2 percent of posts complied, and compliance improved significantly across the five years. Larger enterprises and posts with higher free silica content performed worse, a counterintuitive pattern the authors highlight. The northwest of the province and the machinery industry showed the lowest compliance rates. Statistical modeling confirmed year, industry, region, company size, and silica content as independent predictors. The authors call for risk-based inspections and controls concentrated on the lagging sectors rather than spread evenly.
pmc-13279518:
F Manzi and colleagues published a 2026 study of theory of mind in children with developmental coordination disorder, defined by poor motor control with no intellectual or sensory disability. Theory of mind means grasping what others think and feel. Their social difficulties might reflect a broad weakness there or only specific gaps. Parents rated social difficulties.

The components behaved differently. Perspective-taking tracked with manual dexterity and was predicted by it after accounting for age, gender, and social symptoms. Understanding others' emotions related instead to verbal skill. Advanced theory of mind leaned on IQ and working memory. Second-order false-belief reasoning showed no significant links. The authors conclude the social-cognitive profile is uneven rather than globally impaired. They suggest therapy should consider how motor skill supports perspective-taking.
pmc-13279718:
Cui-Xian Qin and colleagues published a 2026 study of why one sugarcane variety uses nitrogen fertilizer far more efficiently than another. Nitrogen drives yield, but excess fertilizer leaches into water and air, so cane that thrives on less is a breeding priority. The team compared a high-efficiency variety, AS108, with a low-efficiency one, GT11, under normal and low nitrogen supply. They measured growth, enzyme activity, and gene expression.

The efficient variety kept higher biomass, nitrogen content, and use efficiency when nitrogen ran short. The enzymes that fold nitrogen into amino acids worked harder, and the high-affinity nitrate transporters switched on earlier and more strongly. Transport genes peaked 30 to 60 days sooner than in the weaker variety. Network analysis placed those transporters at the hub. The authors offer this timing and coordination pattern as concrete targets for breeding high-efficiency cultivars.
pmc-13280018:
Jonathan Fisher and colleagues published a 2026 review of gamma delta T cells as a platform for cancer immunotherapy. These cells make up only 1 to 10 percent of circulating T cells but concentrate in barrier tissues such as gut and skin. Unlike conventional T cells, they switch on without needing the MHC presentation system. They also do not attack a recipient's tissues, which opens the door to off-the-shelf donor cell products.

The review weighs where unmodified gamma delta cells have produced durable responses and where disease burden has overwhelmed them. It then surveys enhancement strategies: engineering the cells with new receptors or armor, and combining them with other treatments that raise their potency or persistence. The authors' interest is practical, mapping which contexts suit these cells today and which improvements are prerequisites for broader use. The survey speaks to teams designing cell therapies that sidestep graft-versus-host risks.
pmc-13280118:
Besir Salihu and colleagues present a 2026 scoping review of eggshell membrane in bone regeneration. Eggshell membrane is the thin film inside an eggshell, rich in matrix like proteins. Its structure mimics the scaffold round cells, which makes it a candidate for guided bone growth. The review maps proof for the membrane and its derivatives in bone and dental repair. Searches ran in three databases for studies from 2019 to 2025.

Of two hundred eighty records, thirteen studies fit: nine in live animals, three in dishes and one clinical study. Forms held native, modified, mineralized, soluble and composite systems. As a group, membrane materials showed good body fit, bone forming potential and vessel growth support. Bone healing and implant bond also gained in models. Human proof stays thin with just one clinical study, so the map marks promise and gaps at once.
pmc-13280718:
Enis Oğuzhan Eren and colleagues reported a new way to make battery parts in a 2026 study. Sodium batteries could store energy at lower cost than lithium ones, since sodium is common. The weak point has been the negative pole, which must hold a lot of charge. The team grew a thin carbon coat on porous carbon using hot gas. The coat is smooth and joined up across the whole surface.

The coat narrows and partly seals the tiny holes in the base. That curbs waste at the surface and packs sodium in more tightly. Cells built this way held a very high charge and kept much of it at a steady level. The authors say the method can also tune what the coat is made of. That opens paths to better battery parts and other tools.
pmc-13281318:
Carson J Peters studied how teaming up with city neighborhoods can draw people into health research in a 2026 paper. Such partnerships link scholars with the people their work aims to serve. The study grew out of a trial on mother and child health in urban areas. Fifteen community partners sat for long, open talks. The author sorted their words for shared themes with a careful coding process.

Five themes came out of the talks. Strong work builds on systems the neighborhood already trusts. It makes research spaces that feel owned by the community. It treats residents as true stakeholders, not just recruits. The research team itself must share the community's aims. And contact must stay honest and real, not staged. The author says these steps can widen who joins trials and who gains from them.
pmc-13281418:
Zoran Milosavljević and colleagues surveyed medical students in Belgrade on HIV knowledge and behavior in a 2026 study. Young adults in Serbia face the highest rates of infections passed by sex. The form scored knowledge, views of people with HIV, and condom use.

Fifth-year students knew more than first-year students, as expected. Yet their views of people with HIV were no warmer. Only the very top scorers on knowledge held clearly warmer views. pmc-13281818:
Gang Zhong and colleagues probed heat loss in tiny light waves inside crystals in a 2026 study. The waves, hybrids of light and lattice shaking, can focus light far below its normal limit. Their quality score nearly doubled in one crystal. The same lift showed in the second crystal and in side checks on other materials. The authors say cold is a general lever for such devices.
pmc-13281918:

Their patient, a 70-year-old man awaiting rectal cancer surgery, arrived with an inferior heart attack. Angiography found no circumflex artery in its usual place; it arose from the right side and looped behind the aorta, a benign variant that can develop plaque. Ultrasound inside the vessel showed plaque in an elliptical channel.

A round stent forced into an oval vessel risks poor apposition, so the team used a drug-coated balloon, which delivers medication and leaves nothing. pmc-13282318:
Renu Saradadevi and co-authors present a 2026 bean breeding study aimed at cutting cooking time through genomic selection. The authors conclude that hands-on trait measurement in every cycle remains essential to lock in gains.
pmc-13282418:

The team studied five hundred six patients from two cohorts, with scans rebuilt at one and five millimetres.

Only about one percent of thick-scan features met the reproducibility bar, against about twenty-seven percent after synthesis. The authors present synthesis as a practical standardisation step.
pmc-13283118:
Compounds made by gut microbes might slow kidney scarring, the hypothesis behind Weiguo Yao's 2026 network analysis. Kidney scarring worsens kidney function over time and lacks strong treatments. Products made by gut microbes affect body health, but their role here was unclear.

Core targets included JUN, IL6, IL1B, and AKT1 in the network results. Three products stood out as safe lead options: propionate, butyrate, and one indole acid. Docking tests showed stable binding to core targets. Lab proof is still needed before clinical use.
pmc-13283218:

Tests ran in two phases against its parent methods and a density-based rival. The rival gave uneven group counts and needed frequent retuning over ten years. pmc-13283718:

Soft tissue injuries such as meniscus tears add pain and limit function. Kneecap instability does the same. Surgery data in this group were missing. Records from several centres covering 2004 to 2025 were searched for these patients.

Twenty-one patients had thirty arthroscopies, at an average age of fifteen and a half. Meniscus injury, kneecap instability, and fracture were the top reasons for surgery. Half of the operations had some complication, and about one in four needed revision surgery. The report gives families and surgeons a first picture of both the promise and the extra risk here.
pmc-13283818:
Pablo Alejandro Millones-Gómez and a large team examined Peru's national researcher registry in 2026, asking whether it rewards more than raw output counts. The team pulled registry, Scopus, and SciVal data for 9,651 researchers across 2019 to 2024 and scored four dimensions by registry level.

More than 92,000 publications were counted. Output rose steeply by level, from under four papers at the lowest rung to over sixty at the distinguished rung, and top-journal output concentrated at the top too. Lead authorship rose with level but stayed uneven even among leaders. Retractions rose with productivity, reflecting exposure more than uniform misconduct. The authors propose a hybrid system that also credits leadership and integrity.
pmc-13283918:
Shingles in a ten-month-old baby is the rare event in a 2026 case by Seyedeh Mahla Hoseini and colleagues. Shingles normally strikes older adults or people with weak immunity. The baby had no prior chickenpox history recorded before the rash appeared.

Childhood shingles rates sit below two per thousand child-years in cited data. The rash followed contact with a nonvenomous snake by a short interval. The authors suggest that body stress or local skin trauma may wake the sleeping virus. No proof of cause is claimed beyond the timing in this case. Odd blister patterns in infants deserve shingles on the checklist.
pmc-13284018:
Trainee surgeons learned robotic gallbladder removal safely in 441 cases reviewed by Gianpiero Gravante and colleagues in 2026. Robotic surgery is spreading, but its place in structured training was unclear. All operators began with no prior robotic experience in this series.

Cases ran from October 2019 to April 2025 under senior supervision. Mean surgery time was just over an hour for the full set. No injuries during surgery and no switches to open surgery occurred. Only six patients had problems after surgery, and readmission stayed below one percent. Learning curves split into four phases ending in a plateau. Scar tissue removal lengthened operations most.
pmc-13284418:
Carla Franch-Marti and a large team tracked practice effects in 2026 as an early warning sign in Huntington's disease. Modelling found burden thresholds where gains faded, and the highest genetic burden group showed minimal or absent practice effects while lower burden groups tracked controls. The authors built an online calculator for individual trajectories and back dynamic measures as trial endpoints.
pmc-13284518: The notice is a correction only, issued in 2026 for an earlier review on nano-biosensor diagnostics by Shashikant Pathak and co-authors. It restores a missing UCLouvain affiliation for author Shadi Bazazordeh. It also adds Arnaud Delcorte, who had been left off the author list, bringing the list to five names. No findings or conclusions of the review change.
pmc-13284718:

pmc-13285318:

After matching, liver hemangiomas were more common in the Cushing group than in the comparison group in the authors analysis. Higher midnight cortisol and higher daily urine cortisol each linked to the growths in Cushing patients. A prediction model sorted risk well in this set. The authors offer the tool for early risk checks and care planning.
pmc-13285918:

pmc-13286518:

pmc-13286818:

The pump delivers hydromorphone under the skin, letting patients trigger doses when pain spikes, which suits those who cannot swallow pills reliably.

Roughly half the patients improved by at least half. Recorded side effects were rare, and none involved slowed breathing. The authors support the approach for selected patients while asking for prospective comparisons.
pmc-13286918:
Qifang Guo and colleagues chart how lung artery pressure evolves over time in patients whose lupus has caused pulmonary hypertension. The 2026 cohort study follows eighty-one patients from a Chinese lupus registry. Group modeling sorted patients into four paths, from pressure starting high and falling fast to pressure starting high and climbing.

The climbing group was small, seven patients, yet faced by far the worst survival. Its members walked shorter distances and carried higher inflammation and heart-strain markers at baseline. Longer walking distance marked the gentler paths. After adjustment, the rising path still predicted death strongly, alongside lupus activity and inflammation measures. Sorting patients by pressure trajectory, the authors say, sharpens risk judgment.
pmc-13287018:
Srividhya Senthil and colleagues tell of two children with a rare immune disease whose self-attacks beat all standard drugs. The 2026 report covers a disorder of the RAS gene path. In it, the immune system turns on the child's own blood cells. Most cases calm down with immune-damping drugs.

Both children went on to stem cell grafts, the last resort. Each first graft failed and had to be done a second time. The team blames traits of the disease for those failures. Three more graft cases from past reports are reviewed, most done after the disease turned to cancer. A targeted drug that blocks the same gene path also gets a look. Grafts, the team argues, belong in plans for hard cases.
pmc-13287118:
Demirhan Örsan Demir and colleagues chart two decades of publishing on robotic lymph node surgery for testicular cancer in a 2026 bibliometric analysis. The operation removes retroperitoneal nodes through robotic arms, sparing young patients a large open incision, and the literature had never been mapped as a whole. A Web of Science search gathered 93 publications from 2006 to 2025 for network and trend analysis.

Output climbed over time, peaking at thirteen papers in both 2021 and 2025. One specialty journal led with thirteen papers, and Johns Hopkins stood out as the top institution. The United States dominated volume, citations, and international collaboration alike. Keywords clustered on robotic and minimally invasive technique, post-chemotherapy cases, and nonseminomatous tumors. The authors note the field still rests on a small circle of expert centers.
pmc-13287218:
Riccardo Cavuoto and colleagues built a mathematical model in 2026 of the thin sieve-like tissue at the back of the eye, aiming to link eye pressure with damage seen in glaucoma. Their plate-based model treats the tissue as a fluid-filled solid that behaves differently along and across its fibres, and it can be solved directly.

Strain and stress peaked near the tissue edge, the spot where harm is thought to start, and rose as pressure rose. Fluid content fell steadily at higher pressure, which could starve nearby nerve fibres. Simpler uniform models misjudged both fluid and strain. The authors offer the framework for estimating tissue stiffness from future measurements.
pmc-13287418:
Sara Javanparast and colleagues consulted Australian stakeholders in 2026 to set research priorities for unpaid carers of older people and of people needing palliative or end-of-life care. Input came through an online survey, a roundtable, and a focus group, then was grouped by theme.

Priorities covered spotting carers early, fair and timely access to help, and guidance through confusing service systems. Support during care changes and after caring ends, including grief help, also ranked high. Checking whether current services actually work was another theme. Participants asked that future studies involve carers in respectful, flexible ways. The authors aim the list at turning new carer policy into practice.
pmc-13288618:
Liwei Zhang and co-authors map address tags that send a viral protein to the cell nucleolus in a 2026 study. The virus is avian infectious bronchitis virus, a costly chicken pathogen. Its nucleocapsid protein, the most abundant viral protein in infected cells, gathers in the nucleolus, a dense region inside the nucleus. The team cut the protein into pieces and mutated single spots to find the tags.

The authors say the tag details could guide weakened vaccine strains or antiviral design.
pmc-13288718:
Sitraka Angelo Raharinavalona and colleagues test blood iodine and thyroid health in Madagascar in 2026. Their study sat in one large hospital in Antananarivo. It ran for two years to August 2023. In all, 195 patients were tested. Blood iodine stood in for iodine status.

Excess iodine hit 12.8 percent of patients. Thyroid disorder hit 15.4 percent. High iodine clustered in those under sixty. It ran less with high blood pressure. Lipid woes, diabetes, and past smoking also split it. After age and sex checks, the two states tied strongly. Finding one should prompt a test for the other.
pmc-13289018:
John Allotey and colleagues study a seizure drug in pregnancy in 2026. The drug is called lamotrigine. Blood levels of it fall in pregnancy. Doctors often test levels to guide dose. The team asked if repeat tests predict seizures.

Data came from the EMPiRE trial in the UK. Fifty maternity units took part. Of 560 women, 183 gave usable data. Forty-six women had seizures in that span. Repeat blood levels did not predict seizures. Starting dose alone predicted risk. Test scores for level-based models were poor. The authors doubt the worth of serial tests.
pmc-13289118:
Sushan Wang and colleagues review a signaling protein in gut cancers in 2026. The protein is called SHP2. It helps tumors grow and spread. It also helps them dodge immune attack. Its role shifts by cell type and place.

The review covers five major gut cancers. It looks at how the tumor setting shapes SHP2. Chemo and radiation can change its action. Such shifts may drive drug resistance. New blockers aim at SHP2 in fresh ways. Mixes with other drugs are being tested. Trials are under way in clinics. The authors frame SHP2 as a precision target.
pmc-13289318:
Nicolai Leuchten, Ioannis Parodis, Ralph Brinks, and Martin Aringer analyzed a 2026 pooled dataset on belimumab for low blood counts in lupus. Belimumab already helps overall lupus activity and cuts flares and damage, but its effect on low platelets and low white cells had not been detailed. Platelets help blood clot, while white cells fight infection.

Data pooled five phase III trials, with 1769 people on belimumab and 1144 on placebo, both plus standard care. At start, low platelets were uncommon, while low white cells affected hundreds in each arm. Low platelets cleared sooner and more often on belimumab, with a third reaching lasting clearance versus a small share on placebo as reported. White cell recovery showed no clear drug edge.
pmc-13289918:
Nuhad Dumit led a 2026 survey on physical and emotional health among nurses caring for Syrian refugees in Lebanon and Jordan. Crisis and refugee-hosting wards strain staff bodies and minds, yet hard numbers for these settings were scarce. Hospital nurses answered in Lebanon, totaling 976 with a 52 percent response, and in Jordan, totaling 2,012 with a far higher response rate.

General weakness was strong in about six in ten Lebanese nurses and over seven in ten Jordanian nurses surveyed. Strong back pain topped 60 percent in both countries overall. Emotional exhaustion ran higher in Jordan than Lebanon by mean score in the results. Long hours, conflict, and heavy felt workload hurt health, while teamwork and resources protected it.
pmc-13290118:
Training under flickering, interrupted vision sharpened the skills of female boxers in a 2026 trial by Youlin Xiao and co-authors. Stroboscopic training blocks sight at intervals, forcing the brain to process movement from partial information, but it had rarely been tested in boxing or in women.

Twenty-six female amateur boxers were split evenly between a stroboscopic group and a control group for six weeks of thrice-weekly 35-minute sessions mixing general visual drills with boxing tasks. The strobe group improved in eye-hand coordination, reaction time, go/no-go control, perception span, and multiple object tracking, and punching accuracy in bouts also rose. Four weeks later, most visual gains partly held, though reaction time and punching accuracy gains did not. Xiao and colleagues see promise for strobe work in fast-response sports.
pmc-13290618:
Hands-on treatment first, then core exercise, is the two-stage recipe a 2026 trial protocol by Dongming Su and colleagues sets out to test in sedentary people with chronic non-specific low back pain. Guidelines already back core training, but pain and stiffness often block patients from training well.

The single-center, assessor-blinded trial will randomize 88 sedentary adults to core stability exercise alone or manual therapy followed by the same exercise, over 12 sessions in four weeks. The model treats manual therapy as passive preparation that opens a short therapeutic window of lower pain and looser muscles, into which active re-education is slotted. Pain at week four is the main outcome, with disability, fear-avoidance beliefs, and muscle properties tracked up to three months. No results are reported yet; the paper lays out the design and its synergy hypothesis.
pmc-13290718:
China's AI medical device network is reorganizing around hospitals and Beijing, Feng Hu and colleagues show in a 2026 study of patent collaborations from 2019 to 2025. Using social network analysis and geographical detectors, they traced how companies, universities, research institutes, and medical institutions co-develop devices.

Early on, firms dominated; over time universities, institutes, and especially medical institutions moved from the margins to become core go-betweens. Geographically the network clumps unevenly: Beijing's hub status kept strengthening while a multipolar pattern formed. Within-province ties ran mostly firm-to-firm, and cross-province work radiated from Beijing toward the Yangtze and Pearl River deltas. Finance output, trade volume, and technology-market activity explained provincial standing best; education spending share explained little. The authors draw lessons for institutions and public health governance.
pmc-13290818:
Artificial intelligence is rewiring how new crop varieties get bred, Nikita Aggarwal and colleagues survey in a review from 2026. Facing climate change and a growing population, breeders need faster, more precise ways to turn field and genome data into better plants.

The review pursues four aims: mapping AI's overhaul of high-throughput phenotyping, cataloguing AI-driven breeding methods beyond tradition, improving models of genotype-by-environment-by-management interplay, and marking AI's current limits. Case studies from the past two decades show working systems across major crops and traits, from drone-scored fields to genomic selection. The authors also credit AI with sharpening gene editing and selection accuracy. Aggarwal and colleagues close with a roadmap urging interdisciplinary teams to fuse data streams for precision agriculture.
pmc-13291018:
Answers written by two chatbots about adenomyosis, a painful womb condition, are graded in a 2026 comparison led by Ling Tian. ChatGPT and DeepSeek each handled 25 common patient questions drawn from Google Trends, under repeated and fresh-cycle prompting, producing 300 texts for scoring on readability and information quality.

In fresh-cycle runs both systems held steady, yet DeepSeek texts scored as easier to read and higher in quality on both scoring tools used by the team. Under repeated prompting, DeepSeek output varied more across several measures, a point the authors flag for caution. Overall the work gives patients and clinicians a grounded way to judge which system gives clearer, more trustworthy answers on this condition, and where consistency still fails.
pmc-13291218: Fahim Mahmud and co-authors issued a short correction in 2026 to a study on machine learning for sepsis diagnosis. Just the correction notice itself makes up the evidence here. It fixes wrong author names in three in-text citations. It also adds five references that were left out. The added works are now cited in two parts of the text. No results or methods are changed in this note alone.
pmc-13291318:
Quantum pictures need a compact code for three-level units. Mirna Rofail, Rasha Montaser, and Ahmed Younes present a 2026 model called NQQR. It stores gray and color images in qutrit systems. Such units carry more states than normal qubits.

Pixel spots are coded with a stack of qutrits. Color strength takes six more qutrits. Extra helper units cut the cost of complex gates. Tests show the tuned model slashes quantum cost. Gains reach near total savings on gray images. Scaling rules are given for larger image sizes. The model suits future quantum image tools.
pmc-13291718:
Ibrahima Sory Cherif and a large team present a 2026 case study of confirmed Lassa fever in N'Zérékoré, Guinea, dating to 2022. They trace how one patient's lasting fever was managed for 13 days before the viral cause was recognized. A detailed survey in the region also worked to map the chain of transmission.

Suspicion arose only after bleeding signs appeared and antibiotics failed at the regional hospital. A blood test confirmed Lassa virus one day before the patient died, and ribavirin was never given. The authors use the case to argue for faster differential diagnosis and better care pathways when standard antibiotic treatment does not work.
pmc-13292018:
Shota Matsunaga and Kumiko Ando link developmental disorders to reoffending in Japanese forensic outpatients, in a 2026 study. The patients were treated under a national act for people found not at fault due to mental disorder. A national database covered outpatient treatment years from 2005 to 2017. The analysis included 2,135 patients, of whom about ten percent offended again during treatment. The disorders checked were intellectual disability, autism, and ADHD.

Intellectual disability appeared in ten percent of patients and autism in about four percent. Both raised the adjusted odds of repeat crime, autism most strongly at nearly triple. Intellectual disability also tied to higher odds of physical violence and of arson. Autism tied to physical violence as well, with odds near triple. ADHD was too rare in the cohort to judge. The authors call for tailored support that fits each case, from a mixed team.
pmc-13292318:
Meeting abstracts from the 2025 annual gathering of the SCORE centers on sex differences research fill a 2026 proceedings collection. The Specialized Centers of Research Excellence program runs on a U54 cooperative agreement from the NIH Office of Research on Women's Health, co-funded by eight institutes and centers. Each center acts as a national resource for translational research on diseases affecting women, with attention to how biological sex shapes illness and treatment. The program builds standards for treating sex as a biological variable and has added a Career Enhancement Core to fund pilot work and train new scientists. The collection gathers the centers' current projects, carrying forward more than twenty years of investment in sex-informed research.
pmc-13292518:
Martin Nakash and co-authors ask a 2026 dementia question across two big aging cohorts: is it obesity or metabolic ill-health that carries the risk? Midlife obesity is a known dementia factor, but late-life obesity sometimes looks harmless. The team sorted 11,482 Americans and 13,068 Swedes by weight and by metabolic health, defined through blood sugar, blood pressure, and lipids.

Metabolic unhealthiness, with or without obesity, pointed toward higher dementia risk in both midlife and late life. The clearest signals were metabolically unhealthy non-obese women in midlife in the US cohort and late-life men in the Swedish one. Obesity with metabolic health showed no significant risk and even trended protective. The authors argue metabolic health, especially in midlife, deserves the attention usually lavished on weight alone.
pmc-13292918:
Kyotaro Fukuta and co-authors describe, in a 2026 case report, a burst belly aorta aneurysm that first revealed a hidden adrenal tumor. A 57-year-old man arrived with sudden belly pain and heavy internal bleeding.

Scans showed a torn aneurysm below the kidney arteries, fixed at once with a stent graft placed through a vessel. Scans also showed a left adrenal lump with rich blood flow, and a tracer test pointed to pheochromocytoma, a tumor that releases stress hormones. After drug blockade, surgeons removed the gland with keyhole surgery and lab tests confirmed the tumor. Staged care proved safe here.
pmc-13293118:
Lorna McAusland and Erik H. Murchie write a 2026 commentary on how wheat leaves breathe at night, responding to a study of Australian wheat varieties under warmer nights. Nights are warming faster than days in many farming regions, and wheat yields fall as night temperatures climb. Respiration, the process by which plants burn stored sugars, is one night-time process that responds strongly to heat.

The study under discussion found that leaf respiration adjusted to warm nights more fully at night than during the day. McAusland and Murchie argue that this day-night gap has been overlooked while research focused on daytime photosynthesis. They point to breeding and crop management that account for night physiology as a route toward harvests that hold up as nights keep warming.
pmc-13293518:
Asa Farahani and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, how aging and body metabolism each shape brain health across adult life. Brain and body change together, yet studies often treat them apart, missing shared patterns that could guide care.

One axis tracked age, with weaker brain structure and poorer brain blood flow. The other tracked metabolic strain, with low good cholesterol and higher weight, pressure, and blood sugar, converging on reduced brain blood flow. pmc-13293718:
Shingo Katayama and co-authors report, in a 2026 study, autoantibodies against a nerve adhesion protein called L1CAM in a small subset of people with schizophrenia. Immune attacks on brain proteins explain some psychosis cases, and new targets may reveal fresh mechanisms.

Lab mapping showed the first domain of the protein as the main target. Patient antibody given to mice harmed thinking performance, and the two patients also showed marked thinking deficits. A tiny subgroup may have immune-driven illness.
pmc-13293918:
Xiang-Ning Cheng leads a 2026 real-world study of stapokibart, an antibody blocking the IL-4 receptor, for severe loss of smell in sinus disease with nasal polyps. pmc-13294318:
Huber Rizzo leads a 2026 herd investigation of two infections circulating together in dairy goats in Northeastern Brazil. pmc-13294718: A 2026 correction by Jie Liu and co-authors amends their article on carbonic anhydrase-1 in diabetic macular edema. The notice restores an omitted affiliation, the Center for High Altitude Medicine at West China Hospital, Sichuan University, for two authors. It also replaces the funding statement, naming three supporting sources and stating that funders had no role in the work. Nothing else in the article changes.
pmc-13294918:
Yasuaki Ito and co-authors present a web tool that draws molecular orbitals right inside a browser, in a 2026 software paper. Traditionally, viewing them meant generating bulky grid files with a separate program and opening them in installed software. Evaluating one orbital over more than a million grid points finished within a tenth of a second, up to a thousand times faster than a plain processor path. No installation is needed, and the code is open source. The authors aim to make orbital exploration as quick as opening a web page.
pmc-13295018:
Michael Dorogan and co-authors review newer dopamine receptor tools for research in a 2026 article. Twin-headed ligands, light-activated compounds, light-switchable probes, and glowing tracers each let researchers control or watch receptors in new ways. The review gathers these advances as chemical biology tools that can sharpen experiments today and may guide better medicines for brain disorders later.
pmc-13295118:
Xiang Gao and colleagues package healing cell signals into bone-seeking beads in a 2026 study. Large bone gaps cannot mend alone and need immune calm, new vessels, and new bone working together. Tiny vesicles shed by a helpful macrophage type carry all three kinds of signal but wash away too fast.

Lab work showed calmer immune behaviour, more vessel sprouting, and stronger bone-forming signals in stem cells. In rat skull defects, loaded beads grew clearly more new bone than empty beads, offering a gentle, targeted repair route.
pmc-13295418:
Didier Fraisse, Alexis Bred, and Catherine Felgines brew lemon verbena tea and run it through a mock digestive tract, in a 2026 study. The herbal drink is rich in polyphenols prized for antioxidant power and for blocking glycation, the sugar-driven harm tied to aging. Whether those compounds survive stomach and gut conditions was unclear.

Total phenolics and phenolic acids held steady through digestion, while flavonoids dipped a little in the gut phase. The star compound, verbascoside, partly broke into kin such as caffeic acid, and those offspring kept antioxidant scores level or better on two tests. Anti-glycation power also held. The authors credit verbascoside and its offspring as the main radical fighters and sugar traps in the tea.
pmc-13295618:
Xuelian Chen and colleagues trace how a soil bacterium's population sensor doubles as a stress shield inside bean root nodules, in a 2026 study of Rhizobium etli. These bacteria trade fixed nitrogen for plant sugars, and the partnership runs on quorum sensing, chemical votes that report crowding. pmc-13295918:
Francisco Antônio Félix Xavier Júnior and colleagues test a urine marker of kidney tube damage in cats with a blocked urethra, in a 2026 study. A blocked bladder outlet is a common cat emergency, and kidney harm can start before the usual blood marks move. The marker is kidney injury molecule-1, a protein shed by hurt tube cells. The team compared blocked cats whose standard blood waste marks still sat in the normal range against healthy cats.

The blocked cats carried plainly more of the marker in their urine, even though their creatinine and urea stayed in range. That gap suggests the marker flags tube harm that standard tests miss at this stage. The authors call for more work on how the marker could guide care for blocked cats, where early warning of kidney harm shapes how hard vets push fluids and drainage.
pmc-13296018:
Ernesto Martínez-Martínez and Roberto Palacios-Ramírez introduce, in 2026, a journal special issue on oxidative stress in heart and blood vessel disease. The heart's heavy energy demand makes it prone to damage when oxygen-based chemistry slips out of balance.

Eight contributions, mixing reviews and new research, survey how such stress drives inflammation, scarring and stiffening across heart conditions. Topics include mitochondrial stress in heart failure with preserved pumping and added antioxidant effects of standard drugs. The editors frame the collection as a guide to current frontiers in redox biology for clinicians and researchers.
pmc-13297318:
Anjia Huang and colleagues pair phosvitin, an egg-yolk protein rich in phosphate groups, with short sugar chains to make it hardier, in a 2026 study. Phosvitin binds metals strongly and shows useful bioactivity, yet it breaks down easily under heat or acid shifts. The sugars used, called fructooligosaccharides, were mixed with the protein to form a combined system.

Tests showed the two parts join through weak, non-bonded forces, with no deep change to the protein's shape. The combined particles grew larger, carried a slight negative charge, and resisted clumping in cloudy-liquid tests. The pairing also dissolved better and kept its metal-binding and fat-protecting powers across heat and acidity levels. Food and supplement makers gain a steadier form of the protein.
pmc-13297518:
Vincens Kälin and colleagues test a complication grading scale in patients treated for a burst brain aneurysm, in a 2026 single-centre study. The scale, called TDN, grades harm by the treatment needed, the disability caused, and the nerve deficit left. Records covered 355 patients treated by surgery, vessel repair from inside, or both, across more than a decade.

Higher grades tracked longer hospital stays and worse function both at discharge and at last check. The scale sorted patients who ended with poor outcomes well, and likewise predicted who returned to work. Patients with any complication stayed about a week longer on average. A shared grading language could aid counselling and planning in this fragile group, the authors argue.
pmc-13297818:
Red wine color may hinge on two levers used at once: acid level and the size of added tannin chains. Arianna Ricci and her team show this in a 2026 wine study. They made 2023 Sangiovese wine at three acid levels and dosed it with grape seed tannins of short or long chain length.

After the wines sat for 40 days in mild heat to mimic age, the long-chain tannin drove color change at all acid levels. The short-chain tannin's effect bent with the acid level. At the top acid setting, pH 3.8, all of the wines turned cloudy and lost their stable state. The team says wine makers should tune both levers to each batch, since grapes now ripen out of step in a warm world.
pmc-13297918:
Mikhail M. Avdeev and others report a 2026 materials study on wormlike micelles made from potassium oleate, used as thickeners in fields such as oil recovery. Adding carboxymethylated cellulose nanocrystals turned dilute solutions into viscoelastic solids, with very large rises in viscosity and storage modulus. Imaging pointed to a network of fibrillar aggregates formed by micelles together with nanocrystals.

Heating tests showed unusual staying power, with the storage modulus barely changing between room heat and higher heat, plus gel formation triggered by warmth. Scattering and calorimetry data showed hydrogen bonding dominates at room heat, while hydrophobic effects take over when heated. The authors link these traits to thickener use in hotter, deeper wells.
pmc-13298918:
Mohammad Gazali and co-authors test whether face shape predicts jaw joint space dimensions, in a 2026 cross-sectional imaging study. Cone-beam scans measured front, top, and rear joint spaces on both sides for 69 adults without jaw disorder signs. Faces were classified as round, oval, or square using standardised photographs and an algorithm.

Nearly every comparison showed no significant difference between face shapes. Only the left rear joint space varied, with round faces smallest and square faces largest on average. The authors conclude facial form holds minimal influence over these dimensions, so face shape may add only limited complementary value during jaw joint evaluation, pending cautious interpretation.
pmc-13299118:
Jacquelyn N. Zera and co-authors compare firefighter sleep at home against sleep at the station, in a 2026 one-time study. Sixty-six career firefighters filled in a standard sleep quality survey for both settings. Station arrangements, shared bunks versus individual dorm rooms, formed a second comparison.

Sleep duration, efficiency, perceived quality, and overall scores were all significantly better at home. Room style at the station made no significant difference, which suggests on-call stress and night alarms outweigh physical layout. The authors recommend station-wide noise reduction, protected nap policies, and insomnia therapy tailored to first responders, rather than spending only on dorm remodelling for occupational fatigue.
pmc-13299318:
The gut and its germs trade notes with teen hormones, and that trade may set heart risk for life. Natalia Kurhaluk and her team map the trade in a 2026 review. Teen years pair fast body change with a gut flock that is still in flux, so food picks bite hard.
