Junk food low in fiber thins the flock and props the gut wall open, which lets ill ease in. The review adds a new tool: fine-tuned brew tanks that grow set goods, from peptides that drop blood strain to fish-oil fats. The team call for trials in teens and long checks on safe use.
pmc-13299518:
Angeliki Maria N. Matzavaki leads a team testing two little-studied nematode species as biological control against stored product beetles, in a 2026 pest study. Storage insects cause heavy economic losses worldwide, and chemical insecticides carry drawbacks. The worm-like nematodes infect and kill insects naturally, offering a sustainable alternative worth checking.

Larvae of four major beetle pests, including flour beetles and a khapra beetle, were exposed on different grains. Both nematode species proved effective against the majority of the tested insects. The authors supply first evidence for these species in storage settings, supporting their integration into stored product protection programmes alongside other measures.
pmc-13299918:
Pakistani parents can learn children's dental care through Facebook if the lessons are properly built and checked, report Ushna Shameen and colleagues in a 2026 development study. Following the ADDIE instructional design model, they surveyed parents' needs, then created an Urdu-language online module on six oral health topics.

Six experts rated the content highly, with item validity scores from 0.83 to 1.00 and a scale score of 0.94, and fifteen parents gave face validity of 0.97. The authors present the module as an accessible answer to scarce dental education in Pakistan, while noting that trials must still prove it changes brushing, diet, and disease outcomes.
pmc-13301018:
H Matsuura and co-authors weigh the safety of doing atrial fibrillation ablation during an acute heart failure admission, in a 2026 nationwide Japanese analysis. Their linked registries captured first ablations from 2012 to 2024. After exclusions, they compared 3,696 patients ablated mid-crisis against 47,241 with a heart failure history who came in electively. Weighting was used to balance obvious differences.

Even after adjustment, ablating during the acute admission carried clearly higher risk. The odds of a clot event were about two and a half times the elective figure. Major bleeding odds ran about seventy percent higher. In hospital death odds were roughly two and a half times as high. Yet absolute gaps stayed modest, near one percentage point for clot events. The authors advise a careful risk benefit conversation and individualized timing rather than reflex early intervention during decompensation.
pmc-13301418:
Sixteen minutes of bodyweight exercise a week may build fitness as well as ninety, Joshua J. Aube and colleagues report in a 2026 randomized non-inferiority trial. Fifty-eight healthy young adults followed one of three published protocols, nicknamed TAB, 5BX, and AMRAP, at 16, 27, or 90 minutes weekly for six weeks. Fitness was read from peak work rate on a cycle test.

Both short protocols proved non-inferior to the long one for estimated peak oxygen uptake, with confidence intervals staying clear of the preset shortfall line. The authors read the result as backing for minimalist training, which strips away the time, space, and cost barriers that keep many people inactive. Replication in wider groups comes next.
pmc-13301718:
Children with heart defects often swallow a handful of medicines daily, Kim Sarah Fritz and colleagues document in a 2026 nationwide German survey. Run with the national congenital heart defect register in late 2021, the poll covered 894 patients aged six to seventeen. Families listed current drugs, which the team sorted by class and screened for risky combinations.

Of the 372 children taking any medication, 179 met the study's polypharmacy bar of two or more drugs, a 48.1 percent share. Heavier regimens clustered in sicker children with more added conditions. Flagged combinations could clash through kidney electrolyte shifts, protein binding, liver enzyme paths, or stacked effects, prompting calls for routine medication reviews.
pmc-13301818:
Pratik Vijay Shah and co-authors update knowledge on classic hairy cell leukemia and its close relatives in a 2026 review. These are rare, slow-growing cancers of B cells with distinctive looks under the microscope and distinct molecular fingerprints. Treatment has changed greatly over the past decade as targeted drugs arrived.

Coverage runs from cell origins and the signalling pathways that drive growth through modern tests such as flow cytometry and gene sequencing. Most classic cases carry a specific BRAF mutation that switches on growth signals, and the review explains how that shapes therapy choices. Established purine-based chemotherapy is set beside newer targeted inhibitors and immune treatments. Relapse and drug resistance remain open problems that the authors flag for future work.
pmc-13302418:
S Ruiperez-Campillo and colleagues present, in a 2026 study, an artificial intelligence system that tracks wave patterns inside fibrillating hearts to find where the chaos is driven from. Ablation works best when doctors target the right sites, yet sources outside the lung veins are hard to locate. Brief moments of organised wave activity may betray those sources.

The system learned from more than ten million heart signals to separate nearby activity from distant noise, then mapped wave directions in 174 patients. Waves leaving the lung veins marked patients whose vein isolation worked better than in patients whose waves entered the veins. At spots where ablation stopped the rhythm, waves also tended to flow outward. The authors call for prospective testing of this guidance.
pmc-13303018:
Mindful scrolling can now be scored, Mengyu Li and Hao Chen build in a 2026 scale-development study with Chinese Douyin users. Two linked studies drafted items, refined them, and then checked the finished scale against psychological wellbeing. The goal was a measure of using social media with intention rather than compulsion, a habit tied to fewer mental health harms.

Nineteen items survived, grouping into four factors: nonjudgement, attention-acceptance, description, and nonreaction. Every factor related positively to users' psychological wellbeing, supporting the scale's validity. The authors say intervention designers can build mindfulness training for social media around these four dimensions, and researchers finally have a common yardstick for the construct.
pmc-13303818:
Milton Gordillo-Romero and co-authors test how added light colors interact with plant type and salt stress in quinoa in a 2026 growth study. Quinoa tolerates drought and salt well, yet the role of light quality in that tolerance has barely been studied.

Four plant types, two shop varieties and two Ecuadorian landraces, grew under white light plus narrow red, far-red, or blue additions, with and without moderate salt. Added far-red made plants taller in both settings. Added red boosted mass without salt but not with it, while added blue softened salt harm. Breeding that targets light sensors may strengthen future crops.
pmc-13303918:
Julian D Olden and a large team assemble, in a 2026 review, the first global history of paying bounties for killing unwanted species. Governments have enlisted the public this way for centuries, against everything from wolves to invasive fish. The authors gathered records spanning eight hundred years.

At least 283 species were targeted by 449 programmes across sixty countries, covering mammals, birds, plants, insects, and more. Motives split between protecting livelihoods, defending ecosystems, and guarding human health. Designs ranged from carefully managed schemes to hasty reactions with no follow-up. Side effects included killing the wrong species and, perversely, helping targets thrive, while fraud surfaced in several programmes. Keeping the public engaged proved a constant struggle.
pmc-13304218:
Mohammad Ahmad Al-Jazi, Anders Kildahl Johannsen, and Anne Brink Behrndtz describe a 2026 case of neck artery tearing as the first sign of two overlapping immune diseases. Stroke in young adults often stems from artery splits, clotting problems, or body-wide inflammation rather than clogged vessels.

A 37-year-old woman with no heart risk factors developed weakness on one side. Days earlier she had painful leg nodules, low fever, and raised inflammation markers. Workup linked the torn carotid artery to both sarcoidosis and antiphospholipid syndrome acting together. Broad testing and long-term blood thinning are highlighted for such young stroke cases.
pmc-13305218:
Nicolás Ateaga and colleagues make copper nanoparticles inside 3D-printed flow channels in a 2026 study of greener production. Tiny copper particles serve electronics and medicine, but steady control of size and shape in flowing systems is demanding.

Printed reactors with winding channels mixed ingredients smoothly under slow, layered flow. Planned experiments varied reducer dose, channel shape, and acidity. An alkaline mix at a set reducer ratio gave the most even, round, and smallest particles. Flow speed and stabilizer checks fine-tuned purity further. Cheap printed tools could scale clean nanoparticle making.
pmc-13305918:
Kevin Hung built a combined heart and pupil model in 2026 to explain why pupil size varies over time. Pupil change has been proposed as a contact-free sign of autonomic balance, yet its bodily sources have stayed unclear.

A proven circulation model was joined to a mechanical model of iris muscle, fed by breathing and pressure-sensor signals through an indirect nerve path. Simulations reproduced breathing-linked widening and calming nerve effects, and a classic nonlinear trait arose from iris mechanics itself. Rhythm bands in pupil signals resembled heart rhythm bands, though their size depended heavily on body state and measurement setup.
pmc-13306318:
Wei Du taught a robot a packing layout from one human demonstration in a 2026 study of sorting and filling. Factories need robots that copy an in-box arrangement even when boxes move, objects vary or work is interrupted.

During teaching, vision tools sharpen box and object outlines and record category, count and relative position and angle for each item. Those relations become a reusable box-centred template that transfers to new boxes at other poses. Live tracking updates free slots and flags missing or extra objects, and transfer trials reached strong placement accuracy in reported tests.
pmc-13306518:
Sidi Mohamed Mohi Dine designed an energy-saving routing scheme for wireless sensor networks in a 2026 study. Clustering and path choice decide how long a network lives before its first node runs out of power.

Shortest-path routing sets efficient routes, while a discrete swarm search hunts the cluster layout that stretches lifetime furthest. A similarity index watches how close swarm members sit to the best layout, triggering a shake-up when the group stalls too early. Simulations showed richer search movement and longer stable operation in reported results, delaying first node death.
pmc-13306718:
Yuanyuan Zhang improved a vision model for spotting apple leaf disease in a 2026 study. Eye inspection in orchards is slow and subjective, so the team added a sparse attention module to the YOLOv11 detector backbone.

Training used 7594 images across black rot, rust, scab and healthy leaves in the reported dataset. Scores reached precision of 0.973, recall of 0.978 and a top detection average of 0.991 in the authors' tests, beating four rival versions. A desktop viewing tool was also built so orchard staff can run the detector in the field. The tool may help farm staff act fast when sick leaves first show.
pmc-13306918:
Farhana Afroze assembled DNA networks actively with molecular machines in a 2026 study. Living systems build far-from-balance materials by spending energy through stepwise chemical and mechanical work, a feat plain self-assembly rarely matches.

A DNA-copying enzyme grows fresh DNA while kinesin motors drag microtubule tracks, pulling and linking strands into fibrous two-dimensional webs. Tests and simulations showed both DNA stickiness and motor force were needed for the tangled hierarchy that formed. The result points toward synthetic materials built by powered nanomachines rather than settling alone. Such webs could one day grow inside the body with no seed cells at all.
pmc-13307118:
Ye Jun Park and a ten-author team ask in 2026 whether ultrasound can measure liver capsule thickening in Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, an inflammation of the liver surface tied to pelvic infection. Diagnosis now leans on CT scanning, which brings radiation and contrast dye. Capsule thickness was compared between the two methods in women with the condition.

Ultrasound readings appeared to track CT results, suggesting the simpler scan carries supportive diagnostic information. Ultrasound is cheap, widely available, and radiation-free, which suits the young women most often affected. Pain in the upper right abdomen overlaps with many other conditions, so extra signs help clinicians decide. The authors stop short of replacing CT and call for validation in larger, clinically realistic groups. A standardised ultrasound measure, they argue, has been missing from work on this syndrome.
pmc-13308118:
Xiaona Li and co-authors compare in 2026 how three tiny particle pollutants harm the green alga Chlorella vulgaris at low and high doses in water. The set covers plastic particles, silver particles, and titanium dioxide particles, each at 100 micrograms per litre and at 10 milligrams per litre.

Each type harmed the alga by a unlike route in their tests across both doses. Plastic bits mainly clumped with cells, shaded them, and stirred surface slime over a long span. Silver bits changed form inside cells and drove cell stress and membrane harm. Titanium bits stayed available and kept stress high. Stress alone thus fails to capture the full harm, so source based control matters.
pmc-13308618:
Shujuan Liu and colleagues report in 2026 a catalyst trick that flips amide making from one carbon unit to two, by adding oxygen gaps to a palladium doped indium oxide. Amide links sit in many drugs, and picking single versus double insertion of carbon monoxide has long been hard to control.

Gaps far from the active site pulled charge across the surface, stretched key bonds, and eased the second carbon unit in for the double path. The tuned catalyst made 130 varied amides and double amides with strong yield, choice, and reuse across runs. Far site tuning may thus steer other reactions where near site tweaks fall short of the mark.
pmc-13309618:
Xiaoyun Xu and colleagues interview neurology staff in China about patient self-care for long-term brain disorders in a 2026 study. The proactive health idea asks patients to take an active role in daily disease control. Staff views shape how far that idea reaches the clinic floor.

Fifteen professionals at a large hospital took part in semi-structured interviews, read with a seven-step method for lived experience. Five themes emerged, covering teaching and motivation, what drives patient follow-through, tools that help and hinder, weak outside support, and system barriers like short visit time. Staff backed the idea but felt under-supported. The authors call for support at clinic, community, and policy levels.
pmc-13311018:
Yusuf Aggour and Roberto Salguero-Gómez propose a layered frame for judging anti aging plans in a 2026 paper. Aging science has deep facts on cell hallmarks but no shared frame that joins evolution views with practical scoring of new plans. Their Aging Onion sorts aging traits into layers along two broad axes.

One axis tracks growth programs that stay on too long, and the other tracks weak upkeep of body tissue. Food sensing serves as the first test field, with calorie limits as a broad benchmark and rapamycin as a narrow drug contrast. The axes help explain why the two plans differ in reach. Wider tests must show the frame holds.
pmc-13311118:
Ibukun-Oluwa Omolade Abejirinde led a 2026 study that frames how to judge a smart wound care tool in a rural health network. Hard to heal wounds strain rural services, where specialists are few and travel is long. A photo based smart tool may standardize checks, yet rural proof on value and uptake is thin.

Work joined a literature scan, partner meetings, and talks with frontline staff and senior leaders in the Brightshores system. Shared gains and outcome picks were sorted into an evaluation frame. Staff views flagged workflow fit, scaling strain, and equity aims. The frame should guide fair rollout and later impact checks.
pmc-13311218:
Ahmed Ramiz Baykan and co-authors in 2026 report a rat study on whether ATP can shield the liver from harm caused by olaparib, a cancer drug. The drug can injure liver cells through oxidative stress.

Twenty-four male rats were split into four groups: healthy, drug only, drug plus ATP, and drug plus melatonin, over 14 days. Liver tissue was tested for damage and defense markers, and blood tests checked liver enzymes. The design lets the team weigh ATP against a known protective agent. Findings could point to a simple add-on that guards the liver during cancer treatment.
pmc-13311418:
Maradona M Mashigo and co-authors offer a 2026 narrative review of the posterior interosseous artery flap, a reconstructive option for wounds of the hand and wrist. The flap moves thin, flexible tissue from the forearm while leaving the forearm's main arteries intact. The review covers the flap's anatomy, surgical technique, uses, outcomes, and complications, and weighs it against other regional and free flap choices.

Published series report generally good function and appearance, with dependable coverage for the back of the hand, the wrist, the thumb, and the first web space. Venous congestion and variation in the blood vessel pattern remain the main drawbacks, though planning and technique changes can lower those risks. Because most evidence comes from retrospective case series, the authors call for prospective comparisons to pin down the flap's place in modern upper limb surgery.
pmc-13311618:
Hao Liu and co-authors build a 2026 prediction model for relapse in lupus nephritis, a kidney complication of lupus. Spotting who will relapse could guide closer follow-up and drug choices.

The cohort held 831 biopsy-proven patients treated at Xijing Hospital from 2005 to 2024, of whom 27.08 percent relapsed in follow-up. Those who relapsed were younger at onset and had higher disease activity and protein in the urine. A LASSO-Cox method picked the strongest predictors and shaped them into a risk model for use at twelve months after biopsy. Internal checks tested how well the model holds up.
pmc-13311818:
Yen-Chen Lin and colleagues present their 2026 study on a combined blood and waist index and heart relaxation in fit military personnel. The index joins triglycerides, glucose, and waist-to-height ratio.

The cross-sectional study covered 176 personnel aged 18 to 44 who had blood tests, heart ultrasounds, and fitness tests. Men above the middle index value were older, with worse metabolic profiles, slower heart relaxation measures, and poorer run and strength results. The index was the leading predictor of one key relaxation measure in adjusted models. Even in fit young adults, the simple index flags early heart stiffness.
pmc-13311918:
Zhichao Zheng and co-authors, in 2026, report a study on a wound dressing spun in place that slowly releases LECT2, a protein tied to inflammation and vessel growth. Chronic wounds stall in a harsh, oxygen-radical-rich setting.

The coaxial fiber dressing pairs two polymer blends in core and shell for steady release. In cell work, LECT2 mopped up reactive oxygen through the NRF2/SOD path, helped vessel growth under stress, and killed staph bacteria, including resistant strains. It also pushed macrophages toward a repair mode. Animal wounds closed faster with better skin regrowth and new vessels, making the dressing a multi-tool candidate.
pmc-13312818:
Sara Jahani and colleagues describe, in a 2026 materials study, a gentle route to hollow carbon nanoparticles whose shape can be chosen in advance. Earlier methods rarely offered precise shape control, so the team grew the particles on self-assembled soap-like templates inside a reverse microemulsion of surfactant, water, and hexane.

By adjusting the water content, the templates settle into spheres, cylinders, or flat lamellar sheets. A butadiyne monomer then polymerizes at room temperature on the template surface, and simple washing removes the scaffold, leaving hollow carbon copies in the same three shapes. Electron microscopy confirmed the hollow forms, and a battery of spectroscopy methods showed the walls consist mainly of sp2-hybridized carbon. The authors present the approach as a simple shape-writing tool for carbon nanomaterials aimed at imaging, delivery, sensing, and catalysis.
pmc-13313318:
Sarah Juul and co-authors report a 2026 nationwide Danish study of heart-caused stroke in children, a subject with surprisingly thin data. The team reviewed every child registered with a stroke diagnosis from 2013 to 2020. Cases were confirmed from medical records and classified with a standardized childhood scheme. Outcomes were followed for two years.

Cardioembolic stroke accounted for 31 of 126 arterial ischemic strokes. That is an incidence of 0.28 per 100,000 person-years in the population studied. Congenital heart disease underlay most cases, appearing in 26 of the 31 children. Large vessel blockages showed up more often in the heart-caused group among children who had vessel imaging. Rates of lasting neurological impairment looked similar between groups overall. Children with definite cardioembolic stroke, though, fared worse before severity adjustment. The authors call for stronger prevention aimed at children with heart disease.
pmc-13313818:
Hadeer M. Mossa and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a suspension culture platform for growing lumpy skin disease virus. The cattle pathogen's spread from Africa and the Middle East into Europe and Asia has strained vaccine supply. Vaccine production has relied on cells grown stuck to surfaces, which caps scale. No suspension version of the Vero cell line exists. The team adapted the cells to live and divide while floating.

The adapted cells stayed viable and reached high densities in culture. Infected after nine passages, they yielded virus titers of 6.85 in log units per milliliter at 96 hours. That sits above the 5.5 log figure from surface-grown cells. The yield was verified by damage observation, genetic quantification, and infectivity titration. The team mapped the infection dose and cell density that maximized output. They frame the platform as a route to bioreactor-scale vaccine production, while noting industrial confirmation still lies ahead.
pmc-13314318:
Rafael Castro-Fuentes and Rosy Socas-Perez ask whether domestication made dogs more vulnerable to age-related cognitive decline than their wolf ancestors. Their 2025 database-driven study compares risk factors shared by canine cognitive dysfunction and human Alzheimer's disease.

Dogs share genetics and lifestyle with humans, and their cognitive syndrome mirrors Alzheimer's in symptoms, brain changes, and risk factors. The authors compared ageing, oxidative stress, inflammation, sleep disturbance, and gum disease impacts in domestic dogs versus captive or semi-captive grey wolves. Dogs showed more pronounced levels of the key risk factors. The authors suggest wolves may be partly protected from cognitive decline, while noting wolf ageing data remain very limited.
pmc-13314618:
Linlin Zheng and colleagues test mangiferin, a plant compound, against fatty liver disease in mice as a 2026 study. The disease packs the liver with fat, and safe, working treatments are still few.

Past work showed mangiferin eases fatty liver through other paths, but its play on bile acids was untested. The team fed mice a high-fat diet to build the disease, then treated them with mangiferin at a dose of 100 mg per kg as stated in the report. The compound clearly eased the liver state, by the measures reported. Gene sequencing of gut microbes and docking models traced the effect to the FXR signal path, which steers bile acid flow, plus a reshaped gut mix. The work names a food-derived option worth deeper study.
pmc-13316018:
Min Ji Kim and colleagues used court records in 2026 to track unlicensed medical practice in South Korea, a hidden threat to patient safety that normal surveillance misses. Their legal infoveillance approach turns criminal court decisions into public health data with machine learning help.

The study covered 1,532 court decisions with convictions from 2005 to 2023. A machine extraction pipeline with human checking converted free legal text into structured legal and medical variables. Analyses ran at case, charge, defendant, and legal levels, showing how judicial data can reveal patterns in underground medical activity over time.
pmc-13316218:
Brett David Cohen and colleagues mined nearly two million hospital stays in 2026 to weigh how atrial fibrillation and heart conditions affect death during acute pancreatitis. Using the National Inpatient Sample from 2016 to 2022, they examined twelve cardiovascular risk factors in adult stays with pancreatitis as the main diagnosis.

Among 1,919,159 weighted stays, overall death was 0.59 percent of the total in the reported figures. After full adjustment, cerebrovascular disease carried the highest odds ratio at 2.83 in the reported analysis, followed by atrial fibrillation at 2.10 in that same analysis. A cumulative count of risk factors was also built.
pmc-13316618:
Andrés M Rubiano leads an international panel behind 2026 consensus guidance on two fluid-drainage operations for severe head injury, ventriculostomy and cisternostomy. Practice varied widely in when and how surgeons use them, a gap felt most in places with few resources.

The World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies panel, built from 16 expert neurosurgeons, worked through a structured Delphi vote after a full literature review. Agreement needed at least three quarters of the panel, and 69 statements passed. Ventriculostomy earned backing as an early step when drainage is needed, while cisternostomy fits selected patients with heavy bleeding around the brain. Step-by-step algorithms accompany both, giving trauma teams a shared playbook.
pmc-13316818:
Aman Gul and colleagues devised, in a 2026 study, a simple scoring chart to predict moderate-to-severe sleep apnea in western China, without needing a full sleep lab first. Their data came from 11,030 patients who had overnight sleep studies between 2012 and 2020.

Patients split into a building group of 7,721 and a checking group of 3,309. Six factors survived as solo predictors: age, body mass index, neck size, male sex, high blood pressure, and diabetes. The chart fit both groups well in their tests, though accuracy was modest, stronger in the building group than the checking one. The authors offer it as a triage aid for busy clinics deciding who needs testing first.
pmc-13317418:
Xiwen Yang and Sibin Yi ask whether regular exercise before surgery aids mental health after surgery for patients with a mid risk wound class. Mood after surgery shapes recovery, and prior habits may play a role. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

Nearly five hundred patients at one large hospital were split by a survey into exercise and non exercise groups. Two weeks after surgery, mood and life quality were scored. The exercise group showed far lower anxiety scores and higher mental and physical summary scores. In the exercise group, more prior exercise linked to less anxiety and better mental scores, the authors report.
pmc-13318018:
Francis Ssenkuba and colleagues survey, in a 2026 field study, snails and other molluscs in five small volcanic lakes of Uganda and Rwanda. These lakes are overlooked corners of the Albertine Rift hotspot famed for unique wildlife. Big Rift lakes draw the research money, leaving these smaller waters unmapped.

Combining shell study, DNA barcodes, and ecology, they found surprisingly rich mollusc life, mostly widespread species with Nilotic roots. Invaded lakes showed communities growing more alike, a flattening pattern consistent with invaders such as the North American crayfish and two foreign snails, though lake differences cloud the blame. Farming damage, pollution, and building add pressure. The authors urge a full regional survey with DNA water sampling before losses mount.
pmc-13318618:
Ji Eun Jun and co-authors report a 2026 randomised pilot study comparing two add-on drugs for type 2 diabetes that stayed uncontrolled on metformin and a sulfonylurea: weekly dulaglutide or daily empagliflozin. The main phase ran twelve weeks, with observation out to week 36.

Twenty-four patients finished the main phase, thirteen on dulaglutide and eleven on empagliflozin. Both drugs lowered the blood sugar marker HbA1c by week 12, with no clear gap between them. Empagliflozin cut insulin resistance and brought earlier weight and fat loss, while dulaglutide raised a marker of insulin-producing cell function and lost weight more gradually. Blood metabolite and gut microbe checks hinted at modest differing patterns worth testing in bigger studies.
pmc-13319018:
Yuzhen Gao and colleagues present a 2026 one-year longitudinal study of first-year university students in China. They track how critical thinking and academic self-concept influence each other over time. Both are then linked to later student engagement. A large sample of 3,437 students answered measures at two waves.

The two traits pushed in opposite directions. Critical thinking predicted a later dip in academic self-concept. A stronger self-concept, in turn, predicted later growth in critical thinking. Critical thinking also predicted higher engagement at the second wave. Academic self-concept predicted lower later engagement, surprisingly. Patterns held across mathematics and English subjects. The authors frame engagement as a moving system, not a fixed trait, during the university transition.
pmc-13319718:
Rebecca Ertl and colleagues report, in 2026, a first-trimester blood test approach for predicting preeclampsia, a dangerous pregnancy condition involving high blood pressure. Current screening predicts early disease well but performs poorly for disease arising at term, and it depends on ultrasound and blood measurements that limit scale.

The study used cell-free DNA already collected during routine prenatal testing in 125 pregnancies, sampled at eleven to fourteen weeks. Sequencing that reads fragment patterns and chemical marks allowed tissue-resolved analysis. Separate learning models were built for early and term disease. Both models discriminated cases well, beating the standard score clearly for term disease. A simulation in a large population explored predictive values. The authors propose one molecular test for the full spectrum.
pmc-13320018:
Zara Latif and co-authors score heart health in women of child bearing age in the United States in a 2026 study using a national survey. Poor outcomes in pregnancy drive high mother death rates, and heart health before and around pregnancy shapes much of that risk. An eight part score from a national heart group was used to grade diet, activity, sleep, and body measures.

Survey waves from 2015 to 2023 held 3992 women age 20 to 44, standing for a far larger national group. Average scores sat in the middle range for all groups. Pregnant women scored lowest of all, below new mothers, nursing mothers, and women not pregnant, and their swelling marker ran highest too. Mid level heart health at these ages leaves much room to lift.
pmc-13320118:
Shixiang Qiu and co-authors test ozone treated water on liver cancer cells in a 2026 lab study of cell death pathways. Liver cancer grows and spreads fast and carries a poor outlook, and ozone water has shown hints of anti tumor power with unclear routes. A growth signal chain that helps cancer cells live and move was the prime suspect.

Two liver cancer cell lines were dosed with ozone water and checked for growth, drift, invasion, and death. One dose held for a day cut all three growth traits and near doubled the share of dying cells in one line. Signal chain parts fell after dosing, which ties the effect to that chain. Animal and safety work must follow before care use can be weighed.
pmc-13320318:
Lea Fierley and co-authors train learning models to forecast high blood pressure and re narrowing in a pinched aorta in a 2026 study from Berlin. The birth defect narrows the main artery and stays a top cause of high pressure in the young. Return narrowing hits up to one third of people over a lifetime despite standard care. Early flags for who will relapse could sharpen follow up.

Records, heart scans, and long follow up from 218 visits by 160 people fed seven model types, tuned and split into training and hold out sets. Tree based and margin based models led the pack, sorting return cases with strong marks in the hold out set on the scale used. The models may help clinics aim scans and visits at those at most risk.
pmc-13320518:
Jamal Hassan Mohamoud and a large team measure, in 2026, sexually transmitted infections among women in Mogadishu, Somalia, using gene-based tests. Such infections often cause no symptoms yet can lead to infertility, pregnancy problems and higher HIV risk. Local prevalence data and risk patterns were limited.

Testing covered chlamydia, gonorrhoea and Ureaplasma species. Overall, more than a third of women tested positive for at least one infection. Ureaplasma was by far the most often detected organism, while the other two bacteria were found by polymerase chain reaction testing in smaller shares. Women in the older age band studied had higher odds of a positive result. Lower education level was tied to gonorrhoea infection in particular. The authors frame screening and schooling as top needs.
pmc-13321018:
Chang Hee Baek and colleagues study, in 2026, whether patients return to work and sport after a tendon transfer for irreparable shoulder tears. The operation moves the latissimus dorsi tendon to replace a torn rotator cuff at the back of the shoulder. Such tears especially limit people with physical jobs or active hobbies.

Eighty-three patients treated between 2012 and 2020 answered structured questionnaires and completed standard shoulder scores, with average follow-up over five years. Most returned to work, though many at a reduced level, and return was slower and less complete for heavy labourers. About nine in ten returned to sport, most fully. A re-tear of the transferred tendon predicted poorer return on both measures, and heavier work demands also reduced work return. Shoulder function scores improved after surgery.
pmc-13321218:
Xhulio Prifti and colleagues compare, in 2026, two generations of locking plates used to fix fractures near the shoulder joint. Such fractures are common in older adults, and plate position and stability affect healing. A newer plate design promises better hold, but medium-term comparisons were limited.

The retrospective study covered 152 consecutive patients treated at a level one trauma centre between 2007 and 2023, most with the first-generation plate. Groups matched on age, smoking, follow-up and initial reduction quality. At final follow-up averaging two years, the newer plate sat lower relative to a shoulder landmark and showed less secondary loss of the neck-shaft angle, meaning the head fragment had drifted less. The authors judge the newer position acceptable, with less displacement over time.
pmc-13321518:
Na Li and co-authors test a low dose gene therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy in a 2026 mouse study. The disease stems from missing dystrophin, a protein that shields muscle from damage. Gene therapy helps but often needs high virus doses that raise toxicity risks. The team used a muscle seeking virus shell to deliver a small engineered utrophin, a stand-in protein.

Newborn mdx mice got a single low dose, and tissues were checked four weeks later. The stand-in protein appeared across skeletal muscle, diaphragm, and heart, with little spill into the liver. Damage markers in blood and muscle fell, dye leakage dropped, and grip and treadmill performance improved, which supports low dose delivery.
pmc-13322818:
Bingrun Li and co-authors set out a new way to group skin diseases linked to the JAK-STAT signalling path, in a 2026 review. Conditions covered include atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, alopecia areata and vitiligo, where many signal proteins act through this path.

Older grouping by T helper cell type does not separate signals that depend on JAK-STAT from those that do not, which limits its use when choosing targeted drugs. The authors add JAK-linked signal modules into that older scheme and review how these diseases develop. They also weigh trial evidence for JAK blocker drugs such as abrocitinib, upadacitinib and baricitinib, aiming to guide safer and more logical use in clinics.
pmc-13322918:
Qionghui Wu and co-authors single out RAC1 as a prognostic marker and drug target in glioblastoma, in a 2026 analysis spanning cancer databases and cell work. RAC1 helps control cell movement and was checked across cancer types using TCGA, HPA, CPTAC and GEO data.

Glioblastoma showed the strongest link between RAC1 and patient outcome, and RAC1 alone among its family passed their survival models with a notably high risk estimate. Blocking RAC1 activation slowed growth, movement and invasion in tumour cells without lowering total RAC1 protein. Single-cell data placed RAC1 mainly in a neural progenitor-like tumour state. Docking work and cell tests nominated the drug palbociclib as a candidate worth further study.
pmc-13323618:
Joseph Rigdon and team present a flexible method for hunting data errors in multicenter clinical trials, where quality checks must keep pace with growing size and complexity. Their 2026 paper lays out a three-phase collaboration between the data coordinating center and the clinical sites. Participant data are first screened one variable at a time for extreme values outside range checks. They are then checked jointly with machine learning across related variables. They are reviewed at site level against demographic-adjusted expectations.

Applied to the MoTrPAC exercise study, the method sifted more than 1.9 million observations from 1,029 people and flagged univariate, multivariate, and site-level outliers that current checks had missed. Findings go back to sites for discussion, and procedures can change where needed. The authors advise running the algorithm on a subset early in a trial and repeating it at intervals, so errors surface while they can still be fixed.
pmc-13324318:
Kai Uchida and Masami Yokota Hirai mapped the missing steps in making tectorigenin, a valuable isoflavone from kudzu flowers. Their 2026 study notes that kudzu produces several beneficial isoflavones in a tissue-specific pattern, with it and its derivatives gathering mainly in flowers. Demand for it is high, but its biosynthesis had not been worked out, blocking large-scale production.

Using transcriptome analysis and enzyme assays, the team found a new isoflavone 6-hydroxylase and an isoflavone O-methyltransferase behind its synthesis. They then engineered yeast to express the genes for these enzymes, producing it from cheaper genistein at 40 mg per liter after 72 hours. The same route yielded glycitein and afrormosin from daidzein and formononetin, opening a practical path to large-scale supply.
pmc-13325118:
Daniel Ananias Reis de Campos and co-authors build a low-cost dopamine sensor from gherkin extract in a 2026 study. Dopamine imbalance marks Parkinson disease and several mental disorders, and standard lab assays are slow.

Peroxidase enzyme from gherkin was fixed onto titanate nanowires to make four biosensors. Square-wave voltammetry gave a straight response from 5 to 65.4 micromoles per liter for each version. The best unit detected down to 0.400 micromoles per liter with strong sensitivity. On a shop-bought sample it read 4.99 mg per mL against a 5 mg per mL label, an error of just minus 0.2 percent. Urea and uric acid barely disturbed the signal.
pmc-13326118:

pmc-13328518:

pmc-13332118:

pmc-13333518:

pmc-13335618:

pmc-13336018:

pmc-13337718:

pmc-13337818:

pmc-13340318:

pmc-13373818:

pmc-13375818:

pmc-13375918:

pmc-13377218:

pmc-13379318:

pmc-13385318:

pmc-13386818:

pmc-13389418:

Their patient was a 41-year-old mother of four, induced at 39 weeks for diet-controlled gestational diabetes.

All four earlier births had been uncomplicated vaginal deliveries. The team weighed intervention risks against the benign, labor-related nature of the swelling and, with interdisciplinary input and shared decision-making, backed vaginal birth, which succeeded without cervical trauma. A focused literature search found no prior report matching the scenario. The authors offer the case as a judgment anchor for a frightening, uncertain presentation.
pmc-13403418:
Zhipeng Pei headed a 2026 review of how heat moves through ceramics built to survive extreme heat. Such materials serve in fast aircraft, nuclear plants, and new power systems. Their worth depends on how well they carry, block, and shed heat at very high temperatures.

The review covers heat carried by lattice waves, by electrons, and by light, plus how grain size and mix shift those flows. It also weighs use of the ceramics to turn heat into electric power. Computer learning guided by physics may speed the hunt for better mixes. Open problems include making the materials at scale and shaping their inner structure with care.
pmc-13403518:
Carolina Braga Moura headed a 2026 review of how dementia behavior symptoms weigh on family caregivers. Odd or hard behavior often causes caregivers more strain than memory loss itself. The review pulled studies that scored symptoms, caregiver distress, and total burden with standard scales.

Five studies fed the distress analysis and seven fed the burden analysis. Higher symptom scores tracked closely with higher caregiver distress. Average burden scores sat at a moderate level across studies, with wide spread between them. The authors ask for finer tools that capture what caregivers face day to day, so support can match real needs.
pmc-13403718:
Hanxue Chen and co-authors traced in 2026 how a gene-marking protein times the switch from nerve cells to support cells in the mouse brain. Faults in this protein cause a syndrome with small head size and learning trouble. Developing cortex first makes nerve cells, then turns to star-shaped support cells.

Removing the protein in mice cut support cell output late in development, while extra amounts raised it. The protein placed a chemical mark that kept a growth sensor gene on, feeding a key signal chain. A drug that fired that chain rescued the fault in dishes and in mice. Treated model mice still showed learning gaps without rescue.
pmc-13403818:
Hassan, Abdulla, and Qadir test, in 2026, a culturally adapted workplace education program for weight management at two universities in Erbil, Iraq, where about 65.7 percent of adults nationally are overweight or obese. Two hundred employees with body mass index at or above 25 self-selected into intervention or control groups of 100 each. The program delivered five individual sessions of 35 to 40 minutes over 12 weeks, built on the Theory of Planned Behavior, while controls received written materials only.

The intervention group lost a mean of 7.46 kilograms while controls gained 0.58 kilograms, an adjusted difference of about 8 kilograms with a very large effect size in the analysis. About 79 percent of participants lost at least 5 percent of weight, versus none of the controls, and 41 percent lost at least 10 percent during the program. Lipids, glucose, dietary quality, and quality of life improved, retention was perfect, and improved dietary quality accounted for 82 percent of the body mass index effect.
pmc-13404218:
This 2026 public health round-up collects short World Health Organization news items on global health policy. It leads with updated data on air pollution and health drawn from the sustainable development goal indicators, and summarises new WHO guidelines on lowering the risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

The air pollution data show fine particle levels fell globally until 2020 but have since stalled, with low- and middle-income countries still facing far higher exposure than rich nations. The dementia guidelines note that more than 57 million people live with dementia. Up to 45 percent of cases may link to changeable risk factors such as smoking, inactivity, and high blood pressure. The recommendations cover physical activity, diet, tobacco and alcohol, and managing blood pressure, diabetes, and cholesterol.
pmc-13405018:
Jayashankar Rakshitha and colleagues use artificial intelligence to predict obesity in Indian teenagers, reporting in 2026. Adolescence in India carries rising obesity shaped by family habits, sleep, mood and social setting. Checked prediction models for this group are scarce.

The school-based study covered 1,292 students aged 10 to 16 in two Karnataka districts. Because real cases were limited, generative tools created 1,500 synthetic records to enlarge training data, with quality and privacy checks applied. A stacked model combining XGBoost, TabNet and TabTransformer reached accuracy of 0.977 in the reported testing, with sensitivity and specificity also high. The authors present the model as a screening aid, pending checks beyond these districts.
pmc-13405118:
Shadreck Mwale and colleagues set out a 2026 protocol on dementia support for African and African-Caribbean people in the United Kingdom. This group often reaches services late, in crisis, and faces poor outcomes and higher rates of institutional care. The study asks what support they need and what delay costs them.

Work combines a co-produced evidence synthesis with narrative interviews and field observation. Forty people with dementia across four council areas will take part in repeated interviews, some joined by family carers. Researchers will also spend 30 days in each local social care team watching how support is offered. An intersectionality lens guides attention to overlapping disadvantages.
pmc-13405818:
Ayse Ozkan and Seda Demir test carvacrol, a herb compound from thyme kin, against brain swelling in mice, in a 2026 trial. A germ toxin, LPS, fires up the hippocampus, the brain's memory hub, and harms memory. Fats called prostaglandins and alarm proteins drive much of that harm.

Mice got salt water, toxin alone, or toxin plus carvacrol by mouth for seven days. Movement and anxiety tests showed no group gaps, which rules out mere drowsiness. A Y-maze with a new arm probed memory. Brain samples were checked for three prostaglandins and two alarm proteins. The design asks if the compound calms that fat-and-alarm axis in the brain.
pmc-13405918:
Al Robiullah and colleagues ask what college students actually want to hear after failing, in 2026 research across two studies. Instructors respond to poor grades in very different ways, and those messages shape motivation and trust. Students and faculty rated scripted replies to a bad exam result.

Three reply styles were compared: practical solutions, emotional validation and warm affirmation of the student. Students rated affirmation as most effective and solution-focused replies as least, the authors report. Validation sat in between. Faculty guesses about student preferences did not fully match, and open answers fill out what each side would say or wish to hear. The work speaks to everyday teaching practice.
pmc-13407018:
Sharon A. Poessel and co-authors draw on 34 years of field data in a 2026 study of the threatened Mohave ground squirrel, a desert species in the American Southwest. Drought, growing harsher with climate change, can reshape survival and movement for such animals, so the team modelled how climate and site conditions affect the population.

Field crews captured 1,404 squirrels at four sites. Males survived less well and wandered more than females, while juveniles survived less well than adults. Greener vegetation lifted male survival and reduced leaving at some sites. Numbers swung widely over the decades, sometimes dropping to zero locally, and adult counts at the two longest-watched sites ended about 70 percent below their early peaks, underlining the species' vulnerability.
pmc-13407818:
Yoshiya Tanaka and co-authors lay out a 2026 protocol. It covers a six-year Japanese study of a new antibody drug. The target is IgG4-related disease. This body-wide scarring condition can permanently damage organs. Steroids control it but flares force long exposure with heavy side effects; inebilizumab, which targets CD19 on immune cells, won Japanese approval in late 2025 after a successful controlled trial.

The study is called 4SigHT. It plans to enrol 100 patients starting the drug at up to forty sites. Follow-up runs through as many as fourteen visits. Care spans up to 312 weeks from March 2026. The main measure is the share of patients with an independently adjudicated flare by week 52. Secondary measures include steroid-free remission, flare timing and rate, extra treatments started, and total steroid dose.
pmc-13408118:
Anqi Liu, Jianing Liu, and Qing Wu ask, in 2026, whether a genetic score built from fractures themselves beats one borrowed from bone density for predicting broken bones. Standard FRAX assessment uses clinical factors, and earlier genetic add-ons inferred risk through estimated density. Fracture and density genetics only partly overlap, though. The team therefore built Bayesian polygenic scores from a fresh forearm-fracture genome study.

Two scoring frameworks were folded into FRAX and tested in 10,135 postmenopausal women from the Women's Health Initiative. Discrimination inched up from 0.683 to at most 0.693 in time-dependent accuracy, reclassification of individuals stayed low at under two percent, and net reclassification nonetheless improved significantly. Decision-curve analysis suggested benefit at some risk thresholds. A modest, real gain is the measured verdict.
pmc-13408318:
Kai Kean and co-authors take a snapshot of the viruses carried in the blood of healthy UK donors. Their 2026 retrospective study uses a targeted sequencing method to survey pooled plasma donations that NHS Blood and Transplant collected in England, beyond the few viruses donations are routinely screened for.

A representative sample of 5,064 donors, tested in pools of twenty-four over one month, carried far fewer viruses than expected: fewer than ten percent of known human bloodborne viruses appeared. Anelloviruses, a near-universal group of harmless viruses, were detected in 89 percent of pools. Human pegivirus type 1 had an estimated prevalence of 3.7 percent with high virus levels, while hepatitis C appeared once and herpesviruses and polyomaviruses stayed rare. The authors offer the profile as a baseline for judging transfusion transmission risk.
pmc-13409018:
Qin and a very large laser physics team report in 2026 a way to more than double the energy of protons fired by an intense laser. They borrow a push from the electrons racing ahead of them. Laser proton beams interest medicine and accelerator science, yet coupling more laser energy into the protons has been stubbornly hard. Their target was a foam with density near the critical value where laser light stops propagating.

The foam yielded electron bunches carrying enormous charge at high energy. As those electrons burst out of the target they radiated a transition field worth a sizeable fraction of a joule in terahertz waves. Its field strength passed a trillion volts per metre. Added to the usual charge-separation field, it lifted the proton cut-off to ninety million electron volts and stamped a plateau on the spectrum. Simulations confirmed the two fields working in synergy.
pmc-13409118:
Sapna Nayak, Sonali Verma, Ankur Mandelia, Preeti Dabadghao, and Margaret Zacharin present in 2026 three teenagers whose missing periods each concealed the same diagnosis behind a different mask. All three had the congenital absence of uterus and upper vagina known by the initials MRKH, with otherwise normal puberty. The first girl, also short, showed hormone levels suggesting her ovaries were failing, yet a normal estrogen level and repeat testing corrected that impression.

The second arrived with groin swellings that suggested a male-typical condition, but imaging found ovaries sitting in the groin and no uterus. The third had a large spinal mass with nerve symptoms alongside the missing internal structures. Careful repetition of hormone tests and detailed imaging untangled all three. The authors pair the cases with a review of their wider clinic cohort to catalogue the traps.
pmc-13410618:
Md. Asaduzzaman Rakib, Ying Yu, and Jianxiong Jiang review in 2026 a family of fat-processing enzymes as fresh targets for epilepsy drugs. About one person in fifty lives with epilepsy, and near a third keep having seizures despite current medicines. Brain inflammation after injury is now seen as a key spark for those seizures.

The enzymes, called lipoxygenases, turn a common fatty acid into signals that drive swelling, oxidative stress, and cell death in brain tissue. Two branches, 5-LOX and the 12/15-LOX pair, stand out in seizure biology and in linked mood problems. Blocking them calmed seizures in early animal work. The review weighs that evidence and sets out what safer, sharper blockers would need to prove.
pmc-13410718:
Nia Imani Bailey and co-authors pilot in 2026 a small school program that teaches teens about cancer and how to lower its risk. Cancer is rising among young people in the United States, yet many teens know little about habits that drive risk. Baseline gaps in the group were wide.

Only about a fifth of students knew vaccination helps prevent some cancers before the lessons began. Under half grasped risks from smoking and alcohol, and about half could spot warning symptoms. Two structured sessions lifted knowledge across the board, including genetic literacy and sun safety. The team argues that short, early teaching fits school timetables and could scale, especially where health literacy runs low.
pmc-13410918:
David Tougeron leads an international team asking in 2026 whether severe immune side effects during cancer immunotherapy link to better survival. The cancers studied carry a DNA repair fault that makes them respond well to checkpoint drugs. Those same drugs often inflame healthy organs, sometimes badly.

Records from 34 centers covered 1,175 patients with digestive cancers. About a tenth suffered severe immune side effects, most often in gut or liver, arising a median of about four months into treatment. Combination drug regimens raised that risk. Patients with severe events answered treatment more often than others. Restarting the drugs after such an event brought the inflammation back in over half of cases, a caution for clinics.
pmc-13411518:
Bo Zhao and colleagues tracked 3320 older adults in China across 2020 and 2023 to test how views on ageing and digital life shape health together. The pandemic pushed services online, which can open doors for older people or pile on stress when devices and support fall short.

People who viewed their own ageing more kindly tended to stay healthier, and digital skill lined up with better health, while mere access to devices told a less clear story. The paper urges age-friendly programs to teach real digital confidence, not just hand out connections.
pmc-13412018:
Yujie Xie and colleagues pit two large language models against each other in a 2026 multicentre study of thyroid ultrasound reports. Up to 60 percent of adults carry thyroid nodules, and nearly all prove harmless, so reading reports well matters. The team fed 1,063 text reports from three centres to ChatGPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1, asking each model to judge benign versus malignant, assign a C-TIRADS class, and suggest management.

DeepSeek-R1 showed higher sensitivity and accuracy on the benign-malignant call, though senior radiologists with images still performed best overall. DeepSeek-R1 also agreed more closely with radiologists on risk class and repeated its answers more steadily. Both models matched clinicians only moderately on management advice, which the authors flag as a limit.
pmc-13412118:
Dirk Schulze-Makuch and colleagues sample a volcanic steam vent in 2026 to ask how much life and chemistry can vary within a hand's breadth. At the Furnas hydrothermal zone on São Miguel in the Azores, six visibly distinct specimens were gathered inside a circle only 30 centimetres across. Each was checked for elements, minerals, bacterial fat markers, and the make-up of its living microbial community.

Minerals stayed much alike across the six, built mainly from alunite, alkali feldspar, and quartz. Microbes, by contrast, shifted sharply with colour: red and brown growth leaned to Proteobacteria, yellow and green to Thermoplasmatota, and white and grey to Crenarchaeota. The authors say pigments and local chemistry together paint the vent's patchwork.
pmc-13412918:
Yao Zhu and colleagues profile gene activity across the life cycle of the edible mushroom Pholiota nameko in 2026. Growers divide its development into mycelium, primordium, growth, and maturity stages, and knowing which genes switch on at each step can guide cultivation. Comparisons between early and mature stages highlighted protein processing and fat metabolism pathways, including linoleic acid handling. Screening by how strongly genes switched on narrowed the field to thirteen candidates in the analysis. One gene, labelled Cluster-7415.13, showed the highest expression and may drive rapid cell expansion and wall building during fast growth.
pmc-13414718:
Kyung Jong Won leads a 2026 laboratory study of a flower extract from Persicaria senticosa and its effect on skin pigment. The team drew out the flower oil with hexane and read its makeup by gas chromatography with mass spectrometry. Tests then used B16BL6 mouse melanoma cells that make melanin.

Eight parts were found, and doses up to 100 micrograms per milliliter left cell survival intact. Key pigment proteins fell, among them the MITF switch and two tyrosinase kin. Proteins that move pigment granules inside cells also declined, hinting at a second brake on darkening.
pmc-13416018:
Marija Jovanović and colleagues stress test published dosing models for adalimumab in Crohn's disease, in a 2026 Serbian study. Adalimumab is an antibody drug against tumor necrosis factor, with levels varying widely between patients. Eight published population models were checked against real data from 195 patients at one medical center.

No model passed every population level and simulation check. Individual patient predictions still landed within acceptable error for most models. The best performer seeded a new model, described by a single compartment with first order uptake and clearance. Inflammation marker CRP and dosing schedule predicted clearance significantly. The new model links immune reaction against the drug, inflammation, and drug levels.
pmc-13416118:
Yash Agrawal and co-authors present a delayed colon perforation after a road crash that hid for two days, in a 2026 case report. A man aged thirty-five arrived stable with mild belly tenderness after blunt abdominal trauma. Early scans showed a little blood in the abdomen but no clear bowel or organ injury.

He stayed stable for forty-eight hours apart from a stuck bowel pattern. Repeat imaging then showed free air, pointing to a burst hollow organ. Emergency surgery found fecal contamination from a torn descending colon. The damaged segment was removed with a colostomy. Serial checks and repeat imaging are the diagnostic safety net here.
pmc-13416218:
Michael D Anestis and co-authors study why some United States adults say firearms should be kept unlocked for quick access even when that raises suicide risk. Their 2026 survey draws on a nationally representative panel, focusing on 2,963 adults with firearm access at home.

Endorsement was far more likely among people already storing guns loaded and unlocked, frequent carriers, and those viewing firearms as essential for protection. The authors interpret the pattern as a protection mindset: adults who feel personally responsible for defending loved ones accept the suicide trade-off. They suggest prevention efforts must engage with these beliefs rather than storage facts alone.
pmc-13417018:
Anwesa Mondal and co-authors examine blood markers across stages of diabetic eye disease, in a 2026 study of type 2 diabetes. Groups totalled 236 people, from healthy controls to patients with high risk proliferative eye disease. The fat damage marker rose step by step across groups, while hexokinase activity fell. After full adjustment, only the hexokinase link stayed firm. The pattern hints that blocked sugar entry may track with worsening eye damage.
pmc-13417118:
Rayhan Hossain and co-authors compare zinc oxide, copper oxide, and mixed oxide particles as light driven cleaners, in a 2026 materials study. Such semiconductors can break down pollutants under ultraviolet light. Particles were made by combustion or heat treatment and set against shop bought versions, using an orange dye as the test pollutant.

Home made zinc oxide was highly crystalline, while the commercial form was mostly amorphous and still cleaned fastest among zinc oxides. Home made copper oxide beat its commercial rival. The mixed oxide outperformed single oxides by keeping electric charges apart longer. Tests confirmed hydroxyl radicals did most of the dye breakdown.
pmc-13417618:
Vikram Nathan and co-authors check the quality of experiments behind a widely used mouse brain wiring atlas, in a 2026 study. The Allen atlas maps connections from tracer injections, and a popular connectome drew on 437 experiments. Close inspection found injections off target, overly diffuse spread, tiny signals, and alignment errors in some experiments.

Combined automated and hand checks removed 56 experiments, about 13 percent of the set. Rebuilt maps lost some weakly supported links and gained stronger ones, shifting network club and community patterns slightly. The cleaned regional map is offered as the more trustworthy version for brain network studies.
pmc-13417718:
Murtaza and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how computer modelling can guide the design of organic solar cells. Organic solar cells are thin, flexible panels that turn light into power. Older designs used fullerene acceptors, which absorb light poorly and are hard to tune.

The authors show that energy levels, light absorption, and charge movement can be predicted from molecular structure. Changing end groups, lengthening the core, or adjusting side chains tunes these traits in planned ways. Top non-fullerene acceptors now reach power conversion near twenty percent, with strong absorption of near-infrared light and low energy loss. How molecules pack together also decides how charges move and where they are lost. The review argues that data-driven modelling will speed the design of efficient, stable cells fit for the market.
pmc-13418518:
Mario Baratta, Paolo Accornero, Silvia Miretti, and Eugenio Martignani review how heat stress worsens udder infection in Po Valley dairy herds, in a 2026 article. Hot humid summers are lengthening in Italy's main milk region. Heat strained cows fight infection poorly, while warmth helps udder bacteria thrive in the environment, so mastitis cases climb in summer.

High yielding modern cows suffer most because milk production itself generates metabolic heat. The review ties climate trends, cow physiology, and farm economics together, including prized cheese supply chains. Better housing, nutrition, and management are proposed to protect welfare and income as summers intensify.
pmc-13418618:

The European Commission requested the follow up after an earlier opinion could not settle safety for long lived and breeding animals, user safety, or emulsifier performance. Guar gum thickens, stabilises, and gels animal feed.

New evidence included genetic toxicity data and tolerance studies in dogs and cats. The panel found no genotoxicity concern and judged guar gum safe for all species at the proposed maximum levels in complete feed. Remaining earlier questions framed the scope of the new data package.
pmc-13419318:
Li Lei and colleagues built an interpretable machine-learning model in 2026 to predict bad outcomes after heart surgery. Cardiac surgery carries heavy complication risks, and the team used data from 3270 bypass patients at one tertiary hospital, adding operating-room and early intensive-care data to a standard preoperative risk score.

The gradient-boosting model predicted adverse outcomes well on validation data, and counterfactual explanations showed which changes might have flipped individual predictions. Surgeons gain an updated risk estimate at intensive-care admission that they can actually interrogate, not just accept on trust in daily rounds.
pmc-13421118:
Tessa Moleman and five colleagues published a scoping review in 2026 on how pharmaceutical waste is handled in five Southern African countries: Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia and South Africa. Their focus covers waste from health facilities and from households, two settings that are often governed by different rules.

Searching databases and grey literature from 2004 to 2024, the team screened hundreds of sources and kept 28 publications. Most countries had some regulatory framework, yet guidance was often vague, enforcement weak, and definitions of pharmaceutical waste inconsistent. Poor incineration and landfill disposal were reported often. The authors call for clearer local policies, stronger enforcement, better sorting systems, and more research on household waste.
pmc-13421318:

Specialists judged its reasoning no worse than the doctors'. It scored better on exact treatment choices and on staying close to guidelines. A new prescribing test, RxQA, rounds out the comparison.
pmc-13421918:
Alfraih and colleagues describe in this 2026 case report a skin disorder that melted away after cellular immunotherapy aimed at leukemia. pmc-13422118:
Feixiang Li and six colleagues explore, in a 2026 study, an unexpected shield against anaesthetic harm to the newborn brain: a rich environment. Mice raised in enriched surroundings — more space, toys and social contact — kept healthier mitochondria, quieter sensors and better cognition. Impoverished housing did the opposite, deepening injury. The authors argue that early environment tunes vulnerability to anaesthesia.
pmc-13422818:

When staff phoned patients before their visit, about eight in ten were reached; most confirmed they would come, and some cancelled early, which freed their slots for others. The authors note that phone reminders work only when enough booking staff exist to act on the answers. One-way text reminders cut missed visits but could push short-notice cancellations up instead. pmc-13422918:
Shefali Gautam leads a fifteen-author team trialling, in a 2026 North Indian study, whether a medicated mouthwash before surgery prevents infections after routine abdominal operations. The chlorhexidine group suffered far less sore throat, fewer positive bacterial cultures, lower inflammation markers and a fifth as many wound infections. Their hospital stays were shorter too. The authors argue a cheap rinse earns its place even in low-risk, low-resource surgery.
pmc-13424018:
Laitinen and Haapala replied in 2026 to a comment on their eight-year follow-up study linking childhood fitness to artery structure and stiffness in adolescence. pmc-13424218:
Pan and co-authors audit how health survey interviews actually happen in this 2026 qualitative study from Nanjing, China. The focus is the EQ-5D. They answered from their own reading of the respondent's story. Sometimes they asked nothing at all. Three drivers explained the drift. Low-literacy respondents struggled to comprehend. A long survey rewarded time-saving. And interviewers misunderstood the instrument as observer-rated rather than self-reported. The authors link shortcuts to the rosy ceiling effects in Chinese EQ-5D data. They prescribe interviewer training as the first fix.
pmc-13424818:

On-off swings came first for most, while dyskinesias arrived later, at a middle of about fifty months and at higher drug doses. Doses at onset varied widely between patients, and the groups with the longest delay were taking the most drug, not the least. Five patients got dyskinesias before any on-off swings, and younger onset raised dyskinesia risk.
pmc-13425018:
Koushiki Ullal and five colleagues translate a questionnaire measuring how a spouse's hearing loss affects the partner's own quality of life, known as third-party disability, into Kannada, spoken by some 43.7 million people in southern India. The tool proved dependable: internal consistency reached 0.90 and repeat testing agreed strongly at 0.914. Five underlying factors explained 58.3% of score variation. Most respondents reported mild-to-moderate third-party difficulties. The authors supply Kannada-speaking clinics a validated way to hear the family's side of hearing loss.
pmc-13425918:

Their cohort held 56 adult men treated between 2016 and 2024 with severe Gustilo-Anderson type IIIB to IIIC fractures.

Outcomes centered on bone infection, called osteomyelitis, and whether fractures united, related to how quickly soft tissue reconstruction followed injury. Trauma teams gain ballistic-specific timing evidence for planning staged reconstruction in military and civilian settings.
pmc-13426018:

Scaling from the mouse data alone, using an exponent of 1.0, placed 87.5 percent of the drugs within twofold of their true human clearance. The authors present single-species scaling from these mice as a promising early prediction tool.
pmc-13426118:
Pemberton and Mensah examined in 2026 how bias in artificial intelligence tools inside the Epic electronic medical record system affects health care leaders and their public messages. Their framework links open executive communication with stakeholder trust when bias is found and rules are applied. pmc-13426318: Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine retracted, in 2026, a 2017 article by Paul and colleagues on the safety and effects of Garcinia pedunculata in rats. pmc-13427718:

pmc-13428618:

pmc-13429118:

pmc-13430818:

pmc-13431718:

pmc-13431818:

pmc-13432418:

pmc-13432818:

pmc-13432918:

pmc-13433418:

pmc-13433918:

pmc-13434018:

pmc-13434718:

pmc-13434818:

pmc-13435418:

pmc-13436018:

pmc-13443918:

pmc-13448318:

pmc-13449518:
