Combined on hernia mesh, the pair removed over eighty percent of biofilm from three Pseudomonas strains, beating either alone. The authors stay cautious: most data are preclinical, some key results remain unpublished sponsor material, and joint safety testing lies ahead.
pmc-13449918:
Salah and co-authors present seven children whose tuberculosis looked like cancer. Their 2026 case series comes from settings where childhood tuberculosis is common yet hard to prove, and where its pseudotumoral form, large mass-like lung opacities, closely mimics neoplasms on imaging. Each child in the series presented with a pulmonary mass on X-ray or CT that was ultimately confirmed as tuberculosis.

The presentations varied across the seven cases, underlining why the diagnosis gets missed or delayed. The authors stress two things for endemic regions. Clinicians must hold tuberculosis high in the differential for paediatric chest masses. They must also correlate the clinical picture with radiology, laboratory tests, and tissue examination before concluding malignancy. Early recognition matters twice over: timely treatment reduces the child's risk of severe disease, and it interrupts transmission of a highly contagious airborne infection to contacts.
pmc-13450018:
Zhao and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how cell metabolism acts as a checkpoint system in bone remodelling. Bone is constantly rebuilt by osteoblasts, which form bone, and osteoclasts, which break it down. Their fuel choices decide whether bone grows or thins.

Under nutrient stress, bone metabolism shifts from regeneration toward resorption, meaning breakdown wins. Sugar burning, called glycolysis, supports bone-forming cells yet can also feed tumour spread through a chemical tag called lactylation. Osteoblasts differ from each other in fuel use, and those differences open distinct weak points for drugs. The review weighs two drug classes, HIF-1α blockers and sclerostin antibodies, for benefit against toxicity. The authors argue that mapping metabolic checkpoints could turn bone disease treatment toward targeted metabolic therapy.
pmc-13450518:
Jiawen Zhao and others tuned nitrogen and potassium feeds for soft wheat in 2026, to balance crop yield with grain protein. Soft wheat needs low protein for its baking uses, yet nitrogen lifts both yield and protein, which pulls in two ways. Most past work tracked one result at a time, and missed how the two feeds act as a pair.

Two wheat types, Wanximai 0638 and Yangmai 20, grew under four nitrogen doses, three splits of base to top feed, and two potassium plans, with top feed at jointing. Yield, protein, flour tests, nitrogen uptake and shift, use rate, leaf green, and enzyme work were all scored. The work points to feed pairs that lift yield while keeping protein in the soft-wheat range. Farmers gain feed plans tuned to both bulk and grade.
pmc-13451918:
Ken Oshiro models in 2026 how trade in synthetic fuels could smuggle carbon across borders when climate rules differ by region. Such fuels, made from caught carbon and hydrogen, are meant for sectors that are hard to clean. When the carbon comes from fossil sources, the fuel can shift emissions to lands with weaker rules.

A world energy model found that about half a billion tonnes of carbon could move to other lands by 2050 under split rules. That flow equals a sixth of the rich club's own output. Counting the fuel's carbon on the buyer's side, with a real carbon price, near erased the leak. The author urges border carbon charges for fuel trade, akin to those set for hydrogen in Europe.
pmc-13452218:
Manami Misu, Kazunori Goto, and Jun Takanari test in 2026 an asparagus stem extract, ETAS, in adults unhappy with their sleep. Poor sleep tracks heart and sugar disease risk, and early work hinted the extract may deepen one sleep stage. Thirty-eight healthy adults took the extract and a dummy pill in turn, for two weeks each, with a gap between, while brain-wave gear read their nights.

The deep-sleep share did not shift by a firm margin. Yet time spent awake after first falling asleep fell, as did time in the lightest sleep stage. Self-rated sleep scores also rose on set items. Gains ran strongest in those who began with the worst wake time, the authors note.
pmc-13452318:
Steven Silverstein and co-authors set out in 2026 a brain theory that ties the scattered symptoms of schizophrenia to one cell design. Certain pyramid cells take input in two zones, a top tuft and a base, and the top zone brings context that tunes what the cell sends on. Schizophrenia has long been cast as a failure of just such joining work.

On this view, weak top-zone pull and slack in the cortex-thalamus loops that feed it leave perception, thought, speech, and self-feel unbound. The piece walks the claim across illness stages, from early warning years to chronic life. It closes with what the theory says about awareness in the illness, its limits, and next tests.
pmc-13452418:
Donglei Zheng and eight co-authors build a tiny capsule system that carries sialic acid safely through the stomach to the gut. Sialic acid, also called Neu5Ac, is a sugar acid with useful body effects that acid in the stomach breaks down. Their 2026 design wraps it in a water in oil in water emulsion, a droplet with layers of water and oil.

The best mix sealed in over 92 percent of the acid as droplets and kept about 89 percent after spray drying into powder. In lab digestion tests, the powder let go of about 86 percent of its load within 120 minutes in gut like fluid. Fed to mice, the capsules raised gut levels of three helpful microbe groups, among them Akkermansia and Lactobacillus. The design points to a way to add the acid to foods without losing it in the stomach.
pmc-13453918:
Kipp and colleagues follow shoulder stability for two years after the Latarjet procedure. The operation moves a piece of bone to stop a shoulder joint from slipping out at the front. Their 2026 study uses dynamic radiostereometry, a precise X-ray tracking method, plus CT based 3D bone models, to watch the joint while patients turn the arm outward. Each repaired shoulder is compared with the patient's healthy side and with its own pre surgery state.

Before surgery, the ball of the joint sat slightly forward and low, and its contact area with the socket shrank. One year after surgery the ball sat further back and higher, and by two years motion matched the healthy shoulder. Contact area grew back close to normal size. Patient scores for instability improved steadily, dropping from 55 percent before surgery to 27 percent at two years, where lower means better.
pmc-13454318:
Sharvari R. Desai and five colleagues ran a 2026 trial asking whether eating almonds each day improves sleep in adults who sleep poorly. The trial enrolled 175 adults aged 21 to 55 and lasted five months. One group ate whole almonds, while the other ate a snack matched in calories.

After five months, the almond group reported better sleep efficiency and fell asleep faster by their own reports. Their overall sleep quality scores also ended lower, which marks better sleep. Lab sleep recordings, by contrast, showed almost no clear group gaps. Melatonin levels at the end were higher in the almond group. The authors say the benefit looks real for felt sleep quality, while machine measures stayed flat.
pmc-13454418:
Yan Deng, YiDan Zhu, JiaQi Li, and Yu Xiong gather, in a 2026 synthesis, what registered nurses say about using generative AI at work. The team merged findings from qualitative studies found in twelve databases, using a set method from the Joanna Briggs Institute. Nurses use such tools in daily care and in research, and their views shape safe adoption.

Six studies covering 113 nurses fed the synthesis. Nurses said the tools can speed work and support learning and decisions. They also raised ethical, cultural, and practical worries, from wrong outputs to unclear rules. A third theme called for training, workplace support, and clear guidance, paired with hope for future gains. The authors treat the findings as early and thin, urging wider studies across health systems before firm rules are set.
pmc-13455318:
Malaisamy Muniyandi and colleagues weigh a short weekly drug course for latent tuberculosis in a 2026 review of 20 studies. Treating silent TB infection matters for ending TB, yet the older nine- and six-month isoniazid courses are long and hard to finish. The review pooled trials and observational studies of a three-month, once-weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine course, called 3HP, against those older courses, grading bias and evidence quality.

People on 3HP were nearly three times as likely to finish treatment as those on the nine-month course. The edge over the six-month course was similar. Overall harm risk stayed close to the older course. Severe harm and liver harm looked lower with 3HP. New active TB looked rarer, though that last gap was not statistically firm. The grade was low to very low, so the review backs 3HP as a practical option while calling for stronger trials.
pmc-13455418:
Meltem Tekbaş-Atay and colleagues expose dental filling materials to fake stomach acid in a 2026 lab study. Reflux and vomiting can bathe fillings in strong acid, roughening them, dulling shine and shifting colour, yet bulk-fill composites differ in how they endure that attack. Five materials, one universal composite, two packable bulk-fills and two flowable bulk-fills, were cast as discs and soaked in acid at pH 1.2 for periods standing in for one and five years.

Acid raised roughness and colour shift and cut gloss in most materials, with the Tetric packable material roughest after five years and the universal Estelite material shifting colour most. The Filtek packable material held gloss best and kept colour within acceptable limits. Flowable materials proved more vulnerable overall, giving dentists a reason to favour packable options for patients with frequent acid exposure.
pmc-13457518:
Schiavon and colleagues in Italy built in 2026 a stats lens to watch how job worlds shape four health risk acts: smoke, poor food, drink, and still life. The acts drive most long ill loads, and job strain bends each one. Italy's yearly health watch holds free text job notes from each guest. The lens reads those notes for themes, and sorts folk into hid job clans. Risk math then runs per clan, with marks that drift year to year.

Each clan gets its own weights for age, sex, and place marks. A sharp prior mutes weak marks and keeps the strong plain. The lens learns as new watch waves land, with no full re run. Health chiefs can see which job worlds turn which marks sour. Aid can then aim at the clans where it bites most.
pmc-13458918:
Chen and colleagues test a new catheter device for repairing a leaky mitral valve in this 2026 preclinical study. The L-Clip system performs annuloplasty through a catheter rather than open surgery. Annuloplasty tightens the ring around the valve. The target is functional mitral regurgitation. In that condition the leaflets are healthy but fail to meet. The team implanted the device in eighteen pigs and measured the valve ring immediately.

Every implantation succeeded, with the first clip placed in a median of about 28 minutes and the second in about 40 minutes in this animal series. The ring's area shrank by about a quarter and its front-to-back diameter by nearly a third right after clipping. No deaths, valve damage, device displacement, or clot embolism occurred, and the authors call for clinical investigation in patients.
pmc-13459118:
Raphaela Joos and co-authors review in 2026 whether the pattern of microbes colonizing a baby's gut in the first two years can forecast later health. Colonization begins at birth and is steered by delivery mode, feeding, and home environment. Those early communities have been linked with metabolism, immune development, and brain development, yet firm diagnostic tools for many childhood conditions appear only years later.

The review contrasts classic statistical models, which expose associations, with machine learning methods that aim at prediction. Both face problems of data quality, study design, and comparability. Readers interested in child health research get a clear map of what early microbiome trajectories might one day predict, and what must improve before clinics could rely on them.
pmc-13459318:
Mustafa Uçar and colleagues test whether fat around the heart predicts early rhythm return after freeze treatment for AF in a 2026 study. Heart-surface fat drives heart-wall change, yet its value after cold balloon treatment was unclear. Sixty-one patients in a row with on-off AF had heart-surface fat volume measured on pre-treatment cardiac CT, then were followed for six months after a three-month blanking period.

Return hit 23.0 percent, and fat volume averaged 333.5 cubic centimetres in return patients versus 201.2 in others. Fat volume predicted return with an area under the curve of 0.891, beating body mass index at 0.836, and each extra cubic centimetre raised odds by about 2 percent. Doctors gain a pre-treatment CT marker for shaping freeze plans and follow-up strength.
pmc-13459518:
Chauret and colleagues report the first human study of camlipixant, a drug aimed at stubborn chronic cough, in this 2026 trial. The drug blocks the P2X3 receptor, a sensor on airway nerves that triggers coughing, and had worked in animal cough models. Ninety healthy volunteers received single rising doses up to 1,200 milligrams, or twice-daily doses for a period, or a placebo, in a double-blind design.

Side effects occurred at similar rates on drug and placebo. They were mostly mild. The commonest was altered taste, mainly at doses of 400 milligrams and above. The drug entered the blood quickly, peaking within about two hours, and cleared with a half-life of roughly four to eight hours depending on the regimen. Blood levels rose in proportion to dose, supporting twice-daily dosing, and food made no meaningful difference.
pmc-13460218:
Ji-Yoon Jung and Tae-Yun Sung argue in a 2026 commentary that sugammadex, a drug that rapidly reverses muscle relaxants used in anesthesia, has not made measurement of muscle recovery optional. Leftover paralysis after surgery can block the airway and weaken protective reflexes. The piece discusses a large study of more than one hundred thousand cases examining what changed after sugammadex arrived in practice.

Relaxant dosing climbed by about forty-five percent over the study years, including for operations that never needed deep blockade. Roughly eight percent of patients suffered breathing problems afterward, and heavier relaxant exposure raised that risk. Sugammadex softened the link but never erased it. Only monitoring with actual numbers removed the extra risk.
pmc-13461218:
Nwolise and colleagues explore Hospital at Home services for care home residents in this 2026 English study. The service delivers hospital-level treatment in a person's usual residence. Policy in England favors it. Hospital care grows strained, and often distressing, for frail older people. The researchers surveyed 50 care home staff in southern England and interviewed 20 of them about their experiences.

Staff said hospital trips were still needed for fractures and emergencies, but often brought distress, poor communication, and physical decline for residents. Hospital at Home, by contrast, was linked with teamwork, continuity, dignity, and fewer hospital-related risks. Barriers included limited staff capacity, patchy geographic coverage, restricted opening hours, and inconsistent referral routes, which together limited fair and timely access to the service.
pmc-13461318:
Marek Slachta and colleagues reviewed in 2026 thirteen free, open-source deep learning tools that automatically outline gliomas, aggressive brain tumors, on MRI scans so their volume can be tracked over time. Scoring covered accuracy on public benchmark challenges, speed of workflow, and fit with the RANO 2.0 response criteria, which now stress standardized volume measurement when judging whether treatment works.

Translation into clinics lags the mathematics: most treatment response studies carry patient selection bias, and no tool had been formally validated against RANO 2.0 by late 2024. Newer programs are being built expressly for that standard, and the authors favor hybrids pairing open-source engines with commercial clinical plumbing.
pmc-13461418:
Vincenzo Tosco and colleagues present in 2026 three patients treated with vital pulp therapy, an approach that keeps a tooth's living core alive instead of performing root canal treatment. Four back teeth with deep decay and signs of reversible pulp inflammation were treated under rubber dam isolation. They received Biodentine XP, a bioactive cement that substitutes for dentin, paired with adhesive fillings placed immediately or in stages.

Two teeth needed direct capping after the pulp was exposed during decay removal, while one patient's two molars received indirect capping over near-exposed pulp. Checks at six months, one year, and three years found every tooth symptom-free and still responding to sensitivity tests, with X-rays showing no disease at the root tips. Fillings held their margins and structure throughout.
pmc-13461518:
Yamana and colleagues reported a 2026 case report of a forty-two-year-old man whose lung cancer changed cell type under targeted therapy. He had stage IIIA squamous cell lung cancer carrying an EGFR mutation, a change common in another lung cancer type but exceptionally rare in squamous tumours. After chemoradiotherapy the cancer returned.

He was treated first with erlotinib plus ramucirumab and then with osimertinib, both drugs aimed at the EGFR pathway. When the disease progressed, a repeat biopsy showed complete transformation into small cell lung cancer while keeping the original EGFR deletion. That retained mutation proved the new cancer grew from the old one rather than starting fresh. Yamana reports he responded well to carboplatin, etoposide, and durvalumab, and urges repeat biopsies at drug failure.
pmc-13461618:
Zhiping Liu, Mingming Sun, and Zhendan Xu present a 2026 computer framework meant to judge nursing quality in operating rooms and to predict risk after tumor surgery. Care around surgery produces a flood of mixed information, from vital signs to drugs and notes after the operation. Fixed scoring tools handle that changing picture poorly. It tests what might have happened under different care paths. In tests the system beat clinical scores and several other computer methods on accuracy. The authors frame it as support for judgment, not a replacement. Trials across hospitals must come before routine use.
pmc-13461718:
Hongqin Du and colleagues tested whether resting brain-wave patterns track ADHD trait levels in young adults, beyond anxiety and low mood. ADHD traits cover inattention, restlessness, and impulsivity, here measured on a self-report scale in students without a diagnosis.

The link held after accounting for anxiety and depression scores, and across most of 64 model variants tried. Related slow-wave measures, including a theta-to-beta ratio, pointed the same way, Du reports, though the effect stayed modest. The authors stress this is a group-level link, not a test for diagnosing any one person.
pmc-13461918:
Alcamán-Arias and co-authors surveyed a 2026 set of microbial mats across high altitude salt systems in the Chilean Altiplano. Salinity was the only measured factor significantly tied to community composition, though site identity explained even more variation. Alcamán-Arias found salt loving archaea enriched in the saltiest habitats, while brackish sites held more photosynthesis and nitrogen related functions. Only fifteen percent of sequence variants were shared between brackish and hypersaline habitats, yet a small core of keystone microbes linked all sites.
pmc-13462118:

Silencing the gene in cancer cells slowed growth, movement, and invasion. Pathway analysis pointed to energy metabolism, above all pyruvate handling. pmc-13462318:

pmc-13462518:

Protein leakage into urine fell below one gram a day in most responders, and Sun calls for larger studies of this matching approach.

The corrected statement credits support from the Harran University Scientific Research Projects Coordination Unit, under project number 17009. The authors apologize for the error. pmc-13463618:

pmc-13463718: Laura Martínez-Martínez, Achille Schiavone, Juan Orengo, and Eva Armero publish a correction to their 2026 study of the Murciana chicken breed. The notice is a correction only. The authors state that the science and its conclusions stay unchanged.
pmc-13464018:
Gaona and co-authors examined in 2026 why lung repair fails in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, the scarring disease that stiffens the lungs. They focused on two signaling proteins, YAP and TAZ. pmc-13466318:
Stella Karydogianni and colleagues review the bitter soapy compounds in quinoa seeds and their possible medical uses, in a 2026 article. Newer work paints a more useful picture, including promise as vaccine boosters and other drug-like actions gathered in the review. Extraction methods compared range from simple soaking to ultrasound, microwave, enzyme, and pressurized liquid routes, with ultrasound and microwave approaches rated most suitable. The authors weigh benefits against the caution due any biologically active plant chemical.
pmc-13466418:

Potato flesh is about four fifths water with very little air space, which shapes that response.
pmc-13466518:

pmc-13467018:
Wenwen Liu, Renjie Zhang, Haokun Li, and Yuanhong Qi review low-carbon routes for China's ironmaking under the country's climate pledges, in a 2026 article. pmc-13467118:

The virus showed in a small share of swabs, near one in twenty five. All but one of the horses were sound when swabbed, so the germ rides in quiet form. pmc-13467218:
Boyan Zhou and Qiang He propose a sandwich panel whose honeycomb core replaces the usual six-corner junctions with other shapes, then simulate its sound blocking, in a 2026 study. pmc-13467818:

pmc-13467918:
Paul and colleagues test in this 2026 study whether gold nanoparticles can keep boar semen usable for longer in liquid storage, a routine practice in pig artificial insemination. By day five, semen receiving the higher dose, 10 million particles per milliliter, clearly outperformed the control: total motility reached 30.78 percent of sperm and viability reached 47.62 percent in the treated samples, with membrane and energy-producing structures also better preserved. pmc-13468118:
Fusun Erten and co-authors assemble a 2026 expert review on whether food- and plant-derived nutraceuticals can support care for urologic cancers, including prostate, bladder, kidney, and testicular tumors. Their search ran across four databases up to June 2026 and included citation chasing both ways. pmc-13468218:

The authors flag the series as potent starting points needing fuller drug testing.
pmc-13468518:
Muschter and colleagues present a 2026 method for attaching the enzyme horseradish peroxidase to surfaces in a controlled orientation, so its active site stays open for work. pmc-13468918:

pmc-13473918:

The high-cost group averaged about twenty-four family doctor contacts of all kinds in the year, against about seventeen for the rest, and the gap held after health differences were counted. Older age, female sex, several diagnoses at once, out-of-hours use, and longer hospital stays each went with more doctor contact. The authors say these patients are heavy users across the whole system, not just in hospitals, which matters for joining up their care.
pmc-13499218:
Abu Ahmed Shamim and colleagues test in 2026 four front-of-pack label designs on packaged food in Bangladesh, where diet-related chronic disease is rising. Labels aim to help shoppers spot foods high in sugar, salt, saturated fat, or calories, yet local evidence on which format works best was thin. The nationwide randomised trial covered all eight divisions and included teenagers aged 10 to 18 alongside adults up to age 60, using mock packaged foods.

Warning labels performed best, lifting correct identification of unhealthy products far above the no-label group for both age groups. A traffic-light design ranked second, ahead of a guideline-amount design, and warning labels most reduced adults' intention to buy harmful products. Every format improved how unhealthy products seemed, which supports making interpretive labels, above all warnings, mandatory in the authors' view.
pmc-13499818:
Timothy J Craig and a large team pool in 2026 long-term data on garadacimab, a monthly antibody injection that blocks an activated clotting factor to prevent hereditary angioedema attacks. The disorder causes unpredictable swelling episodes, and prevention is lifelong, so durability and safety over years matter. The pooled analysis combined a phase 2 study, a pivotal phase 3 trial, and an open extension study, with results cut off in June 2024.

Median exposure reached two and a half years, stretching beyond five years for some patients in the safety set of 172 people. No deaths occurred, few patients stopped treatment over side effects, and injection-site reactions were the most common drug-related complaint, mostly mild or moderate. Attack rates fell by roughly ninety-five percent from the run-in period in the efficacy set, a benefit the authors describe as durable across the longest exposure reported for this drug.
pmc-13500818:
Ivan Kirilov Kostadinov leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 experimental study of a gold vapour laser that emits ultraviolet light. The team built and tested six laser tubes of different diameters, lengths, and active volumes to see how output scales with the size of the glowing region. Gold vapour lasers are the only metal vapour source working on this ultraviolet transition, yet they run at extreme temperatures and remain far less developed than copper vapour lasers.

The best tube delivered a maximum average output power of 1.07 watts at a wavelength near 312 nanometres. Output per unit volume reached 56.3 milliwatts per cubic centimetre, more than six times the best previously reported figure. An unstable cavity with a Glan prism produced polarized, high-quality beam output for the first time in such a device. Mixing the lines near 312 and 628 nanometres generated a new deep-ultraviolet line near 209 nanometres.
pmc-13501618:
Siyuan Tan leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 study of two blood proteins as warning markers after acute myocardial infarction, a heart attack. The proteins, angiopoietin-2 and its receptor TIE-2, regulate blood vessel stability and remodelling. The team enrolled 180 heart attack patients treated at Hunan Provincial People's Hospital between July 2020 and March 2021. They measured both proteins at baseline and followed the patients for major adverse cardiovascular events after discharge.

Follow-up averaged 444 days, and 55 patients suffered a major event. Adjusted Cox regression identified both proteins as independent predictors, with hazard ratios of 2.400 for angiopoietin-2 and 2.004 for the receptor protein in this cohort. Angiopoietin-2 discriminated future events with an area under the curve of 0.756, ahead of 0.664 for TIE-2. Patients above the chosen cut-offs, 1.896 and 21.886 nanograms per millilitre respectively, faced roughly triple the event risk.
pmc-13501718:
Martina Krofič Žel leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 veterinary imaging study comparing two ways of measuring adrenal gland size in dogs. Adrenal size guides the diagnosis of hormone disorders and tumours. Earlier work suggested CT reads larger than ultrasound, but the two had never been measured head-to-head on the same day. Thirty client-owned dogs with no suspected adrenal disease had both scans in one anaesthetic session. Pole diameters and gland length were recorded for both glands.

Agreement analysis showed a positive bias: CT returned larger values than ultrasound for every dimension. For the left gland, both pole measurements differed significantly in every weight class, while the right differed only in some. Discrepancies widened in bigger dogs. The authors advise following patients with whichever method produced the original measurements. They note the caudal pole size travels between methods more reliably than the cranial pole.
pmc-13503918:
Jinpeng Wu and three colleagues hunt for a weak spot in triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive type with few targeted drugs, in a 2026 study. They joined single-cell and spatial gene data with network and machine learning tools. The goal was to name the cell states that drive the disease.

One cell group stood out: fast-dividing, inflamed-looking cancer cells at a late state in their growth path. A twelve-gene score drawn from this group split patients by survival and by likely drug response. One gene, RPN1, drew focus tests in a cell line. Cutting it lowered cell life, raised stress signals, and pushed cells toward death. A stress-soothing chemical partly undid those effects, which backs a stress-based attack on this cancer.
pmc-13505018:
Burak Ezer and Rifat Bülbül review five years of hepatitis A test results from a hospital in central Turkey, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Cleaner water and child vaccination since two thousand twelve have cut early-life contact with the virus. That shift can leave teens and young adults open to later, harsher illness.

More than seven thousand people were tested, and fresh infection was rare. About two thirds showed past immunity overall, but teens aged fifteen to eighteen had the lowest rate by far. Young adults also showed a large immunity gap, while all older adults tested were immune. Readers see a clear case for catch-up shots for the teen and young adult groups.
pmc-13505918:
Laura Ceballos leads a team on drug barriers to oxfendazole against liver flukes. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with sheep infected with Fasciola hepatica. The drug is used at higher doses against flukes.

Plasma spread and fluke uptake were mapped at two doses. One dose was the standard worm dose for sheep. The higher dose was six times that standard level. Blood exposure rose near fivefold at the high dose. Peak levels were about fourfold higher as well. Fluke drug levels more than tripled at the high dose. Dose thus shapes how much drug reaches flukes.
pmc-13506118:
Neil V Shah and colleagues studied spinal deformity surgery outcomes for adults with and without rheumatoid arthritis in New York State records. Among 6,020 patients who had fusion for adult spinal deformity, 238 had rheumatoid arthritis. The team tracked complications and repeat surgery through two years, taking account of age, sex, fusion length, and general illness burden.

Patients with rheumatoid arthritis had complications in about sixty-one percent of cases, against forty-four percent without the disease. Surgical and medical complications were each more common, and repeat surgery was needed in about twenty-seven percent versus nineteen percent. Once those factors were counted, rheumatoid arthritis stayed a predictor on its own of both complications and revision. The authors say these figures should feed straight into how surgeons counsel patients with the disease about the risk of surgery before deformity correction.
pmc-13506218:
Claire C Russell and colleagues report an 80-year-old man whose swallowing tube had stretched to about eleven centimetres wide after years of achalasia. In this disorder, the valve into the stomach fails to relax. He arrived after two weeks of worsening swallowing trouble and several days of tolerating no food at all. Scans showed the gorged esophagus packed with retained food and a lung abscess blamed on inhaled material.

His achalasia had been stretched open years earlier and quiet spells had discouraged follow-up. Surgeons' endoscopy team crossed the tight junction under X-ray guidance and balloon-dilated it successfully. Because he was frail and aspirating, the surgical team added a stomach feeding tube to protect his lungs and restore nutrition. Care needed gastroenterology, lung, and surgical teams working together. The authors warn that long gaps between achalasia treatments allow extreme widening and dangerous complications.
pmc-13507118:
Fischbein and co-authors track wasps that may attack an invasive fruit fly in the Andes. The fly, Drosophila suzukii, harms soft fruit crops worldwide. The team watched three local wasp species across farms and wild land. Each wasp peaked in a distinct season of the year. One peaked in spring and one in summer.

The third wasp leaned toward autumn activity. Field proof showed that wasp can grow inside the pest fly. That is the first such proof for the region. The fly also used wild fruits as backup hosts. The authors flag the pupal wasp as a lead for pest control work.
pmc-13507418:
Tsuyoshi Kawai and Yasuhiro Matsunaga present AFM-Fold, a computer method that rebuilds three-dimensional protein shapes from microscope images, in 2026 work. High-speed atomic force microscopy can film proteins moving under near-natural conditions. Its images, though, show only the outer surface, not the full atomic structure. Their system pairs a neural network that reads key shape features from an image with a guided diffusion step that builds matching forms.

Tests used the enzyme adenylate kinase, and the method recovered its open and closed forms plus the states in between. The authors then applied it to 159 real frames of a flagellar protein called FlhAC. Results fit the images better than fitting a fixed crystal form, and each frame took about one minute. The work offers a faster route to watching proteins change shape.
pmc-13507518:
Yu and colleagues examined whether four weeks of resistance training shifts inflammation, a brain-growth factor, and thinking performance in midlife adults, in a 2026 study. Five hundred adults aged fifty to sixty-five trained three times weekly, with blood tests and executive-function tasks before the program and three days after the last session. There was no comparison group, so results are before-and-after associations.

Yu found two inflammatory markers fell while brain-derived neurotrophic factor, a protein supporting neuron health, rose. Working memory accuracy improved and reaction time quickened, and performance on a color-word interference task improved. Participants who completed nearly all sessions showed larger numerical changes, though attendance was not randomized, so that pattern is only descriptive. The authors present the program as a feasible exposure for studying body-brain links and call for controlled trials with follow-up to test durability.
pmc-13508118:
Puneet Gill and Daniela Yepez review whether a drinkable X-ray dye helps doctors manage bowel blockages caused by scar tissue, in 2026 work. Such blockages are a common surgical emergency, often after past operations. Many clear with rest, a stomach tube, and fluids, yet waiting too long to operate on the rest raises harm. The dye can show whether the bowel is opening, predict who will settle without surgery, and perhaps help clear the blockage itself. The review followed standard reporting rules and gathered 21 clinical studies.

Some studies found faster clearing, shorter hospital stays, and fewer operations with the dye. Others found no clear gain on those measures. The authors suspect differing study designs, patient mixes, and dosing plans explain the split. Their reading favors the dye mainly as a guide for decisions, rather than as a treatment in its own right.
pmc-13508218:
Farah Munirah Mior Mazlan and four co-authors look for factors tied to autism diagnosis among children seen in primary care clinics in Kelantan, Malaysia, in 2026 work. Spotting autism early is hard in routine clinics, above all outside big cities. The study ran from March to September 2025 in five districts and enrolled 207 children aged 18 months to 12 years. Each child had a sensory and behavior screen, then a full clinical assessment against standard diagnostic rules, whatever the screen showed.

Twenty-nine children received a new autism diagnosis during the study. Two factors stayed linked to diagnosis after full adjustment. Older age at assessment raised the odds, which the authors read as late recognition rather than a true cause. First-born children were also more likely to be diagnosed than later-born siblings. The authors urge stronger routine developmental checks in primary care so cases surface sooner.
pmc-13508418:
Dibyajyoti Nath leads a ten-author field study testing silicon plus a helpful bacterium to lift coriander growth on silicon-poor soil in India, in 2026 work. The trial ran at a coconut farm research site in Coimbatore, using a local coriander variety. Seven treatments mixed two silicon sources, a mineral form and rice husk ash, at two rates, with or without a Bacillus bacterium. Plots followed a standard repeated layout, and growth, leaf chemistry, defense enzymes, and yield were measured.

Silicon plus the bacterium beat other mixes across the board. Plant height rose by up to about three fifths over untreated plots, and leaf silicon climbed sharply. Defense enzymes and quality compounds surged, with leaf protein nearly tripling in the best plots. Top leaf yield came from the higher ash rate plus the bacterium. The authors back the combined chemical and biological route for poor soils.
pmc-13509918:
Niusha Raeesian and David J. Riese ask whether a familiar growth-signal network sits at the center of eye melanoma growth signals, in a 2026 review. Uveal melanoma starts in the pigmented tissues of the eye and spreads often, with poor outcomes once it does. The review covers the cancer's biology and drug treatment, then lays out how the ERBB receptor family and its growth factor partners pass signals inside cells.

A separate pathway driven by altered G proteins is known to power most of these tumors. The authors argue the two systems talk to each other, so part of the driving signal may flow through the growth network as a side effect of that crosstalk. If so, drugs aimed at the growth network could offer a new line of attack. The piece presents this as a reasoned proposal for testing, not a proven therapy.
pmc-13510318:
Siphosethu Mgwili-Qikani, Guillermo Pulido Estrada, and Constance Sewani-Rusike report a cross-sectional survey, published in 2026, of how children with lower limb amputations judge their conventional artificial legs. Fifty-two children aged 4 to 17 at three centres in South Africa's Eastern Cape, with their caregivers, rated comfort, function, and overall satisfaction after at least a year of use.

Average overall satisfaction was modest, while comfort and function scored higher. Comfort correlated strongly with both function and satisfaction, and children born with limb differences were significantly more satisfied than those who lost a limb later. The authors argue that socket comfort and working performance should drive design and rehabilitation choices.
pmc-13510818:
Yiyuan Yu and nine co-authors characterize an enzyme from a virus that infects Vibrio bacteria, germs that drive costly disease outbreaks in fish farming, in 2026 work. Such enzymes, called endolysins, chew through the bacterial cell wall and are eyed as antibiotic stand-ins as drug resistance grows. The team pulled the enzyme gene from the virus genome, built the enzyme in lab bacteria, purified it, and tested its wall-breaking power across conditions.

The enzyme hit hardest against host bacteria in their fast-growth phase, with peak action at a set dose, warm temperature, and neutral acidity. A common chelating additive boosted activity, while high levels of metal ions nearly shut it down. The enzyme broke down six Vibrio species, a wider range than its parent virus manages. The authors say its heat and acidity tolerance suit farm use.
pmc-13511518:
Chliapnikov and Bernstein review seizure related decline in treated brain tumors, in work from twenty twenty-six. A glioma patient who suddenly worsens may have hidden seizures, a seizure linked scan change, treatment damage, or true tumor growth. These look alike on imaging.

Misdiagnosis can delay the right therapy, the authors warn. Their narrative review synthesizes evidence for a framework that joins electrical, clinical, and imaging data. Nonconvulsive status epilepticus, ongoing seizure activity without shaking, is a key hidden cause. The framework aims to help teams sort reversible seizure effects from real progression before changing cancer treatment.
pmc-13511618:
Giada Pauletto and twelve co-authors test whether nerve signal shifts during brainstem tumor surgery forecast how patients fare soon after. Watching nerve signals in surgery aims to cut harm, but its forecast value for this tumor type is unclear. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

The team reviewed just over twenty adults who had brainstem glioma surgery with full signal watch across more than a decade. Five signal kinds were tracked, from touch and move signals to hearing and face nerve reads. Warning marks were met in near half the patients for some signals. Yet neither touch nor move signal drops linked in a firm way to function at discharge.
pmc-13512718:
Lian and colleagues compare two ways plant genomes gain extra gene copies, using the tea plant in 2026 evolutionary research. Whole-genome duplication copies every gene at once, while transposed duplication moves single genes to new locations. The team combined gene activity data, chromatin maps, and DNA methylation data from eight tea tissues to ask why copy pairs from the two routes behave differently over evolutionary time.

The analysis covered 4,071 whole-genome duplication pairs and 10,174 transposed pairs from the tea reference genome. Whole-genome pairs stayed co-expressed, meaning switched on together, in 44.3 percent of cases, against 33.0 percent for transposed pairs in the same dataset. Transposed genes also showed heavier methylation, a chemical mark that quiets genes, even where chromatin was equally open. Damaging variants near transposed gene promoters hurt their coordination most. Lian links the gap to combined genetic and epigenetic pressure.
pmc-13513418:
Telmo-Fernando Basantes-Vizcaino, Luis Marcelo Albuja-Illescas, Julia K. Prado, and Bolívar Xavier Aguirre Valencia review the white peach scale, an invasive armored insect not yet officially reported in Ecuador, in 2026 work. The pest attacks more than two hundred plant species, from fruit trees to ornamentals, and causes heavy losses worldwide. It tolerates a wide temperature range and survives cold storage, which helps it ride international plant trade into new regions.

The review gathers nearly seventy years of research on its spread, hosts, biology, and control options. Andean fruit zones in Ecuador offer climates where the pest could settle if it arrives. The authors urge preventive watch systems, early detection programs, and joined management that mixes field monitoring, biological control, and steady inspection of nurseries and imported plants. Acting before arrival, they argue, is far cheaper than fighting an established invader.
pmc-13514618:
Pennipat Nabheerong and colleagues report a validation study, published in 2026, testing whether a simplified dental method can estimate age in Thai children. The Demirjian four-teeth methods score tooth development on X-rays, but accuracy varies by population, so the team checked both versions in Southern Thai children and teenagers aged 7 to 15.

Using 360 panoramic X-rays, split evenly between boys and girls, the researchers compared estimated dental age with true age. Both methods overestimated age, by roughly half to three quarters of a year on average, with typical errors near one year. Method II was marginally more accurate, and the authors recommend Thai-specific calibration before forensic or clinical use.
pmc-13515118:
Shuhua Ma and five colleagues review, in a 2026 article, the use of metal-organic frameworks in membrane distillation, a desalination method that pushes water vapour through a water-repelling membrane. The method uses little energy and handles very salty wastewater, yet wetting, fouling, and low flow hold it back at scale. Metal-organic frameworks are crystal-like sponges with tunable pores, and makers now blend them into membranes or grow them as films.

The review compares these two designs and explains how the sponges ease the heat and salt build-up that drag on output. Their channels let vapour pass while their surfaces can be tuned to resist wetting. The authors close with the hurdles that remain before such membranes serve in working desalination plants. Readers get a map of a fast-moving materials niche aimed at freshwater scarcity.
pmc-13515418:
Junshen Wang leads a ten-author team testing fertiliser mixes for greenhouse soil in a 2026 field study. The team compared five regimes: plain soil, chemical fertiliser alone, mushroom-growing residue paired with chemical fertiliser at high and low rates, and organic fertiliser pairings. Gene sequencing mapped how each mix changed soil nutrients, microbe communities, and the cycling of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur.

Every treatment raised soil nutrients. The high mushroom-residue mix led on organic matter, total nitrogen, nitrate, and available phosphorus, while chemical fertiliser alone led on potassium and ammonium. Mushroom residue lifted microbe richness and diversity, and both organic pairings enriched helpful microbes. Chemical fertiliser alone pushed oxygen-free metabolism, an effect the high residue rate reversed. Available phosphorus, potassium, and ammonium steered the community shifts most. Wang's team recommends residue pairings with proper dose and tillage for worn greenhouse soils.
pmc-13515718:
Seungmin Song and six colleagues build memory devices from silk protein in a 2026 materials study. Memristors store data as resistance states that persist without power, and silk fibroin suits versions meant to dissolve safely in the body. Pure silk versions leak current and hold their states poorly, though. The team mixed titanium dioxide nanoparticles into the silk film at four loadings, from none up to one percent by weight.

Adding the particles steadied the high-resistance state and cut leakage. Devices switched cleanly within one volt either way, with on-off current ratios around ten thousand to one hundred thousand. They survived one hundred switching cycles and held their states for the full test window. Charge storage also rose in the low-resistance state, which the team ties to filaments and particle-assisted effects at the interfaces.
pmc-13515818:
Jing Li and colleagues report a plant study, published in 2026. It covers the root fungus Serendipita indica. This fungus lives inside the roots of many plants. The team asked how it helps wheat seedlings grow. They suspected chlorophyll plays a role. This green pigment captures light for photosynthesis.

Wheat colonised by the fungus grew taller. It also grew heavier. It held more chlorophyll than uncolonised seedlings. Gene activity profiling of leaves showed clear changes. Genes for building chlorophyll switched up. Genes linked to leaf ageing switched down. Related pigment pathways were also enriched. Targeted gene tests confirmed the pattern. The pattern sits behind the stronger growth.
pmc-13515918:
Rihwa Choi and co-authors examine in 2026 how different cutoffs for a blood inflammation marker change heart risk classification in Korean adults, beyond what cholesterol tests already reveal. The marker, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, flags the low-grade inflammation that feeds artery disease.

Using a national 2024 health survey of about fifty-eight hundred adults, they applied three cutoffs. Over a quarter of adults passed the lowest threshold, while under nine percent passed the highest. Among people whose lipids looked completely normal, the marker still flagged a sizable extra share, up to about fifteen percent of all adults at the loosest cutoff. The authors say thresholds shaped on Western data need population-specific reading in Korea.
pmc-13517318:
Corrales-Hernández and colleagues studied how caffeine combined with a birth-inducing hormone affects sows during farrowing, comparing first-time mothers with experienced ones in a 2026 animal study. Pig research usually centers on piglets, leaving the sow's own response understudied, even though intravulvar caffeine is authorized in Europe. The team measured hormones, behavior, and delivery performance under different induction protocols.

Corrales-Hernández found that a split-dose hormone protocol plus caffeine clearly shortened total farrowing time and the intervals between piglets in both parity groups, increased piglets born alive. Reduced perinatal deaths, especially in experienced sows. Treated sows also changed posture less often, a sign of discomfort, and rested more in favorable lying positions. Stress and reproductive hormone patterns during birth depended strongly on whether the sow had given birth before, showing the maternal response is parity-driven and the combination a useful welfare tool.
pmc-13517518:
Arianna Sgariboldi, Nicola Chirico, and Ester Papa build prediction models for chemicals' climate impact in a 2026 study. Life-cycle assessors need each substance's global warming potential, yet measured values exist for few. Their structure-activity models infer warming potential straight from a molecule's shape, using plain regression on a small set of readable input clues.

The models follow the OECD rules for official acceptance: open maths, checked validity, a defined zone where predictions hold, and input clues a chemist can read. They stay simpler than rival models of similar accuracy. A test run screened over thirteen thousand candidate replacement chemicals, ranking safer options by predicted climate cost. Sgariboldi's team offers the tools as practical support for assessors and for industry hunting replacements for harmful substances before new products lock in avoidable warming.
pmc-13518918:
Guanran Zhao and six colleagues make carbon hollow fiber membranes in 2026 for separating ethylene from ethane, two gases so alike that cryogenic distillation eats about 0.3 percent of world energy. Such sheets could slash that cost, yet few can split the pair finely enough at scale without defects.

Their nonstop process blends tailored metal-organic framework particles into polymers drawn from farm biomass, then carbonizes the fibers in semi-batches. The three-phase nanostructure that results passed ethylene fast while blocking ethane, reaching a selectivity of 75 at high pressure with 21 days of stable running. A palm-sized module kept its strong showing, and cost checks backed its market case. Zhao and co-authors frame the route as a factory-ready toolbox.
pmc-13519018:
Giulia Parovel and Stefano Guidi document a visual quirk in 2026: a smiling mouth makes the eyes above it look brighter. Earlier work on mixed expressions focused on emotion reading, not raw appearance. The pair ran two within-subject experiments where volunteers rated eye brightness and smile strength for whole faces and for isolated features.

Eye brightness ratings climbed steadily as the paired mouth smiled more, even when the eyes stayed neutral. A smiling mouth also lifted genuine Duchenne smiling eyes above their solo baseline, while a neutral mouth dimmed them. The effect showed up in photos, paintings, and even face-like patterns. Parovel and Guidi frame the mouth and eyes as one integrated expression.
pmc-13520118:
Tao Hua leads an eleven-author team in 2026 setting out design rules for ultra-narrow light emitters in organic displays. Pure colors need emission bandwidths under 10 nanometers, yet finding such molecules has been trial and error, since a narrow spread is hard to foresee. Their scheme treats ring layout, meaning how fused rings connect, as the control knob.

High-throughput screening across fusion patterns of boron-nitrogen doped triangulene found a taking-turns layout that cuts the energy lost as the structure relaxes. A ground-state score then foresaw the narrowing without costly excited-state math. Guided lab builds yielded sky-blue emitters with light bandwidths down to 9.1 nanometers. Devices made from solution reached 10.9 nanometer bandwidth with 38.1 percent external quantum efficiency.
pmc-13520318:
ShengSheng Liu and colleagues built machine learning models to forecast long-term survival after surgery for invasive breast cancer. Published in 2026, the study used United States SEER registry data from 2010 through 2020 plus an outside patient group from a cancer hospital in Guangxi. Four models competed to predict cancer-specific survival at three, five, seven, and ten years.

A random survival forest model led the field, scoring strongest on the training data and holding the best accuracy on both internal and outside checks. Its calibration was sound and its clinical value stayed stable on decision analysis. Feature-importance diagrams showed which patient factors drove the forecasts, and the model sorted patients into distinct risk bands. The authors present it as a tool for tailoring follow-up and treatment talks. Readers get a validated predictor, with the usual caution that models need local testing before routine use.
pmc-13521618:
Yoo and colleagues built an open, reproducible workflow for mapping city tree canopy from free aerial photographs, work that usually demands commercial imagery or lidar. Urban trees cool streets and clean air, but canopy changes block by block across public and private land. Their 2026 framework pairs a U-Net segmentation model, which paints canopy cover pixel by pixel, with a YOLOv9e detector that pinpoints individual trees, both tuned for America's free NAIP farm imagery programme.

Across two Los Angeles neighbourhoods the segmentation model scored strongly on the standard Dice overlap measure. The detector found trees with moderate accuracy against a held-out test set containing over seventeen thousand hand-labelled trees. A sufficiency experiment gave practitioners a concrete annotation target: performance levelled off at about 130 labelled trees per image tile. Early tests also suggest the workflow transfers to unseen neighbourhoods without retraining.
pmc-13522318:
Nyall R. London leads a 2026 first immunotherapy trial in recurrent or spread olfactory neuroblastoma, a rare nose tumour with no established treatment at that stage. Eleven patients received a dual-action fusion drug that traps a growth signal while blocking the PD-L1 checkpoint, dosed every two weeks.

Enrolment stopped early when drug development was discontinued. No tumours shrank objectively, so the main goal was missed. Half of evaluable first-cohort patients held stable disease, some durably, with one showing complete metabolic clearance on specialised imaging. Severe drug-linked harms affected three patients, including immune diabetes and bleeding events. Longer stable control hints at benefit for a subset.
pmc-13522418:
Nathan L Dowling and collaborators report a 2026 Australian pilot study of a concentrated four-day program for obsessive-compulsive disorder, known as the Bergen 4-Day Treatment. Twelve inpatients received the brief program and thirteen received a standard three-week inpatient program. Neither group was assigned at random, so the comparison is presented as early feasibility work.

Independent ratings used a standard obsessive-compulsive severity scale before treatment, shortly after treatment, and three months later. Symptoms, depression, and anxiety fell in both groups, while the four-day group scored lower at both follow-ups and showed higher response and remission rates. No one dropped out of the brief program, and satisfaction was high, supporting a larger and more rigorous trial.
pmc-13522518:
Hye Hyun Kim and co-authors present a direct test for cancer-linked microRNAs in blood in a 2026 diagnostic study. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA molecules whose levels shift in many cancers, yet current tests need several amplification steps that can introduce error. The new platform uses a glowing protein cage carrying a DNA probe and an enzyme-linked partner that changes light output when the target binds.

No amplification step is required, and the system can tell apart targets differing by a single letter of genetic code. Applied to blood serum, the test distinguished lung and gastric cancer patients from healthy donors with high accuracy. The authors argue that simpler, direct measurement could support earlier and more reliable cancer diagnosis, possibly even outside large laboratories.
pmc-13522618:
Rajesh Soma introduces an artificial intelligence framework for checking contract risk inside a business quoting system in a 2026 paper. Contracts for software services carry complex privacy, service-level, and pricing clauses that manual review often misses. The framework pairs a large generative model with a language model for meaning matching, scanning contract text against major privacy and security standards in real time.

Testing used five hundred synthetic contracts, with manual legal review and a rule-based method as baselines. The framework cut contract errors by roughly a quarter to a third, shortened deal cycles, and reached about ninety-two percent compliance detection accuracy. The author notes that the figures come from simulation and need real-world validation, and the design includes encryption, bias checks, and audit trails.
pmc-13523518:
Xiao-Yu Zhou and colleagues pool, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, cardiovascular outcomes for two diabetes drugs, semaglutide and tirzepatide, in adults living with type 2 diabetes, overweight, or obesity. Both drugs are widely used, yet heart outcome evidence differed in maturity. The reviewers searched six sources through November 2024.

Forty-seven randomized trials with 59,352 participants were included. Semaglutide was linked with lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, cardiovascular death, heart attack, and heart failure, while the stroke estimate fell short of statistical significance. Tirzepatide showed a lower heart attack risk, but its other cardiovascular estimates were not significant. Because most trials compared each drug with a control rather than head to head, the authors warn against reading the results as proof that one drug beats the other.
pmc-13524418:
Erin A. Hirsch and colleagues describe, in a 2026 cross-sectional survey, behavioral factors tied to yearly lung cancer screening participation. Low-dose CT screening works best when eligible people return annually, yet adherence determinants are multifaceted and poorly mapped. The team applied a cognitive-social model of how people process health information.

The survey reached 143 screening-eligible adults who had recently completed a scan with annual follow-up recommended. Respondents reported high confidence in handling the screening process, saw strong benefits, and named few barriers to returning. Fatalism about cancer was low. Knowledge specific to screening, however, was suboptimal. The authors suggest communication efforts should target knowledge gaps while building on existing confidence, and they offer the findings as groundwork for future hypothesis-driven adherence research.
pmc-13524618:
Monique M. Ridosh leads a large team in a 2026 scoping review on what parents and caregivers say about self-management for youth with chronic conditions that began in childhood. As these young people move toward adult care, families help them learn to manage their own health. The review asked how much of that literature actually includes family voices.

From a parent review of 640 articles, 218 studies published between 1992 and 2025 included parent or caregiver data for young people aged 9 to 35. Just over half reported the caregiver's relationship to the child, and far fewer reported age or race and ethnicity. Most studies were quantitative and cross-sectional. Topics centered on the individual young person, then family support, with health system and environment rarely addressed. The authors recommend richer reporting and stronger designs.
pmc-13525518:
Alshami and Kattan tested dental adhesives upgraded with light-activated antimicrobial particles for bonding fillings to decay-affected baby-tooth dentin, in a 2026 laboratory study. The additives were erythrosine, a pink dye that kills bacteria when lit, loaded onto either zirconia nanoparticles or sepiolite, a clay mineral nanoparticle. Caries-affected dentin, the softened layer dentists often leave behind, bonds weakly and harbors bacteria, so a germ-killing glue could help.

Alshami split specimens into four groups, from plain adhesive to the two nanoparticle versions, then measured bond strength by pulling the joint apart and counted surviving Lactobacillus bacteria. The sepiolite version performed best on both measures, with the fewest surviving bacteria and the strongest bonds, while plain adhesive was worst on both counts. Both nanoparticle adhesives beat the control, and the authors suggest testing them in multispecies bacterial films and after aging to confirm durability.
pmc-13526218:
Alasgarli and co-authors recount a stroke that unmasked a hidden infiltrative heart disease. Their 2026 case report describes a 43-year-old woman came to hospital with an ischemic stroke whose origin was unknown. Checking for a heart source, ultrasound scans showed diffuse abnormalities of the heart muscle and left atrium. Her electrocardiogram paired low electrical voltage with thickened ventricle walls. That classic mismatch pointed to infiltration.

Blood and marrow tests were inconclusive, but a kidney biopsy confirmed deposits of monoclonal lambda light chains, establishing AL amyloidosis. She received heart failure treatment and daratumumab-based chemotherapy, yet rapidly progressed to kidney and multiorgan failure and died after the second cycle. The authors stress considering amyloidosis in younger stroke patients with this imaging signature.
pmc-13526718:
Xiaojun He and colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, how interleukin-10 helps surgical incisions heal during sepsis, a severe whole-body infection that delays wound repair. The anti-inflammatory signal IL10 was suspected to act through fibroblasts and macrophages in the wound, but the cellular details were unclear. Human skin samples and a mouse sepsis model were combined.

Sepsis raised natural killer cells and macrophages and expanded two harmful subsets, PI16-positive fibroblasts and CCL8-positive macrophages, with stronger crosstalk between them. IL10 treatment shrank those subsets, calmed the crosstalk, and prompted macrophages to release signals that drove fibroblast growth. The authors nominate PI16 and CCL8 as treatment targets for septic wound healing.
pmc-13526818:
Tan and colleagues published a 2026 study on checking AI guesses about gene jobs with hard statistics. Language models can now guess a gene set's role from its list alone. Those guesses sound plausible but lacked a rigorous way to be tested. The team turned gene and role descriptions into number vectors for testing.

Top embedding models recovered known gene relationships with high accuracy overall. They caught gene-role links with sensitivity above 95 percent in benchmarks. The framework separated real signals from model-made noise better than rivals. An open software package puts the method in other labs' hands. One drug-response gene set gained meaning through the new approach. Language-model guesses thus gain a proper gatekeeper for research use.
pmc-13527618:
Qinni Yang reviewed a protein best known in ovarian cancer as a possible marker for autoimmune disease. Published in 2026, the single-author review covers human epididymal protein 4, or HE4, a secreted protein that tracks ovarian cancer with better accuracy than older markers. Cancer and autoimmune disease share overactive immunity and inflammation, raising the question of whether HE4 also tracks autoimmunity.
