The review walks through HE4 biology in these conditions and weighs its promise for diagnosis and monitoring of chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease. Readers get a candidate marker with a plausible mechanism, still needing prospective validation before clinical use.
pmc-13527918:
Zainab M. Al-Zadjali and eleven colleagues examine late HIV diagnosis in Oman in a 2026 cohort study covering diagnoses made from 1992 to 2024 at the Royal Hospital in Muscat, the national referral center. Records of 549 adults were reviewed, with late diagnosis defined by a low CD4 cell count at the time HIV was found.

About thirty percent of patients were diagnosed late, and most of them had felt no symptoms and had no other illnesses recorded. Younger adults carried strikingly higher risk than those over 47, as did people with low hemoglobin, heart disease, or high blood pressure. Sex and route of infection showed no clear link. The authors see missed chances for earlier testing, especially among young people.
pmc-13528018:
Md Feroj Ahmed and eight colleagues mine gene data in a 2026 study for links between type 2 diabetes and triple-negative breast cancer. The two diseases often occur together, and their drugs can clash. The team combined gene activity datasets for both conditions. They used an explainable machine learning method with SHAP values to rank shared genes.

Thirty-six shared genes separated patients from controls in both diseases. Four stood out as key shared genes: S100A9, CIRBP, USP10, and PSMD1. Network analysis found the switches that control them. Pathway analysis pointed to common disease mechanisms. Docking tests then screened known drugs against the key genes. Two candidates emerged, tepotinib and ursodiol, as possible shared treatments. The authors offer them as leads for lab testing, not proven therapies.
pmc-13528418:
Luis Alejandro Barrera surveyed rare disease policy in Colombia and proposed a better path forward. Published in 2026, the Spanish-language essay untangles two labels often treated as one: orphan diseases, lacking commercial drug interest, and rare diseases, affecting very few people. Colombia counts as rare any disease under one case per five thousand people, recognizing 2,273 such diseases today.

Colombia led Latin America with its 2010 orphan-disease law, covering caregivers, reference centers, central drug buying, research funding, and training. A 2015 statute then tightened the threshold from one per two thousand to one per five thousand, dropping the more frequent diseases from the list. The author weighs what that shift cost patients and what reforms could restore broader protection. Readers get a compact policy history with reform ideas attached.
pmc-13528518:
Jiamin Wang and six colleagues protect glycerol's shape to steer its electric conversion in a 2026 study. Glycerol pours out of biodiesel plants as cheap surplus. Turning it into glyceric acid is valuable but messy, since reactions split the carbon chain. The team first locked glycerol into solketal, a ring form that hides two of its three reactive arms.

A copper-molybdenum catalyst then oxidized only the exposed arm. In strong alkali the setup hit about ninety percent selectivity for glyceric acid. Conversion neared ninety-five percent within five hours. The rig ran steadily for one hundred hours. Making the protected form and purifying the acid both proved practical at high purity. The authors offer protection-first thinking as a general route for upgrading biomass leftovers.
pmc-13528718:
Ayşe Gülden Bekgöz, Kerem Dost Bilmez, and Muhammed Saltuk Deniz review helicopter ambulance trips for infection patients across Türkiye in a 2026 study. Registry data held 543 such patients. Breathing infections led the list, with COVID-19 next. Most trips, about seventy-three percent, stayed inside one province. The rest crossed to other provinces.

Median flight time was sixty-three minutes overall. Cross-province flights took about one hundred fifteen minutes at the median. Local flights took about fifty-seven. Brain and membrane infections were far more likely to fly far. Sepsis and skin infections usually stayed local. The authors read the pattern as need-based triage, not distance alone. Time-critical brain infections gain most from fast hops to specialist centers, they argue.
pmc-13528818:
Bhavanam and colleagues reported in 2026 a hard diagnostic case: a toddler with five months of painless rectal bleeding traced to a Meckel's diverticulum hiding on the wrong side of the bowel. This congenital pouch, a remnant of the duct that feeds the embryo, almost always sits on one bowel border. The mesenteric form is rare and easily confused with a duplication cyst. The child had already had normal endoscopies elsewhere and a camera operation that found nothing.

Repeat scopes were again normal, but a tagged red blood cell scan showed blood pooling in the small bowel. Open surgery found the pouch buried in the mid-ileum mesentery with its own blood supply; surgeons removed it and rejoined the bowel. Lab study confirmed a Meckel's diverticulum carrying stomach-type lining, the usual bleeding source. The child recovered with no further bleeding, and the authors stress keeping the rare variant in mind.
pmc-13529018:
Chia-Wei Tsai and colleagues published a 2026 cryptanalysis of a quantum communication protocol. The protocol promised provably secure direct messaging. A controller supervised exchanges between two parties. The original authors assumed the controller might be hostile. Their security proof claimed protection even then.

Tsai's team shows the claim fails. The controller can send hidden probe particles. Those probes quietly reveal the secret encoding keys. Combining probes with public data recovers every message bit. The attack leaves no errors for checks to catch. The result exposes a blind spot in the proof. Quantum security claims need attacks tested, not just theorems.
pmc-13529718:
Zengjing Chen and four colleagues use quantum walks to hunt new uses for old drugs in a 2026 paper. Finding fresh purposes for approved drugs is cheaper than inventing new ones. Their method, DRQuantum, walks a layered network linking drugs, diseases, and proteins. Quantum walks explore many paths at once through entanglement effects. Standard random walks check one route at a time.

The walks turn each node into a compact feature code. Matching codes suggest drug and disease pairs worth testing. Scores beat classic repurposing methods on ranking and accuracy measures. Case studies on single diseases showed practical hits. The authors say the quantum view captures tangled network structure better. It reads both local neighborhoods and the whole map. The tool is offered for early candidate spotting, not proof of effect.
pmc-13530118:
Changqiang Yang and Yue Song report in 2026 on a special T-cell type in children whose IgA vasculitis has reached the kidneys. Kidney involvement decides the long-term outlook for this vessel inflammation illness, yet its immune drivers stay partly hidden. Blood testing covered 88 children split among three groups.

Children with kidney disease showed more of these gamma delta T cells, with more switched into an active state. Cells making the signal IL-17A raised the odds of kidney involvement and tracked with protein lost in urine over 24 hours. That measure proved highly specific, hinting at a future blood marker.
pmc-13530218:
Dezheng Wu and co-authors build a 2026 product rating system that learns its criteria from shopper reviews instead of fixed checklists. Fixed scorecards and personal weighting miss shifting market tastes. Review mining first extracts hidden themes, which become the scoring dimensions for a candidate product.

A fuzzy ranking method turns qualitative judgments into numbers, while a swarm search refines the weights and repairs inconsistent scoring. A smartwatch case test showed the system capturing what users actually valued and producing balanced overall ratings. The authors offer the framework as a guide for design choices and market positioning.
pmc-13531818:
Jihun Ryu and Kwang Shik Choi project in 2026 how climate change will reshuffle 18 mosquito species across South Korea. Nearly two thousand location records fed mapping models using climate, land shape, and land cover data. Future ranges were drawn for three decades under three emission paths.

Ground wetness, elevation, and land cover shaped current ranges more than climate alone. Under the harshest 2070s path, two major disease carriers more than doubled or tripled their suitable ground. Two northern malaria mosquitoes lost all suitable habitat in that scenario. Five species, mostly malaria carriers, ranked highly vulnerable overall.
pmc-13531918:
Maylen Reiersøl Dahl and co-authors follow in 2026 how adult children fare in the weeks after an older parent moves into a nursing home. Eight adult children gave narrative interviews three times during 2022 within a larger qualitative project. Two exemplar stories, a daughter and a son, carry the shared patterns.

The son account breathes calm and relief, while the daughter account hums with stress and tension, despite similar circumstances. Personal resources, organizational support, and social ties tilted each path. Staff can lighten the passage by supporting role mastery, personal wellbeing, and family relationships.
pmc-13534418:
Ning Chang and colleagues report in 2026 compounds that lower DUX4 activity in facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, a disease with no approved cure. Faulty release of the DUX4 gene in muscle drives the damage, so most drug hunts target it. An artificial intelligence screen picked molecules predicted to bind BAZ1A, a chromatin factor tied to DUX4 control.

One compound, C06, strongly cut DUX4 and its target genes in patient muscle cells. At low doses it matched a known blocker yet stayed more specific, restoring a healthier gene pattern with little disturbance elsewhere. Readers see a candidate for further drug development.
pmc-13534718:
William Darch and colleagues test in 2026 whether proteins from tardigrades, tiny animals famed for surviving extremes, can help human blood vessel cells handle stress. Vessel lining cells face heat and salt stress in culture and in engineered tissue. Four tardigrade proteins were added to the cells through gene transfer.

During stress itself, cell activity fell in protein-bearing cells. After a recovery day, most protein groups rebounded far above control levels for both salt and heat stress. Protection thus appears context linked, aiding recovery more than the acute phase, which invites deeper study.
pmc-13535218:
Arsene Djoko Nono leads a team in Douala, Cameroon, on drug proof gut germs. Their study from twenty twenty-six spans people, birds, and waste water. The germ type makes a shield that blocks many key drugs.

The team took blood, swabs, bird gut, and waste water samples. They grew the germ, tested drugs, and read full gene codes. Rates and risk traits are set out for each source. Gene reads show how strains link across the three sources. Such cross checks are rare for Cameroon and aid control of spread.
pmc-13536118:
Xu and colleagues laid out a review plan for lung cancer team care in this protocol from twenty twenty-six. Care by a multidisciplinary team is a cornerstone of cancer treatment, yet delivery varies worldwide. Low-resource settings face the steepest barriers. No global review has yet mapped how such care is organized and where practice lags evidence.

The planned scoping review follows established frameworks for mapping studies. Six databases plus trial registries will be searched, in English and Chinese sources alike. Two reviewers will screen and extract data independently, with a third settling disputes. Findings will appear as charts, tables, and narrative. No ethics approval is needed since all sources are published. The protocol is registered openly.
pmc-13536218:
Rutter and colleagues expose a counting flaw that hides how deadly rural head injuries are: hospital statistics never see the patients who die at the scene. Their 2026 retrospective study gathered every adult traumatic brain injury in one Australian trauma system during 2019, hospital admissions and prehospital deaths alike, 266 people in all. It compared outcomes by where the injury happened.

Nearly half the cohort never reached a hospital alive, and just under two thirds of injuries occurred outside cities. Rural patients carried roughly double the adjusted odds of death compared with urban patients. They arrived with similar coma scores, pupil findings, injury patterns, and scan severity, which points away from injury mix and toward distance and delay. The single strongest killer was polytrauma, injury to several body regions at once, which multiplied the odds of death about eightfold in the model. The authors demand that rural injury statistics always include prehospital deaths.
pmc-13536818:
Abdulaziz Bakhsh and colleagues assess training gaps in palliative care for adolescents and young adults in Canada in a 2026 national survey. Patients aged 15 to 39 years face distinct medical and life-stage needs near the end of life, yet adult training lacks specific skills for this group. Doctors who finished adult palliative training between 2019 and 2024 rated their exposure, knowledge, comfort, and learning needs.

Fifty-five eligible replies showed that under one third had received group-specific training in residency. Most reported low comfort with the youngest patients, aged 15 to 18 years. Largest gaps covered moving from child to adult services, sexual health and fertility, and finding social support. Limited hands-on exposure and few mentors were leading barriers. The authors propose a dedicated skills curriculum.
pmc-13537518:
Adeel Anwaar and four co-authors report surgery for a large kidney stone in a rare case of a kidney on the wrong side. Their case report appeared in twenty twenty-six. In crossed ectopia, one kidney sits on the other side of the body. The non-fused form is very rare, and odd shape and tube paths make stone care hard.

The stone was large and dense, yet a scope passed up the urine tube cleared it in full. No cut from the back was needed. A review of past cases backs a wider role for this scope route in odd kidneys. The authors present the case as proof the route can work even with a big stone load.
pmc-13538318:
Man Bo Lee and colleagues disable a candidate gene for pre-harvest sprouting in rice using gene editing in a 2026 study. Sprouting means grains germinate on the plant before harvest in wet weather, spoiling quality and yield worldwide. Fine mapping had pointed to OsERF94 on chromosome four. Two edited lines carrying disabling changes were tested under sprouting conditions, with genome checks and gene activity profiling.

Edited lines germinated far more readily than normal plants under sprouting conditions, showing greater vulnerability after gene loss. Genome resequencing found few or no stray edits, supporting precise targeting. Activity shifts hit hormone pathways that wake seeds, with growth hormone making genes rising and breakdown genes falling. Reporter tests hinted at wider promoter effects. The authors propose the gene as a breeding target for sprouting resistance.
pmc-13538418:
Piero Calosi and co-authors compare chemical profiles of giant Antarctic sea invertebrates with normal-sized relatives in a 2026 study. Giants may have evolved under rich oxygen in icy water, yet molecular proof of metabolic adaptation was missing. Giants across groups shared a shifted use of energy-making pathways, suggesting common metabolic rewiring for large bodies in harsh cold. Giants also broke the smooth size scaling seen in relatives, marking them as more than simply enlarged copies. Acute warming triggered no short-term chemical rewiring in giants or relatives. The authors conclude that giants look no more heat-sensitive than relatives in brief tests.
pmc-13539918:

Using public tumor datasets and laboratory cell lines, the team showed that losing ALDH2 created resistance only when p53 was mutant. The loss raised a second enzyme, PDE4B, which matched poor outcomes in patients. A licensed drug that blocks PDE4B, roflumilast, restored the cancer cells' death response to oxaliplatin. The authors suggest testing this pairing in p53-mutant disease.
pmc-13540718:
Andries Janse van Vuuren and colleagues studied cooperative breeding in babblers in two thousand twenty-six. Helpers raise others' young instead of their own. pmc-13540818:

The authors caution that perfect use might still have failed, since the cabinet's basic efficacy was never proven under Korail's contamination load.
pmc-13540918:
Şeydanur Urhan Güçlü and colleagues survey Turkish jaw surgeons in 2026. The topic is psychological checks before jaw surgery. Such surgery reshapes the jaw and the face. It strongly affects how patients feel about their looks. Missed mental health problems can hurt satisfaction and adherence.

pmc-13542218:
Peymaneh Davoodi, Marzieh Atapour, Arezoo Shahsavari, and Roozbeh Kiani design, in a 2026 computer study, CRISPR gene edits for the honeybee's vitellogenin gene before anyone attempts the difficult laboratory work. Their pipeline generated about fifty-seven candidate guide RNAs for each of two gene segments and scored them for structure, cutting precision, and repair bias. The best guide for one segment favoured enzyme access, while the other segment's leader promised stronger disruption of the protein.
pmc-13543418:

pmc-13543518:
Matteo Zanchetta's team studied ultrasound markers in 2026 for delayed graft function after kidney transplantation. Delayed function struck about nineteen percent of the retrospective group. A Doppler measure called the resistive index ran higher in those patients at both scans, tying sluggish blood flow to poor early function. In the small contrast pilot, the area-under-curve measure of enhancement separated the groups, with lower values in grafts that went on to delayed function. Standard Doppler already helps, the authors conclude, and contrast measures may add value once larger studies confirm them.
pmc-13543618:

The third cancer had no virus insertion and a separate origin. Multiple primaries in one organ, the case shows, can hide behind an imaging diagnosis of spread.
pmc-13544618:

Both choices are standard in Dutch burn centers. Patient values should weigh in that close call. Shared choice needs clear facts in plain form. The aid packs facts, value prompts, and talk guides. Patients and staff both helped shape the aid content. Trials will test if the aid lifts choice quality.
pmc-13545418:

Sixty-four male veterans over 55 were assigned to either a standard protein diet or a higher protein diet, both calorie-reduced and paired with exercise. Function was tested with a standard performance battery, walking tests, and grip strength over six months.

The higher protein group lost slightly more weight by three months while keeping more fat-free mass at six months. Their performance scores, walking distance, and grip strength also improved more than the standard group's. The authors treat the findings as early evidence and call for larger trials in this understudied group.
pmc-13546718:
Konan Ange-Sylvestre Goli and a regional team characterized in 2026 the virus behind peste des petits ruminants, a deadly disease of sheep and goats, in the Savannah District of northern Ivory Coast. The sequences fell into two distinct clusters, suggesting the virus entered the area more than once, probably through uncontrolled animal movements across borders. The authors call for stronger molecular surveillance and cross-border vaccination planning.
pmc-13547218:
Fan, Hsieh, Lai, and Chen trace how a dividing cell keeps its spindle centered. Their 2026 paper studies the protein EPLIN during mitosis. The spindle must anchor to the cell cortex correctly. pmc-13548218:
Elizabeth O'Nions and eleven co-authors lay out a study protocol on fairness in multiple sclerosis care in a 2026 paper. The planned study gathers routine records from five specialist neurology centers covering about seven million people in England and Wales.

Everyone newly diagnosed from 2018 through 2024 enters the cohort. The main measure is time from diagnosis to first disease modifying treatment, with time from first symptoms to diagnosis and use of high strength treatments as secondary measures. The team will test whether age, sex, deprivation, and ethnicity predict delays, adjusting for clinical factors. Results aim to expose inequities worth fixing.
pmc-13548518:
Ebru Guney Sahin reports a 2026 case of a two-year-old girl who inhaled aluminum phosphide, a grain-storage pesticide, and developed severe heart failure. Poisoning by swallowing this chemical is well known for causing collapse, yet dangerous heart damage after breathing it in is rarely described. The child arrived previously healthy, then suffered repeated cardiac arrests within her first hours in hospital.

Her heart recovered enough for the machine to stop on day eleven. She later developed severe lung injury and died after another arrest on day twenty-one, a course the author uses to argue for very early heart support in such cases.
pmc-13548618:
Zhila Maghbooli and colleagues review whether immune-system genes that raise the risk of getting multiple sclerosis also drive how fast it worsens, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. One variant, HLA DRB1*15:01, roughly triples the chance of developing the disease, yet its link to progression was disputed. Across all variants, the pooled link to progression was modest. The famous risk variant itself showed no significant tie to worsening. Three other variants did look harmful, most strikingly DRB1*09 with about fourfold odds. Effects also split by region, appearing in Asian and North American studies but not European ones. The authors conclude that the genes for catching the disease and the genes for its course are largely different sets.
pmc-13548718:
Yunling Long, Zhuoyuanyuan Chen, and Yuling Xie interview nurses who deliver home care booked through an internet platform in western China, in a 2026 qualitative study. The service sends hospital nurses to the homes of elderly and chronically ill patients, extending care beyond the ward. Twelve experienced nurses, all women with an average of eighteen years in practice, described what the work is really like.

Four themes emerged. Nurses valued professional growth, patient convenience, and the hospital's good name. They also hit logistical snags, safety worries on home visits, and clumsy procedures. They asked for stronger teamwork and policy backing, and they proposed simpler processes, better protection, and wider publicity. With no insurance reimbursement and thin institutional safety nets in their setting, the authors name safety training, insurance coverage, and interprofessional support as make-or-break priorities.
pmc-13550618:
Qingfeng Guo, with six colleagues, published a 2026 method for spotting gas entering a drilling well before it becomes dangerous. Gas intrusion can lead to blowouts, so the team used ultrasound Doppler sensors, which track flow by sound frequency shifts, around a wellbore pipe. Their framework counts gas channels, measures frequency shift ranges, and sets thresholds that separate flow patterns.

A laboratory system with a circulation pool and sensor array mimicked downhole conditions, injecting gas at speeds from 0.1 to 5 meters per second at several positions. The method followed how two-phase flow evolved and flagged pattern changes early. The authors present the non-invasive setup as a fast-responding option for gas kick monitoring.
pmc-13551118:
Halet Türkantoz, leading eleven colleagues, published a 2026 report on breakthrough bleeding in the GTH-AHA-EMI study of acquired haemophilia A, a rare disorder where antibodies attack clotting factor VIII. A preventive drug, emicizumab, reduced bleeding overall, yet 22 clinically relevant new bleeds occurred in 14 of 47 patients during twelve weeks of prophylaxis. The team pulled study records and surveyed investigators for details.

Nine bleeds counted as major, fifteen arose spontaneously, and twenty needed treatment, most often with recombinant factor VIIa. Eight patients went to hospital and nine needed intensive care or invasive procedures, though most bleeds resolved and permanent harm was reported in two patients. No clotting complications appeared, so the authors call treatment safe and usually effective.
pmc-13551718:
