The team searched six databases to September 2025 for randomized trials, pooling results with a random-effects model and grading evidence quality.

Five trials with 5,903 women, run in Uganda, Kenya, and the United States between 2009 and 2021, qualified. Structured contraceptive counseling was the commonest intervention, joined in some trials by vouchers, outreach, and safe-sex education. The pooled analysis began from a significant association between such programs and contraceptive use, and the authors present the trials as the available randomized evidence base.
pmc-13551818:
Emrah Harman, with eight colleagues, published a 2026 study of gut problems in an immune deficiency disease. The disease, called CVID, weakens antibody defense. Gut involvement is common and serious in these patients. The team reviewed 109 adults at one center. They compared patients with and without gut involvement on clinical, scope, tissue, and immune data.

Gut involvement appeared in well over half the patients. Those patients had lower IgA and IgM antibodies. They also had fewer switched memory B cells, a mature antibody cell type. Low IgM and low switched cells stayed linked in the final model. IgM alone split the groups well. Most scoped patients had abnormal findings, often like bowel inflammation. The team links the gut problem to stalled B cell growth.
pmc-13551918:
Chiara Riccietti, with a large Bologna team, published a 2026 study of thinking in a brain fluid disorder of older adults. The disorder is idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus. A shunt operation can relieve it. Many patients also carry Alzheimer's changes, which may blunt the gain. Patients had full workups from 2015 to 2025. Workups included deep thinking tests and spinal fluid markers.

At the start, 226 patients showed the classic pattern of weak attention and executive skill. Of these, 102 had surgery and were retested at six months. Thinking improved overall after surgery in the reported results. The core aim was to compare patients with and without Alzheimer's markers. That split, before and after surgery, shows how a second disease shapes who gains from a shunt.
pmc-13552218:
Jianing Wang and co-authors test whether a blood protein, C1q, can foretell delirium after emergency surgery for a torn aorta. Acute type A aortic dissection is a surgical emergency, and delirium after the operation is common and harmful. C1q is part of the complement system, an early arm of immune defense. The team enrolled patients having dissection surgery and drew blood before the operation and on the first day after.

Delirium was checked daily with bedside methods. In all, 67 patients were studied. C1q ran higher in those who became delirious, both before and after surgery. Preoperative C1q predicted delirium on its own, with an odds ratio near 1.38 and fair accuracy on the prediction curve. A blood draw taken before the knife could thus flag who needs delirium watch and preventive care most.
pmc-13553318:
Valeria Calcaterra leads a six-author team testing simple blood scores for metabolic syndrome in young people with Down syndrome. Their 2026 study drew on sixty patients and forty peers without the condition. Metabolic syndrome means a cluster of risks, such as high blood sugar, poor blood fats, and high pressure. The team set a score built from blood fats and sugar against older measures, alone and mixed with body size.

One in seven of the Down syndrome group met the full cluster of risks. The fat-and-sugar score matched the older insulin-based test in spotting cases, and it gave the best overall score for sorting who had the syndrome. Mixed versions were less sharp but rarely gave false alarms. The authors call the simple score a cheap early warning tool.
pmc-13553718:
Katsunori Kouchi, Takashi Fumita, Chikako Nakata, and Keita Kagaya report scope-based treatment of children's pancreatic duct injuries, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. Blunt belly injuries can tear the pancreas duct, and care without surgery often breeds fluid sacs and organ shrinkage. Their center has used duct stents placed by scope since twenty nineteen.

Ten injured children were graded by the current trauma scale. Three with severe grades received stents; in two, the stent bridged the tear, and the organ stayed healthy, with one sac that faded on its own. The third child needed drainage through the duct when a sac grew infected, and it cleared fast. One unstented severe case fared worse, with heavy shrinkage. The authors back scope care as a safe option.
pmc-13554118:
Kimihiro Yamazaki and ten colleagues build a digital twin of biomacromolecular thermodynamics from cryo-EM data. Their functions hinge on thermodynamics, from small local wiggles to large shape changes on the free-energy landscape. Cryo-EM now resolves large, complex static structures, yet their full energy behavior stays hard to pin down. Their 2026 paper presents a deep learning frame with a theoretically guaranteed isometric autoencoder.

The frame rebuilds the thermodynamics recorded in cryo-EM data and maps mixed shape states and transition paths partly on its own. Tests on a 50S ribosome and two SARS-CoV-2 spike proteins yielded fresh biological insights with no added assumptions. Unlike similar methods, the approach guarantees exact construction of the free-energy landscape. It promises to advance biology by exposing the energy flows of complex systems.
pmc-13554318:
Dunliang Ma leads an eleven-author team comparing a backward-route heart artery procedure in patients with and without diabetes in a 2026 study. The procedure reopens arteries blocked for a long time by approaching through side channels. In all, 836 patients at one centre qualified for review. Success rates for tracking channels and reopening arteries matched closely between the two groups.

Hospital complications stayed rare and alike in both groups. Follow-up covered most patients for a median near three years. Patients with diabetes faced more major heart events overall, driven by higher death rates from all causes and from heart causes. After adjustment, diabetes still predicted worse long-term survival. The authors call the procedure safe for both groups, with harder long-term odds in diabetes.
pmc-13554618:
Ralf Gold and colleagues reported final results in two thousand twenty-six from the SISTER study of natalizumab given under the skin for relapsing multiple sclerosis in Germany and Austria. The drug was first given by vein drip, and the under-skin route was approved later. Clinics needed real-world evidence on preference, safety, and results.

Hundreds of patients were followed for about a year in three groups: switchers to the new route and starters on each route. Satisfaction and preference were the main measures, alongside safety and disease control. Neurologists gain everyday practice evidence that the more convenient route holds up outside strict trials.
pmc-13555918:
Houyun Zhang and three colleagues uncover a long non-coding RNA that brakes stomach cancer in a 2026 study. The RNA, named SOCS2-AS1, does not build proteins but steers other molecules. Tissue pairs from 102 patients, plus several cancer cell lines, supplied the test material. Levels of the RNA and its partners were measured, then functions were probed in growth and invasion assays.

The RNA ran low in tumours, and low levels tied to worse patient outlooks. Restoring it curbed cancer cell growth, movement, invasion, and shape shifting. It works by soaking up a small RNA, freeing a receptor gene that the small RNA normally silences. Reversing any link in that chain cancelled the benefit. The authors nominate the RNA as a marker and target.
pmc-13556018:
Qian Zhu, Guang-Nao Zhou, and Jing Guo studied in 2026 what drug-resistant tuberculosis costs patients in Lishui City, Zhejiang Province, and how a local subsidy softened that cost. They surveyed 117 people treated for multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant disease between 2017 and 2022, collecting treatment histories, medical bills, insurance payments, and subsidy records.

Median direct medical costs came to roughly sixty-five thousand yuan per patient. Insurance covered a large share, subsidies cut what remained, and families still paid a median of just over eight thousand yuan themselves. Patients whose subsidy fell below the median amount had notably worse treatment outcomes, while about three quarters of the group completed treatment successfully. The authors say the policy helps, though stronger study designs are needed to prove its effect.
pmc-13558618:
Yulika Yoshida-Montezuma and ten colleagues followed Canadian children and their parents in 2026 to see how obesity odds moved before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. The prospective Toronto-area cohort held 1,163 children and 653 parents, each measured at least once in the five pre-pandemic years and once between 2020 and 2023. Piecewise models split the trend at the pandemic's start.

Children's obesity odds had been climbing steadily before the pandemic, then jumped sharply in its first year before easing in the second, while remaining above the old trajectory. Gains concentrated in younger children and lower income families. Parents' obesity odds, also rising beforehand, levelled off during the pandemic years instead of accelerating. The authors read the child pattern as a shock that partly, not fully, unwound.
pmc-13558718:
Zhaofan Li and eleven colleagues trained in 2026 a deep learning model that grades anaemia from photographs of a patient's lips in a working emergency department. Blood tests remain the standard, yet their invasive nature delays diagnosis where resources run thin. The team compared a lip-focused model, built on a detection transformer, with a full-face version, and both against the bedside judgements of senior and junior doctors.

The lip model classified severity correctly in eighty-five percent of cases. It beat the full-face model by eight points and the senior physicians by a wide margin. Each answer came back in a small fraction of a second. Medical knowledge shaped the three severity classes the model predicts. The authors present the tool as automated decision support for triage, where a fast non-invasive screen can decide who needs blood drawn first.
pmc-13559318:
Dozier and co-authors compared a 2026 single centre cohort where early lung cancer diagnosis and surgery were combined into one anaesthesia event. Standard care splits robotic bronchoscopy biopsy and robotic resection across separate days, and delays beyond eight weeks worsen outcomes. The combined event does biopsy, rapid pathology, and resection under one anaesthetic.

Sixty-one patients were included, nineteen in the combined pathway and forty-two in the traditional staged pathway, Dozier reports. Median time from diagnostic scan to resection fell from about eighty-five days to forty-eight days with the combined approach. Time from first lung specialist consultation to resection also shrank significantly, from about sixty-three to thirty-eight days. Direct costs did not differ significantly between pathways, and the combined group's nodules were somewhat smaller at pathology.
pmc-13560218:
Ali Utku Şahin, Hasan Yücel, and Bircan Kara examine household earthquake preparedness in Türkiye through the lenses of Maslow's hierarchy of needs and the risk perception paradox. Their 2026 survey reached 1,193 households in districts mapped at high seismic hazard, administered online between May and September 2025. Awareness campaigns are widespread nationally, yet home readiness stays thin.

Earthquake salience was high: most respondents had lived through a quake and nearly all perceived local risk. Even so, only 19.3 percent felt sufficiently prepared, while about half felt partly prepared in the reported shares. Money was the dominant barrier, named by almost ninety percent, followed by lack of time and worry about sustaining daily life. Confidence in one's readiness varied by gender, age, and income. Training participation lifted perceived preparedness. The authors recommend pairing campaigns with financial support and tenant-inclusive housing safety steps.
pmc-13562218: This 2026 correction notice by Manon T. Lachmann and colleagues amends their paper on iron-iron hydrogenase enzymes engineered with modified azadithiolate bridgeheads to act as one-way hydrogen oxidation catalysts. Figure 5 of the original article, which diagrams proposed hydrogen oxidation pathways through the enzyme's H-cluster, was replaced with a corrected version. The notice prints the incorrect and correct figures side by side for transparency and makes no other change to the paper.
pmc-13562318:
Abdelwahed Yahmadi and colleagues compare the two standard rescue operations for patients who regain weight after sleeve gastrectomy. Their 2026 retrospective study follows 109 patients converted at their institution between January 2014 and December 2016, forty-seven to one-anastomosis bypass and sixty-two to Roux-en-Y bypass. Outcomes were tracked at one, five, and seven years.

Both operations held their weight loss durably to year seven. The one-anastomosis route won on weight: greater total loss and body mass reduction at both the first and seventh year checks, with a shorter operation to boot. Roux-en-Y won on reflux, resolving heartburn significantly better. Diabetes, hypertension, and lipid remission rates matched between the groups, and complications stayed low in both. Iron deficiency and other nutritional gaps appeared more often after the one-anastomosis operation. The authors advise matching the procedure to the patient's dominant problem.
pmc-13562418:
Jesus Barriguete and Juan Gutierrez review sensors built from stimuli responsive materials for medical uses. Soft matter can blend stability, bend, and body fit, traits key for wearables and implants. The review came out in twenty twenty-six.

Smart materials change their structure when heat, light, or other triggers hit them, while they keep their core traits. Mixed with soft bases, they gain bend, strength, and body fit. Recent gear uses them in body and nature sensors, smart films for fluid chips and drug dosing, and bendy electronics for support and coats. The authors look ahead to bio inspired implants and wearables with sharper sensing.
pmc-13562618:
Manoj Kumar Rout and Sunita Keshri build light sensors whose response can be tuned with a magnet. The devices stack thin films of cobalt-zinc ferrite on silicon, topped with a transparent conducting layer. One version adds dysprosium, a rare-earth element, into the ferrite. The 2026 team sputtered the films, checked their structure and magnetism, and measured how the devices answer broad light, spanning 300 to 1100 nanometres, under a small applied voltage.

The dysprosium version delivered nearly three times the photocurrent of the plain one, switched faster, and scored higher on sensitivity measures. A magnetic field up to 3000 oersted boosted the current further in both devices, apparently by lining up charge carriers and cutting losses. Some photocurrent even lingered after the field was removed. The authors see promise for sensors whose light response can be dialled magnetically, with uses in optical sensing and spin-based electronics.
pmc-13562718:
Shankargouda Patil and two colleagues test, at country level, whether eating more microplastic tracks with higher rates of lip and mouth cancer. Plastic particles pervade food and water, yet population evidence on cancer is nearly absent. Their 2026 ecological study covered 106 countries with 2020 as the anchor year. Estimated dietary intake was set against age-standardised cancer rates, adjusting for smoking, alcohol use, wealth, and urban living. Checks included placebo tests, seafood-based sensitivity runs, and spatial models that account for neighbouring countries resembling each other.

Early unadjusted curves hinted at a bent, non-linear link. Smoking and urbanisation also predicted rates, unevenly. Once the chosen spatial lag model absorbed the geographic clustering, the microplastic contrast collapsed to a null result, at minus 0.41 with a p-value of 0.85. Their own decision rule labels the finding hypothesis-generating only. They call for person-level exposure studies rather than country averages.
pmc-13562918:
Nesrine Benkhaira and her team set thymol and limonene side by side as germ drugs, in lab tests and on screen. Their study from twenty twenty-six does the side-by-side for these two plant compounds. Drug resistance drives the hunt for new germ drugs. Plant compounds are an old ground for that hunt.

Disk tests, dilution tests, and kill tests covered many microbes from real cases. Germs of both wall kinds, yeasts, and mycobacteria all went through the tests. Thymol beat limonene against each kind tried. On screen, models told how each one binds to germ targets. Drug-like fit and safety marks were also worked out. Lab proof and screen proof side by side make the case stronger. Thymol looks the stronger hopeful for new drugs.
pmc-13563718:
Ahamad Salman Amathullah and three colleagues adapt a pregnancy-anxiety questionnaire for Sri Lanka's two main languages, Sinhala and Tamil. Anxiety specific to pregnancy, fear of birth, of a disabled child, of bodily change, is often missed, and no checked tool existed for these speakers. Their 2026 study recruited 200 pregnant women, 100 per language, at antenatal clinics in two Western Province hospitals during 2024 and 2025. Translation followed World Health Organization steps: forward and back translation, an expert panel of psychologists, obstetricians, and midwives, and pretesting with real users.

Statistical structure checks in both languages recovered the original three themes exactly, and every question loaded acceptably onto its theme. Reliability scored well, at 0.86 in Sinhala and 0.81 in Tamil. Every subscale held up as well. The authors declare both versions valid and reliable, giving Sri Lankan clinics a fair way to spot pregnancy-related anxiety in either language.
pmc-13563918:
Shin-ya Takizawa and three co-authors build a light-driven system to turn carbon dioxide into useful fuel, in this twenty twenty-six study. Their model copies the leaf membrane where plants split water and fix carbon. The system needs a light catcher and a catalyst sitting close together, so energy can pass between them.

In older setups the parts were scattered at random in a fat bubble membrane, wasting energy. The team fixed the light catcher on the membrane surface and let the catalyst partner form right beside it. That pairing passed energy far more smoothly. The design points to better artificial leaves for cutting carbon dioxide.
pmc-13566418:
Emily Jay Nicholls's team synthesised qualitative research on hunger and food access for people with HIV in wealthy countries, in a 2026 systematic review. Food insecurity worsens HIV outcomes, yet most first-hand accounts came from low- and middle-income settings, leaving high-income experiences underexamined. The team screened 2,772 records down to 12 studies from the United States and Canada and graded the studies.

Three themes emerged: structural inequalities shape and complicate access to food, insecurity harms health and well-being, and obtaining food itself becomes demanding labour. The authors frame HIV and food insecurity as syndemic, each amplifying the other through poverty, housing instability, and stigma. Interventions, they argue, must tackle those reinforcing conditions together rather than food alone.
pmc-13568718:
Sai Say Han, writing alone, makes the case for the humble bedside exam in finding artery disease spread across the body. When plaque narrows arteries in two or more zones, heart attack and stroke risk jump well past single-zone disease. Plaque is a body-wide process, so disease in one zone should prompt a search in the rest. Scans can do that, but they cost money and are not always at hand.

The review walks through a full hands-on check: listening at the neck, comparing pulse and blood pressure in both arms, feeling the belly, and working down the leg arteries to the feet. It also notes where touch and sound mislead, and when a scan must settle the question. A careful exam costs nothing and points the costly tests where they count. That is the heart of the twenty twenty-six review.
pmc-13569018:
Milad Masrouri and colleagues combine, in a 2026 study, X-ray imaging, AI generation of bone microstructures, and computer simulation. Their aim is to learn why spongy bone loses stiffness in a pattern that simple density rules miss. Thousands of tiny bone cavity structures were simulated, with AI-made copies expanding the sample while keeping realistic shapes.

At the millimeter scale, stiffness followed the classic density rule. At the tiny cavity scale, stiffness depended far more steeply on density because stress fields around voids merged into weak corridors that guide cracks. Load then travels through connected solid paths rather than through bulk material. The shift matters for designing light, damage-tolerant porous materials.
pmc-13569218:
Leimarembi Devi Naorem and colleagues profile, in a 2026 observational study, bacteria inside root canals during regenerative dental treatment, a procedure that tries to regrow tissue in damaged young teeth. Nearly two hundred samples from tooth surfaces and canals at five time points were sequenced and compared between treatments that succeeded and those that failed.

Failed cases consistently carried more of one bacterial phylum, and final samples showed distinct species enriched on each side, with two species marking success and several marking failure. Diversity shifted over time more than by outcome. The signatures could one day help dentists predict which regenerative treatments will heal and adjust care early.
pmc-13569418:
Katharina A Zientek's team mapped the wider brain architecture of panic disorder beyond classic fear circuits, in a 2026 meta-analysis. It brings recurrent attacks and high treatment resistance, yet research had centred on fear regions while the drug pipeline stayed empty. The team pooled functional neuroimaging experiments to find steady patterns of altered firing.

They found heightened firing along a prefrontal-hippocampus-brainstem axis, not confined to fear areas, linked to serotonin and dopamine receptor maps and explained in part by candidate-gene patterns. The pattern also showed low developmental expansion and reduced oxygen metabolism, fitting brainstem hypersensitivity. The work points to molecular and practical targets that fear-circuit models alone would miss.
pmc-13569518:
Chu Zhang, Yanping Wu, and Xin Li interview, in a 2026 qualitative study, twenty-one hospital pharmacists across fourteen Chinese provinces about research on pharmacy practice, a field still young in China. Pharmacists from top-tier hospitals described why they do or avoid research, what they need, and what helps or blocks them, in talks analyzed with a behavior framework.

Most valued research tied closely to daily clinical work, driven by professional fulfillment, career growth, and curiosity. Needs centered on better service models and information systems that ease data access. Hospital support, a positive research culture, and teamwork with other professions encouraged engagement. Pharmacy leaders get a grounded list of levers for growing research capacity.
pmc-13569818:
Vultaggio-Poma and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-six on a soluble inflammation receptor as a pregnancy marker. Ninety pregnant women are tracked across all three trimesters. Thirty non-pregnant women serve as controls. The soluble receptor runs higher in pregnancy and climbs steadily. A standard blood ratio marker trends the same way but adds different detail. First-trimester levels run higher in women with prior pregnancies. Thyroid underactivity and male fetuses also link to higher levels.

The marker appears in cord blood and tracks the mother's level. Body size, diabetes, and blood pressure show no links. The authors propose it as a marker of pregnancy immune tuning. It is the first such study of this receptor form.
pmc-13570618:
Afaf Ennahal and colleagues mapped where a protein called PAPP-A appears in chronic sinus disease in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Earlier work showed high levels in sinus disease with nasal polyps, and the protein matters in inflammation and cancer. They stained tissue from patients with and without polyps, plus healthy controls.

Staining patterns in polyp tissue tracked with counts of eosinophil immune cells. Those cells made the protein strongly, along with some T cells and mast cells, and levels in mucus matched a related inflammation marker. Sinus specialists gain a candidate signal for sorting patients by inflammation type.
pmc-13571918:
Li Chan and colleagues compare, in a 2026 multicenter retrospective analysis, higher versus standard radiation doses inside bladder-preserving treatment for muscle-invasive bladder cancer. Return of cancer inside the bladder remains a risk in this approach. One hundred seven patients treated between 2015 and 2025 were followed for a median of twenty-three months.

Boosted dosing, delivered as a focused extra dose during the same sessions, clearly improved two-year control of invasive disease inside the bladder after accounting for tumor stage. Control of noninvasive disease, spread-free survival, overall survival, and bladder preservation did not differ, and side effects on urinary and bowel organs were similar. The gain is narrow but real: fewer invasive returns at no extra toxicity cost.
pmc-13572118:
Beppe Benedetto Consentino and nine co-authors report a crop study from twenty twenty-six on pea and arugula microgreens. Microgreens are young greens prized for nutrition. The team tested plant based stimulants that are not microbes, given in distinct ways, to see effects on yield and food value.

They tried a protein mix from plants and an extract from seaweed. Each was given by soaking seeds or by feeding roots. Soaking seeds raised pea yield a lot compared with root feeding. The seaweed raised nitrates, while the protein mix lowered them. The team also ran a simple cost check, so growers can weigh gains against the price of treatment.
pmc-13573418:
Emomine Odjesa, with two colleagues, describes a 2026 study of what shapes contraceptive choice among married women in Nigeria who want family planning. Methods differ in how long they act: permanent options, long-acting and medium-acting reversible ones, and short-acting ones. The team asked which traits of a woman and her household go with each kind.

The analysis used national survey data on women of reproductive age who were married or in a union. A multi-level model weighed personal, household, and area factors at once, since women cluster in communities that share services and norms. Sorting users by method length matters for programs: long-acting methods need trained staff and stocked clinics, while short-acting ones need steady supply and refills. The results aim to show planners where each method finds its users and where gaps persist.
pmc-13574518:
Ara Cho and co-authors review cases where a fabric graft lengthened a short kidney vein in transplant surgery, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Short veins make living-donor kidney placement hard, and fake grafts raise fears of infection and clots. Eleven cases at one Seoul hospital were tracked.

Most grafts served right kidneys, and follow-up ran near four years on median. Kidney function at discharge was sound. No clots or narrowing showed in any graft during follow-up. One patient needed rework for bleeding not tied to the graft. The authors call the fabric graft a safe, lasting option under blood-thinning care.
pmc-13574918:
Gustav Lind and three colleagues test a new type of CT scanner for tracking wrist implants in a 2026 study. Loosening is a serious problem after wrist joint replacement, yet tiny implant movement is hard to measure. Their method uses CT-based motion analysis that needs no implanted marker beads.

One cadaver wrist with an implant was scanned 40 times on both the new photon-counting scanner and a standard scanner. The new scanner measured rotation more precisely while using half the radiation dose. Eight patients were also scanned after surgery and again at six and twelve months, showing only very small early movement. The authors call for larger, longer studies to set firm limits for what counts as loosening.
pmc-13575118:
Paz García-García leads a 2026 study using a common bacterium to recover rare earth elements, metals vital for magnets, batteries, and screens. Standard mining and processing of these elements cause heavy environmental harm. The team worked with Pseudomonas putida KT2440, a microbe known for handling tough chemistry.

Their key step used resting cells, which avoided a common problem where the metals form solids with phosphate on their own. Recovery began with fast sticking to the cell surface, then grew into mineral particles outside the cells. The particles were cerium and gadolinium phosphates shaped as tiny rods. Cerium particles kept their glow and gadolinium particles kept magnetic behaviour. The authors present the method as a cleaner route to useful materials.
pmc-13575618:
Puneet Samaiya and five co-authors review the two-way conversation between gut microbes and mitochondria, the cell's energy producers, as a driver of brain and eye disease. Their review came out in 2026. When gut communities fall out of balance, mitochondria suffer through several routes at once.

Disturbed microbes make fewer helpful fatty acids, the gut wall leaks, and bacterial toxins raise inflammation and oxidative stress. Those hits are linked to Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases and to several retinal diseases, from macular degeneration to diabetic eye damage. Diet, heavy antibiotic use, and excess blue light may worsen the imbalance. Candidate treatments include next-generation probiotics, dietary change, and mitochondria-targeted antioxidants. The authors caution that most treatment evidence is still preclinical.
pmc-13576318:
Xin Liao and three colleagues examine a breakdown in staff talk during an operating room handover, in a 2026 case study from a large Chinese hospital. Turnover between operations demands fast, tight coordination across many roles, and breakdowns there feed surgical harm. Rather than blame individuals, the team read the incident through a human factors framework.

Interviews with five staff involved in turnover coordination produced six linked themes. Information got distorted in transit, no standard talk protocol existed, and professions worked in fragments. Wider problems included clashing hospital norms, staff skills mismatched to roles, and weak tech support. Together the themes showed system layers stacking pressure onto frontline talk. The authors argue fixes must target that system stack, not single speakers, to make surgical teamwork safer.
pmc-13576518:
Weiyi Qin and three colleagues present CLEAR-HPV, a 2026 method that makes AI predictions of virus status in cancer slides both accurate and readable. HPV status strongly shapes outlook and treatment in head and neck and cervical cancers. Deep learning models can read it from stained tissue slides, yet they rarely explain what they see.

Their framework reshapes the model's inner space so it sorts tissue into plain concepts without being taught labels for them. It found keratinising, basaloid, and stromal patterns on its own, mapped where each appears, and summed each slide as shares of just ten concepts. Those shares kept the predictive power of the original 1,536-number fingerprint. The concept structure held steady across three large cancer atlas datasets. The authors offer the method as a general add-on for slide-reading models.
pmc-13577518:
Shenming Qu, Zhiheng Liu, Huazhen Zhao, Yichao Wu, and Yang Yang published a computer vision study in twenty twenty-six on spotting maize pests in field photos. Pests change shape as they grow and hide against messy backgrounds, so detectors miss them. The team rebuilt a lightweight YOLO model with three new modules and named it WSD-YOLO.

One module sharpens sensitivity to pest textures from several directions. A transformer block adds global attention to suppress background noise cheaply. A dual-attention module blends features so varied pest shapes register. Across repeated training runs on a maize pest dataset, the model averaged about seventy-nine percent mean average precision. The design targets accurate scouting without heavy computing.
pmc-13579518:
Sonia Redhu and co-authors make four glowing dysprosium compounds and test how helper ligands change their light and power traits, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Each compound pairs the metal with a fluorinated light-harvesting part plus a second binding part. Heat tests, light tests, and power tests map how the four differ.

All four held up well under heat, which suits device making. Their energy gaps sat in a range that marks wide-gap semiconductors. Strong yellow light from the metal plus blue light from the ligands mixed to near-white light overall. Readers in display work see a candidate material for white light diodes.
pmc-13580118:
Chen and five colleagues build an uneven boron cation and probe its wild chemistry in twenty twenty-six. Boron cations with two open slots are among the most electron hungry species known. A bulky guard group let the team hold one with two unlike arms. That uneven build unlocked reactions a symmetric form cannot reach.

Adding one electron gave a radical that broke down in ways set by the solvent around it. Swaps at the boron center let the team make short lived forms with hydrogen or chlorine attached. A fluoride trap proved one such form exists, backed by computer models. The work shows these fierce species can be made and steered.
pmc-13581018:
Kelly Chimpén Mac Leod and colleagues assessed rhinoceros temperament in North America in 2026. Captive breeding supports African rhino conservation. Temperament knowledge could improve rhino wellbeing. Keepers rated animals they knew well. Novel object tests added behavioural data. Black and white rhinos both featured.

Dozens of black rhinos were rated. Well over one hundred white rhinos joined. Fearfulness and exploration tendencies emerged clearly. Activity and human comfort varied individually. Managers can tailor housing using profiles. Training can also adapt to temperament. Enrichment choices may fit each animal. Positive mental states are the goal.
pmc-13581318:
Khaled Alebrahim writes to the editor about kidney injury after heart surgery. His point is simple: prediction helps only when paired with prevention. The letter answers a biomarker study. That study found four blood signals high in patients who developed the injury. A combined panel forecast the injury sharply. Alebrahim cites his own team's earlier work on over nine hundred patients. It covered adults and children. Injury rates ran near three in ten adults and two in ten children.

His letter lays out a prevention ladder across the operation. Before surgery, tune kidney health and fluids. During surgery, shorten bypass and clamp times. After surgery, guard blood sugar and flow. Start kidney support early when needed. New markers and machine learning earn praise. Their value lands only inside strict prevention routines, he insists.
pmc-13581918:
Huang and three co-authors cataloged rare thalassemia variants in Ganzhou, southern China, in twenty twenty-six. Thalassemia, an inherited blood disorder, is the commonest single-gene disease worldwide and is frequent in China's south. Mapping rare variants supports genetic counseling and prenatal diagnosis.

Over eighty-four thousand people were screened between twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-five, and one thousand eighty-one carried rare variants, about one point three percent. Rare alpha and beta variants were roughly balanced, and twenty-six variants were newly identified, six classed as likely disease-causing. One new beta variant was linked to a specific anemia pattern. Rates varied by district within the region. The authors stress that the variant spectrum is complex and uneven, so screening programs in high-incidence areas need methods that catch rare forms, not just the common deletions.
pmc-13582218:
Tom Folkerts and a team of co-authors track how neck muscle quality changes after front-of-neck spine fusion surgery. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Fatty muscle in the neck tracks with worse disease and poorer surgical results, but change over time was unmapped.

Thirty-five patients with scans before surgery and one to five years after were analyzed. A deep back muscle and its small partners were measured at the top, middle, and bottom of each fusion. Fat content fell clearly at the bottom level only, dropping about seven points. Other levels held steady. Working muscle area showed its own pattern by level. The authors link the map to how surgeons plan and judge recovery.
pmc-13583218:
Toth and coauthors track human brain slices as networks settle in culture. Slices of adult human brain give rare access to live circuits. Slice prep is a harsh shock to those circuits, though. If networks keep true function or rebuild anew was unclear.

The team joined signal reads, calcium imaging, and tissue checks. Slices were tracked for weeks as they sat in culture. Early weeks showed wild swings and weak firing rates. Brain cells fired in bursts more than in fresh tissue. Tissue form also shifted a lot in that span. Later weeks showed a more stable network state.
pmc-13584018:
Lauren Kari Dixon and nine colleagues published a national audit in two thousand twenty-six on lung cancer surgery in England. Surgery offers the best cure chance for non-small cell lung cancer. The team used linked cancer registry and hospital records to track practice from two thousand fifteen to two thousand twenty-three.

Of over three hundred eight thousand patients, about eighteen percent had lung surgery. The surgery rate rose from about fifteen percent to about twenty-one percent across the period. Smaller partial lung removals grew, full lung removal fell fourfold, and keyhole surgery became the norm. Centres still varied widely in how often they used the smaller operations for small early tumours. Short-term outcomes were also tracked.
pmc-13584218:
Rui Wang and a large team present 112 ancient genomes from China's middle Yellow River region in this 2026 study. The river valley is a birthplace of East Asian farming culture, yet its early people left few genetic records. The new genomes come from eight dig sites and span a long stretch from about 6200 years ago to recent centuries.

Later people in the valley traced most of their ancestry to the earliest local group, farmers of the Yangshao culture. Two later shifts reshaped the picture: one near 4500 years ago tied to the Longshan period, then a slow spread of central Henan ancestry across the basin. Two burial sites also showed how status could pass within families, or how marriage ties could matter more than blood lines.
pmc-13584518:
João Rufino and colleagues make a protein isolate from Brazil nuts for food use. Their study from twenty twenty-six applies a pH-shift extraction method. Brazil nuts are rich in protein and selenium naturally. A purified isolate could serve sports and health foods.

The isolate reached a high protein share by weight. Its proteins were small, suggesting easy digestion and absorption. Selenium content stood out in the mineral profile. Key amino acids included the sulfur carriers of selenium. Flow behaviour was moderate due to particle charge forces. Antioxidant-linked plant compounds also carried into the isolate. Food makers gain a functional Amazonian protein ingredient.
pmc-13586218:
Yemko Pryor and colleagues built matched national and state sets on United States forensic DNA banks from 2001 to 2025. These banks grew hugely over two decades, yet full data on their shape and makeup stayed limited. Their 2026 dataset paper offers three linked sets for studying that growth, policy differences, and report practice across states.

The first rebuilds monthly National DNA Index System counts from FBI files, tracking convict, arrestee, and crime-scene records, labs, and cases aided. The second gathers state counts and policy facts on arrestee gathering, family searching, and gathering laws in all 50 states. The third evens out population and yearly gathering data from public-records requests. The authors offer the series as a base for over-time and cross-state research.
pmc-13587018:
Kun Chen and five colleagues published a lung cancer study in two thousand twenty-six on why tumours resist the drug cisplatin. Resistance is the main barrier in treating advanced non-small cell lung cancer. The team focused on a stemness factor called SOX2 and a copper-linked form of cell death named cuproptosis.

Resistant cancer cells held more SOX2 and were harder to kill by copper-driven death. Silencing SOX2 restored that death route and raised cell death overall. A blocker of the copper pathway undid the benefit, confirming the link. SOX2 switched on a signalling path that raised a copper pump protein, which helped cells dodge the copper effect. Blocking that pump or path weakened resistance. The findings suggest new drug targets.
pmc-13587318:
Jayesh Sheth and a large team gather India's cases of the severest form of Gaucher disease. Gaucher disease is a storage disorder where a missing enzyme lets fatty material pile up in organs. Type 2, the acute brain form, strikes infants and usually takes life before age two. Reports from India were scattered, so the team pulled together 19 diagnosed children referred from across the country for this 2026 series.

Swollen liver and spleen, low platelets, eye movement faults, and poor feeding and growth marked most cases. Gene testing found the causal changes spread across the GBA1 gene, with one exon carrying the largest share and one change turning up in over half the children in a mixed form. Four children from Gujarat shared a rarer change, which hints at a founder effect in that region. The series is India's largest for this type so far.
pmc-13590418:
Wang and co-authors review how three layers of molecular data together illuminate chronic sinus disease with nasal polyps. The disease mixes lasting inflammation, a weakened tissue barrier, and tissue reshaping. It returns often after treatment, and patients respond in varied ways. Most studies so far read only one data layer at a time. Few join the layers into one picture.

The review weaves lipid, protein, and gene activity data into a single disease network. Cross-layer markers that hold steady could guide patient sorting. Sorted care may match the right therapy to the right patient. The authors argue joined data, not single snapshots, will move precision care forward.
pmc-13592018:
Diego Caproni de Morais and five colleagues probe how selegiline, a drug used in Parkinson's care, nestles inside ring shaped sugar hosts in water. Such hosts, cyclodextrins, can carry drugs and improve how they dissolve. The team paired heat based binding tests with magnetic resonance checks and computer simulations. Two host types were compared, a plain ring and a modified ring carrying extra chemical arms.

The modified host bound the drug more tightly and with better energy terms, the tests showed. Binding was driven mostly by entropy, pointing to water release and greasy contacts inside the ring cavity. Odd ratios near one and a half guests per host hinted at larger stacked assemblies. Simulations supported a neat three to two host drug arrangement.
pmc-13592318:
Zakaria Anfar leads a 2026 team anchoring single iron atoms onto molybdenum sulfide sheets for splitting water into hydrogen without platinum metals. Cheap, lasting catalysts for proton exchange membrane electrolyzers remain a bottleneck for green hydrogen. A cysteine coating coaxed iron atoms into a bridge pose across sulfur sites, tuning their electron density. Inside a working device of modest size, the catalyst delivered strong current at two volts.

The unit then ran stably for 360 hours after a short break in period, the team reports. Spectra taken during and after work backed the claim that the bridge sites stay put under harsh acid duty. Anfar and colleagues frame surface tailoring as the lever that made the sites both lively and tough.
pmc-13592418:
Zhou and colleagues designed in 2026 a catalyst that splits water into hydrogen and oxygen across acid, neutral, and alkaline conditions. Single iridium atoms sit on nickel oxide sheets in two distinct forms: some embedded inside the sheet and some adsorbed on its surface. The team tuned the iridium share and tested the best mix in a membrane electrolyser, a device that splits water using electricity.

The eight-percent iridium catalyst needed only low extra voltages to drive both halves of water splitting at working current. Embedded iridium atoms pushed nickel toward its active oxidised form for oxygen release. Surface iridium atoms instead gave sites where hydrogen atoms bind, favouring hydrogen release. The authors argue that controlling where single atoms sit is key to all-pH water splitting.
pmc-13593818:
Wen and six colleagues clone a gene from blue green algae that helps make melatonin, and hunt drug leads for child sleep apnea in twenty twenty-six. Melatonin may aid children whose sleep breathing is blocked, often by swollen tonsils. Plant melatonin is slow and costly to extract. The algae gene, when placed in lab bacteria, made an enzyme that works two steps of the melatonin path.

In parallel, the team mined tonsil gene data for drug matches. Four known drugs stood out as leads. Computer docking showed each fits its target protein well. Two of the drugs have past links to the melatonin path. The two halves of the study meet in a plan for new care.
pmc-13594818:
Jorge Sánchez and colleagues evaluated whether the medical tests commonly used for chronic hives actually help doctors make better decisions. Chronic urticaria means hives that keep returning for weeks, and many tests are ordered despite guidelines backing only a few.

The team first listed the tests in use, then graded each for accuracy and for real usefulness in guiding care. Few of the common tests performed well in practice, which capped how much good they could do patients. Photo records of the hives and drug challenge tests showed the clearest real benefit in the review. First clinical impressions alone misclassified nearly 30 percent of cases, Sánchez notes, so proven tests still matter.
pmc-13596018:
Hong and co-authors report a teen patient with severe electrical burns and a stubborn hospital infection. The 16-year-old boy faced repeated infection with Acinetobacter baumannii that resisted carbapenem antibiotics. This germ haunts intensive care units and can cause grave wound and body-wide infection in burn patients.

Electrical burns damage skin and deeper tissue in ways that differ from flame burns. Broken skin and mucosa let hospital germs enter and persist. The case traces the long, recurring course of infection during his hospital care. It highlights the hard fight against drug-resistant germs in burn units.
pmc-13597218:
Rong Ji, Xialin Chen, Juan Lang, and Zhongkui Xiong report a lung cancer case with a long response to a drug mix, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. A seventy-four-year-old man had widespread small cell lung cancer with liver spread. After first chemo and chest radiation, tumors reached his brain nineteen months later. Whole-brain radiation followed, but the brain disease returned in five months.

He then got an immune drug plus chemo. A daily targeted pill followed as upkeep care. The cancer vanished fully and stayed away for twenty-four months. His total survival reached sixty-seven months. The authors propose this sequence for like hard cases.
pmc-13597518:
Noshine Mohammad and colleagues tested deep learning systems that read MALDI-TOF mass spectra, the tool that names microbes in minutes, across three public health jobs. Their 2026 study used 7,424 spectra to test naming of a difficult mycobacterium's subspecies and its drug resistance, plus mosquito species naming and age guessing from body parts.

Balanced scores ran from the mid-eighties to mid-nineties percent for species tasks, and resistance calls scored higher still. Mosquito age estimates landed within roughly two to four days of the truth. Prep choices and tweaks for machine and sample spread proved key. The team also weighed computing cost and energy use against the score gained. The authors argue the pairing of the device with tuned AI could carry high-end testing into field and low-resource settings.
pmc-13600218:
Natalia Jędruchniewicz and eleven colleagues set out the plan for RESET, a very large trial of a smoother path through major surgery. Long stays, complications, and bounce-back admissions still dog older patients and cancer patients after big operations. The trial tests one joined-up pathway against usual care.

The pathway links tailored exercise and prep before surgery, tight teamwork during the stay, early discharge planning, and support after the patient goes home. Near nine thousand patients at two centers will be assigned, nine to the new path for each one on standard care. Three main outcomes anchor the trial: stays of two weeks or more, readmission within a month, and complications within a month.
pmc-13601518:
Erik Vanegas Müller leads a ten-author systematic review in 2026 on sudden cardiac death in young athletes and two tools that might predict it. Sudden cardiac arrest during sport is the leading medical cause of death in young athletes. The team searched eight databases for studies from 2013 to 2025. Topics covered how often these events happen, explainable AI for dangerous heart rhythms, and computer models of the heart's electrical activity.

From 9,574 studies, 84 met the criteria: 16 on incidence, 30 on explainable AI, and 38 on modeling. Reported incidence of sports-related sudden death ranged from 0.1 to 0.6 per 100,000 participants per year. Among AI studies, heat maps showing which parts of a signal drove the decision were the commonest explanation method. Models mostly worked at cell and tissue level. The authors call for shared definitions and for joining risk data, explainable AI, and heart models into one athlete-specific risk system.
pmc-13601718:
Theresa J S Wallner, Nora Christlein, and Laura M König interview people in Austria about how menstrual distress plays out inside romantic relationships. Menstrual distress means period symptoms felt as threatening or hard to manage. Partners can ease that strain, yet research had rarely asked how. The team ran semi-structured interviews with 27 people aged 19 to 59 who were in relationships and had lived with menstrual distress.

Partners shaped the experience whether they engaged or not, the interviews showed. Relationships built on openness, authenticity, and teamwork made coping easier. Dismissive or awkward partner responses did the opposite, feeding stigma and the trivializing of symptoms. Most participants were in heterosexual relationships, with a few in queer ones and one unlabelled. The authors recommend early menstrual health education for everyone, and guidance for couples on handling the monthly challenges together.
pmc-13602218:
Yuji Maruo and colleagues describe a two thousand twenty-six case report of pneumococcal meningitis from a vaccine-missed strain in a toddler with cochlear implants. Modern conjugate vaccines prevent most invasive pneumococcal disease. Strains outside vaccine coverage still threaten children whose inner-ear anatomy links to the brain's fluid space.

Their two-year-old had both ear implants placed despite fluid leaks during surgery. His vaccinations were fully up to date, including the broadest conjugate vaccine. Fever, vomiting, and lethargy signalled meningitis, and spinal fluid grew serotype thirty-four, outside vaccine coverage. High-risk children need vigilance beyond the schedule.
pmc-13602518:
Tara Maria Hoffmann and colleagues explored identity strain in parents of children with rare, undiagnosed conditions. Caring for such a child strains emotional health, yet lived experience research remains thin. Their 2026 interview study spoke with 24 parents of undiagnosed children undergoing whole-genome sequencing across English NHS sites, sampled for high anxiety, family impact, or low resilience, before results returned.

Parents rebuilt their sense of self around caregiving, torn between heroic carer and ordinary parent, while grieving the family life they had pictured. Health-system navigation and social expectations deepened the strain, with mothers most often adopting the heroic role. Uncertainty itself weighed on mental health. Hoffmann and colleagues call for counselling support across the testing journey and research on how result return affects wellbeing.
pmc-13603618:
Rahul Patil, Shweta Patil, Joyce Gonzales, and Alexander Verin review a modified form of heparin with therapeutic ambitions, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-six. Heparin thins blood, which limits its use against inflammation. The derivative, called ODSH, has most of that anticoagulant power removed.

What remains is a strong grip on inflammatory troublemakers. The review covers ODSH's structure, mechanisms, and disease applications. It damps signals from HMGB1, limits neutrophil enzyme damage, and interferes with platelet activation and cell adhesion. Vessel leakiness driven by thrombin is also reduced. Inflammatory and vascular diseases are the target territory. The authors assemble the case for trials of a heparin relative that does not bleed.
pmc-13607418:
Beatrice Foglia leads a team that reviews a cytokine axis in liver disease. Their review from twenty twenty-six deals with oncostatin M and its receptor. Fatty liver disease is now a top cause of chronic liver ills.

Its spread tracks obesity and type two diabetes rates. Two drugs were lately approved for the condition. Their power to slow advance helps only some patients. No data yet cover cirrhosis or liver cancer outcomes. Marks to flag patients at risk are lacking. Swelling signals drive disease advance and cancer growth.  Inflammation signals are central to that story.
pmc-13610018:
Stefano Benvenuti studies urban weeds as pollinator support in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Cities drive biodiversity loss, yet they can shelter pollinators when flowers are diverse and steady. Benvenuti surveyed wild flowering plants and their visitors in three Mediterranean cities in central Italy.

Over three years, about one hundred fifty insect-pollinated plant species were recorded across five habitat types. They supplied nectar and pollen through the season. Bees dominated the visitor mix, which also included flies and butterflies. Visits ran highest in grasslands, road verges, and wetlands, and lowest in woods and paved areas. Benvenuti argues that sparing wild flowers should be a core part of urban green planning.
pmc-13612418:
Congwang Chang and six co-authors report robot aided surgery for a rare urethra cancer in a woman. Their case report, from twenty twenty-six, deals with primary clear cell adenocarcinoma of the urethra. It is scarce in the books, with no set care plan. The patient was a fifty-seven year old woman with half a year of worsening hard pee and two months of repeat blocks. Scans, scope, and tissue reads set the call.

She then had a full removal by robot aided keyhole surgery. The team adds a read of past cases to frame traits, hard calls in diagnosis, care picks, and outlook. Readers learn how to spot and stage a cancer most will never see.
pmc-13613318:
Shuo Cao and five co-authors review artemisinin drugs as candidate treatments for metabolic syndrome, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. The syndrome bundles insulin resistance, belly obesity, blood fat problems, high blood pressure, and poor sugar control. It sharply raises the risk of diabetes and heart disease, and single-target drugs often fall short.

Artemisinin comes from malaria treatment, but lab work shows wider effects. In cells and animals it improved insulin sensitivity, steadied fat metabolism, calmed chronic inflammation, and reshaped gut microbes. Several signaling pathways sit behind these gains. Direct evidence in patients, though, remains scarce. The authors weigh what must happen before these drugs can move into routine metabolic care.
pmc-13615418:
Rafaela Makri and a large research team published a trial report in two thousand twenty-six on diet advice plus digital tools for Greek adults. The GATEKEEPER study enrolled adults aged fifty-five and over at risk of metabolic syndrome. It asked whether apps and devices add anything to regular dietitian counselling.

Nearly one thousand adults were split into three groups for three months. One group got monthly counselling alone. The others also got a web platform, or the platform plus digital devices. Waist size shrank in all groups, slightly less in the digital groups. Weight, body makeup, and blood sugar improved alike across groups. The device group did move more each week. The authors conclude counselling did the heavy lifting.
pmc-13615618:
Zhu and colleagues test a guided way to help new medical students learn from watching surgery care. Early ward time can confuse beginners, who may not know what to watch for. Anesthesia work is fast and much of it hides inside team routine.

Twelve student groups, with more than one hundred fifty students, were split by chance into two arms. One arm used the guided model, built on set goals and checks before and after watching. That arm scored far higher on clear goals and focused watching after the placement. It also gained more knowledge and rated the placement better. Gains held across study tracks and past time in operating rooms.
pmc-13617118:
Tania Gonzalez and co-authors present hard cases of high blood pressure in infants' lungs in a 2026 paper. Newborn lung hypertension comes in three forms, driven by resistance, by flow, or by pressure after the lungs. Heart shunts can confuse the usual ultrasound measures.

The series covers eight patients in three groups, including premature infants with lung disease and infants with chronic breathing failure. Ultrasound first suggested resistance-driven disease in these cases. Invasive testing then showed that flow through heart shunts was a main driver instead. The authors warn that shunt flow can mislead treatment choices and stress careful testing.
pmc-13617218:

These are rare and severe skin reactions that often follow drugs or infection. Existing guidelines give advice, but hospitals in Australia and New Zealand differ in staffing, burn care, and referral routes. Local agreement on practice was missing. The team drafted guidance from guidelines and reviews, then asked clinicians to rate 130 items on urgency, routine testing, and care steps.

Thirty-one clinicians took part, twenty-two from one center and nine from eight other centers. Agreement ran high on history taking, examination, supportive care, team involvement, discharge planning, and follow-up. Doubt remained over fluid amounts compared with burn care, the scope of first tests, and drugs that dampen the immune system. pmc-13618918:

They enrolled one thousand four hundred five confirmed mumps cases under fifteen years old from 2021 to 2025 and two matched controls per case. Controls were matched on sex, schooling stage, neighborhood, and birth date. They then modeled which vaccination factors changed effectiveness.

Unvaccinated children were far commoner among cases than controls. At least one vaccine dose gave seventy-six percent protection. It climbed with age, from no clear effect in toddlers to fifty-five percent in kindergarten children. It reached eighty-seven percent in primary schoolers and ninety-three percent in secondary students, though tiny numbers make the youngest estimates shaky. A two-dose analysis found no significant effect. The authors warn this reflects missing data, not vaccine failure, and neither dose spacing nor time since vaccination changed protection.
pmc-13619918:
Mashael Alnowaiser, Wissal Boughattas, and Safiya Alshibani study Saudi athletes who also run businesses, in a 2026 paper. They ask how an identity built around sport carries over into business life. The study sits in the context of national reforms that have grown the sport sector and opened new paths for athletes.

The authors interviewed twenty four athlete founders in depth, most of them amateur or recreational athletes. Four themes described what sport gave them: personal traits, work skills, a sporting legacy, and community values. Many also felt a tension between how they saw themselves as athletes and how others saw them as founders. That tension was strongest among women in the study.
pmc-13620118:
Kathleen Hatch and five colleagues examined rat brains six months after whole-body exposure to oxygen ions, a heavy component of space radiation, in a 2026 study. Astronauts on deep space missions cannot shield against such particles. Two low doses were tested, and the team measured inflammation and synapse markers in four brain regions tied to memory, movement, and attention.

Changes varied sharply by region and dose. The hippocampus showed raised immune and synapse markers at the lower dose and a mixed pattern at the higher one, while the front cortex stayed almost untouched. The striatum raised synapse markers at both doses. Some molecular shifts tracked behavior on social memory and vigilance tasks. The authors read the pattern as lasting synaptic remodeling that could underlie uneven cognitive risk after particle exposure, with certain regions more exposed than others.
pmc-13623118:
Moumita Tanjila and colleagues study what keeps women employees engaged at work in Bangladesh, where social norms and workplace barriers can hold women back. Engagement means a worker's emotional and mental investment in the job. The team tested five possible drivers, from leadership support to career development chances.

A survey of 242 women across four industries fed a statistical model of the links between the drivers and engagement. Supportive organisational culture, supportive leaders, and good blending of work and home life each went with stronger engagement. Social and cultural pressures showed no direct link, and career development chances mattered only in workplaces with solid human resources systems behind them. Industry-level backing for gender equity did not change the social pattern. Because the design captures one moment in time, the authors treat the results as associations, and they advise managers to shape strategies to each workplace rather than each sector.
pmc-13623218:
Leonor Teles and colleagues review radioligand therapy for children with solid tumours, a treatment that attaches a radioactive atom to a molecule that seeks cancer cells. The approach delivers radiation from inside the body while sparing much healthy tissue, a pressing need in children whose growing bodies suffer lasting harm from standard treatment. Adult cancers have gained from the method, but child evidence is scattered.

The review gathers the early clinical experience, centred on neuroblastoma, a nerve tissue cancer of young children, and lays out the targets, radioactive drugs, outcomes, and safety reports study by study. Most series are small, and results remain early. The authors discuss the hurdles specific to children, from dosing by body size to long-term effects on development. They close by mapping where trials should go next so the field can move from scattered reports to firm guidance for young patients.
pmc-13624818:
Nair and Mistry wrote a 2026 letter to the editor about a review of ketamine drugs given around surgery. Seo and co-authors had pooled trials to ask whether ketamine or esketamine lowers nausea and vomiting after general anaesthesia, meaning sickness felt once patients wake up. Nair questions how that review defined and grouped its outcomes.

Nair argues that mixing nausea alone with combined nausea and vomiting blends two distinct problems into one headline result. Guidelines instead call for each outcome to be defined and reported apart, with standard watching periods after surgery. The letter also warns that some placebo groups really received active background drugs. Other comparison groups mixed medicines with very different actions and anti sickness effects. Those choices, Nair says, can blur what the pooled numbers mean for practice.
pmc-13625318:
Jin Liu and co-authors issue a correction to their 2023 study of asthma in rats, first published in Respiratory Research. The original work tested whether a protein called MIF worsens airway remodeling, using rats sensitized with ovalbumin and a MIF-blocking compound named 4-IPP. In assembling Figure 5, the team uploaded a wrong tissue image, so a Masson stain picture meant for the control group also appeared in the treated group row.

The notice shows the wrong and right versions of the figure side by side. That figure gathered the study's core measures, from airway wall thickening and mucus cell counts to collagen laid under the airway lining and muscle growth. Correcting the swapped panel keeps the published record honest about which image came from which group of rats.
pmc-13626318:

They ran accelerator radiocarbon tests on twelve plant samples. Short-lived grasses and outer wood layers were favored, to dodge the old-wood trap. Bayesian modeling then bound the results, alongside dates from Tibetan mural inscriptions and prayer texts. Three building ages emerged for the city's key structures.

An early phase in the later fifteenth century raised one complex, dated to a tight window in the 1450s and 1460s. A White Temple phase followed in the mid-sixteenth century, and a long defensive phase from the mid-seventeenth to late eighteenth centuries strengthened a watchtower, perhaps against regional wars. Grass samples cut through a calibration flat spot that had blurred the sixteenth century.
pmc-13626818:

Their central claim is that these drugs directly switch on HMGCS2, a liver enzyme that helps make ketone fuel, backed by animal, genetic, cell, and test-tube evidence. Dr Taylor objected that the drug strengths used in human liver cells and in one binding assay far exceed what patients' blood ever carries.

The authors answer that those high strengths served target hunting, not dose claims. Free blood levels may also understate liver exposure. Carrier proteins pull the drug into the liver, and animal data show it pooling there. Mice fed the drug showed dose-linked enzyme activation at exposures matching human data. The exchange, printed as a formal reply, turns on how far lab doses can speak for the clinic.
pmc-13627918:
Alexander Muacevic and four colleagues surveyed junior doctors in two Sydney hospitals about artificial intelligence in medicine. The pilot study asked how much these early-career clinicians know about AI, how they feel about it, and whether they would use it in their future practice.

Responses showed mixed self-rated knowledge and limited day-to-day use, yet attitudes were broadly positive. Doctors named help with paperwork, searching large amounts of data, and note-taking as the biggest gains, while wrong output from AI tools was the main worry. Most said they would use AI more if their health district endorsed it, and most wanted AI taught during medical training.
pmc-13628518:
Maximiliane Sehn and colleagues asked how measurement choices change heart wall readings in cats in 2026. Wall thickness of the main pumping chamber helps decide whether a cat has hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a common heart disease. Experts disagree on whether inner border layers should count in the measurement, so fifty-two cats classed as healthy, borderline, or diseased were measured several ways.

Septal wall thickness came out significantly larger under one edge-to-edge method than under the alternatives. Because the included borders shift the number, the same cat could cross a diagnostic line depending on technique. The authors conclude the border rule must be standardised so clinics and studies compare like with like.
pmc-13631318:
Dingyu Wang and eight colleagues show that knee bone shape carries a measurable sign of ligament injury risk. The ligament is the anterior cruciate ligament, or ACL. Their study appeared in 2026. ACL tears strike athletes and teenagers at high rates. They recur suspiciously often. That hints anatomy, not just bad luck, loads the dice.

The team built a deep learning model that classifies injury status from 3D bone point clouds. It trained on five thousand MRI scans. It was tested on nearly eight thousand civilian knees plus a professional athlete set. Accuracy was strong in both. Performance held across acute and chronic injuries. It also held regardless of joint dislocation. Bone shape barely changes after trauma. The authors thus read the result as proof that shape is a genuine risk factor.
pmc-13631518:
Zhuyang Wu led a 2027 mouse study pinpointing where a safety tag on the cell-death regulator RIPK1 matters most during development. RIPK1 balances survival and death signals, and adding ubiquitin chains at lysine 376 normally restrains its kinase activity. Mice lacking that tag everywhere die around embryonic day twelve and a half, yet adding a kinase-dead change rescues them, showing that runaway kinase activity kills. The open question was which cells need the tag.

The team made mice lacking the tag only in endothelial cells. No such pups were born alive. At day eleven and a half, mutant embryos looked normal, but by day twelve and a half they showed widespread bleeding, slowed growth, delayed hearts, vessel thinning, and inflammatory signals. By days thirteen and a half and fourteen and a half, severe anemia and defects followed. Endothelial cells alone require this ubiquitin brake to keep embryonic vessels intact.
pmc-13632018:
Weight-loss medicines known as incretins are followed inside a Texas cardiology clinic in a study led by Patel. Although trials show clear heart and metabolic benefits, cardiologists have been slow to prescribe these drugs, partly because they are seen as diabetes drugs and partly because of cost and insurance hurdles. Patel and colleagues reviewed how a dedicated clinic, staffed by heart specialists, a nurse practitioner, a dietitian, and a coordinator, actually used them.

Among sixty-nine patients with follow-up visits, most started on semaglutide, and weight loss grew steadily with time in care. Median loss reached about seven percent at six months and nearly fourteen percent after two years. Most patients stayed on the same drug, and only a few stopped for cost or stomach side effects. The authors present the clinic model as a workable route for bringing these medicines into routine heart care.
pmc-13632718:
Claerwen M Jones and fourteen colleagues studied the immune cells that drive celiac disease. In this condition, eating gluten triggers T cells that attack the small intestine. Most of those cells target four small pieces of gluten proteins. The team profiled single T cells from patients' blood after a gluten challenge, reading each cell's gene activity and its receptor, the part that recognizes gluten.

The same cell types appeared across all four targets: aggressive helper cells, regulatory cells, and killer-type cells. No target produced its own special cell type, so function did not follow which gluten piece a cell recognized. The team also found shared receptor patterns that mark which target a cell sees. Those patterns predicted a cell's target from its receptor alone. The findings give researchers a way to track the exact cells that matter in this disease.
pmc-13635018:
Livio Vitiello and ten colleagues published this 2026 review of an eye injection drug for swelling caused by blocked retinal veins. Retinal vein occlusion, a leading cause of vision loss from vessel disease, often floods the central retina with fluid. The drug, faricimab, blocks two growth signals at once. The team gathered the major phase three trials and real-world studies of the drug in branch, central, and partial vein blockages.

In the big trials, faricimab matched the standard rival drug on vision and anatomy during monthly dosing. Gains held under stretch-out schedules lasting over a year, and many patients reached longer gaps between injections. Real-world reports confirmed the anatomical gains, though vision gains varied more, especially in long-standing or stubborn cases. The safety record looked favorable overall. The authors stop short of claiming longer durability than rivals and ask for longer comparative studies.
pmc-13635618:
