The fungus, Ustilago maydis, infects living plant tissue, secreting small proteins called effectors in waves. Each wave matches a stage of infection, yet the DNA switches setting that schedule were unknown. The team reanalyzed gene activity data and compared promoter regions, the DNA stretches in front of genes, across related fungi.

Three candidate switch elements emerged, one each for early, middle, and late infection stages. Their positions in front of genes backed their regulatory role. Cutting into three promoters showed each element's effect depends heavily on its surroundings. In synthetic promoters, the early element switched genes on while the middle one held them down. The authors describe a combined code: activating and repressing elements mix in each promoter. That code could let engineers build fungal promoters with dialed-in timing.
pmc-13636618:
Griffin P Thomas and seven colleagues published this 2026 case study on watching glucose live inside a vaccine factory fermenter. Pneumococcal vaccine production grows bacteria on glucose, and knowing the sugar level steers the batch. The old method pulled samples for lab testing, which costs time and money and exposes workers to a pathogen. The team replaced it with a probe that reads light scattering, called Raman spectroscopy, directly inside the vessel.

A statistical model trained on the light patterns predicted glucose levels in real time with small error. The method passed formal validation and entered the control strategy of a licensed commercial plant, a company first. Operators now trigger the next process steps when readings hit the target window. The authors report lower costs, better process control, and a safer posture for staff. The case shows real-time sensing moving from pilot curiosity to licensed routine.
pmc-13637618:
Suha Naser-Khdour and three colleagues report a simulation study testing how badly evolutionary tree-building fails when its simplifying premises break. Standard methods assume evolution runs stationary, reversible, and homogeneous: base frequencies steady, changes equally likely in reverse, and one rate pattern everywhere. Real genomes violate all three through shifting makeup and uneven pressures. The team simulated sequence data under graded levels of violation, using values drawn from real datasets rather than worst cases.

Maximum likelihood tree-building proved broadly sturdy. Across a wide range of realistic violations, the inferred trees stayed accurate despite the wrong premises. Failure arrived only at the extreme, under strong convergent evolution where unrelated lineages arrived at similar sequences on their own. The authors' message is measured reassurance: ordinary departures from the textbook model rarely mislead, while convergence deserves the field's worry. Their graded design also gives future studies a fair benchmark.
pmc-13642518:
Dong Xu and five colleagues report a new way to control tiny swirling patterns made of light. The patterns, called optical skyrmions, are stable twists in the way light waves are oriented. Their stability makes them attractive for data storage and fine measurement. Practical use needs a way to switch their form on demand.

The team focused tightly wound, radially polarized vortex light. They used a property called polarization helicity, which captures how the light's orientation twists as a whole. By setting the starting phase of the light, they could flip the pattern between forms. They could also control which way the pattern handed. The results offer a fresh handle for shaping light at very small scales.
pmc-13643318:
Lulu Yu and twelve colleagues present a mouse study on SRSF3, a splicing factor, and the sex gap in liver cancer. Men develop this cancer far more often, and the estrogen receptor plus FOXA factors help protect female livers, yet what controls those protectors was unknown.

Deleting Srsf3 only in liver cells erased the sex gap, raising cancer incidence in both sexes after chemical induction. The missing factor cut expression of the estrogen receptor and FOXA genes and their downstream targets, and it binds the FOXA1 promoter directly. In breast tissue, by contrast, the same factor promoted tumors, showing organ-dependent behavior.
pmc-13645518:
Ayame Tamura presents a study of how Dark Triad personality traits relate to workplace deviance among Japanese employees, and how office culture changes that link. The Dark Triad bundles Machiavellianism, narcissism, and psychopathy, all tied to bullying and counterproductive behavior.

Surveys from 387 employees fed regression and mediation models. Psychopathy and a high power-distance climate, where authority goes unquestioned, each predicted more bullying and counterproductive acts. Narcissism turned harmful only under high power distance and slightly protective under low. Flattery, or ingratiation, carried part of the effect for several traits. Climate can license or restrain dark traits, Tamura concludes.
pmc-13646118:
Kana Khairunnisa and Yusuf Alam Romadhon present a small case series on what listening feels like, pairing personal reports with brain wave recordings. Four healthy nineteen-year-old women each listened to a favorite song and to a recited Qur'an passage called murottal, three minutes apiece. Brain activity in the alpha band was compared with an eyes-closed resting baseline. Heart rate and spoken impressions were gathered at the same time.

Each woman's brain wave pattern broadly matched the state she described, whether calm, picturing images, or concentrating. The side of the brain showing the stronger response differed from person to person. With only four participants, no random ordering, and no statistical testing, the authors label their observations as leads for a larger, balanced study. The series shows how spiritual listening can be studied with the same tools as music research.
pmc-13649418:
Yanzhen Xu and four colleagues asked how grandparent care links to young children's feelings and behaviour in China. Grandparents often share child care there, which helps working parents but also packs more adults into daily care. The team surveyed 729 parents of children aged three to seven at three points in time.

More grandparent care linked to more emotional and behaviour problems in children. Part of that link ran through weaker social skills. The tie between grandparent care and social skills was worse in homes where family life ran poorly, and milder where it ran well. The authors suggest that family climate and children's social skills are good targets for support work.
pmc-13650618:
Jessica Ledesma-Aparicio and ten colleagues propose a workflow that puts tau protein at the center of Parkinson's disease research. Tau is famous from Alzheimer's disease, and its abnormal chemical tagging with phosphate groups is increasingly implicated in Parkinson's as well, where it interacts with the signature protein alpha-synuclein.

The plan starts with phosphoproteomics, a census of tau's phosphate tags, in brain tissue, body fluids, and patient-derived dopamine neurons, hunting for signatures tied to vulnerable regions or disease pace. Computer simulations then test how each signature bends tau's shape, weakens its grip on cell scaffolding, or invites clumping and partner binding. Those structural clues feed drug screening for molecules that fit specific tau shapes. The authors insist that biomarkers and drug candidates be rechecked in Parkinson's cohorts and models, since most structural knowledge still comes from other diseases.
pmc-13650718:
Gabrielle Wong-Parodi and seventeen colleagues study whether a stormwater planning tool can raise the adaptive capacity of small and midsize cities along the United States Gulf Coast. The region floods often, its stormwater systems are aging, and city staff in smaller places rarely get research attention, so the project paired a tool called FloodWise Communities with sustained researcher engagement.

Forty-six cities took part between 2021 and 2023, with staff surveyed before and after the intervention and interviewed afterward. Use of the tool tracked with stronger feelings of having usable knowledge and with changed intentions about adaptation. Staff whose jobs already touched adaptation gained the most in both measures, which hints that role and authority shape what a tool can achieve. Unexpected uses of the tool also shifted how capable practitioners felt. The authors present the work as the first test of its kind in these cities.
pmc-13651618:
Isabella R Clemmer and seven colleagues shrink a heart protein analysis down to biopsy scale. Their target is phospholamban, a small membrane protein that helps govern calcium handling in heart muscle. Their method reads whole intact proteins rather than chopped peptides, preserving how chemical modifications combine on a single molecule.

A light-cleavable soap-like reagent makes greasy membrane proteins analyzable, and the team's earlier workflow needed ten milligrams of heart tissue, far more than a biopsy yields. Their streamlined one-pot extraction cuts the requirement tenfold to a single milligram while keeping detection, quantification, and modification mapping reproducible by liquid chromatography and tandem mass spectrometry. Multiple natural variants of the protein, differing in their modifications, were cataloged from that speck of human tissue. The authors offer the protocol for the many heart studies where tissue is precious.
pmc-13661218:
A team led by Muhammad Shoaib asks why a key blood fat fades so fast after cardiac arrest, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The fat is lysophosphatidylcholine, or LPC, and past work showed that giving more of it helps patients and animals survive. What no one knew was where the LPC goes.

With a tagged form of LPC, the team tracked its loss in the blood after arrest. The fall was not even: LPC types with chains rich in double bonds dropped the most. The cause was fast breakdown in the blood itself, not lower output from the liver or uptake by tissues. Changes in LPC also tracked with changes in related fats, which hints at a wide upset in blood fat balance. Care, the authors argue, must either slow this removal or top LPC back up.
pmc-13689418:
Emilie Racine and co-authors pinpoint the single amino acid that lets a bacterium's own enzyme disarm its antibiotic, and show that swapping it foils the defense, in work from twenty twenty-six. Odilorhabdins kill bacteria by jamming their ribosomes. The producing bacterium protects itself with an enzyme that tags the drug and kills its power.

A scan swapping one residue at a time flagged the first lysine as the tag target. When the enzyme was switched on in test bacteria, the natural drug's strength fell sixty-four fold. The swapped variant stayed almost fully untagged after hours and kept killing. The enzyme ignored other common antibiotics. Design rules for tougher versions follow.
pmc-1382018:
Voight, Kudaravalli, Wen, and co-authors map signs of very recent positive selection in the human genome. Selection leaves marks when a helpful gene variant spreads fast through a population. Finding such marks reveals how modern humans adapted to local foods, climates, and diseases.

The team scanned the whole genome for variants that had risen quickly but had not yet taken over completely. Each strong signal points to a trait that mattered in the recent past. Their map gave other researchers a list of regions to study for links to health, diet, and survival.
pmc-3241518:
Morris, Wooding, and Grant examine time lags in translational research, the path from discovery to patient benefit. Their study reviewed literature that describes and quantifies those lags in developing health interventions. They identified a small set of papers that actually measured the delays.

Few of those papers could be compared directly, they found, despite the famous claim that translation takes about seventeen years. Measuring lags honestly matters because funders promise faster translation to patients. The review shows how thin the evidence behind that promise was, and what better tracking would require.
pmc-4595218:
Benchimol, Smeeth, Guttmann, and their co-authors issued the RECORD statement in 2015. Routinely collected health data, gathered for care and administration rather than research, were being used for studies more and more. Their speed and scale raised issues that older reporting guidelines did not address.

RECORD extends existing guidance for observational studies that use such data. It asks authors to describe data sources, coding, and linkage in enough detail for readers to judge the work. Clear reporting matters because routine data can hide errors in records and coding. The statement helps journals and reviewers hold this fast-growing research type to a sound standard.
pmc-5241818:
Zheng, Terry, Belgrader, and their colleagues described a droplet-based system in 2017 for profiling single cells. Reading the full set of gene messages in single cells is basic to grasping how complex living systems work. Older methods could handle only small numbers of cells at a time.

Their system counts messenger RNA from tens of thousands of cells in a single sample run. Cells are encapsulated in droplets, up to eight samples at a time, and each cell's messages get a unique barcode. That scale reveals rare cell types hidden in bulk averages. The approach powered the wave of single-cell atlases in immunology, cancer, and development.
pmc-5496518:
McKeith, Boeve, Dickson, and their team updated the rules in 2017 for diagnosing dementia with Lewy bodies. A consortium for this disease refined its advice on both clinical and tissue-based diagnosis. The prior report had been in wide use for the last decade.

The new rules draw a clear line between the clinical signs used at the bedside and the lab markers that support the call. This dementia mixes memory loss with vivid visions, swings in alertness, and stiff, slow movement. It is often mistaken for Alzheimer's disease, which can lead to harmful drug choices. Clearer rules help doctors spot it sooner and care for patients in a safer way.
pmc-6821018:
Catherine Kelly, Alan Karthikesalingam, Mustafa Suleyman, and coauthors listed challenges for clinical artificial intelligence in 2019. Health AI research was racing ahead, with demos across many branches of medicine. Yet very few tools had reached real clinical use.

The authors name the gaps: messy real-world data, workflow fit, regulation, and proof of benefit. They warn that models trained in one hospital may fail in another. Fairness and monitoring after launch get equal weight with accuracy. The paper became a sober checklist for teams moving AI from papers to wards. The authors also address who stays accountable when an algorithm's advice is followed or ignored.
pmc-7095418:
Peng Zhou, Xing-Lou Yang, Xian-Guang Wang, and coauthors reported the pneumonia outbreak virus of probable bat origin in 2020. Since SARS emerged, many related coronaviruses had been found in bats. Some were already known to be able to infect human cells.

The team sequenced the new virus and showed it shares most of its genome with a bat coronavirus. Lab tests confirmed it enters cells through the ACE2 receptor, like the SARS virus. The evidence pointed to bats as the likely original host. Their report anchored early scientific agreement on the outbreak's origin.
pmc-7164518:
Linlin Zhang, Daizong Lin, Xinyuanyuan Sun, and coauthors solved the crystal structure of the SARS-CoV-2 main protease in 2020. The main protease cuts viral proteins into working pieces, so the virus cannot mature without it. That makes it a prime drug target.

The structure revealed the enzyme's shape in fine detail. The team also improved an earlier inhibitor design against the related SARS enzyme and showed strong blocking in tests. A shared structural blueprint let chemists worldwide start designing drugs at once. Protease inhibitors later became a real class of COVID-19 medicines.
pmc-7285218:
Fabien Magne and co-authors asked a pointed question in 2020: can a simple ratio of two gut bacteria groups serve as a sign of an unhealthy gut in people with obesity? The two groups, Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes, dominate the human gut. Researchers had proposed that when their balance shifts, it marks a disturbed microbial community linked to inflammation and metabolic trouble.

The authors review what studies actually show about this ratio in patients with obesity, and how consistent the pattern really is. They weigh its promise against its limits, since diet, medicines, and lab methods can all sway the numbers. Their cautious account is a useful check on a popular shortcut that is sometimes read as more certain than the evidence allows.
poems-pg10518:
John Hay, the American diplomat and man of letters, prefaces this revised edition of his poems with a long, rueful note about Spain. The pages, he explains, grew out of the first half of 1870, when he was in Madrid during a time of intense interest for that country. He left in the August of the Franco-Prussian War, passing through a Paris stunned between excitement and the catastrophe of Sedan. He never returned, though he dreamed of it for years.

Hay refuses to rewrite the youthful book, arguing that its merits and faults alike belong to youth and cannot be amended without tearing it apart. He corrects only the flagrant errors and sends the poems out again with their prophecies unfulfilled. Readers get both the early verse of a future Secretary of State and an old man's honest audit of his young enthusiasm.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-158-19:
Punch readers on February 18, 1920, found Charivaria at the front of volume 158, turning the week's reports into short, dry jokes. Politics in Paris and London, sport, and money matters share the column.

A Paris writer asks Lloyd George for a clear statement, and the column marvels at such innocence. Professor Waller is said to have measured emotion by experiment, while Sir Thomas Lipton's challenge for the America Cup wins acceptance in New York. Alarm over a planned Futurist portrait of a typical O.B.E., a will worth over seven hundred thousand pounds written in under a hundred words, and new jobless insurance fill the rest.
rilke-poems-1918:
Rainer Maria Rilke was a German-language poet born in Prague. Jessie Lemont translated a selection of his early poems in 1918, the first book of Rilke in English. The poems come from his work before the famous later collections. They already show his eye for objects, angels, and inner life.

Many pieces are quiet prayers, portraits, or scenes from nature and art. Rilke turns simple things into signs of a deeper world. Lemont's versions are free at times, yet they carried his voice to new readers. This early selection lets readers watch a major poet taking shape. It is a gentle entry into his work.
robert-browning-pg14618:
C. H. Herford, professor of English literature in the University of Manchester, wrote this study of Robert Browning for the Modern English Writers series. William Blackwood and Sons issued it at Edinburgh and London in 1905, the year given as MCMV. A list at the front prices the series at two shillings and sixpence a volume.

Herford opens with a letter to the Reverend F. E. Millson, the friend whose reading first brought him to Browning. A generation has passed, he writes, since Millson read Ben Ezra aloud at Brackenbed Grange. Millson had known Browning's worth early, when few did, and Herford's standpoint in the pages ahead stands close to his friend's.
rodkinson-talmud-vol-5-1918:
Michael L. Rodkinson gave the Babylonian Talmud English dress in a vast set. Book Five of that set came out in 1918. The Talmud is the great store of Jewish law and lore. It grew from talks of rabbis over scores of years in Babylon.

Rodkinson's set was the first bid to give the whole Talmud to English readers. Book Five is one step in a set of twenty in his full plan. Law, tales, and keen debate on the Torah fill its pages. The work is rough in parts, but it broke new ground in its day.
russell-logical-atomism-1918:
The Philosophy of Logical Atomism prints the lectures Russell gave in London in 1918. They are his clearest public statement of the system he built with the young Wittgenstein in mind. The world, he argues, is made of facts, not things.

Lecture by lecture he analyzes statements, names, and descriptions. He shows how language can be rebuilt to mirror the structure of fact. Particulars and universals, the atoms of logic, replace the grand systems of older thought. Russell speaks with unusual openness about a philosophy still in motion. These lectures are the best spoken introduction to the founding program of analytic philosophy.
russell-mysticism-logic-1918:
Bertrand Russell published Mysticism and Logic in 1918, a set of essays for general readers. The title essay contrasts mystical insight with logical clarity in philosophy. Russell respects the mystic's vision but defends reason as the safer guide. Other essays treat mathematics, causation, knowledge, and free will.

The book includes work from the era of his essay On Denoting, a classic of analysis. Russell writes with wit and unusual plainness for a technical thinker. The collection sold analytic philosophy to the public as no book had before. It remains a fine first Russell. Its defense of reason still reads as bracing and humane.
russell-roads-freedom-1918:
Bertrand Russell published Roads to Freedom in 1918, a work of political philosophy written during the First World War. Russell weighs three rival paths: socialism, anarchism, and syndicalism. He finds merit and danger in each. His own hope is a form of guild socialism with wide personal freedom.

He attacks the wage system, the power of the state, and war as linked evils. Education, leisure, and free thought receive strong defense. Russell wrote as a pacifist facing prison for his views. The book is a classic of libertarian socialism in English. It shows his moral passion alongside his logic.
sandburg-cornhuskers-1918:
Carl Sandburg published Cornhuskers in 1918, his sweeping second collection of Midwest harvests, wars, and workers in verse. The book confirmed Sandburg as the prairie poet of the American heartland in 1918. Harvest fields and troop trains share its pages, for America was feeding armies and sending its sons abroad.

Prairie, the long opening poem, rolls through grass, corn, railroads, and the peoples who layered the Midwest over centuries. War poems mourn and honor the young men leaving farms for France in the great conflict overseas then raging. Work songs, folk figures, and love lyrics keep the collection varied in mood and music from piece to piece. Sandburg's free verse stays plainspoken, built for the ear and the platform as much as the page in print. The volume deepens Chicago Poems' promise into a whole region's epic of labor.
simmel-konflikt-modernen-kultur-1918:
Simmel's Conflict of Modern Culture appeared in German in 1918, the year of his death and of Germany's defeat. The short book grew from a wartime lecture on the spiritual crisis of the age. Simmel, Berlin's most brilliant essayist on modern life, turned his method on the war-torn present itself.

His theme is the clash between life and form. Life forever creates forms, works of art, institutions, and creeds, then chafes against them and breaks them to live again. Modern culture, he argues, has sharpened that old conflict until form itself seems the enemy. The lecture reads as a farewell to a breaking world by a man who had taught Europe how to see it. Short as it is, the book distills Simmel's philosophy of culture into a single, somber argument.
solovyov-justification-good-1918:
The Justification of the Good, published in English in 1918 in Nathalie A. Duddington's translation, is Vladimir Solovyov's moral philosophy. Solovyov, Russia's greatest religious thinker, set out to ground ethics in an absolute good rather than in custom or command.

He builds morals from three natural roots, shame, pity, and reverence, and develops them into a full account of personal and social duty. Against both empty formalism and crude use-ethics, he argues the good must be justified as a whole way of life. The book is the centerpiece of his system. It introduced many English readers to Russian religious thought.
soviet-constitution-1918:
The Russian Soviet Republic adopted its first constitution in 1918, months after the Bolsheviks seized power. The All-Russian Congress of Soviets approved the text in July, in the middle of a civil war. It was Lenin's October Revolution given the form of law, the first constitution of a self-declared socialist state.

The charter declares all power to lie with the soviets, the councils of workers, soldiers, and peasants. It strips former exploiters, landlords, capitalists, and priests, of the vote, and weights city votes above country ones. Private ownership of land is abolished in its opening declaration of rights. The founding document of the Soviet order was bold in promise and brief in life, replaced as the Union took shape. Its model, class rule written as law, influenced communist states for the rest of the century.
spr-proceedings-vol29-1916-1918:
Parts seventy two through seventy four and an appendix fill volume twenty nine, for 1916 to 1918. The war years weigh on every page of the SPR record. Sittings multiply as the bereaved seek word of the dead. The Society for Psychical Research tests those sittings with its old rigor.

Telepathy trials proceed in the background of the grief driven work. Apparition reports from the front and from home enter the files. The appendix gathers society business from three hard years. Volume twenty nine shows the archive under maximum strain. Its standards bend far less than its subject matter grows. Historians of the war's inner life use it.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5018:
John Tyler gives four yearly addresses, from December 7, 1841, to December 3, 1844, parted by three stars. One date is given as December 1843, with no day. The first finds great cause to rejoice in the country's broad thriving as Congress takes up its duties once more. Peace has held within the borders and plenty in the homes through the year now closing.

Sickness struck a few parts of the land with grief and death, Tyler grants, yet the people's health was in the main kept safe. Growth past all past measure shows in numbers, strength, wealth, knowledge, and all that feeds human and social joy. Such gifts, he warns, rest on the guard of a kind Providence, and call for fresh thanks. He then turns to affairs since the last parting, among them the case of Alexander McLeod, a British subject.
stopes-married-love-1918:
Marie Carmichael Stopes, a doctor of science from London and of philosophy from Munich, published Married Love in 1918 as a new word on the sex difficulties of married life. Her preface says happy homes are needed more than ever, and that the book aims to add to their number by showing how much sorrow can be dodged.

Stopes argues that many middle-class marriages look fine on the surface yet fail in private, often through plain ignorance rather than ill will. She urges knowledge as the base of a sound state and a sound home. The book became a landmark in frank, plain talk about marriage for ordinary couples.
stopes-wise-parenthood-1918: Only the opening pages are present here. They hold a bookplate recording a gift from the Paul Hamlyn Foundation to the British Museum, opened in December 2000, followed by a list headed Books by the Same Author. That list names science works on old plants and plant life. It also names Married Love and a letter to working mothers. But no title page or text of Wise Parenthood itself appears in these pages.
symmes-circular-no-1-1818:
John Cleves Symmes, a former army captain in Ohio, sent this short circular round the world in 1818. In it he made a bold claim about the shape of the earth. He asked learned men and the public to hear him out.

Symmes held that the earth is hollow, with wide holes at both poles. Through those holes, he said, ships could sail to warm seas and lands inside the globe. The one page claim is the birth writ of the American hollow earth craze that ran for a hundred years.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Three tales make up the eighteenth volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels. They are The Case of Conscience, The Devil of Pope-Fig Island, and Feronde. Questions of conscience and purgatory get the poet's most teasing treatment in this set.

The Case of Conscience opens by noting the storyteller's ease. Those who deal in fables bestow names and titles freely. Every girl is a nymph or shepherdess. Some are even goddesses moving below. Horace, the poet says, followed the same art with superior skill. Behind the compliment stands a tale about a scruple carried to a confessor. Pope-Fig Island brings Rabelais's islanders, who once insulted the Pope, and Feronde is the brute who is purged of his sins by a trick and comes back preaching purgatory from experience.
taylor-life-of-pythagoras-1818:
Iamblichus wrote the Life of Pythagoras in the late Roman age. Thomas Taylor gave the work English dress in 1818. Pythagoras was the Greek sage at the root of math, music, and soul lore. Few lives from the old world are so wrapped in myth.

The life tells of the sage's trips to Egypt and the East for lore. It tells too of his school in Italy, its rules, and its strange bans. Short wise rules of the sage close the book. The text is the base life of the man who shaped the West's hid line.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-18:
The Caxtons reaches Part XVIII with Pisistratus still at the pen. His chronicle of the family, told as his own story, here turns outward. The scholar father's household, so long the tale's center, gives way to a farewell addressed to a whole new land.

The narrator bids farewell to a fair land he calls the Canaan of exiles and an Ararat for shattered arks. He praises it as the cradle of a race with a vast future no sage can guess. Its climates, he says, can ripen earth's products and shape the families of man in many ways. The part opens on this grand, parting note, far from the quiet rooms where most of the tale has lived.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: No. 18 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated March 11, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls, published in New York. Only front matter and a book notice are present here. The notice praises Simple Lessons in the Study of Nature, by I. G. Oakley. It calls the book handy for teachers who want true nature study for children. Its subjects lie right under children's feet: a twisted shell, budding twigs, fallen leaves, feathers, and grass.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part:
John Ormsby translated this stretch of Cervantes' Don Quixote, Volume 1, Part 18. Chapter fifty-one deals with what the goatherd told those who were carrying off Don Quixote. A new tale begins as the caged knight is borne along.

Three leagues from the valley, the goatherd says, there is a small village that is one of the richest in the neighborhood. In it lived a farmer, a very worthy man, much respected by all who knew him. The goatherd's story opens a fresh inset tale of village life while the main party travels on with its prisoner.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, August 29, 1829, No. 387, crowns Constantinople queen of the morning and sultana of the East. The engraving covers only a section, from Seraglio Point to the Janissaries' Tower. Within it rise the domes of Santa Sophia and the Ahmed mosque among towers, palaces, and minarets in every style. The editors fear recapitulating the city's splendour, so often touched on, would prove uninviting.

War news keeps the city topical, coupled with talk of expelling the Turks from Europe. Its position, the article argues, seems fit for dominion over the whole world. Constantinople stands at Romania's eastern edge on a neck of land toward Anatolia. The Sea of Marmora washes its south, the Golden Horn its north-east, and it climbs seven hills like ancient Rome. The irregular triangle runs about twelve miles in circumference. Readers get an imperial capital measured as a temptation to surrounding nations.

Saturday, January 22, 1831, brings the Mirror's No. 472, which illustrates Christ Church, Doncaster, drawn from the Gentleman's Magazine. Doncaster is celebrated for beauty, cleanliness, its race course, and its venerable Gothic church. The new Christ Church, with an elegant spire, adds a feature to every approach. One benevolent man founded and endowed it: John Jarrett, whose family had long connected with the town.

Jarrett made his fortune as a partner in the Low Moor ironworks near Bradford during the war, then retired to his native town. Years of kindness earned him his townsmen's respect and esteem. The church's first stone was laid on October 9, 1827, but Jarrett died the following January at eighty-three, before completion. His gifts began with 10,000 pounds, the account continues. Readers meet industrial money converted into a parish church within one lifetime.
the-money-moon-a-romance-pg10418:
Title page, dedication, and contents only are present here for Jeffery Farnol's The Money Moon, a romance of 1911 with a frontispiece by A. I. Keller, so the narrative itself does not appear. A sibling record of the same edition carries the same opening leaves; here the contents run further, through Chapter IX.

The dedication to Jennifer, dated February 10, 1910, thanks her for unswerving faith and famous generosity. Chapter headings follow George Bellew from counsel with his valet to a haycart dispute and his arrival in Arcadia. Small Porges finds an uncle while fortune-hunting for another. Miss Priscilla, peaches, Sergeant Appleby late of the 19th Hussars, and gooseberries in Arcadia fill the later headings.
the-narrative-of-gordon-sellar-who-emigr:
The Narrative of Gordon Sellar, who emigrated to Canada in 1825, was printed at Huntingdon, Quebec, by the Gleaner Book Room in 1915, with Canadian copyright held by Robert Sellar. Chapter I opens in Glasgow, where Gordon's mother worked as a servant and married a soldier. The boy remembers a tall man in a red coat tossing him toward the ceiling on afternoon visits.

In his fourth year, his father's regiment was rushed off to Belgium to fight Bonaparte. News of Waterloo brought crowds, illuminations in Argyle Street, and men drinking Wellington's health at the Cross. His mother shivered as she carried him past the drunks. Weeks later a sergeant left a paper on their table, and she came home to snatch it up with a cry her son says he hears yet.
tob-0118:
John Robison taught science at Edinburgh. In Proofs of a Conspiracy, from 1797, he held that the Illuminati of Bavaria had lived on past their ban. Through lodges and clubs, he said, their agents worked to bring down the faiths and thrones of Europe. In his view, they had helped spark the French revolt.

Robison wrote as an insider of the world he charged, which gave the book force. George Washington got a copy and wrote back on it. Sound or not, the book is a founding text of plot lore. In it one can watch two hundred years of distrust of secret groups take shape.
tob-10418:
Edwin Arnold titled his Victorian rendering of the Bhagavad Gita The Song Celestial. Arnold gave the battlefield dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna in flowing English verse rather than prose. The same scripture that other entries present in plainer dress sings here in nineteenth-century poetry.

Arjuna's doubt about fighting his kin opens the poem, and Krishna answers with teaching on duty, devotion, and the deathless self. Arnold's version was beloved in its day and introduced many English readers to the Gita. Readers comparing translations will notice how verse changes the pace: argument becomes song, and Krishna's counsel arrives with a hymn-like lift.
tob-10818:
Lewis Spence wrote An Introduction to Mythology for the curious beginner, ranging across Greek, Norse, Egyptian, and Celtic traditions and the mythologies of the Americas. Before retelling tales, Spence asks basic questions: what myths are, why societies make them, and how scholars read them. The survey ranges widely without drowning in detail.

Gods, creation stories, heroes, and flood tales are compared across cultures, with attention to ritual and nature explanations current in Spence's day. Some of his theories have aged, as introductory theories do. Still, as a friendly first expedition into comparative mythology, the book gives newcomers a map before they enter any single tradition deeply.
tob-4118:
Plotinus, the last great philosopher of the ancient world, taught in Rome in the third century. His pupil Porphyry arranged his essays as the Six Enneads, fifty-four tractates in six groups of nine. Stephen MacKenna and B. S. Page translated them into English of rare beauty.

All things flow from the One, says Plotinus, through Intellect and Soul, and the soul's task is the flight back to unity. His prose rises from strict argument to sudden rapture. MacKenna spent years polishing each page. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. The translation's fame rests on making a hard thinker readable.
town-system-of-speculative-masonry-1818:
Salem Town, an American Masonic educator, published A System of Speculative Masonry in 1818. Town set out the history and moral teaching of the craft in a clear, ordered form. He wrote for Masons who wanted a defense of their order and for readers outside it.

Town explained the degrees, symbols, and duties of speculative Masonry, which uses building tools as lessons for conduct. He argued that the lodge taught virtue, charity, and faith in God, not a threat to church or state. His system became a standard early American statement of what Masonry claimed to be and why its members valued it.
un-ga-res-a-69-18:
Afghanistan's long war and slow rebuild fill Resolution A/69/18, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the vote of the year before, and the Security Council's texts on the land, among them votes of October 2013 and March 2014. It states firm fealty to Afghanistan's freedom, unity, and whole land. The land's rich mix of peoples and its deep past are honored in the text.

The world pledge to Afghanistan runs long, the text holds, and it must grow ever more Afghan-led. The Bonn meeting of December 2011 frames the path: from a time of handover to a decade of deep change. States back the Kabul path, by which Afghan hands take the lead in rule, safety, and growth.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly resolution 69/18 (2014), titled 'The situation in Afghanistan,' is the Assembly's annual omnibus statement on the country at the moment the international combat mission wound down. It reaffirms Afghanistan's sovereignty and unity and reviews the transition of security responsibility to Afghan forces, due to finish at the end of 2014.

The Assembly pledges continued support for Afghanistan's government and people, condemns violence by the Taliban, Al-Qaida, and other extremist and criminal groups, and deplores the heavy toll on civilians. It backs the Kabul process of Afghan ownership, the Tokyo partnership framework, regional cooperation through the Heart of Asia process, and the coordinating role of the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan. It also presses for refugee returns, human rights, anti-corruption work, and counter-narcotics efforts. The resolution sketches the international community's terms for staying engaged through Afghanistan's transformation decade.
un-sc-res-1018: United Nations Security Council Resolution 1018, adopted on 7 November 1995, is a brief procedural text about the International Court of Justice. A judge of the court, a Venezuelan jurist who had served since 1991, died on 24 October 1995. His seat stood empty for the rest of a term due to end in February 2000. The Council fixes 28 February 1996 for the election to fill the seat. The Security Council and the General Assembly vote on the same day, each on its own.
un-sc-res-118:
Egypt had seized the Suez Canal in July 1956, and talks were under way that autumn. On 13 October 1956 the Security Council set the terms any settlement had to meet. Foreign ministers of Egypt, France, and Britain had spoken. The Secretary-General had reported on their private talks. The Council distilled the talks into a list of requirements. They became known as the six principles for Suez.

Transit through the canal must be free and open, without hidden bias. Egypt's sovereignty must be respected. The canal's running must be kept apart from any country's politics. Tolls and charges should be set by agreement between Egypt and the users. The principles were agreed days before Britain, France, and Israel attacked Egypt.
un-sc-res-1418:
Nine days of grace for a set of terms on the former Yugoslavia were granted on 21 June 2002. Those terms had been set a year earlier, in Resolution 1357 of 21 June 2001. They concerned the peace force and the arms embargo in the region. Resolution 1418 was adopted unanimously, and it is very short.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decided that the terms of Resolution 1357 would continue in force until 30 June 2002. That nine-day span is the whole extension the text grants. The Council also decided to remain seized of the matter. A bridge of days, rather than months, is unusual in this series. It held the legal position steady while the Council prepared its next, fuller decision on the former Yugoslavia.
un-sc-res-1518:
Iraq led to a Council vote: Resolution 1518, adopted unanimously on 24 November 2003. The old sanctions committee from 1990 had been wound up in May. Work remained to trace money taken out of Iraq by the fallen regime. Those funds were meant to pass to a fund for Iraq's recovery.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council creates a new committee of all its members. The committee will keep naming people and bodies whose assets abroad must be frozen. Frozen funds then move to the Development Fund for Iraq. It takes over the old committee's lists and its working rules. Its mandate stays open to later widening.
un-sc-res-1618:
Iraq's terror campaign drew a blanket condemnation on 4 August 2005. Attacks in recent weeks had killed more than one hundred people. Thirty-two children died in one bombing, and election staff and a member of the constitution-drafting commission were also killed. Attacks on foreign diplomats caused deep concern. The Council praised Iraqis who kept the political transition moving under the threat.

The Council condemned without reserve, in the strongest terms, the terrorist attacks in Iraq. Any act of terrorism counted as a threat to peace and security. Deepest sympathy and condolences went to the victims and their families. The Council affirmed that terrorism must not be allowed to break Iraq's transition to democracy. Member states' duties under resolutions 1373 (2001) and 1267 (1999) were restated. All states were urged to deny terrorists safe haven, bring them to justice, and stop funds and weapons from reaching them.
un-sc-res-1718:
North Korea's claimed nuclear test of 9 October 2006 drew sanctions within five days. The Council voiced the gravest concern at the challenge to the Non-Proliferation Treaty. It noted Pyongyang's refusal to return to the six-party talks. It deplored the North's announced withdrawal from the treaty.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council condemned the test as a flagrant breach of its resolutions. It demanded no further nuclear test or ballistic missile launch. The North had to retract its treaty withdrawal and return to the treaty and to atomic agency safeguards. Its missile work would stop, and it had to abandon all nuclear weapons and programs fully, in ways that could be checked and not undone. The Council then barred the supply of heavy weapons, missile and nuclear goods, and luxury goods to the North, under a new sanctions committee. This text built the core of the North Korea sanctions regime.
un-sc-res-18:
General disarmament machinery was set in motion by the Security Council on 13 February 1947. The General Assembly had resolved on 14 December 1946 that the regulation and reduction of armaments was a top task for peace. The Council accepted that charge as one of its most urgent duties.

The Council resolved to work out practical measures on arms reduction and on information about United Nations forces. It set up a commission of its own members to draft proposals within three months. The new body would cover general regulation and reduction of arms and the safeguards to enforce them. Atomic matters were kept outside its reach, under the Atomic Energy Commission. The Military Staff Committee was asked for urgent advice on the forces to be put at the Council's call. The body became the Commission for Conventional Armaments.
un-sc-res-1818:
Cyprus, split between Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities since 1974, is the subject of Resolution 1818 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 13 June 2008. It belongs to a long series of votes that keep a United Nations peacekeeping force on the island.

The text extends the mandate of that force, called UNFICYP, through 15 December 2008. It welcomes the opening of the Ledra Street crossing in Nicosia. It also welcomes new promises by the two leaders to seek a shared federation. The Council urges both sides to start full talks soon and keep the peace process moving.
un-sc-res-1918:
Somali piracy reached into the courtroom in Resolution 1918, adopted in April 2010. Pirate attacks off the Horn of Africa were capturing ships and crews for ransom at record rates. Navies could seize pirates, but states struggled to prosecute and jail them.

The text asks the Secretary-General to report within three months on options for trying pirates, including special courts in the region. It urges all states to make piracy a crime in their own laws. Readers get the legal half of the piracy crisis, the part that continued after the warships left.
un-sc-res-2018:
Adopting Resolution 2018 on 31 October 2011, the Council acted on Piracy in the Gulf of Guinea. Pirates and sea robbers off West Africa threatened shipping, trade, and growth. Crews were seized as hostages, and attacks turned violent. Nigeria and Benin had begun joint patrols off the Benin coast.

The Council condemns all such attacks and urges a full regional answer. States should pass laws that make piracy a crime where none exist yet. West and Central African bodies should build a shared plan with information sharing and joint patrols. Flag states must warn their ships on how to avoid and resist attack. The text also welcomes a United Nations team sent to study the threat and report back.
un-sc-res-218:
Portugal's colonies were judged a threat to the peace on 23 November 1965. Thirty-two African states had brought the question to the Council. Portugal refused to apply resolutions 180 (1963) and 183 (1963). Instead it was stepping up repression and military operations against the African population. Their hopes of self-determination and independence were being crushed by force.

The Council affirmed that Portugal's policies toward its colonies and their neighbors gravely disturbed international peace and security. It deplored Lisbon's failure to recognize the right of the peoples under its rule to self-determination and independence. Portugal was called to give that right immediate effect in its territories. The Council restated its urgent demands: free the political prisoners, stop repression, and let the peoples choose their future. All states were told to give Portugal no help that let it continue the repression. States had to report the steps they took to the Secretary-General.
un-sc-res-318:
Rhodesia's sanctions machinery was strengthened by the Security Council on 28 July 1972. The sanctions committee had delivered the special report the Council requested in resolution 314 (1972). Some states still traded with the illegal regime against resolution 253 (1968) and their Charter duties. The Council said the sanctions would stay until the aims of that resolution were fully achieved.

The Council reaffirmed the right of Southern Rhodesia's people to self-determination and independence. It recognized the legitimacy of their struggle to win those rights. It approved the committee's recommendations for tighter enforcement. All states still holding economic ties with Rhodesia were told to end them at once. Member states had to carry out resolutions 253 (1968) and 277 (1970) in full, and acts breaking them were condemned. States were asked to give the Council every help needed to make the sanctions bite.
un-sc-res-418: The Security Council's numbered decisions include Resolution 418, entered in this catalog under the year 1978. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-718: Adopted by the Security Council and numbered 718, this formal text is catalogued under the year 1991. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Resolution 1018, adopted on 7 November 1995, is a short procedural text on the International Court of Justice. The Council notes the death of Judge Andrés Aguilar Mawdsley on 24 October 1995, which left a vacancy on the Court for the rest of his term. Under Article 14 of the Court's Statute, the Council fixes the election date. It decides the election will take place on 28 February 1996, at a meeting of the Security Council and at a meeting of the General Assembly during its fiftieth session.

Egypt seized the Suez Canal in July 1956, and the world held its breath. Britain and France were furious. Egypt's leader, Nasser, claimed the canal as his own. Talks ran in New York through the fall. Resolution 118 passed with no dissent on 13 October 1956. It set six tests for any deal on the canal.

Ships of all flags must pass freely, with no bias. Egypt's rule over the canal must be honored. The canal's work must sit apart from any state's politics. Tolls would be set by pact between Egypt and canal users. A fair share of fees would fund the canal's growth. Fights with the old canal firm would go to judges, not guns. Two weeks later, war came anyway.

Resolution 1318 is a brief UN Security Council decision adopted on 7 September 2000, during the period of the Millennium Summit, when world leaders gathered at the United Nations in unusual numbers. Its entire operative content is a single act of adoption.

By it, the Council adopts an attached declaration on making itself more effective at keeping world peace, with a special focus on Africa. The declaration committed the Council's members, many represented at head-of-state level for the occasion, to strengthen peacekeeping and conflict prevention, with special weight on Africa's wars. The hosted text carries the decision itself; the declaration it incorporates set the tone for peacekeeping reform debates that followed.

Nine days of cover for Balkan rules came from this brief text of 2002. On 21 June, the Council adopted Resolution 1418 without dissent. It acted under Chapter VII. The text concerns the wars in the former Yugoslavia. It extends a deadline set a year before in Resolution 1357. That text dealt with the arms ban and linked steps for the region.

Two short lines do the whole job. The rules of Resolution 1357 stay in force until 30 June 2002. The Council stays seized of the matter. The bridge kept the legal frame from lapsing. A fuller step on Bosnia's post-war order came next.

After the 2003 invasion of Iraq, loose ends from the sanctions era remained. Resolution 1518, adopted unanimously on 24 November 2003, created a fresh committee to handle one of them. The earlier sanctions committee had been shut down in May 2003. Yet lists of Saddam-era officials and entities still needed maintaining.

The new body includes every Council member. Its task is identifying people and groups whose assets states must freeze and transfer. It inherited the old committee's list and its working rules. Members acted under Chapter VII, the Charter's enforcement chapter. The committee kept the financial pressure of Resolution 1483 alive after the old machinery was gone.

Resolution 1618, adopted on 4 August 2005, condemns the bombing campaign then tearing at Iraq's transition. The Council reaffirmed support for Iraqis building representative government under the 2004 framework, and praised their courage in pursuing political and economic change under constant terrorist threat. Iraq's government was commended for steps toward national dialogue and unity.

In the strongest terms, the Council condemned without reservation the terrorist attacks in Iraq, treating every such act as a threat to peace and security. It singled out the shameless and horrific attacks of the previous weeks, which had killed large numbers of civilians. The text ties the condemnations to the Council's wider counter-terrorism resolutions, from 1999 and September 2001 onward.

North Korea's first nuclear test brings sweeping sanctions in Resolution 1718, adopted unanimously on 14 October 2006. Pyongyang claimed it had tested a nuclear device on 9 October, defying the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty it had quit and ignoring warnings from the Council days earlier. Members called the test a grave challenge to the non-proliferation regime and a danger to peace in the region and beyond.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council condemned the test and demanded no further nuclear or missile launches. It barred the sale to North Korea of heavy weapons, missile and nuclear-related materials, and luxury goods, and imposed travel bans and asset freezes on people tied to the programs. States were told to inspect suspect cargo within their laws.

Resolution 18, adopted on 13 February 1947 by ten votes to none with the Soviet Union abstaining, takes up the postwar call to cut armaments. The General Assembly had resolved in December 1946 that regulating and reducing weapons and armed forces was a top task for strengthening peace. The Council accepted that assignment and organized itself to act on it.

It created a commission, made up of the Council's own members, to draft practical proposals within three months at most. The proposals were to cover general arms reduction and effective safeguards to police it. The Council also agreed to take up the Atomic Energy Commission's report quickly and decide how to speed its work, an early pairing of conventional and atomic disarmament.

Cyprus sees a fresh opening in Resolution 1818, adopted on 13 June 2008. The two sides' leaders had agreed in March and May to work toward a bicommunal, bizonal federation with political equality. The Ledra Street crossing had opened, building trust. The Green Line stayed broadly calm, and work on missing persons and mine clearing was moving ahead.

The Council gives full support to the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, and extends its mandate until 15 December 2008. It urges both sides to build on the momentum and prepare the ground so full talks can start smoothly. It asks them to consult UNFICYP on marking out the buffer zone. It also calls on the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to restore the earlier military position at Strovilia. A report is due by 1 December 2008.

Piracy off the coast of Somalia is the subject of Resolution 1918, adopted on 27 April 2010. Pirates were seizing ships in busy shipping lanes and holding crews for ransom. Yet many suspects caught at sea were released without any trial. Courts in Somalia and nearby countries lacked the laws, staff, and prison space to handle the cases.

The Council said that failing to prosecute pirates weakened the whole effort against piracy. It called on all states to make piracy a crime under their own laws. States were also asked to look favorably on trying and jailing suspects caught off Somalia. The Council ordered a report within three months. The report had to set out options for new courts, including special chambers in national courts, a regional court, or an international court.

Piracy in the Gulf of Guinea draws a regional response in Resolution 2018, adopted on 31 October 2011. Attacks and armed robbery at sea off West and Central Africa threatened shipping, seafarers, who were sometimes taken hostage, and the region's development. Nigeria and Benin had begun joint patrols off Benin's coast. The Council said a fix was needed, led by the region's states.

The Council condemns all piracy and armed robbery in the Gulf of Guinea. It encourages ECOWAS, the Economic Community of Central African States, and the Gulf of Guinea Commission to build a joint strategy. It covers laws criminalizing piracy, a framework for sharing information and coordinating operations, and bilateral or regional patrols that respect freedom of navigation. It calls for cooperation in prosecuting suspects, including financiers, and asks flag states to issue defensive guidance to ships. A UN assessment mission is welcomed, and international help is encouraged.

Portugal's colonial wars are judged a threat to peace in Resolution 218. It passed on 23 November 1965, with seven votes in favor and four members not voting either way. Thirty-two African states had brought the case to the hall. Portugal had spurned the Council's 1963 texts on its colonies. In their place, it stepped up harsh rule and armed sweeps against Africans who sought freedom and self-rule.

The Council held that this course, toward both the colonized and their neighbors, gravely shook world peace. It deplored Lisbon's refusal to act. It pointed back to its 1963 steps, which told states to halt arms sales to Portugal for use in colonial wars. The case fed the long squeeze that ended the empire a decade later.

Resolution 318, adopted on 28 July 1972 by fourteen votes to none with one American abstention, works on the machinery of Rhodesia sanctions. The Council had asked its sanctions committee in February to propose ways of making the measures against the illegal regime bite harder, including changes to the committee's own terms of reference. The committee's special report was now in hand.

The Council reaffirmed that sanctions against Southern Rhodesia would remain fully in force until their objectives were completely achieved. It deplored the states still defying the 1968 sanctions resolution in breach of their Charter duties. And it restated the Rhodesian people's right to self-determination and independence, recognizing the legitimacy of their struggle to win it.

Arms sales to South Africa became a binding ban on 4 November 1977. Resolution 418 was adopted unanimously that day. South Africa had built up its armed forces and attacked neighboring states. It also repressed its own people at home. There was concern that it stood close to making nuclear weapons.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council ruled that South Africa's drive to acquire arms threatened world peace. All states had to stop supplying South Africa with arms and related material at once. The ban covered weapons, ammunition, military vehicles, and spare parts. States had to review their existing arms contracts and licenses. They also had to refuse all cooperation with South Africa in making nuclear weapons. It was the first time the arms embargo on South Africa became mandatory for everyone.

Peace for Cambodia was signed in Paris on 23 October 1991, after years of war. The Paris agreements set out a complete political settlement of the Cambodian conflict. A transitional United Nations authority would help run the country toward elections. Resolution 718, adopted unanimously in 1991, gives the agreements the Council's full support.

The Council authorized the Secretary-General to name a special representative for Cambodia. It welcomed his plan to send a survey mission there at once. The mission would prepare for the United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia. That authority was the body the agreements created. All Cambodian parties were called on to obey the cease-fire in full. They also had to cooperate with the Supreme National Council of Cambodia and with the United Nations. The text opened the door to one of the largest United Nations operations of its time.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s21-18:
Section 21.18 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers tables of contents in CFR parts. It sits in Part 21, on the preparation of documents subject to codification. A table of contents is to be used at the head of a part in three cases. The cases are a new part, a full revision of a part, and a set of sections revised or added as a subpart or like group.

The table is to follow the part heading and come before the text of the rules in that part. It is also to list the headings for the subparts of the part. It lists headings set without a designation and the sections in the part as well, as the text goes on to state. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6318:
Section 6318 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers added home state office space for Senators in a disaster. It sits in Chapter 63 of that title, on Senate Members, among the rules on staff, costs, and allowances. Part (a) holds in spite of any other law or rule. It needs the approval of the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration.

With that approval, the Sergeant at Arms and Doorkeeper of the Senate is cleared to give added aid to a Senator. The aid is in the form of facilities, services, equipment, and office space in the Senator's own state. It must tie to a disaster or emergency in that state, as the text goes on to state. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6518:
Section 6518 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with pays for harm to workers. It sits in Chapter 65, on Senate officers, in a general part of the chapter. The old sums of past grants that are in the hands of the Secretary of the Senate are put to a use. Those sums are the left sums of grants whose time has run out. The Secretary may use them to make a set deposit.

The deposit is the one that must be made to the credit of the Employees' Compensation Fund. That duty is set by a part of Title 5, named in the text. A second clause sets the start date of the rule. The section is to apply to grants for the year 2014. It is to apply to grants for each year from then on as well.
valentia-rosa-florescens-1618:
Florentinus de Valentia, a Benedictine monk, published Rosa florescens in Latin in 1618. The title means the blooming rose, and the work answers slanders by F G Menapius from 1617. Menapius had attacked the Rosicrucian society in print, and Valentia rose to defend it.

Valentia rebuts the charges one by one, in the manner of a formal defense brief. His side of the exchange speaks for those who took the manifestos in earnest. The pamphlet war of those years was fought by such short, hot replies. Rosa florescens is the defense at its fullest, and it pairs with Menapius's attacks across the record.
veblen-higher-learning-1918:
American universities fall under Veblen's knife in The Higher Learning in America, from 1918. Business principles, he charges, have captured the schools meant for disinterested learning. Boards of businessmen govern, and presidents act as executives chasing funds and growth. Scholarship bends toward show, numbers, and vocational training.

Veblen contrasts that order with the higher learning itself: inquiry pursued for its own sake. His subtitle, in effect, is a plea for scholars freed from captains of erudition. The attack became the classic institutionalist critique of education. Faculty still quote its charges a century later. Its satire stings because readers keep finding it true.
waley-170-chinese-poems-1918:
Arthur Waley opened classical Chinese poetry to English readers with A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems in 1918. The anthology runs from the ancient Book of Songs to the Tang masters, above all Po Chü-i, Waley's favorite. His introduction explains Chinese verse with a clarity that taught a generation how to read it.

Farmers, exiles, courtiers, and old friends drinking wine speak in these short, luminous pieces. Waley's free renderings favor sense and feeling over rhyme, a method that reshaped translation itself. The book remains a landmark: the door through which English poetry first entered China's long tradition.
ward-psychological-principles-1918:
Late in his career, James Ward set down Psychological Principles in 1918 as his full system of psychology. Ward was a Cambridge philosopher who also helped shape British psychology as a field. His book treats the mind as active from the start. That stance set him apart from schools that built mind from passive sense data.

He covers attention, feeling, memory, and will as acts of a living subject. Each topic ties back to his wider view of a world of active agents. Teachers of his day treated the work as a standard statement. It sums up decades of his lectures. Modern readers meet here a rich, older psychology.
warfield-counterfeit-miracles-1918:
Benjamin Warfield taught at Princeton and defended the full trustworthiness of the Bible all his life. His Counterfeit Miracles, published in 1918, argues that true miracles belonged to the age of the apostles and then ceased. It is the classic Princeton case against later miracle claims.

Warfield tests the wonders claimed in his own day: faith healing, cures at Catholic shrines such as Lourdes, and the gifts claimed by new Pentecostal churches. He finds each claim weak where the miracles of the New Testament are strong. Churches that share his view still use the book to judge fresh reports of wonders.
wlewis-tarr-1918:
Tarr, published in 1918, is Wyndham Lewis's novel of Parisian art life before the First World War. Frederick Tarr, an English artist, tries to free himself from his German fiancee Bertha and from the bohemian swirl of studios, duels, and dances.

Around him, the painter Kreisler careens toward violence and absurdity. Lewis writes in a hard, glittering style meant to match his vorticist painting: people as machines of appetite and pose. The comedy is savage and the energy enormous. Tarr is modernism's most aggressive novel, a blast against sentiment from the movement's wildest talent. It still divides readers sharply.
yeats-per-amica-1918:
Per Amica Silentia Lunae, published in 1918, is Yeats's short book of occult philosophy, written as he began the system that became A Vision. Its Latin title means 'through the friendly silences of the moon'.

The book holds two essays, 'Anima Hominis' and 'Anima Mundi', and the dialogue poem 'Ego Dominus Tuus'. Yeats argues that each soul seeks its opposite, its anti-self, and that a great soul of the world stores the images poets draw on. The ideas are strange, but the prose is among his finest. It is the seedbed of his later work and thought.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol18:
Liverpool issued Volume XVIII of the Journal of Discourses in 1877, the year Brigham Young died. Sermons by Young fill much of the volume, preached near the end of his thirty years of leadership. His counsellors, the Twelve, and others speak beside him, all preserved in shorthand reports.

No reader in 1877 could know the era was closing, which gives these pages their poignancy now. The teaching voice sounds as firm as ever, guiding a church about to pass to new hands. Volume XVIII thus holds a special place in the set: the founder-generation's near-final word.
